If you loved Company of Heroes 1 and are looking for that same great WW2 commander experience, CoH 2 is not for you! This is definitely a great game and all, but is is NOTHING like the original game. As a player coming from the first Company of Heroes, I was very much suprised and a bit confused at the changes to the game. Im not talking visuals or anything (we'll get to that later), I mean the mechanics of the game. It was certainly a good suprise, but I had no idea what to do at first. I didn't get the whole leveling up your tech (Apparently there are no longer buildings where you make units), but after experimenting and reading a bit I started to understand. It was a bit dissapointing that you could no longer build a base but just had one there from the start. After playing a few matches, however, everything started to make sense and after a while I actually started to get pretty good. This game gets very strategic, and if you want to survive you can't just spam one unit and think you're going to win, or go for the early rush anymore and expect to overun your opponent. There's no more massing artillery units and just barraging your opponents until they either rage and quit or until their base crumbles, which is very nice because arty was so OP in CoH 1. Oh and sorry but im talking about the western front expansion btw. I think I've rambled on long enough, but in my opinion CoH Western Fronts is worth every penny, much better than getting Company of Heroes (WF is a standalone). Oh and one last piece of advice: Dig in and cover you your units weaknesses. That is the only way to survive an advancing enemy.

Grim Dawn is an ARPG that harkens back to the era of Diablo 1 & 2 and Titan's Quest (some of the people who worked on TQ formed Crate).  No frills or bell and whistles, just your character, loot, and monsters to click to death, but for me that is what makes it so much fun.  You can see it is a labor of love from the Crate Team as they continue to improve, add to it, and tweak it while remaining responsive to the community.
If you like massive open world games, cutting edge graphics, and strong multiplayer support this may not be the game for you.  But if you like to play in short bursts, solve a few side quests, and pick up loot I recommend it.

Overcooked works best when played with friends, which makes the fact that you cannot play online an unforgivable oversight. There is, at least, a local competitive mode to compliment the cooperative campaign. Two teams of two cook across a series of symmetrical kitchens to see which pair can churn out the most dishes. It's a simple addition that makes no meaningful changes to the core gameplay but provides a welcome diversion from the campaign nonetheless. And recruiting people to play either mode should be relatively easy. Overcooked is not only extremely accessible--with intuitive, pick-up-and-play controls--it's also adorable. Who wouldn't want to chop onions as a racoon in a wheelchair?

-Free

I have used Blender since version 2.1, before the user interface was remodeled.  It sucked back then, but it was still better than its competition... and it was free!
I love the user interface changes since then.  They remodeled the entire program to be easily customized and tweaked.  If you don't like it, change it!  The default layout is fairly basic, but you can complicate it and add other panels to the window or change settings and then save all those changes to the default file for later use.  It is a very nifty design that continues to wow me.
There are no tutorials built into the program.  You'll actually have to do your research, maybe watch a few YouTube videos explaining the interface and shortcut keys.  You may find bits and pieces of the interface confusing at first, but it's a lot easier to navigate than 3DS Max or Modo or 3D Coat and offers more of a technical charm than Maya. Once you learn how to do some basic navigation in Blender, you can basically explore the program to figure out the rest.  It's a very technical program, mind you, and it does not cater to newcomers as well as commercial, for-profit software.
Overall, Blender is the best at what it does, because it is worked on by many bright people and contributed to by its community.  It is an open-source, free 3D tools suite that offers practically every feature you could possibly require.

DOW is an RTS with a bit of a deviation from the standard resource/base model seen in the likes of Starcraft or C&C. Instead, you obtain resources based on captured points and relics found around the map. Doing so prevents the "turtle in/mass army" tactic, as you are forced to expand outwards in order to gather. Gameplay wise, the game is very clearly a Relic game; and anyone who has played Company of Heroes will pick it up right away. Rather than build one unit at a time, you build squads of units. These squads can be upgraded with special weapons, or even link up with hero type units to greatly boost their ability. While members of the squad can die, you can reenforce them on the fly, making a squad feel more valuable than the sum of it's parts. Give it a try!

This hex-based, turn-based, post-apocolyptic, survival exploration game is quite unique and fun. The gameplay largely centers around exploring abandoned cities searching for useful items and shelter. One of the best features of the game is the level of detail in everything, every item serves a purpose and every decision has its pros and cons. The combat is extremely brutal in spite of being text based, as the descriptions are very specific and make you think about what exactly you have done; eg 'You kick the enemy breaking their ribs and punctured their lung, they bleed to death.' There are a lot of hazards you can succumb to, such as temperature, sickness, bleeding and starvation.
Overall I reccomend this game to anyone who likes challenging tactical turn based games, particularly permadeath roguelike style ones.

The 4th edition in the comical Tropico Series. I've only played this and #3 at the time of review, but I can tell you the series is fun, as is this game. Each subsequent game doesn't see many improvements other than in graphics, but that's not what this review is about is it?
Tropico is a city-building game set in the cold war where you create your benevolent, malevolent, or anything in between dictatorship. It focuses on a single island on a time for you to develop, each with different resources and prime strategies to exploit the island. From tourism, to exporting raw materials, to exporting finished goods. Maintain good relations relations with the super-powers or risk invasion. Receive foreign aid from those you are close to, and military protection from those whose♥♥♥♥♥you kiss. Or create and independent tropico for all of your natives, imported workers, and tourists (or lack thereof) to enjoy!
+The graphics are superb
+The sounds are good
+The controls work just fine
+It contains enough improvements over #3 to be worth the purchase from recurring fans of the series.
+Has enough content to sustain the price.
-Has a really bad marketing strategy. Just look at the DLC list.
-Has some bugs.
If you're new to Tropico then this is as good of a place as any to start. If you're old to the series, this is a huge improvement over everything before it. I give this game a 4/5. It's almost perfect for what it is, but needs some bugs ironed out (And this far from release? They never will be). Full price of $20? Totally worth it.

An extremely disappointing game with deceptive and misleading marketing. They promised the players the ability to make choices and decide the fate of the protagonists but we cannot make any meaningful choices whatsoever, their fates have already been decided by the devs before the game even starts, they only present you with the illusion of choice. The only choices that you get to actually make are minor and irrelevant and by the time you've realized that it's far too late for a refund of your money and your time.
This game is basically a linear cutscene story that's occasionally interrupted by quicktime events. And you're probably not going to enjoy the story at all, because of 2 main reasons. First, the story itself is not original because your protagonist house (the Foresters) is modeled after the Starks so everything will seem very familiar and unoriginal, lazy writing at its best. Second of all **SPOILER ALERT UNTIL THE END OF THIS PARAGRAPH**, the game much like the show itself follows the same "dark fantasy recipe" which means that it will use cheap tricks to try and get you to care about your characters and protagonists just so it can shock and hurt you later when they inevitably get brutally murdered. Rinse and repeat. Because of that there is no such thing as a "good ending" in this game, there is only bad and worse. I actually mean that, for me the game finished with a scene of my head being chopped off. The end.
So no, I cannot recommend this game to anyone else, not even to the fans of the show. It's no surprise that there was never a sequel to this game and I hope there never will be. The only good thing in the game is the fact that you get to interact with popular characters from the show because they were involved in the voice acting work and they've done great, but the game needed a lot more than that to be considered good.

I genuinely feel bad about this review. I don't recommend this game, and yet, I do. I did not particularly love my time with this game, but I have family members who would. Its charms were fairly lost on me, but I have no problem imagining that others would be completely absorbed.
The reason for my conflicting emotions is that this game does not have any specific failings. It is enormously adorable,  has a great visual style, pretty tight controls (including controller support), a charmingly cute soundtrack, and simple level design / gameplay.
The only real problem is that it is not captivating at all. It is spectacularly simple, and fairly repetitive. I could have kept playing without really forcing myself, but I also would have been just as happy to stop playing and turn on an old rerun of Top Gear.
So, I'm torn. Do I review a game for how I could see others taking its charms? Or, rather, do I review a game with my own personal opinion of it? I tend to lean more towards the personal aspect of reviews, so that's why I chose not to recommend it.
It's not that I think it's stupid. It is cute, it is easy to play, and it is incredibly cheap. If you have a young child in the house, they will probably love this game. In fact, I will be recommending this to my father, since he loves buying games for my nephews to play when they visit. I tend to like my sidescrollers with a bit more substance, however. Give me Cave Story+, Chasm, Guacamelee, or any 2D Castlevania any day of the week.

Not a game I hated, but one I grew exhausted with fairly quickly and wandered away from without really meaning to do so.
The setting is great, the parkour is well executed and fun, and the atmosphere is solid, but it all becomes a slog pretty fast. An open world game needs either fast travel or a good measure of freedom. While you're free here to roam as you see fit, no progress can be made unless you trigger story events - which often puts you in the now very tired "moral conundrum" position of either being a terrible person or not advancing the story.
Forcing the player to be evil works sometimes if the writing is excellent, but here it's just okay, and that old "not this again" feeling sinks in repeatedly. This doesn't just make for unpleasant story, but also affects the gameplay, requiring you to make "decisions" which put you needlessly in peril and force you into ambush situations. For players who like scripted events and on-rails campaigns, this probably won't be terribly aggravating. Having avoided that sort of thing for most of my life, I found it jarring and depressing.

If you loved Company of Heroes 1 and are looking for that same great WW2 commander experience, CoH 2 is not for you! This is definitely a great game and all, but is is NOTHING like the original game. As a player coming from the first Company of Heroes, I was very much suprised and a bit confused at the changes to the game. Im not talking visuals or anything (we'll get to that later), I mean the mechanics of the game. It was certainly a good suprise, but I had no idea what to do at first. I didn't get the whole leveling up your tech (Apparently there are no longer buildings where you make units), but after experimenting and reading a bit I started to understand. It was a bit dissapointing that you could no longer build a base but just had one there from the start. After playing a few matches, however, everything started to make sense and after a while I actually started to get pretty good. This game gets very strategic, and if you want to survive you can't just spam one unit and think you're going to win, or go for the early rush anymore and expect to overun your opponent. There's no more massing artillery units and just barraging your opponents until they either rage and quit or until their base crumbles, which is very nice because arty was so OP in CoH 1. Oh and sorry but im talking about the western front expansion btw. I think I've rambled on long enough, but in my opinion CoH Western Fronts is worth every penny, much better than getting Company of Heroes (WF is a standalone). Oh and one last piece of advice: Dig in and cover you your units weaknesses. That is the only way to survive an advancing enemy.

My Sains Row 4 review.
Simply put, so long as you can run it, it is one of the biggest laughs and to be perfectly honest, one of the funnest games ive played for a long loooooooooong time, it has sequences that made me burst out laughing, made me feel awesome, and generally is just one of those games where if all you really want from a game is some nice flashing lights and lots of fun, its absolutely perfect, in fact even if you dont like flashing lights and lots of fun.
Details wise, i guess ill go in the standard format of graphics, gameplay, performance etc etc.
First up, and to get it out of the way, graphics.
They're pretty good based on what ive seen on my office laptop (will touch on it in the performance section) it looks pretty good in places and it usually looks fairly good, though ive noticed some weird visual glitching (may be down to my system, and i cant tell if its intentional on the games front). a solid 7/10, would rate higher if i could actually max it, although im sure itll look acceptable to anyone.
Gameplay, the meat of any game. Its your standard GTA-esque third person sandbox world shooter/racer/thing, but with a slight, tiny addition..... SUPER POWERS, one of the things i adore about SR 4 is that its essentially the same as saints row the third, but with more content and more awesomeness, and a half decent story at the very least. I do need to mention that i used an Xbox 360 controller for the majority of my play time but only because i found it more comfortable (due to owning SR 3 and SR 2 on the Xbox 360) if you do use the keyboard and mouse i can say it felt ok and tolerable to use. Little sidetracked, i know, the super powers are one of the reasons this game feels so awesome to play, they literally let you run around faster than cars, blow everything up without using guns, pick up and throw objects, etc etc, its incredibley satisfying sometimes. The shooting also feels solid and very well done with a large arsenal to pick from, and customise to your hearts content. It also features the series staple, character customisation, and its so damn good, can customise practically anything, and everything you could want to. Finally i come to the vehicles and extras, Vehicle wise i dont see much use in them but they handle pretty well with a controller, but from past experience with driving around with a keyboard, its a little clunky. Extra's wise its got some fun activities and the like, and its free roam.....with awesome super powers...
Gameplay is a 9/10 overall, the only thing i wish it did differently would be the top end of the heat meter, without spoilers, it just stops after a boss battle.....which kinda makes it feel pointless to rampage but its fun while it lasts.
Story: no spoilers, at all......rating is a good solid 8/10, reason with no spoilers: great writing, good voice acting, laugh out loud sections occasionally. There is no more on this section.
Performance: this one i undoubtedly will probably be heavily discredited on, but i can run SR 4 on an Acer office laptop that was never once intended for gaming, while this should not compel you to go buy it if you cant run it at all and its specs are way higher than your systems, chances are it wont run, obviously. I got extremely lucky as my graphics card is not suppose to do this kind of thing in this much detail, or on this scale. Actual in game performance is therefore hindered severely, but at worst my game dropped to about 2-5 frames per second when i spammed one of the powers in a mission, and this happened twice, due to my own combat needs, on average it hits 25-30 frames at the very least and is playable, again, at the very least. I cant stress enough that if you arent sure you can run it, dont try to.
Performance rating: 8-9/10, it undoubtedly can run pretty well on a proper gaming system, but i did notice when i tried using steam broadcast the game slowed to a crawl, whether this is related to my system or anything is kind of out there in the realms of mystery, but i can say that no other game (even ones that are as needy, or needier than this one) has this broadcast problem.

The unique style of NEO Scavenger is not that unique as they want you to believe. It's very reminiscient of the original point and click games such as Fallout and Baldur's Gate with even similar typed "cells" you interact with. Now, that's not necessarily a bad thing. In this case it works great for the way the game wants you to play. Finding resources and survival are obviously key to this type of game and they don't fail on that note.
However, the combat seems way too strange. Albiet, if you have a weapon (melee or ranged) the fights are much easier to succeed; my encounters with fights early game with no weapons lead in instant failure. I don't know many people in an apocalyptic setting that can take getting punched, tackled, kicked, and mercilessly harrassed for very long. Yet the survivors you fight, have exceptional durability. You can kick a person 10+ times on the ground and they still somehow manage to stand up, punch you and break your shoulderblade. After a 12 minute fight with the first random stranger outside ends, I freeze to death and all of that was a waste of nothing.
I understand this game is not to be taken lightly and stroll through it, but I haven't made it far past the first main objective. I have frozen to death at least eight or so times because of how the world is roughly randomized. Sometimes you're lucky and fight resources to keep you alive and buildings to sleep in so you can make it there, but other times, you will freeze to death before you can find a shack.
No matter how unsettling this sounds, I truly have been enjoying myself everytime I play. Simply because the story has already captivated me into wanting to hear more on the story. As well as enjoying the game, minus the few listed, I have had no complications with playing this game and I'm excited to see any possible additions and hoping for better luck in my coming ventures.

One of my favourite strategy games of all-time, Dawn of War is a real-time strategy game set in the futuristic Warhammer 40000 universe.
Like most strategy games, you have a base building. You build more buildings which give you access to units and abilities. You can then uprgrade units and building to improve your army. To build buildings or units you need resources which can be acquired by capturing points and buildng power stations. Buildings, units, abilities and playstyles change according to the race that you choose. In the original Dawn of War, you have access to 4 races: Space Marines, Chaos, Orcs and Eldar.
In the single player campaign mode, you play as the Space Marines in a story driven campaign. The storyline is interesting enough to keep you engaged and maps are varied enough to stay interesting for whatever difficulty level you have selected.
There are also single player scenarios, where you pick and any army and map and then play. Also there is online multiplayer to play with human opponents. Maps can hold between 2 and 8 players who can be divided into teams if desired.
There is also a customiser where you can choose a race and customise the look of your units and buildings to create a unique looking army for yourself.
There are also 3 expansions which further build on this: Winter Assault, Dark Crusade and Soulstorm.
Winter Assault features new maps, storyline and the addition of the Imperial Guard race. The storyline features the option to play through it as Good (Imperial Guard and Eldar) or Evil (Chaos and Orks) with an ending that changes depending on who you pick to play the final mission with.
Dark Crusade again features completely new maps, storyline, addition of the Tau race and the Necron race as well as new units for existing races. The single player game is changed slightly as you now have an overworld view of the planet that all these races are fighting on. You choose which areas you wish to battle in first. The more areas you acquire, the more resources that are open to you. You can also acquire honor guard units (rare powerful hero units) as well as equipment to give to your race's leader, which enhances their stats and abilities. This gives the game a pseudo-RPG element. You eliminate other races by invading their home region and taking it, but they can do the same to do.
Again, the storyline is engaging enough, but not as immersive or as intense as in the previous games.
Soulstorm once again builds further on what has come before by featuring more completely new maps, storyline, addition of the Sisters of Battle race and the Dark Eldar race, as well as even more units for existing races. The single layer features an overworld view of several planets and maintains the pseudo-RPG elements of Dark Crusade.
Overall, this is a great strategy series to get is you are a fan of the genre or of Warhammer 40000 in general.

First things first, if you are intending to play this game then I strongly suggest putting it on its hardest difficulty. This is a casual point and click and it is one of the easiest I have played so you don't really need the extra help that the game offers.
This is a puzzle and point and click adventure game. I know that most point and click games have puzzle elements but this one has a stronger focus on them. The main gimick seems to be item searching. You are presented a few times thoughout with a big pile of items and a check list to find them, it's a little bit like one of those games they have in the pub that promises to pay out but in the later levels most likely doesn't even have the items you want to find. The game also has detective mode where you click on a few of the background scenery and your character who puts sherlock holmes in the shade uses her powers of clavioyance to describe exactly what happend! Yes it does stretch the imagination a bit but that's what games are for right? :) On the harder difficulty it supposedly gives you a penalty for miss clicking but I missclicked a load of times to test it out and nothing seemed to change for me which is very strange. Could be a glitch? Or maybe you really do have to miss click like crazy before anything happens.
Although there is detective work I wouldn't really say this is very film noir. It almost felt like a game for children but there was quite a lot of potty mouth at the end of it which was quite surprising for me. It has creepy moments but it is toned down a lot, this won't cause you any fright or jump scare but it is still somewhat disturbing.
The art work is very nicely done and an awful lot of it is voiced which is nice. Only 3 hours of gameplay though although your milage may vary. If you already own it like I do then it is worth your time and is a nice distraction. I have been suffering like mad with my GID over these last few day and maybe I am being a little more charitable then at a more relaxed time, but it took me out of this world for a few hours and that is worth a lot for me at the moment.
I hope you enjoy it! I did!

Chances are  you'd have heard of Game of Thrones. A popular show, based on an acclaimed series of novels called "A Song of Ice and Fire", which now gets attention from TellTale, the ones who are famous for their episodic point and click games. Is it a good match? One doesn't need to know a lot to bet on "yes". But is it worth the players while? Introducing to this new series, House Forrester is the one who's family members are mostly spread throughout the world, taking their shot at the game for the sake of not losing everything they have, a consequences of being on the losing side of the war.  At a first glance, fans would feel that this family is heavily inspired on the Starks. While true in a sense, it's not a "The Force Awakens"  similar to "A New Hope" situation. As the story progresses, you can see that they have their own personalities and they handle the events better. While you don't need to be a fan of either the show or the books, the main episode may be lacking tense feelings and wow factors, as it starts with the brutal event that had people talking for a long time and put the show on the map. Since it's the world of Game of Thrones you can expect things to not go your way, it will be unfair and you'll ask a question along side a character "Why do the Gods keep ♥♥♥♥ing us?". The main characters won't feel weak though. Even with a crippled one you'll have the option to make a stand, although it won't lead to glory. Political machinations, bloody deals and forced changes, that's what the story is about.
I've played through the game twice. Had I written the review after the first play-through, I would have rated it negative. Second time around, one year later from playing it, I've made different choices, but I've also seen the same things with different eyes. Perhaps knowing the story, not having the tension of what comes next changed my perspective on things. Perhaps I've gone soft. The problem I've had the first time around was that it all felt to brutal, like they writers were going to much with the "unfair" and the "murder". Characters would die before you'd care for them to live. Then the other main issue was that whenever things would lighten up, dynamic consequences were you could bring changes for the better, there was always a plot bomb to put the character down, neutralize everything. Add a perceived as a cliffhanger ending, which I see as a teaser trailer for the next season(it might be, considering it takes place after what felt like a final scene), and you can see why most people are displeased with it.
Playing through the second time around, in a time where I played mostly TellTale games, the loved and the loathed, I could say that Game of Thrones-A TellTale series is not the one to be dismissed and watch somewhere else online. I've noticed in the analytics regarding choices how extreme the unbalance is, as most people go for the same thing, disregarding the alternative. Most of my choices were in the 6.8% to 39%, while having a few of little over 60%. Certain characters make it through the season at inhuman costs or cheap tricks. Picking an ally means making a secret enemy of someone else. Making a choice of who lives and who dies changes the course of the final episode, which is not a short one. The length of most episode is close to two hours, the fifth one being a short one, being ten minutes over an hour.
Following the formula from the books and the show, the story is divided into different point of views, the main characters being in different places yet tied to each other, in this case by blood. There's the crippled former warrior that stands high as a lord, the squire that wants to prove himself he can do more than serve wine, the little boy that has to grow up faster to be a lord, the handmaiden that sets her own webs in a place of intrigue and deceits, the exiled brother who's in an exotic place and is the charming fellow with something sharp in each hand. You'll have three dialogue types, ranging from diplomatic to aggressive, however tied enough together to show their uniqueness to their character. While silence is an option, it does feel like an absence of your character's implication most of the time. In certain key moments, you'll have the big choices to make. Just like in any TellTale game however, you may change how a thing happens, but you won't stop the plot from happening. That said, the game won't impress you with its variation if you replay it at once, but it's story, design of the characters  and well-crafter soundtrack may warrant a replay across the years. I feel the disappointment of the ones that wanted to have the option of triumph and it's a bile to swallow the fact that the only thing it goes down to is delaying the loss, but such are dark fantasy stories that are made with multiple parts, in this case seasons to follow. Enjoying the characters, the QTE (yeah, first time I've said that, maybe the only game where I've enjoyed Quick Time Events, finding them fluent and entertaining), and trying out the other options for the sake of seeing small scale changes, it's a way to pass the time without regretting it.
While it's not everyone's cup of tea and me not being a fan of the show, after playing this, I feel like saying: "Iron from Ice!".

Tropico 4 is yet another sequel to Tropico, still being about dictatorship, and a direct sequel of Tropico 3, being almost like expansion pack. Yep, it's like a building sim, but more centered around small populations of Banana republic, so to say. It was released in 2011 by Haemimont and Kalypso, being on PC and Xbox 360. Steam apparently got this version where they added one more sandbox map and some player costumes. In other words, this is probably the best version.
Not much to say technical wide, but the engine was updated and seems to be even more optimized now. I didn't expect it to work better than Tropico 3, so that's great!
Albeit they implented Steam achievements in silly way. It only checks when you startup the game. That means that if you want in-game achievements to be noticed by Steam then you have to restart the game after your session of play.
And well, what can I say. Tropico 4 without any add-ons feels like a mere expansion pack to Tropico 3: Absolute Power. Sure thing, it came out 2 years after the third one. I am not even sure what to write about.
Well, there is now a new campaign which seem to be fun and with humorous characters. Now with proper main story lines. Still given only through text with potraits.
It was still a bit of a drag, so with it being so similar to Tropico 3 I didn't feel like beating it.
There are a few new buildings, like firehouse. Or salt mine, which promises infinite recources.
It still is easy to keep yourself in power and to have money rain on you from indursty. Actually, you can now import recources, making it possible to run pure industry busyness. And if you are tired of waiting for construction workers wasting time with fiesta, then you can now Quick Build construction with money. Which is great, but seeing how money rains on you, it kinda removes a bit more challenge.
Disaster are now better implented. You can now actually watch hurricane wrecking up your plans in real time.
It's nice to be given side-quests by both campaign and by factions.
And now I think I already ran out of any big things to mention.
As for those who never played, this game is about building your island nation, by placing buildings, issuing kinda-dictatorship edicts and keeping all political factions happy. Also, unlike first game, it's very easy to keep in power and keep factions happy, so 3 and 4 are very laid back games. Actually, it's easier to be democratic and honest, then try to be dictator, so forget about this part. Sadly. Still will steal hours of your time.
It's still is a bit more than Tropico 3 with Absolute Power, so newcomers should buy this one. Just watch it, there is one expansion pack and dozens of lazy tiny DLCes.

BTW I bought this game for five bucks since I was NOT going to buy this game at full price! Nope! Just like ESO, there's no way I'm gonna waste that much money. (I am very stingy yes)
What I do not like:
- Fishing is awful, FFXIV does it better.
The way you fish in the game is very clunky. The controls are barebones and auto fishing in this game seems like such a hassle. The way it's implemented in this game, for me, feels very inconvenient. If it was faster then I wouldn't be complaining. My thoughts on fishing in video games are as thus: If it is not a fishing game, then don't make it one. Both heartfelt and cerebral, a solid platformer as well as a very sharp and entirely self-aware deconstruction of platforming as a genre. People throw deconstruction around as a cheap buzz word, but here it actually applies. "Braid" quite literally and systematically disassembles the most common and basic mechanics of the past 30 years of platformers and both isolates and reassembles them in new ways on a level by level basis--all leading up to its brilliant twist ending which turns the conventional narrative of the genre completely on its head.
Plus, it's one of very few games which use "game mechanics" and "gameplay" as languages and means of expression in their own right. You can learn as much of the philosophical nature of time and paradox just from playing Braid as you could from an entire undergrad course on the topics, not to mention about more ephemeral topics such as the nature of love, obsession, and regret.
Pretentious? Maybe. But luckily it's also fun to play as well.

There’s something special about a game where you can choose to reroute power away from the vital life-support system to the weapons and coax one last shot out of your crippled, flaming wreck of a spaceship. It’s the kind of desperate, so-crazy-it-just-might-work move James T. Kirk or Han Solo would attempt to reverse his fortunes and save his crew. And even though it doesn’t always work – or perhaps because it doesn’t always work, and sometimes everyone dies and you have to start again – it’s those moments when it does that make FTL: Advanced Edition one of the most memorable and replayable games I’ve ever played.
FTL is a story generator more than it is a game of skill. After countless hours of the PC and iPad versions, I’ve effectively mastered its amazing ship-to-ship and somewhat weaker hand-to-hand combat systems – it doesn’t take too long, as it generously allow you to pause at any time and consider what to do and where to move your tiny crewmembers. (That makes it an excellent fit for the iPad’s touch controls, too.) But because it involves so many random factors, from whether a missile hits its mark to if your crew can rescue a space station from giant spiders in a miniature text adventure, FTL is often cruel to the point where a few bad jumps can render a playthrough effectively unwinnable. That’s the joy of it: you never get to feel safe.
Combat seems rudimentary at first, since both 2D pixel-art ships sit still on the screen trading blows, but its wide variety of offensive and defensive options give it surprising legs. The many ways in which multiple versions of blasters, beams, flak, missiles, ion blasts, teleported bombs, attack drones, boarding parties with six distinctly different races, and mind control interact with shields, cloaking devices, defensive drones, engine speed, medical bays and cloning facilities, reinforced doors, and more is endlessly interesting. Success in battle involves timing your most powerful shots to hit when their shields are weakest, which effectively creates some great “Fire on my command!” moments.
FTL is a spaceship simulation roguelike-like. Its aim is to recreate the atmosphere of running a spaceship exploring the Do you target their shields first and make them more vulnerable to your next attack, or try to knock out their weapons with the first volley and spare yourself the repair bill of having to take some hits? Do you concentrate on raw firepower, or throw in some ion weaponry to quickly disable enemy systems, drones that can attack or defend, or send over boarding parties and use mind control to turn the enemy crew against each other? Or try to power up your FTL drive and run? Whatever you decide, no plan survives contact with the enemy, and FTL does a great job of throwing unexpected and unlikely attacks at you to force you to pause and reconsider.
The one spot that could use some work on the iPad’s touch interface is the weapon panel. As the most frequently accessed part of the UI, it’s almost always either covering up vital crew health information or constantly needing to be reopened to target new enemy systems. On PC, that’s not an issue.
As you’re driven forward through the five-sector map of randomized navigation points by an unstoppable rising tide of Rebel ships, it forces still more decisions. While you never know exactly what’s waiting for you at each point, I’m always tempted to explore as much as I can and upgrade my ship as much as I can before I reach the extremely tough battle at the end. Sometimes that backfires, and I have to bite my nails as I desperately limp to the nearest repair shop, hoping there’s not a heavily armed pirate waiting to exploit my moment of weakness.
Every jump is just as likely to land you in a well-written miniature text adventure that often feature interesting moral choices. Should fool an alien into joining your crew by telling him you’re a god? Or abduct docile aliens to sell on the black market? Those moral choices almost never have direct good/evil consequences, so there’s no one judging your actions but yourself. Some of your options will change depending on your crew composition and equipment, like if you send your robotic Engi crewmember into a quarantine zone, and that keeps them fresh for replaying. Some even turn into quest chains that unlock new ships for your next playthrough.
Those ships can dramatically change the way you play. Playing as the armored Rock cruiser, for example, makes me less afraid to take a few hits, and more inclined to send over boarding parties while using flame weaponry to kill the crew (since Rock crewmen are immune to fire). The same goes for the ship augmentations, which can change your viable strategies by giving you nearly infinite drone parts or allow you to fire your weapons once without waiting for them to charge.
The free Advanced Edition update (the only one available on iPad) added a new eighth race called the Lanius, which drain oxygen from any room they occupy, making them good for deterring boarding parties and for attacking drone ships. There are a ton of other additions as well, and even after dozens of hours I’m still discovering new quests.
FTL: Advanced Edition is an incredibly replayable game, and each run gives me something memorable and rewarding – even the ones that end with my entire crew dead. The excellent iPad version has just become my go-to mobile game, since it includes all of the tense decision-making and unpredictability that make it endlessly entertaining on PC. Though I still prefer the speed and accuracy of the PC’s controls, the iPad version is very smooth and a close second.
Score: 9.6 / 10
"A Tough, memorable and endlessly replayable, FTL: Advanced Edition is an outstanding simulator on both PC and iPad."

I played Company of Heroes before I started Dawn of War, and I absolutely love both games. Disregarding the several very awesome standalone expansions to Dawn of War, I have to say the original is ♥♥♥♥ing kickass. When I first picked it up, I played it for the classic skirmish option, and set up my own custom games against the AI so I could have massive battles within this awesome universe. But when I really got sucked into this game was when I fired up the campaign with the nice little story, for an RTS game, and the varied missions that escalated the scale and availability of troops as I progressed. If you like RTS games, then Dawn of War is a must-buy. And I would even recommend it to those who've never played an RTS game before because it's very accessible given the less complicated base-building and resource system (no gatherer units, you just build energy generators with workers and capture points with infantry). I often have a difficult time playing the likes of Age of Empires and other games of a similar vein because I'm too lazy to manage everything economy after playing this game.

As a post apocylipic survival game, Neo Scavenger serves as a (probably) pleasent diversion from the typical zombie survival genre. In this game you are faced not only enemies from both the earth and beyond, but also with realistic factors to your person that may prove your undoing if neglected, and you are also faced with perma death.
Combat in this game makes up with it's lack of action with it's in depth desicion system that controls how you approach situations, which also comes to play in miscelanious events that fall outside of regular gameplay. These 'events' will grant you with better outcomes if you select the right perks for your character at the beginning the game. Select the wrong ones during character creation, however, then you might as well let the dogmen (not to be confused with werewolves) eat you where you stand.
The cruel realism of the game forces you to think, making this game fun to play and giving it it's strategic element. And now that modding is becoming available, I personally cannot wait for all the crazy - or scary - ideas the comunity can grant for this game!

"Save Game usage for Dummies: The Reimagining" is a lighthearted RPG romp. Set in Wisconson, 1956, the game was first released by Blizzard in 2004, then picked up by Ubisoft in 2009, who added tactical and strategy elements, including the ability to customise your Ken and Barbie dolls.
SGUFD, as it is known by fans, is rumoured to be one of the most difficult games of all time, with a full 88 keys assigned to various aspects of pitch and yaw for the sea-faring sections. You'll never look at a humpback whale quite the same way again!
A literary classic, SGUFD is known to be highly prized amongst collectors of fan fiction, with a level of subtlety, terror and suspension-of-disbelief which is only matched by Independence Day, the movie. Unlike Blizzard's tepid original, Ubisoft's version ditches your favourite Starcraft characters, making up for it with lots of jump-scare shots, which incidentally later inspired the game "Five Nights at Freddy's". And Oh! What a stupendous ending - with at least 30 minutes of closure! (wait did I say 'minutes'?) Not like all those other games that tail off with no satisfying ending in a blatant attempt to set up a sequel.
One for the christmas stocking.

After a particularly long 4-hour session (of multiple deaths) and many other playthroughs, I'm going to give a review of this game, and it's pretty harsh.
Neo Scavenger is a game that has possiblity emanating from its mechanics. The writing is beautiful and manages to capture most any scenario that you're put into. Generally, it prides itself on being a survival, inventory-managing (think Deus Ex) roguelike that is incredibly unforgiving. Maybe a little too unforgiving.
Generally, when I lose a roguelike or a game in general, it'd be nice to have some idea of what I was doing /wrong/. I don't have that sense while playing Neo Scavenger. Most every playthrough, I think I am playing at the top of my game, as best as possible. Enemies can randomly hit you in the head with their fist and instantly kill you, even if you're geared up to the max. Unless you get ridiculously lucky, the cold of the environment WILL kill you. Eating the wrong things WILL kill you. If you got unlucky and didn't find a town, the cold or wolves or zombies or bandits WILL kill you.
It has stopped being fun to play. The UI is there. The mechanics are all there. The combat is thrilling. The art is there, the writing is there, and dammit I want this game to be so much more than it actually is. If you really want a hyper-realistic survival game, especially one as complicated as this one, then I can recommend it wholeheartedly. But if you're looking for an enjoyable, frantic gaming experience (as so many other survival games hope to achieve), Neo Scavenger unfortunately is far, far too luck-based to give any sense of accomplishment.
In addition, over the 5 months I stopped playing, the "skill ceiling" or "endgame" has gotten no higher or larger as far as I can tell. A legendary melee weapon (the crowbar) is handed out basically for free, the warmest clothing can be found in nearly every building, and one corpse's food can sustain you forever, as can the numerous woods, rivers etc. If you don't start out with certain skills (botany comes to mind) then you'll be stuck relying on finding towns to survive. and you CAN'T get new skills aside from the implants that I've never seen.
Overall, I think that with a bit of patching Neo Scavenger could be a great, renowned game. It's not that it needs polish; it needs content, and it needs a difficulty that scales directly with how skilled you are, and skill should /matter/ more than it does.

Written in a win-win perspective.
This game is fantastic.
The graphics are good for the time, enemies are unique and constantly changing, and as a bonus, the game actually requires you to THINK to get the best performance out of any mission. Currency managing is a must, as doing so will reward you when something bad DOES happen.
Breakdown:
Pro(s)
+Good graphics. (Customizable for higher-end PC's like mine.)
+Smart enemy AI - It WILL kill you if you don't pay attention!
+As your forces get better, they can be customized to fill the role that you want them to fill.
+Has a very interesting mechanic of researching and constructing facilities to further your "Rush to the top!"
+Story is..Well..Interesting! It won't bore you to death, if you're into that kind of thing.
+Overall a well made game. Enemy within Significantly adds to the game, and fixes some annoying bugs, too.
+Really nice customization. Especially the customization DLC "Elite soldier" which gives you some sweet power-ranger lookin' crap.
Cons:
-After a while, the aliens begin advancing so damn fast, that it's mentally straining to know that it will only get worse.
( At first, this is 100% OK, keeps you interested and won't allow you to become overpowered. BUT, eventually, it just gets ridiculous..)
-Some pretty annoying state-of-the-art bugs. (Honestly? You can easily look right past them, so it's all good. )
-System can often screw you violently. A 90% shot can miss really easily. (Realism. Realism hurts.. )
-Some aliens are outright overpowered no matter what you upgrade. (Ok at early stages - Later becomes annoying, as you know "Okay I'm definetly going to get one guy seriously injured after this.. )
Middle:
-/+ System can and WILL cheat you, with insane amounts of aliens to fight at once. (This, again, is okay at the early stages. But eventually - - It's too much to handle, no matter how advanced your guys are. )
-/+ The maps repeat. ( This is kind of OK, as you become familiar with maps and learn the best tactical approuch to overcome odds at them. )
-/+ Aliens advance just like you. (Is okay at early stages - But they can and WILL start advancing 3x as fast as you, and suddenly, out of the blue, have MANY, new, powerful units. )
-/+ The "Will" stat on soldiers. (While this is reasonable, sometimes, it makes you want to bash your head in with a rock. You'd think a soldier's will would seriously increase if you win - But no, this game pretty much says "This, this is your soldier's will. THIS is how it will stay-, and annoy the hell out of you when one of them panics randomly because their will is slightly lower than the next guy. OR, worst case, gets mind controlled because of it. Really annoying, but I guess understandable. )
Overall: 8/10. Very good, and very fun. Early stages become fun, while keeping the difficulty up there. Later stages..Well, become significantly more annoying to deal with and overcome.

NEO Scavenger is a pretty tough survival game. Unlike most other survival games, this one is more strategic, and isn't first/third/ResidentEvil camera. It's like a hex-turn-based board game.
When you begin a new game in NEO Scavenger, you're greeted with a page. Basically, you can pick traits to help you in your adventure (Botany lets you see if a certain mushroom is safe to eat, Lockpicking lets you break into locked buildings, etc.). There's also Flaws. Things like Insomniac will make sleeping more difficulty, and Metabolism will require you to eat more. Of course, some Flaws have positives. Metabolism, for instance, slightly increases healing.
It's possible to encounter friendly NPC's, or ones that want to punch you until you recieve a concussion and die. Of course, there's a way to protect yourself from hostile NPC's (or you just want to kill friendly NPC's). There's a variety of weapons. It could be a Butcher Knife, a Shotgun, a bunch of pebbles (for the daring), and a Crowbar. There's obviously more, but those are a few.
Speaking of NPC's, there's strange critters roaming around the world of NEO Scavenger. Ever wanted to encounter a DogMan? Or this creepy humanoid-like thing that wants eyes? It's in this game, and the latter is pretty creepy.
NEO Scavenger has random encounters. You can encounter things like: a broken-down car with a sleeping bed inside, a tank with people inside, a dog, or some other stuff (that can be a little screwed up). There's also some set locations in the game. The game is randomized, but there are a few areas that are always there. For example, a large city, and a strange house. There's a few more, but you can look for those (or just Google them).
NEO Scavenger has a looting feature. You can scavenge abandoned houses, buildings, and more. You might find worthless junk (like the almighty pebbles), or you might find a backpack, or even a gun! There's also left/right shoes.
The quest for shoes begins begins as soon as you begin. Walking barefoot is no fun, and neither is freezing! Finding shoes and warm clothing is important at the beginning. You game will be cut short if you don't find these items ASAP.
Well, there's probably a bunch of other stuff I may have forgotten to mention, but if I remember, I will surely add it in.
Do get this game. There's also a demo, so try that out, too.

Whimsy! If you're looking to add some whimsy to your life, this is a great choice. If not, this probably won't be your cup of tea (haha). The gameplay is very simple - you're a dude who floats around in a magic teacup collecting sugar cubes and stickers and avoiding obstacles. Obstacles include lava, angry clouds, pits and various pointy things which cause instant death. What I think makes SIT special is that there is a meter that controls your ability to jump/float that rapidly depletes when you press jump but immediately starts to fill when you release it. This means that you can do a variety of midair maneuvers such as changing directions and jumping higher than you would expect. You can customize your little dude with stickers you collect (mostly just color choices, but boy, do I enjoy the different colors of magic teacup trails). There are a few different game modes. Story mode is 40 levels with no unifying theme per cluster of levels and no appreciable increase in difficulty. Some levels sprinkled in are randomly a little more difficult, but nothing frustratingly so. There is some variety as far as grassy level, boat level, underground level but like I said, there seems to be no rhyme or reason to level order. A few levels add wind obstacles or little shooting mini games and I guess this is called story mode because there are a few pictures at the very beginning and there is a quasi boss battle at the end. The 10 bonus levels add a cool new element - blocks that allow you to rotate the level. Survival mode consists of 5 levels of collecting sugar for two minutes while avoiding obstacles. You get an achievement for collecting 30 sugars in each, but I collected 50 in each in only a few tries. Challenge mode is 5 reworked levels that you have already played that have more obstacles thrown in to make them more of a challenge.
Tips & Tricks - So this is the first Steam game that I have unlocked all the achievements on. They are pretty straightforward except for 3. I got the no jump achievement on level 21. (It isn't possible on many of the levels because you cannot reach the goal without jumping unless there are wind boosts on that level). I got the no sugar achievement on level 12. (Again this is not possible on every level because the sugar cubes are often between you and the goal). Lastly, I was stumped at first as to how to get the achievement for perfecting the credits level because the credits did not roll after completing story mode or after completing the bonus levels, although there was a congratulations screen after each. To play the credit level, pick Cobra from the main menu and then click on credits. (Weird).
Bottom line - Whimsy! Fun, not overly challenging but decent challenge if you are going for all the achievements which requires perfects on the levels. A nice little diversion. If you're looking for something low stress and sugar-coated, I definitely recommend this. I picked this up during the summer sale for $0.74, so just keep an eye out during the upcoming fall and winter sales if you are interested.

Well, I did not expect 232 people to find my review helpful. That probably means I need to improve it. I mean, diarrhea is only one of the many things in this game.
NEO Scavenger is a pretty tough survival game. Unlike most other survival games, this one is more strategic, and isn't first/third/ResidentEvil camera. It's like a hex-turn-based board game.
When you begin a new game in NEO Scavenger, you're greeted with a page. Basically, you can pick traits to help you in your adventure (Botany lets you see if a certain mushroom is safe to eat, Lockpicking lets you break into locked buildings, etc.). There's also Flaws. Things like Insomniac will make sleeping more difficulty, and Metabolism will require you to eat more. Of course, some Flaws have positives. Metabolism, for instance, slightly increases healing.
It's possible to encounter friendly NPC's, or ones that want to punch you until you recieve a concussion and die. Of course, there's a way to protect yourself from hostile NPC's (or you just want to kill friendly NPC's). There's a variety of weapons. It could be a Butcher Knife, a Shotgun, a bunch of pebbles (for the daring), and a Crowbar. There's obviously more, but those are a few.
Speaking of NPC's, there's strange critters roaming around the world of NEO Scavenger. Ever wanted to encounter a DogMan? Or this creepy humanoid-like thing that wants eyes? It's in this game, and the latter is pretty creepy.
NEO Scavenger has random encounters. You can encounter things like: a broken-down car with a sleeping bed inside, a tank with people inside, a dog, or some other stuff (that can be a little screwed up). There's also some set locations in the game. The game is randomized, but there are a few areas that are always there. For example, a large city, and a strange house. There's a few more, but you can look for those (or just Google them).
NEO Scavenger has a looting feature. You can scavenge abandoned houses, buildings, and more. You might find worthless junk (like the almighty pebbles), or you might find a backpack, or even a gun! There's also left/right shoes.
The quest for shoes begins begins as soon as you begin. Walking barefoot is no fun, and neither is freezing! Finding shoes and warm clothing is important at the beginning. You game will be cut short if you don't find these items ASAP.
Well, there's probably a bunch of other stuff I may have forgotten to mention, but if I remember, I will surely add it in.
Do get this game. There's also a demo, so try that out, too.

SAWA represents, to me, the ideal cheap game. It's inexpensive, it's a game you can pick up and play for 10 minutes, but it has plenty of unlockables, divergent events, and so on.
Basically each 'level' is dodging enemies or projectiles.  There are also plenty of bosses and minibosses, and each time you play is different.  What makes SAWA different is that the each event is insane, from accidentally jumping into outer space, to taking shrooms and fighting off your inner demons, or my personal favorite, fighting glitches in the game as they attack and try to break the game.
There's not much to say, the replayability is great but does run dry and is completely randomized, so there's no way of knowing if you'll ever unlock some of them.  It's cheap, small, and a great time waster for a few laughs.

Random citizens at diners use laptops, call their friends via phones, eat things and drink popsicles. The best thing about it is that all parts are connected to each other and interacting in different ways. Walking with a straight back katana holder stumbles across a policeman. After yelled curses they start to shoot in each other. Suddenly a driver decides that it's enough red lights on this street so he jammes a gas pedal on the floor and turns on a sidewalk where are the first two men are. On top of that is ability of all characters including the player's to use drinks and food and weed at any time.  All this makes exploration in this game is so amazing. Visiting the same place makes you recall different facts that you discovered. It makes exploration a rewarding system in which you always look up for something amazing around a corner. There are many different buildings you can enter and explore. Some of them are parts of missions and some are not. For me-this game's world is the best of GTA 1-4 and other saints row games because it's living and it's awesome.
Saints Row 3 looks the same at the first sign - the same pedestrians and random folks outside in parks, on piers and in shops. Their look is more casual like what you see in real life. Rarely you come across individuals such as a peeing old man and weird black man with a chicken commercial on a t-shirt underneath weird massive rags. Character's movement is slower and actions they make when something's happening around are slower as well. Overall it feels like the world has less energy in it. The same is about Steelport itself. Everything is sleepy and doesn't catch your eye like in SR2 or GTA Vice City.
Saints Row 4, however, is a different story. Weird virtual effects on buildings, water and citizens are catchy and interesting to explore. Everything implemented connects very well with the whole idea of a matrix world. The more you progress in the game the more weird everything becomes. It's easy to just jump from a roof to roof, then go explore that big glowing alien tower, then suddenly become interested in something red below you and finally find yourself doing that for hours. Since you're acting in Steelport again, it's always cool to find places that you remember and compare them in both games. Until the final mission you're stuck in the night.
Difficulty
Saints Row 2 is the hardest game of three. I can't say how many times I respawned in front of hospital. What makes it so hard? Firstly, there's no upgrades likein  the other two. You simply start and end with the same amount of health + bonuses from side quests. The game itself is much faster and random events occur all the time. It's way harder to fly helicopters. During shooting you want to hide behind something like trashcan. Does it make game more interesting? Yes!  It doesn't look hardcore but provides some challenge which for me is an essential thing for any game.
Saints Row 3 throws at you masses of enemies. A fight may start calmly but be warned! In a few seconds you'll be overwhelmed by enemies. They will send simple cars, then mutants and then brutes and everything times 10! The same thing is going on during missions. Also there are upgrades that help a lot especially when you hit a high level and become unvulnarable to bullets, car explosions and fire. Overall yes it's a hard game at the beginning and then it becomes easy.
Saints Row 4 has spawning aliens and robots and cars with cookies. It has upgrades as well that protect you from certain types of damage and increase health.The main difference from SR3 is an enemy spawnign rate which is much lower. The increased amout of danger levels all the way up to six means that you'll be dealing with various enemies as it grows and at the 6th it'll be a 1v1 fight agains a guard.
Driving, Cars and Driving Cars
Saints Row 2 has the most types of cars I've ever seen: all your normal and fancy defaults as well as busses, bulldozers, weird food vagons, limos, airport baggage carts, trailers, trucks, bikes.
Saints Row 3 appears to have a little bit less amount of 'normal' cars but definately has more weird cars developed mainly for combat and destruction. My favorite feature is drifting. Using cars such as Bootlegger and Churchill allows you to do long around the corners, 180 degrees and spin drifts. Everything about it feels and looks good!
Saints Row 4 is more about super jumps and running so it's not much to say about cars because they're more just of a things somewhere below. You use cars mainly during missions where using of superpowers are limited or disabled. The game still offers you some new fancy crazy vehicles.
Story
Saints Row 2 has three main scenarios each of them is a story of how a gang died. Missions vary in places and objectives and events. For example, sneak into a power plant and steal a radioactive barrel. Escape with it on a heli and mess up with an enemy boss by using it as a ... in a different way. Homie characters are developing during cutscenes.
Saints Row 3 has even more variety and characters and things. It's one big quest about restoring control over Steelport. Missions and sidequests come along.
Saints Row 4 has the most epic story that involves so many crazy and awesome ideas. That's where the creativity flows. Characters development uses connections to the previous games as well as explanations of past events. Although the game features only a couple new characters it keeps it on a high level.
Co-op mode
Saints Row 2 is running without Steam features such as Achievements and Steam Hud menu and Join Game options. If you're not playing with a friend in the same network you'll have to use a third party programm such as Evolve. However, connection is pretty smoove even though between me and my friend are 7.000 miles. The guest has all features that the host has except: no crew and homes costumization, can't buy property and no side quests progress will carry on in singleplayer and games with other folks online. The gameplay is pretty awesome where you drive around together and do missions and even control your roles in side quests.
Saints Row 3 has an easy to connect Steam support to all players - just start a game and right click on your friend and press 'invite'. You can do things together, you explore the city together, you do missions together. Everything is easy and works just fine. The guest cannot costumize crew or houses but is able to purchase property to recieve an hourly income.
Saints Row 4 has the same easy way to connect to each other. Co-op game still exist on missions and on some side quests however is almost dead during free roaming and collecting stuff. Players use super run and super jump but there's just no way to do it together or simultaniously. So the gameplay looks like this. You and your friends are doing things and sometimes start missions and do them together. After the missions they again move in different directions.
Have fun.

Imagine Diablo 3...but better in nearly every metric.
Grim Dawn is an ARPG Dungeon Crawler...so most people will compare it to the Diablo series...and I will be no exception.  Having played both...I will share why I think Grim Dawn is a superior experience.
Diablo 3 was a game where I could play an entire 4-6 hour session and come up with little to nothing to show for it save experience.  No legendary items...no set items...finding them became an exercise in frustration rather than a fun evening.  Since reaching the level in Grim Dawn where legendaries can drop (50+) I have not had one session of the same length where I didn't get at least one item of value and usually a decent handful.  So the game feels more rewarding of your time.  And yes, you get the problem of things dropping for classes that aren't yours...but this game more than D3 ever did makes me feel compelled to make alt characters.  This is reinforced by the class system wherein you not only have 6 classes to choose from (8 with expansion that I highly recommend), but can also early on dual-class to create a wide range of combinations.  An arcanist that dual classes Soldier will play and feel entirely different to an arcanist that chooses Shaman.
The world is huge...like really huge.  You can call that a positive or a negative but I consider it a good thing because it helps slow the problem these sort of games get where everything becomes routine and samey.  You don't have to do loot runs on just the final boss to farm gear...in fact there are things hidden in the world even more powerful if you're willing to search them out.  And crafting is important in this game...and resources to do so are always in demand...giving you reason to keep killing even the common trash packs...aside from building reputation with local factions for very useful gear augments and items that can be passed to alts to make their rep grinds go by up to twice as fast.
Graphically...going back to Diablo 3 there is a small graphical dip...call it Diablo 2.5.  But I found I quickly got over it.  Customization of your character is nearly non-existant...you get to choose male or female.  This lack of customization is mitigated somewhat by the fact that by the time you're max level...regardless of class you'll barely see yourself (if at all) under all your armor.  And with the expansion they added an NPC to allow you to transmogrify your gear into any other appropriate slot item you own...and yes you can turn swords into axes and maces to scepters or whatever you fancy.
If I had to pick something to gripe about...it would be that the levelling takes a painfully long time at levels 60+.  At time of writing I have logged 270 hours...which has been enough for me to get one character maxed out and in mostly highest tier gear...and a few alts in their 20's.  Keep in mind though I am not only a completionist nutter, but also didn't level quite as efficiently as I later found out I could.
But if you like this genre of game...I can't recommend Grim Dawn enough.  Vast world...rewarding loot system...pretty good story (though the base game ends on something of a cliffhanger the expansion picks up from).  Lots of creature and location diversity.  Stop reading...buy the game...it's worth it even at full price.  As someone who typically gets bored of this type of game fast...I have no plans to stop playing this game even after 270 hours.
Buy it!

Thank you Crate, for getting me back into ARPG's
You guys did a phenominal job, I love nearly every aspect of this game. I only have 36 hours so far, and I haven't completed my first play through, but I'm really excited to discover the rest of the game world and complete the story.
The environments are dark, and gloomy, but colourful and vibrant somehow. It's a delicate balance that was achieved pretty well.
Combat feels sharp and well put together, you actually do feel your hits connecting which was one of my biggest grievances in TQ, the combat just didn't feel solid.

The skill/tree/devotion point system didn't feel great to me however, it seems a little confusing, the descriptions don't really make sense for them and it makes it difficult to know whether or not you're choosing what you actually want, the secondary class system seemed completely unneccesary imo, but other players who like more variability among classes would disagree. I like to have a handful of classes to choose from, then customize that class to suit my playstyle. Choosing a secondary class leaves people vulnerable to choosing classes that completely hinder one another and ultimately lead to progress being made in one class much more than the other,
The story isn't the greatest but it is pretty good, and has just the right amount of voice acting. Characters seem well thought out and reflect their personalities accordingly. That's a big plus from me.
I don't really know what else to say. This game is really good, for any ARPG fan this is a must have, I lost my job recently and haven't been able to purchase AOM, but when I can I certainly plan on updating my review to reflect what I've heard is nothing short of an amazing expansion.

Quick Summary Version:
Company of Heroes 2 is one of the top 10 RTS games out there, it's an arcane RTS game with ww2 elements putting the axis vs allies in intense battles ranging from 1v1 battles to 4v4 in multiplayer and got a very mediocre campaign that I won't go into detail. Company of Heroes 2 has changed allot since its early days and is better game if it´s compared when how the game was back in 2013, which allot of people seem to cry about.
The game itself got some of the base building stuff and teaching, though the game focuses more on the battlefield rather than the base building moment of the game. Another thing that company of heroes 2 got that other RTS games don´t have is the RNG element of the game and it´s destructible battlefields that give a nice element to the game.
RNG means random generated number, what it does have to do with the game is to give this risk/reward feeling while you send your units into battle. When your units shoot their guns, the game will select a random number, depending if the number was good or not will determine if the unit made a hit or not. Sometimes a tank shell can destroy a whole squad because of that, and can be very frustrating, but also when you manage to do this against the enemy, it feels rewarding. Though some people might hate this RNG system that relic has added to Company of Heroes 2 as a feature, cause of the frustration it can give while you're trying to finish that last squad or tank and your units miss all there shots to finish the job.
Company of Heroes 2 got allot of DLC that's mostly just skins or commanders that give you a different playstyle, though nowadays relic has fixed the major issues the game had back in 2013 when some commanders were just pay to win, you needed to own these commanders to play decent against others players and the game has become much more stable since then. Relic has also added a "War spoil" system that enables all players that have purchased the game to get the DLC(expect Theater of war and new factions) while playing the game. Though, this system is very close to the drop system in tf2 and is very random. The only really garante for you to get all the DLCs for free is just to play allot over the time and hope you get the DLC you wanted for free. They haven't added any kind of a crafting system with the duplicates you sometimes to get while getting war spoils which mostly leads you to remove them because of the item limit with 1000 slots. They haven't added any trading system for players to trade items with each other which is a bit sad, though it seems like relic is hinting on adding these features with how they drastically changed their business model.
Though, the games got some unpolished features like: how the game lacks an ingame leaderboard to show players what´s there rank and relies more on you using a browser to check your rank from there website which is annoying. The game is also pretty badly optimized and really needs to be worked on. Even the main menu got problems with giving a very unpolished feeling, while starting the game up the screen will lock itself to 30fps cause of the movie that is played behind the main menu.
Another issues is that some animations with the new factions are very clunky and gives a very unpolished feature to the game while playing also, I´m talking about the infantry units animations in the game.
The game doesn't have a option to change your hotkeys which is a bit sad and gives you only the option to change between Classic Hotkeys(hotkeys from coh1) or grid hotkeys.
The ranking system in coh2 is also very unbalanced and will sometimes match you up with a completely new player against players that have 800h+ ingame. Another thing is that they almost never reset the ranks. That means if some player managed to become maybe top 200 or so, it enables him to stay at the rank pretty much with just not playing. It´s a bit shame they haven't really inputted a same kind of a feature that Cs:go got with it´s "accept to play" feature. What I mean is that, when you search for a game and accept, you comply that you are gonna play a game for 30-60 mins, and if you leave, you're gonna get a punishment for breaking the "accept to play feature". This enables players to leave right when a match starts and ruin the fun for other players in 4v4 (for as an example), and make them lose right of the bat and decrease their rank thanks to him/her.
I would recommend this game for people that want something else than Starcraft 2 in the RTS genre and want something new with its own elements. It´s a bit sad that Company of Heroes 2 isn´t really that big in the competitive genre of games, and the game has the ability to be there, though there are some things that need to be changed before it can see that light of day.

It changes the formula significantly in some aspects in comparison to the original titles, and a lot of them not for the best. There is only one base, only one troop transport craft, interception mechanics are emasculated. The way that tactical combat handles enemy spawning("pods") and line of sight is dubious at best. But on the other hand soldiers now have a lot of customization and newly introduced RPG mechanics give each recruit one of the four classes, which greatly predetermines their tactical role, not to mention the cover system which shapes the battles and make them a lot not like in the older titles.
It will easily provide you with several dozen hours of very enjoyable gaming experience and a great potential for replayability. So grab it if you haven't already.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a Turn-based, tatical, Sci-fi stratgey game that I was sceptical about going into to, seeing as console ruined my first impressions of this game. When I got into PC, however, I was amazed at how good the game actually was.
In XCOM, you are the commander of a strike team, under the project XCOM opperation, to liberate all the aliens on Earth, and save the planet. It is VERY turned based, and forces you to think on the spot, most of the time, when you are pinned to walls against hostile ailens. The game is also very difficult. Even on normal mode, the game is tough. There will be times when you are yelling at your computer screens to try and tell your team to "learn to aim", and other times, you will hoping that they recieve promotions and don't die.
There are some more aspects of the game, however. You need to manage the research department, to make sure the stuff that you salvage off of the remains of aliens can be studied and more thoroughly understood. There is also the workshop, wheer you can craft items to help your strike team in battle, to help other nations, and to help to fight against UFO's. You also need to manage your crew, make sure they have the best stuff they can, and make they get their promotions.
Overall, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is an amazing game, that I will definitly play more of. This is a game that I HIGHLY recommend to all players out there who REALLy like to think and analize things in games, but also, have a great time and feel satisfied after each victory.
