This is your typical Telltale game, with all it's charms and faults.  But what made me make this a negative review was that it has some additional issues in it.  And, let me make this clear, if you have not seen Game of Thrones or read the book, avoid this game.  Aside from having major spoilers for what happens in the source material in it, this should not be your introduction into the franchise.  Its writing quality is vastly inferior and could turn you off from an otherwise fantastic franchise.
So I'll start off with the general Telltale issues, in case this is your first Telltale game.  The game lies right off the bat, your choices do not matter.  At all.  The only choices that matter are the ones made at the 11th hour of the final chapter.  Everything else is completely negligable.  It doesn't matter if you save someone from dying, or if you're nice or a♥♥♥♥♥♥ every action you make has the same result.  Stand up for yourself in a confrontation?  The other party will beat you up because you♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off.  Redo that confrontation but this time be submissing and try to appease them?  They'll beat you up because now they're cocky and think they're better than you.  Either way, you're getting beaten up.  There is no choice.
Other standard telltale issues being graphical glitches, and bad animations.  Characters do not have nuance in their expressions.  If a character is fondly remembering a moment about a family member at that family member's funeral, they will rapidly shift from happy smarmy cocky face, to sad about to cry scared face.  There's no transition, there's no middle ground, it is a rapid jolt.
But those aree just the normal telltale issues and those can honestly be overlooked.  If you go into a telltale game and just expect a fun narrative, you can have a good time.  But unfortunately this game has its own unique issues, and those issues involve the source material and the narrative structure.  And I will do my best to describe these without spoilers.
Unlike other telltale games, you are in control of 4 categories of characters, each with their own plot, much like the show.  In Game of Thrones, the show, you'll see multiple stories and perspectives that will eventually tie into each other.  Every story is important, every action progresses the overall story.  Unfortunately, this game fails in that on two fronts.  One of the stories has nothing to do with the others.  You could cut it entirely and the overall narrative of the game would be 100% unchanged.  Nothing that character does ever, at any point, ties back into the other 3 plots.  (minor spoilers for Season 6 of the show)  This would be the equivilent of Arya dying in Bravos.  If she dies in Bravos in the show, nothing would have changed with any of the other characters, or the overall plot.  It would have been a lot of buildup for absolutely no pay off.  Her arc could be cut and nothing would change.
This falls into the second character's issue, which is that while it does impact the other 2 arcs, it is almost entirely tell and no show.  This character's accomplishments are all told, they are merely talked about but we never actually see the results of her accomplishments.  Nothing she does is actually shown, no impact is displayed, it's just mentioned.  And given the end of the game, her arc, much like the first character's, could entirely be cut and nothing would change.
So that leaves us with 2 out of 4 arcs that actually progress the story along meaning that literally half the game is completely pointless.
and then there's the ending.  This will contain spoilers for the end of the game, nothing specific but it will still be spoilers.  You have been warned.  The end of the game has a no win situation.  This isn't like other telltale games, where even though things may not go perfectly, characters you like may die or have to be left behind, there is still triumph, there is still hope and you know that none of your actions were in vain.  This game does not have any triumph in its ending, leaving the entire experience feeling completely unsatisfying.  It ends on a loss and a cliffhanger for a season 2 that may likely never happen.  There is a point halfway through the game where you're given a dialogue option that results in the death of your main enemy but also kills you and is thus a failure state.  However, this  option is actually better than the genuine ending.  Something is wrong with a narrative when a failure state is more satisfying than the actual ending.
To wrap this up, I will name one good thing about this game, something it does better than other recent Telltale games.  This game does allow you to fail.  A big issue I had with The Walking Dead Season 2 was that you couldn't fail. Somehow this game gives the video game experience of a classic, 80s-era space 'Choose Your Own Adventure' novel.
Take your ship with its small crew and meager weaponry, and make critical decisions, attempting to survive pirates, pulsars, and the occasional giant spider, all with a deadly rebel armada right at your heels. Do you fight, or run? Is it worth the reward, or will you risk losing crew? Do you take down that rebel ship, even though it's bringing food to innocent refugees? Take the moral high ground, at the risk of failing your critical mission?
Surprisingly, FTL is quite extensive in the weapons and systems your spaceship can obtain. What flavour of laser gun do you like? Multi-shot, quick charging, slicing beam or even chaingun style? Or do you want disruptive Ion guns? Shield ignoring Missiles and Bombs? Maybe swarm the ship with attack drones, or even ignoring all that and teleporting over a boarding crew and mind controling the enemy.
I've played big production space-sim, rts, or turn-based games that have less gameplay options than this simple top-down 2D rogue game.
All that said, it is also unforgiving in it's gameplay, at a level where one might bandy the words "Nintendo Hard" or "Ninja Gaiden on Hard Mode".
There's a learning curve in this game, and it goes beyond knowing the stats of your weapons, crew or enemies. You can't plow through the game picking a single tactic or weapon combo and expect to win in the slightest.
The game gives you a wide array of tools, and expects you to use them all in varied combinations to win. Learning to recognize the combos your playthrough is giving you, and responding to the events and enemies you find, or picking the path that best fits your combo or situation, really is how to play this game on a winning level.
Seriously, do not expect to breeze through this game like most other current games. Expect failure in your learning process, and learn to love the "Aha!" moments, where you suddenly realize a new level to the game and can't wait to test it out on your next playthrough.

Game of Thrones: A telltale game series
I decided to try this game out because I am a fan of the TV and book series. I was interested in what this game had to offer to expand on the already existing universe. The story is compelling, and the characters were convincing. If all you are looking for is an expansion on the story, I would recommend you to buy this game. That is -- if you are willing to look over some problems.
Before I bought this game, I encountered the term 'illusion of choice' quite often in other posted reviews. I understand that as a protagonist you should not have the power to control the world around you, but I think the term is still justified. Sometimes you would want to try and better the outcome of the game, and discover that it did not matter at all when you used te rewind function. To save you the dissappointment -- stay away from rewinds.
Furthermore, the game appeared unpolished, at least on my computer. I had quite alot of mouse acceleration, what made it hard to play the quicktime events, but sometimes even select the right chat dialogue options! I appreciate that you can play the mute in the game if you choose to do so, but I was disappointed that I sometimes was forced to do so because of this.
Lastly there are some discrepancies in the story that I would not say are canon, but I do not blame the developers for changing details, they made the story more streamlined.
What I did enjoy was that the 'important' characters were voiced by the actors from the TV show, this helped immersion. Apart from the minor problems I had with the game, I think it was still enjoyable to play. If you want to support Telltale, I would just buy the game at its normal price, but other than that I would recommend waiting for a sale to pick this game up.

This game is like a drug, the well known syndrome of "one more turn". There is always something to discover, something to scare you or something to kill you. After countless deaths by ghosts, dogmen, cannibals and once because of very bad diarrhea, I still come back to the game, trying out different skill combination. The semi-random layout of the map (random scavange locations + fixed special locations), there is always an insentive to explore and see the world. Random encounters make every venture to a city that much more interessting.
The slow pace of the game is perfect for people who want to take it slow, or like me, need time to actually figure out what they want to do. Combat is also refreshingly slow, gives you time to think over your moves and select the best option at the given moment (will you headbutt your opponent or dodge his next attack, hoping he will be vulnerable to counter attack).
I hope the game evolves in the same way, presenting us with more dangerous creatures that stalk you in the night and more unique places that make you sit for a moment and carefully choose your next action, because permadeath is never that far away.

An excellent game, blending in turn-based tactics with base management. Each fight fuels you with resources and valuable tech, which is needed to improve your base facilities, which then produce the equipment your squad needs to survive every fight. This is accentuated by the fact that the opposition starts out much stronger (and gets stronger each month) than you, whereas your soldiers can get killed by a single shot.  This loads each fight with additional stakes, and promotes predictative thinking,  whereas you attempt calculate the probability of success for every move you make, in an attempt to stack the odds in your favor. It's a compelling package, where different elements work in unison to provide an engaging gameplay-loop.
As far as turn-based games go, this one's pretty all right.
PS: Try to get this bundled with the expansion, Enemy Within. It has mechs.

Game of Thrones - A Telltale Games Series  (No significant spoilers)
In this game you are placed into a family, The Forresters, who are loyal to House Stark in the war in the North. You will play a multitude of characters within the family, and while it doesn't seem like your actions really change the outcome at all, you still get a very interesting and well developed story; that is right in line with the TV Series and Books. They capture the traditional "no one is safe" feeling of GoT very well, and while some people will feel unhappy that it feels you never come out ahead I would challenge you to try your best to play with game from the perspective of more of a spectator. I did not approach every character with the same mindset I would take for myself. You can tell by the tone they take with their answers just what kind of person they would be. People naturally  will make all the characters work in unision to one common goal that the player wants to see, and I think that is why they feel so let down when nothing goes the way they planned and worked so hard but the game rips everything from them, me on the other hand I had some characters seem merciful and forgiving, others manipulative, and some I played to be more arrogant. After all was said and done I felt just like I do at the end of each season of GoT, and I feel like that is what TTG was going for here.

Is it the best? No. Is it a staple of the video game industry like Maya? No. But Blender is free, which is the best part. And just because it's free doesn't mean it's inferior: I learned everything I know just tinkering around with Blender, looking up tutorials whenever I get stuck on something. And even now after trying Maya, I still prefer Blender. Partially because my computer isn't top of the line, and Maya causes a lot of lag, not to mention uses a ton of storage.
I've used Blender for three years and counting. I've even found success with Blender, with two of my models being sold in Team Fortress 2. I owe a lot to the program, and I cannot recommend it enough to those curious about 3D modelling and design.
But all this applies to Blender in general. How about Blender on Steam? I think it's pretty great. There's the Community Hub to ask questions and show off your work, and automatic updates mean that even lazy people like myself can consistently have the latest version of the program. Blender hitting the Steam store is as good of a time as ever to give it a shot.

Completely luck based video game. You might as well spend your time playing a slot machine.
Furthermore, this is not a challenging game, it’s a punishing game. Highly unenjoyable.
Also, how hard would it have been for the Devs to give players the option to restart from their current sector in the event of player death, like a checkpoint for each sector you clear? Since death occurs frequently and *spoilers* the final flagship of the game has three forms to fight through (which you’ll only find out about when you’re actually fighting the flagship meaning you’ll have no time to prepare or strategize unless you look up a walkthrough in advance) not granting players checkpoints or for that matter any kind of meaningful save state is just terribly bad design. What is offered in the way of a save state is more akin to pausing the game then actually saving your progress. Why sacrifice your personal time to put yourself through the rigors of unenjoyable frustration? Think of all your favorite videogames and how many of them send you back to the very beginning of the game in the event of your death. No auto saves, lives, checkpoints, or save states. In FTL if you die, you go all the way back to the beginning of the game. Imagine sinking one, two, or even three hours of your life into this game and then having to start all the way over from scratch - not fun. People claim these design choices are what make roguelikes quote unquote fun. If you’re truly interested in the rougelike genre might I recommend The Binding of Isaac, a much better game (also available on Steam).
Stay away from FTL and its crippling, broken, and player hostile design philosophy.

In this way it is almost like a bitcoin mining system, and more importantly, the rootkit they install in the background for "anti cheating" remains active while the game is.

The armor and weapon upgrade system is setup into such a nonsensical way that it relies entirely on not just one, but two or more levels of stacked korean RNG. An excellent game, blending in turn-based tactics with base management. Each fight fuels you with resources and valuable tech, which is needed to improve your base facilities, which then produce the equipment your squad needs to survive every fight. This is accentuated by the fact that the opposition starts out much stronger (and gets stronger each month) than you, whereas your soldiers can get killed by a single shot.  This loads each fight with additional stakes, and promotes predictative thinking,  whereas you attempt calculate the probability of success for every move you make, in an attempt to stack the odds in your favor. It's a compelling package, where different elements work in unison to provide an engaging gameplay-loop.
As far as turn-based games go, this one's pretty all right.
PS: Try to get this bundled with the expansion, Enemy Within. It has mechs.

1. No, you don't step outside of the spawn area and "very commonly" die immediately.

trying to offer you the most authentic and realistic experience of surviving in a wasteland.
5. It's not DayZ. You won't find bandages every corner where you look. You will, however, find enemies that are equally as equipped as you and have the exact same amount of health, strength, and endurance. If you can land a lucky one-shot, so can they.

One Part Fallout/Wasteland, One Part Text Adventure, One Part Roguelike (or Dark Souls if you're trendy), and One Part Survival/Horror make up this indie game. You wake up in a cryogenic sleep chamber with no clues as to who you are, where you are, or what the hell is going down. All you wake up with is a hospital gown on your back, and a dogmanbeast right down the hall way that looks hungry.
The game at first is hard as balls as you learn to survive out in the wilderness. Combat is brutal, with the persistent wounds (bleeding, head trauma, cuts/scrapes/scars) that affect your performance. Survival is even worse as you need to juggle hunger, hydration, and health all at once as you travel the wasteland. But after your few first brutal deaths you will eventually start to catch on and make your way further into the harsh post-apocalytpic scenery. Eventually you'll make your way into an actually populated city where the story begins to develop and the game begins to flex its Text Adventure muscles.

Completely luck based video game. You might as well spend your time playing a slot machine.
Furthermore, this is not a challenging game, it’s a punishing game. Highly unenjoyable.
Also, how hard would it have been for the Devs to give players the option to restart from their current sector in the event of player death, like a checkpoint for each sector you clear? Since death occurs frequently and *spoilers* the final flagship of the game has three forms to fight through (which you’ll only find out about when you’re actually fighting the flagship meaning you’ll have no time to prepare or strategize unless you look up a walkthrough in advance) not granting players checkpoints or for that matter any kind of meaningful save state is just terribly bad design. What is offered in the way of a save state is more akin to pausing the game then actually saving your progress. Why sacrifice your personal time to put yourself through the rigors of unenjoyable frustration? Think of all your favorite videogames and how many of them send you back to the very beginning of the game in the event of your death. No auto saves, lives, checkpoints, or save states. In FTL if you die, you go all the way back to the beginning of the game. Imagine sinking one, two, or even three hours of your life into this game and then having to start all the way over from scratch - not fun. People claim these design choices are what make roguelikes quote unquote fun. If you’re truly interested in the rougelike genre might I recommend The Binding of Isaac, a much better game (also available on Steam).
Stay away from FTL and its crippling, broken, and player hostile design philosophy.

I have been a casual Blender user outside of Steam for almost five years now, and I think it is an amazingly capable piece of software. It's free, it's powerful, and I love it. However, if you want to jump right in and create your very own cg masterpiece or low-poly game assets, you'll have to deal with a very steep learning curve. Blender does not hold your hand, and to make matters worse, the interface is a confusing mess of buttons, sliders and graphs that don't make a huge amount of sense at first sight. This is probably due to Blender's attempts at covering functionality outside of 3D modelling, for example video editing or even game design (yes, Blender is also game engine).
It is confusing to learn, but after all incredibly satisfying when your render finally ends up looking the way you want it look. If you want to get into Blender, I would recommend working through some tutorials at Blenderguru.

In short: Do you enjoy GoT? Would you spend all the hours feeling like you did while watching the end of the Red Wedding? Do you enjoy Visual Novels? Then give it a go....when it's on a discount.
A bit longer: This Game is a Visual Novel with quick time events. You have choices but they don't matter in the overall story. It changes the look a bit here and there but never in a significant way.  The story is not bad and you feel the GoT feeling with some significant differences. During the whole game and I mean the whole game, you'll feel like you are watching the Red Wedding, no matter what you do. In the tv series at least you have some positive things happen, that makes you relieved for the character you're rooting for. Here you will not experience that, just the bad feelings, it won't end with a happy ending, heck, it's not even ending with a high note. Except for  one characters ending part at the end, and that won't be the one you want happy ending the most for.
It definitely gets the part right though where you want to punch characters on your screen just like in the tv show.
The voices and music are great in it too.  The parts that are in Essos you will enjoy the most.
So, if you love GoT and it's world then if it's on a discount then buy it. Otherwise watch it on youtube because no matter what you do, you won't get a happy ending here, not even a high note at the end.

The only Tropico I've had the pleasure to play, This is a simple city builder; you don't need to manage detailed finances like the old Sim Citys, or zone sections off of the land or deal much with traffic. Just simply pick a building, find a spot, and plunk it down. The meat and potatos is in the export based economy. Find resources to utilize, and "design" an efficient economy that keeps goods moving from the initial point, to the docks and out of the country. Important to a lesser extent are the tourism and service industries. Look for a nice part of the Island, and turn it into a kitschy tourist district. You can have them mingle with local Tropicans, or keep them away.
Other things to deal with: keeping the various factions happy, and keeping the foreign powers happy. Set in the 1960s, it behooves you to keep the US and USSR content in relations. Otherwise an implied invasion force ends the game. You can also lose the game by losing elections. Keep the people happy, and they'll vote for you. You can be Presidente for life. That is of course if you allow elections in the first place.
There's lots of humor to this, and it doesn't take itself seriously. The soundtrack is great, especially if you've listened to the Salsa and Merengue. The graphics and art is beautiful, yet it can look like a slum if you want/cause it to. In the end, this game is perfect if you want to get your city building fix in, it doesn't require much time, and the learning curve is simple.

In all honesty, it's pretty boring. The story is nonexistent - which is fine, if not to be expected considering the subject era.
It's not a BAD game, but the gameplay is just a rehash of every other FarCry, without any strong exciting characters (Vaas) to drive things. The weapons are every bit as lukewarm as you'd expect.
The stone age AS AN ENVIRONMENT is refreshing, but unless this era is 'your thing', it's going to go flat VERY quick. Terrain is so similar I couldn't describe a single area or location to you other than the village you found. You'll perk up when you encounter a new 'biome', but for the most part, it's just white noise. If I think back on terrain/atmosphere - it's almost like I'm blind. I simply don't remember ANYTHING about the environment.
As for the village building - that was a hook for me, sucker-as-I-am. There's no village building, though. Everything is placed by the designers (no big deal), but consists of a half dozen build stones. You sidle up to the stone if you have resources, click build hut, and the named NPC gets a hut. You can upgrade each once. Other huts and signs of civilization pop in based on those upgrades, but it's not interactive to any degree.
A lot of these complaints are my personal take. If someone didn't have much FarCry experience, and had a thing for 10,000 BC - you're probably going to LOVE this game. I can't speak to that though.

I wanted a good tactical game - this would be it if not for the poor line-of-sight implementation.

It's easy to be pulled in by this games great look and superb soundtrack but it won't be long before you relise how completely unbalanced this game can be. Unless you pick the engi ship in the hanger you will have no way of reliably defending against missles and if you get unlucky enough to find a bunch of missle launching enemies in the first or second sector, you can easily get picked down before your space adventure even starts. From then on its merely a matter of hoping the FTL deity grants you the luck of a space leprechaun. FTL is a roguelike game in that the early game is where you prepare and get stronger to counter any late stage bad luck, however in good rougelikes such as The Binding of Isaac or Rogue Legacy they are essentually skill based games in that while extremely difficult the entire game can be won without ever taking a hit. However in FTL's case you'll need to prepare for things you may not be able to effect at all. For instance the final boss. If you do decide to sport a full bording attack strategy, that can very well get you through the entire game save for a few auto scouts. However the final boss is almost completely immune to this strategy, as even if you kill the entire crew the ships previously unmentioned auto AI takes over, and if you plan on your bording team to damage the rooms until the ship is destroyd you'll easily get picked down by drones or missles before such a thing can be accomplished.Overall FTL is not a bad game if your looking for a more casual space ship battle sim but if you really want to sink your teeth into a a more skill based game you'll need to look elswhere.

When I first started playing FTL what surprised me the most was just how much attention I had to give to the game. The idea is simple enough: send your spaceship across the galaxy to reach your federation base and take down the main command ship of the rebels to restore peace and order.
But that's easier said than done. Do you have ANY idea how hard it is to maintain a spaceship? You need fuel. You need energy. You need energy to make shields to protect yourself. You need weapons to fight back. You need ammunition to fire the weapons. You need a crew to fly the ship. You need to protect your crew from incoming missiles, enemy intruders and give them enough skill to make sure they know how to do all that.... ect...ect...ect...
On my first few plays through I was totally shocked at how often I was defeated. On my first round I was blown to bits, so my next round I built up my shields. But then came stronger ships, and I had to buy new weapons but I couldn't afford it... and I died again.
On my third round, I finally had a knack for building up my ship's offence and defense, and felt very secure... when a Mantis army charged in, and annihilated my entire crew. So, on my fourth round I finally found a way to protect them as well...
And I enter the next galaxy to find... I had run out of fuel. Game over.
FTL is a real time strategy game that I highly recommend with multiple reasons to play through. Every round is a new scenario and new opportunities. The music is fantastic, and while the graphics and story are light, the entire game has enough charm to make it fun. And yes, after hours of playing, I still haven't "beaten" the game. Not yet.
This time, for sure.

This is a great 3D Tool. Professional and straightforward! It is great by itself, but using it with Unity3d makes it a bliss!
A great example for it is for character animation for games: In other 3D tools you have to put all your cycles in a timeline, export and set it up in Unity. In Blender you can save each animation separately and yet Unity will import it AUTOMAGICALY! Even if you change the length of any animation. You can even export Blend shapes animations; you can have a complex 200 bones+controllers for a character and easily export the only 20 deform bones for Unity and bake the animation automaticaly; you can do a batch export by groups from a single blend file; etc. etc... And I'm just talking about exporting to Unity! Imagine all the other stuff!
And I give you a tip: don't import the .blend directly to Unity; export a .fbx file for a good measure. Trusth me on this one! ;)

While I applaud the developers for trying to think "outside the box" on this iterration of the Farcry series, something just feels ... off.  It is by no means a "bad" game.  I was entertained all the way until the end - which is why it gets a positive review from me - but this is perhaps my least favorite Farcry game.  I think it comes down to the fact that in this version we are using spears and clubs instead of AK 47's and grenades - which isn't necessarily a bad thing - but the weight and heft of the weapons feel off.  The ability to tame animals and use them against your enemies works brilliantly. No regrets about buying this game, except perhaps that I hadn't heard about summer sales xD ! In any case, totally worth its money. Has an excellent singleplayer campaign which features every type of battlefield you could think off (entrenchments, villages, river crossings, shelled cities etc.), as well as a shocking and saddening story to it, showing the nature and horrors of war as well as the Soviet Union's way of handling its soldiers. Last but not least the Multiplayer! 2 game modes, a variety of maps depending on the number of players and the fact that you are playing against humans ensures that no two matches are the same, even if they are fought on the same map with the same tarting locations (which are also not set for every map). Bought it approximately 2 months ago and played very often since then, I must admit I am very satisfied with this game, had quite some fun, and the achievement/army customization/commanders options  make sure that you have a personalized game experience and playing style. The only negative aspect so far is that sometimes you are matched with players that seem to posess not much more that the basic skills, due to the matchmaker looking to build even teams, and not find players that are on the same level (meaning that it will try to get 2 teams with the same average level, no matter if one team has 2 players with levels 1 and 50 and the other one 2 players with levels 24 and 26).
Hope you found this review useful, it is really worth buying it, especially now that it is on sale!!

Ariel is a first-person science fiction walking simulator / survival horror game from indie developers, Nuclear Fiction.
You play Professor Ferdinand Ludec, a physics researcher and expert in electro-monopole theory who has been abducted and forced to fly to Ariel, one of the moons of the planet Uranus. Though the game's introduction doesn't immediately give you any indication that anything is amiss on Ariel when you land, you receive a radio message from someone sending a rescue party out to collect you. All you have to do is survive until it reaches you.
The game's introduction explains that the mission to Ariel was a secret, and certainly one would think that kidnapping physics professors is unusual, but Professor Ludec seems to be fairly unfazed by the idea that he's been flown across the solar system to find himself on an inhabited moon of Uranus.
Exploring the moon, you soon find evidence of life -- both flora and fauna -- and evidence of foul play, with increasing numbers of Earth's intrepid scientists having met their grisly end.
The graphics seem to be the main draw for the game at the moment. The game is ostensibly set on Ariel, a moon of Uranus, and that planet hangs large and impressive in the sky. There's a good feeling of desolation as you explore the scientists' camps, but everything starts to look very similar rather quickly. It's easy to get lost when everything looks the same, especially when you don't have access to any navigation equipment.
The graphics overall are quite detailed, impressive, and colourful, and look great as screenshots. However the game moves painfully slowly, even when Ferdinand is sprinting. And everything is WAY too dark during the night-time hours, turning much of the game into a headache-inducing squint-fest. With technology to fly to Ariel and live there for a time, I have to wonder why the scientists didn't bring brighter lights with them.
There are a few graphics options, but the game seems to pick an overall level and set them for you. Other than that you can adjust a slider through a number of categories: low through ultra. This adjusts the various settings automatically.
The music in Ariel is another of its strong points. There's a great mix of classical music, such as the mournful violin-heavy music during the introduction, and electronic ambient-style tunes during the game. It's eerie and fits the setting well.
Sound effects are pretty terrible, with your plasma weapon sounding very weak and your footsteps sounding like you're walking on amplified seashells inside a metal auditorium. The default volume levels need adjustment, too, as they're all over the place; the music will often as not drown out the voices, while the footsteps wake up your neighbour's sleeping children.
I like speech in games; generally I think it can enhance the immersion and suspension of disbelief. But there is a point at which voice acting becomes bad enough to make it detract from the experience, and the speech in Ariel is very close to that point. The voice actors have strong accents, which is fine, but they're also often stilted and mumbling, and don't seem to know what they're supposed to be saying. They don't sound professional at all.
Ariel plays like a slow-moving first-person walking simulator, but I don't think it's really supposed to. The game basically involves walking around very slowly, collecting as many food and drink items as you can carry before reaching your even-slower 'overweight' speed, looting chests, pressurising and depressurising habitats so that you can eat and drink, and occasionally reading or listening to logs that you find lying around. Oh, and sleeping when you find a bed and it's become too dark to bother trying to make out what's going on.
This sort of game needs more than fancy graphics and nice music to carry it, and in Ariel's case it's presumably supposed to be the story. The overall situation is deposited on you in a great wad at the beginning, when you sit through a painfully slow-moving introduction, and then the rest of the story is revealed to you as you progress, through written documents (on paper -- why would anyone cart paper documents with them on such a journey?) and computer and audio logs.
This would be fine and it's been done before many times -- I think the original System Shock was the first game I remember playing that did this exceptionally well -- but Ariel does it so poorly that most of the messages are painful to read. The writing is of awful quality, with basic grammatical errors littered throughout, but even if you're able to ignore that and try to take it seriously, the plot is so hackneyed that it's simply uninteresting. It's not surprising the voice actors sound so bored.
Ariel features three difficulty levels, with the hardest featuring perma-death. The levels apparently adjust the number and difficulty of enemies, as well as the rate at which your basic statistics -- oxygen, hunger, hydration, and fatigue -- change over time. Regardless of your chosen difficulty, you can only save and restore your game at a save point, which you'll find in some of the habitats. I don't know why the developers chose this instead of allowing saving anywhere; it just makes the game more of a chore.
The base statistics all drop way too quickly to make the game enjoyable. Ferdinand will die of thirst and hunger within a day or so, and doesn't seem to be able to stay awake for that long either. Thankfully the scientists must have also suffered from the same metabolic disorder, as there are countless bottles of water and snacks to eat scattered around everywhere, and you can always harvest meat by killing the native creatures. In order to eat or drink you'll have to find a habitat to pressurise (so you can remove your helmet), which is sort of cool, but after having to wait for the pressurisation/depressurisation sequence once or twice, you'll want to do it as rarely as possible.
Speaking of the natives, they're rather boring, too. I've encountered a weird bipedal thing with pointy, blade-like arms, which I killed before it got anywhere near me, and have seen a number of flying squid-like things that just ignored me. The moon also has a number of weird weather events that can affect you in different ways, and you can adjust these by playing with various machines you find. I'd recommend that you don't; they're nice for a change.
I did die from climbing a hill, though, so that was, um, interesting.
As with many Early Access titles, Ariel also has a number of bugs that I assume will be fixed while it goes through the EA process. The developers have been releasing updates regularly.
Pros:
+ Nice music
+ Nice graphics, though half the time you can't see them
+ Steam Achievements.
Cons:
- A silly script with terrible grammar
- Bad voice acting
- Time passes too quickly, statistics decrease too quickly
- Long load times
- Far too slow
Ariel tries hard, but, so far at least, falls far short of the mark. The action is sporadic and lifeless, which would be absolutely fine if the story carried the game, but it doesn't. The script and story-related messages are silly and littered with poor grammar, which carries over to the in-game interface; the voice acting is robotic and mediocre; and the game is boring. It's billed as an "intense survival experience," but it's just not, or at least not yet.
If you're interested in the game then I'd recommend that you wait a while and see how it progresses through Early Access. Even better, go and play the original System Shock while you wait; it's a much better game.

NEO Scavenger now has my full recommendation.
This game has some deep tactical roots to it. A turned based rogue-like where you start off in the most startling position of weakness I could possibly imagine. “Scavenger” is the name of the game but this key aspect and function serves as a means to an end, and that end is survival.
You wake up in a cryogenic facility with nothing of use but a hospital gown, medical bracelet. You're soon attacked by a supernatural creature, setting the tone for the brutal reality of survival, which seems to be the biggest note of the game. Notice I didn’t mention any shoes or memories. You’re barefoot and it’s autumn. No way to go through life in my humble opinion. I guess there’s a story about finding your identity or finding out what happened to the world.
Sounds interesting, right? Like “28 Days Later” meets “DayZ”. I couldn’t tell you, because basically I’ve spent my hours just trying to survive against... get ready for it...
. Food is scarce. I once savored a small packet of crackers for sustenance. I recently died trying to hunt a dangerous creature in what felt like a very realistic and thought out exchange in combat.
. Water is not as scarce, but takes up storage space and the effects of dehydration can onset quickly leaving you weaker to take on the rigors of survival and ultimately lead to death.
. It always seems cold and rainy. One play-through I traveled west for 12 hours and died of hypothermia desperately trying to find some degree of shelter or warmth.
. Some people seem to be opportunists in this new and horrifying setting, attacking you on sight. You can try to reason with them or beat them to death or submission. Either way combat has to be dealt with or avoided one way or another. There are also inhumane beasts, such as the dogman who(that?) recently severed an artery in my leg, taking a fluke victory in what was described to me as brutal combat.
The turned based combat plays out very interestingly, giving you often unique choices based on your surroundings, tools and skill set. In addition to normal attacks with your weaponry you often have different tactical options in a fight, like a trip or a head-butt. Leaving your opponent stunned and vulnerable is a key to winning conflicts and staying healthy.
Wounds need attention and in a very animalistic way you need to learn that just because you can best a being in mortal combat it doesn’t necessarily mean he can be your prey.  The spoils of war are all well and good but damn well better be worth the cost of an open wound or wounded limb.
Luckily there seems to be a wide array of technology, pharmaceuticals and med-kits to be found in your mysterious surroundings, everything seems to have something more to it. There's a vast world of crafting, trapping and other skills I've only touched the surface of. Hacking with a laptop can be far more effective than hacking with a cleaver.
Storage plays as big of a roll as anything I have mentioned thus far. I really enjoy the vast inventory options and the various challenges that arrive. The tools available to you in moving your life supporting cargo are just as varied. Plastic bags can be used as a light and spacious backpack but they quickly deteriorate under such use, a true backpack can handle much more rigors. Sleds can be used to drag your sleeping bag and other supplies but is outclassed by a modified shopping cart as a vehicle.
Light sources can play a big part in safe scavenging, night time or not. Lighters run out of butane though, and flashlights need batteries. You often consume some of your items durability upon use as you scavenge for that rare useful weapon and equally sparse ammunition.
There are some hiccups in this surprisingly immersive experience, like a lack of a local leaderboard and tracking or rating of your statistics and progress. The game doesn’t seem to integrate with windows well on start-up, but this is easily fixable in the settings. The aural potential of this game seems unrealized and the atmospheric tune that plays throughout doesn’t do enough for me. The lack of sound just about the only thing holding me back from having a more immersed experience.
The slightly crude graphics and the fact that it is a Java game may be off putting to some, but those willing to look past the amateur feel will be rewarded with a view into this game’s deep, brutal, intelligent soul. The sense and reality of a true, terrifying post-apocalyptic survival setting seems fully represented. Made by Blue Bottle Games, which from what I can tell is just one dude, this frisky indie title feels like a true labor of love towards the bleak reality of our impending doom.

I love the GoT universe and deeply appreciate everything George R.R. Martin has to offer with his profound intellect and deeply moving ability for storytelling, and being new to the Telltale series I was willing to trust this could at least emulate his universe and provide an entertaining story to fans desiring more from the universe. However, I was deeply dissapointed at the end product. There is nothing but fanservice to a superficial understanding of GoT, where I found intrigue and suspense was shallow and no sense of progress was achieved. Every decision either set you back or put you at a standstill, and any victory was wrenched away with various excuses for more drama and a supposed "GoT feel", meant to put you in the place of a fatefully miserable character in Game of Thrones, on the inevitable track to death.
Even with all this we have the failure of the subtleties of immersion. Even with what bones were thrown to those knowledgable about the universe, my suspension of disbelief for the animations and quality (which I believe to be rather significant) was yet broken with the bugginess of the game and how unpolished it was for me to click off of the screen twice an episode. Perhaps this is me being new to Telltale, but I would still count off for these failures.
The most damming quality of this, however, is its knack for not representing my intentions in the narrative given prompts available. I have nothing to blame except my apparent disconnect with the writers and/or the quality of representative choices. It is immesurably disappointing for decisions to be made contrary to my desire especially when stacked upon an intrinsic dissatisfaction wrought with every move one makes.
Overall, I would not recommend this to anyone. It's unsatisfying, not immersive, and hardly responds to one's actual intentions. I'm left feeling it's just not faithful to the Game of Thrones experience in the end.

"Grand Theft Awe...some!" 10/10
Assuming it was just another 'Grand Theft Auto' clone, I grabbed 'Saints Row IV' while it was on sale and then proceeded to forget about it for months. Then one rainy day I decided to boot it up and was more than pleasantly surprised with what I discovered. Essentially the movies 'Independence Day' and 'The Matrix' bashed into one action packed escapade, this game is chock-full of witty dialogue, pop culture references, and explosions; lots of explosions. And for those of you who still think this is just another 'Grand Theft Auto' clone, I've got six words for you: you barely drive In this game. It's based much more on pedestrian missions as opposed to car driven ones. There, I said it and I'm glad that I got it off of my chest.
The best part of the single player campaign in 'Saints Row 4' is how it never grows stale; constantly changing perspectives, situations, characters, and even genre, this game keeps you own your feet and never lets you down. In just a few minutes you'll go from platforming, to 2D side-scrolling beat em' up, to sitting in a turret blasting alien spaceships out of the sky. But the game doesn't stop there, it also adds in super powers to really make things fun and gives you the ability to jump as high as buildings, run faster than the speed of sound, shoot fire out of your palms, and basically any other awesome power you can think of; yep, this game has it all.
I'm so glad that I finally gave 'Saints Row IV' a chance, because this is one of those games that  you sit down to play for an hour and end up beating the whole damn thing. It instantly grabs you with it's balls to the wall attitude, tosses you up against that wall, and then proceeds to give you the thrill ride of a lifetime. The story doesn't take itself too seriously, the cut-scenes don't feel like a chore to watch, it's fast-paced, it's entertaining, it's got sex, it's got cars, it's got guns galore; it's basically the best action movie you've ever seen. Aliens have come to take over the planet, and it's up to the president of the United States to save the day. What else is new. Welcome to Earth.

Having used it for years before it came to Steam, I can attest to Blender's incredible efficiency as a one-stop program. Many projects can be done start-to-finish without ever minimizing the window. Blender has an incredibly comfortable and intuitive interface for basic functions like creating materials, modeling objects, mapping textures, rendering and compositing. But it is also well prepared for less common/more advanced users, capable of sculpting shapes, implementing complicated physics or particle systems, rigging models for animation, and motion-tracking your real-life footage (an unbelievably cool feature, I must say). Blender even comes with UI for animation keying, sound and video clips, and it's own programmable game engine.
Often times developers sacrifice comfort and built-in technology for freedom, but Blender manages to be both a more comfortable software and a more free environment for creation than technology like 3DS, Maya, or Rhino. On top of being an enormously powerful and impressive software on its own, It also comes with hundreds of valuable plugins, and  an alternate rendering engine called Cycles which I used for my thesis.
All of this, and it's also a FREE open-source program, constantly being updated and improved? You might as well try it, and I promise you will find everything you had in Maya and more.

As a long time Blender user. I can easily say this is the best Free and Open Source 3D Modeling/Sculpting/Rendering program out there. I'm excited for it coming to Steam for several reasons:
I'm lazy and Blender doesn't have auto-update in the non-Steam version, now Steam will download it for me when Steam launchs. 'murica
The community hub is going to be filled with amazing artwork, I can't wait!
Now for my review:
Blender is an open source, free 3D modeling program which features easy to use features and a powerful rendering engine. Capable of outputting high detail characters, environments, props and more; Blender is the tool you'll need if you want to get started on your own Indie Game's Graphics.
Blender has several major features and more:
Animation, bring your characters to life with Key Frames and an inbuilt Animation image/movie output.
Rendering, turn a simple cube into a cube with fancy lighting and material effects such as reflectiveness and more.
Physics Simulation, simulate water, cloth, wind and more using Blender's physics.
Game Engine, not as good as Unity; but this one is completely free and included in Blender. It runs off of Python scripting and doesn't look half-bad.
Pros of Blender:
The program is very powerful and Renders (if setup properly) look amazing.
The interface is very easy to get used to and can be easily modified to fit your preference.
There are tons of well-made community videos that are easy to understand and will get you started making artwork with your imagination.
In built game engine, which isn't half-bad.
Completely price free, royalty free and constantly updated.
Performs really well, I've never had Blender crash on me; even while Rendering a 4 million polygon scene with Textures, Shading and some fancy Reflective Materials.
Cons:
If your PC is not really powerful, Blender will have frame drops when you are modeling really high-poly scenes.
Blender takes a lot of learning and a lot of patience to become a master of. I'm nowhere near this title, and I've been working constantly almost every day for the past four years.
That's pretty much it for the Cons, and the second Con goes for any 3D Modeling program where you start from scratch.
-----
I'd really recommend giving Blender a try, it's not bad to pickup 3D Modeling skills. It's a fun hobby and if you work towards it; you can make some really cool things.
Some websites I'd recommend visiting if you're new to Blender:
Really great tutorials for new, intermediate and advanced Blender users, created by expert artists!
Blenderguru has some really great tutorials as well, which are all free to watch.
Good luck to all the aspiring artists out there!

FC:P puts you in the boots of a prehistoric hunter named Takkar; your people are scattered and are going insane. You reunite your people against the other tribes, build up a village, and ultimatley slay the enemy leaders. Then you control Oros and the game just sort of ends. This standard Far Cry storytelling (Introduce world, introduce enemies, kill enemies, run around in sandbox) falls sort of flat in the setting; as the majority of the story revolves around the other tribes having ran to Oro's beleiving their gods are angry at them.
So the ending when it finally comes is underwhelming. Progression is stopgap, as it's the same handful of weapons the whole game. Building up your village is mostly just a chore. So the crafting is just a laundy list of things. And then there's the five or so different types of collectibles scattered throughout the map. What this means is that most of the game is busywork. Delicious to look at busywork.
Oros is just big enough to feel intimidating, but you quickly unlock abilities that let you very quickly traverse it. You never feel like you have to move too far out of your way to get something done. Combat remains the same throughout the game; which the exception of the final boss fight being an insanely annoying video game archer battle.
Get it on sale if you like shooting games. It's an interesting game for folks that just wan to expore and slaughter.

NEO Scavenger now has my full recommendation.
This game has some deep tactical roots to it. A turned based rogue-like where you start off in the most startling position of weakness I could possibly imagine. “Scavenger” is the name of the game but this key aspect and function serves as a means to an end, and that end is survival.
You wake up in a cryogenic facility with nothing of use but a hospital gown, medical bracelet. You're soon attacked by a supernatural creature, setting the tone for the brutal reality of survival, which seems to be the biggest note of the game. Notice I didn’t mention any shoes or memories. You’re barefoot and it’s autumn. No way to go through life in my humble opinion. I guess there’s a story about finding your identity or finding out what happened to the world.
Sounds interesting, right? Like “28 Days Later” meets “DayZ”. I couldn’t tell you, because basically I’ve spent my hours just trying to survive against... get ready for it...
. Food is scarce. I once savored a small packet of crackers for sustenance. I recently died trying to hunt a dangerous creature in what felt like a very realistic and thought out exchange in combat.
. Water is not as scarce, but takes up storage space and the effects of dehydration can onset quickly leaving you weaker to take on the rigors of survival and ultimately lead to death.
. It always seems cold and rainy. One play-through I traveled west for 12 hours and died of hypothermia desperately trying to find some degree of shelter or warmth.
. Some people seem to be opportunists in this new and horrifying setting, attacking you on sight. You can try to reason with them or beat them to death or submission. Either way combat has to be dealt with or avoided one way or another. There are also inhumane beasts, such as the dogman who(that?) recently severed an artery in my leg, taking a fluke victory in what was described to me as brutal combat.
The turned based combat plays out very interestingly, giving you often unique choices based on your surroundings, tools and skill set. In addition to normal attacks with your weaponry you often have different tactical options in a fight, like a trip or a head-butt. Leaving your opponent stunned and vulnerable is a key to winning conflicts and staying healthy.
Wounds need attention and in a very animalistic way you need to learn that just because you can best a being in mortal combat it doesn’t necessarily mean he can be your prey.  The spoils of war are all well and good but damn well better be worth the cost of an open wound or wounded limb.
Luckily there seems to be a wide array of technology, pharmaceuticals and med-kits to be found in your mysterious surroundings, everything seems to have something more to it. There's a vast world of crafting, trapping and other skills I've only touched the surface of. Hacking with a laptop can be far more effective than hacking with a cleaver.
Storage plays as big of a roll as anything I have mentioned thus far. I really enjoy the vast inventory options and the various challenges that arrive. The tools available to you in moving your life supporting cargo are just as varied. Plastic bags can be used as a light and spacious backpack but they quickly deteriorate under such use, a true backpack can handle much more rigors. Sleds can be used to drag your sleeping bag and other supplies but is outclassed by a modified shopping cart as a vehicle.
Light sources can play a big part in safe scavenging, night time or not. Lighters run out of butane though, and flashlights need batteries. You often consume some of your items durability upon use as you scavenge for that rare useful weapon and equally sparse ammunition.
There are some hiccups in this surprisingly immersive experience, like a lack of a local leaderboard and tracking or rating of your statistics and progress. The game doesn’t seem to integrate with windows well on start-up, but this is easily fixable in the settings. The aural potential of this game seems unrealized and the atmospheric tune that plays throughout doesn’t do enough for me. The lack of sound just about the only thing holding me back from having a more immersed experience.
The slightly crude graphics and the fact that it is a Java game may be off putting to some, but those willing to look past the amateur feel will be rewarded with a view into this game’s deep, brutal, intelligent soul. The sense and reality of a true, terrifying post-apocalyptic survival setting seems fully represented. Made by Blue Bottle Games, which from what I can tell is just one dude, this frisky indie title feels like a true labor of love towards the bleak reality of our impending doom.

Hoplessly addicted, thats what I am. There are several indie gems out there but I have to admit that this one is the best I've played. Why? Probably because it reminds me so much of the original Wasteland and does well to hold me over till the I get the money for the second. You play as a man with no real memory of who he is and wakes up in a post apocalyptic world, except it doesn't use the cliched desert wasteland or zombie infested urban feista. No, it sets itself apart by creating its own twisted world. In the game you move along a hex map and scavange for supplies. These supplies range from balls of twine and floss to civilian grade weapons and military grade technology. You are able to craft a varity of things out of seemingly usless items. My favorite being the sled (plastic sled + medium length twine, rope, floss, etc.) which allows me to carry more things BUT i am unable to run making combat difficult. Combat takes a bit getting use to but not for very long. It's turn based where you select what you do and you do it then your opponent takes their turn. Simple and when combined with your imagination, downright enjoyable. Even in early acess this game is so well polished I would believe it to be complete, though I'm glade it isn't because I would love to see more and more items and craftable objects. This is a must for fans of classic RPGs, Fallout(original), Wasteland, The Road(both book and movie), and Fallen Paragon(a book I highly recommend find it on Amazon).

NEO Scavenger is a great Turn-Based Survival Roguelike, where you wake up in a cryobay in Michigan, with no knowledge of how you got there. After a quick encounter with danger, you're thrust into the world with nothing but a hospital gown, bracelet, and an odd talisman around your neck.(do NOT take off the talisman).
From there you see the hex based map you'll be spending a good time looking at, along with the inventory management screen. From here, you're free to do as you wish, though you're soon given a main objective that you may CHOOSE to do. While there's plenty(a lot) of free roaming options, they also give you a quest, a sort of main story to follow/do if that's what gives you your jolly's.
That, along with the fact you can choose several perks/skills at the beginning can really change how you approach the world.
Do you make a life in the wilderness, using your trapping and knowledge of plants to ensure you thrive where others would struggle?
Do you use your superior stealth and tracking, flitting from ruin to ruin, scavenging what you need, and stealing from bandit camps when you stumble upon them to make your living?
Maybe you can live in or around Detroit, making week-long trips into the wilds and ruins of Michigan, taking items of value to not only equip and feed yourself, but to use your experience as a electrician and mechanic to get the most profit back at the market.
Or maybe you want to use your superior skills in close and/or ranged combat to take down every sumbich' you see and feast upon their flesh?
Or maybe 72 hours in you'll die of diarrhea/dehydration/starvation/cholera because you ate some random berries in the forest, then blow out everything you eat and drink from every orifice.
Or maybe you'll get jumped and killed by bandits in the middle of the night.
Perhaps freezing to death because you couldn't find warmth in time tickles your fancy.
Or maybe die due to infection because you bandaged a wound with a filthy rag.
All these options are available to you. You can even mix and match them. Some of your actions in the world and the skills you take will even influence the main story.
With randomly generated world, permadeath, selection of skills, and randomly placed loot and enemies ensure that no run is ever the same as the last.

Blender isn't like your other Modeling programs, like 3ds max, maya, or even milkshape, Blender is perhaps the best choice in game creation, animation making, MOVIE making, sculpting, or even just pictures. Plus, it's free.
You might ask "Why Blender? Why can't I use 3ds max?" well, 3ds max is expensive, too expensive for most people, however, Blender is free, and will always stay free.
Now, before you go ahead on modeling masterpieces, it might take a while to get used to the UI and such. In this case, there are thousands of tutorials on almost every single feature on Blender, either it be fluid creation, sculpting help, and even more. Don't be afraid to search how to do one thing towards the other, because EVERY single system has a tutorial. This way, being stuck will be a breeze to escape!
Blender even features motion tracking, wind dynamics, cloth simulation, fluid simulation, ray casting, and even more amazing features.
And that rendering thing? Good lord, it's so realistic, you'll think you're looking at a picture taken from a phone! Blender has the ability to render EXTREMELY Realistic scenes!
So, if you're interested in trying out modeling, making a game, or maybe even a movie, go ahead, get this! It's the perfect piece of software!

Yeah, sometimes you die within 15 minutes because the game refused to drop any good weapons, but other times you end up with an unstoppable juggernaut by the halfway point. This game isn't about long-term strategy; it's about making do with what you have. You might tell yourself you're not going to make deals with pirates this time, but when you're limping through space with damaged weapons and no scrap for repairs, that bribe starts to look awfully nice...
The tactical combat is excellent too. Having to prioritize systems when you don't have enough power, being forced to change tactics when an enemy missile knocks out one of your critical systems, panicking when your life support gets taken out by an enemy boarding drone...
I will say that the game can feel a little bit long for a rogue-like, meaning that it can be quite disheartening to play for 45 minutes before realizing that you don't have the upgrades necessary to survive much longer and then inevitably dying. I think a slightly shorter game length might have been less frustrating at times, but to be honest this is such a small criticism that I rarely noticed in my 100+ hours of playing.
Absolutely recommended.

It's a freaking poker game. How can it not be more straight forward than that. The side conversations and the unlocks are nice. As it stands however. The game isn't all that great. For three simple reasons
1) Facing the same characters over and over again. No multiplayer. And no "DLC" or "extra content" where you can switch out the other characters for brand new faces. While it is nice to hear the side conversations. It can get pretty old. Pretty fast.
2) Luck. Now while this may sound dumb and stupid. There are instances where you might have a lousy hand, but! In some odd concidence you won. Outta nowhere! Where as the other card players could've easily beaten you. Now this might be a game mechanic or just sheer dumb luck. Whatever the case maybe this shouldn't be a thing.
3) Weird A.I. Now, if this was against other players then the game might be more fun. But the A.I. in this game is weird, For example, and depending upon how lucky you are when you start a new tournament. The other card players might go all in. Outta nowhere! Which means if you got a great hand than the other opponents. You might actually win the game right away with no real sense of tension OR knock out half of the competition before the game can really progress anywhere.
In the end Poker Night is a perfect game for Poker fans and achievement hunters. Yes, this game does have a tutorial and a cheat sheet to understand the 'card hands' and whatnot. But like what I stated; luck really runs the show in the game. If not then the weird A.I. does. If your an achievement hunter and a poker fan. This game might be up your alley. But for anyone else, you might want to pass.

An alright game crippled by techical limitations.
The story of this game centers around a family that is a lot like the Starks, but not the Starks. A seriese of unfortunate events befall them and they are forced to hunker down and fight for survival in a suddenly hostile world. Again, they're not the Starks, but they're a lot like the Starks. In fact, they're so much like the Starks that this game feels more like a fanfiction than an official GoT game. That's how like the Starks the not-Starks are. Add to that the persistant misconception that these games are a choose-your-own-adventure book made binary and you've got something mildy dissapointing. This game is linear, all paths lead to the same outcomes, you have no control. The only control you have is how characters think of you, which means diddly.
The technical aspects of this game take it from alright to not alright in several distinct ways. For one, the world is dead. A maximum of about 12 people are ever on screen at once. In a game like The Wolf Among Us or The Walking Dead, this makes sense, because the characters are all, in their own ways, a dying breed. There aren't enough of them left to have a gathering of more than 12. In this game, where you're supposed to be in an established town with a castle and bustling masses, this limitation is significantly immersion breaking. At one point, you're supposed to have a small army of mercinaries at your back, when in reality it's 4-5 burly men with swords. Truly, the smallest army.
This game is dissapointing, and we all should have seen it coming. That's not to say it wasn't enjoyable, it was just dissapointing.

Among the many 3D software options that cost hundred of dollars, and use a ton of space in your hard drive (5gb most of them!), you find this little, yet wonderful 3D application. It doesnt cost even one dollar, will take less than 100~mb of space of your hard drive, and you can actually do most of the things you can do with any other 3D application.
You could even call Blender 3D a suite: You can Model, Animate, Paint, Sculpt, Particles simulation, Composite images and Videos, you can track videos, put sound on them. Virtually, you can do everything in this software. And it costs nothing. (Sure, After Effects, Zbrush, are way better at what they do than Blender. But still, Blender can, and that means a lot to freelancers)
Is Blender worth learning when there are other professional 3D apps? Yes. Blender is a tool, and a tool is as good as the person using it. I have worked with 3dsmax and Maya in the past, softwares where I thought I wouldnt be able to get good at modelling at all, until I met Blender. I have also never missed 3Dsmax or Maya, mainly because Blender is so Shortcut dependant that it makes you work faster. As simple as that.
Also, Blender has probably the most active community. You found a bug and reported it? Probably it will be fixed the next morning, or in a couple of days.
Blender is a really good, free and OpenSource application. It is still a necessity to know other and more common softwares like 3dsmax and Maya for most of jobs, just to include your Blender work in a pipeline correctly.

Blender is an extremely powerful piece of software which can potentially allow you to accomplish any task from modelling, animating, texturing, rendering, video editing, audio editing to even compositing and motion tracking.
I am certainly no professional but I have been using Blender for years for various smaller projects.
While very hard to get into at first, once you grasp how everything works and how flexible this application is, the only thing really separating you from fulfilling your ambitions in 3D graphics is your own skill.
That last part should not be underestimated, as from personal experience I can tell that it is easy to try to create something and never end up with a satisfactory result (or any result at all!) and blame it on the software.
But the truth is, while any software has its limitations (Blender has some relevant ones that I will discuss further down), creating something beautiful in the space of 3D graphics takes lots of experience and skill.
Luckily there is a large amount of learning resources on the internet, both paid and free, that allow for learning Blender as well as the necessary skills (even at the same time! :D).
Just be warned that this is no simple weekend task.
Blender itself is, as already said, a very powerful piece of software and some say that it even surpasses the industry standard tools in many areas. I can't confirm or deny that, as I have not used those tools for any longer amount of time.
What I can say though, is that while Blender has most of the features those tools posess and certainly is able to allow you to produce very professional results in an efficient way and therefore might be a great choice for teams and individuals, it is not one of the major tools that are used by most of the larger studios.
Therefore it might not be an ideal choice for individuals trying to gather skills mainly with the goal of starting a career at a large studio.
The other implication of this is that some tools that have been built (e.g for Unreal Engine 4) are not designed to be compatible with Blender. It is also a bit tricky to set up a reliably working import-export pipeline to certain engines.
But these are not as big of a problem as they might seem, and the situation is improving a lot these days.
Both Valve and Epic Games (developers of Unreal Engine 4) have sponsored Blender development of game specific features (especially when it comes to importing, exporting models and animations to game engines. Epic Games even started a tutorial series on making Blender work with UE4 as good as possible and improves their own importers).
There are also tools, that already have great support already, such as Unity 3D.
Personally I have tested both Unreal Engine 4 and Unity and I can confirm that Unreal Engine is a bit tricky but can be made to work nicely with the right settings and Unity works just about fine more or less out of the box. It can even import .blend files directly.
Overall Blender is a really great piece of software (especially for the price!) and if you can deal with its "limitations" it will serve you well and allow you to fulfill your dreams if you have the patience to gather the required skills :)

I may catch some flak for this review, as "Puzzle" is right there in the user-defined tags for this game. However, I had hoped that the atmosphere and voice-controlled spells might temper my usual aversion to this type of gameplay.
The game is very pretty, and the signature mechanic works exactly as advertised. You indeed cast spells verbally through your microphone, and this works pretty reliably. However, I could not get excited about the remainder of the experience.
My first hiccup (and likely that of many players) was immediately before gaining the third "spell," in which players are expected to "show deference" to an eye shrine. I only learned of this solution by consulting a walkthrough, and feel pretty confident that it would never have revealed itself to me, as it's quite obtuse. Shortly thereafter, I walked into a room with stones floating in a gap I needed to cross. I scoured the room as best I could for around 10 minutes, and could see no clear way forward. Then, upon consulting the walkthrough again, learned of a small symbol over an arch that I was expected to notice and activate.
Around this time, I decided that this one wasn't for me. Again, perhaps this review will not be a useful one. However, suffice it to say that if you don't typically like puzzle games, the inclusion of voice commands will likely not change your mind.

So this really happened: Blender is now on Steam. What can I say? as a user of Blender since 2004 I've hated it at first and started to love it once I "got" it. Prepare for a steep learning curve if you want to achieve cool results.
Having said that I can assure you Blender is one of the most competent and powerful 3D-production suites of the current generation and can compete with the likes of Max, Maya and Cinema 4D. The sourrounding ecosystem of plugins is much smaller which is the reason the uptake of Blender in highly-evolved production environments is slow. In the world of asset-creation and smaller animation projects things are different, though, and Blender is a widely used tool.
I'd definitely recommend it for anyone looking at 3D-animation and modelling. Once you get used to it you will have a real frame of reference for competing tools.

This game is fantastic. The randomness of each playthrough makes it endlessly replayable. Yeah, sometimes you die within 15 minutes because the game refused to drop any good weapons, but other times you end up with an unstoppable juggernaut by the halfway point. This game isn't about long-term strategy; it's about making do with what you have. You might tell yourself you're not going to make deals with pirates this time, but when you're limping through space with damaged weapons and no scrap for repairs, that bribe starts to look awfully nice...
The tactical combat is excellent too. Having to prioritize systems when you don't have enough power, being forced to change tactics when an enemy missile knocks out one of your critical systems, panicking when your life support gets taken out by an enemy boarding drone...
I will say that the game can feel a little bit long for a rogue-like, meaning that it can be quite disheartening to play for 45 minutes before realizing that you don't have the upgrades necessary to survive much longer and then inevitably dying. I think a slightly shorter game length might have been less frustrating at times, but to be honest this is such a small criticism that I rarely noticed in my 100+ hours of playing.
Absolutely recommended.

I love visual novels, and love zombie games wih resources and group managing. And so I really wished I could recommend this game but I really can't.
The first biggest issue, is that the game is short or incomplete. While is not uncommon games that have are launches as only chapter 1, this one is sold as full price complete game and not advertised as a chapter 1 of a story or work in progress. You can finish the game in one sit in a few hours (5-9 hours gameplay I would say, even less if you rush things) and there's a bug where you literaly skip a part of the story straigh to the end, may you want to do it or not.
The game was described as "As an ex-military officer looking to rebuild your relationship with your teenage daughter" but said daughter is barely seen apearing in a single scene the entire game.
The story is interesting, only major issue is that a lot of the interactions with your group members are pretty random, sometimes members of the group apear wanting to talk to you in a new day, and the small story they tell it's cool, but being random if you need to load a previous save (or the game crash and need to rollback to the previous night) you lose those relation progress. That make hard too to actually choose when you want to get closer or have a relationship with someone.
The resources management portion of the game is interesting and even fun, but can be pretty frustrating some moments, as the resources that apear on the map are random, sometimes causing a shortage of food that can not be avoided but by luck (as you may find food while collecting other resources) what can be annoying when you're "working hard" to keep everyone fed and in a single day everything go down, sometimes for the next day be all fixed for a lot of food apearing (or not).
On mechanics, I've played just the 2nd edition, that don't have the fight roulette or lockpick system, so can't really say about it. Maybe I'll try to play a the story a 3rd time to try the 1st edition and see it. On the 2nd edition it's story only, you can never lose a VIP member of the group in combat, but the no-VIP survivors will at random still get hurt or die.
As I said in the start, I really want to recommend this game, and it is actually kinda fun to play, if you get cheap in a sale or something is actually worty spending a few hours on it, maybe, but have in mind this is just a "chapter 1" the story ending with a ton loose ends (almost all if not all).
If the developers eventually finish the story, be on update, DLC or continuation of the game would be 100% worthy playing, but the unfinished story while interesting leave you hanging in the end right now.

3. You can skip dialogue by pressing the right mouse button.
Anyways, this is an alright timewaster. I suggest waiting for a sale, I wouldn't neccasarily say it's worth 5 dollars; this is more like a phone app then it is a game.
