If you don't like the voice casting you won't like it. Atmosphere is beautiful, surreal, sometimes creepy. This is a puzzle-exploration game, not combat-focused; even combat is best handled like a puzzle. The puzzles are not obvious and the game doesn't hold your hand about solving them. There is no map function, and the in-game maps aren't especially helpful.
Half the point of the game is its voice-cast mechanic, and the other half is to tell its story, which is dark, kinda sad, and takes place in a pretty, creepy, pretty creepy world. The primary two complaints about it are "microphone doesn't work" (I have no firsthand experience with that) and "puzzles are not intuitive" (which for some people they aren't, but for some people having to think outside the box is part of the appeal).
+ The game is pretty. Really pretty. The first chapter has a mushroom-crystal-caves-and-gothic-architecture aesthetic, chapter two takes the gothic architecture and adds a dash of fever dream, doll-head-masks, and even a touch of chinese imperial. Chapter three goes into angelic astronaut energy engineer territory. Very unique.
+++ Provided it works for you, the voice-casting practically guarantees a nerd-gasm the first few times you cast a spell. I'd recommend you use the game's language rather than english, so you can copy their pronunciation (open the journal and click the phrase to hear her say it) without fear of your accent causing trouble. Plus, speaking Maha'Ki helps put you in the game.
++ The story is actually pretty good. The bits of lore you can find give tantalizing glimpses into a dark world, and the character's goal and motivation will tug your heartstrings. Though, the good ending managed to wreck me enough that even now (months later) I still haven't scrapped up enough heart to go back and play again to see the bad ending.
+ The controls are reliable. The physics are pretty good, but the fall damage is a bit punishing. Tip: teleporting out of a fall does
cancel fall damage.
+ You
actually find the information you need to proceed, defeat your foes, and solve certain puzzles, in the world. Just check every nook and cranny.
- It's not terribly well optimized. I have a mid-powered rig, and have to run the game on suboptimal settings.
- The puzzles really are a little surreal, which can make them tricky to solve. You can use environment queues to help (
) but there are a few things that require an intuitive leap.
-- Combat is clunky. Vermin can be killed with the light beam, but everything stronger needs the firebomb, which is... well, clunky. That and getting tongue-tied can literally kill you, particularly when you're fighting
because even if you've found the note that explains its spells, its voice (sorta like blood sloshing through gravel) makes understanding it, and therefore knowing what spell to cast yourself, difficult.
- You cannot cast "Tial Udah" while telekinetically holding something. Why not? Because the thing is in your reticle.
If you're impatient, if you don't like weird, or if you have any problem with the thought of the voice casting, don't bother.
If you are patient, if you're fond of hard puzzles (or linguistics), if you like strange, dark, or morbid stories, or if you like novel mechanics like the voice cast, try it.

Your hitbox is the entire wagon (large), but the area your default weapon can attack is one small line right ahead of you. You will get hit many, many times by enemies just above or just below this area charging toward you. Anyone who makes it to the Buffalo will know what I mean. There are other weapons, but there's no way to store or change them, so if you get something that could help you later you can prepare to fire it off about two minutes before you really need it.
Your wagon has three passengers, among whom damage is "shared". Hits land not-really-randomly on your party members, often hitting and killing one person before the other two. It's possible to get hitpoints back but this happens on a purely random basis, and consists of either events that may or may not happen or medkit pickups you may not be able to reach. The frustration that comes when you find a rare event only to realize it's your 1-HP guy instead of your 4-HP guy that you have to try to finish it with... agonizing.
There's some laughs to be had here; I thought it was hilarious when I had the option to either ford a river or jump over it, and then later either go around or swim under the river. There's also a ton of content and different paths your adventure might take; I was still finding new ones until I finally quit playing.
It's a shame I'm not going to see the end of the game though because I cannot put up with these deaths that I have no real control over. If the hitbox on the wagon was a lot smaller and my gun could aim a little I'd probably play the hell out of this game. Sadly, I'm sick of it and going to see if I can get a refund.

I've always thought I have a chef in me. Oddly my fascination with cooking doesn't come from watching real chefs work, or the food itself. Instead it comes from watching mobster movies. For some reason most of them had a part where an old Italian dudes cooked. I don't know, they just made it look cool. After burning regular rice, chicken breast, eating uncooked oatmeal, etc, I can confirm there is no chef in me. And now I relay on wife to keep me alive.
Overcooked doesn't particularly concentrate on the cooking itself, but rather on coordination to get the food ready on time. You will be given a set of meals to prepare and serve. You start by receiving the order, prepare the ingredients, cooking them, and finally arrange them for service. You'll also handle washing the dishes, and in case of overcooking fires will breakout and you'll have to extinguish them.
The whole process in itself starts simple by giving you easy orders of Onion soup or Tomato soup, but in no time you'll be cooking burgers. You will have to cook the burger, cut the tomatoes and lettuces, put it all in a bun, and serve it in a sandwich. The first difficulty comes when playing co-op is who will do which part to run the process as fast as possible. The need for coordination could test your relationship with the other player, as it tested my marriage.
The developers up the difficulty, brilliantly, with terrific level design. Some levels will have rats stealing any unattended food, floors made of ice, another level where the whole kitchen is on two moving trucks on a highway. The trucks move away from each every couple of minutes, splitting the kitchen in two. The level design is terrific and varied keeping the experience fresh.
The narrative part, which is odd for it to have one to start with, is really well done. You're a cook in the Onion Kingdom, which was invaded by a horrific monstrosity that will destroy the kingdom if not fed enough food, in a short time. You start the game by cooking for the monster, then beaten by the fact that you're not good enough. At that time the Onion King save you and travel back in time so you would have enough time to travel the world, and sharpen your cooking skills, so when the day comes you will be ready.
The biggest problem with the game is that it doesn't support online co-op. I get the idea that the experience is so much better as a couch co-op, but still why not provide a practical option.
Overall Overcooked is a simple game, with simple mechanics and graphics, put together to shape a smart, funny, couch co-op experience that will test your patience, and relationships, especially with your significant other.

XCOM : Enemy Unknown / Enemy Within.
I'm reviewing both at the same time because when I bought XCOM I got both the base game and it's expansion.
This game is so damn addicting, I would play countless hours and dying a little inside everytime one of my soldiers die. You get attached and have fond moments of where they do either really bad misses or perfect kills across map. That's what makes this game so unqiue compared to the triple A watered down games we usually have these days. Game developers get in a comfort zone and make it easier for new players.
Thank god, XCOM is not one of those series. You will lose, a lot.
That's the fun of it in all honesty though, you learn from mistakes and I highly recommend first playthrough on ironman it will teach you a lot.
There is somewhat of a storyline, it's very simple design basically just do 5 main missions and that's it. Took me around 20 hoursish on my first playthrough on Normal difficulty. Wide range of enemies, espically thanks to Enemy Within. The flying aspect of the game with interceptors is very basic but it does matter a lot in the game, you'll have to keep a good amount of interceptors in each country to defend your satellites from getting destroyed by enemy UFOs.
You can customize your XCOM soldiers and choose their loadout which is a game in itself to make sure you have the best loadouts for a tough mission ahead.
X:COM Enemy Within adds Mechs,Psi units and new enemies to shed a tear for. A beautiful expansion but I would recommend it on steam sale, $32.99 is a bit much and same with the Slingshot Pack that only adds about 30 minutes of gameplay to our game and a new character for $7.79
Overall I'm extremely impressed with XCOM and I'll be sure to do a review soon on XCOM 2 and if it can live up the gameplay of the first game.
PS: There is a mod called 'Long War". I highly recommend it after beating the main game as the main game basically is a tutorial for Long War. It's turns it into a brand new game with the mechanics of XCOM:EU/EW.
Good luck, Commander.

I was so excited when I saw COH2 was out. I loved the original. Perhaps that's the problem. COH2 is just no where near as good as the original.
For starters, there's only one single player campaign, as Russia. No German campaign. How cheap is that?!
For seconds, the game is a rampant money grab, everything is for sale, uniforms, badges for the main menu, hell, you can buy a silver or bronze border for a dollar. And of course, there's two more factions you can buy for multiplayer (only), and there's the add on packs that add an odd mix of single player, multiplayer and co-op. Just to give you a clue, the total expenditure (not including the game itself) on packs could be up to $212?! I think it's easily possible to spend over $300 on this. Whatever you do, don't do it...
And perhaps most importantly, the core gameplay seems like more of the same, but...somehow less (probably due to the lack of Americans and German factions). Due to the ham fisted story, the game wants you to throw men forward to slaughter, just to prove how brutal to their own soldiers the Russians were in WW2.
Somehow COH has lost it's soul, and lost it's way. I wonder if the publisher Sega had anything to do with that? Most likely...
UPDATE: So, after a lot of playing I think my final anlysis is this:
The game is still a big money grab, content that should be free has to be paid for.
The single player campaign is still not as good as COH1, but at least there is now also the US campaign (if you pay for it). Still no German or UK campaigns.
The multiplayer is better than the original, only in the sense that in the original I lost every time, but COH2 seems more balanced (despite imbalances), and at least I can win sometimes now! :)
Overall, I have changed it to a thumbs up, because the positives outweigh the negatives, but I still think the DLC format sucks, and that a campaign for UK & GY would have been good.

Don't let the boardgame hex look and turn-based gameplay fool you: This is a complex survival simulation, one of the best I've played and almost certainly the best on Steam. Even in early access, the game is in a completely playable and mature state, a notable contrast to the buggy, imbalanced status of almost every game available in this genre.
The drag/drop crafting system is intuitive yet almost too simple, at once the game's greatest asset and biggest barrier to sinking too much time into it. A few minor ease of use tweaks would go a long way. Still, conceptually, this is the kind of system RPGs need to return to, especially outside of the roguelike/survival setting.
The far less accessible UnReal World is the only game I can think of that compares. This game drops a lot of the old-school roguelike cruft in a positive way (usually that's a bad thing!), so I would honestly recommend this to anybody interested in this sort of game first.

Anyone who tells you this game is bad is either lying or doens't know how to enjoy this game.
Like the last one, the only way to really enjoy the game is to take nothing seriously and just have fun, and that's really easy in this game.
Once you get past the opening segment and start getting your super powers it's an absolute blast.  You can't have multiple powers available at once, but you can easily switch between them, and traversal powers like super speed and super jump are always at your disposal, eliminating the need for any vehicle once you level up stamina and get certain upgrades, but you'll get in vehicles anyway for the sweet neon cars and monster-truck versions of pre-existing vehicles, and if you get the presidential dlc you get the most hilarious jet which you will probably not be able to resist riding around in either.
Add to that all the sci-fi movie and game references (the whole thing is almost a parody of Mass effect, with "loyalty missions" for all of your homies, romance options [where all you do is shag, but like I said: parody] and of course the space, 3rd-person shooter theme) and throw in ways to feel closer to all of your friends, which was unexpected but endearing when you start learning how they cope with the situations they are or have been in, and their views on you.  Put all that together and what you have is a game that will give you hours upon hours of entertainment.
The worst thing I could find about this game is that they (SPOILERS) killed Oleg.  I guess when Deep Silver bought the franchise they took some kind of poll to figure out who everyone's favorite characters were and went with them, which explains why Kinzie is such a central character this time around.  Still doens't explain why Oleg (whom I always thought was wildly popular) was "cut" (possibly to remove the brute class altogether, which is also a weird/dumb play,) so that and not only Angel's death, but complete absence from the story were the worst things about the game for me.
If you have a sense of humor and want to play something that's just a fun, dumb good time, this game is a must-buy.  I'd suggest picking up the edition that comes with all the dlc which is nearly all costumes and cosmetics(which is all dlc should be,) with some weapons, vehicles, and even some side-missions thrown in for end-game content, as it just makes the game more fun/silly, and it's a fairly common thing to go on sale.  Hell, if it's on sale then the Saint's franchise pack is also probably on sale, which I'd suggest even more.
So get out there and see how corny/silly/badass you can be gosh-darnit!

I've used Blender for many years now. This is an awesome tool for 3d animation, modeling, green screen chroma-keying, planar tracking, roto-scoping, and even has a built in game development suite.
It's ironic to see it available on steam kind of to me, being that blender's original form was created by a video game development studio, Neo Geo, who originally had a vision of an all-in-one development software package. Years later, the software hit the open-source scene and has since taken on a life all it's own. It's currently developed by a team with love, and there are quite a selection of add-on packages to add extra features created by the community, not to mention how many add ons come in the "trunk" of the initial software when installed by default (they are available in 'File' >'User Preferences'>'Add ons').
The default setup for mouse may seem awkward to many at first, with left-click setting the "origin"-cursor in 3d space where clicked (used for some referencing and also as the point where objects you spawn will appear), middle mouse being used for rotation of the view in the 3d space, and right-click being the action that selects 3d objects. These can of course be changed in the user settings.
But so much can be done with this software, and again, for free!
Here is a music video that me and my drummer did for our 'symphonc-metal' band, with my using Blender and his using Adobe After-effects. We did this in about a month by ourselves with a $40 budget!

Pff. I am quite torn whether to put a thumbs up to this game. Do not get me wrong: I absolutely LOVE the graphics, I like the setting and even the storyline. I am okay with the map being a copy of FC4. But at this point I feel the game has some major issues. First of all: there are WAY! TOO! MANY! enemies and animals. I know the devs wanted us to not be safe but this is just ridiculous! In previous titles you could plan your stealth approach without worrying too much for the occasional predator that will attack you and most of the time you were just an arrow away from getting rid of the nuisance. In Primal, however, wherever you turn, every 2 feet you stumble upon hordes of animals and enemies! Feels like you are walking in Hong Kong - it is so crowded (I am really NOT exaggerating about how crowded the game is). Heck, it feels like a storm in a Call of Duty game. Needless to say, you get killed so often that you HAVE to use the fast travel. Either that, or the game quickly becomes boring. You have to be constantly attacking just to get the next collectible. That screams that the game lacks content. And indeed, as much as I love the setting, I think it isn't suitable for a FC game. All the explosions, wingsuit, flying, etc, etc - GONE. Sure, control of beasts is there as to try to compensate for the fireworks but it is just not enough. The content is so sparse that it feels the game has been released unfinished. While the graphics are even better than the already very beautiful FC3 and FC4, I thinkt Primal is actually a step back. Overall I recommend the game but only if you get it on a sale. Otherwise, it is not worth the full price.

The spell casting is actually very engaging but the level design and puzzles are so abysmal I can barely even articulate the extent of it.
Real example for the choosy buyer:
In one instance you have to activate a panel to open a door, laser a crystal to spin a platform, then do a running jump into lava and teleport at the last minute get through the door, all on a five second timer. The jump requires so much precision it's hard to tell that you're even supposed to be doing that in the first place (and then you'll look it up and, yes, that is the solution). All of that uses multiple voice commands which actually feels pretty slick, but in practice pushes the limits in terms of the precision being demanded. Then when you miss the jump, you take damage. If you finally make the jump, you have to fight a room full of enemies with 10% of your health left (they have horrible AI, but there's like 4 of them) and your fireball spell does almost no damage. And if you die, you have to do the stupid platforming again.
And that's just one example, the whole game is like this. You take an unintuitive 'puzzle' that punishes you for trying to solve it (there's a reason Portal and Talos Principle don't have fall damage), then follow it up with a combat or platforming sequence that's needlessly difficult because you have no health left. What makes this even more horrible is that there's a healing spell that is overpowered but it only works in water; so every time you'd want to use it you can't, but whenever there's water around you're literally immortal because it just channels forever keeping you at max health. This means you'll incrementally be whittled down by the aforementioned stupid hazards then one shotted by a brain dead enemy or a 10ft drop, but when the first actual boss battle happens you literally cannot die because the arena floor is water.
As good as the visuals and voice recognition are, they're just wasted potential tacked onto hot garbage.
Get it when it's on extreme sale (like >70% off) if you're very curious, otherwise save your money.

A parody of The Oregon Trail edutainment games.
Graphics are intentionally retro 8bit, with a CRT monitor filter you can optionally enable. Simplistic, low-detail sprites represent your wagon, your party and anything else that may or may not want to kill you - and the former grossly outnumber the latter.
Equally retro are the sound effects, with beeps and blops and a catchy MIDI-ish soundtrack.
Gameplay is like a sillier Oregon Trail - normally you control your wagon along a linear course, avoiding obstacles and shooting at things that (rarely don't) want to kill you. Your party has individual life bars and you lose once all of them are dead or missing. Events pop up after every gameplay section, ranging from shooting train robbers, to choosing between fording or jumping a river, to some rather spoiler-y occurences.
There's the main campaign mode, and progressing through it and beating certain challenges can unlock survival modes (last as long as possible in a gauntlet of enemies), shuffle modes (your starting settings are randomized from what I understand) and new wagons (which change your speed, party's health and firepower).
It's a small game and gets you a few laughs when you play short sessions of it, and it's probably in your best of interests not to take it too seriously, even if it does get a tad dark and difficult (especially difficult).
Modern economies wouldn't have any problems if a) we had enlightened rulers and b) they had access to this sort of tool for IRL use. Socialist utopia ftw.

I was a big fan of Far Cry 3 and 4, and Primal kinda fills the gap while waiting for Far Cry 5.
Visually the game is beautiful, the light in particular (the moon through the trees at night is stunning), but the world itself is quite repetitive.
The mechanics are very similar to the previous episodes, although of course without vehicles and guns.
The weapons are fairly limited, but it feels like the game is not taking advantage of it: I prefer assassin style gameplay, but there is very little emphasis on this in the game: none of the "climb the ledge and takedown" from the previous episodes for example.
The storyline is not bad, but nowhere near FC3 or 4, and the game ends up being quite repetitive.
All in all it took me ~30-40 hours to reach 100% in the game. At time it brought me back to the fun of the previous episodes, but simply felt too repetitive. I'd recommend it if you're a fan of the series, or fancy  trying something a bit different, but only if you can get a good price on sales.

I was so excited when I saw COH2 was out. I loved the original. Perhaps that's the problem. COH2 is just no where near as good as the original.
For starters, there's only one single player campaign, as Russia. No German campaign. How cheap is that?!
For seconds, the game is a rampant money grab, everything is for sale, uniforms, badges for the main menu, hell, you can buy a silver or bronze border for a dollar. And of course, there's two more factions you can buy for multiplayer (only), and there's the add on packs that add an odd mix of single player, multiplayer and co-op. Just to give you a clue, the total expenditure (not including the game itself) on packs could be up to $212?! I think it's easily possible to spend over $300 on this. Whatever you do, don't do it...
And perhaps most importantly, the core gameplay seems like more of the same, but...somehow less (probably due to the lack of Americans and German factions). Due to the ham fisted story, the game wants you to throw men forward to slaughter, just to prove how brutal to their own soldiers the Russians were in WW2.
Somehow COH has lost it's soul, and lost it's way. I wonder if the publisher Sega had anything to do with that? Most likely...
UPDATE: So, after a lot of playing I think my final anlysis is this:
The game is still a big money grab, content that should be free has to be paid for.
The single player campaign is still not as good as COH1, but at least there is now also the US campaign (if you pay for it). Still no German or UK campaigns.
The multiplayer is better than the original, only in the sense that in the original I lost every time, but COH2 seems more balanced (despite imbalances), and at least I can win sometimes now! :)
Overall, I have changed it to a thumbs up, because the positives outweigh the negatives, but I still think the DLC format sucks, and that a campaign for UK & GY would have been good.

Anyone who tells you this game is bad is either lying or doens't know how to enjoy this game.
Like the last one, the only way to really enjoy the game is to take nothing seriously and just have fun, and that's really easy in this game.
Once you get past the opening segment and start getting your super powers it's an absolute blast.  You can't have multiple powers available at once, but you can easily switch between them, and traversal powers like super speed and super jump are always at your disposal, eliminating the need for any vehicle once you level up stamina and get certain upgrades, but you'll get in vehicles anyway for the sweet neon cars and monster-truck versions of pre-existing vehicles, and if you get the presidential dlc you get the most hilarious jet which you will probably not be able to resist riding around in either.
Add to that all the sci-fi movie and game references (the whole thing is almost a parody of Mass effect, with "loyalty missions" for all of your homies, romance options [where all you do is shag, but like I said: parody] and of course the space, 3rd-person shooter theme) and throw in ways to feel closer to all of your friends, which was unexpected but endearing when you start learning how they cope with the situations they are or have been in, and their views on you.  Put all that together and what you have is a game that will give you hours upon hours of entertainment.
The worst thing I could find about this game is that they (SPOILERS) killed Oleg.  I guess when Deep Silver bought the franchise they took some kind of poll to figure out who everyone's favorite characters were and went with them, which explains why Kinzie is such a central character this time around.  Still doens't explain why Oleg (whom I always thought was wildly popular) was "cut" (possibly to remove the brute class altogether, which is also a weird/dumb play,) so that and not only Angel's death, but complete absence from the story were the worst things about the game for me.
If you have a sense of humor and want to play something that's just a fun, dumb good time, this game is a must-buy.  I'd suggest picking up the edition that comes with all the dlc which is nearly all costumes and cosmetics(which is all dlc should be,) with some weapons, vehicles, and even some side-missions thrown in for end-game content, as it just makes the game more fun/silly, and it's a fairly common thing to go on sale.  Hell, if it's on sale then the Saint's franchise pack is also probably on sale, which I'd suggest even more.
So get out there and see how corny/silly/badass you can be gosh-darnit!

As a big fan of visual novels and zombies, I was excited to get this one. The classic, TWD inspired story about the group of survivors with tough moral choices meets the easily approachable format of visual novel should be an easy win in my book.
Unfortunately, the great (if not the most innovative) idea is hindered by less than stellar execution, and while "Dead But Alive" is far from bad, I cannot reccommend it for the full price.
Apart from game's length (about 2 hours), the storyline is not complete - the game ends with "to be continued" and it's not clear whether the next episodes are coming. That's the main problem of the game - lack of content and lack of variety. Both the the resource management (managing the camp of survivors) and visual novel (choices, romances) aspects have not enough depth. There isn't enough control of the survivors - you cannot assign them tasks or roles; it's not even possible to dismiss them after they join your ranks (unless it's driven by the story), so they end up eating your food until the end. With so limited control, you're not going to feel like a boss. The game also suffers from technical issues (for instance, clicking on any resorce image leads to script error), but it runs well enough on Win7.
Visual novel part of the game is quite short - there are some decisions and moral choices to be made, but despite their serious tone, the game doesn't let you feel their weight upon you. And while characters look interesting, there's too little interaction and dialogue for them to really come alive. Romance part, from my experience, is not an inch deeper than that - a few dialogue lines and one scene per character. You can be involved with as many NPC's as you wish without any consequences, which makes the whole thing even less believable and less exciting.
Despite all negative stuff, I enjoyed "Dead But Alive!" to a degree. It can be fun for a while, it has nice visuals, a variety of characters and a promise of grim, post-apocalypse world waiting to be explored, but unfortunately, it doesn't fully deliver. With the recent update, however, there is a glimmer of hope that developers will fix the bugs and add more content (or change the pricing) in the future, and create a bigger, better sequel that would finally let me party Rick Grimes style.

I've been a fan of Winter Wolves games for quite some time now. I've played all of their titles that allow same sex (M+M) relationships and have never been displeased. In this game there are three men and three women (I believe?) who may be romanced; I chose two of the men and there were no consequences do to having more than one lover.
The game takes place, for the most part, in a small camp which you must build up defenses for.  This requires you to go out into the world and gather food and materials so that you can survive. I found it extremely easy to have more than enough food; I never fell into starvation mode. Gathering materials did eventually become tedious, particularly for the defenses, which get torn down constantly.
Occasionally you will come up against zombies and have to play a ridiculous “slot machine” battle system. I hated the system, but fortunately there is an option to disable it and just focus on the story.
The game is very simple to play, the dialogue is absurd, childish, possessed of terrible grammar and horribly misspelled; the graphics are dreadful.
But please dear reader, these are not actually criticisms. These are factors which make Winter Wolves games sweet, charming, addicting and very fun to play.
I absolutely loved the plot, the romances and the character development. Just a warning however: this game has a “to be continued” to it. You will not meet certain objectives, which I am assuming will come about with a new title.

So it's obviously aesthetically wanting, the "story" is wanting, and we're left with "is it fun?".  This is a personal question, but for me it is a resounding "no".  The initial "strategy" is simple, but can't scale up to harder enemies:  take out shields, then weapons, then powerplant.  You better get some good weapons, but where?  Oh, that's right, it's an iterative game--keep looking until it spawns.  But stay alive until then.  I find that level of difficulty capricious, without meaning.  Terrible, in a word.
In short, I bought this game at a time when $10 was a lot of money;  I still want my money back.

Permadeath has never been so fun!
It's so hard to find a good survival game that doesn't feature hordes of the undead - often in place of more creative challenges to, well, staying alive. Similarly, it's the rare title that does anything very well at all for less than $10 these days. NEO Scavenger fits both bills and still has more to come (I guess... I haven't noticed many bugs and I think I've progressed a fair distance). You'll probably need the wiki to help you get started, if only because you have to get the hang of some of the craftable items. I played the demo for about forty-five minutes before grabbing the full version and only had two or three things I'd count as bugs:
1) My save data was inexplicably lost once, but I didn't mind starting over
2) It seems to me that there's really only one way to start with any decent chance but that's not necessarily going to stay true in the final version (and I could be wrong - there's a decent amount of randomness with each play)
3) Sometimes you setup a camp site and it disappears later, sometimes re-appearing on a later visit to that hex
None of these, for me, are game-breakers because I'm not playing NEO Scavenger to win - I'm playing to -survive-. This means battling cold weather, raiders and dogmen, hunger, thirst, fatigue, and the dangers of exploring/scavenging ruined buildings that might collapse on you at any moment. I simply include most of the bugs along with the other dangers and keep on truckin' (or start a new game). I highly recommend that anyone looking to play a game that focuses on those things as NEO Scavenger really does it well. Happy Gaming!

I strongly support this tool.

Blender has been around for years and is the most comprehensive CGI suite I've ever come across (even when compared to paid software).
Is it easy to use?
Hell no! But what did you expect? This is a creative tool not a game.
Once you've learned how to use it you'll find that it's powerful and comprehensive but at first it will crush your dreams of becoming an amasing 3D artist.
A great deal of perseverance is required in the first few days but it's well worth it!
Can I make games with it?
Once you've learned how to model with blender you should have no trouble creating assests for games. You can make use of the in built game engine if you really want but it's very bare bones. I reccomend using something like Unity instead but making the assets in blender.
All in all it's 100% free, comprehensive to the point of removing the need for other tools that would usually feature in the modelling and texturing workflow, has a huge and helpful online community and a huge library of FREE addons.
I can't recommend this enough.

I quickly finished The Farm (5 minutes tops) and wanted to try other levels. Remember, I have to go back to the launcher to select a level. So I must completely exit the game to go back to that. Awkward af.
Some other notes:
-I finally discovered the options menus. They're only accessable while actually in the level and oh boy are they limited.
-Graphics settings is literrally just 3 options: High - Medium - Low. Despite the fact that this game looks equivilant to a game made in 1999, my somewhat capable gaming rig couldn't handle it running on High, so I ran it on Medium with still lots of frame issues.
-Music is class. Banjos, violins, just wish it wasn't SO LOUD. Luckily, there is a audio levels settings in the options. There's also a slider for SFX but I have no idea why since I didn't hear the animals or anything else making sound besides the music. Maybe the music was just still too loud IDK.
-The game has 2 odd inclusions: 1. A flashlight, even though it's never dark enough to need it unless there's some hidden cave I never found or something. There's no day/night cycle here. 2. A SAVE feature?!?! What on earth are you saving?? There's no collectables, no map unlocking, no achievements, nothing!
All in all, despite the many things in with this game that could make someone pull their hair out, I got about a half hour of solid entertainment out of it. I laughed. I cried. And at the normal price of $.99 and currently on sale for $.59 I'd say it's worth the tag. Even better if you're lucky to get it bundled. Try it out, you'll get some laughs. Or perhaps some deep thoughts pondering how games like this still get made.

TL;DR: Grim Dawn is more beautiful, stable, complex, and interesting than Van Helsing.
Grim Dawn is beautifully rendered.  The settings, armor, and weapons change appearance as you move up the ranks.  When you start the game, your weapons and armor look like nothing more than wooden boards that have been nailed together.  As you progress through the game and levels, items change in material, enchantment, and animation.  The enemies also scale accordingly to provide a reasonable challenge without inducing frustration, even at the Veteran level.  As the game increases in difficulty, the type and build of your character begins to influence your play style more and more.  The elegant musical score subtly fills the quiet moments of the game and rises to match exciting moments (e.g. boss battles) without becoming a cacophony of sound.  The voice acting is decent and you can skip most of it, if you're not interested.
The game's story is told through character missions and pieces of lore, which can be interesting to read, but not necessary.  The pieces of lore tell the story of other people who have been caught in the Grim Dawn conflict.  Some people decide to wait it out; others decide to fight.  Sometimes you meet these people later on; other times you find their eviscerated bodies.  If you remove the magical/steam-punk component to these stories, they are very similar to real-world stories of families and people living through an armed conflict.
On the technical side, I've only had one "crash" where my screen went blank.  There have been a few graphical or find-path glitches here and there, but nothing game breaking.  Grim Dawn does not suffer from any of the progress-blocking bugs (e.g. Van Helsing).  The load times are surprisingly fast, given the gorgeous settings and items.  Animations are smooth and silky.
For a game that's < $10, it's definitely worth buy several copies and having a party with friends and family.

As a long-time fan of Path of Exile, I'm always a bit apprehensive about trying other ARPGs--the extreme level of customizability and theorycrafting in PoE are a major draw for me, and I have a hard time appreciating games with cookie-cutter characters/builds like D3 because of how great PoE has been. That said, Grim Dawn has exceeded my expectations in this and many other regards.
While the base system of choosing two different classes and putting points into a wide variety of options across one or both trees gives quite an amazing variety of options, it alone wouldn't hold my interest. However, there's a second system for character progression--Devotions--which are all interconnected, and combining the two is absolutely fascinating. Just like in PoE, I now have way too many builds I want to try, more than I'll ever have the time for.
I suppose most people probably care more about, you know, actually playing the game than about character builds and theorycrafting, and Grim Dawn is excellent in that regard as well. It allows and even encourages a more tactical style of gameplay than PoE; I have yet to encounter any real one-shot mechanics, though the boss fights are interesting and difficult; and the story told as you play, plus all the lore you can find if you look for it (which also gives xp! yay!), are well-designed, interesting, and well-written. I can't think of any real complaint I have with the game, other than perhaps the inability to abandon an optional Bounty quest after you accept it--until you complete it, you're stuck with it--but that's really such a minor issue I wouldn't mention it normally. At the moment, it's literally the only negative thing I can think of in the entire game. That, I suppose, explains the quality of the game better than any review.

Britain is struck with a zombie plague, and you must lead a ragtag gang of survivors in a search for supplies and your own missing daughter. Why are zombies rising up in Bournemouth? Does it matter?
If you're looking for a first person shooter, this isn't it. This is resource management - maintaining and upgrading your camp, searching for supplies and looking for clues. It can still be quite tense! You may struggle a little with combat at first, and lockpicking takes a while to get the hang of, but persevere and you'll soon be hooked. It's hard to leave your camp when you still need to stock up on supplies and you're only a few materials shy of that next fence upgrade.
Combat is done in an unusual style - rather than simply rolling dice, you have a sort of fruit machine. Spin the wheels and try to score more than your opponent. Score a skull, and you've automatically been hit. But there's a twist - get three skulls and, unless your opponent somehow does the same, you've automatically won.
If you don't have the time for combat, you can simply hit the Auto button to resolve combat instantly. And if you never want to do that again, there's always "Visual Novel" mode, in which you focus on the resources and the plot and skip all those pesky puzzles. But why would you do that?
DBA is an unusual and entertaining take on the much-visited zombie apocalypse genre, and a more realistic view of the collapse of civilisation than many. Now I'd best get back to it - the camp's low on food and we've heard rumours of a stockpile nearby.

The subject might lead people to believe that I will be too easy or maybe too harsh, I will try to be as fair as I can in my assessment.
A couple of disclaimers before I begin:
1) I am not a fan of Zombie games, movies or anything else. I think the genre is overused and played out at this point.
2) I have liked or loved every Winter Wolves game I have purchased(Loren & DLC, SOTW & DLC, Roommates, Planet Stronghold and Spirited Heart Deluxe)
3) I know it says I have little to no time playing the game, but I bought the game through Winter Wolves website and then only got my steam key recently when the game was released here on steam.
Okay, now on to the critique. I have 2 complete playthroughs of Dead But Alive and feel I have pretty much reached conclusions about how I feel about the game. I am going to lay out a list of the pros and cons as I see them.
PROS:
*The atmosphere is pretty solid and true to itself. The game is a zombie survival game, and it makes constant reference to this throughout.
*The game makes you make apparently(I will get to this more in detail later) tough decisions right from the start.
*The writing is true to the game's atmosphere and does a solid job of conveying character development
*The game is largely glitch free and is pretty clean in the writing with few typos or grammatical errors.(This is a big one for me)
*Having 3 ways to complete the final quest was a nice touch
CONS:
*While the writing is solid and conveys character, I find it lacking. It feels unnatural, largely because people don't say just one sentence at a time.
*This leads to the second con, which is that with no text speed adjustment, I occasionally missed things that were said and just had to guess. I think this also created the issue with why the first con happened.(This and the first con were big ones for me)
*The combat system was just clunky and unwieldy as far as I was concerned and it didn't take long for me to just turn it off
*The rewards for the red, green, and yellow zones along with the resistance seemed contradictory to what the game states and to what seemed logical
*The romances appeared so late in the game that I completely missed them the first time around due to finishing the last big quest before any of them had the chance to start, only realized after choosing a different approach to that final quest in the second run through.
EDIT: I APPARENTLY MISSED AN OPTION IN THE OPTIONS MENU THAT MAKES THE TEXT CLICK TO ADVANCE. DOH!
Conclusions: I think the game is okay, but a few things really bugged me, while the writing was solid in content and emotion, is was sorely lacking in the delivery. I think this was heavily impacted by the way the dialog was delivered. No ability to change the speed of the dialog and the fact that it just advanced automatically was a big thumbs down for me and probably(I am guessing) led to all the one line dialog that is simply not natural. I hope that can be blamed on the game engine. The next big issue for me was the slot machine combat. That just really broke immersion for me, I understand the attempt to create drama, but there just has to be a better way than that. Also, not having any of the romance initiating dialogs occurring until such a late point in the story was a bit off putting. Also being able to follow up with some of the characters on their personal quest would have made each character more memorable, you know like the personal quests from Loren. I don't want people to think I hate the game, just these things really kept me from liking or even loving a game that I would not have played normally. I tried out a genre I don't generally like because of Jack and his track record of delivering great VN games, and were it not for these issues I would be here gushing about a genre that in general I don't like.
A few other smaller issues, that I had were things like my base camp was never attacked by zombies on my first playthrough and only after starting final preparations for the final quest on my second playthrough. This could have increased that dread feeling. Another small issue, probably a bigger issue for others, is that no matter what decision you make in certain situations, the only thing it seems to impact is how you are viewed by certain other NPCs. I have kind of gotten used to this in games, but it would nice for a game to really have a truly branching storyline sometime.
There you have it.
TL;DR I think it is an okay that could have been so much better with just a few changes.

This is by far the BEST RTS experience I have ever played in my 20 years of gaming.  Do not trust the meta scores on metacritic because it was a bunch of negative reviews due to Russian controversy. But as far as gameplay, you will NOT find a better RTS game. Not even close.

CoH 2 is yet another wonderful strategy game that features in-depth variants of strategic gameplay using a wide variety of infantry, armor, and other means of destroying your opponent.  The gameplay is similar to the first game, but has an added feature of weather effects.  Rain and snow can drastically change the 'climate' of the battlefield.  The joy of this game is that it features an alternate front of WW2.  Russians versus Germans.  The sadness of this game is how certain strategies work SO much better than others.
In the original game, the sides were relatively balanced.  People try to argue this point all the time, but the generals (special abilty trees) you can select made the game decently even-footed between Germans and Americans.  Every unit had a purpose.  In CoH2, however, it feels like there are certain units that just aren't worth building...at all.  Only a handful of the strategies (generals) available seem effective.  However, there are other elements to the game that give it more depth.  Minor upgrades to particular TYPES of units (i.e. 3% faster reload on MGs) and things like that allow for customizability of your army's loudout.
The new setting and new units are all quite fun, though, and clogging German guns with Russian bodies never gets old.
I'll give the game 7/10 because despite the setbacks of minor imbalances, the game has a lot going on for it.  It's still ridiculously fun.  I'll always prefer the western front to the eastern one, but this is a solid game with an amazing campaign and wonderful multiplayer.

You can look around the review pages for this game and see a sea of "recommend" posts, thats for good reason, and I will get to that. First however, I would like to try and define what NEO Scavenger is, though that may be difficult.
NEO Scav is a survival game in its simplest form but the title of "Survival" doesn't do it justice. I would like to define it as a "Turn based RPG", but that too doesn't quite fit the bill. "Sandbox"? no, not that either . Now I'm not saying that all of these traits and aspects are not included in NEO Scav, but each one does not define it well alone. The only thing I can think to do is paste all of them together (using medium string and a sharp edge) making it a Sandbox Survival Turn Based Role Playing Game (a SSTBRPG), now all we have to do is throw a H in front of that acronym for "Hardcore" and its shaping up to be a decent genre description, a bit of a mouthful though.
Not that (H)SSTBRPG's really exist (that I know of aside from a few indie titles scattered about the web) as a gaming norm, just kind of an acronym I made up on the spot, but the idea isn't a norm. Why is that? The only answer I could think of was that it is too much of a risk for large companies to make a game like that, one that would truly test a person's ability to survive in the wilderness  and deal with day to day threats like hunger, thirst, sleep, and warmth. I don't know if that's true or not, and looking at the amount of people who play games like NEO Scav, I can't see how that theory could hold together.
I'm getting off track.
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
NEO Scavenger is created (to my knowledge) by one person, Daniel Fedor. That alone when looking at the game is an amazing feat, especially considering how in depth NEO Scav truly is. Whether its crafting or just scavenging there is plenty of things for you to make or find.
The first day is the hardest, you wake up in an odd place with something scratching at the door (I won't go into detail as, well... Spoilers) , but you immediately have to escape. Using skills to selected at the start, a set of four with the ability to add more at the cost of negative traits, you venture out into the world.
You walk out into the sunlight of the world, its dawn,  its cold, and you don't have much in the way of clothing save a hospital gown. Immediately you're struck with a problem, find clothing or die of hypothermia. This is what kills most new survivors, and it took me a while (and a few protagonist deaths) to find my rhythm. This first day is brutal, but once it's over, a whole new day begins.

Now you're warm-ish, but the previous days exertions have caused you to grow quite thirsty. You see that there's a water source nearby, a river, but you don't know if the water is safe to drink. You have no method of checking if its "infected" or if its "sterile" but  you don't have the luxury of waiting. This is something that kills off a lot of the players that make it past day one. Let's say you were lucky, and now you're no longer thirsty, and you didn't manage to acquire some form of disease or infection, now what.
By this time you're starting to feel a little hungry, while scavenging you manage to find a couple of mushrooms and some berries, but without the proper skill (which you can choose at the start of the game, it's called "Botany") you can't tell if these are poisonous or not.  You pick them up all the same, if it comes to it, you might have to take the chance.
But whats that on the horizon, it looks like another scavenger is none too pleased with you stealing his supplies (or for any myriad of other reasons), and now he wants you dead. You can't escape, you have to fight. You pick up a large nearby stick and prepare to defend yourself.
The fight is frantic, messy, and results in both parties getting pretty bruised up, but eventually the other scavenger retreats from battle, leaving you to treat your wounds...
The point is that NEO Scavenger is relentless in its urge to kill you, but it's not like you can't combat this. You can cover you're tracks so that enemies have a harder time following you, you can hide in urban areas and ambush scavengers to steal their stuff, you can apply bandages to your wounds and take pain pills to deal with blood loss and manage the amount of pain your character is in. All the while traveling for some far off goal.
And there is SO much more, and even more to be added I'm sure.
-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------
In short try the demo, it's a pretty accurate but  slimmed down version of how the game plays out, if you like it, buy it... you can't go wrong. The creator is pretty active in the forums, discussing current game bugs and ideas with the community, both here on steam, as well as on his site at Blue Bottle Games.
Take care, good luck surviving, and hopefully this was helpful.

NEO Scavenger has to be one of my all time favorite games. Even when it was back in early access. The first time I tried it out, I played for six hours straight. That's a long time for me. I was just so in love with it.
There is a storyline to follow, but you don't have to watch the story unfold with each playthrough, because NEO Scavenger doesn't hold your hand...at all. Whether you want to find more information about your life and what has happened to the world is up to you. Personally, I just like to see how long I can survive in this messed up wasteland.
This game does have a steep learning curve, but once you figure things out, you'll be set to survive for weeks. And while some say the graphics are too unbearable to live with, I don't mind them. I think they are part of the charm that sucked me into the game in the first place.
To be sure that this game is for you, check out the demo before you spend your fifteen bucks. That's what it's there for, right?

First and foremost, do not take my above playtime as my experience, I've bought it on Desura and the Website, and I wanted a third save and to give an additional amount of money to the devs. (Why can't I just give you money?!) Anyhow, this is Neo Scavenger in a nutshell:

Cold. How long has it been since I've been warm. A day? Ten? I don't know any more, time seems so eternal out here, and I've lost track of it. I don't know anything but pain, fear, and cold these days... and hunger. I tried building a campfire a while back, and that damned Bandit left me bleeding and scarred. I went looking for some medical equipment later that night, an an apartment collapsed on me. I'm weak and tired, but I'm too afraid to sleep... But I can afford to close my eyes a bit, right?...
"Give up all your f***ing gear if you want to live!" Before I'm even fully aware, I'm staring into the muzzle of a revolver. I panic and begin to scream, and he whacks me across the face with the revolver's butt.
"What? You f***ing deaf? Hand it all over!" I'm not deaf, but I'm not stupid either. If I hand over all this gear, I might live a while longer, but I'd still die. Slower and even more painfully than if he shot me. Besides, he might even be bluffing? Before he knows what's happening, I slam a heavy punch into his chest, knocking the wind out of his lungs and freezing him for a moment. Not one to waste, I use that moment. I grab a heavy-looking stone on the ground and begin to pummel him. In the dark, I see nothing but a vague grey shape. I slam the stone into his stomach, and he screams in pain. I pummel him even further, and further... Long after he dies, I'm still hitting him with the stone. My arms are aching and my head is pulsing, but I keep hitting the battered corpse. Finally, I relent. More out of exhaustion and pain rather than any sense of logic.
Then, I sleep. Fitfully and weakly at first, but soon enough, my fatigue catches up to me, and I rest. When I wake up, the full realization of what I'd done caught up to me. The "bandit" was a starving emaciated skeletal husk, and his revolver was a rusted abomination that was more likely to explode rather than fire. I begin to suck in a hitching, weak breath as I sob. That could have been me, and it probably would be before long...
It's been a while since I killed that man, but the heavy black weight of it hangs heavily on my shoulders. I hate my own existence, and have long considered suicide... If this isn't hell, then what is it? Just as I begin to slip the bottle of sedatives out of my pocket, I see a man approaching me. I haven't seen another sould in so long... and I feel genuine joy and excitement at the prospect of talking to someone... Maybe even make a friend? I begin to rush towards him, hands in the air to signify my friendliness. Before I know what happens, I am knocked aside the head, and looted.
This is Neo Scavenger, and though your adventure may not last as long, or be as miserly, you will experience the highs and lows of survival. You will wonder: "Why? Why did it have to end this way?" And you will face many hard choices.
Do both your practical intellect and your inner masochist a favour, and buy this game. It's well worth it's price.

I heard about this game from a friend and decided to play the demo to see how I felt. About two hours passed and I purchased the actual game, to spend another two or three hours playing the balls off of it.
At first a first look I was unsure about the action events (fights, encounters etc.) seeing as it was primarily text and seemed like it would be a little dull. I was very wrong, while yes the action events are just text along with some other info (character portraits, conditions and so on), it doesn't detract from the intensity at all. If anything imagining what is happening as it's described to you makes the whole fight even more tense.
I think the most appealing thing about this game is how realistic it is. You can (and will) die in so many different ways, it's fantastic! You can be beaten to death, bleed out, get poisoned, mauled, shot, etc. But what I love is how indirect it is. You can go into a forest and eat some berries, a few turns later you get some pop up text informing you that your character is vomiting. What caused that? Was it the berries? The dirty bandage giving you an infection? The water from the lake? Along with hunger, thrist, sleep deprivation, temperature and the horde of melonheads closing in the game becomes very stressful. But in the best possible way.
Besides the many ways to die, the scavenging is top notch. Far better than say Fallout for the sake of argument, where you gather stuff for a while and then you're good till end game. In NEO Scavenger you need to keep scavenging to survive and you will not find guns in every house, or food in every cabin. Chances are you'll die before ever using a gun, but when you have one with the right ammo, you feel worried about using it in case it's wasted. This combined with the crafting and character skills to open up new options, makes each playthrough very different.
The best part is the game isn't even done yet, so new features are being added to make this experience even better. So if you're reading this right now and you're still unsure I really reccommend you at least try the demo. I think this game is fantastic and would really sing it's praises to anyone who's looking for a challenging and realistic survival game.
I'd give it a solid 8/10 so far, would be swarmed by melonheads again.

Easily one of the smartest and well-constructed games I've played, Braid is a puzzle game disguised as a platformer.  And don't be fooled by the demo, as there's a lot more to the game than rewinding to avoid death.  Like Portal, Braid takes just a few concepts (e.g. rewinding time, enemies immune to time manipulation) and hammers out puzzles that make the most out of only a few mechanics.
Do you suck at puzzles and get easily frustrated? No problem!  Braid is designed so that you can skip over tough puzzles and come back to them later. And when you come back and solve a difficult puzzle, the feeling of accomplishment will be great.
And the rewind mechanic is guaranteed to lessen the frustration associated with platforming games.  If you mistime your jump, you simply rewind the game and do it right the next time.  Trust me, instead of making the game too easy, it makes the game more playable.
This game will make you feel smart.  Play it!

If there was an "unsure/maybe" option for a rating, I would give this game that.
Poker Night at the Inventory is unforgiving if you're new to Texas Hold 'Em poker, but can be manipulated if you're patient and lucky enough. A tutorial or guide of sorts in the game itself would help out tremendously, and having a switchable difficulty from the get-go would really help (There's a difficulty setting in the menu technically, but it's set to Normal by default and can't be changed.) Every character has their own play style, and range from daft to impeccible.
-Max is fairly reckless with his bets and doesn't seem t have a grasp on when to fold. He's the easiest to eliminate for this reason,
-Strong Bad knows a good hand when he has one but is so absorbed in himself that he doesn't take the others' behavior into account.
-The Heavy takes into account every action taken by the other players when making his choices. If he goes all-in, you're up♥♥♥♥♥♥creek without a paddle.
-Tycho seems to have 2 modes: Fold at the start, or keep raising the stakes throughout.
Like I said, Poker Night is unforgiving if you're new to Poker. You may get some good, lucky hands when you first start playing but within an hour or so that luck will be gone, and you start getting crappier hands (or possibly, the opponents get better ones.)
There's an exploit to get around this however; If you go All-in at the very beginning of a hand, 9 times out of 10 everyone else will fold and you'll win the pot atuomatically. Do this enough times and with enough luck and you can eliminate everybody without actually playing.
The game also seems to have performance issues, as framerates are relatively unstable (though still within 18FPS at the very least and 30 at most) on a moderately fast system with a 1366x768 screen and the graphics set to preset number 4.
Overall, Poker Night is a fine game, but if you're new to Hold 'Em then you're in for a hell of a ride.

TLDR: Choices are ultimately irrelevant, no dramatic satisfaction at all. Good world-building but poorly excuted narratives.
Though their lore is interesting, House Forrester is a hamfisted Stark knock-off. Most characters are enough of their own person, but their aesthetics and family position are very lazily imitated (Lady Foresster may as well be Catelyn Stark, they're basically the same person).
Of the four storylines, only two (or one and a half, really,) have any dramatic payoff/resolution. Given this game came out three years ago and there's no sign of a second season, this was poor storytelling and forward planning. Of the other two stories, one is simply packed with infuriatingly impotent choices that just serve to put the player through some sort of masochistic fantasy of the greatest hits from the Stark Family Tragedy, and the other is completely and utterly redundant! An entire storyline ends with literally zero impact on the overall plot, let alone any of the other main character's arcs.
Fewer characters in fewer places would have probably been a far more cohesive story. Sure, it's nice to see as much of the world as we see in the show/books, but for the sake of a few (well performed) cameos it's not really worth it at the expense of good plot.
Frankly, I couldn't give a♥♥♥♥♥♥about a second season. TellTale would be better off putting their resources into fresh material rather than trying to tidy up this mess.

My first playthrough I kept getting random strange freezes throughout the first episode. Usually at QTE's. Shortly after I started the second episode the game crashed, and refused to launch. The only way to fix this was to delete my save file.
Second playthrough - still strange random momentary freezing at QTE's. Didn't put me off too much but frustrating at times when I died. This seems to be a trend in some Telltale games, and might well be considered an "era" within their development, as I didn't notice anything like this in The Walking Dead Season 1 or 2, but did in the DLC "Michonne", saw it again in Game of Thrones and then did not experience it in Batman. I have yet to play "The Wolf Among Us", but hopefully it isn't plagued by this.
For a game that prides itself on "Choices Matter", they largely don't. A death couldn't be avoided regardless of how you treat a guest. At one point an NPC steals wine, my decision to not indulge in the wine (as I didn't want to be caught) was rendered pointless as after the conversation briefly ended, my character went to drink the wine anyway, and was caught. Infuriatingly, one of my final (and most important) decisions was absolutely pointless - rendered void because of a choice earlier in the episode with no real rhyme or reason behind it. TellTale Games are pretty well known for this issue but Game of Thrones was particularly egregious for it. On a similar note, one problem I thought was really bad in this game was the answers you pick weren't always the same as what would be said. Not infrequently the response you gave was much more aggressive/cowardly than the option you wanted to give.
I went into the game expecting a game that wasn't truly linear and would change based around my actions and choices. They had no affect whatsoever, and I really can't recommend this "game" which should really be sold as an interactive movie. I stuck with this game because the characters enthused me and I was rooting for the Forresters. Furthermore the game was a serious effort to play through. I tried it on different hardware and still the QTE's were buggy, both sets of hardware were more than enough to play the game.

I've used this program for years now.. (I'm a game developer who work in my own firm) And I simply love it.
I used to use "3Ds Max" (which I used for quite a few years, and is ridiculously expensive), but I switched to Blender because Blender was open-source, which means that I can sell whatever I make in Blender, without worrying about buying expensive licenses from the software developer.
I've also found that Blender is much more stable and less buggy than 3Ds Max, and support Multiple computer monitors, so you can split your views up on different monitors. (Good luck trying to make 3Ds Max do that..)
Bottomline:
Blender is a super useful 3D program that is 100% free, and I see no reason to use any other 3D program (maybe except zBrush) since they usually cost a lot of money, but does pritty much the exact same thing..
Keep in mind:
Every 3D program has a learning curve, and Blender is no exception. Starting out in Blender can be a frustrating experience, but is worth learning. So, if you are a newcomer, I recommend going to YouTube and watching beginner tutorials. Good luck!

X-COM: UFO Defense was a terrifying and terrific game that was well overdue for a modern update, and what better developer than Firaxis to take up the charge?
XCOM: Enemy Unknown (and Enemy Within) offers a modern take on a great theme: aliens have arrived and they're taking over the Earth. They're going to succeed, unless you, the player, stops them. The player takes over the role of The Commander of XCOM, a last-ditch international cooperative force of the best of the best of humanity's soldiers, scientists, engineers, and pilots. Your squads of soldiers will be deployed on missions to recover alien technology, defeat alien terror attacks, and uncover the mystery of the invasion in hopes of ultimately thwarting it. This side of the game occurs on a turn-based tactical combat layer that will be familiar to those of you who've played the original, or even games like Final Fantasy Tactics and the like. For a good chunk of the game, the aliens have better guns than you and are often statistically superior, so your soldiers must make good use of cover and positioning to overcome that challenge.
The rest of the game (research technology, training soldiers, building equipment/facilities, managing aircraft) occurs on a base management strategy layer. It's a fairly light take as far as management games go, but it gets the job done, and there are multiple ways to go about things. You need to deploy your squads, aircraft, and launch satellites in such a way as to minimize global panic and keep your benefactors (countries) on your side
One of the best parts about XCOM is that it mirrored facets of the original well: the game can be deadly. You can lose your campaign, and then boom, game over, the aliens won. A tactical battle can quickly go awry, resulting in you losing your top squad of soldiers and forcing you to field newbies once more. This terror is best exemplified in the game's Ironman Mode, which only allows a single autosave file, and the game autosaves with every single turn. Lose the campaign, and your save is deleted. Combine that with one of the harder difficulties (Classic or Impossible), and difficulty junkies will surely get their fill.
All in all one of the best strategy games to come out in the past decade. The expansion (Enemy Within) and other DLC (Slingshot) add more missions and options to the game in a great way. A must buy for tactical/strategy lovers and a great "first strategy" game for newcomers, though they may want to start on Easy or Normal.

First - try the demo. The game style is somewhat of a niche, so it may not be for you. After that... well if you're still reading, perhaps a review is in order.
Perhaps the best way to explain why NEO is worth a shot is the fact that I've introduced three players to it, with each having exactly the same responses (almost stages of grief style). First is the inevitable freezing to death ("What? What did I do wrong? This game is stupid!"). Next is figuring out how to survive that part ("Ah, I can use that sleeping bag until I find clothes, or possibly light a fire"), normally followed by having your head bashed in by someone ("What? What did I do wrong? This game is stupid!").
Next run through you figure out how to make weapons ("Now I can go take on those damn bandits!"). And, after killing a couple, you WILL get cocky and drown on your own blood ("What? What did I do wrong? This game is stupid!").
By about the fourth serious run (normally with a half-dozen freezing to deaths in there) you're surviving, and doing it well. You start analysing the risks of combat (he has a machete, I have a bow... how close do I let him get?). From there your deaths are almost always due to errors on your part - surviving can be time consuming but is generally not hard, unless you want to deliberately handicap yourself by not taking the easy way (no trapping skills, no botany skills) for a difficulty boost - and all three players were hooked. At each stage you could see them figuring out what to do next, how to avoid the mistake they made last time.
Despite what some reviews have said you do not need to find the recipe papers to make anything - they tell you how to, but if you put the ingredients in the crafting screen it will let you know what you can make. Generally it's pretty intuitive too - large stick plus knife equals sharpened stick, for example, but you soon learn the crucial recipes by heart.
Yes, it's unpolished. Yes, it's flash. Yes, the story and interface leave a lot to be desired. But it's still well worth the time.

I have to admit I was very skeptical of this game at first but now after buying it on sale and giving it a chance I have to say that this is by far my favorite Far Cry game so far. After loving FC3 and Blood Dragon I was very much looking forward to FC4 but after playing FC4 for a while it really bored the hell out of me and everything felt the same as FC3 but in a different location so I thought I was burnt out on this series, that was untill I played Primal.
Playing Far Cry Primal is a much different experience to 3, BD and 4 mainly because of their being no firearms or cars or any other modern human invention since this is set in 10,000 BCE and I have to say it is a very welcome one. The bow and spear is very fun to use, the club is just a standard mele weapon and isn't anything special but overall I enjoyed the combat in this game very much.
The missions were fun in my opinion, they were captivating enough to keep me interested throughout the game.
The side missions are very abundant and I still haven't done them all yet but plan to.
I also love playing Takkar the Beast Master, riding a sabertooth tiger into battle is so much more fun than driving cars in the previous entries. The hunting in this game is so much more fun than in the previous two games also because you are playing as what is essentialy a glorified Caveman it feels right that you should be naturally good at hunting since that is what they had to do to survive. There are plenty of upgrades for your gear that will have you hunting all different types of animals. There are also the special hunting missions which have you track Boss animals and fight them and afterwards you can tame them and even ride them.
The world map is very similar to FC4 but I don't see a problem with this at all because the landscape and setting is so much different that it was never at any point noticable but even if it was so what? I love going back in time and adventuring in an area thousands of years before, its great fun honestly.
On the technical side of this this game ran at a very smooth 65 + FPS on very high settings and I only noticed it drop below that when using the owl.
Overall I would reccomend this game to anyone who is a fan of this series or is new to it, this game offers so much and I wish I gave it a chance earlier but better late than never! Don't pass this game up, it's a gem.

Grim Dawn has all the similar and expected aspects of its genre. Loot farming, boss battles, character customization, and tons of baddie stomping. All packaged in a grim, dark, and fantasy setting. While everything is done well, nothing really stands out either. It looks like Diablo 2, has the story of Torchlight, and mechanics of Titans Quest. It feels very much like every other ARPG of note that has come out in the last 10 years. Not that this is nessicarily a bad thing, many fans of these previous games will be delighted to have a new, updated, and familiar continuation of the things they love. However, this also means that those looking for something new and refreshing to push the genre forward will be dissapointed.
Really, I am not sure what else to say. The game is good and well done and has everything that is expected of this type of game. Well put together art and setting, decent challenge, a lot of character customization, and with few techinical issues. I have enjoyed it for what it is, but ultimately I also feel a bit of dissapointment or perhaps futility. I have done all this before, multiple times with just different art assets. I think the games biggest short coming is the engine itself. Grim Dawn uses an older game engine originally designed for Titans Quest, and as such many of the same mechnics and shortfalls of an old game engine are very apparent. As a small indie dev it is understandable why this route was taken but I think the game has much more potential it could have lived up to if given the proper tools from the start.
So for those that really enjoy this style of game and are looking for a new challenge, this is a very good choice and a good game to buy. It does take a slower more methodical, and technical appoach to other games and some experience with ARPGs will definitely help with the learning curve. Those brand new to the genre may find this a bit overwhelming at first but it is certainly something anyone can become knowledgable in given a little dedication. For those looking for a more casual and faster approach may want to skip this one for some the other entries of the genre. Also for those looking for multi-player, I would say beware. I do not have experience personally with Grim Dawns multiplayer but I have heard it can be a bit finicky compared to others as well.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a roguelike space-sim. Despite it's rather lackluster appearance, (text boxes, no voices, action is borderline turn based) I can't recommend FTL enough. If gameplay were a person, it would be an elegant british person, sitting in a fine chair drinking whiskey from a glass next to a fireplace with a hound curled up at his feet.
It's clean and elegant.
And expect to get roflstomped.
FTL, being a roguelike, is harder than hell. Given the way that the RNGod can occasionally ruin you, it wouldn't be unfair to say that when you start out, your advancement is partially just statistical chance that *eventually* you have to get a little further.
Massive variance between ships, crews, strategies, weapons, and events ensures that each consecutive run, even with identical starting conditions, will be different.
If I had to put a downside to FTL, it's the game length. When you start, a run can be measured in hours (if you don't have what napalm does to my rose garden done to  your ship), and it can be very frustrating to have a long run go to hell. In a way, this means it punishes you as you improve, because your investment before failure increases. (And yes, failure is a forgone conclusion).
Still, the pros outweigh the cons. You'll easily get your money's entertainment out of this one.
