Personally, my favourite Telltale GAME. The best narrative being awarded to the first The Walking Dead season.
The game follows multiple characters which can at first seem annoying and badly paced. After the first episode you'll get used to it though and if you like Game of Thrones' formula, then this will serve you better than you might imagine.
After episode 1, all stories leave you with some sort of cliffhanger before going to the next character.
The stories are really interconnected only through name and relationships. Some stories have little or no connection with the main narrative, which undoubtedly is the Ironrath's story. The seemingly most interesting stories (like the "squire" and "lord") mostly turn out to be pretty weak and relatively empty. The handmaiden's story stays comfortably in the middle with it doing almost nothing out of the ordinary or interesting.
I read the reviews. The most popular ones describe the game as "unnecessarily cruel" or just plain "unfair". To those people I have to say... You do realize what you're playing, right? This isn't your happy-go-lucky Tales From The Borderlands or just some comedy thing. It's Game of Thrones. The show is one of the cruelest shows out there. Some people felt like they were out of control at some key moments, to which I say that that is the point. You don't play the extremely influential people. Just because you have choices, doesn't mean that anything's possible. Some people expect that when you're talking to a mad person that's in power (most of the powerful figures in S03-S04), that they'll just accept what you say and lend you a hand. Support you or even admire you.
As an example, minor spoilers for S01 of TWD. If you thought as the character, then it was an extremely tense narrative with you not feeling safe at all. But if you thought as the player, then you were able to calculate the real risk. You knew who would die, who would always live. Where you'd be safe and where you wouldn't be.
In GoT, this isn't the case. I tried to analyze everything. Predict what would be thrown at me and what was an actual threat and what was theatre. In here, I never knew. I genuinely started thinking like the characters. What to do to ensure my safety and the safety of others. To prevent as much damage as possible. No one was ever safe. You knew only your goals while being oblivious of your actual end destination.
That's what a Telltale game is supposed to do. Make you worry, make you care for others because them leaving/dying or doing whatever could seriously hurt you.
I do have real complaints now though. The conversation timer is too short. Telltale's trying to make conversations real and fluid, but they fail to realize that they're not. You have certain choices and you have to choose from them. In real life I'd know what I'd say, but sometimes you either lack the options you want or they're just written in a way that you might not understand properly.
I'm officially a C1 level English speaker while most likely becoming a C2 (on the level of a native speaker) in the near future. Around 30% of the time, I wasn't able to really properly read the options and because of that either chose wrong or had to "cheat". The cheat being just pressing spacebar to initiate a "soft-pause". You see the options but the time doesn't move. That's not how it should be. You should have enough time to read what you'd say while also feeling the pressure of time. In the last episodes, I lost that worry because I started depending on the soft-pause to help me.
This is, from what I remember, the first Telltale game to be 6 episodes long. Each episode is around 100-130 minutes in length, which makes this a very beefy experience. I wholeheartedly support that. People tend to hate filler because of the overuse of it, but TWD: Michonne showed us all how having too little filler makes the game mean almost nothing. This way, the game was able to flesh out characters and make you care for them. It gave you time to think about your situation too, making you care more and decide accordingly.
The graphics are a small part, but they're pretty weak and it's starting to finally show. For the performance and system requirements, the game itself looks like a prettied up 90s 3D game. Empty environments and flat textures. The animations are also laughably choppy. Characters can't even turn themselves while walking. Instead having to stop and then turn. Also, camera angles are like from a bad student film. Camera cuts to a person with around 2 seconds of just nothing moving and then the character either starting to talk or move. It happens too often and it just shows where Telltale's priorities seem to be.
TL;DR
This game is on the higher end of the Telltale games. Good characters, good story and a type of storytelling that makes everything unpredictable. If you don't like something that can be unfair, then you're obviously not a GoT viewer anyways and in that case this game isn't for you.
The game's very good, but the short decision times and the sometimes disappointing sub-plots might persuade you enough to not get it.
Overall
8/10
For what it does, it does it extremely well while adding enough to keep the Telltale formula fresh.

Telltale's Game of Thrones Season One takes place in the show's continuity, starting near the ending of three, and carrying through season four. However, the show (and books, for that matter) do not take the game into account when going forward in their plot. This makes sense as the game was written neither by George R. R. Martin, author of the book series, or any of the writers for the show.
The main cast of the game is House Forrester, bannermen to House Stark who specialize in the producing and selling of special, hardened wood made from the ironwood trees in their local area of Ironrath.
If you haven't watched up through season three of the HBO show, then you will probably be confused in the first episode of the game. While it is not a necessity to watch the show to enjoy the game (although people may say it is), the plot doesn't go out of it's way to explain what is going on, and relies on the player having some existing knowledge. The game ends during what would be late season four of the show, and as before, while it isn't necessary to have watched it, there are very heavy spoilers for that season.
Episode One introduces the player to three playable characters. Gared, who is squire to Lord Forrester, Ethan, who is third son of Lord Forrester, and Mira, first daughter of Lord Forrester and handmaiden to Margaery Tyrell in King's Landing. Gared is the player's eyes to the outside world, Ethan gives us insight to what is directly happening with the other Forresters in Ironrath, and Mira is the window to King's Landing, capital ot the Seven Kingdoms. These aren't the only playable characters, as more get added in the next episode.
As any Game of Thrones fan knows, this franchise can be brutal. Viewers and readers alike will
be dissapointed from this angle. Lies, murder, intense fight scenes and more are all seen in plentitude. Taking after it's origins, the narration style flits back and forth between the point of view characters, giving almost equal screentime to each storyline. While this story element succeeded at showing the different events in the world, the cut times were somewhat questionable at points, making an intense atmosphere drop into a happy or calm one and then back. While some may see this as good, it also makes the player
invested emotionally with what is going on.
Anyone going into a Telltale game can expect tons of differing choices to be made, which have various outcomes on the story. While some say that Telltale as a company is not very good in this field due to the lack of outcomes available, I tend to see it as an interactive book. The overall story is going to stay mostly the same, beginning to end, but small things might change depending on playstyle. However, even I was a little disheartened by the little effect my decisions had throughout the season. Some characters had more impact than others, namely Ethan's line, while characters like Mira seemed very straight forward. Some chalk it up to lazy writing, while others say that it's because the game outcomes would be
different if they branched off that much. While I agree more on the latter side, it was frustrating to try your hardest every chapter to make an impact and still end up in the same place.
As a fan of both
and
, I adored this games story. From the multitude of characters introduced, to the risks and choices taken by the playable characters, I couldn't put the game down for long periods of time. While frustrated with the lack of outcomes for my decisions, I was able to enjoy the game as a piece of lore to the existing franchise, and I am excited to see what the writers and developers will do for season two.

I'm going to be clear from the beginning. This game is a mess. It really is such a shame since it had huge potential. A proper game set in the ASOIAF universe and even with some of the actors from the show could have been a fantastic gaming experience.
Cons:
- The art style. I will not lie that in this game there are a few moments of stunning beauty (like the north grove) but the rest of the game just looks like unfinshed concept art that has been poorly animated.
- Character interactions. These are weird in places. Sometimes I would click an option, trying my best to be nice to another character but they would take it as an insult and there are some severe consequences because of this mistake.
- Time limits. You are often rushed to make major decision you later regret because you didn't have the time to think it through.
- Controls when you are fighting or moving your character around. These controls felt very overly sensitive and difficult to control and they are almost always accompanied by a poor camera angle that makes it hard to see what you are doing.
- Your choices seem to have relatively little effect. For example the handmaiden section felt completely useless and accomplished nothing for me. A great deal of the choices cause the last episode to end in the same way which I won't spoil for those who haven't played.
- Its predictable in places. This may just be because of the choices I made but in many cases I felt that I could tell what the next part of the story would be and what the big 'twists' were.
Pros
- The story is good. Even if it is predictable there are still parts where I couldn't stop playing as I was eager to discover what was next.
- Its Game of Thrones. Anyone who's read the books or seen the show wants to be in the G.O.T universe and this is your opportunity

Imagine the original Fallout set in Michigan, with text based combat that goes into far more detail- well, nearly every aspect of this game involves detail, detail, DETAIL! I died so many times in the beginning because I failed to realize you actually have to boil water, lest you will sooner or later drink something nasty and slowly die (that is, if a raider, bandit, or mutant does not take advantage of your weakened state first). Events utilize traits choen at the beginning to provide you options based on your skill sets, such as using medical knowledge to release a cryogenic tube's inhabitant as bait, so you can make a clean escape from a mutant freak. Pressing survival issues also include sleep, hunger, hypothermia, health status (pain, poison, infection, bleeding, all of which can be combatted with aid such as banadages and antibiotics.... or even scotch as a painkiller!). It really is too bad though that you can only wear boots, but cosmetics aren't much of an issue when the average character lifespan in the beginning is less than 3 days.

NEO Scavenger is a fun little indie title by Blue Bottle Games, if your vision of fun is watching your character slowly dehydrate to death after you develop diarrhea from a diet composed of berries and swamp water. Despite being incredibly unforgiving the permadeath mechanic makes it an excellent game to play in short bursts, and death itself is not that much of a frustration.
In its early access state it has a great crafting system and survival mechanics that can only get better, but it suffers from a combat system that needs a lot of work and a big lack of NPC interactions.
If you enjoy the survival genre or even turn-based games this little gem is a nice title.

FTL: Faster Than Light is a roguelike space-sim. Despite it's rather lackluster appearance, (text boxes, no voices, action is borderline turn based) I can't recommend FTL enough. If gameplay were a person, it would be an elegant british person, sitting in a fine chair drinking whiskey from a glass next to a fireplace with a hound curled up at his feet.
It's clean and elegant.
And expect to get roflstomped.
FTL, being a roguelike, is harder than hell. Given the way that the RNGod can occasionally ruin you, it wouldn't be unfair to say that when you start out, your advancement is partially just statistical chance that *eventually* you have to get a little further.
Massive variance between ships, crews, strategies, weapons, and events ensures that each consecutive run, even with identical starting conditions, will be different.
If I had to put a downside to FTL, it's the game length. When you start, a run can be measured in hours (if you don't have what napalm does to my rose garden done to  your ship), and it can be very frustrating to have a long run go to hell. In a way, this means it punishes you as you improve, because your investment before failure increases. (And yes, failure is a forgone conclusion).
Still, the pros outweigh the cons. You'll easily get your money's entertainment out of this one.

If you are a die hard GOT fan and need your fix, get the "game", just wait for it to be on SALE first. Telltale are supposed to be making "choose your own adventure games"... but this "game" is prime example of 'you know nothing John Snow'. None of your choices matter, nor does it effect the story at all, you will always get the worst outcome and most of the time even if you think carefully about your characters responses, the game makes you say something completely different. To call this a "game" is kind of insulting, its like handing a controller to a kid while watching a cartoon and making them think they are controlling what happens on screen. Honestly the story is decent as is the voice acting, but Telltale would be better off just making an animated series than these "games". One thing that I notice in Telltale "games" is NPCs you talk to can have moments where it will say "such and such will remember that" as a reaction to your chocies.... but not ONCE have I seen this come back into play later on. It is not a game if your choices have no consequences and your actions have not effect on the story. So again, if you like GOT and want a decent stoy, buy this on SALE, its not worth $30. Enjoy it as a cartoon and dont expect much else. I miss an age where choose your own adventure was just that, where your choices mattered. Old Sierra games like Monkey Island and Police Quest from 25+ years ago had better interactive stories and puzzles. Telltale NEED to do better and stop with this holding your hand stuff, make it a challenge and worthy of being called a game.

The first Telltale game I played was "The Wolf Among Us" and it was an intense, fresh take on a series I knew nothing about. It felt ike choices mattered, especially at the end, and what you had was an interesting story that you felt hopeful you coud win.
These key elements are missing out of Telltale's "Game of Thrones".
First of all it truly feels like nothing you do matters. Right out of the gate, all these choices you make have little to no impact on the general storyline besides changing some dialogue trees. In the end the same plot points happen to the major POV Forresters regardless of whom you picked or where you went. There are certainly some major decisions to make, especially when it comes to who lives or dies, but the little things leading up to these moments don't make any difference, and once again, Telltales over-arching plot matters more than these decisions.
Secondly is the matter of hope. There is absolutely none in this game, and that made it unbearably unfun for me. I've watched the Game of Thrones show, and read all the ASOIAF books, and I know this is a bleak, unforgiving universe where a lot of the major villains are protected by seemingly unpenatrable plot armour. What sets the show and books apart from this game, and what has us coming back, is that there is always a sliver of hope that the ones you root for can pull it off. There is none of that here. Not once does it feel like the Forresters get a leg up, no matter what master plan they institute, they falter, no matter how badass a character, they make bad decisions, and no matter how carefully you work, you will lose. How is this fun? If I wanted a "life sucks" simulator I woud have just gone to work.
While the game is appealing in terms of lore, art design, and stellar casting, it unfortunately becomes an unfun, hopeless, and impactless game, with your decisions making no difference and the plot consistantly beating you down.

This game not only embodies that but hammers you over the skull with it at every single turn. Every victory is met with a bigger defeat, every joyful moment met with greater tragedy. You are not going to win and nothing you do will actually matter in story (as is the norm for Telltale).
I'll keep it short - Poor writing, unclear choices (answers that seemed to convey one thing were preformed in a completely different manner), choices having no bearing on the story whatsoever, myriad plot holes that exist just to ensure that the main characters are always in the worst possible situation, and finally intentionally not wrapping up the story for the expressed purpose of selling a second season.
It's not worth $30 under any circumstances. If you are a die hard GoT fan you should wait for a steep sale before picking it up.

In summary, Double Action: Boogaloo is a creative game comparing to most Source engine games, where the goal of the game is not to get the most kills or secure a checkpoint, but take out your enemy with style. Depending on the method of how you take on your opponent, you get rewarded "Style Points," which determine who is winning. You can do various things to obtain these points, such as completing an objective whether that be delivering a suitcase stuffed with cash or to race through certain checkpoints. These objectives spice up the gameplay and make things very chaotic since eveyone is going to want to get those extra points. You can also obtain points by attacking other players, where you get some points for kills, headshots, being as the game says "tacticool," meleeing, long range, etc. But, the main way to get these points is introduced by a unique parkouring system within the game. You can dive, slide, and backlip while shooting for extra points, and to make movie-like battles. But, this mechanic can take a bit to get used too, it can be exploited to pull off ridiculous stunts, and looks pretty wacky. For example, you can endlessly scale a wall by doing a backflip off of it then diving at it, as each backflip "restores" your dive and each dive "restores" your backflip. This can make designing custom maps a bit tricky. Also, the stunt key is your right-click button. This takes a bit of getting used to, as most games on this engine have right-click as a scope, but it ends up making sense since diving is a key element to the game. That's all remarkable that I have to say about the game, since it definetly will allow you to sink a few hours into the game, but you probably won't be returning for a while. And to end off on a cliche note, I hope this review has helped you decide if you want to download this game, although it is free, so why not?

As a long time Blender user who usually just uses it and doesn't bother to check updates for months at a time, it was a pleasant surprise to see it on Steam. It's difficult to find a completely accessible, full-featured 3D application such as this one for the low price of $0.00, but, if you're a Steam user, look no further!
If you've been browsing the catalog on Steam, looking for an application that will take care of just about everything in regards to asset creation for Workshop projects, hobby animation, or visual assets for an entire game, Blender is one of the best. With far more features available than Maya LT, MODO Indie, or just about anything else, there's pretty much nothing you cannot do in it, plus it beats out the competition in price alone.
In the past, it has received a bad rep due to a messy UI, but that has been cleaned up in recent years, and it is no longer as intimidating to learn. Even if you don't like the way it's set-up, if you take the time to learn the features of the UI, you can customize it to fit just about any workflow that works best for you. Practically the entire interface can be dragged, split, doubled, tripled, minimized, or maximized at a whim.
Few other 3D applications are as all-in-one as Blender. You can go from start to finish on just about any project all within the program, though certain third-party applications can be handy to speed the process and generally help workflow, but to be able to model from a box, to sculpting, to rendering, to rigging, to motion capture for animation, and do damn near anything beyond and in between all within? It's amazing, really.
The only thing you have to lose by giving it a whirl is time. There are dozens of resources for incredibly in-depth tutorials and courses, and thousands more stand-alone tutorials from various places around the internet, so you can really learn the program and use it for absolutely nothing.
You can go from never having modeled to creating completely rigged and animated pieces within weeks, if you set your mind to it, for free. So, why not? Even if you plan to move on to a different program, there's no reason not to get your feet wet with Blender.

Concise Remark: This is a content-laden, exciting romp through a dark, oppressive narrative, a truer successor to Diablo & Diablo 2 than anything come before, and the eternal shame of Diablo 3.
More in-depth, and consequently less flippant, observations:
Grim Dawn is a lot of fun, and after another installment of content, continues to shine as a modern hack-n-slasher. The writing is top-notch, and doesn't shy away from the horrifying circumstances of its setting. Most of the lore can be read leisurely via a game tab, and richly world-builds in the background of the narrative as it unfolds.
Classes are meant to compliment one another, so solo-classing will ultimately leave you at a disadvantage- this is not a real issue, as dual-classing supports pure-melee, pure-magic, and a wide variety of hybrids therein. You will WANT to multiclass. As of the expansion, there are six classes in the base game (Soldier, Demolitionist, Nightblade, Occultist, Arcanist, Shaman), and two extra (Inquisitor, Necromancer) that come with the expansion- which is a must-buy if you're even considering Grim Dawn.
The world map is huge, and all connected. Aside from magical tears in the fabric of space, you will literally fight cross-country across a very, very large world. Deserts, forests, swamps, snowy peaks, ruined cities, and otherworldly elsewheres, crypts and fortresses- all find representation.
There are a ton of factions in game, and the friendly ones all come with quests, some of which are locked depending on your relationship with them (meaning you'll have something to look forward to in late-game). There are many secret areas to discover, optional bosses, enemy heroes (which increase in population if you switch on "veteran" difficulty). Factions have their own stores, separate from the public fare, and have varied tiers of loot relating to your relationship level.
Enemy factions, on the other hand, have ranks in how much they hate you. The more they hate you, the more populated their mobs become, the more numberous their heroes, and ultimately, "nemesis" rank heroes that act as optional bosses- again, something to look forward to in late-game.
There are multiple levels of difficulty, which have to be "Unlocked" ala Diablo. Beginning the game, you have a choice of Normal or Veteran, which cranks up the mob and hero spawns. I recommend Veteran, as Normal will leave you feeling underwhelmed.  Following Normal/Veteran is Elite, and then Ultimate after that. There is also a Hardcore mode, which is immediately available. I have a friend who swears by Grim Dawn's Hardcore mode.
Some downsides to consider: the engine is very old, and sometimes has some performance problems, even in higher-end machines. There's not a lot that can be done at this point, but the Devs are constantly trying to refine what they can. That said, it's my current understanding most people don't have crippling issues. There are some hitches in frame rates, this is because the game is saving your character state, and isn't indicative of any problem (it has caught some players off-guard, but being forewarned, you won't be one of them, will you?). Lastly, the base game ends on a cliffhanger, and since there are no "endgame" cinematics in Grim Dawn, it can be a little jarring. The expansion syncs up with the cliffhanger, however, but also doesn't end with any traditional "endgame" cinematic. This is due to the open nature of Grim Dawn's development- the devs want to keep supporting the game so long as there is a demand for it.
I run Grim Dawn at a fairly consistent state of good performance on High graphics settings, using an ASUS ROG G750jm, for what it's worth.

I jumped in hoping for a new Titan Quest and sure enough I got one! Overall I find it a good game, confined in the hack 'n' slash genre. Below I 'sketched' a few pros and cons based on my finding, based on the things I like or dislike and based on the fact that I haven't finished it yet.
PROs:
- the maps / areas: I like the fact the fact they are larger although the were times when some of them felt waaay to big
- the skill system: very much like it; one of the main reason I liked TQ also
- the devotion system: I liked it; I also like how the whole point gathering works (with all those shrines and the special items you need to offer in order to be rewarded)
- the skills / weapons / spells 'feel' good when used
- liked the books / journal system. Made me hunt for them immediately :)
CONs:
- the maps / areas: way too big sometimes
- the save system: in the first half or so of the game, when you log out you always go back to Devil's Crossing. I liked better the save method in Titan Quest, where you would save and continue your progress from the last Fountain you visited
- the loot / gear variety: once you spent a decent amount of time in the game (maybe around 10h) and progress, you kinda seem to have seen all the possible combinations of sufixes and prefixes and special attributes etc. Please bear in mind that I have not unlocked and/or played at Epic or Legendary diff.
- the story: not that keen on reading something which to me seems like a text having a wierd font, wrong size and at first glance not that interesting. Also, the audio part is not enough.
- the side quests / questing system: same old, same old: go there do that, come back. I just did them for XP
- the reputation system: a good idea but for me it didn't really made a difference: haven't bought any special gear, haven't gained any special traits / quests / experiences off of it.
- the graphics: I am more of a guy who likes to see more bright color, who likes to see some green here and there. To me, GD is having a combination of gray and brown. But hey, that's just me.
Although I realise I've given more CONs than PROs, I still consider it is, somehow, a good game, I still like and will continue to play it. I guess this is because I am a huge nerd when it comes to hack 'n' slash games, TQ and all that related stuff.

Usually, I'm not a big fan of science fiction. Aside form the Star Wars extended Universe, I never cared for it much and found it boring.
And usually I'm not a big fan of strategy games and micromanagement either.
So, I didn't really expect much when this game was on sale for 5 bux and I bought it, thinking "why not"
However, unexpectedly, this game has absolutely blown me away, and I count this now to one of my favorite games of all time.
It's like a crossover of Fire Emblem, Counter Strike and Chess, and while I'm not a big fan of Fire Emblem, I absolutely love both Counter Strike and Chess, alas, I absolutely adore this game.
Just one thing: Just like Fire Emblem, this game can be pretty hard. BUT: depending on your playstyle and the limitations you give yourself (no saving mid-game etc.) this might not matter. I for instance, I play with "save scumming" and on a rather low difficulty, however I still find myself really enjoying it and my mind being challenged in a stimulating way, resulting in a very pleasant gameplay experience for me.
And if I can enjoy a sci-fi turn based strategy game with perma death, despite disliking strategy games and sci-fi and generally being bad at both game genres and micromanagement as well, so can you.

GTA and Just Cause walk into a bar.  They're good friends even though they move in different circles.
However, for some reason tonight is different.  The air is sweeter, the colors richer, the bourbon tastier and the conversation more lively.  GTA's smile comes a little easier and Just Cause's eyes shine a bright blue that belies the insanity that lurks behind them.
Maybe it was fate.  Maybe it was just happenstance.
Regardless...after the quick and awkward sex in the handicapped women's stall of the bathroom, a miracle occured.
A child that tempers both of the parents personaities- more liberally and not as firmly entrenched in "realism" as GTA and not as likely to stick it's face in a mixing bowl of cocaine while already high on acid like Just Cause.
That child is Saint's Row.  Tongue is planted firmly in-cheek for every aspect of the game and if you're a fan of movies, you'll get a TON of references here.  Totally almost lost my♥♥♥♥♥♥during the Aerosmith song in the prologue chapter.  Open world, but with very "relaxed" rules...this is a great buy for $10-15.
Also, Volition made Freespace.  So...y'know...maybe they'll make another one if they sell enough Saints Row.  Hopefully.

A very great city building game.
Tropico 4 is a build on the pervious Tropico 3. You are El Presidente! and it's you're job to over see the island micronation of Tropico. Tropico takes things above and beyond the ordinary city builder however, not only do you need to establish a thriving economy and order the construction of buildings but you'll face other challenges as well. Every single Tropican citizen is known to you, no random little ants just to simulate a living city here! Every Tropican has personal thoughts, personal priorities on what's important in life, faction affiliations, and a family history. There are numerous conditions around the island that effect the residents, like pollution or crime saftey and liberty. Tropicans welfare also becomes part of the flow of resources, jobs are divided up into 3 educational categories and you'll need to make sure you have a steady supply of highschool and college graduates to man the more important jobs on the island.
Unlike other city builders you'll also need to contend for your reign's continuation, several factions on the island have demands on how the island should be run and often they conflict with each other. Foreign powers can also be angered or endeared to help the island or potentionally end your reign themselves! The approval of the common Tropican matters as well, either you'll have to please them enough to win their votes in elections periodically or you'll have to make sure your army is well enough equiped to contend with rebels.
El Preisdente is fairly customizable, there are a handful of costumes and other cosmetics though it's not enough to knock your socks off or anything. The trait system will allow you to describe who El Presidente is by choosing a backstory, a raise to power, and several traits. They all give small bonuses from making certain workers more efficent or giving you a free building to making certain factions more friendly to you or certain foreign powers.
Graphics aren't amazing but they do work pretty well and this game should be pretty friendly to some lower end systems.
Gameplay wise you can choose between a story mode that will take El Presidente through the turmoil of a cold war, a scenario option allowing you to play though little challenges requiring you to complete several objectives just like in story mode, or you can just play sandbox and build your island up until you retire... or are deposed...
Overall I give this game a firm 8/10 and this is a definite buy for anyone interested in a good city builder! If this game is too easy for you than I'd recommend checking out the very first Tropico, and I'd also recommend Tropico 2 if you like pirates...
Tropico 3 is basically the same game so I'd avoid that even for a little cash this game is defintely a worthy upgrade.

Half Life 2 is considered one of the great classics of PC gaming. Sequel to the sublime Half Life 1, it earned renown for its visuals (HDR lighting, facial animation, and water-effects), game-play (especially its use of physics-based gameplay), and story. It is the title upon which Valve built it's Steam empire and is the #1 game for which people demand a sequel. It is a must-play game and all PC Gamers adore it.
Except for me. I think it stinks. Half Life 2 is a terrible game wrapped around some interesting technology.
This isn't just me trying to be controversial; even when it was new I was less than impressed with the game, although my opinion wasn't quite as negative. Nor am I simply judging an older game by modern standards; I still love older titles like Ultima 5, or Doom, or - yes - even the original Half Life despite their lack of modern conveniences or graphic fidelity. I might not want to play them anymore but that doesn't mean I can't appreciate their brilliance. But with Half Life 2, I don't see a clever game; I see a title beloved more for its neat-for-the-time technology and its association with its predecessor.
And Half Life 2's technology was - and still is, to a degree - impressive. While the limitations of the Source Engine are increasingly becoming obvious, it still is a capable platform. HL2 ushered in an age of HDR lighting, high-resolution textures. It's water effects were second to none when it was released. The facial animations - especially the spectacular opening sequence with the G-Man - was a technical tour-de-force, daring comparisons to the sort of CGI earlier seen only in big-screen movies. Its physics engine was remarkable; HL2 wasn't the first to make use of physics, but it was one of the earliest to make it a core part of its gameplay. No longer were physics simulations relegated to ragdolls or other special effects; in HL2, it was an essential part of the game.
But for all that, the game just wasn't very good. It was exceedingly linear for one, on par with later Call of Duty games. There are, on occassion, small side areas where you can go and explore, but by and large the only path available is the obvious one laid out for you by the developers. It relied heavily on gated arenas to set the pace of the gameplay, forbidding progression until each and every monster was killed. For all that its engine allowed fairly expansive (for the time) levels, the maps were divided by very noticable load points, breaking up the gameplay... and this from the same developers who made the original Half Life a virtually seamless adventure from start to finish. Those maps were all far too long too, each set greatly overstaying their welcome. While there was some good variety between "worlds" ("City 17" had you dodging trains, the "Water Hazard" levels had its airboat, "Sandtraps" the ant-lions), the units kept going on far longer than needed. Worse, none of the gimmicks (airboat, sand-lions) were shared in later units; no fighting alongside sandlions while driving an airboat and fighting striders, for instance. Nor did it help that - the developers did little to leverage the technological power of the Source engine; there were no breathtaking visual set-pieces and far too much of the game was  set in grey and beige tunnels. I am convinced that the fan-favorite "Ravenholm" levels wouldn't have gotten half as much praise if they hadn't offered some much needed variety after trudging through two hours of brown swamp-water in "Water Hazard".
Worse was the protagonist himself. Gordon Freeman's infamous silence was acceptable in the original Half Life because the story was so straight-forward: disaster strikes, fight off monsters and soldiers until you get to the end of the maze and kill the big boss. Although rampant with aliens and super-science, the setting itself was still familiar enough as to need no comment, beyond perhaps an exclamation of wonder. This was definitely not the case in Half Life 2, where nothing is explained and Gordon remains curiously, stupidly silent - and so do all of his associates. Everything is just taken for granted and Freeman's silence hurts the story far more than it helps, an issue that Valve obviously noticed in the DLC episodes, since they added Alyx to provide the commentary they stubbornly refused to allow Gordon. His silence was an interesting take in the first game, but feels like a gimmick in this sequel.
Some of these issues were fixed in the DLC episodes - a better and more mixed variety of gameplay, better set-pieces, stronger story-telling by adding more talkative NPCs, larger levels to offset the load-zones - but the original game suffered greatly from these issues. It was too much a tech-demo with none of the cleverness of the first Half Life. It was linear, too gimmicky and generally an uninteresting game. Seperated from its franchise, it almost certainly would have floundered in the market.

is a tower defense game set in space, where you have to defend several space stations from the invading Zotrix aliens.
First of all I must say that the UI itself is somewhat hard to understand at first, especially the level selection menu. The levels of the game are divided into several space stations, each one having 3 different missions, and while I must say that it becomes clear once you play the first three levels, I guess the game could do a better job in showing the different levels and sections. The game does offer you 3 different difficulty settings for each mission, as well as 6 different modes to choose from such as the Classic, Endless and Max Credits. That said, even though I tend to get stuck on a tower defense game when I start to play one, I usually don’t delve into other modes besides the classic one, I do try however to achieve the best star rating on each level though, which in this game might take a while.
Each of the levels gives you a small introductory text that provides some background as to why the Zotrix are invading that station and what is their purpose but that is pretty much as far as the storyline goes. Each of the level is however very different from each other, some just have you keeping the enemy from reaching a certain place while others require you to protect certain structures. The levels also vary a lot in terms of layout, some levels have a single route that the enemies will follow, while others will have several routes or even one route that splits into different routes. Not only that, but you’ll be facing some pretty dramatic changes in terms of where you can place your turrets from one level to the other, which requires you to think through and adapt to different enemy types.
While the tower design isn’t particularly pleasing to the eye, it is however easy to differentiate one tower type from another. Towers come in various different shapes, formats and colors that help distinguish laser towers from missile towers for example. The game offers 15 different towers and while upon reading the description of some of them you might feel like they’re pretty much the same, on the playing field they differ a lot. You’ve got towers that stun and slow enemies, single and dual laser turrets, beam turrets, missile turrets and so on. They might not sound interesting in paper, but in action some of them are pretty cool like the missile towers. There’s this one that fires 4 missiles each second and then there is another that fires one missile every few seconds but it deals a ton of damage.
There is plenty of different ways that you can build up your defenses on any given level since you have so many towers to choose from and, you can also upgrade each of these up to 3 times, increasing their range and strength. You can also change the way turrets behave, like targeting certain targets such as, the closest, the first, the strongest or the weakest enemy within their range. One thing that I believe is unique to Solar Division, when compared to other Tower Defense games, is the fact that you can build drone towers and set routes for them to patrol. If an enemy gets within the range of these drones they will be shot. While they can’t be upgraded, this was by far my favourite defensive mechanism to use, especially when several enemy routes meet in a line on a level and you can just have drones flying through and attacking them at all times.
While there are plenty of other great tower defense games on Steam, I’d say that Solar Division is worth checking out, especially if you’re a fan of TD games. The game might not look or sound particularly amazing but it has some nice little features such as the drones, which I’ve mentioned above, and offers a
that force you to change your defensive tactics. Overall it is a pretty
that could perhaps use some UI polishing and some more interesting plot.

Solar Division is a tower defense game in space. Your goal is to build a variety of towers to combat an alien menace. Does this sound generic? Well yeah, it kind of is, but if you're a sucker for addictive and strategic tower defense games, Solar Division may be right up your alley!
So, clearly this game isn't trying to be anything incredibly special, though nor does it need to be in my opinion. The tower defense genre is inherently a simple one (place a bunch of towers, wait, place more towers, wait, rinse & repeat), so innovation is a bit tough to accomplish. Usually, I like when games try something new, and even though Solar Division doesn't really do this, I think it still is a well-made game that may or may not deserve playing if you're into tower defense games or not. If you are, Solar Division is not a bad option by any means.
The gameplay is what you'd expect: place towers to shoot down wave after wave of aliens, collect money, and then upgrade old towers or buy new ones to stop the bigger and badder enemies. This continues until the waves are all complete. From there, you can play the next level, or repeat the same level with a variety of options - 3 difficulties and a few different types of modes. The game consists of 30 levels, some of which have some interesting objectives in them. Most levels are typical for the tower defense genre (if enemies reach the end of the map you lose a life, which you have a set amount of), but some involve the player defending a ship or surviving for a set time limit. I like these conceptually, but the time limit one was a bit silly because the timer started before I had even hit the key to launch an enemy wave, so all I had to do was sit there and wait for a few minutes. It's not a huge deal, but just a small noticeable gripe.
In terms of the towers themselves, there's 15 in total, most of which are fairly unique. Some are quick lasers, some shoot powerful lasers that need to reload, others fire rockets, one tower slows down enemies, and a few of them provide bonuses to other towers like increased money from killing enemies or added damage. There's even a drone tower that launches drones from a line that moves across the map. So in terms of tower variety, I think this game does pretty well. The enemies aren't super varied, but they certainly differ in size, armor, speed, and appearance.
Something unique that this game does is that it has a checkpoint system. Every few levels, a checkpoint will be saved so that if you happen to mess up horribly, you can simply just press backspace and go back a a bit instead of having to retry the entire level. It's honestly a great feature that I think should be mandatory in any tower defense game by now.
The maps sort of confused me initially - both in the menu and in the levels themselves. See, after beating a level you have to click on the next level and then hit the play button, which sort of just makes level selection needlessly confusing. Again, it's a minor complaint, but still a noteworthy one. In the levels themselves though, the map is just sort of a cluster of floating debris that you place towers on. It confused me at first, but after a while I got used to it.
Graphically, Solar Division looks....well, not great. However, it also doesn't look too bad, just certainly not incredible. The maps, enemies, and towers all just sort of look bland to me. Perhaps that's a personal complaint though, and regardless, the game is still pretty fun so it's not too big of a deal really.
I will say though that the sound design is a bit annoying. The music is fine, nothing special though, but the sound effects got a bit annoying to listen to after placing dozens of towers and hearing the same announcer guy say what tower I place each time. Most of the towers make annoying noises too, but luckily there's an option in the menu to turn off tower SFX, so that's nice I suppose.
This game's difficulty progression seems to be just about right, which was perfect for me since I sometimes suck at tower defense games if I don't have time to get down a good strategy for clearing levels. One thing that was noticeable was that it was pretty much a breeze if I just spammed one of the towers (the "Shocker" - the one that slows+damages aliens), but the devs actually balanced some of the towers today so this strategy is no longer viable. Still though, I felt as if I were playing normally I would both find the game challenging and yet also not too hard, if that makes sense.
All in all, Solar Division is a fun game that's probably worth your time. Is it fantastic? Eh, I'm not sure on that one. I'd definitely say though that it's a great game for fans of the tower defense genre or for anyone who enjoys a little bit of strategy in their games. It's simple, fun, and contains a decent amount of content for its price. Plus, my complaints are mostly personal gripes, really. Overall, it's not a game that does anything incredible, but for a tower defense game it's a great inclusion to the genre.

In Solar Division you must use the various towers at your disposal to defend different space stations against the Zortix alien invasion. Like most tower defence games you'll progress through various different maps (3 per space station) facing wave after wave of enemies which you must destroy without losing your lives. There are a few different types of missions all involving wiping out a set number of waves of enemies but some missions have additional objectives such as defending one or more moving or stationary objectives or destroying all the waves within a specific time limit adding a nice little bit of variety and challenge.
You start straight off with a tutorial which explains to you the basics of gameplay, what the various options in game do and essentially how to play before you get straight into the action. You will begin only with a few towers but as you progress you'll unlock new ones along with new maps. The game starts relatively easy but the difficulty curve is very nice and I haven't found myself too over or underwhelmed yet.
The default mode for each map is Classic which is the 'story mode' and will allow you to unlock the next level when completed but each map also has 5 other game modes including Endless (where you play until you die), Max Credits (where you start with 40,000 credits), Limited Towers (where you can only place ten towers in total) and a few others that I haven't really tried yet.
The multitude of maps you'll unlock greatly increases the playability of Solar Division because you'll need to play each level different from the last. Some levels will have many enemy routes forcing you to find choke points so your towers can have maximum efficiency while others will have moving objectives you have to defend so you'll have to spread your towers out to protect yourself from all angles.
If you take too much damage or lose too many lives you can take advantage of the games handy checkpoint feature which is a great little addition to the game. At various points in the level you'll hit 'checkpoints' which by pressing backspace at any time will allow you to revert to that previous point. This comes in handy when you make a mistake that could cost you the game and don't want to lose money by simply selling the tower; though you'll lose a few waves of progress you won't have to start the entire level over again.
There are plenty of towers in game, all with their own damage, range and special effects and each tower can be upgraded a maximum of three times. You can also choose how towers interact with enemies by choosing to attack mobs based on their strength, position in line or distance from the tower. Aside from the basic attack towers there are also 'upgrade towers' which, if placed within range of other towers, can do things like increase money earned from them, increase their attack range or boost the amount of damage you can do. My favourite tower is a rather awesome drone station which if you place two down you can set a drone patrolling the map instead of having only stationary towers. This can be great for catching any little sneakies that might slip past towards the end.
You'll also find a multitude of enemy mobs also but these only seem to differ in speed or strength with no special abilities that I've encountered yet. You can view the stats of each different type of enemy by clicking on their icon where you'll find a small amount of information, their shield type (if any) and what they are vulnerable and resistant to.
I only had a few issues with the games, none of them gamebreaking but some were very noticeable. The first being you're not really told how to change maps. I assumed once completing the first level it would automatically select the next one for you but it doesn't. This is made even more confusing by the fact that the levels aren't named, they simply have a different picture which you must click. I have read a few people commenting saying the game on has one map because of this. The second is only a small issue but there are various spelling mistakes in game such as 'highlighted' being spelt 'hilighted' . I think this is likely due to the developer not having English as his first language and as I said before it's not a huge issue, it's just something I noticed whilst playing.

It's a punishing but rewarding experience that rewards careful planning. You WILL lose soldiers unless you save scum/play on easy mode or you're just that good. I personally hate myself enough to go for a "no soldier left behind" playstyle, but even I'll admit sometimes it's better to cut your losses.
Also, despite not having any official modding tools, it has one of the most comprehensive ground-up overhauls of any game I've ever played--if you for some masochistic reason decide the vanilla game is too easy for you, check out The Long War. Even the developers have gone so far as to admit the vanilla game is basically just an extended tutorial for The Long War, and it convinced them to actually add modding tools to the sequel.
Highly recommended.

It is here that Grim Dawn makes a grand entrance. Built upon the Titan Quest engine, Grim Dawn's sublime gameplay improves upon Titan Quest in every single way, except atmosphere and lore; Greek mythology is unmatched in this regard. It does not, however, mean that the world of Grim Dawn is

If you like ARPGs, you should give Grim Dawn a chance. It might just surprise you with how good it is.

I've been using Blender regularly for a few years now. The first time I opened the program I was overwhelmed and closed it immediately.
When Source Filmmaker was released, I got more interested in 3D graphics. I wanted to be able to create and modify assets, so I turned to Blender. This time I actually bothered to watch some tutorials on youtube and gave myself permission to just "play around" and try new things.
Over the years I've grown madly in love with this tool. Initially I only used it because it was free, but now it's my go-to tool for my entire pipeline. Modeling, sculpting, rigging, texturing, animating. Hell, Blender is even slowly replacing Adobe Premiere for my video editing needs as I become more comfortable with the Movie Clip editor.
There are wonderfully robust addons that allow me to export content to my favorite game engines: Arma 3 and Source SDK. It also works well with Unity and UE4.
Blender takes some getting used to. At first the right-click to select, and the myriad of keyboard shortcuts will seem like insurmountable challenges, but stick with it. It's worth it.

Play This Game If:
-You love the Sci-Fi Genre
-You like Star Wars or Star Trek
-Are interested at juggling a spaceship and crew
-Finding weaknesses in enemy ships and building your own craft fit to travel the galaxy
-Enjoy Rogue-like games/RPGs
Don't Play This Game If:
-You are easily frustrated by defeat/repeated death
-You won't play games without a New Game+
-You scoff at complain when the random nature of a game "gets the better of you"
-You are a Rebel scumbucket
Additional Points that make the game worth it:
-Great Modding community if you're into that.
-Choice based text conversations throughout that really make you feel like you are traveling the galaxy
-Unique fun and balanced weapon system
-Massive replayability.  Each session lasts anywhere from 10 minutes - 2 hours
-Tons of extra ship unlocks.
I highly reccomend this game, as it can be played with almost any computer build and will bring you hours of enjoyment.

There are six "episodes" to this game so far and at first it seems like no matter what you do the outcome for the episodes will be the same. For some plot points this is true (and I wish there had been a way to get around some of them) but in a game like this, you have to have some fixed things to build a world on. What you don't know until you've been moving through the game is that by episode six everything comes back to bite you. Choices I made in episode one finally meant something- and I have confidence that when they release season two they will mean something there too.
Bonus things? You get to learn how everyone else made decisions, which is rad. And at the end of the last episode it tells you how you play! Apparently I play with "instinct and nobility". Which I mean, got me killed, but it wasn't wrong for how I tried to play and how I try to live my life.
I had a lot of fun and would recommend it 100%. Wish the company made more games in my interest areas.

Aesthetically this game is absolutely beautiful, you can turn almost every step into a wallpaper.  The developers used a real mix of texture, colour and light to create a very convincing world that oozes a history you don't know.  In particular the use of light and dark is very effective.  Many of the elements used are very familiar to those who have experience with fantasy and sci-fi genres but still feel very foreign and alienating.  Obstacles and enemies are visually striking but they also look like they fit into the environment.

The sound design in this game is very simple but very effective.  The developer knows that silence is sometimes the best option and they use it very well.  There isn't much music but what is there is well composed and adds to the experience.  It's the ambient noise that really stands out.  There are times when you'll hear nothing but your own footsteps echoing off the stones walls, or water in the distance, or another sound that can't be identified.  There are some enemies that make noise, which you'll learn through play.
The most important sound you'll hear of course is your own voice, which you will be using frequently.

The controls in this game are very simple and standard, they'll come naturally to anyone with FPS experience.
The part you're most likely to get tangled up in is remembering the voice commands.  The developers took a lot of care in creating a language that shouldn't be too difficult for anyone to pronounce, and none of them are long incantations, but it will be a foreign language that you'll have to learn through practice.  The game doesn't pile these spells on all at once though, so if you don't wait months between sessions you shouldn't have too much trouble with the learning curve.  Spells are staggered out and introduced in tangible, practical ways that give you a full understanding of the use before you move on to the next concept.
Having given this aspect of the game some very thorough testing I can say that the system can't be tricked, you can't just throw sounds at the wall and have them stick.  However that does not mean it's tedious to cast the spells, the game is very good at picking up what you're saying and responding instantly.
If you have a mic and want to be an actual wizard this is the game for you.  An in-depth and beautiful world, haunting sound design and simple, tight controls have all been well thought out and built to compliment some largely unexplored vocal mechanics that just work.  Everything just works.

It's hard to stop hitting the retry button on this game. While there's no hand-holding in this survivalist/sci-fi RPG, every loss gives you a bit of knowledge about how to survive better on the next playtrough. While most everything about the game is minimalist (lofi-graphics and text/icon turn-based combat), the game's approach to describing characters and events forces you to assess your decisions not based on a sheet of numbers or a cookie-cutter game sprite, but on what you know about your capabilities, and what you can see of the problem(s) you face. It's a great aesthetic that forces you to be your character instead of just playing them. It's a great game, and getting better.

i suggest checking out the blender basics videos on
as well as getting through at least units 1 and 2 of
finishing the whole thing will help you but that much at least should get you familiar enough using blender to be able to move on to other tutorials.
i've got little actual experience with other 3d programs (outside of CAD specific ones that is and those tend to do things differenly, on the surface anyway, than this type of 3d software.  i'm pretty good with  Inventor, Revit, and i guess i'll throw autoCAD in here too though most of my work in that wasn't 3d.) what little experience i do have with other 3d programs is being able to figure out basic use of maya on my own relatively quickly as well as somewhat recently watching a lot of professionally made tutorials where other programs were used (mostly max and maya) just to learn techniques and workflows.
the basics of 3d modeling and such is the same in maya, 3ds max, blender, and other 3d software in the same vein so if you know your program well enough you can usually (and usually quickly) figure out how to do the same thing in your program of choice.  however that doesn't mean the process is as quickly or easily done in every program.  while whatching tutorials using other programs i've seen far more times where they've had to break the flow to get to someing in a menu or do something else in a more roundabout way that i just wouldn't have to do in blender.
i'm not saying blender has the best of everything.  i've seen a few things so far that i've thought it'd be nice to have in blender but overall using blender is just so much more smooth of an experience than what i'm seeing in these other programs.  so much so at times that these tutorials using other programs seem to be torturously slow and roundabout.
there's people saying blender is the easiest to use in these reviews and other people chiding them for it.  mostly i think the people disagreeing are confusing ease of learning with ease of use.  there is a difference.
blender isn't the easiest to lean 3d software out there but from what i've seen there are a lot of things that are easier to do in blender than in other software.
blender is great. 10 out of 11 and with plans in place to get better still.

Blender, like many other 3D modeling and animation packages, has a reasonably steep learning curve, but can be very rewarding. Blender is very versatile, but I'm mostly writing from a game developer/modder perspective.
Blender is most adept at polygon modeling although NURBS modeling is also supported to a lesser extent. The UV mapping tools are solid and fast to use once you are familiar with the process. Animation is straight forward and depending on the game you are developing for, you may be able to export your animations for use in the game. Mesh importers and exporters for most common formats are provided, and many more may be installed as plugins.
Protip: If you are interested in modding Bethesda games (like me) such as Fallout or any of the Elder Scrolls games, have a look at blender_nif_plugin over on Github.
Outside the relm of game content creation, Blender also has good support for scene rendering using both rasterization (blender renderer) and path tracing (cycles renderer). Smoke, hair and liquids can be simulated internally and produce nice results. There is also a built in game engine which is scriptable in Python, although it has not received as much developer love in the past as some would like.
Blender also has a built in node based compositor (again with a learning curve) which can be used for everything from general video editing to rotoscoping and green screen.
In Blender, keyboard shortcuts are very much your friend. This adds to the learning curve, but becomes a necessity when you want to learn to work quickly.
I've been following tinkering with Blender on and off for about 10 years. The developer and user community is very active, friendly, and helpful. It is great to see Blender on Steam. I hope this helps more people discover and use blender to make awesome games and mods.

First and foremost, let me start off by saying that there will be spoilers throughout this review. If you’re even remotely interested in keeping the story for when you run through Episode 1 yourself, I’d suggest waiting to read this. If you’ve watched season three of the HBO T.V. series or read “A Feast For Crows”, you’re probably OK reading through this as there will not be many surprises.
The last three to four years have produced quite a few shoddy games based in the world of A Song of Ice and Fire. The abysmal RTS, and the better-but-not-great attempt at an RPG. It’s also pretty widely known that I’ve been a gigantic fan of George RR Martin since middle school, that being over ten years ago now. I’ve read and reread that entirety of the book series quite a few times, and have dabbled in the various communities that have sprung up to discuss the legitimacy of various children, hierarchy of families, and the events of Westeros. With that being said, I’m usually a giant stickler that a game stay true to the lore, or spirit of writing, that comes across in dialogue and plot. Telltale games did an absolutely phenomenal job at erasing the damage that the previous games had inflicted upon me.
A bit of a background on the political landscape that the game takes place in. Eddard Stark has been murdered at the hands of Joffery Baratheon. The North has risen under the banner of his son, Rob Stark. The rest of the realm, save Dorne, is in turmoil at the hands of the various men who have attempted to claim that they are the One True King of Westeros. The game begins with you playing the role of a young squire in service to House Forrester. Specifically, you are the squire of Gregor Forrester, the lord of the lands and titles of House Forrester. You are camped out at The Twins, the home of House Frey, and the downfall of Rob Stark, King of the North.
The Red Wedding is just about to take place, and with it, the fall of The King in the North.
Game-play & Mechanics
At first, I wasn’t thrilled with the game-play. The game is more of a visual story than a real attempt at wandering around Westeros, leveling up a character, or anything you expect in a typical adventure style game. This was my first foray into a story-based Telltale game, however, and from everything I’ve read about their other titles, this seems to be fairly commonplace. The longer I played, the more I came to like the system. The quick time events were fairly clever, if not a bit confusing at first, and lead to a couple of deaths before I truly figured them out. Several times throughout the story there were invisible walls that kept you from exploring other areas of the game. I first noticed this inside Fort Ironrath, the home of House Forrester, but on my second play-through noticed it more in the wooded areas and places you’d expect a bit more openness. While it was a bit annoying and killed the immersion a bit, Telltale did a good job of adding in other areas that were there solely to be explored, such as the tower in Fort Ironrath. It had no purpose other than to venture to the top, and watch your citizens go about their daily lives.
The ability to inspect most things in the game coupled with the deeper meaning that a lot of the objects held was a trait that I liked very much. A great example of this was procuring the Sentinel bracer as Ethan Forrester. This opened up new dialogue with your uncle, your mother, and the candidates for Sentinel, as well as your siblings. You could even have unique dialogue or description options just by looking at something prior to talking to someone. I’m not one to stave off excess description, and Telltale did a fine job supplying me with things to study and read.
Though the few shortcomings that I’ve noted here were not game-breaking or ridiculously unpleasant, ultimately at the end of the episode I would say that the mechanics and game-play were the one true weakness of the title. The quick time events weren’t repetitive, but you did find yourself wishing for more things to do. More interaction outside of the plot/story. For example, I would have loved to been able to, as a squire, help Rodrick or Gregor don their armor, or suit up for battle. Or, upon my return to Ironrath, to have a brief time where I could fight with the other squires in the courtyard during training. Even having the ability to fight a wooden practice dummy would have been engaging enough to dispel this complaint.
Dialogue & Voice Acting
The voices in this game were a bit surprising to me. It’s not very often you get to hear the voices of a very prominently placed TV show like “Game of Thrones” make their way into a video game, or, I should say, a video game you want to play. I could poke a stick at the other titles stemming from A Song of Ice and Fire, but it’d be a bit redundant. The voice acting was pleasant, well manicured, and did a very nice job making the story both alluring and compelling. I did not have any real complaints about any portion of the acting bit of the first episode.
Story & Plot
Upon receiving a review copy of Telltale’s apparent successful foray into Martins mind, I was extremely worried. The story was the most important piece to such a grand undertaking, and George Martin left plenty of pitfalls and snares along the way to destroy even the most solid of attempts at creating parallel dialogues and sub-plots within the Game of Thrones. My first instinct proved to be false, however, because worry was not needed. The way that Telltale managed to fashion a seemingly unmentioned house, portion of the North, and still remain realistic and true to George RR Martins characters still has me astounded. Throughout my two times through the story, I found no major plot holes, and was even impressed with the timing in which they had the events of House Forrester unfold. Telltale did an excellent job of staying true to the characters set forth by Martin, particularly Ramsay Snow and Cersei Lannister. Ethan Forrester was also a welcome addition to a story line that had a hidden dagger in the dark. True to his style, the ending twist had me up and out of my seat before I knew what I was doing, something that had not happened since I had read “A Storm of Swords”. All-in-all, this is a story that, so far, I can genuinely say belongs in the world of A Song of Ice and Fire.
Graphics
Though the least important, in my opinion, criteria for measuring the depth of a game, Telltale’s A Game of Thrones Episode one did not fall short. The quick time events had great animations, with nothing too jittery or glitchy. The limited amount of landscape you were able to see had quite a bit of detail, particularly playing as Ethan Forrester in the courtyard of Ironrath, and playing as the young squire Gared during his journey North as he is hiding from Ramsay Snow. Though not the games strongest point, I would venture to say that a lot of thought and talent went into the seemingly hand painted environments and impressive looking quick time events.
In Conclusion
It’s not very often that, as gamers, we are given the opportunity to buy a story and watch as it unfolds around us. Here lately it seems we are bombarded with launch day DLC, or essentially paying money to beta test developers games. With Telltale’s A Game of Thrones, we are given more than that. We are given the ability to play an interactive story with incredible lore that has, in my mind, stayed true to the spirit of George RR Martins works. Right now, the game is retailing for just $30 on the Steam store. While this review only covers the very first episode, there are a confirmed six planned in all, and by purchasing Telltale’s latest work, you receive access to all the episodes as they launch. If you enjoy the world of A Song of Ice and Fire, and can enjoy an Episodic point and click adventure, this title is well worth the money.

NEO Scavenger is a turn-based, post-apocalyptic, survival roguelike with perma-death. I also now sometimes fondly call it a Procedural Death Michigan. It's mean, immersive, annoyingly addictive and seems to strongly dislike players wearing right boots (left boots are fine).
Basically, you scavenge around (and die after the building crumbles on you), fight other people scavenging around (and die valiantly with monkey wrench in hand) or try to talk to them (and die a turn later by drinking a celebratory made-it-through-the-turn sip of poisoned water), try to kill creatures that would like to eat you almost as much as you'd like to eat them (and die hungry), craft items to help you survive (and die warm because your fire alerted every deadly thing around), keep track of your hunger, thirst, diseases and injuries (and die very informed) or try to get to the seemingly last big hub of civilization (and die trying to get there; or trying to get in; or after you get in; or on your way back out).
In short this is a game where you try to make it through the day while figuring out what has happened to your hero and the world - and die trying. I really don't want to spoil this too much for you, but rest assured, whether you prefer dying by traumatic brain injury, blood loss, cholera, dehydration or an angry mob, there are enough options there to suit everyone's tastes. And if that doesn't sound fun to you, go away, I don't like you.
-----
NEO Scavenger is the chess of survival games, if chess came without an instruction manual and forced you to scramble to understand its rules. It's all about making tactically sound moves, about the constant weighing of risk-reward decisions, but without ever feeling certain you made the right choice. Very much like real life in that way. The gameplay mechanics, while seemingly unforgiving, are actually there to remind you that you are not a badass superhero, just an average person thrown into a huge mess. Combined with the deliberate obfuscation of the player stats, this feeling of vulnerability makes the game surprisingly immersive. It's an exercise in role playing and player driven choices based on gut feeling rather than number crunching.
Quite realistically for an average Joe, going in situations guns-a-blazing will rarely be rewarded, running away and hiding your tracks from a bunch of stray dogs may. The combat is a constant dirty struggle of trying to get the upper hand while dancing around your opponent, surprisingly complex and rewarding for something delivered with a few buttons and a bit of text. But even with great equipment and a character with decent combat skills, every fight you survive will leave you weakened, hurt, tired and more vulnerable to the next threat that comes along. In that way, the combat, as well as the deeply simulated survival and sickness mechanics, enhance the constant feeling of being exposed and alone, afraid and uncertain in the middle of a hostile world. You are never allowed to feel safe. You are never allowed to hunker down, build a huge base, put fences around it and kill everything that dares come through. Throughout the game, the mechanics drive you to keep moving on, keep surviving day to day, keep doing mundane inventory management, and keep trying not to die. And almost always failing.
But dying here isn't always a bad thing. Since you can't really improve your skills, (though you can add to them in a limited way) you need to die to improve, to learn, to realize how to make better choices next time. You even need to die to learn more of the world, simply because you can never uncover everything in one playthrough. Which brings us to the story.
Behind the immersive atmosphere and the fun, unforgiving gameplay mechanics, hides an interesting, complex, well-written story and huge amounts of lore and flavour text delivered both in long screens and in tiny bites literally everywhere you look. The story will never beat you over the head with what you should do next (and it's fair to say you should remain doubtful when it seems to do that), so it is perfectly ignorable if you just enjoy the sandbox game. But it's worth getting into, and it's also worth remembering that every time you think you know all the possible answers to a question, there's likely more there to discover, if only you do things slightly differently next time (by having a different build, carrying different items, making different choices, going down a different path, uncovering different information). The mystery of the story is a sprawling, complicated puzzle, one you will not solve easily, even by finishing the game the first few times.
If it looks as if I'm ignoring the game's flaws, it's because to be honest I enjoy the game too much to notice them most of the time. That said, the UI could be friendlier to newcomers (which is a polite way to say it's pretty unintuitive); thankfully it's perfectly serviceable once you get used to it. Also, while obfuscating stats is an interesting and perfectly valid design choice, obfuscating some of the less intuitive game mechanics is simply an annoying hurdle to climb over when you first start out. In more technical matters, the cookie-based save system (one of the few elements there to constantly remind you that this is still a flash game) can be a real pain, the game doesn't play well with many commonly used modern resolutions and the process of adding mods is a bit too archaic and involved for most players these days. Even more importantly, there is a very valid argument to be made about how well a perma-death roguelike game with unforgiving mechanics can still make for a deep story-based experience that is more enjoyable than frustrating.
But even with all its problems, as you may have gathered I think this is a great game: the perfect flawed little gem, and in my head already a cult classic.

Fantastic program that i have used for about 4 years. Blender is a 3d Modeler, Animation Suite, Video Editor, Game Engine, and more all in one program. Just as a warning, the program is much easier to use once you learn some key combinations (s for scale, r for rotate, and tab to go into edit mode.) I cannot recommend this program enough, with enough experience you can make some really fantastic renders and animations.
For anyone open to learning this software i cannot stress one point enough: This program is shortcut based NOT menu based, so if you are coming into this expecting all of the stuff to have buttons somewhere, they don't. space is the closest you'll get to that.
There are two main rendering options inside of blender, the Blender Render and Cycles Render.
-Blender Render (in my opinion) is good for beginners, you can make very nice looking renders and stuff in this. (I don't use it so i can't say much.)
-Cycles render is much more difficult to use, but is ridiculously powerful once you learn how to use it. You can make a large amount of content, like metal and glass, with this without even using materials. Just as a warning, rendering a very detailed scene in this renderer will likely make your computer useless during the hour or two a render can take.
-----------------------------------------
For new users i reccomend a few things to start off:
If you have been using any other 3d software: go into file > user preferences > input and change "Select With" to Left, this will feel infinitely more comfortable to you.
If you happen to be using blender to export to Unreal Engine: Set your scale in the export to fbx menu to 50 to 100, otherwise your models will be really small (also triangles will disappear when importing onto UE4 in my experience).
If you are modeling in unity: unity supports importing of .blend files directly into the engine.
If you are using Cycles: Click the button on the bottom left of the window and change it to the Node Editor, this is how everything works in cycles.
If you have an nvidia graphics card: You can use CUDA to speed up your renders! go to file > user preferences > System and change "Compute Device" to CUDA.
If you are using cycles: for your FINAL render, go to the camera tab and change your sampling preset to FINAL, this will remove fuzzy stuff from your renders (this does not show up in blender renderer)
Your number pad changes your perspective in 3d, 0 on the num-pad will go into camera view. big tip: shift + f will allow you to position your camera from inside of your camera view.
In user Preferences, there are a MASSIVE amount of addons, ranging from tree generators to exporting to 3ds formats.
Tab brings you into edit mode, google how to use edit mode.
This software may seem difficult at first, but remember: This is free. You can make renders, models, and animations on the level of $1000 software once you learn to use it, not to mention this can export to almost any file format of any software ever.
Remember: Google is your friend, if you're stuck someone else probably was too.
Enjoy! :D
