Downloaded this just to write a quick review.
Blender is the program that started my my love with 3d art.  I taught myself all about the program back in 2001, when it was in early development.  At the time most 3d tools where very hard to aquire, either because of cost, or just lack of access, not to mention very few schools had any sort of graphics programs outside of autocad.  Without Blender i would have never had the exposure to the world of 3d graphics,  the barrier to entry was just too high.   It helped form the foundation that helped me build my skills in maya, max, zbrush and various compositing tools.  To see how far this program has come, in the 15 years since i used it is not only impressive but surprising.  I am glad blender survied and grew in spite of the domination of the indusrty by a few giants.   This is the perfect program to experiment with and create new things and learn your own methods and techniques for acieving results in 3d.  That said, the workflows and tools are quite different from inustry standard programs and some things learned might not carry over well, but there is always more than one way to accomplish your goal in 3d.  Blender will challenge you to find unique and creative methods, that will help you see outside the box that is inustry standard workfow.   You will not find a better tool to experiment with, and since its free, not only is it a gift to the community, but society as a whole, and i hope will continue to provide the tools that are creating new artists.

To sum it up: brilliant ideas buried by poor design decisions.
Instead of making this game action-oriented, with awesome spells that can turn legions of enemies to cinder, the devs produced a very slow-paced walking simulator where once in a while you get to cast something to light a path or open a door.
Most of the time you're just wandering through endless corridors, hoping to find some hidden inscription or button you've missed, because the puzzles are unsolvable without it. Combat - as little of it as there is - is incredibly clunky and redundant. The only thing that keeps you going are the new spells you get from time to time. But then you get slowed down even more by things like corridors that drain your health. And to save the game you've got to find a checkpoint, so after another 30 minutes-long stroll you can easily lose all your progress by taking a wrong turn and dying randomly.
Overall, while the spell mechanic actually works and feels great, the game does not capitalize on that at all.

extended:
This is more or less a series of extremely simple minigames strung together seemingly at random.  Most can be summarized as such: clumsily move around on the screen while dodging pixelated blobs and clicking to fire slow-moving bullets at such.  It can be amusing to see some of the situations described or depicted in the game, but the gameplay itself is lacking.  The controls are just clumsy enough that you never get into that addictive, edge-of-your-seat frenzy that the best arcade games can inspire.  Still, they are not so bad as to incite you to throw your peripherals at the monitor, and there is something to be said for character.

To put it in perspective, if I had paid $5 for this game instead of $2 on sale, I would feel extremely ripped off.  But for what I paid, I can appreciate the value.  Given all of this, I will err on the side of being positive and recommend the game.

Thompson got lost, beat up, hunted and otherwise left for dead in Blue Bottle Games' NEO Scavenger. Here's what he had to say about it.
NEO Scavenger: First Impressions

It was raining. Corporal Mayweather adjusted the sights on her laser sniper. It was pretty fancy but she almost preferred the standard issue rifle, not this alien junk. She hated them. It was still hard to believe this was even happening: aliens, abductions, death. It was all she knew now. For the last 6 months she jumped from mission to mission. Quickly falling into the role of squad sharpshooter. Her lightning reflexes and dead aim kept the others alive, and she could never take her job seriously enough. This particular day they had been flown to Germany to invetigate a downed UFO, a milk run, command had said. She was beginning to doubt it. The squad leader had her positioned on a ridge, providing overwatch to her comrades below, and watch she did. Suddenly out of the corner of her eye she saw them. Three sectoids. Thats what the scientists called them. They had that "classic" alien look to them and they carried plasma rifles attached to their wrists. She alerted the rest of her squad and they took up position. Stevens ran up to the ridge and took cover behind a stump. "You all set up there?" he asked. Mayweather looked down and gave a nod, her bright purple hair soaked and matted on her head. Stevens was the squad medic and she had taken a particular liking to him. He was always quick to run in the line of fire and rescue a downed squadmate or provide moral support. The sectoids approached cautiously, and as they closed in a few shots rang out from the east. It was the rookie, Himata. He had panicked and taken a few shots at the sectoids, but was nowhere near his target. Mayweather shot a glare in his general direction, but she remembered how it was during her first mission. The poor guy could barely keep himself alert and mentally intact. Wait... Had she heard those noises before? The downed UFO echoed something fierce and suddenly three Floaters shot out of the hangar bay. She had a few confirmed floater kills from previous missions and she knew they were a force to be reckoned with. Her training and reflexes kicked in and she snapped a quick shot at the nearest floater. As it always did, the shot connected with a crisp burning sound and the floater dropped, lifeless, to the ground. The other two quickly hovered into positions and began their counter attack. Their heavy plasma rifles flashed in a series of shots that seemed to casually drift not to her, no. Stevens was their target. Desperate not to lose him she shouted: "STEVENS GET DOWN!" He was hit, badly. She jumped down from the ridge and ran to his side, struggling to give him any kind of cover. "Mayweather, what are you doing!" It was the seargent, he sympathized with her but he knew she was their only chance at getting out of this mission alive. "Get back on overwatch!" She was torn, conflicting emotions tumbling around inside her. She looked down at Stevens and as their gaze connected two things happened. First: she realized what stevens would have her do, he wanted her to do her job, to kill those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s that had caused the human race so much pain. The second thing that happened was that a plasma shot from a previously unseen sectoid came flying through the air straight at Stevens. Time seemed to slow as it lazily drifted into the side of his head and continued onwards, as if the human life it had just taken didn't phase it at all. Even though her sights were muddled from the tears, Mayweather stood and took her shot. The sectoid fell, then another, and another. Her thoughts lost in a cloud of rage, she let loose and gave the aliens what they deserved. Justice wasn't as simple as paying them back, and it was small compensation for what they had taken from her, because she knew none of her missions would be the same again.
There is enough emotional material in this game to write a million books.

NEO Scavenger
NEO Scavenger is a game that wants you to die. Even more than that, it is a game that wants to kill you. Brutally and rapidly if possible, but slowly will work just as well. From hypothermia to bandit attacks to starving to death, it pulls no punches in the “you’re going to die” department. It is an unforgiving game and makes no apologies about it. Quite frankly, that’s one of the reasons it succeeds so well. Before you go running off without reading further, allow me a moment to elaborate. A single paragraph is all I’m asking.
You see, NEO Scavenger also wants you to succeed. It does supply you with the tools and skills you need in order to survive. It simply doesn’t hold your hand or coddle you along the way. You begin simply enough. You start the game by picking your few basic skills and you wake up on the floor of a cryogenic freezing lab with something mean heading your way. Your journey has just begun in earnest. You may use your chosen skills to assist with the incoming creature, via feeding it another survivor or simply locking the door. The skills you have chosen to outfit yourself often change the game in this way, leading to all kinds of different outcomes to little problems like this. It’s undeniably gratifying to halt an enemy attack by using your hacking skill to drop a cryogenic tank and feeding the creature a reality television star. Let’s be honest; who hasn’t wanted to do that at one point or another?
Are you still with me? I thought that might get your attention. The aim of the game is fairly simple; find out who you are and what happened to the world. Things take place in a post-apocalyptic environment, and you have no memory of any of it. It’s fairly standard, but it plays out relatively well nonetheless. Hints are revealed through old newspapers you find scattered about and obvious visual cues. Your hand is never held at any point, there is no tutorial, and there are no retries. When you die, it is game over and you start again from the beginning. NEO Scavenger is a harsh, unforgiving piece of work. But you also get a little better each time, get a little further, and learn a little more. It’s tough, often seems unfair, and is always exciting.
Technically, it is a pretty solid game. It’s still in development, so it does have its share of bugs and incomplete features, but what is currently present does work well and you shouldn’t be deterred from giving it a shot if you find yourself at all interested. Over the course of the next few months it will be fleshed out and cleaned up, and it’s looking like it will become a great little game. I would recommend it easily enough, especially considering the $10 price tag attached to it. If you think you might be interested, and don’t mind a rough edge or two, give it a shot. If you think you can take the abuse, that is.

The short of it: a turn based early access title with a ton of potential. Despite being rather bare bones as of this review, there seems to be very regular updates from the developers leaving me hopeful that this title will blossom into something brilliant.
The long of it:
I've just got to start this review by gushing over the gorgeous visuals that are on display here. Enemies and allies alike are detailed extremely well in addition to having smooth animations. The backgrounds look gorgeous whilst your character zips across an iced over lake with his huge badass final fantasy-eque sword in hand. There is no doubt that you will have a feast for your eyes (providing your computer can run the higher settings).
The gameplay comes of as being rather basic throughout the tutorial, but i can already see, even from my short time playing, that there is quite some depth to be explored. The concept of harmony and dissonance tiles do bring a nice flavour to a genre im not particularly a huge fan of. Every action you can perform possesses one of two variations: harmony or dissonance. Harmony variations are weaker than dissonance variations, but upon performing a dissonance action your characters tile turns red and only dissonance actions can be used when this tile is stood on. If there are too many dissonance tiles on your side then you can risk blowing up your grid, dealing damage to all of your guardians which increases with more dissonance tiles on your side. This mechanic creates for a risk versus reward mindset which can make for some exciting moments. There are many more elements to the game such as combo- based moves but this review is already long enough as it is.
Characters are designed brilliantly and all possess unique abilities and gorgeous animations of their own. Despite the character pool being somewhat low as of this review, you can count on there being regularly introduced characters if the developers history is to be counted on. It would be nice if there were more animations for each character, but i can confidently say that they are likely to be added later on.
My main gripe about this game is the lack of content as of this review. There are only training, tutorial modes and a wave-based mode against ai controlled monsters (which are as well designed and animated as the main cast) for single player content which i find rather dissapointing, but it is worth mentioning that the game is very much still in its infancy as of right now.  Additionaly, due to the currently small playerbase it is difficult to play multiplayer matches. I believe to my fullest that new content will be added very soon.
All in all, this is a title im glad to support. I am looking forward to the game growing from its strong base, and I am confident in this being the case as the developers are both very active and keen to improve this game. They listen to community feedback well- a sign of a passionate team. Even if the game is potentially not to your liking i would recommend giving it a go. after all, in the worst case scenario you can still refund the game anyway!

Blender is a fantastic program to model objects for games. You can go from making incredibly detailed objects to use in scenes for making animations (Blender also simulates some fluid dynamics), to making efficient, lower poly models for games.
There are many tutorials on the internet. If you have a question about how to do something, then there's a good chance that someone else has already asked it and received an answer.
Blender also allows people to use python to create modules, that add features not normally present in Blender, and, there are some libraries that allow you to open/import and save/export different types of file formats not included in Blender, such as .x (directx) files.
What's even better is the fact that Blender, and the libraries mentioned above, are completely free. Which is great considering Blender is equally, if not more, powerful than many other modelling programs that cost money.

Half Life 2 is one of those games that is considered the best of all time. Why's that?
Because it did pretty much everything right. The graphics, game engine and physics were a breakthrough for a game in 2004. The combat although simplified from Half Life 1 was still satisfying with more creativity using the Gravity Gun. The level design was brilliant with each chapter being unique from the rest. The story and presentation was decent with great characterisation and decent voice acting. The music while not as exceptional to the likes of other composers is still enjoyable to listen to. Any negative I would have with this game will be greatly overshadowed by a fantastic singleplayer experience. The same can be applied for both Episodes 1 and 2.

Initial Review from 16/11:
I cannot recommend Prodigy Tactics in the current state (as of 16th of November 2017).
TLDR: The game has been in developement since 2014 (and was supported via kickstarter) has undergone significant problems in its developement and is currently still only in a state that I would describe as "early alpha". The game itself has massive potential to be very good but is nowhere near fulfilling its potential right now. The game has crashes, gameplay bugs, partly questionable gameplay deisgn choices and little content right now.
Background of the game:
In april 2014 Hanakai Studios opened a kickstarter campaign for Prodigy Tactics and were successfull (212.194$ raised). It was, if I understood it correctly announced as a boardgame / videogame hybrid, by using a video game and a board to place your physical figures in the game. If I also understood correctly this idea was scrapped, obviously♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off most of the customers which are right now asking for a refund (look in the comment section under kickstarter). The rewards for the kickstarter campaing were announced to be distributed in October 2015.
Content:
9 Characters, 2 Maps (which is just a cosmetic thing), an archaic tutorial, a training modus and a bastion modus. Also an encylcopedia about the characters, what they do and tips on how to use them. The game has been in developement for at least ~ 4 years and thats all the content there is right now? Despite them cutting the main feature (boardgame hybrid)? And the game is supposed to be out in a year? The one thing that makes me hopeful that it might indeed be fully released in 2018 is that there are lots of videos from the developers that show other characters are already in developement (there are a lot of short gameplay videos of a lot more characters out there, showing completed models and animations).
Bugs and Engrish Translation:
The game's translation currently is terrible. Its amateurish translation at best but fortunately its mostly understandable. But a few times during the tutorial it was so terrible that I didnt even understand what they were trying to tell me. The game also crashed a few times upon starting a game. The Report a bug feature is currently unusable as the game crashes upon sending the ticket. There is a button in the menu that doesnt do anything (bottom left, the middle one). Sometimes upon using a harmony move, no harmony mana field is spawned. There are also a few things that I'm not sure are bugs or gameplay features ... more on that in the gameplay section
Characters:
Obviously one of the main drawing points of the game is the cast of characters. They are pretty unqiue, all have different gameplay mechanics, different stats and special abilities and are connected via affinities that can launch combination attacks upon using special attacks. Also some characters synergise with others making teambuilding important and interesting. The game really shows a lot of potential here. If there were to be lets say 20-30 characters in the finished game, the team building and team combination attacks could lead to a really deep and complex game.
I have read in another review, that the characters have unique stories and motivations. Uhm not really. They have 2-5 lines of story in their encyclopedia that just give a brief overview of the character at best.
Gameplay:
Has really good features but also really weak and wonky ones. I wont give an overview of the system because it would take too long. I really like the choice of playing safe with harmony moves or risky with dissonance moves. Balancing them out and using the resulting mana fields to your advantage should lead to a deep and complex combat system. However I'm not sure I like the involved RNG with the dissonance moves / squares. Also I really think the targeting is weird. You choose the opponent you want to attack by placing your character in the opposite row of the character you want to attack. But even with ranged you can only attack the foremost character. I'd really like this system to be changed because it heavily limits the possibilities of who to attack.  Also the combat damage calculation is useless and wrong in about 80% of the time and doesnt even change upon chosing a harmony or dissonance attack. Power buffs appear to not be working as they haven't done anything in the games I have been playing. There is a lot more that I didnt like but I'll stop here to reduce the length of the review.
In the end I would advise you not to buy the game as you really don't know what you will be getting and especially when. I have the feeling that this might be one of the games that stay in early access for far too long and don't end up the way they were supposed to. The current amount of content, gameplay wonkiness, engrish translation and bugs really keep me from playing the game more. However I also believe that if the developers push this game in the right direction it will be a very deep and complex tactical game that you can play online. I will update my review accordingly if the developers update the game. Hopefully it will be a recommendation as soon as possible.

DISCLAIMER: This review is from someone who has minimal experience with platformers (both historically and currently).
I am one of the few people on the planet who has no real opinion about platformers. I didn't play them as a kid so they hold no nostalgic feelings.  I've also never been struck by platformer-fever; I have no strong feelings on the genera whatsoever.  I have played a small number of platformers (Mario, Super Meat Boy, DK, Blackthorn, & does Spelunky county?), I'm not inexperienced necessarily but rather a combination of unfamiliarity with the genera and general apathy.
With all that out of the way let's focus on Top Hat.   I'm not sure how I acquired this game, but I installed it because hey, why not? After a very cursory glance at the reviews and it’s % standing (62% positive) I assumed this was gonna be pretty lame.  Low and behold it turns out that Top Hat is a resounding ‘decent’.  I’m not sure if it’s because I expected so much less or what, but I’ve been really enjoying my time with Top Hat.
Top Hat wants to be an NES game.  Everything about the aesthetic of this game screams 1991 nostalgia.  The 8-Bit sound is fun and the sprite work is solid.  It looks way too clean to actually be an NES game (there is far more detail in the environments & sprites than an NES game).  Regardless of the aesthetic not being perfect ‘NES’ the visuals are pleasing to look at and the sound is right there pleasing away too.
I think what really shocked me about Top Hat was how it controls.  It works really well.  By no means is it Super Meat Boy perfect but it’s accurate and reliable.  Even with my miniscule experience I’ve played a few badly controlling platformers and have heard/watched about how many there are out there.  Platformer controls are apparently one of those things that’s very easy to ♥♥♥♥ up.  I was surprised Top Hat controlled as well as it does. Because of it’s mixed reviews I expected something approaching Digital Homicide levels of bad mechanics.  What I found is a solid and acceptable “physics” system. My only issue with the controls is that the default settings for a gamepad are stupid and hard to get used to.  Luckily the devs N94Games are better than most AAA devs and allow full button mapping on the keyboard/mouse and gamepad.  TotalBiscuit would be proud.
There are two major, universal problems with Top Hat.  The first issue is the fact that even though it’s fun and functional, Top Hat is absolutely unremarkable.  This game is like a piece of plain toast and butter.  A totally legit food item that doesn’t taste bad in any way but there is no glamour, mystique, or excitement with a piece of toast.  It’s just toast and butter.  Same with Top Hat.  It’s a platformer that functions great and is engaging enough to keep me playing but at the same time it’s not all that interesting, kinda safe/boring, and ultimately forgettable.
The second and more prominent issue is the price.  $10 seems way too steep for Top Hat.  A quarter that price sounds much more reasonable to me.  It just isn’t exciting enough to warrant dropping 10 bucks on.  This is the kind of game you buy for $0.75 during a steam sale and then are pleased when your expectations of meh are surpassed with “mmm….not bad.”
So what’s the TL;DR?  Buy this game when it’s on sale,  For me, the full price is WAY to high for something of this calibre. It’s good, just not $10 good. If you can pick it up on sale I think it will surprise you with how competent it is.  It’s most definitely fun, a slightly less exciting form of fun when compared with something like Rocket League or The Binding of Isaac, but, it is fun none the less.  Pop Top Hat onto your wishlist and next time it’s on sale for anything under $2.50 grab it.  At that price this is definitely worth playing.

I'd consider giving this game another try if some of these issues are resolved.

Alright, so there's going to be 2 parts to this Review. 1: Why i nominated this game for an award, and 2: The actual review.
1: Why i nominated this for an award.
First off, I nominated this review for "A game within a game" And i did so because The base game is so much fun, it has 2 giant maps you can mess around in and slaughter zombies and whatnot, but also there is The Following. The Following is like both maps from the base game COMBINED. It's like a whole other game, that you can access from Dying Light. The mechanics are a bit different, but it's the same game, just different maps!
TL;DR This game is like 2 different games because the 2 maps base, and the Following DLC are all like seperate games. Especially The Following.
2: Actual Review.
I really, really love this game. It is so much fun, running around and killing zombies, in fun, creative, and awesome ways. This game makes me happy when i play it, in fact, it's so fun, i've played through the campaign about 4 times now. The many variety of weapons, cool moves (and sometimes hilarious) like the Kick, Dropkick, stun, and max legendary level punching things. I also like how you can have silent ranged weapons, such as the bow and crossbow, but the guns are sometimes fun to kill zombies with. I think the most efficient way to review this would be a non (slightly) biased comparison of this Battlefront (Lucas Arts / L.A) with EA's new Battlefront.
-GAMEPLAY
L.A take the lead with this one. Pretty easily to be honest. Much more game modes, maps, factions etc.. 1-0, to L.A.
-GRAPHICS
What do you expect. L.A's is 10 years old. 10 YEARS OLD. 1-1.
-REPLAYABILITY
While EA's multiplayer leveling system offer some replayability, L.A's wider range, and much larger density, of content give L.A the point. Also, and i will refer to this quite a bit, not everyone likes multiplayer. 2-1 to L.A.
-SINGLEPLAYER
EA doesn't really know how to create a good singleplayer. At all. In fact, it seems they've given up on the idea altogether. Rest in peace EA - post Battlefield 2 / Bad Company. The lack of singleplayer is a negative point for EA, and L.A's extremely well done singleplayer, including a campaign, critically acclaimed Galactic conquest, and instant action give L.A a well-deserved point. 3-0
-MULTIPLAYER
EA get a point by default, as L.A's multiplayer was decommisioned a while back. While i deducted a point from EA for not having a singleplayer, i will not do so with L.A for the lack of multiplayer as, a) there was once upon a time, and b) the expansive singleplayer more than makes up for it. There are dozens of singleplayer only games and L.A's Battlefront is one of the best. 3-1 to L.A.
-MOD SUPPORT
Time has been of L.A's side, with multitudes of mods being released, a lot of them can be considered as unofficial expansions. A conversion pack has been developed, adding the favourite instant action maps from L.A's 1st Battlefront. Who doesn't like free additional content. 4-1 to L.A.
-PRICE
L.A's Battlefront is $15 on steam (I got my copy on special for $5). Fair enough for an old game. EA's is around $80. L.A's has a LOT more content, + mods such as the conversion pack. 1/5 of the price for (in my opinion) a much better game. 5-1.
-ACCESSABILITY
I can run L.A's Battlefront with 128 bots, maxed settings, easily over 60 fps, on my laptop. While L.A's Battlefront is only available on steam, Xbox + Xbox 360, and PS2, EA's is only available on the newer platforms (so tough luck for fellow laptop users). Also, for console users, EA's is multiplayer only (effectively) so hooray for online costs. Close battle, but point to L.A. 6-1.
OVERRALL
If this was a football match, L.A's Battlefront would be Barcelona, and EA's would be Norwich. EA has yet again disappointed with its money-mongering and lack of singleplayer ability. I'm pretty sure EA have just produced the 1st clickbait-like game, not sure why they didn't call it Battlefield: Star Wars and save the royalty costs. Congrats to L.A's Battlefront for beating a game 10 years newer,

I'm way behind with this review of XCOM: Enemy Unknown (played with the Enemy Within and all DLC) since it's been out 4 years and XCOM2 is now available. Still, here goes.
XCOM is a highly strategic turn-based game, which requires management of multiple different resources in different circumstances, which gives you a constant stream of tough choices to make. The game is quite hard and can be quite unforgiving; when something goes wrong it can escalate from bad to disaster very quickly.
For me, those are all good points and I am thoroughly enjoying the game.
If you like turn based strategy, this is one of the better ones that I've played for the gameplay. Graphics and sound are both perfectly acceptable, but not breath-taking.
The biggest problem with the game for me is that even 4 years after release, I'm finding it buggy. Regular saves are necessary just in case things don't work. Sometimes the menu with the save and quit options stops functioning, so you have to kill the game and lose any progress made. One of the missions (the train mission in the Slingshot DLC) has failed to realise that I've completed it; with similar results. Sometimes the game gets stuck on the aliens turn and there is no way to do anything except close the game and restart. These are things I might have expected if the game was new, but at 4 years old I'd have thought this would have been ironed out.
The positives outweigh the bugs for me, and I can see me getting many more hours of play time out of the game, but the bugs do leave me cursing it from time to time, especially if I haven't hit Save for a little while.

What can I say about this game that hasn't already been said?  Alot.  In order...
1 - Graphics - This is what attracted me to the game in the first place.  The graphics are simply gorgeous.  They are a delight to behold, even at lower resolutions, and if you are fortunate enough to have a 4k monitor you will be amazed at the animations, the color, the detail - everything.  At HD levels they are still far above the par that any game has set for your brain intake.  Quite simply, looking at this game is like... making love to your eyes.  Yes it looks that good (sorry for the GRAPHIC description :P )
2 - Characters - The core of any game that is in this genre is it's characters.  Are they memorable?  Are there any single characters that just make you want to say, "Nah, that's for n00b's", or "I've seen enough of him\her"?  With Prodigy Tactics, the characters are as memorable as they are diverse.  Each has a background that is as well writen as any RPG character could be.  They each have a story, a motivation, and each is wildly different from the other.  I don't want to spoil any surprises, but lets just say that if you locked Dr. Seuss, Jim Henson, and a vial of LSD in a room you STILL wouldn't be able to come up with better and more imaginative characters then they have.  Which leads nicely to...
3 - Variety - Not a single character is like another.  They do have "fucntions" which may be similar (IE - Gaurdians, Attackers, Supporters), but the way they act, look, and sound are so unique from one another that it is almost like the best brains in the business came up with a character each and then accidentally discovered eachothers e-mail addresses and said "Hey - lets stick these dudes in a game!".  Yup.  They ARE that different!
4 - Uniqueness And Depth - The gameplay will be familiar enough to feel comfortable playing for the first time, but different enough so that you don't say, "Oh - another one of these!".  There are many aspects to this game which bring a fresh breeze to a stale genre of "Ye olden chess like game that hath fancy moves".  The gameplay is simple enough for a child to learn, but deep enough for Stephen Hawkins (and if you are him, I formally challange you to a game.  The winner gets a lifetime supply of Playboys - I heard you have enough Penthouses already (if you don't get this joke, just do a little biography on him at another bet he made)) to... errr... Hawk at.  Sorry Mr. Hawkins, but it's not like I choose your name.  In all fairness, you didn't either, but still.  Back to the point.  The theory is a simple one - the board is made of 24 circles, 12 per player, 3 rows deep, 4 circles on each row.  You put characters down on circles, and then they attack other characters.  When you kill a character, it counts as a point.  The first person to get to 3 points wins.  Simple?  Not quite.  Throw in things like turning the playing circles from nuetral to harmony or dissonence that altar gameplay, call in support in the form of backup characters, bond team-mates together for attack or defense, PLUS characters have more then just one move available to them, and much, much more!  Yes, this game is unique enough to attract beginners, but deep enough to make Bobby Fischer say that "Prodigy Tactics is ALIVE!" and challange Boris Spassky to a game of Prodigy without disagreeing on rules AND have the pressure of a couple thousand nuclear warheads without a sweat (I hope I am throwing in enough weird references for you all).  It's THAT good.
5 - Sound - The sound is as memorable as - well - all of the above.  It matches the games other incredible qualities perfectly.  You know how memorable Darth Vadar's voice, sound, and lightsaber were the first time you heard them?  Those are the sound effects.  The music?  When it's used, it's as apropos as the "Jaws" theme is when you see a shark, or "Ode To Joy" when you get a job promotion.  It isn't over or underdone - it is like that bear's porridge that's juuuust right.  But don't worry, you won't get eaten if you play this game.  *DISCLAIMER* YOU MAY GET EATEN IF YOU PLAY THIS GAME
6 - Interface - This game is not only on PC but it is coming to Nintendo Switch - and perhaps other platforms as well.  I just mention that because while the mouse functions perfectly well, the game just BEGS for a touchscreen interface.  If you have a touchscreen monitor, you are in violation of a new federal law if you do not buy this game.  Everything just WORKS, it's intuitive, and user friendly like the original I-Pod was when you touched it for the first time.  It is THAT good with a touchscreen!
7 - WHY ARE YOU STILL READING THIS?! - If you have read this far, you are obviously interested, so why not download the demo and find out for yourself what you've been missing out on?  And then buy a copy of the game!  Heck, go crazy and buy 3 copies!  Buy them for your friends.  Or buy them for strangers and then suddenly you will HAVE friends!

So, you're wondering about Blender ehh?
So I first started using Blender about 10 years ago and crikey has it come a long way since. Now you can do smoke/fire, sculpting, model and do most other things a lot easier than before, get great renders from cycles (which is improving all the time), do VFX if you wanted, use some freakin awesome new plugins (retopoflow and molecular script ftw), etc. Okay I'm waffling on but it's a great 3D package, I mean the fact that it's free too is excellent because it's not often you get free software that matches up to the paid for software, although each has its own particular strengths over the rest (blender is known for great modeling, UV unwrapping and animation tools). Blender is used by so many more professionals now from a few years ago, it's being taken a lot more seriously and is becoming better and better with each release. One of the other nice things about blender too is that if you're poor and penniless, you can still do pretty much anything of the norm 3D wise in blender. I've found that this is handy because I've had projects where I say, needed to sculpt on a piece of my mesh, so instead of exporting the mesh, using other software, importing it back, I instead just switched to sculpting mode, did what I needed to do and was done. And once you get to the level where you've learned the interface nicely and the hotkeys relevant to you, you can do what you like (e.g game assets, 3D printing, animation, etc) and you've got something very good in its own ways.
I should talk about some of blenders shortcomings now... So first off if you are new to it, be wary of using Crtl+Z in object mode, you can lost a lot of modeling work doing that! Also get familiar with layers, the hide keys and the blender stack exchange, this will save you a few headaches late). Note that I only speak from my perspective of someone who doesn't do animation (excluding dynamics), VFX, video editing, scripting or anything with blenders own game engine.
As far as blenders feature set weaknesses go... I'm not big on its baking tools (I prefer xNormal) although there is a good plugin you can use for that anyway (Meltdown). The game engine is not terribly relevant anymore since you now have all the more developed game engines free to use now (Unity, which works superbly with blender I might add, Unreal, Source 2 soon, etc). Blender is pretty nice for dynamics (nice smoke/fire tools in my experience, and you can export fluid animations too. Plus, hair/fur!) but when it comes to making objects that break I've found it's really not very good at it... (Update: Looks like someone is working on that anyway
). The learning curve is steep, blender can be confusing at times. And whilst Blender does have great sculpting tools it doesn't match up to zbrush and mudbox (but it's slowly getting there!).
All in all though, not terribly bad shortcomings (unless you do forget to save or press Crtl+Z in object mode!) :)
I've not talked about a heck of a lot that Blender can do and is good for, I could go on for ages but it'd be better if you are intereted to just go to
and read up on it. Otherwise this is a very worthwhile package, it's got a steep learning curve but it's worth it and you're never far from help if you need it. Blender has been a pleasure to use (despite the odd expected headaches XD) and I love using it, I'm glad I took an interest those 10 years ago and got the skills I have. So get Blending!

Ah NEO Scavenger, I've seen you grow from a tiny early access game to now a fully fledged game.
I'm a sucker for these kinda games, turn-based and almost entierly text based. I wish I could re-live my first expierence with this game, it started with me waking up in the Cryochamber pouring over every line of text. I read that an entity was coming for me and I had to think fast, so first thing I did was jump out of the window, wouldn't anyone want to get away as fast as possible? Well that wasn't exactly a great idea, as I jumped out in my reckless haste I had mangled myself up real bad on the broken glass, not good. Not only am I now bleed profusely from everywhere, I have a hospital gown on, a weird necklace, a hospital band saying "Philip Kindred," and a hulking werewolf following me. I took my first steps out into the world, only to die later that night from hypothermia and blood loss.
NEO-Scavenger puts you in a post-apocalpytic Michigan with a slew of crazy characters and horrifiyng monsters. It's brutal and unforgiving when you start out, and your first (and many) deaths will come from hypothermia. The scavenging and loot system for this game is completly random but not unfair and makes finding that one piece of equipment feel so good. Finding a gun is a hell of a lot harder then finding a jacket or some food. You're more likely to find clothing in an apartment than a storage shed. It's satisfying seeing your character grow and aquire new gear and become a true badass of the Michigan area, that is until a random thug comes up to you hits you in the head once with a rock and kills you instantly. Then he's the new badass Michigan. Did I mention this game is hard? Well at least the first few hours are. This game kicks your♥♥♥♥♥when you first start out, once you get your berrings and figure out what works best (Strong+Melee+Trapping+Broad Spear = OP) then the game really does get a lot easier and a lot of the challenge goes away. As other review's have stated once you hit end-game and beat it you really have seen and done everything there is to see and do. "Quests" are not random, story events are not random, and the ending is not random. What happens happens, but, getting there is where all the fun is at. Looting everything you can while staving off hunger, thirst, and keeping your own wellbeing while fending off Bad Motha's, Blue Frog's, and Dogmen are what truely make this game entertaining. I've seen this game grow up and it is still as fun when I first started playing it. Open the Wiki and just go at it, every death is a learning expierence!
If you are looking for a unique game that kicks your♥♥♥♥♥in the beginning and makes you feel like a badass later, with a killer story and fun gameplay then look no further than NEO-Scavenger!

I just have to say that on an indie dev working on a shoestring budget, Blender has been an absolute lifesaver for me. I can actually learn 3D modeling without having to pay thousands of euros for a modeling software. I use Sculptris for sculpting game models and Blender to retopo, rig and animate. Once you learn how to use it, it's quite quick and powerful.
Blender is actively developed and new and exciting features come with every new version. Currently, I'm eagerly awaiting for the new viewport and maybe the possibility of writing my own shaders.
You can also extend Blender as much as you want. Everything is open source. If you need a new feature, just download the code and start hacking. I've made several Python addons for my own needs. While there are limitations on that API, it's still ridiculously powerful.
There are some quirks. Like having separate workflows for different rendering engines. I wish they just somehow took all the good parts of Blender Internal and put them on Cycles. Having to work with Blender Internal just to get GLSL viewport is a little silly.
The software would be easily worth 200 euros for me. But it's free, and I'm very happy with that.

An enjoyable platformer,  many of the negative reviews adress wierd controls and lack of controller support.  Both of these issues appear to have been fixed as you can now change the bindings on all controls and I was able to play with a wired 360 controller.
-Music is fitting and enjoyable, goes very well with the game.
-Art looks nice and there is a good deal of variety from world to world
-Gameplay offers a good deal of challenge that gets more difficult as the game progresses, especially with the boss fights.
-Unlimited continues, when you get a game over on a boss, you don't have to go back to the begging of the world, you start back at the beginning of the fight
-Enemies and hazards vary enough to not become boring, the enemies have different attacks and mechanics, not just different appearances.  The hazards have set mechanics or timed patterns that make them easier to avoid once you learn them.
-Health system, this contributes a good deal to the difficulty of the game.  The coins you collect give you lives back when you get 100, but there is no way to get health back during a level other than dying.  Your health is replenished once you beat the level though.
-English translations, the game was localized from Polish and many of the translations are very (possibly intentionally) goofy.  The story itself is pretty light so this is very likely, but it does take you out of the game a bit, certainly makes you laugh.
Overall I would reccomend the game,  It will only take 4-5 hours to beat the game depending on how proficient you are at platformers, but there are hidden collectibles and achievements that add a bit of replayability if you're into that.
At 10$, it is a very good difficult platformer for people that enjoy genre.  On sale, the game is certainly worth picking up for someone who has a passing interest in a short, fun game.

So happy to finally be able to say I've finished this game. I played on the hardest survival setting and It was a long 60 hours of enjoyment mixed with way too much, unnecessary frustration. This could have been an amazing game but it's still got that UBISOFT janky-ness that rears it's head every 30 mins or so. To keep it brief:
+ The graphics and sound are impressive. A very enjoyable world to experience.
+ The combat is great due to the new restrictions. Using a bow and arrow and perfecting your aim is really rewarding.
+ Great value - Plenty to do and a captivating world to get lost in.
- The AI is very good one minute then laughable the next. Buddy AI is just a joke. Enjoy getting trapped in an area due to your buddy blocking the entrance? Plenty of that!! Enemies can be impossible to it as they Michael Jackson all over the place. Good luck perfecting those long distance arrows!!
- Day night cycle is like someone switching a switch - One minute it's dark and then...boom, morning!!
- Navigating the terrain is just unbelievably tricky at times. It needed Dying Light's movement and nearly got there...just too many slopes to slip down when you should be able to climb.
If you love Far Cry due to nostalgia then this is more of the same with enough changes to make it feel worth while. Just expect the usual UBISOFT weirdness to show up now and again...well worth picking up in a sale! :)

Let me start off by saying: I bought it for 8€ and if you paid more, I'm sorry :P
This is a Telltale game. Telltale is famous for letting you decide the course of the game. But if the game shows you, even throws it in your face, that you can't change anything, it's very frustrating.
I won't put spoilers in here, but let's just say that it's more like watching a movie than playing a Telltale game, which is already an interactive movie.
To give an example of how much influence you have on the games outcome:
If you make a good decision, the game goes on and you get the ending.
If you make a bad decision, some character scolds you and you get the same ending.
It's very sad that something like this was done with the concept of a GoT Telltale game. GoT has so many opportunities for awesome intrigue and choices that have effects that you couldn't have imagined in the moment. This is still true, but the choice doesn't matter, so basically you get three choices that all have the same unpredictable outcome, which feels wrong. I understand Telltale isn't that big of a company and their bugget isn't very big, but it's just so disappointing...
I suggest this game for people who have never seen a video of it, had any spoilers or any other contact with the game. Because if you don't have that, you won't notice the pointlessness on you first playthrough. Also, even then, I wouldn't pay more than 10€, because you don't get a lot of playtime out of it (I got 15 hours, but that includes going out of the house with the game still running paused a bunch of times)

C'est alors que Descartes reprendrait la parole et dirait à ce rustique, à ce buté : je veux bien que vous ne soyez pas fou, puisque vous ne vous y résolvez pas ; mais souvenez-vous cependant que toutes les nuits vous rêvez et que vos songes quotidiens ne sont pas moins fous que cette folie que vous refusez. Et la réticence naïve de l'objecteur qui ne peut pas douter de son corps parce qu'il ne veut pas être fou serait vaincue par l'exemple du rêve, tellement «plus naturel», «plus commun», «plus universel».
Séduisante hypothèse cette de Derrida, qu'a dit que «Grim Dawn c'est il meilleur Diablolike de tous les tempes». Elle résout au plus juste son problème : montrer que le philosophe va droit à la mise en question de «la totalité de l'étantité», que c'est là justement la forme et la marque philosophique de sa démarche ; s'il vient à s'arrêter un instant à une «étantité» aussi singulière que la folie, ce ne peut être que si un naïf le tire par la manche et l'interroge ; de lui-même, il ne se fût point attardé à ces histoires de rois nus et de cruches. Ainsi le rejet de la folie, l'exclamation abrupte «mais quoi, ce sont des fous» se trouvent eux-mêmes rejetés par Derrida et trois fois enfermés à l'extérieur du discours philosophique : puisque c'est un autre sujet qui parle (non pas le philosophe des Méditations, mais cet objecteur qui fait entendre sa voix mal dégrossie) ; puisqu'il parle d'un lieu qui est celui de la naïveté non philosophique ; puisqu'enfin le philosophe, reprenant la parole et citant l'exemple plus «fort» et plus «probant» du rêve désarme l'objection et fait accepter bien pire que la folie à celui-là même qui la refuse.
Mais on peut voir maintenant de quel prix Derrida a payé son habile hypothèse. Omission d'un certain nombre d'éléments littéraux (qui apparaissent dès qu'on prend soin de comparer le texte latin à la traduction française) ; élision des différences textuelles (tout le jeu des oppositions sémantiques et grammaticales entre le paragraphe du rêve et celui de la folie) ; effacement enfin et surtout de la détermination discursive essentielle (double trame de l'exercice et de la démonstration). Curieusement, Derrida en imaginant derrière l'écriture de Descartes cette autre voix, objectante et naïve, a soufflé toutes les différences du texte ; ou plutôt, en effaçant toutes ces différences, en rapprochant au plus près l'épreuve de la folie et l'épreuve du rêve, en faisant de l'une le premier brouillon, pâle et manqué, de l'autre, en résorbant l'insuffisance de la première dans l'universalité du second, Derrida poursuivait l'exclusion cartésienne. Le sujet méditant devait pour Descartes exclure la folie en se qualifiant comme non fou. Or cette exclusion à son tour est trop dangereuse sans doute pour Derrida : non plus à cause de la disqualification dont elle risque de frapper le sujet philosophant, mais par la qualification dont elle marquerait le discours philosophique ; elle le déterminerait en effet comme «autre» que le discours fou ; elle établirait entre eux un rapport d'extériorité ; elle ferait passer le discours philosophique de l' «autre côté», dans la pure présomption de n'être pas fou. Partage, extériorité, détermination dont il faut bien sauver le discours du philosophe s'il doit être «projet d'excéder toute totalité finie et déterminée». Il faut donc exclure, parce que déterminante, cette exclusion cartésienne. Et pour ce faire, Derrida, on le voit, est obligé de procéder à trois opérations : affirmer, contre toute l'économie visible du texte, que la puissance du doute propre à la folie est incluse, a fortiori, dans le rêve ; imaginer (pour rendre compte qu'il soit question malgré tout de la folie) que c'est un autre qui exclut la folie, pour son propre compte et selon la diagonale d'une objection ; enfin ôter à cette exclusion tout statut philosophique en dénonçant sa rusticité naïve. Renverser l'exclusion cartésienne en inclusion ; exclure l'excluant en donnant à son discours statut d'objection ; exclure l'exclusion en la rejetant dans la naïveté préphilosophique : il n'en a pas fallu moins à Derrida pour venir à bout du texte cartésien et pour réduire à rien la question de la folie. On peut en constater le résultat : l'élision des différences du texte et l'invention compensatrice d'une différence de voix reconduisent l'exclusion cartésienne à un second niveau ; il devient enfin exclu que le discours philosophique exclue la folie.

Being the first game I ever bought on Steam all those years ago, I feel like I should recommend this game. I already had written two seperate reviews in favor of it. So why do I feel like flipping that  big thumb upside down? Well, I've realized that this just isn't a good game. My issues with it just pile up when you actually look at it objectively. (Skip to the list now if you just want a brief overview without too much reading.)
For starters, the RNG is ridiculous sometimes. I've had some playthroughs were I magically managed to kill one of the most powerful things in the game with nothing more than a hoodie and a stick. Other times, I take about three steps away from the start and a thing called a Mega Wraith comes by and slaughters me. Both of these things have happened at least twice.
OK, lets say that RNGeezus is on your side and you managed to become an absolute tank. Now what? To be honest, I'm still not sure. I've got to the lengths of cheating the game and there's nothing else to it. You can go and do the story for a bit. A really small bit. I mean,
No really, I've tried every dialogue choice and item combination allowed in the first "encounter" of the story. They all end with you being given a task -- a fetch-quest to get the "Vase of McGuffin" or something equally ridiculous -- that will either kill you if you're not a tank and bore you to tears if you can survive. Oh, did I forget to mention that it never tells you were the dang thing even is?! This is where my playthroughs tend to end.
Last thing before I let the bulletpoints take over. Did I forget to mention this is as polished as a rusty machete? It's running in godforsaken,
Adobe Flash for crying out loud! It also barely understands what a 1080p screen even is. I never noticed this for a long time but I used to play this exclusively on my laptop from... huh... it was from 2005 as well.
- More in-depth than any other post-apocalyptic survival games I have ever played.
- Kinda funny predicaments like getting your head LITTERALLY CRUSHED by something called a "Mega Wraith"
- Story is not necessary. Really, you can just jump in, not read anything and still have a good time. Great for when you don't have a lot of time to spend
- Addicting. Beacuse you die so much, you constantly have that Flappy-Bird-ish, "Just one more turn" mentality (see CONS)
- More expensive than I would like. Maybe thats just me but it just doesn't feel all that polished. In fact, it's still running in Adobe Flash!
- Really hard. Since it's randomly generated, it takes a whole lot of luck to not die before you can even have a fighting chance.
- Too much cussing in the main story. This might be my personal taste but some of the cursing in the game feels forced and unnecessary.
- Ultimately pathetic story. If you do choose to play the main story, you'll eventually feel either A) disappointed with how it's handled or B) be completely and hopelessly lost. After the first meaningful encounter with the story, they pretty much give you the boot out of anything you might find helpful and pretty much tell you to do a fetch quest. A quest, mind you, that never once tells you how to complete it.
I'm disappointed to have to turn my back on this game but I feel like it's just not good enough to recommend. Play the demo and leave it there. You've already played all the fun bits.

Yup, There are many other available software programs similiar to blender, here are a few:
- 3DSmax 2018 (USD) monthly: 185$ // yearly: 1470$ // 3 years: 4410$
However, 3dsmax is concidered as a very solid software toolkit, it has more options than blender and you can rely on Autodesk for good support. Blender will also offer you support but it's a foundation and not a company.
-MODO (Indie) 10: This software goes for 279,99$ on Steam (or their website). Without doubt it's better for hard surface than vanilla blender, modo offers tons of breat boolean options. And ofcourse you're able to do other things with it like uv unwrapping, but personally i prefer blender for that.

I wouldn't get it straight away but if you wanna go into a even more professional direction you can concider to pick this up.

+ Regulair updates, but randomly.

I started to learn modelling using Maya. I'm not gonna say that Blender is better- feature wise, it's still behind. But if you're considering learning 3d, Blender is a good way to get into it without breaking the bank. A polygon is a polygon, whatever software you use to build it. Proper topology, UV layout - you're going to be using  the same concepts... In terms of modelling, Blender is pretty good and pretty fast (provided you learn the hotkeys very much the same as how you use Mayas hidden marking menus)
Blender's renderer is pretty good too. Cycles can get you amazing results pretty quickly. since it's node based, it's pretty easy to build up complex and realistic materials. It also has real time viewport rendering so you can see what your changes does on the fly. It also supports GPU rendering-- which is damn fast. (as of right now, blender officially supports NVIDIA CUDA cards... though AMD has submitted a patch for openCL and you can get the experimental build at

dont be worried about the Blender's limitations (viewport, particles, multires sculpting) if you're just starting out, it's unlikely you're going to reach the limits of blenders capabilities. Artists have been putting out some impressive works out there using blender.
Blender is always changing and evolving. they release a couple of official builds each year. each one improving on what's there. what's great is that you can be a part of it as well. You see a lack in blender and you've got coding skills, you can contribute to the code.
Blender has a wealth of tutorials out there for you to learn from, from cgcookie to blenderguru... the resources are pretty widely available. The community is pretty helpful if you get really stuck..
overall I'd rate blender 9/10 would blend again.

I never intended to buy this, thinking I'd hate it. Instead I received it as a gift and found I really liked it. Graphically it's wonderful and you can travel about freely into snowy mountains, down lush valleys and in lakes and rivers. It's basically a survival game in pre-history where you kill and skin animals and fight off people of enemy tribes. I can't say I'm keen on slaying animals but accepted it as an essential aspect of play. There are numerous missions, although some very samey, and as you develop your tribal population you gain experience with basic weapons and your skills improve via an allocated points system.
There is a lot of collecting and crafting involved, which gives you something to do other than fighting enemy neanderthals and fighting off all the animals that are intent on attacking you at every opportunity. This is a bit overdone I think. A useful deterrent is brandishing a flaming club or spear, especially at night.
The best part is (a bit like FC3 and FC4) where you infiltrate and conquer enemy camps. Usually this requires subtlety rather than charging in recklessly. However, I found a flaw. If you go to an elevated position overlooking the camp you can rain down flaming arrows almost with impunity. A few enemy dunderheards
attempt to reach you but they're easily picked off! And the arrows fired at you are easily dodged.
Without any spoilers, the main downer for me is when you get to fight prominent enemy characters. It harks back to old computer games of the 1990s where you had to 'kill' the enemy countless times to succeed. I think this is a cop out these days because with a bit of creativity you can make a task difficult wiithout resorting to this old nonsense!
For instance, let's say you had to fight someone across a log over a deep ravine. You'd have to skilfully maintain balance while weilding a weapon and evading enemy blows. I reckon this would be far more entertaining than running about like a lunatic on steroids with an axe trying to dispatch the enemy countless times before he drops.
Aside from my one gripe the game is a worthwhile purchase for the open world experience.

As of writing this I had just completed the main story and quite a lot of content so all that's left for me is some of the special beast missions and other side quests. To put it simply, this is my favorite entry of the recent Far Cry games. I haven't played 1 or 2 but I'm sure many people can say the same. The story is simple, your tribe is at the brink of total annihilation and you have to lead them to become the top of the food chain while also battling two other warring tribes. I was never lost during the main story, except for that one time I stopped playing for a few months (I'm sure some of you guys switch between games constantly and forget to finish them) but I was quickly able to catch up.
Combat was one thing I was concerned about seeing as how it was mostly melee combat and Far Cry was know for the gunplay, but the combat is well done. Hearing the crunch of a dude's skull as I clobber him with my club is always satisfying. Bows were my go-to before I became comfortable with the other weapons and I found it easy to score headshots in this game, more so than FC3 & FC4. I'm guessing they made the hitboxes a bit bigger? I don't know, but it's definitely easier to score headshots. The whole beast master thing is pretty neat, my only complaint being that animal AI not being responsive. And not the "realistic animal behavior" type of unresponsive, just plain ol' annoying AI beahavior. But nothing that will make you do anything more than shake your mouse back and forth out of annoyance; a flaw for sure, but a forgivable one.
However, the most fan to be had is when you are able to tame a sabertooth tiger and unlock the perk that lets you ride it around as a mount. HOLY♥♥♥♥♥♥ easily the most fun mechanic to be put into any of these Far Cry games. The tiger controls the same way as Takkar does on foot, but he runs BLAZING fast and leaps forward like BAM. You can swing your club, throw your spear, use your bow and all that fun combat stuff. My favorite part though is the fact that you can loot, gather, and skin stuff without having to dismount, you can basically freeroam while never getting off the tiger(within reason of course, there are some terrains where you have to hop off)! Of course, your animals also have health meters so you will have to heal them if need be. If they die, you can revive them no problemo. Havent't used the owl much, but it's a useful mechanic from what I've gathered.
Not much to say on performance, I ran it beautifully with my Strix 1070 and Skylake i5 on 1440p at 70+fps. If you can run Far Cry 4, you can run Primal. All in all, I enjoyed the hell out of this game and I think it tops the others. The caveman thing definitely works for the series. It is a breath of fresh air from the modern day setting of the main installments and I would give it an 8/10. I am satisfied with my purchase.

I don't often write reviews for games, but this one actually deserves one.
The premise of the game is incredibly unique, and the developers did an amazing job at making it feel like you're truly learning and casting spells derived from a language of power. The backdrops are beautiful, and as I go further through the game I find the story itself intriguing. It's gameplay is simple, but challenging, though not enough to make you frustrated.
The story and Temple itself are the real good points though. It has a very Lovecraftian feel to it, but not in the most well known cosmic horror stories, but more from his Dream cycle. I find that extremely poetic, and to see that sort of story in a game is refreshing. Just the general premise makes me hunger for more, not just the same sort of game or the same temple, but just more of the -world- itself.
I would say the game isn't for everyone, but it's definitely an experience. I would *LOVE* to see this in VR, but from the forums it appears like it's unlikely. I think that would bring an entirely new level of immersion to an already immersive game.

I've seen some complaints that this game is "too similar" to the other Far Cry titles, and is not innovative, etc. As I have not played the other FC titles, I can't speak to that. I can, however, speak to the quality of this game, and it is extremely impressive. The environment is both highly vaired and immersive, from frozen wastes to the north, coniferous forests throughout and riverlands which permeate through the lower areas, one truly gets the sense of a primeval world.
Adaptive animal behavior makes hunting an actual challenge, as opposed to many open world games which use the "Shoot, Skin, Repeat" cycle. Combat is surprisingly fluid and seamless, with different weapons being required for different enemy types. The stealth system isn't ideal, as one can be detected fairly easily, and summarily rushed by every enemy in the area who all somehow know your exact location. However, that difficulty makes a successful stealth raid all the more satisfying.
The campaign isn't overly complex, which is fine with me. (How much political intrigue does one REALLY expect in a Neolithic culture?) One weak point which I found extraneous is the use of a scouting system a-la Assassin's Creed's Eagle Vision. However, this is mitigated by Survivor mode, which I cannot praise highly enough. Survivor mode can be selected at the start of a new game, and is where this game truly shines. It's almost as if this was how the game was originally built, then was remanded to an optional method to make the game easier. Survivor mode removes much of the scouting system's unrealistic features, removes several tiers of skill and equipment upgrades which drastically change the overall difficulty of the game, and adds a new level of difficulty to the survival aspect of the game, modifying the stamina supply to reflect fatigue and hunger which accumulate over time. I stop just short of recommending that first time players engage in survivor mode, as the difficulty can dissuade a player after awhile. But it truly enhances the experience of the game.
In summation, I must again hearken back to the overall beauty of the world which was created here. It's perfectly satisfying to go about harvesting and hunting in this visually stunning representation of early Man's stomping grounds.
PS- If anyone is brave enough to try Survivor mode on the highest level of difficulty with permadeath on, good luck.

Sid Meier's Civilazation V is a game which provides many things in its gameplay and overall experience however, much like previous installments in the series this game will pull you in as though Scorpion himself had some form on involvement. This could largley be due to the fact that while keeping to the general gameplay flow of the previos civ's it amazingly manages to refine and polish it for a much sleeker and smoother gameplay experience which will have you consistently saying to your self just 5 more minutes for this turn to which will turn into several paths that the player is provided with. Do you wish to be a warmongering leader destroying and elimating all other forms of existance within your path or do you want to culterally advanced becoming the peace keeper of the world who dabbles in sea trade or culter advancements for bigger hold boosts etc. Or just straight rush for science advancements making you the most technologically advanced civilasation within the game. (However, no matter what you do Ghandi will be centuries ahead and WILL nuke you if you get on his bad side) In additon to these gamplay paths are several dozen civilasation leaders of whom are all unique in their own way with bonus and advantages in certain environments or situations such as elite units or gold boosts. However, in addition to this, the gamplay while being extremely simplistic does provide some form of enjoyment as unit battles are tense to watch when fighting a more advanced civ and on higher difficulties will result in a loss if you fail to become advanced. Despite all these however, the games UI does become extremely annoying and an eye sore in many situations often leaving much to be desired, in addition, larger game varients on much larger maps can be a pain and will often result in the player getting bored due to the amount of time it takes to wait for a turn to end. Moreover, some of the dlc does change certain hings within the culture tree that make the game much more irritating however, it is easily worked around after an hour or two.
To conclude if you much enjoy the previous installments of civ you will for the most part very much enjoy Civ V however, without much motivation playing becomes a chore and a bore to finish. If you wish to wait id recommend getting the Collection with all the dlc as many annoyances in the game are fixed but also provide at least 30 more civs play as this extending the overall game experience and replayabilty to an extent most games in the series fail to do.

First Try on Top Hat
The Video can be found here:
First off, the options menu is relatively simplistic. You have 3 seperate sliders for audio options. Apart from that you can adjust the screen size(which I would not consider resolution options). Last, but by no means least, you can rebind the controls for keyboard and controller.
Going into the game, the first thing I've noticed is that the dialogue is well translated and the jokes came across fairly well. The music is also quite good, the only minor complaint I have is that the looping of the music is a bit clunky.
Gameplaywise I have to say that the gunplay(if can call it that way) and the platforming feel nice.
The enemy variety and enemy design is simplistic, but it does the job. The bosses so far feel relatively underwhelming(the mechanic of the first one is easy to dodge, the second one is quite tedious to fight), but it might change later on.
One thing I'd like to add before coming to the conclusion is that one of the "selling ponits" of the game is "Challenging. Really". So far I have to say, the game is not that challenging. It is more the case that the game is unforgivable in terms of mistakes. Since there are no savegame slots, you will only have one savegame. Apart from your progress your current lifecount is saved as well, which can end in a mess when you are only on one life bevore hitting a checkpoint. I can imagine that it is getting frustrating when you hit harder levels(or even bossfights) with only one life left.
The question I suppose is: Is the game difficult, because it's genuinely difficult, or is it because of design decisions in terms of savepoints, etc? And in the case of top hat, I say, it is "difficult" for the wrong reasons.
With that out of the way we come to the tl:dr: Is the game worth it?
It is not a bad game that is for sure, but as I've stated above, I went about 1/3 through the game within 30 minutes, so you can say that your average playthrough will take you somewhat around 2 hours. And apart from Achievments and a higher difficulty levels there is not much replayability available.
With that said, I'd say it's a definite buy at a sale, but if you are desperate for a nice action plattformer, you might consider buying this game even on full price.

I've seen some complaints that this game is "too similar" to the other Far Cry titles, and is not innovative, etc. As I have not played the other FC titles, I can't speak to that. I can, however, speak to the quality of this game, and it is extremely impressive. The environment is both highly vaired and immersive, from frozen wastes to the north, coniferous forests throughout and riverlands which permeate through the lower areas, one truly gets the sense of a primeval world.
Adaptive animal behavior makes hunting an actual challenge, as opposed to many open world games which use the "Shoot, Skin, Repeat" cycle. Combat is surprisingly fluid and seamless, with different weapons being required for different enemy types. The stealth system isn't ideal, as one can be detected fairly easily, and summarily rushed by every enemy in the area who all somehow know your exact location. However, that difficulty makes a successful stealth raid all the more satisfying.
The campaign isn't overly complex, which is fine with me. (How much political intrigue does one REALLY expect in a Neolithic culture?) One weak point which I found extraneous is the use of a scouting system a-la Assassin's Creed's Eagle Vision. However, this is mitigated by Survivor mode, which I cannot praise highly enough. Survivor mode can be selected at the start of a new game, and is where this game truly shines. It's almost as if this was how the game was originally built, then was remanded to an optional method to make the game easier. Survivor mode removes much of the scouting system's unrealistic features, removes several tiers of skill and equipment upgrades which drastically change the overall difficulty of the game, and adds a new level of difficulty to the survival aspect of the game, modifying the stamina supply to reflect fatigue and hunger which accumulate over time. I stop just short of recommending that first time players engage in survivor mode, as the difficulty can dissuade a player after awhile. But it truly enhances the experience of the game.
In summation, I must again hearken back to the overall beauty of the world which was created here. It's perfectly satisfying to go about harvesting and hunting in this visually stunning representation of early Man's stomping grounds.
PS- If anyone is brave enough to try Survivor mode on the highest level of difficulty with permadeath on, good luck.

If a game gets the important things right then I can forgive alot in terms of design and execution, and In Verbis Virtus leaves me overflowing with magnanimity toward it in spite of its obvious (and not so obvious) flaws. The atmosphere and tone of the game had me forgetting that I was wandering through an--at times--poorly designed maze because the sights that maze had to show me expertly sold the premise of the game: that this was a place where pilgrims underwent a rite of passage. Confusion, disorientation, exhaustion. . . these things are par for the course when it comes to religious experiences, and I can accept that as justification for all the backtracking I've done thus far. The resemblance of the temple's facade to the famous treasury building of the city of Petra was another wonderful touch, and the piecemeal revealing of our not-so-silent protagonist's backstory had me willing to suspend my disbelief from quite a height, even though I ocassionally had to check the internet for hints.
If you're thinking about buying this game for its unique selling point I can only say that if In Verbis Virtus has managed to pique your interest you will find your curiosity aptly satisfied time and again. Being able to directly communicate with the game world adds a unique layer of immersion to the story, and one which is not only easy to get to grips with, but well paced and thought out. Sure, being able to call down fire on your enemies is one thing, but being able to *literally* do it is another thing entirely. Yes it's a gimmick, but as a gimmick it is well executed and it showcases what more games can, should, and will be making use of in the future. One thing I would recommend is taking the time to generate a voice profile before you start playing. I haven't had an issue being understood, but I didn't bother with the defaults either.
All in all: In Verbis Virtus is one of those games that I can see myself playing over and over again simply because it really puts me right in the middle of the action. It is not perfect by any means, but what it doesn't do perfectly it still manages competently, and what it does differently it does exceptionally well.

Before I review the game I have to say, I was a huge fan of the Walking Dead and The Wolf Among Us made by Telltale Games. Because I had experience with Telltale I knew to expect more of an interactive story rather than a game and I was fine with that. Given I enjoy the Game of Thrones TV series a lot. And it is exactly what I expected, so I am not disappointed by the lack of gameplay.
I have to say though, gameplay is really put to a minimum in this series. Other than say The Walking Dead series the only thing you are doing here is watch cutscenes and pick dialogue choices. I won't count the numerous quick time events as gameplay, they are more a nuisance than interesting gameplay and there are no choices to make other than press the right button or you die (or someone else will save you anyway). While you could walk around the set pieces in The Walking Dead, exploration in Game of Thrones is set to bare minimum. There is nothing you can really see or learn about the game world other than following the main plot.
While this sounds negative, I had fun with this story. It captures the feel of the TV series pretty well and left me shocked at points. You get the feeling of treading water, fighting against an inevitable doom for House Forrester and every choice you make seems to make everything worse. I give the game credit for that. I haven't played it a second time but I guess in the end only few of your choices really impacted the general outcome of the story. It is okay because characters refer to your choices anough and you get a feeling of consequences of your actions. But don't be mistaken. You'll get confronted with big decisions regarding the fate of the protagonists. You will be part of "the Game" while playing and it feels terrifying.
There were situations where I found all of the given choices to be lacking and I could only choose between two terrible answers. Some of the things the protagonists did were utterly dumb and out of my control, as well. But ultimately I got what I wanted: Another story set in the world of ice and fire and this time from the perspective of a lower house. And it was a good one. Fans of the TV series will probably enjoy it.
On the technical side the graphics feel a big outdated now. The Telltale Engine is old and you feel it at times. The voice-acting however is top-notch and manages to draw you in. Well done.
One last disclaimer: To understand the plot you need to have watched Seasons 1 to 4 of Game of Thrones. Many things and characters are not introduced properly or characterized enough that you understand what is going on without knowing the overarching plot. But if you intend to buy this game you probably have watched them anyways.
I recommend this game to fans of Game of Thrones who want to experience the events of Game of Thrones from another perspective. And you have to be okay with it being an interactive story. If this sounds like you: You are safe to buy.

Braid is a thought-provoking, yet short adventure that will puzzle you to the very end.
Pros:
- Beautiful visuals. The game feels like a watercolor painting.
- Pretty soundtrack that never feels stale.
- Unique puzzles based on time manipulation that are a fun challenge.
- Very intelligent, though purposefully ambiguous storyline.
- Fun secret areas with some of the game's most difficult puzzles.
Cons:
- Some puzzle elements lack explanation (which may be a plus for those who prefer it) and may add unnecessary confusion to a task.
-  One (optional) secret item in the game requires the player to wait nearly two hours for a simple task.
Braid is a challenging puzzler that requires out-of-the-box thinking and will keep you in a problem-solving state of mind from the title screen all the way to the inspiringly well thought out ending. This indie classic is something that all intelligent gamers should experience at least once.
