Imagine the scene at Ubisoft: “Far Cry 4 (FC4) made us oodles of cash, but how do we squeeze even more out of it?”
“I know. How about we re-package it, but this time set it in the Stone Age?”
“Hey, that’s a good idea, let’s do it!”
…which is, of course, exactly what they did, although with a few refinements thrown in for good measure. Far Cry Primal (FCP) is a thinly veiled version of FC4, but without the carefully crafted theme-rich story, the sharply drawn NPCs, the stunning vistas and the cultural immersion. However, you do get the option of playing the game in “permadeath” mode, which means that if you die, you have to start over from scratch (sic). Instead of FC4’s mercenaries for hire option, you now have the assistance of a tamed beast, if you want it. As such, FCP is a pale facsimile of its big brother FC4, but setting it in the Stone Age does steer it refreshingly away from being “more of the same”. However, this positive aspect of the game is more than offset by its whopping triple A price tag of GBP39.99, which means that I can only recommend this game if you can get it on sale.

♕ Gameplay
For being a story rich game that resembles an interactive movie, it lets you make choices ranging from mere insults to crucial decisions that could cause many deaths in the near future. Besides that, sometimes you're able to walk around and interact with surrounding people or objects and participate in quick time events. That's pretty much it for gameplay, thus don't expect any intense action or exploration.
♕ Story
Storywise it's a treat to Game of Thrones fans. Just 2 minutes in and it already feels like an actual episode of the show (excluding boobies, of course) thanks to wonderful voice acting (with original cast), immersive music and even the original intro in the beginning of each episode. The plot itself showcases the story of House Forrester, a briefly mentioned family in the books that strongly resembles Starks. These characters are well-written and interesting to play as, thereby you start to get emotionally attached to them. In terms of timeline, the first episode takes place right after the Red Wedding and 6th ends somewhere around the beginning of season 5, leaving an unfinished story that demands a continuation.
♕ Choices
Naturally, Telltale games are prominent for good storytelling, however, they're also well-known for creating illusions to make you feel that you're in control of the situation. In the end, the result is usually the same anyways with some minor changes. But still, it's always going to be satisfying to make your own decisions and, for example, make those who murdered your family or friends suffer.
♕ Graphics and optimization
This game looks like a watercolor painting and at first it was hard to get used to it. However, some shots probably couldn't look just as good in different graphic style. Moreover, the game runs just fine for the most part. My only complaint is the stuttering in one of the episodes that forced me to restart the game and some minor texture clipping issues throughout the whole playthrough.

Blender is user-friendly, it has high perfomance, modeling is really fast (though, some of this fastness comes from user-made addons), and, what's most important, - it's free.
But despite of everything above, Blender is underrated in industry for no real reason.
Or, I may guess, it's underrated because Blender's learning curve is merciful, which leads to a huge number of artists with undeveloped skills, who don't really want to become professionals. This kind of community creates a stereotype around an app itself as well.
Now, talking about the cons: simulations are quite bad for animation purposes, rigging is a little nightmare, in-built texturing is kind of painful as well, sculpting isn't based on voxels - it sometimes creates artifacts. Some are quality-of-life features are missing (e.g. rotating view in image editor or offsetting edge loop). But all these things are not critical, as you often can find user-made addons to compensate for them, or even make your own addon with a little bit of Python knowledge.
IMO, if you want to make masterpieces, it's better not to use Blender solely for everything. It's power is mostly in modeling and raytracing rendering engine. Combine this great-great power with, I dunno, PS, SP, Houdini, 3d Coat, etc.

I write 'yes' as recommendation, but with some reservations...
Notice: A microphone is required to play this game. Also, nerves of friggin’ steel.
Welcome to a land of magic. You are a wizard in search for a strong, ancient power for reasons I will not spoil; but to get to it, you will have to explore the temple, solve its puzzles, and battle unspeakable evil! That last part is more annoying than exciting, by the way.
In Verbis Virtus is, in essence, a fantasy RPG halfway between puzzle and action. Do not that you are required to own and use a microphone in order to play this game, for that is the whole point of it. As a wizard, you will be doing the spell casting via voice commands. That’s right, that means the game depends on a voice recognition system. That could only bode for fun and frustration, right?
But lets take it one thing at a time! Because in order to play the game, I had to be able to open the game, which in itself was a puzzle. I have no idea why, but the game alternated between crashing and freezing; probably something related to the resolution.
On the upside, In Verbis Virtus has a “safe” mode that opens it in a window on super low res. On the downside, that it has a safe mode because you may need to use it to get into the game is kind of a sad state. Once I was able to start it without crashing, the game ran fairly well only getting a bit choppy when entering a new area for the first time that day.
Visually, the game is quite stunning. even in low settings it didn’t look as bad as other ‘better’ games do, so there’s something to be said for that. The music was really nice too, and what voice acting there was (to show you how to pronounce the spells and in cutscenes) was… I wouldn’t say good, but it wasn’t bad either. The ambient sounds left something to be desired, however, though they weren’t too bad. The fire for some reason sounded fairly similar to the critters, and while I’m guessing the idea of keeping a semi-constant critter-like noise in the background was to keep you on edge, it became annoying as you couldn’t be sure when they were actually coming for you unless you’d been in the area before.
The game mechanics are pretty nice. Controls are basic: you jump with space, move with wasd, use mouse to aim and look around, shift to run - there is no ducking, however. In order to cast the spells, you interact via voice. Just aim your mouse at something, click and call out the spell name, and release your click. The spell will be cast. To stop the spell, right click. There are checkpoints that auto-save when passing a chapter, and save points spread out through the game, not nearly close enough to what I’d normally like, but not too far apart either. I just like to save every time I accomplish something, I’m obsessive like that.
Surprisingly, the voice recognition system works fairly well, and it has plenty of ways to be used. In the game options you can choose to cast the spells in English or the made-up language of the game, Maha’Ki, I went back to try them both (though my original playthrough was in Maha’Ki) and both worked pretty well. There was the occasional moment where a spell wasn’t cast, which included times such as slightly panicky, rushed casts for getting my♥♥♥♥♥kicked by enemies, the infuriated “I’ve said it three times already, would you please cast it??” rushed casting, and the “I clicked after I started casting” casting. But overall the spells cast 99% of the times, and when it didn’t, it was user fault.
Within the voice recognition options you also have the choice to record your own words for the spells. Now, I didn’t try this, but I can only imagine it can be great fun, and it’s a neat option to have.
As for the puzzles themselves, some are easy, some are hard, some are really not overly intuitive kind of hard, but for the most they were fairly good. Until, that was, you reached a timed puzzle. Really now, why would you do that to me? Is casting and running and casting while running not hard enough that you have to put the time limit so that we barely make it?
There was quite a bit of backtracking to be made from some of the puzzles to other parts of it, which would have been much less annoying without the critters roaming around, but I can overlook that since they had pretty scripted areas in which they appeared and paths they followed, so they were entirely predictable.
All in all, I was pretty content with the puzzles except for the timed ones, and then I was a slightly less happy camper until that was over.
I knew there’d be some fighting when I went into this game, I just didn’t expect them to be that annoying.
Now, your mileage might vary, but I feel like the greatest downfall of this game is precisely that: the fighting. Ahhh… what can I say about it other than I completely hated it, and it got me stuck in each encounter I had to the point where I didn’t get to finish the entirety of the story because of it. I got completely stuck, not even because I didn’t know how to beat the bad guys, but because they were so friggin’ annoying, and casting while trying not to die while trying to time something else was just not my thing. The very first fight you encounter is not just a fight, but a bit of a timing puzzle as well, and I seriously spent way too long trying to pass it, to the point where more than once I considered quitting right there. I didn’t. I quit further ahead, but I still quit.
Could this game have done well with fighting? Yes, if enemies had been defeatable via actual fighting spells, as opposed to trying to make them puzzly-difficult for the sake of making you use the several spells. Now, don’t get me wrong, while it could have been “fun” to fling an enemy across a room with my spell to stun him before putting a fire ball on his face (note: you get a fire spell, and then an explosion spell, not a fireball spell, making it even more annoying), you can’t really base the entire experience on the player’s timing skills with juggling 3 different spells in a moment of heated combat. Particularly if the enemy isn’t even a boss.
I feel like maybe if casting spells hadn’t been dependant of you clicking, calling out, then releasing the button to get it to actually cast, and it would have just recognized voice commands without the need of any clicking (and unclicking) in between, it would have made things much easier and I wouldn’t have been quite so frustrated with it all.  I can see where they wanted to go with the fights in terms of creativity, I just feel like it wasn’t well handled, or just… didn’t belong in this particular game.
As it was, most the fights I came across were just annoying and brought down the entire experience for me.
Bug wise I didn’t come across anything very obvious, except for the problems I had getting it to start and the occasional crash which happened mostly when I started a game, usually before I even loaded a save. But there were some crashes after as well. They really added to the frustration.
There’s little else to be said about In Verbis Virtus, I wish the puzzles would have been more open, giving you a chance of using various of your spells in order to complete it creatively, instead of “here is this rune or button, so this thing requires this particular spell while you stand in this particular spot.” (The fights suffered from this too; certain enemies required certain particular series of spells, except for the occasional one “easily” defeatable with fire, which still took two spells.)
You don’t need mazes and hours of backtracking to make good puzzles, you just need to give the user more creative ways to solve it in a single room.
I also wish there would have been a “no monsters” option, it would have made my experience much more enjoyable. I could’ve probably done with just the critters and a final boss at most.

Equal parts fun and "make you hate your friends" managerial nightmare.
Overcooked makes for an excellent couch coop where you and your friends try to manage a kitchen and push out as many correct orders as possible within a limited time frame.  While simple enough at the start, the levels quickly grow in complexity as the shapes of the kitchens become more obtuse and the hazards (like rats stealing your ingredients or counters sliding and changing the shape of the map) become increasingly difficult to circumvent.  Deft coordination and communication is necessary to manage the kitchen with 3 or 4 players in these situations, but such cooperation does not come easily.  It can take more than a few tries to get the best rating on every level, which if your friends aren't all on the same page, can make for a frustrating affair.  The light hearted visual style and storyline makes it hard to get mad at the game, but the same can't always be said for your friends...  Luckily, there's built in "swearing" and "punch" buttons in the game, so they've got you covered as far as venting those frustrations.
The game is at its best when you have 3 or 4 people, in my opinion, as much of the resource management puzzle solving is oversimplified with only 1 or 2 playing (although, that can be helpful if you're trying to get better ratings on hard levels).  That said, it can be difficult to gather so many people and controllers locally at times and the game does not currently include online play, so bear that in mind before purchasing.  The game is also fairly short, but like Portal, the experience is unique enough that I think it more than justifies its pricetag.
Even with it shortfalls, Overcooked is a refreshing and excellent addition to the couch coop collection and easily earns my recommendation.

Super Amazing Wagon Adventure is a game that made the YouTube rounds a while back and for very good reason.  It's one of those absurd hilarious games that just refuses to stop surprising you hour after hour.  It starts off as a pretty standard Oregon Trail inspired adventure as you customize your party, and pick a wagon.  Then after that first ten seconds I'm pretty sure the game takes a handful of shrooms and maybe coke right to the face and goes completely off the rails.  This game isn't trying to have a compelling narrative, it doesn't want to be IGN's game of the year, and it's not trying to tun the industry upside down with it's wicked angsty edginess.  No, SAWA is a game that just wants to be fun.  It wants to take you an adventure infused with pure randomness and heart of comedy gold.  You'll jump rivers and end up in space, you'll go looking for food and end up tripping balls, you'll be making your way across the plains and then fighting a Buffalo filled tornado.  A FREAKING BUFFANADO!
Visuals- The atari style graphics are simple yet endearing, and the color is perfect for the cartoony feel.  It's not winning any awards but it's perfect for the game.
Replayability- This game has it!  Not because this game offers new wagons and things to unlock, but because you just can't stop from wondering what could be next.
Sound-  Similar to the visuals, it's good but not mindblowing.  It's everything this game should be.
Gameplay_  The shooting can be a bit on the garbage side which is a shame.  You'll die a surprising amount, and what you die from will usually be even more surprising.  This game at points doesn't seem to follow any rules either.  I was once killed by a bear with no way to defend myself.  If this kind of thing bothers you, may be best to look else where.

first and foremost, I have been using blender for 3d models and assets for game development and design pieces over the past 5 years. I am a daily user of this software. So regarding anything i say about it, is mostly geared towards blender render, poly modelling, UV work, and object orientation. All big renders are usually done with BPR technology now, along with specialized programs such as keyshot, marmoset, etc. i do not work in cycles, nodes, or game development within blender, but use blender as a solid tool regardless. just a disclaimer.
do i recommend this software for anyone starting out in game design? yes. do i recommend it for concept artists who are kitbashing and want basic lighting and set ups? yes. indie film creators? yes. need effects for your games? yes. need models? yes.
The controls take a bit to getting used to, as well as the interface since its constantly changing and rearranging. but for the most part, the basics are there.
blender has been a solid indie development tool for an extremely long time. the reason for its easy popularity, is its free. and not just in the sense that its free to download. But free as in, licensing, distributing models, creations done in it, etc.
with that being said, its also something to note that this program is extremely feature rich and powerful if you know what you are doing.
lets just get the basic terminology down for areas it can conquer no problem:
- game engine: CHECK
- poly modelling: CHECK
- Animation : CHECK
- Node Based Material Creation: CHECK
- Rendering tools : CHECK
- Armature, IK rigging, bare rigs, solid constraints, bone rotation modules: CHECK
- 3D organic sculpting: CHECK (need a ton of rework as well)
- UV Tools: CHECK
- Particle simulations: CHECK
- Physics Modules :CHECK
im sure i forgot a pile of stuff. basically, blender has everything. even if its lacking a feature, knowing python and applying it to blender can conquer your issue, since its open source.
for those complaining about controls, interface, etc. you are a brat. nothing more. to have this tool at my fingertips at its reasonable price of free, THEN anything i even create in this program can be monetized at no royalty cost, it is the best.
once you do get your feet wet. Partner this software up with GIMP, Inkscape, xNormals, for free stuff that works well.
I am a proud blender user, and i am greatful it exists at all. for how powerful it is, its amazing the work and time thats gone into it.
bit recommendation to the developers though. better exporting for rigs and armature to notable engines like unreal and unity would be solid. also your texture paint mode and sculpting mode need a serious revisit as well. only issues i ever had is all.
another request is a less complicated layering system for UV work and textures. It would be awesome if i could stream line my texture work from outsourced software such as photoshop, gimp, etc. and have it react in real time on my model and UVs. its a long shot, but a solid addon would be nice. either or. keep up the good work. glad you guys are on steam.
i think you guys should open up steam workshop features as well. be cool to download and see other peoples work.
cheers! long live blender!

This game is a lot more fun than I thought it would be.  My friend and I were looking for a game that we could play co-op together and this game is almost perfect for that.
There are only 3 things I wish they would change about the game.  I wish the main menu navigation to start a co-op session were better.  It is a little frustrating to have to load into the game then connect and load into your friends game.  Second is the way the game transitions from co-op to single player.  When you go from co-op to single player mode it stops you from playing and loads you to a safe house.  I wish it was more seamless.  Finally is the way the single player story progresses when you co-op with another player.  If you and the person you are playing with are in the same place on the story you will both progress your respective story campaign.  If you are the slightest bit behind the person who joins the session will not progress.  One time we began playing and both of us had only played together, however in the time it took me to load into his game he had accidentally progressed the story and didn't realize it and therefore several hours of gameplay was not saved on my campaign.
Borderlands 2 is a great example of how to do co-op.  If this game worked like that it would be great!  These are definitely not game breaking issues though, so I would still highly recommend this game.  A lot of great moments.  If you are easily frightened I would only recommend playing with other people.  Once you get familiar with the way the game works (especially at night) it is not nearly as terrifying.  The first time that we got stuck outside of a safe zone at night we ended up being chased by a ton of zombies and volatiles (we might have been screaming in panic) and in that moment it became every man for himself.  Now that we know how to approach the night, we can help each other and not be so terrified.  Your first encounter will be adrenaline filled! And you will like it.

Excellent visuals, excellent atmosphere, excellent technology (the voice recognition works far better than i expected).
However...
Some of the worst level design i have seen in years. You never know what you are supposed to do and often you can only find out by trial and error.
There are too many puzzles that require exact timing, overly precise positioning etc. The voice recognition is good, but it's not good enough for that.
For instance, in chapter 2, there is a labyrinth. you don't know where to go at first. easy enough, right? now imagine there being enemies in the labyrinth. bit tougher, you have a fireball spell but it needs to be detonated with an additional spell, and the enemies don't seem to die in one hit. bit harder, but still managable.
Now imagine that you also CONSTANTLY TAKE DAMAGE while in the labyrinth. Have i mentioned there is a health bar? have i mentioned some puzzles involve platforming, and not making a jump yields fall damage?
tl;dr: I came for spellcasting, i stayed for the H.R.Giger inspired visuals and rich atmosphere.
... but then i left for obtuse and frustrating gameplay.
So only get it if you can deal with that frustration. I also recommend playing this like a point'n'click adventure: with a guide at the ready.

Half roguelike, half text adventure RPG/adventure game, NEO Scavenger is definitely something new.  I picked it up after watching a couple of YouTube videos, planned on playing for a few minutes, and found myself trying to beat a bandit to death with a rock while I coughed up blood.  Limping away from the fight, I died moments later from acute blood loss.
It's a brutal but phenomenal game.  It relies heavily on your own imagination which, in my opinion, makes it that much more powerful.  It is one of the only games that captures the bleakness and terror of the situation.  One moment you're strutting along with a shotgun in hand, a smile on your face, and the next, you're panicking because you drank contaminated water.  You're sick, coughing, vomiting, and it's all over.
Phenomental, wonderful game and a great replayable experience.  Just be prepared to lose because it is a *difficult* game.

Company of Heroes 2 plays like a well-polished, stand-alone, overpriced expansion pack to the original Company of Heroes 2. It introduces the Soviets as a new playable faction, comes with a shiny campaign, new maps, and a few new mechanics. Aside from that and the enhanced visuals it's just about the exact same game. Even the in-game interface is damn near identical.
It makes for a game that plays well and fans are certain to enjoy, but simultaneously isn't very appealing to non-hardcore fans. CoH2 does bring some improvements, like an ongoing player advancement system that unlocks statistical upgrades and aesthetic enhancements for multiplayer. Theatre of War is another great addition that adds tons of story-driven co-op vs ai, solo botmatches, and solo challenge missions.
The rest of the new mechanics are mostly fluff. Ice, snow, and cold weather are notable new game mechanics, but it never feels like they have a major impact on the way the game is played. You can blow up ice beneath units to sink them, you can track units through snow, and units can die from cold. It sounds impactful, it should be in theory, but in practice it doesn't really change the way you play the game all too much. This is further worsened by the fact that most of the campaign - and multiplayer/ToW maps - doesn't involve ice, snow, or cold weather at all.
The singleplayer campaign is simultaneously better and worse than CoH's. Its structure is similar to the original CoH, not Tales of Valor, but its missions aren't quite as obnoxiously long-winded: they're just long-winded now. There also seems to be a bit more variation in objectives and limitations during missions. Yet the game is riddled with grossly exaggerated parodies of things-that-ocassionally-happened in the Soviet army during WW2, which eventually ruin the experience even for westerners.
Company of Heroes 2's multiplayer is very much like the original CoH. It still works well. There's not much to talk about here other than said ongoing progression system that allows you to build up a custom loadout of enhancements and commanders. That makes for a bit more variation, but the enhancements are mostly minor.
Visually Company of Heroes 2 is a notable improvement over the original game, but not as much over Dawn of War 2. The benchmark seems simultaneously uglier and underperforming versus playing a regular match, but that's likely a matter of perspective. Textures are still a sore point even with everything cranked to Maximum. Most importantly, Company of Heroes 2 is easily one the more demanding games out right now and it certainly doesn't look the part.
The major DLC packs are Theatre of War campaigns. Those include botmatches / co-op vs ai / solo challenges in a campaign-like narrative structure. That's actually a substantial amount of content for the price if you like CoH's singleplayer gameplay.
Company of Heroes 2 is a solid entry in the Company of Heroes series that's sure to please fans. But it's not a substantial improvement over Company of Heroes in any regard. Recommended for fans of the franchise. Anyone else might want to look twice or wait for a sale.

Equal parts fun and "make you hate your friends" managerial nightmare.
Overcooked makes for an excellent couch coop where you and your friends try to manage a kitchen and push out as many correct orders as possible within a limited time frame.  While simple enough at the start, the levels quickly grow in complexity as the shapes of the kitchens become more obtuse and the hazards (like rats stealing your ingredients or counters sliding and changing the shape of the map) become increasingly difficult to circumvent.  Deft coordination and communication is necessary to manage the kitchen with 3 or 4 players in these situations, but such cooperation does not come easily.  It can take more than a few tries to get the best rating on every level, which if your friends aren't all on the same page, can make for a frustrating affair.  The light hearted visual style and storyline makes it hard to get mad at the game, but the same can't always be said for your friends...  Luckily, there's built in "swearing" and "punch" buttons in the game, so they've got you covered as far as venting those frustrations.
The game is at its best when you have 3 or 4 people, in my opinion, as much of the resource management puzzle solving is oversimplified with only 1 or 2 playing (although, that can be helpful if you're trying to get better ratings on hard levels).  That said, it can be difficult to gather so many people and controllers locally at times and the game does not currently include online play, so bear that in mind before purchasing.  The game is also fairly short, but like Portal, the experience is unique enough that I think it more than justifies its pricetag.
Even with it shortfalls, Overcooked is a refreshing and excellent addition to the couch coop collection and easily earns my recommendation.

Tropico is a unique franchise. It is a city builder that takes its strength from the historical, socio-economical and geographical context it is based in.
First of all it is FUN. It is easy to play and understand in the city builder aspect of it.
You play through a series of missions which basically give you a few buildings and a context, and you need to build from there. (sometimes, you will have access to only one type of resource... or specific goals)
The game is set in a cold war period on various paradise islands of the caribbean.
Basically, you need your people to be happy, they need buildings, buildings need money, you need to make money.
there are several ways to do that : tourism (make your island nice, build tourism buildings) , farming (different crops in different places like high or low altitude, humidity for example), industry (transform farming products, or use mining/logging resources.) Or all of them combined.
You can be a "good" dictator, trying to please the people, you can be a ruthless leader, with police control, fake elections, strong army presence, or a combination you want of these.
Many of the missions and dialogs are humorous and tongue-in-cheek in nature, and often makes me laugh aloud. This is quite an addition for this genre, and coupled with the geographical setting and rich historical period, it makes quite a unique game.
The background music is very well made and feels right at home in this setting. It makes you hum the salsa tunes all day.
If you have played tropico 3, well this is almost the same, with some notable additions in terms of buildings and missions but basically it's the same engine, same graphics, same everything. I would still recommend getting it with all DLC on sale.
If you haven't played any of the tropico series, you will no doubt enjoy this very funny - nice to watch - easy to get into city builder

tl;dr - I recommend this game and to those who say it is bad: try again and stick with it instead of giving up on it, use your imagination a bit as well, if you have one after playing COD.
When I played the first 7-10 hours of this I actually found it hard to go on and even boring (and badly made), I almost retired, but instead I didn't and I was rewarded. This game is both hilarious and gruesome at the same time. It is easily as addictive as Farcry 3, and more barbaric. The only place I really fault this game is the beast AI - oh, beastie I need you to be stealthy with me, so that means you run into the crowd of enemies and set all the alarms off (and that's with the stealth pet).
The brilliance of this game comes from its primal stone age setting, the mortal fragility of the starting character, and the attention to detail.
The weapons and mounts are really funny and you can do some very creative things with them (if you have more imagination than is required to play COD), especially with civilians :P.
Almost everything in Primal can kill without warning, there are no "safe spots" in this map and your character is extremely fragile for the first half of the game, all of this put together means the game is easy in "comfortable" gameplay but also challenging when you want to push the boundaries (it is your choice how you play...).
You can really see the attention to detail in this game, it might be a mod but the map and the characters are really unique and well done. You can see how someone really put in the effort to make the map as primal as possible.

A few hours in, while some of the conversations are repeats, there's enough variety that it's still cool to listen to. I especially like the occasions when Strong Bad manages to get on Tycho's nerves. In general, Tycho has great lines, Strong Bad and Heavy are good, and Max... not so much.
In terms of atmosphere, the visuals are good and consistent enough between the characters, and there's nice relaxing background music. Some of it sounds like a jazz-lounge version of the Team Fortress 2 music.
Overall, I quite enjoy the game.

Remember those emotions you had while watching Game of Thrones ? The goosebumps during the opening ? The anger and sadness when a character you liked died ? The hatred and irritation every time you saw those characters who only deserve it ? The surprise and concern every time you realized that someone is a manipulative sl*t ? The relief when something went the way you wanted it to go ? Let me introduce you Game of Thrones : the game that will manage to get you through all of those emotions again.
You play as several members of the House Forrester from the North and loyal to the Starks. The game starts at the Twins, during the Red Wedding ; imagine how things will go from there (spoiler :
). You will try as hard as you can to save your House with every scattered member : visit Ironrath, King's Landing, the Wall and even Meereen ; a wonderful journey across this incredible, ambitious and vast world.
Some will complain about the "illusion of choice". Be no fool, you can't change everything : the main storyline is already set. But isn't it so in every game you'll play ? Still, you'll be able to change many things ; sadly, this is Game of Thrones and you won't be able to give everybody a happy ending.
As a Game of Thrones fan, I loved playing this game : it makes you "live" in this universe, the story is well written and narrated, the plot drags you along the chapters. An amazing experience next to the Forresters. Iron from Ice !
However, be warned : this game will not please every kind of gamer. If you want to be rewarded by playing or making the right choices, know that there are not really good options : only terrible choices and less bad choices - it really feels like a Game of Thrones game should feel. If you're expecting to magically win every impossible situation (for example
) and save everyone do not buy and play this game : you won't feel any satisfaction. But if you like Game of Thrones, intriguing stories and, like me, you can enjoy a game whose unfortunate plot can surprise you, go ahead. I managed to
, which felt rewarding, and I would really like to play a second season.

This game came out in 2013 and I only learned of its existence a few days ago. The surprise for me was seeing how good it was received back then, so I wonder who else, besides me, also let this little game slip past their fingers. That said, I was given the chance to check this game out, and I’m glad I did so.
is the name of a place, somewhere in the depths of Hell, a place made of bones where you arrive without knowing who you are. What is curious about this place is that nobody knows where all the bones come from, considering that no one has ever witnessed anyone dying. I’ll refrain from mentioning anything related to the plot and the story of the game for I think that is the best the game has to offer, my goal here is to expose the mechanics of the game.
As a game,
is hard to describe, it has some puzzles in it but the main focus is on dialogue and interacting with various NPCs, which there are plenty - I think at least over 80 different NPCs. The puzzles themselves might not be that easy to spot at first, it’s only when you’re further into the game and come upon certain things or pieces of dialogue that you’ll start to wonder about something that you saw when you first came into this place. If you’re expecting this to be a game with engaging gameplay you’re out of luck. The game is pretty much just running around from place to place while attempting to solve conversation puzzles.
That is what made the game and the dialogue so engaging for me. As you play and talk to people you can get infected with one of the 7 deadly sins. These sins can be used on every NPC and each of them will trigger a different piece of dialogue. The NPCs response to you sometimes can provide a little background to the game world, sometimes it helps you accomplish an objective but, overall, it all happens behind this great satire and exposure of interesting and thought provoking philosophical, moral and ethical paradoxes, positions and dilemmas. That is what makes this game great.
Overall, I wasn’t expecting to enjoy
as much as I did. It features an excelent atmosphere, albeit repetitive, excellent thought provoking and, at the same time, funny dialogue, conversation based puzzles, a rather unique and intriguing setting and a particular set of extremely well done riddles. I highly recommend it if you’re into games that deviate from the traditional meaning of games or if you’re looking for a great satire.

Well, I can't say that I have completed this game. From day 1, I had a commitment to play this game with friends. We started to, but then problems happened and now we're waiting on another friend to buy this game. Nonetheless, I keep wanting to come back and play it, and recently I decided that I was going to play until I got to where we left off because there is nothing else I want to play, and this game is pretty great.
So is it good?
If Dead Island and Mirror's Edge had a lovechild, this would be it. That is to say, it's killing zombies and running around an apocalyptic nightmare as if you're the master of it all.
But PsionicPhazon, is it good?
I felt that the story was a little bit lacking. Pretty straightforward. Main character good. All people he likes are good and have the exact same opinions. All the bad people are bad. The main character's boss is all like, "Are you and Jack an effective team?" (Yes, that's from that one terrible movie with Tom Cruise that was also predictable and lacking). All-in-all: good people are good and have the same opinion, bad people are bad and only do bad things. Normal people like you and me are good. Rich and/or powerful people are bad. Same yawnfest of a story you see in every game and movie these days. Very black-and-white.
Okay, but... is it good?
I'm one of those rare people that just didn't like Skyrim. I don't know. I just don't like going on a quest to fetch a sack of sugar from a hoard of bloodthirsty orcs for grandma so she can use it to resurrect a demon soul (you thought I was going to say bake cookies), all the while there is an evil plot, which realistically would have a time-limit on it. Why the hell would I go through all that trouble to do these side-quests so grandma can have her way? F*** your cultist ways, grandma! I'm gonna go mount Alduin and force-feed his innards to useless Lydia! Buuuuuut even that gets boring, so I always start a new game and never finish it.
Not with Dying Light. Nope. For me, the side-quests are interesting enough, and the trouble I have to go through to get to these stupid side-quests is fun enough, that I am interested and I remain so. Even the annoying main quest-line is interesting enough that I will ocassionally do what they ask, forgetting that normally-looming time-crunch I feel like I need to do. Right now, Jade's brother has been sitting in the middle of the night zombie's nest for days and I've just been doing side-quests for some stupid twins who look down on me as their intellectual inferior.
BUT IS IT GOOD?!
Yes! It's awesome! Stop asking me that! Of course it's awesome! I'm not some loser who writes a bazillion lines of words just to say it's bad!
Overall:
9/10 (story needs work, but I really like the sandbox I was dropped in)

In Saints Row IV you are the President of the United States and the Earth is attacked by aliens. After failing to defeat them, you find yourself in the Matrix and you must learn to use this to your advantage to stop the alien invasion.
Saints Row IV plays just like Saints Row: The Third. But early in the game, you start picking up data clusters and taking down the Wardens of the simulation, allowing you to unlock special abilities. You will be able to be as fast as a car or to jump like Spider-Man, later you will be also able to glide around.
There are a lot of movie and videogame parodies in the game such as They Live, The Matrix, Inception, Mass Effect 2, Mortal Kombat, Metal Gear Solid, Streets Of Rage, Riddick and many many more.
There is a wide range of things you will do in story missions. There are lots of throwbacks to Saints Row 1,2, and 3 throughout the game. You also have a space ship very similar to Mass Effect where you can chat with the crew and romance everyone. So, the story will never become boring.
Activities have taken a big change, instead of a pass or fail system, it is now bronze, silver and gold. You will also unlock more powers, perks for powers, costumes and weapons through beating activities.
There's a lot of new stuff like a telekinetic Professor Genki competition, platforming rifts, speed rifts.
Saints Row IV has nearly all of the original character voices from the first 3 games. There is also again a big music selection. A great selection of dance, hip hop, 90s and more you can listen from the in-game radio stations.
The graphics are nearly the same as in Saints Row: The Third.
Overall I think Saints Row IV is also a fantastic game. It is a lot of fun to play, especially if you play with a friend.

Oh boy, this game was such a pleasant surprise from start to finish. When I initially found out about this game, I was interested in it because hey - I like "off the beaten path" type games that seem to invoke a bit of thought that you normally wouldn't have when you play your average platformer or fps. So I bought the game, started it up a few days later, and low and behold I see the developer's name: Gregory Weir. I was shocked and amused by how I managed to pick up a game by a game dev I've really admired for quite a few years. I've lost count of how many times I've played How to Raise a Dragon, Bars of Black and White, Looming, and, most of all, The Majesty of Colors. So needless to say, I was stoked to play this game, and it did not let me down.
I pretty much finished this game in one day. It is based off of Principia Discordia, which is a book for a religion of sorts called Discordianism. I cannot  figure out if this relgion is a satire or 100% serious, and I guess thats, in some ways, a good thing. You play as a character trying to escape from the Ossuary. The gameplay mostly consists of solving puzzles and encouraging the seven deadly sins on people in order to progress and gain information for the four members of the sacred order who each seem to have their own agenda in order to protect the Ossuary. Along the way, you will expose the truths about the Ossuary and what they tell to their people in order to keep up a facade and keep everyone in check. There is a lot of humorous dialogue that seems to poke fun at religous and politcal stances; from a museum filled with impure things that you actually aren't allowed to see, to two political parties in which membership you are allowed to switch back and forth with as you so choose. Also, cabbage people.
The puzzles are not terribly difficult, but are a nice challenge to figure out nonetheless. The gameplay adds nicely to the story as it allows you to figure things out at your own pace. The fact that every person in the Ossuary has different dialogue depending on what sin you impress on them is a very nice touch as well and offers some amusing conversations. I can tell the game was lovingly made, and the ending notes added yet another pleasant surprise to my experience. There is another game by Gregory Weir that might be easy to forget, but by playing Ossuary, I remembered it. Checking on the Ludus Novus website I found the "game" Narthex. It is a very short game with pretty similar graphics and art to Ossuary that advertises itself as having an ending that's "not worth getting". It is also a game that was made to try out a conversation engine. Its the game Ossuary was born from. Another nice surprise to see after finishing the game.
I reccommend this game to people who thought what I initially thought when buying this game. It is not a game with a ton of "gameplay" but it is every bit as engaging as any other game. Its a fun experience and now I know a little bit about this bizarre religion of Principia Discordia. And most of all, I was reminded of why I enjoyed Gregory Weir's games in the first place.

I didn't play arpgs in years, frankly i got sick of the grind, the most common element in the genre, no matter what other good aspects a game offered, -it always let back to the grind,
Then came Grim Dawn, and i was (sadly) hesitant, didn't back the kickstarter, didn't buy in on early access, nor did i buy on release, -all of which i regret now
But as they say, it's never too late
and so when i got Grim Dawn at the end of summer 2017, i was instantly hooked and sucked in deep, it just blows me away
from a game standpoint, if "new to the genre", it's rivaled by few, PoE and D3 are maybe the only, slight, contenders(each for different reasons), and yet i feel Grim Dawn offers something even to new players, but also to "veterans" -that makes it worthy of fanboi arguments fighting over

and i can't recommend it enough
the effort and care put into the game clearly shows,
the content is massive, and considering it's an Indie, the polish is there no doubt. Sure, ofc it wont be "aaa" lvls of polish and magnificent splendor, but you know what, it doesn't matter
the game doesn't "lack" anything, and Crate shows they still have more to give, -content being released, and patches tweaking the already existing, + constantly dashing extra sprinkles of polish on this goodie good yum-yum cake too for constant extra lovin'
The world is "grim", gorgeous in its own right,
-the lore more than satisfactory,
and most importantly, for an arpg, the build depth, combinations and potential are massive, with no shortcomings in terms of loot to blend it all together
Secrets galore to discover, large areas to scourer, grand bosses to get utterly roflstomped by -because your arrogance didn't hold up to a god in the end
Grim Dawn is not only the game that brought me back into the arpg genre with delight, it did so without draining me and making me quit, because even tho the "grind" is there, it never makes me notice, -because i'm always busy trying something "new" even tho i'm still "running that same content", -which no other game has done in years
and no "AehAehAeh" game (besides WoW) comes even close to matching the time and enjoyment i've spent in the world of Cairn
More than decent graphics
solid mechanics, combat, etc
interesting setting and quest+factions vary enough to make different playthroughs' "actions" considerable enough and different on their own
8 classes to date, with dual class system -and each class having massive potential on their own, equating to a grand total of
character build possibilities
etc etc etc, i feel like i'm rambling and babbling at this point and would just make an endless list with, in the end, not much point other than: the game is amazing imo, and my opinion is fact, -and now it's law, so you should give GD a shot too
Grim dawn will likely keep me hooked for a long while, and even more likely make me return more often -even after when i finally manage to grow "tired" of it
it's a magnificent game, and utterly grand arpg, easily one of
best arpgs made to date,
-not since the days of D2 have i enjoyed this genre so much, and truly makes me reminiscent of the hours "wasted" as a kid, -but looking forward to waste even more now
9/10 if new to the genre 11/10 if you're already arpg familiar or 13/10 if you like the genre

Half-Life 2 is a great game, It has some fantastic sections and few tedious ones. The game begins with a fantastic introduction into the world of Half-Life 2, It allows the player to explore the world a bit before getting you into the action and gives you all the motivation you need to want to save the day. This is largely due to the fact that The combine are a great enemy that the game really make you despise and they have some pretty cool designs as well.
Even though this game is fantastic it will most likely have a level or two that you won't like, for me this was Water hazard and Ravenholm. Water Hazard just doesn't work for me, the boat isn't really fun to use and their are too many moments where you need to get out of the air boat and open a gate or solve some physics puzzle, these parts just feel like they're there to make the game feel longer. Ravenholm on the other hand just feels like a source engine showcase. The only parts I liked about Ravenholm was Father Grigori and the atmosphere.
The moments where this game shine however is when you get to interact with characters such as Alyx, Barney, and The G-man. Most of these sequences don't even have the player doing anything action packed but instead just listening to some really well written dialog.  You really start to like these characters and the game makes you want more once it's over.
Any how if you haven't checked this game out and enjoy a good FPS every now and then, then I'd say check it out. It's only $10 and you'll get a quite a few hours worth of entertainment.

Enjoyable philosophical puzzle game.
Make no mistake: Ossuary is a highly intellectual pastime. But it is not pretentious. It shows you different moral or ethical positions, but doesn't assign any one to you. The philosophy is not retrofitted to some pre-existing puzzle gameplay (*cough*Talos*cough*), but rather integral to the game: as you explore your surroundings (some sort of afterlife?) and talk to people, you acquire the seven deadly sins, only there are two sides to them: they can do harm or they can do good (e.g. envy might make you respect someone else and motivate you to become more like them). When you talk to the ~100 characters in that limbo (each with their own little dialogue), you'll encounter quests: to solve them, you need to explore, and you need to ply the "gatekeepers" with just the right sin to make them want to do what you want them to do. But there's more: puzzles that don't advertise themselves as such. 6 endings that can be experienced on the same save game slot. There's a lot done right in this game.
If you like to read, to think, to puzzle, to explore people and concepts and game levels, then you should play Ossuary. Few games come with so much in such a small package. If you don't like to explore, you might find it rather short and not worth it; but it lasted me 3 hours and was very much worth its reduced price.
Well-designed, thought-provoking, original: recommended!

Ossuary might be the most fun religious game I've ever played since the Shin Megami Tensei series. Ossuary is basically Bible Adventures but for Discordianism - and actually fun to play.
But what's Discordianism, you ask? Well, in the late 1960s, a small group of american counterculture theorists, magicians and writers decided to sketch out a parody of all religion - which turned out to be a completely valid religion in its own right. This religion has as its "main" texts several editions of The Principia Discordia. These editions laid out the contradictory, absurd, non-foundation for a religion that has somehow stuck in culture.
Discordianism, the world's first open source religion, is basically a collage of Zen Buddhism, western philosophy, parodies of ceremonial magic and a healthy dose of drugs. And you're one of its Popes.
Ossuary is a clever way to express the views of the Principia Discordia in game form. The world of Ossuary is an allegory of what is called the Aneristic Delusion and the Curse of Grayface: the current "fallen" state of humanity. It's a world where people take themselves too seriously with ridiculous results. What the Principia presents as metaphorical, Ossuary represents as literal. All of the factions in Ossuary come from the Principia Discordia. Your quest in this game is to collect Sins and share that corruption with others, hopefully helping them chill out a bit.
Ossuary is only very slightly a "game", it has minimal interaction. But it's an excellent way to immerse yourself in Discordianist thought. It's a way to interact with the tenets of a religion.
If you care for useless philosophical navel-gazing, enjoy paradoxes or are in any way attracted to any occult tradition, I strongly recommend Ossuary. If you're a serious person who wants serious action-packed games, you might want to skip this. Or better yet, open your pineal gland and try something outside your comfort zone.

In exploring the yard and talking to the people around you, you are slowly burdened with sins which you can then use to infect other people and get different response from. Spend time around the particularly lazy, and you’re infected with Sloth, which is the perfect remedy for that highly-wired guard who’s been watching that key for several days without sleep. Talk to the right people and use the correct combination of sins and it won’t take you long to collect all seven -- it’s then that you realise just how many words have been ploughed into Ossuary; every single person has unique responses to all seven sins. In the heart of the fortress, sixteen soldiers stand in formation and, should you like, you can prompt eight unique responses from all of them. It doesn’t advance the plot any, but every one of them has their own insight and reactions to the world around you that could have effortlessly been written off with the adventure game trope of “That does not work here”. You could spend a lot of time coaxing these response out of people. If they don’t actually offer any responses, well, odds are you found a cabbage. Deal with it as you please.

Buyer beware: Treat this game as if it were a visual novel with very little to no gameplay. It's more of an interactive venture into philosophy and whatnot. A "Talk N' Walk" if you will. Gameplay amounts to talking to NPC's over and over and collect a variety of four particular "core aspects" each of the 4 main NPC's will require of you. In doing so, you get an "ending" which is a summary quote of the ideologies behind that particular NPC's beliefs.  There is very little to play here. A very loose definition of what a game is.
You really need to understand this BEFORE you spend $8 on it. To re-emphasize my point: it is not so much a game, as it is more a visual novel. I impulse bought and I will admit I was a bit annoyed. Especially since I got all 6 endings in under 2 hours. The disappointment subsided however due to the amount of text that is included and the atmosphere the game gave. So, when you see it as more of a sprawled out book while you keep your hands busy doing other things, then it becomes a bit more tolerable.
Also, tagging it horror is a bit poor taste. it isn't really "horror." The aesthetic gives it a "horror" look but it isn't really. It's all atmosphere. The cool thing is when you get 6 endings, the developer opens up to you via a notes page so it is always nice to have that kind of transparency. There is also 26 achievements with the bulk being secret ones, so I imagine that will be where most of the "replayability" will come from. Finding all those. There is also a couple other things I couldn't figure out post game, so I imagine there is even more hidden stuff or whatever if that is your bag.
The developer was kind enough to release a demo. Play THAT first. In doing so, it's basically playing the actual game for free. The gameplay does not change, and what you get in the demo is what you get in the real game.

Company of Heroes 2 is just a shell of what Company of Heroes used to be. Generic combat, underpowered feel, gimmick blizzard conditions, and absurd multiplayer DLC requirement; CoH2 is nothing suprising, a very average RTS; from what was an outstanding franchise.
CoH2's combat feels very generic. Every explosive weapon feels about the same, regardless of whether it's an anti-tank gun, or a high explosive shell. Infantry combat seems to suffer the same problem. The units in CoH2 also feel horribly meaty, like someone used a keyboard while wearing mittens, and ended up with a few extra zeros added onto everythings health. There is nothing outstanding for the vast majority of units; even extremely expensive high caliber AT or HE howitzer guns.
The lack of large scale battles is also a very large minus for what era this game is designed around. A hard limit of 100 population, when most units are 4-8; and many larger units are 10 or more population. The lack of units makes every unit lost a massive investment, as replacing it could be equivalent to several minutes of resource production.
The meaty units, combined with the very slow pace of production, along with the lack of tactical usefulness for most units; makes combat uninteresting at best.
The blizzard conditions are a very haphazard addition to the game. Requiring very little back-end and actual game design to implement, and adding almost no value. Blizzards are a minor annoyance at best.
While the game does cost some money to purchase; Company of Heroes 2 is listed as a balanced multiplayer RTS. Which CoH2 utterly fails at. The inclusion of a rediculous pay wall for any decent commander doctorine, locking out a majority of the basis of multiplayer; is pay to win at its finest. The fact that you purchase the base game, just to be required to buy DLC to be competative in multiplayer is horrid. There are MANY free to play games without a multiplayer DLC paywall; and CoH2 is not a free to play game.

As a long time fan of the Far Cry series (as in I had the five disc CD set of the original in 2006) and someone who owns every game in the series, this one was a let down. It might be right for some people who might take the setting as a breath of fresh air, but for me this is a "far cry" from the run and gun shoot em up like every other game in the series. Its also sad to see that this game is obviously not meant to be played on PC, which is a shame considering the series started out as one of the best PC exclusives of the mid 2000's. All the cutscenes run at 30 FPS no matter the resolution or framerates you are getting, which is unique to this game compared to the rest of the series. The main menu and options all run at 30 fps with significant input lag, which makes changing options using a mouse seriously disorientating, also unique to this game compared to the rest of the series.
Other than that, the graphics are amazing, it would be challenging to find a game that looks better. The gameplay is great, but it does still feel like a re-skin of the other games in the series. And with so much fewer options in terms of weaponry, much of the gameplay feels repetetive, although hunting animals in this game feels much more lifelike.
Overall I honetly like the game, but if I could i would get my money back and skip this one, so im giving it a negative review. Sorry ubisoft.

The rerelease of Quake Live on Steam has definitely reinvigorated the QL community.
While autojumping and the addition of loadouts make the game more user friendly, QL is still the same skill based, hi-speed FPS it always was. To be honest, I was never into Q3, but I liked the older Quakes from demos. I've always felt Unreal Tournament was superior to Quake 3 because UT can do practically anything Q3 could do, but with more customization. After having a chance to play it legitmately online, I can definitely see the appeal. Jump into some matches and frag. Improve your aim, learn how to dodge and study the map to get better. Admittedly, weapon balance feels all over the place and many match ups can feel unfair. But it is very fun to blast away with rockets, earn a shotgun kill or rail somebody with a railgun or instagib. A variety of modes are avaialble to make things, most notably Freeze Tag (Frag enemy to freeze them, thaw teamates to revive), Red Rover (Hunt the enemy team, switch teams when you die) and Quad Hog (hunt the person with quad damage and take it to kill fast).
The subscription offers some usefulness including the ability to host your own servers and host servers with your own game rules, but most players will be satisfied with the F2P model so I do wonder how well QL can survive despite the increased interest. Regardless, the game is super fun when you're not getting destroyed and thanks to QL, I have a new found respect for Quake multiplayer.

It should have been longer and could have had more consequences, certainly. It is one of the weakest Telltale has produced from a thematic and gameplay perspective. For people who never played this game: just do it. If you get it while on sale (I bought it for $25 a while ago), it's a bargain for how much content you actually get.
The number of missions/side missions/challenges from the main game + The Following (about 100 hours of content or so, chalenges and quarantines included) make it worth it's price, especially if you're a fan of zombie games (I wasn't actually a fan, this being my first such game, but I really enjoyed it and finished it 3 times).
However, there's always something that's not quite right, and for this game that something is called "The Bozak Horde". Some people call it hard/tough/impossible whatever. It's not, not at all, I was able to finish it from the 2nd try or something like that. What it IS, actually, is bugged.
For the people that don't know, this game has 3 achievements that you can only get by playing the Bozak Horde challenge: the first one you get for just finishing the challenge. After you do that, you get a blueprint for the "Bozak bow".
You need to craft the bow to get the 2nd and 3rd achievements: Electric whisper (the blueprint for electric arrows) and Things That Go Ka-Boom (the blueprint for exploding arrows).
You get the Electric whisper by killing 10 virals with the bow. This one is bugged, I actually killed them 2 times without getting the achievement. I thought that you only get it after you FINISH the chalenge, so I stopped playing (not having the time to finish the whole thing).
Then, the 3rd time that I've done it, I got it as soon as I killed the 10th viral. So bugged and annoying. If you don't get it as soon as you kill them, just restard the challenge and don't waste your time doing the whole thing.
And the last and most frustrating one: Things That Go Ka-Boom. You only get the achievement (and blueprint) if you finish the challenge (20 trials) in 31 minutes or less. This is hard enough, but definitely not impossible.
However, when you get on 12th trial (killing a bunch of virals on an elevator) and then the game just won't open the next door for you, you probably tend to get frustrated. That's what happened to me. I was about 3 minutes faster than my best time, but had to wait for 2 minutes for that ♥♥♥♥ing elevator door to open (and it still didn't), so I just ALT+F4 that♥♥♥♥♥♥ 12/20 trial and you get that..it's annoying.
I hope the devs actually find a way to fix those, even though they're just achievements (it's the first game that I've tried to get 100%, only this one and co-op remaining).
Other than that, if you're only into single player: get it, it's worth it!

I love city builders and nation building sim games, and Tropico 4 combines both for one of the best experiences every produced. The humor that doesn't simply drip but gushes from every pore further adds to the replayability and fun of this game. I played the Original Campain and the Modern Times Campagin months ago, and came back recently to tackle the extra missions, and the charm is still there. Takes forever to build stuff, running into the red happens easily and way too often whcih can lead to spiral of death until the rebels come, a coup storms the palace, or the superpowers finally dispatch troops. But when everything comes together, it's a great feeling of achievement and pride as I bring a impovrished island to glory and power.
Though, if you really dig down and strip away the humor and fun, you are still left with a solid game, only dealing with dark and depressing subject matter: executions, labor camps, the seemingly never ending struggle between the US and USSR, the threat of being overthrown and disposed. It's not a "historical" game, but many of the things that took place are based on history and events of the Cold War in the Caribbean, so I have to give props to that.
It's a great game, and worth every dollar thrown at it, all of course from my secret Swiss Bank Account.

This game is unlike any I have played in the last two decades. I recommend it to anyone who wants a turn-based hex RPG. Set in a post-apocolyptic Lovecraftian Michigan, your character emerges from a crygenic vat to step into a race against time. You can die from dehydration, starvation, disease  and hypothermia, in addition to wounds inflicted by the various denizens surrounding the Motor City's wastelands.
This hard setting is further amplified by the decision not to include a leveling system. Each time you play, you learn more about the game mechanics and possibilities. You can augment your character with four of a dozen advantages, as well as about six disadvantages. Thes combination of these influence your play style, as some opportunities only present themselves to those with a given trait.
For those who love to play first-person shooter "RPG" as murder hobos, this is not the game for you. It is more reminiscent of games from the late 1980s and early 1990s in that it tells its story in a piecemeal fashion with only one Rouge-like save option. While you can engage in combat, you will frequently die. Stealth, scavanging and crafting reveal much more of the story, and further contribute to the desperation as you try to unravel not only how you came to be cycled out of the cryogenics tank, but also what happened to create this near-future landscape.
Expect to die a lot. And enjoy it.

Having never played an XCOM game before, I went into this game very cautiously. I've been hearing about how great this game is for quite some time and since the entire XCOM: Enemy Unknown package was on sale, I thought I'd give it a shot. After playing for quite some time, I wish I had encountered this game sooner. At first, the resource management, perma-death, and complexity of the game mechanics made the experience a little bit intimidating. However, after about an hour of play I found myself successfully leading a well trained squad through every combat scenario with ease. Every decision you make can have serious lasting repercussions. One wrong move and a squad-mate is dead. All that training for that squad is rendered worthless, making it a frustrating experience at times. Once you finally complete the mission and successfully exterminate the alien menace however, it becomes one of the most gratifying experiences in video games. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a well made game and I highly recommend it to any fans of turn-based strategy games. Even if you're not a fan of those kinds of games, it's worth trying out and a good starting point.

This Telltale series of Game of Thrones was more than I was expecting. I started watching The Walking Dead after playing through the Telltale game, but with Game of Thrones I did the opposite.
For those of you that are not familiar with the show, all of the people that live in this world are separated by House. When you begin the game, you are given your own house (which is not one of the familiar houses known from the hit TV series). You play your game through the eyes of a handful of different characters; allowing you to like the show, bounce between the many plots and storylines.
In the game, you are in the house Forrester, which is a small house in the North. Ironwood trees surround your land, which is your key resource that you provide to the kingdom. Through your journey you will visit the familiar locations like The Wall and Kings Landing, but you will also visit some new locations as well.
When you play through as the five different characters in this series, you will be able to get a whole new love for the series; I know I did. You will visit some familiar characters you have learned to love (or hate), but you will also create relationships with new characters that you may not have known from the TV series as well.
I strongly encourage you to try this game; especially if you are a GoT fan. It will shed a new light on the series as well as give you a few surprises that you did not see coming.
If I spent the time I played this game on something productive I could have made the world a better place. I don't regret it.

Multiple Stressors Affect Bee Health
Scientists and regulatory authorities agree bee health is a complex issue, and researchers are continuing to seek answers to general honey bee colony declines. While the specific cause of these colony losses remains undetermined, several studies have indicated this delicate balance may be affected by a variety of factors, including introduced pests and parasites, microbial diseases, inadequate diet, bee management practices, habitat loss, loss of genetic diversity and improper use of pesticides.
Specific factors affecting bee health, include:
Parasites (Varroa; tracheal mites) - Most scientists now agree that honeybee colony losses are the result of multiple causes, with no single factor being responsible. This Forbes article explores the myriad of factors contributing to honey bee losses. This Bayer brochure explores the many factors affecting honey bee health, especially the Varroa mite. Also read the Overwintering Fact Sheet.
Nutrition deficiencies - Bayer's North American Bee Care Center Manager Dr. David Fischer testified before the Horticulture, Research, Biotechnology and Foreign Agriculture Subcommittee of the House Agriculture Committee to discuss research and management strategies regarding pollinator health in April 2014. Panelists agreed (archived webcast) that the two top factors impacting bee health are parasitic Varroa mites and lack of adequate nutrition and forage.
Diseases (Nosema; bacteria; viruses) - Honey bees are impacted by the Nosema ceranae fungus, the American foulbrood disease, and more than 20 viruses.
Weather - The weather can exacerbate other problems that honey bees face.
Beekeeping practices - Research has provided new management recommendations that beekeepers have begun to adopt.
Pesticides (hives; agriculture) - Some critics contend that neonicotinoids may be involved in honeybee losses; however, there has been no demonstrated effect on colony health associated with neonicotinoid-based insecticides when used according to the label. In fact, the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency stated in 2012 that it "is not aware of any data indicating that honey bee declines or the incidence of CCD in the U.S. is correlated with the use of pesticides in general or with the use of neonicotinoids in particular." This Bayer fact sheet takes a close look at the data behind neonicotinoids and the role of the compound in crop protection.
Genetic weakness - One effect varroa mites have in severely attacked colonies, is to cause deformities.
Queen issues - This report on the National Stakeholders Conference on Honey Bee Health considers much of the research done on honey bee health and considers the impacts of nutrition and food diversity on the longevity of queens and workers among other issues.

PROS:
*Voice recognition works most of the time
*Good spell variety
*Beautiful environments
*Good atmosphere
*Appropriate music and mostly appropriate sounds
*Lore is interesting for the most part
CONS:
*Too many puzzles where even the
is unclear and where necessary items are hidden away
*Voice recognition still sometimes fails, which can quickly lead to death during combat or dangerous platforming
*Spell potential is untapped
*Writing quality is inconsistent
*Lore is conveyed entirely through easily missable "documents"
*Some parts of puzzles are reset upon loading a save
GAME LENGTH:
If the player follows a guide and has good luck with voice recognition, this game could last around 10 hours.  Achievement hunters will need a bit more time to hunt down all 35 documents.  Without a guide, this game could last over 20 hours.
SCORE:
6 out of 10
This game's best features are its voice recognition concept and implementation, visuals, and spell variety.  It is impressive to me that such a small team pulled all of this off.  Unfortunately, core design decisions regarding puzzles, combat, and direction dealt a serious blow to my enjoyment of the game.
I like to know what my goal is in a puzzle game so that I can consider the tools at my disposal and develop a logical plan for how to achieve it.  I don't mind a bit of experimentation and exploration, but they are taken to extremes here.  Puzzles frequently lack clear objectives even when one is halfway through them, objects necessary to solutions are sometimes hidden away or meant for
rooms' puzzles, repeated platforming around death traps is often necessary to get perspective, it is not always clear if a player is equipped to solve a puzzle he finds yet, and the player frequently does not even always know what solving a puzzle will accomplish.
One room in the last chapter of the game stands out to me (spoilers ahead):  after going through several steps to lift or move platforms and open up floor and wall panels, the player is "rewarded" with a mysterious ball of ice.  Like the room in which it resides, it has no obvious purpose, but as the player considers it, he realizes that it is growing smaller.  It is melting.  Now the player, with no sense whatsoever of what to do, feels rushed to do
.  It turns out that the solution here is to cast a fiery bomb spell on it, get out of the underground corridor where it was found, take it to
room, place it in one of three holes in the wall that lead to an opening in the ceiling, walk a particular path around a large room while using telekinesis on the ball in the ceiling (because the floor path matches a path in the ceiling that the player cannot see), freeze the ball in place at the end of the path, and make it explode, all before it melts to nothing.  If he fails, he has to start the process all over again.  And this is just one part of one puzzle.
Even if I had the time to devote to reaching such a solution on my own, it would not be time well spent.  Worse, if I need to leave the game, parts of the puzzle (e.g. object positions) may be reset.  Thus, in the absence of a hint system, busy players may find themselves frequently starting the game up to face not just the same puzzle again, but parts that they have already solved.  It is no surprise, then, that only 5% of players reach the end of chapter 2, according to the Steam achievements.  This is a shame, as chapter 3 is the best-looking part of the game and has more spells to introduce.
Players who are interested in challenging puzzles or willing to use a walkthrough may still find a reason to walk away from this game:  the combat.
There is only a handful of normal enemies:  walking and flying swarms that follow a set path and die easily, wisps that follow a set path and die easily, bipeds who charge the player, and floating mages who can cast three spells.  Dealing with the first two types is no big deal, but the bipeds (Saevar) are another story.  One-on-one, they are a joke:  the player can simply cast a bomb spell on them, then stun them to give the bomb enough time to charge.  But since they can spawn in twos or threes, the player never gets any great area of effect spells, and voice recognition may fail, these creatures can actually pose a challenge sometimes.  The floating mages (Shar-Seth), in contrast, are somewhat fun to fight because the player has to listen to the words that they chant for their spells, then act accordingly.  But these are much deadlier if the voice recognition happens to fail.  This would all be fine if battles were always preceded by healing ponds and save points, but they aren't--and sometimes the battles are surprises.  Death means having to re-do whatever platforming was necessary to reach these battles in the first place.
Then there are the three bosses:  the first is almost like a battle with the Shar-Seth, but requires a trick to kill it when it heals itself; the second is a two-part chase involving the ice, teleport, and telekinesis spells; and the third is a battle against clones with powerful spells.  Fortunately, the game either saves automatically at the beginning of these battles or has a save point right before them.  Unfortunately, voice recognition failures tend to result in instant death and the third boss in particular is very frustrating.
Clearly, imperfect voice recognition is my biggest reason for judging the combat negatively.  But there are other annoyances.  Every spell cast requires that the player hold down LMB, speak the proper words, then release LMB.  This is obviously to let the game know when to "listen" for the player's voice and when he is done speaking, but since it makes actions take noticeably longer to perform, situations that require quick reflexes become all the more tense.  Additionally, if the player casts the wrong spell, he has to first cancel it before he can cast another, interfering with the flow of combat.  Two spells--the light beam and the ice beam--even look similar, so it may not be immediately apparent that the wrong spell was cast.  Finally, releasing projectiles caught by the shield spell too often sends them flying everywhere
where the player is aiming, which can make the final boss battle take much longer than it should.
(NOTE:  It has come to my attention that the game offers the player the option to record his own voice for spells to improve voice recognition.  I will not be playing the entire game again to test this, so I can't say if this would have improved the speech recognition.  Regardless, the game's obtuse puzzles and awkward combat were enough to hurt my experience.)
The story is all right:  the player character is simply out to bring his loved one back to life by using the magic he finds in the temple, while the god who guides him wants him to do something else.  Occasionally the journal will update with a little bit of his backstory or his feelings about what he is experiencing, but it didn't add anything to the game.  The 35 hidden documents, however, provide a good deal of lore, explaining some of the history of the temple, the gods, and the civilizations that worshiped them.  It's just a shame that so many of them are hidden (why hide the meat of the story?) and that the writing is a bit inconsistent, sometimes sounding proper and authoritative and other times sounding modern, even sloppy.
I would like to give this game a higher score and a recommendation for its unique mechanic (an experience in itself), visuals, and spell variety, but the core aspects of gameplay--the puzzles and the combat--just don't work for me.  As another reviewer remarks, this game has a lot of wasted potential.  I give this game a 6 out of 10, though more hardcore puzzlers might get more enjoyment out of it.
Be wary of reviewers with only a few hours played:  chapters 2 and 3 are longer and harder than 1.
