Short version: This game has unicorn ambushes, rabid squirrel attacks, and river jumping. You should buy it.
Slightly longer version: This game is merciless, unforgiving, and totally ruthless, just as an Oregon Trail homage should be. You are in a wagon and have a gun to shoot things. Sometimes you get out of the wagon to shoot things. If you are lucky you get medical recovery items and better guns, from shotguns to carpet-bombing airplanes. If you are not lucky, your three characters get horrible diseases and die to machine-gun-armed bandits and Civil War fights. More often than not, the latter will build up and have your journey end terribly.
What keeps the game from getting overly frustrating (at least for me) is the humor. This game is hilarious, and it has everything from dinosaurs to satellites. The narration is fantastic, and it is worth playing for that alone. It's why I got the game, despite usually not being a fan of these types of games. Super Amazing Wagon Adventure was just too funny to skip.
It controls well, once you get the hang of it. I personally am terrible with keyboards for games, but from how it felt, I'm fairly certain a keyboard-savvy player will usually be perfectly fine. There are plenty of options as well, ranging from a number of wagons you can unlock to survival modes. With the numerous scenarios your playable party can get into, it has high replayability.
This game is $3 for a base price, and the witty narration is worth that alone. Add in the other great factors, such as the unlockables and tight controls, and you have a huge winner. Now if you'll excuse me, I need to go back to dying to buffalo.

I am an old timey MMO fanatic. I started Ultima Online in 1999 and have played MMORPGs daily with very few breaks ever since. I've got thousands of hours if not tens of thousands of hours in Ultima, Dark Age of Camelot, Everquest 1 & 2, Guild Wars 1 & 2, and have played significant amounts of other similar action combat MMOs like TERA and Neverwinter. That's my perspective going into this review.
My TL;DR is that BDO is essentially the best currently supported MMORPG on a modern feeling game engine. It is far from perfect, but it is significantly better than it's key competitors like GW2, TERA, and Neverwinter.
The positives:
-The game is vibrant and alive, players are everywhere and even if you're alone there's an immersive atmosphere
-Combat is extremely well designed
-End game is spot on, high risk high reward gear crafting, world bosses, lifeskilling, economics, grinding
-Nonconsentual world PvP
-The worker system, building a global empire is very satisfying
-General character progression and account progression is highly segmented and very satisfying
The negatives:
-Business model is sinister in some areas (pets and dyes are some of the most brutal RNG crap I've ever seen)
-Siege combat for territory control is plagued with technical problems

First off I gonna say that I love this game for those who probably will hate this review.
General things:
To start off this game is not just the price you looking in the store, to be able to farm without getting suicidal feelings you will need to spend 40~ more euro to buy pets so they will loot for you; yes you can farm manually, but you will be killing millions of monsters.
Will crouch to loot every single one? - Quick answer = NO.
Yes you can buy this pets from the market but hey! Good luck!
Another thing that you get a bit forced to buy (not as much as pets) is a ghillie costume, this one hides your name when you playing against other people, it won't ensure you a victory though those players you fighting will have to focus you like the double to be able to see you. Against some classes in the night you fight looking the map not the enviroment which is sad..
This costume is not sellable throught market so is completely pay to win (even if it would be sellable throught market it would be kinda of p2w since get pearl items from the market is very hard).There is an item called "flare" which allows you to see their name but hey it only lasts for 5 seconds or so, so this won't counter pay to winers.
PvE:
The thing which we call PvE in this game is not as other MMORPGs, you are not doing raids/dungeons with your guild every friday neither find parties to do them. You just got spots with mobs, TONS OF MOBS. You wanna be farming them to level up your character, get money or simply get a item drop from them.
Another PvE concept in here is lifeskilling, the lifeskilling in here is way more extended than other mmo's. You can almost play like a lifeskiller in here without doing any other PvE content and you sure won't get bored of it if you enjoy the lifeskilling thing (get money from it, upgrade your lifeskill rankings, etc..).
PvP (this is not the main concept of the game in my opinion because is greatly unbalanced):
Let's be honest, to feel yourself able to kill your adversary in a PvP arena/battleground you will need around 2.500 hours in this game to be able to get the gear to do it, so just simply forget about arenas/battlegrounds.
As a guild member you can be part of a higher tier PvP (Conquest wars, Node wars) those you do with your guild, but as arenas/battlegrounds, you won't do anything if you are not correctly geared (here you can miss some gear since you got a team, you will need to play 1500 hours or so to get the gear to be able to do something more than just see)
The PvP content you are going to do a lot likely or unlikely is PK (Player Kill), in this game you can turn on/off PvP (with ALT+C) which allows you to kill other players or allows other players to kill you. There's a main stat in here called "Karma" which allows low players to don't get camped by higher geared players. If that karma drops below 0 the guy is going to "Negative Karma", this guys can only go to their city Muiquun (which is located at the desert). If those die while in negative they can get their gear downgraded, crystals blown, exp reduce. To raise the karma you need to farm.
There's a big bad thing here which are guild wars, If a guild is able to war your guild (it must be both prepared or both non prepared) these players can kill you anytime they want without any consecuence which is kinda sad if you are low geared and you are getting camped by a high gear guy.. You can of course leave your guild (you won't be able to join it or another back in 1 day) to make karma system do its job which I recommend if you suffer this from other players.
With all this said, I gotta recommend this game because I'm in love with it. I got so funny times with my friends that i wouldn't take away for anything.

Having never played an XCOM game before, I went into this game very cautiously. However, after about an hour of play I found myself successfully leading a well trained squad through every combat scenario with ease. Every decision you make can have serious lasting repercussions. One wrong move and a squad-mate is dead. All that training for that squad is rendered worthless, making it a frustrating experience at times. Once you finally complete the mission and successfully exterminate the alien menace however, it becomes one of the most gratifying experiences in video games. XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a well made game and I highly recommend it to any fans of turn-based strategy games. Even if you're not a fan of those kinds of games, it's worth trying out and a good starting point.

A failed attempt to capture Game of Thrones' glory. For anyone who hasn't read the books or watched the show, this game will probably be alright and provide a decent story, but your choices will seem to not matter at all (which they don't). For people who have watched the show or read the books, this game may be worse. The game has you play a number of different characters from House Forrester, a minor house in the North, which begins to fight with house Whitehill, another minor house near it. As a result of this, the game does not capture the show's feeling of a large scale conflict taking place in many different areas around the globe with high stakes; it feels very small and insignificant (because it is). Battles or ambushes will only involve like 10 men. The final battle of the first season may have like 100 men. The game tries to include characters from the show, including Tyrion, Cersei, Ramsay, Jon Snow, Daenerys, Margaery, but most don't have a whole lot of screentime. The game also tries to replicate the shock of main characters dying, but fails to do it in a meaningful way. In the show, when a main character dies, it leads to events that introduce new characters or make other characters more prominent. In the game, main characters will die often no matter what you choose, making you feel like your time playing and making those choices were wasted. Characters will die...and the story will not introduce new or just as interesting characters. The worst offense of all is the illusion of choice. For example (minor game spoilers) you have the choice between making peace or continuing a war... but no matter your choice, a fight still ensues and war continues. Or when you can make a series of choices, but in the end, your character dies. There are also some strange low texture graphics and some odd animations. I would not recommend this game really unless you have extra money and nothing else to buy, or if it goes below $5.

I enjoyed the game for what it was but it's undeniable that there's much wrong with it. The best part is most definitely the atmosphere and worldbuilding.
The world is amazing. It feels primordial and alive. The amount of foliage is astounding and the lighting effects are superb as well. The two rivalling tribes you're fighting against are visually very distinct, going as far as to even speak different languages.
The combat is servicable but quite shallow. Nothing to write home about, except that smashing someone with a two handed club is fun for a while.
The biggest problems with this game are:
1.) Lack of meaningful content
2.) Short and weak story
3.) Runs out of steam very fast --> disappointing endgame
The world is huge and beautiful, but it's just filled with the same boring missions over and over and over and over again. "kill all animals in the area" great you did it! now do it 12 times more!
"Kill all enemies without alerting them" Great! now do it 12 times more!
"Burn the huts", "kill the big guy", "run around in a cave" It's the same everytime, on all the 200 dots on your map.
You do these missions a few times and then you'll ignore them.
The "Story" Missions aren't any better. Usually they're very random and most of the time lack any coherent story.
Some Missions are nice, You track the source of poison water, poisoned animals, collect glow-in-the-dark mushrooms etc.
Look for the village Missions, at they're somewhat unique.
Later in the game you get the chance to hunt legendary beasts, nicely done, although a bit contrived. I'm getting to that later.
The main story is quite short. You probably only need a few hours if you focus on them. In general you complete some tasks, then go to the Udam/Izila homelands where you complete ONE, yes that's one as in 1, mission and then you're done there, roll credits.
the enemy tribes homelands should be extremely challenging and hostile, the ultimate challenge for your skills, but nope it's quite disappointing. The Izila don't even have a big Village. The Udam do, but like almost all settlements, they're eerily empty. ALmost no people/enemies actually occupy the camps you'll find.
when you reach the Homelands, you'll probably already have upgraded most of your stuff. IF not, you'll find plenty of the most rare animals there, whose hides you need for upgrades. Congrats, those are completely useless now. Hunting very quickly becomes meaningless, as you can't use their hides for anything else but very specific upgrades. f.e You only need 1 rare elk skin in the entire game. FInd one and you'll never need one again.
The rewards for completing... well.. anything really, feel unsatisfying to me. You get exp, skill points, meat, or village upgrade materials... for literally everything you do. Sounds good on the surface but then you ask yourself why you do this boring mission in the first place, when you could do any other... equally boring mission... so you breeze through the story missions and some village missions with the occasional generic one between and you'll finish the game with almost max upgrades anyway.
Oh, and just FYI, your village stops growing after 80 pop. going up to 300 only gives you a % bonus in exp.... yaaaay..
Soooo why am I recommending this anyway? and why is it a story of unfullfilled potential?

Farcry Primal is an unique experience, and I'd rate it as a good one.
The game play was immersive. I found all the NPC's in the game to be interesting characters, as much as pre-historic characters could be.  There's the Farcry style of upgrading your gear via animal skins, a fairly well developed skill tree, and the ability to use various beasts to aid in your progression.
The beast taming is easy to understand and to implement. Each animal type  has it's own unique abilities. Opening higher skill tiers grants the ability to ride certain beasts, which makes traveling across the map much easier. Taming predators at the top of the food chain and then using that pet can make the game a little easy (go go Gadget Sabertooth Tiger).  My only disappointment here was a greatly scaling down of the badger (Quote from Farcry 4 Honey Badget Don't Give a F***).
Hunting animals is fun all in itself. Hunter vision allows you to see animal tracks, blood, and certain cents. And of course you're hunting with spears and a wooden bow, although at high speeds (with the right skills unlocked) clubs make excellent weapons for hunting.
The game allows for a variety of play styles. The Day and Night Cycle exist, so you can pick the time of day you want to do the majority of the game play in. If you want a tactical approach, you can use the owl to scout ahead. Possibly drop various bombs upon unsuspecting enemies and then together with your black leopard, you can begin to silently eliminate the enemies. Or if you're more of a HE-MAN Caveman type you can charge into battle followed by your battle scarred Cavebear to soak up the damage and quite literally eat your enemies.
Storyline....no complaints here. Primal powers like cold and fire were present in the storyline, which is actually fairly common themes among early mankind.  I enjoyed all the characters, I felt like the game ended in a satisfying way.
Other thoughts. I enjoyed the game, I liked the progression and the RPG elements. I love the interactions that can happen with the wildlife, which seems to want to snack on any of the NPC's they could find. Although I enjoyed the caveman theme by the end of the game I was itching to get a fully automatic weapon into my digital hands once again. I found myself missing much of the technology that I had taken for granted in other Farcry games. The Squirrel Suit. A car with a RADIO in it. Or simply a larger arsenal.
I highly recommend this game.

Tropico is a brilliant spin on the classic city builder genre. Instead of the old Sim City formula, you have to build each and every building on your small island nation. This is fine since in many cases, space is limited since your island is, after all, surrounded by water. The goal of the game is to build a successful Banana Republic and remain in power as "El Presidente." You can remain in power through a variety of ways. You have to keep all of the people of Tropico satisfied with your job as "Presidente" but be warned that keeping everybody happy all the time is impossible. You have to please different factions such as the Capitalists, Communists, Militarists, Religious, Environmentalists, Intellectuals, Nationalists, and Loyalists to keep them willing to vote for you whenever (or if ever) elections come up.
Plus you have to keep the foreign powers satisfied. The biggest threats in terms of foreigners are the US and the USSR (The game starts in the 1950s so Cold War politics come into play here). The Europian Union, Chinese Empire, and Middle Eastern countries won't pose a threat but♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥them off can put you under a trade embargo from them. To make things more interesting, you have access to a variety of Edicts that you can issue such as instituting prohibition or a contraception ban. You can praise either the US or USSR and invite them to build a military base on your island (for a yearly rent of $2000 of course). You can order literary courses for all students, declare martial law and forbid elections, permit free housing for all citizens, establish the secret police (piece of advice, use a Cabaret for the Secret Police station, then all your secret agents look like showgirls), invite the Pope to visit your island, and many more fun options that will determine how you rule Tropico.
This is a rundown of my typical playstyle.
I've never played the campaign since I'm more interested in Sandbox mode but in my sandbox mode games I've largely stuck with a Capitalist playstyle. I tend to run the country by refusing to allow free housing, using a "You do not work, you do not eat" ideology.
Whenever I see a shack and I know that there's ample housing availible, I demolish it. (Shacks pop up whenever there's not enough housing availible and/or whenever the occupant(s) can't afford even so much as a monthly rent of $1.00). All must work and pay rent. No exceptions. If there's too many unemployed, time to build some new farms or lumber camps (which offers the most jobs for uneducated Tropicans).
Criminals are arrested and sent to work in the labor camps, producing cash crops such as tobacco, sugar, or coffee. There are no free meals in Tropico (which, ironically, allows for free food via a marketplace provided there's enough produced domestically or imported via the dock).
Environmentalists only serve to stifle and choke our progress by demanding the removal of all logging and mining operations and unfairly taxing businesses that happen to release pollutive elements into the air. Therefore Environmentlists are shunned in Tropico.
Recommended DLC for this game would be the Vigilante DLC for certain as it gives you the Labor Camp building which is superior to the Prison as it functions as both a farm and a prison which you can use to produce cash crops or even produce food for the citizens of Tropico while using prisoner labor. All you need is to spend a few thousand dollars to arrest a few people to send to the camp. Advisable that you just arrest criminals and the leaders of any political factions you disapprove of. :)
The Propaganda DLC is also advisable since you can build Propaganda Towers which turn citizens into loyalists (who are loyal to you and will vote for you every time). This DLC also provides the grey ushanka (Russian hat) and coat of the steriotypical Soviet Union garb. I might play with a capitalist agenda, but I do like me an ushanka.
A few things I'd like to see added to Tropico (granted this is Tropico 4 and Tropico 5 has been out for some time by now so I don't know what is and is not an option)...
1: Customizable flags. Being able to create my country's flag would be an interesting if not fun immersive feeling. FPS games allow us to create personalized tags, why not RTS games like Tropico?
2: More in depth control over what is and is not provided for free. Food, healthcare, and religion are the big three things that are provided for free to Tropican citizens, no matter how you choose to play. Being able to decide whether or not you have "Presidentecare" or requiring a monthly offering from all of Tropico's faithful churchgoers, or truly instituting a "no free meals" rule would allow players to experiment with different styles of governance.
3: More female avatar options. The Male Custom Avatar has the lion's share of customization options while the female Presidente is limited to only a few. A little equality in the customization would be nice. The ability to choose what voice El Presidente uses would also be a great idea.
4: Establish relations with foreign nations. Being able to forbid specific imports from certain countries like forbidding all trade between Tropico and the Middle East, allowing a foreign embassy onto Tropican soil, forbidding the importing of weapons or the exporting of specific goods to specific countries would be a nice touch.
5: Name the Nation! Tropico isn't just the name of the game but it's also the name of the nation too. In game tips and other aspects refer to the nation as Tropico. Not really a complaint but I'd like to be able to name my country instead of just having to go with the generic "Tropico."
6: Legality. Being able to determine what is and is not legal is an idea. I'm mostly just asking for the ability or edict to enact a law that cracks down on the people living in shacks and forces them to move into proper housing. Cruel? Perhaps but then again, that's what this game is about, being as nice or as cruel as you want to be.
To summarize: Tropico 4 is a great spin on city builders and is an interesting medium in which to test differing styles of government. It has plenty of campy and commedic elements to give the game a lighthearted feeling. I mean when you select someone who works as a lumberjack and their thoughts read "I'm a lumberjack...and I'm OK!" you know you're not playing a game that takes itself too seriously. Definately give this game a try if you want a good feel for the Tropico series.

I hear a lot of people saying that saints row 2 was the best in the series. Whereas I think the 3rd was the standout title. It really branched away from "GTA clone" to it's own unique game. And I'm sorry but it seems like the saints row series, always ends up doing what the GTA series promises. The distinction is that this series doesn't take itself seriously at all.... ever. And in this installment, the craziness gets kicked up a notch
I'll get the negatives about this game out of the way first: this could have been a DLC (on top of the million other DLCs for the 3rd). The new mechanics they add in this game are really FUN. Flying, jumping high, running at crazy speeds, the super powers. Theyre all fun and fluid and great..... the only thing is that they make a LOT of things from this series, obsolete! Once you get your powers.... well why do you need a car? or your crew, for that matter. In the 3rd, I had a lot of fun customizing my cars and my crew, and used both quite a lot. In this game I never felt the need to use either, and when I did it was more because I felt I should, not that they were necessary. Its like in their attempt to give us all these fun new powers they just kind of dumped everything else by the wayside. Which is a shame... there was a lot of great stuff there (that's STILL in this game, despite there being no need for it). What they also need to do is put more actual content in these games. map completion just doesn't fly with some people as a reason to keep going. I've played through a LOT of the 3rd.... so why would I need to re-complete that whole map when all of the mini games are the same? This is even exponentially worse with 'gat out of hell', where the whole game is just that
HOWEVER
This game is pure entertainment. You have to sit back and enjoy the absurdity that this series will fling at you constantly. Saints Row knows exactly what it wants to be, as a series... and even the disjointed mechanics fall in with that. It's fun and engaging which is what gaming should be.
What I would love to see, is them abandon all these bells and whistles for the next installment. with gat out of hell, this series is now bigger than itself and theres nowhere really left to go. Building a new installation from the ground up, with new characters, more of an emphasis on the mechanics in 2 & 3, and focus on content, not mini games. That would be fantastic. Untill then I wouldn't buy any new saints row games because once you've played 3, you've played them all

A completely new and entirely obtuse enemy murdered me. I am legitimately not sure if I could even damage this guy, but if I could it would have required super accurate aiming on my part anyways. I had no old saves to load to because making new ones required me bending over to use my keyboard, and reloading my only save left me with almost zero health and no other way to proceed but that awful timing puzzle. I had no other option but to quit.
I think the dev team lost focus of what they wanted to make. The game should have been either about puzzles or killing monsters, probably the former to be honest, but the way they mashed those two goals together doesn't work. In Verbis Virtus really is not that far away from a pretty good game, but the designers at Indomitus Games seem to lack discipline in their work. Actually, that probably isn't fair, maybe the publisher meddled too much or maybe the team had bigger ambitions and it fell flat; but in all honesty I'd rather see the spell selection mechanic sold to a bigger developer who could handle it better. I don't think In Verbis Virtus is worth your money. Maybe if you really want to check out the voice mechanic take a look, but don't spend more than five bucks.

Before I begin, let me just clarify why I would not recommend this game. It's a good game, really good in fact. Graphics are nice, though there is a bit of stuttering here and there. The story is deep and interesting, and who doesn't want to be able to cast spells with their voice? However, there is one MAJOR drawback to all of that, and that is this: It's a puzzle game. I know it may seem like a stupid reason to not recommend a game, but let's be perfectly honest. Even a puzzle game like this is boring, even with the ability to cast spells with your own voice. And to be brutally honest, that's this game's only selling point; "cast spells with your voice!". It's a great concept, but I just cannot recommend a game that takes a good concept and puts it in a game it doesn't belong in. This game would've been much better off as an RPG with Co-Op and/or PvP, where you fight other people and hear them cast spells and have that one split second to think of the proper counter-spell. Instead, we get a game where you roam through a boring (though well-designed) crumbling temple that makes you feel like Indiana Jones while you beat your head against a wall trying to figure out what the heck you're supposed to do next.
Bottom Line: Beautiful game, well designed, good concept but in the wrong type of game. If your only reason for buying this game is "Oooh, I get to cast spells with my voice? Heck yes!", don't buy it. It'll just disappoint you. But if you love puzzle games, then this just might be your cup of proverbial tea.

Thirty minutes into Saints Row IV and you’ve shot our way through a military base before disarming a nuclear bomb in flight, winning the hearts of the nation and the presidency of the USA. You’ve signed off on a cure for cancer or ended world hunger, and fended off aliens from a turret gun on the White House lawn. It’s immediately clear that Saints Row has finally abandoned any of the pretence at gritty underworld realism that was so at odds with the slapstick of previous games in the series. This is the game that finally provides an appropriate thematic context for Saints Row’s mechanics, one that sees the Steelport Saints emerge from Grand Theft Auto’s shadow once and for all.
In Saint's Row IV, you once again take on the role of the leader of the Saints, a now globally recognised gang. After a series of events culminating in you riding a nuclear missile through the air to attempt to disarm it before it reaches Washington (don’t ask), it isn’t long before you become President of the United States yourself (of course). The good times don’t last long though, as humanity’s worst fears are realised when an evil alien race known as the Zin invades Earth. You and the other members of the Saints are held hostage in a simulated version of Steelport. With the help of your hacker friends Kinzie and Matt, and combat backup from the rest of the crew - including Vice President Keith David - you must disrupt the system enough to break free and hopefully save the human race.
The Matrix came out fourteen years ago, and it’s getting to the stage that movies get to when you hear yourself saying “What do you mean you’ve never seen The Matrix?”, and then think to yourself “...oh I’m getting old”. However, as one of the most important films in its genre, you can forgive Saints Row IV for making quite so many references to it. Everything from “finding an exit”, down to diving into the very bodies of enemies and destroying them from within gets a mention. The pop culture references don’t stop there either, in fact I’m sure the rest of this review could be composed simply of the names of games, films and television shows Saints Row IV leans on. Some of them might seem a little outdated, maybe intentionally so, but if you just take everything the game throws at you as it comes, you’re certain to have a much better experience.
Although it is a simulation, you will be familiar with Steelport if you played the previous game. The landscape is much the same, with most of the old locations in the same place. It is noticeably different though, with a liberal scattering of alien hardware, and a lack of sky and water. Since this world is simulated, the laws of the universe can be bent and broken. You now have what can only be described as super powers. Super sprint allows you to travel faster than any car ever could, and combined with Super Jump you can clear multiple city blocks in a matter of seconds. You have a limited stamina bar, but it isn’t long before you upgrade your powers and it becomes irrelevant. At this point you can leap around to your heart’s content. The movement in this game is stupidly fun to control, making the usually boring matter of getting to your next quest location a joyous exercise. Your powers also stretch to you being able to shoot out fire and ice from your hands, smashing down into the ground with great force, and even letting you move objects, and people, around with telekinesis.
The combat still holds up well too. In addition to all the weaponry from the previous game, you have access to all kinds of alien tech. The Dubstep Gun, The Singularity Gun and the Inflato-Ray are some of the most amusing, and most satisfying things to use in any recent video game. As before, you will still be upgrading your character as you play through the game using Cache, which accumulates by performing pretty much any action in Steelport. Mayhem missions return, where you cause as much damage as possible in the time limit. Insurance Fraud has you playing in traffic to generate money. Instead of car racing, you will be racing using your super jump and sprint. You will be hacking shops in a minigame which is a slightly altered version of Pipeline. These side activities provide a distraction from the main quest line, but none of them are particularly worth spending too much time on. In fact it is the most basic of video game concepts that ends up being the best thing to do in your downtime. Collecting Clusters, found on rooftops and walls throughout Steelport, allows you to upgrade your special powers. Since the platforming is so good, it almost becomes a compulsion to head straight towards a Cluster when you see it.
The main story missions are where Saints Row IV shines. The writing is top notch, although you will definitely want to have played at least Saints Row The Third to appreciate a lot of the referential jokes. The game is filled with laugh out loud moments, not only from the dialogue, but often even just from the very situations you find yourself in. Each of your crew members has their own Loyalty Mission, which grants them superpowers of their own upon completion. These are side missions worth doing, while other quests in the game aren’t really necessary unless you’re going for all of the achievements. The main missions alone will take you a decent amount of time, and to complete everything in the game will take up to around twenty hours, especially if you want to get Gold in all of the challenges.
I have mixed feelings on the way the game looks. I wasn’t a big fan of the dark and gloomy visuals of the simulation, but the way every texture shimmers every now and then as the computer program occasionally slows up is pretty cool. The frame rate remained pretty constant, even when it seemed like the entire screen was exploding, or when I was running at hundreds of miles per hour through city streets leaving a trail of destruction in my wake. The only time it occasionally hitched was during an autosave, but it was barely noticeable. The customisations are as deep as ever, and still allow you to look pretty much however you want, as well as bringing in a “Nolan North” option for your character’s voice.
Overall Saints Row IV is a marvellously enjoyable game, while still suffering from a few of the complaints that the series has always had. The main quests are great, and although the side missions are not painful to play, they don’t pack the same punch. If you played and enjoyed Saints Row The Third, then picking up this sequel is a must. Equally if you’re looking for a game that lets you act like a badass with special powers, this might be a better superhero game than many others that are actually billed as such

This is the kind of game that makes me question if I should continue to bother with video games or not. Am I just wasting my time? Are these games that've been hyped to heaven with almost no backlash just bald-faced lies spitting in my face? I have come to this point after wasting so much of my life, throwing myself over 20 hours closer to my death, playing this repetitive, poorly balanced, poorly made-in-general piece of ♥♥♥♥ing garbage. Yes, I despise this game. I have finally come to terms with that conclusion. I tried giving it one more chance after my first (also negative) review that's now deleted, unlocked a few more wagons and modes, but nothing changed for me except the growing hatred for this game, my grown distrust for popular consensus and for sources of game coverage I thought were reliable, and the weariness this has brought upon my life in general. I really, really hate this game.
OK to start: what it looks like: an absurdist, tongue-in-cheek parody of Oregon Trail (obviously), like the video game equivalent of a Mel Brooks or an old Zucker/Abrahams movie. And that description is accurate to some extent. This is a game full of zany, random occurrences, ridiculous humor, and gameplay that, to put it one way, bears little resemblance to the original Oregon Trail. This is all just window dressing though. Strip it aside and what you have instead is a really awful vertical shmup mixed in with awful twin-stick shooter segments with a factor of randomization added to try to give it variation but they bungled it up so badly that it makes already badly done mechanics more frustrating.
If there is a singular goal in this game, it's to unlock all the wagons, since doing so requires accomplishing pretty much every possible task in the game. One wagon requires you not only unlock all five levels in survival mode, but get three full stars in all of them (which means surviving three or more minutes), another requires unlocking "shuffle mode" where you must survive as many randomly ordered scenes from the main game in a row (to get the wagon you need to survive 50), and unlocking the final wagon means completing the main adventure with ALL the wagons. Most of the wagons are unlocked by stumbling upon and surviving random scenarios, some rarer than others, in the game.
The main adventure allows you to ride a wagon with three attendants, which you can customize to some degree by gender, hair style, hair color, manner and color of dress, skin color, eyes, and facial hair (reserved for the men only). This is probably the most fun part of the game, not that it's necessarily interesting in itself, even if it is amusing, but because it's the one and only thing in this game that doesn't cause immense suffering. Then you pick your wagon which you only have one to start with and, if I'm being perfectly honest, is probably better than the majority of wagons I've tried so far. It sucks, but it sucks less so than some of the other crap you get. Now the concepts for the wagons sound fun but actually playing with them? No. The magic wagon has probably the worst default weapon of everything in the game, firing spread "magic" shots in wide angles, too wide actually, and disintegrates things when it kill them meaning you can't collect precious animal hides with it (better get a power-up!), and it fires slowly at that. The invisible wagon starts you off with 1 health for everyone, no joke, as a compromise for how small and easily maneuverable it is. If you survive the first areas and can grab full health for everyone it's great, otherwise, good luck. The space shuttle starts you all off with TWO health, has an even larger hit box than the other wagons (which are too big as it is, making the NES Silver Surfer's seem like a pixel by comparison), has only the same regular attack as the main wagon, and is faster, meaning, harder to control when you're faced by a barrage of enemies and herds of buffalo who will most assuredly kill you much faster. I could go on about how annoying and unfun some other wagons are but really it's the game itself that's out to get you more than the crappiness of your wagons (though that doesn't help).
OK like I said the game is randomized, but not to the extent a roguelike or even some roguelites would take it. It's more like a Tower of Guns roguelite where there is a small amount of randomization but with mostly clear-cut, set paths, level designs and so forth, the difference being that Tower of Guns was actually not a terrible game (I gave up on some of its frustrating challenges eventually but for the most part had a good time with it). The game begins the same way every single time - you kill animals for fur, run into some bandits, seek either wild berries (or if the game wants to ♥♥♥♥ you over, shrooms, though surviving that once does unlock a wagon - but after that, it grows tiresome), then you come to a river crossing, where you can either jump or ford it. Most of the wagons are too slow, clunky and big to bother fording, so I always jumped (which sometimes landed me in the river anyway, getting me hit by boulders coming downriver). There is one set of boulders where you must wait for them to come down, with a space opening up to go through but I swear unless you have a fast-moving wagon this is literally impossible to get through without getting hit. And it goes on and on and on. The game itself is not that long, but you will be assuredly killed repeatedly due to the crappiness of the mechanics and the random events which will screw you over big time.
Sometimes the game asks if you want to investigate something, like distant gunfire (which is either a bank or train robbery), but a lot of times it forces you into situations that you don't want to go into. Like, no, I don't want to save the injured falcon or get the poison gun for the billionth time, especially if I'm at the brink of death and have a perfectly capable gun already at my disposal. But it will anyway and you have no choice but to go along with it. Some situations you may as well quit your game since you will get bent if you encounter them. Like having to travel to a distant trader for a new wheel with the falcon with coyotes all over you. These segments are long and the falcon really sucks at taking down large numbers of fast-moving enemies at once. Then you die and you must repeat the process with one of the other surviving characters and you die again. And if you're forced to meet a woman in a red dress and she turns into a bandit, just... quit right there. After that you will be assaulted by bandits you have no chance of winning against. Oh, and buffalo. I don't know how you're supposed to survive the large herds of buffalo with a large wagon without a decent weapon, and if your characters (idiotically) decide they're "bored" and speed through the herd, you're dead, and frankly they deserve it for being so goddamn stupid as to speed through buffalo to be trampled to death by them and your poorly handled vehicle. Oh yeah there are "twin stick" segments where you might be alone on foot and fight enemies without your wagon or compadres. Your hitbox is more reasonable, but movement never felt "right" nor did the mouse aiming. There are too many fast-moving, tiny enemies hard to hit with your puny weapons with you being too slow to outrun them and eventually you'll be circled and killed. That's actually more a complaint of the survival mode than of the main game but it can happen.
But no matter where you die, whether by buffalo, by wolves on a mountain, or river boulders, the game always feels so inanely repetitive. You will encounter every scenario, of which there are very few, so many times trying to complete the game with one of your many crappy wagons and failing that it becomes a mentally numbing experience. I don't want to hunt more wildlife, bandits, berries, or choose to cross or ford rivers ever again. This is sheer endurance, not fun.

One of the best survival games I have played; where it's a dog eats dog world. Hunger sets in if you don't consume food, you can die from dehydration, freeze to death, bleed to death, die from infection and poison; the odds are stacked against you. However, the same goes for everyone else in Neo Scavenger, as well. It isn't like other games, where they severly penalize you but the conditions does not effect the enemy. Far from it, scavengers you find along the way can bleed to their demise and freeze and perish in the cold if they have no clothing, just like the way you can in the given conditions.
If you pick this game up, be prepared to scream at times, and die countless more. Each death comes with learning to play better, and the learning curve is extremely steep. This game is literally based on Marxism, and it truly is a brutal, unforgiving atmosphere. Do not underestimate the enemy, and if you encounter two or more at once, do not be frugal. It's better to use that ammunition and live another day, than die and start over. Gear up and learn how to survive; and good luck.

Games with wasted potential like this make me angry. The graphics, controls, and atmosphere are superb. The voice recognition is great and casting spells by voice is a blast. Shame it's wasted on such a lame and incredibly obnoxious puzzler.
I don't think I could design more annoying combat or puzzles if I tried. There's very little combat, and thank goodness for that because enemies are as much of a threat to your patience as to your health bar.  Either they're swarms of critters you have to either back away from awkwardly or whittle away, or they're poorly programmed humanoid enemies who spend half the time sitting there and half the time charging you, and only react to your spells half the time.
As for the puzzles and exploration, there's very little thinking involved. It's 5% thought, 10% trial and error, and 85% scouring every last area for some easily missed scribbling, statue, hidden mechanic, or other piece of junk you need. The map in the start of the second level is either completely unreadable or for another area, because I spent a good 10 minutes looking at it and looking around trying to orient it and figure out where I was. There's an area where you take damage as long as you stay there for literally no reason, with no indication except for a small grunt when you enter the area.
You barely even get to use your spells creatively. They may as well just be keys for various locks.
If you will excuse me, I'm going to go pull out all my hair now.

I love this game, despite how difficult it may be. I give it an 9/10
You command a crew on a starship that is attempting to outrun the rebellious scum that has caused havoc in this war. Everything you do will have consequences; thus you need to chose your actions wisely. This game gives so much detail to the little things too.
Pros:
-There are a handful of alien races that do different things. For example, Humans learn things quicker, Engis repair things quicker, etc. Their health also varries due to their race. They can also level up when they work at a certain place for long enough.
-There is a "scrap system that plays into a few things:
--Buying things from stores. Yup! There is an "economy" in this game that focuses on scrap. You can buy things from fuel (which is needed to make jumps from point to point) to weapons to ship enhancements to even crew members!
--Upgrading your ship. Each ship has "active" and "passive" equipment. Active equipment you have to dump power into whereas passive equipment just needs to be upgraded. Active equipment takes a more active role in combat, such as weapons and shields whereas passive equipment makes it easier to regulate you ship, such as making sensors more powerful or making your doors stronger.
--Upgrading your power supply. During your game, you will most likely NOT have enough scrap to completely do what you want. This makes spending scrap dangerous but fun at the same time. This also means you probably won't have enough power to go around, so you will have to make sacrifices.
-There are different situations your ship can run into. This ranges anywhere from a distress signal being a trap to a legitimate distress signal to fending off people from giant spiders (because giant space spiders are no laughing matter!)
-There is a different play experience every time. This adds varriety to the game, giving it a high replay value.
-There are multiple ships that unlock when certain conditions are met.
-There are trading cards for the game.
-You can control your crew as individuals! This makes the game have another level of complexity. Do you want to put that crew member in the engine room or the shields room?
-It's a space "roguelike."
Cons:
-It's a little difficult (but hey, that is part of the fun! It gives your brain a workout).
(Seriously, that is the only con I can think of.)
Tl;dr: It's a space "roguelike" that offers a unique gameplay. The game give the ability to control every aspect of the ship. It's a great game!

After spending more time in Starward Rogue. I have 30% of the game unlocked.  I wanted to modify my review to be a bit better reflection of the game. If you want the super short review: The game is very good, even at full price. If you want the short 'comparison' review : the game is like The Binding of Issac, or Enter the Gungeon in spirit and replay-ability. Starward Rogue and those other two games I would consider the best top-down rogue games currently available on steam. For a side scroller: Rogue Legacy is good.
So now a further examination of this game:
Lets face it, this is why you play a game like this. This is going to be affected by the quality of the levels, enemy variation, 'responsiveness' and controls. The developers have done a lot to improve upon the genre. Secret rooms are not as much of a guessing game ,
. there's plenty of different characters to pick from out of the gate. they are different, and fun. One very esoteric (and challenging) bot controls time. The game only progresses when you move. Really interesting feature.
This is its own category, because it merits discussion. Is the level generation algorithm good? Well offhand it looks like a modified BSP tree, and it works well. the levels balance well. They generate quickly, more quickly than BOI did. The item synergies feel good, and the path to progression being a combination of leveling, shopping, hunting and luck seems to be a nice mix. I havent had many 'broken' runs. Small modifications to the level, such as teleporters at the ends of leaves in levels to get around are nice additions, and make the game less tedius when you are in a run.
I will say that the very jarring increase in difficulty on level 5 even in normal mode is pretty surprising. Why did I take off 2 points?
Firstly I wanted to see more thematic variation between levels. This is something BOI and Gungeon do well. The levels ARE different, but not
different. This could be improved.
Secondly, because of the intersection of sound and procedural generation. I'll explain more in the next section.
In most roguelite games this is the most overlooked thing, and it is here as well. Firstly, the sound is adequate, and the music is adequate. Its not 'bad'. Its just a lot of missed opportunities. The music track does not change thematically much from room to room. Exceptions are the silence in sacrifice rooms, and a few other notable things. Otherwise the track just seems to sort of play. The music was offputting at first -it felt like a 90s rave dance track. Over time its grown on me, and I'd even say its fitting of a mirthful bot-game. Some ways it could be better? How about change the instruments when health is low? What about changing the instrumentation based on the room enemies? Like a big powerful monster is a low booming synth, lots of little bots are like arpeggiators. By picking the 'robot' genre you have so much possibility to tightly couple the music and sounds you hear to what the player sees and experiences. Missed opportunity for greatness here, but not categorically 'bad' either. Its barely above average, hence 6/10
Ok I am a programmer, so I can probably weigh in on some of this. Firstly a TON of options are exposed in the settings and menus and thats just awesome. Hats off. There are some issues with UI scaling at large resolutions that needs to be configurable, and also issues with very wide monitors as well. the second part is more forgiveable.
Things like collision detection, and overall physics seem to be 'ok'.
When it runs the game performs well, and you can see you usually are getting 100s of FPS. So that's good.
The low score however is due to frequent crashes, which is unfortunately unacceptable. Not sure what is the right move there.
The art is good, but not 'amazing'. The bots look cool, the usage of 'energy' projectiles was smart, because the game gets a glow-y tech-y vibe. Befitting of a bullet hell game.
I do feel like the projecticles coudl benefit from more animation. Sometimes the projecticles looks like a lot of very static lifeless decals. What if the glow pulsated? what if the projecticle spins as it comes to you? some Do but a lot of them look rough. On the other hand the projecticle 'pathing' is awesome, and they make very interesting fun patterns.
The ship is neat, and I like that you can see through the floor. It does take a little time to learn which tiles are traps. There's a spike trap that I did not 'percieve' as a trap until I had already been hurt by it. Again. Animation could fix this. what if the spikes popped up? Its moving so i know its dangerous.
Overall the art looks good, but the game needed more animations to convey its ideas.

Starward Rogue's truly an excellent game.
You might want to add "- wars" in your research while looking for gameplay on Youtube, though, else all you're getting is Star Wars : Rogue trailers.
It's a really polished gem, that wonderfully mixes up the rogue-like genre, that everybody seems to know and unconditionally love (Thanks, Isaac ?), and the niche-targetting, fantastic but unfriendly Bullet hell genre (get outta here, Isaac.)
Mechs are usually a turn-off for me, but there's clearly enough variety and vivid colors to make me love the artistic direction. I've got to mention the soundtrack, though. I guess it's some kind of ambient trance or something (I'm not very good with names), and even though it felt weird in the beginning, it actually fits the action quite well. Alas, there are very few tracks, which to me is the only downside of this game.
Gameplay-wise, it's really refined. The game has an excellent progression curve (even though you'd better get familiar with danmakus if you weren't in the first place.) There's lots of enemies, which all come with cool, inventive patterns, and the rogue-likey character customization gets pretty relevant here. No doubt the devs were shmup addicts who wanted to give the genre some fresh air by getting rid of scoring and linear progression and adding lots of new features, and the result is lovely.
Finally, the bosses really are badasses, and the fights are accordingly rewarding. Getting to the end of the game is going to be tons of pain, so be prepared. Regular not-so-hardcore players should be able to get to the end of floor 5, though, and I think for 12$, Starward Rogue's definitely worth the shot. Just don't inflict that to your family and friends if you're the yeller type, of course. :)

I suppose I liked Telltale's attempt at Game of Thrones more than I disliked it, but it was a fine line indeed. Chief problem being a lack of any real choice and almost constant frustration that ensues when the game brushes off player decisions and twists the narrative toward a predetermined plot point. You can replay a chapter six ways from Sunday, put guards on walls and bar the doors, but a character that is meant to die, will die regardless. Technical limitations of an aging engine aren't helping things either. Lack of ultrawide resolution support, mouse that freezes during action sequences, and cumbersome menus only add to the overall frustration. First time, I rage-quit immediately after the end of Episode 1, and it wasn't until my second attempt a year or so later that I was able to enjoy the story for what it is, without expecting it to play out like an RPG with multiple endings. It is not so much a game, as it is a good Game of Thrones story with a heap of interesting characters. R. R. Martin would feel like a kid in a candy factory with so many fresh faces primed for slaughter.

Far Cry Primal is an interesting game because it is set in the stone age, but despite that, it's a true Far Cry game, with the series main strenghts and weaknesses. For me, this means that it's a good first person open world game if you play it at your leisure, but a chore if you want to 100%. Especially because the side missions are repetitive and the collectibles pointless. The game of course lacks the modern guns, but still gives you plenty of ways to deal with your foes. The combat is definitely more personal, and it feels brutal. Taming animals to aid you is awesome, especially the stronger ones. And speaking of which, they play a much larger role in here, and are more dangerous. The world is alive and you can see plenty of interactions. The map is big but a bit repetitive. There's no money system, so gathering materials and crafting are very important. The story is nothing special, but manages to express some emotions. In the end, if you like the franchise, you'll like Primal. If you don't, it won't change your mind. The game does a great job at introducing new ideas and adapting to the historical setting, but like i said, it's definitely Far Cry at it's core. The survivor mode definitely gives you a more immersive experience, but unless you really loved the game, there isn't much reason to bother.

First of all this is the only game from whole Far Cry series I like and that is due to game world setting. I enjoy running around with a club and bow not to mention the pets.
Right after starting the game with the better texture pack you will be struck with very pleasant graphics and sounds. No complaints there. There is no music, but that is absolute must - you need to listen to the sounds around you for your own survival. Music would be game breaking.
Gameplay wise I was soon bored of normal gameplay (open world games are meant to be played on permadeath settings, else there is no thrill to it), I started to do silly things like running through areas without even caring if I die or not etc. So soon enough I have switched to survival permadeath playthroughs and the rest of my review will be based on my experience there.
After you learn your way around, you will find out there are only 2 kinds of enemies in the game you should fear - bears and sabercats. Against normal bears, you can stand a chance even pretty early on but it´s still risky. They can usually be avoided though in one way or another. Sabercats are another story. Fastest and strongest predators in the game, they can two hit kill you, means dying within few seconds. And basically most of my playthroughs end up being killed by sabercat.
The second thing you need to fear are in-game missions. There is a mission kinda early in the game (like within 5 hours of gameplay), actually two of these, that spawn sabercats and one of these in a cave where is no room for anything but pure luck. I got through these two missions alive only once. My last 3 games ended in the same mission being killed by the very same sabercat. Too bad these missions are kind of needed to finish, they grant basic NPCs whom gives you better crafting and skills...
Pets are great but need a lot of micromanagement. When you call a pet it spawns randomly around you in a distance, means it can actually attract enemies to you, it can even spawn in enemy village you wanted to sneak into. ;-) Pets and especially cat pets are quite fond of falling from cliffs and dying. My best playthrough was ruined when my sabercat pet commited suicide and I have died trying to tame a new one.
I like the weapon choices. And there is not much to tell about them... Club for melee, bow for distance, spear when all clubs break (for melee) or for throwing at close distance (heavy damage). Didn´t get to other weapons much, mainly due to fact my longest playthrough was 7 hours 44 minutes before death.
Combat is fine. Some people complain there is no dodge and parry. But hey, how would you parry with a club... Or against a beast. I like it as it is.
Now in-game events. There are three kind of events or missions:
- Main story missions - these tend to be difficult and rewarding and they are preset. I have one major complaint here. If you start such mission, you will be forced to stay in certain path/area on map before you finish it. Now imagine you kill a rare beast and it runs off behind the border of this path/area - yeah, you are screwed. You saw a beast you wanted to tame behind this invisible border - you are screwed. This is a very very bad design for open world game. When I saw this in Far Cry 3 (the only other game from Far Cry series I tried) I have requested refund straight away. I like Far Cry Primal, but I repeat - this is horrible design. Rather apply time limit or something (ANYTHING) else, certainly not invisible border in "open world" game. I guess in permadeath game I should avoid these missions until I get much better gear (but I will get killed before that anyway or die in those missions even with the right gear... permadeath game is more about the path than result, at least in my case).
- Prescripted events - these appear on the map and they are always the same and on same spots. It gets repetitive. Also some of them are straight lying. Like this "easy" event (game description) which spawns a bear attacking your party. Won once, failed twice. Certainly not easy with "starting gear".
- Random events - these are similar to for examply Skyrim events - they are always the same (types) but randomized over map. My only complain is event where you have save someone from animal attack. This event spawned on me several times right at the beginning of a game when I had a basic bow, one club and one spear. Young woman attacked by bear. You don´t have means to kill him... I managed to run him off once but game didn´t recognize that as a victory (stuuupid), obviously to save the woman you must kill the bear or he will find her later that evening in a tent-bar or something.
I wish there was an open play mode. Seriously. Permadeath over and over while playing the same story over and over and over and OVER. THERE SHOULD BE OPEN PLAY MODE... Just start at the starting village and skip the starting missions. It would start right after the part when you start the fight with other tribes for map control. Sadly there isn´t one and that is a big let down.
This game is like this - you enjoy your lovely life in prehistoric era with awesome graphics and sounds, clubing your enemies, shooting arrows at wildlife and all is sunshine. Then out of nowhere or in a certain mission, sabercat comes and your game is mercilessly put to an end. YOU ALREADY FOUND OUT HOW TO TRY DEAL WITH THEM, but there is just no time. Sometimes they completely surprise you, sometimes you know what is coming and yet you manage to screw up. Death in few seconds remember? Still I would not exchange this for boring normal playthrough with loads/saves and respawns. I would not care one bit about deaths and soon enough I would not care one bit about the game as well.
Recommending the game although I will never ever finish the main story. I don´t posses the ultimate skills to not die once and I haven´t see most of the game yet - I guess the missions later on will be even more brutal. Still worth it. :-)

Team Fortress 2 and Minecraft had a baby and they named it Block N Load.
This game is indeed a lot like TF2 and MC but I think what makes it unique is the characters that you can play as.
Let's take two of my favorite heroes as an example, Kreepy The Klown and 'Doc' Eliza Doolally.
Kreepy is very interesting to me because it's extremely rare for me to find games that involve clowns. Besides the fact that he's a clown he also has interesting equipment like trick bananas and a balloon shovel. 'Doc' Eliza Doolally is kind of common because she is a chemical type but she's designed to be like a doctor which is not something you see everyday in games.
Now when it comes to actually playing the game it can seem a bit boring and unoriginal. But because of the game's style it can be ridiculously fun. The learning curve isn't big at all because it's pretty straight forward and as soon as you get into the game there's a learning tab that contains a video tutorial and solo practice rounds. The waiting time for matches can be long but not all of the time, I could wait 5-10 minutes for one match and then get another one in seconds.
A lot of games have a bad commmunity but I never ran into anyone mean or anything. Most of the time people are quiet and keep to themselves each match but sometimes you can run into very chatty but friendly people who like to help newcomers.
I tried my best to go over most of the things in this game while keeping a short review, hopefully this helped. If it didn't that's OK because guess what...the game is FREE. You can try it out and if you don't like it simply uninstall.
Hope to see you in the goofy battles! <3

This is one of those obscure games that, in all respect, deserve to stay forgotten, for various reasons.
First thing first: the graphics of the game look atrocious.I'm usually not someone who will pick on such when reviewing a game but even for a DOS game, this isnt a good looking one. I would go as far to say that even Bubsy 3D (where the dev or devs had no idea what they were doing with the engine) had better scenery than  Xenophage.
The basic gist of the game is very simple: you are fighting against other characters in a row of 5-6 opponents in the so called story mode (assuming this game had any sort of story to begin with than this paper-thin 7 lines excuse of introduction), as well as you can play in free-play or train against a dummy in story mode. ....yeah, it isnt.

I didnt had the occasion to try out the other characters yet and see if they handle in any shape or form differently (assuming they even do), but bluntly put,  Im not really sure  I could force myself to ever launch this hideous garbling mess ever again.

Developed and published by Tayfun Tuna, The Orphan Dreams is the kind of game I knew it shall rue the day I’m going to write a review to it. Relatively recent and with so far, many positive reviews from others, I thoroughly despised playing it myself and couldn’t find almost any redeeming point to it. The following review may or may not upset those which have played and found it fun. But I shall never abandon my honest opinion for the shelter of positive review ratings. So the least you can do is respect my opinion, even if you disagree with my views regarding this title.

The Orphan Dreams would have been a somewhat decent game if priced for let’s say…1 dollar/euro. Sadly it’s currently “worth” five times as much. Its failed attempt at offering an emotional experience in laughable at best and the few mini-games and puzzles it tries to sprinkle between one tragic scene to another offer little diversion from noticing just how bland it actually is.

The poorly animated and drawn images couldn’t have been worse. And I played my fair share of shovelware, on Steam and before it. You couldn’t even find it an excuse for “artistic interpretation” since it’s pretty obvious the dev team simply didn’t care polishing the game at all. As if the shoddy graphics weren’t enough, the sounds are just as atrocious and seem recorded and then played  through a cheap mobile phone.

+ A few of its puzzles were interesting
- Generic and repetitive sounds and graphics
- No Steam Trading Cards or Achievements
- Unbalanced difficulty (through annoying puzzle timers)
- Highly overpriced for what it currently offers

This is Tayfun Tuna’s debut on Steam but they certainly started off on the wrong foot. No Achievements or at least Trading Cards? Even Digital Homicide provides those and I’m sure almost everyone on Steam knows the general quality of the games those guys publish and develop. How can Orphan Dreams be so highly rated right now, is beyond my understanding. I shall not accept or recommend the title in its current form and I suggest to any potential buyer to avoid it unless it’s being sold for the sum I mentioned previously or given away for free. Remain reluctant even then.

Though the controversy surrounding BDO inevitably scares away far too many potential new players, this game is the farthest from "dead" you can get. There are, as of me writing this review, over 10,000 players online. And that's just on Steam, let alone the official launcher.
There is no other MMO like BDO. The amount of freedom to do whatever the hell you want is wonderful, horrible, and awe inspiring all at once. It sets off OCD, ADHD, and an inevitable streak of psycopathy in every new player.
You want to level to 56 to get this "Awakening" you've heard so much about. Oh, but you can fish. And gather. And process. There's quests and side quests that reward knowledge and contribution, and oh now I have a trade empire of mindless beer swilling slaves spanning the entire continent.
Oh, there's a sailboat? How many logs? Be right back, I'mma cancel that dinner date with my definitely-not-from-Canada girlfriend.
I'd also like to touch on that "P2W" tag thrown around like chicken skin at a South Park viewing party. The only things I can conceivably see as P2W are only mild. The Artisan Memories you can purchase triple durability recovery on gear after a failed upgrade, and while you will be failing A LOT and repairing max durability A LOT, you can get Artisan's Memories for free just by logging in and getting a free currency called Loyalty. 4 days login is enough for 1 Artisan's memory, and honestly as a new player with small amounts of income you should be going slow on the upgrade stuff anyway as you learn the mechanics and systems of the game.
By the time you have the income to really start upgrading, you can literally just buy either the materials needed to repair max durability quickly, or just buy the fully upgraded gear. The in-game marketplace has fixed prices, leaving market crashes and sniping impossible.
The graphics have a MAJOR pop-in issue. And on a fast enough mount, you'll have to pause often for the world to load on weaker rigs. My Tier-5 horse sends me jerking to a stop every 5 or so minutes for the world to load on my laptop, but...the game runs serviceably on my laptop. A small price to pay.
The voice acting is atrocious. Turn it off. The game's music is serviceable. Turn it off. The natural ambience of wagon wheels, wind in the trees, rushing water, and salty tears of RP chat is wonderfully immersive, despite the UI designed by a mentally deficient toddler and the rare visual bug (textureless boulders in the middle of roads appearing for a few moments, mild lag with mobs as they spawn in, etc.)
The servers have their on and off days. There will be weeks you go by playing 12 hours a day with the normal lag expected of an online title with a metric♥♥♥♥♥load of stuff happening on the screen, and then for a week or so every 10 minutes you'll be disconnected. This is the CURRENT controversy of BDO, but as of today (NOV 22, 2017) the servers have been reported fixed by the devs and AMPLE compensation have been given to those most affected. As I said, over 10,000 players are online as of this moment, so I'm guessing the problem is (at the very least) better.
PROS
* Character customization, graphics in general
* Sound design
* Combo-based action combat
* Waifu-sim 2k17
* Ample♥♥♥♥♥♥to waste time on instead of progressing like you should be doing
* Varied classes that do about anything you'd want them to
* mini elephant mount
NEUTRAL
* Sound design
* Story (interesting, but overall too long and a bit cliche)
* Class balancing. Picking the right class (witch/wizard) means being a God, picking the wrong class (Kuno/ninja) means being left behind somewhat
* Graphics. Again, if one can look past the pop-in like I do it's simply a mild annoyance, but it can turn one away)
* Cash Shop. Some very nice things for productive members of society or those with access and permission with mom's card. I have no qualms dropping 10-20 bucks a month for a game of this quality)
CONS
* Community can be...eclectic. Block RP chat immediately if you want to spare yourself from arguments over whether traps are gay and if Trump is ever gonna build that gattdern wall
* Voice acting is truly horrendous. Like, some of the worst I've ever come across. And I've played plenty of Korean MMO ports to the states with terrible VAs.
* The grind can be all encompassing. Hours spent moving in a circle through a cave killing the same enemies only for the XP bar to raise by 2 percent. This is at end game, however
* PVP is forced upon you after lvl 50 in many areas. This is a pro for some, and a con for many. The majority rules.
* Server instability. Can be a real problem sometimes.
All in all, I wholly recommend BDO for those with the time to play, the patience to learn the mechanics, and the willingness to drop a few bucks on something they enjoy.

The Quake series is classic. It's probably the most influential shooter when it comes to online arena/deathmatch  gameplay. If you haven't spent time playing it yet, you've missed out, and now is your chance to make up for that by testing out the waters with Quake Live.
So what exactly is Quake Live? Quake Live is basically a free game of the year edition remake for Quake III Arena. Same graphics engine, very similar gameplay, except it has significant patches to the netcode and functionality. But best of all, it's on now on Steam. Unlike modern shooters, Quake won't reward you for getting kills with airstrikes and UAVs or ammo drops. The only thing rewarding in Quake is your skill.
Quake III Arena in particular had a lot of gothic art and influence, which hasn't been dropped out of Quake Live, although it seems a bit minimalized. Quake is probably the reason I turned out emo/goth/scene/indie. When I was a kid it exposed me to blood, gore, and gothic art. It's weird to say but Quake was my first FPS ever, and actually had a profound influence on how I turned out.
If you loved Quake or even if you still haven't played it, download Quake Live now and start fragging away.

Why do people keep on making roguelites with scarce health?
Roguelites are fun as long as they do ANYTHING BUT THAT.
There's a perfectly good reason why this is bad.
Say that the player has 10 health, gains 1 health every 4 rooms, but loses 1 health every 3 rooms.
Will the player be thinking "Wow, that was a tough fight, but I made it!" at any point?
No, because everything is so weak that it's rarely damaging the player at all, let alone single-handedly life-threatening.
Everything will seem like a pushover.
And yet despite this, the player will eventually lose because although they get hit rarely, they get healed even more rarely.
So, a long game with scarce health can seem too easy yet be too hard at the same time; and if it isn't too hard, then it will seem way too easy. If the game seems adequately challenging, then the player will lose in only a few minutes.
This is the absolute worst way to balance a game's difficulty, and I do not believe there is a game in existence that is better for having done this, yet thousands have.
Could this easily be fixed?
Yes, just make everything more lethal, but make shields way better.
Say that the player has 10 health and 10 shield, but gets hit an average of 8 times per room.
Will the game feel challenging at first? Yes, they'll often be losing a good chunk of their total health pool.
Will the game continue to feel challenging? Yes, because obviously the maximum number of times they'll get hit in a single room will be higher if the average is higher, so it's entirely possible for a single room to kill a player outright; whereas if the player rarely gets hit more than once in a room, it's unlikely that there'll be a room that hits them enough to take them from full health to zero.
But health shouldn't be pure shields, because otherwise the only rooms that matter are ones that are likely to kill the player outright. If health is 50% shields, then to matter in any way, a room must be at over 50% as lethal as a room that kills the player outright; and that seems perfectly reasonable.
Currently, health is 9% shields, so a room that over 9% as lethal as a room that kills the player outright will end up doing lasting  damage.
