I'm pretty good with twin stick shooters, and I haven't found one I liked in a while. A lot of people compare this game to Binding of Isaac, but IMO the similarities only amount to "top-down shooter in a randomly constructed dungeon with prefab rooms." For my personal taste, Starward Rogue is a lot more fun.
Configurable inertia. Weapon sounds range from light to weighty and generally feel right. Nothing feels "unfair"; if I die, it's my own fault.
Looks great to me! Bullet visibility is good. It can get confusing when a lot of things are shooting at once, but that's how it should be, right?
Surprisingly, this Arcen game has a good soundtrack. I keep it off now, because (1) I've heard it too many times, and (2) it gets me so pumped up I start making mistakes from being too aggressive.
The room layouts require attention without resorting to gimmicks more than once in a blue moon. The enemy movements are mostly ho-hum, but their bullet patterns require focus to deal with while still feeling well balanced on normal difficulty.
There's tons of content. I just finished beating the game a couple times with the default mech after 13 hours. I expect at least 20 more with the remaining mechs and the extra floor unlocks when I win one more time.

This game was unlike no other game in the Telltale videogame franchise. It combined Game of Thrones, a book and tv series with so many twists and turns through characters deaths and characters betraying one another and shocking plot twists, and was packed into Telltale's lovely art style and atmosphere which every game from the company has.
To myself, this felt like I was actually in the Game of Thrones universe, and I felt as if the game itself was almost a movie. Telltale games also have a unique value to them where they have the ability to make you feel genuine sorrow for characters; it started with the walking dead series, and I didn't think I would say this, but the Game of Thrones Telltale game also bestowed in me a genuine sense of sadness, for House Forrester and its losses.
To anyone who likes the Game of Thrones franchise, I definitely recommend this game. To anyone who likes Telltale games I recommend this game to those individuals as well.
A fair warning however to those who love to be invested in such glorious story-driven video games; you are going to have one hell of a roller coaster ride with this game.
I give this a solid 9.6 out of 10, for its beauty as both a Telltale game and as a branch off of the Game of Thrones franchise.

Writing a review to help give this game the support it and its creators deserve.
I'll be honest, Starward Rogue didn't leave the best of initial impressions. The tutorial was sloppy and abrupt, the UI is average, some of the visual elements fall flat, and the soundtrack is rather repetitive.
In spite of all of this, I am going to recommend this game.
Put simply, this game completely nails the most important elements in this genre. The game handles well with a gamepad, the variety of rooms is staggering, there are plenty of different weapons to choose from, and the game handles the balance between the player's three guns (one of which has infinite ammo, one of which has finite ammo that requires pickups to be refilled, and one of which has finite ammo that recharges between rooms). There's also six classes that all play completely differently and a few frustration-reducing features like a Borderlands-esque shield that lets you take one hit per room without losing health. Special commendations, however, go to the enemy bullet patterns. Every foe has a distinct and elaborate firing pattern, some of which require thinking ahead or precision to successfully avoid. In this way it's closer to a bullet-hell style than other games in this subgenre.
I must also note that balance-wise the game is still rough around the edges in a few places, but Arcen Games seems to be vigilant on fixing issues while adding small amounts of additional items and minor refinements. Not enough to detract from a recommendation, but I feel it would be amiss to not mention this.
If you enjoy other games in this style, pick this one up. I can say with certainty that this is the best twin-stick shooter I've played since The Binding of Isaac: Rebirth. It's also worth recommending to anyone who likes arcade shooters of any type, as the RPG elements one would associate with a roguelike are very downplayed, leaving only a XP system and currency.

I decided to get dreadlocks and dye them pink before streaking around town, mass murdering middle aged inhabitants. And  then I bought this game on sale for 5,99.

Have you ever listened to the news, or reading a newspaper and you hear about those dictators who care little of their citizens, exploit their own homelands, or even assassinate political enemies?
Guess what! there's a game where you can do just that! No, not Roller Coaster Tycoon
Tropico 4, is a simulation game, much like Rollercoaster Tycoon, where you attempt to accomplish various goals and earn money to get a higher score.
You are "Presidenti", a fictional character who can be pretty much whoever you want him to be. Personally I can't shake the name "fidel castro" From my mind. Anyway, I digress; You're whole goal is to shape the Island of "Tropico" into a paradise/world-power/luxury-resort/tourist-attraction.
There are a number of missions or quests that you complete as you progress through the game, you start out with a tutorial where you're being taught about "rule and politics" by "generalissimo". (aka, the tutorial)
There's several different modes, but generally it comes down to two ways to play: Missions, and Sandbox mode. On missions you have various objectives that you must succeed in to unlock the next mission.
The controls in the game feel like Rollercoster tycoon had woohoo with the Sims3, I've always disliked moving around the world with the cursor or the arrow keys, because whenever I press ASDW I bring up some rogue menu. However it's not too difficult to overcome the movement keys and zooming methods (mouse wheel).
Fair warning: There's a lot to take in when you start this game. Most people who have played Simulator games should already be aware of this quality, you micromanage a whole Island and have different objects that show up that you can choose to complete or not.

My achievements wouldn't appear until I leave the game and re-enter, most the achievements require really getting into the game and accomplishing various tasks, you would do well to just play through the campaign and worry about what achievements are left once you're finished.
Tropico is priced at $19.99, which is a fair price for how much content is in the game, as always; I suggest waiting for a sale so you can get the most out of your money.
One last thing to keep in mind about Tropico 4, it was released in 2011. Meaning the graphics look dated, since the graphics tried to go for "realism" it's quite obvious the game was designed in 2011.
Here's the real question: Do I like the game? Yes, and no. The game is fun, but I need to spend more time learning the mechanics. It's a sound working game, so there's that. But I didn't particularly enjoy this game more then other strategy games I've played.
In the end I don't feel one way or another about this game, there is a PC Demo, if you're considering getting this game I recommend trying that Demo to know for sure if you want it.

HALF-LIFE 2<
The long awaited sequal to half-life came in 2004. The game was a hit for fans of the original and brought some new elements and features to the battlefield. The plot takes place two decades after the black mesa incident and earth is under siege by a seemingly unstoppable alien race, the combine.
PROS:
-The story is very well paced and put together very nicely as all the others. You play as Gordon Freeman again during the aftermath of earths defeat in the Seven Hour War. Not spoiling the rest in case you haven't picked up a copy in the 10 years its existed.
-The environment is very immersive as it is a long seamless road to the end of the game with, as the definition of seamless implies, zero cutscenes or immersion breaking interruptions.
-The gunplay involves the same weapons from half-life with plentiful new additions such as a combine rifle and different grenades. The arsenal available is pleasently loud, very powerful feeling, and quite fun to use when eliminating the enemy as per tradition.
-The game gives players a little down time after a while with some dialogue heavy playable "cutscene" like segments. Four in total.
-New engine means new physics, and new physics means a whole new realm of puzzling to do.
-The ending is fantastic with closing out the game but certainly could have been better.
CONS: (Not even half-life is safe from sin, sorry) Please note that i am extremely aware that this game is sorta old.
-Controls feel less floaty than half-life 1 but there's still some slip n sliding.
-The combine is a painfully easy enemy throughout the entire game and even when their ranks change.
-Cutscenes are replaced with you being essentially trapped in a box and forced to listen to dialogue every playthrough. There are four instances of this happening throughout the game but all are spread vastly apart from eachother.
-The games puzzles and other logic based conundrums are bonehead easy and will just seem like annoyances on successive playthroughs. Sad part being this seems to be the games only ace in the hole as it will sometimes FORCE mundane puzzles(hope you like box stacking) on the player in order to continue.
This game is about as much of a must have as the first one. I picked the entire series up in a frantic buy in a summer sale and it was worth it. The game is very replayable to me, i went through it about twice a year ever since i picked up the orange box for the xbox 360. The game has some very valid criticisms from fans of the original and while i see almost all of them i still can't help but come back. if anything it's textures for gmod if you don't have much interest in it.

You came here to see bullets flying across the screen by the hundreds and to fling lead at dozens of enemies, all of whom have their own quirks. Arcen Games does Strange Things. They do Good Things. They do Fun Things.
They are not a big corporation, and I doubt they ever will be, because they most of all do Unsafe things.
Starward Rogue is, functionally, much like Binding of Isaac; But whereas most games look at Binding of Isaac and say 'Okay, let's basically make it like that', this game took Binding of Isaac far beyond what it should be. The characters are very, very different- One of them even turns the game into a Frozen Synapse-esque strategy, with the action only moving when you do. The controls are crisp and ultra-responsive. Unlike Binding of Isaac, I have never had a moment where I ran into something because the character was moving like they were on a patch of ice- Except for that one game where I picked up the item that specifically makes your sprint movement faster, and slippery. Controls are completely amazing.
The vast breadth of items and monsters makes the game hugely fun. There are tons of different items, and enemies, and each enemy works in a different way. The roguelike bullet hell is endlessly entertaining, always throwing new challenges at you. Bosses aren't AS varied, but there are twenty of the damn things, each one of which is very unique in its fight style, and insanely fun. The items vary from simple passive boosts to the vast variety of different primary and secondary weapons, which encouage different gameplay styles.
It's insanely fun. It is definitely worth more than 12 dollars. And Arcen Games needs your help, because they do strange things that don't slot easily into other people's labels. They deserve to be rewarded for doing something that is not only different, but amazing.

Starward Rogue is a shoot-em-up/bullethell rogue-lite that is often compared to Binding of Isaac or even Nuclear Throne.  It is fun, fast-paced, graphically well-polished and unique, with a lot of customization options and smooth, fair controls.  A good coffee-break sort of game that is easily played in short bursts, or as long as you like.
Your goal is to clear a dungeon room-to-room, floor-by-floor, using your primary weapon with infinite ammo; your secondary weapon that uses energy that refills every time you (re-)enter a room; your finite supply of missiles; findable modules that give unique passive effects or abilities; 1-shot uber consumables; and your ability to WASD-dance your way between a hail of living, oft-unpredictable bullets.
You can find or purchase power-ups, health restoration pick-ups, ammo for your missile launcher, new weapons for your primary and secondary slots (which can be a HUGE boon in either case), etc.
Your choice of class at the start of a run can have a huge impact on your run based on their various strengths and weaknesses and starting weapons, but once you start picking up new weapons and power-ups, the character you started with may be a different one entirely from the one you die a painful death as. :D
You will lose.  A lot.  But this game is fast-paced--you can rest between clearing rooms, though--and fun, and death never really feels unfair.  The wide selection of difficulty levels also ensures you'll always be able to have a good time, as well.
Highly recommended either for casual fun, masochistic self-harm, or anything in-between.

Starward Rogue is a roguelite/bullet hell game made by experienced indie studio Arcen Games, previously known for games like AI War or Bionic Dues. Developers obviously favor the sci-fi theme so Starward Rogue is no exception. You'll control a mech that will venture into "The Megalith" to destroy every threat on sight.
To do that important task, you'll be assigned with many weapons. From the start you'll get a basic rifle, energy rifle (with limited energy for every room) and missile launcher. That doesn't mean you'll keep those through your run, as you'll be finding many great weapons and tools (some apply as a permanent passive bonus, others are only for one use).
Before you start, you'll select a mech that you want - if you don't like the basic one, you can pick a mech that focuses on treasure hunting, or a mech that can manipulate time (in a Superhot style), for example. Don't worry, there are even more unique mechs for you to pick, providing more variability for your runs, which is necessary for every roguelike/roguelite game.
Variability of runs is also high because of two important things: There are many room patterns that can surprise even experienced players, and every enemy has a unique way of attacking. Every type of enemy has a different way to turn your run to inevitable end. This fact made me really excited for more runs, seeing the awesome developers' creativity for bullets and attacks. This applies also for bosses and though there aren't many of those, they still offer a great bullet hell experience.
Besides of health (and shield), you'll be also taking care of money that will drop from several objects in the rooms, and shopping - you can spend your money for bot helpers, new weapons, upgrades, heals or experience. Starward Rogue follows classic leveling system, where every level up offers you a special passive upgrade (you pick one from three possible upgrades). Through the levels, you'll be also collecting a health shards that can upgrade your maximum health.
From the presentation point of view, the visual style of the game feels pleasant in terms of the sci-fi theme. That applies also for the soundtrack, which belongs into electronic/dubstep genre and though I don't listen to that music genre, it felt fine there.
To make it a great experience for both newbies and skilled players, Starward Rogue has five difficulty options. Unlocking achievements tends to be really satisfying, as developers made them only for challenges that truly tests your skill... to a certain extent, since you can unlock them even on the easy difficulty (
).
Developers definitely deserve praise for this game, which they even continually update with new content and bugfixes. They also support mod creators, with their active Arcen Games forum community and detailed documentation on wiki.
Starward Rogue is a great case of using currently popular roguelite and twin stick shooter formulas into developers' favoured futuristic theme. With continued support, great room, weapon, item and enemy variety, there aren't feature that would deserve a negative critic. I can recommend this game with a clear conscience. Great game!

Diablo 2 used to be the game to which I would compare every other Diablo-style ARPG I came across.
Not anymore.
Grim Dawn is now my new standart for the genre.
Only thing it's missing are the randomly generated levels. I even held of buying GD for awhile because I knew the levels where pre-designed... I shouln't. I honestly don't even miss that feature now when playing GD, since everything else is just so good.
But even though the levels are pre-designed, there are still some randomization going on. On diferent playthroughts the game will place some blockades/walls randomly on certain areas, which means that even if the area is the same, your path might be different now. Plus, loot and mobs are obviously random.
Besides the amazingly fun gameplay and the gazillions of possibilities for diferent builts to fit your style, Grim Dawn also has a great setting and world-building, a nice Lovecraftian narrative and a great sense of progression. All things that the first two Diablo games did very well, but similar games like PoE and Torchilight dind't (at least not to this standart, in my opinion).
Grim Dawn can be finished in about 30hrs (not counting the expansion) but it took me 70 becouse I just din't want it to end. I was having so much fun and the game has lots of things to do if you want to extend your time with it. There's plenty of secret areas to find, including a few optional rogue type dungeons.
After a couple months since I first finished the game, I'm now starting my second playthrough, and I'm having just as much fun as the first time. Or maybe even more since now I have a better idea of what I'm doing with my character built.
I predict there will be more playthroughts after this one.

I remember back in my days when I'd saddle up on my horse every night, sneak downstairs, and quietly start up my most prized relic... The Playstation 2. Once it was up, I would insert the holy Battelfront 2 disc and begin the game. My excitement grew as I picked the galactic conquest mode and join the Galactic Empire as a grand admiral. Commanding fleets and destroying rebel scum in a first or third person fashion was so relieving. And after a night's work I'd shut the console down and sneak back up into my room right around 2 in the morning, hoping my parents didn't hear me.
In conclusion, this game has made more childhood gaming memories and fun than I can count, and I absolutely love looking back on them. This game has also represented the most godly fashioned strategic gameplay with a fast paced first/third person Star Wars shooter mix. I owe the devs a lot for what they did to me.
Sure this might seem a little over dramatic, but in a nutshell it's all true. And because of the ridiculous amount of love I have for Battlefront 1 and 2, I decided to support and buy this game once more, but this time for computer. If your a lover of Star Wars, or even shooters in general, BUY THIS GAME.

Half-Life 2 is a first-person shooter taking place after the events of Valve's Half-Life. In this game, you play as Gordon Freeman, an ever silent character who wields a crowbar and dons an HEV (Hazardous Environment) suit. I remember seeing this game years ago when I was young. Though, I mainly got it to run Gmod. However, I did play through it... a lot! And it was pretty fun. The mechanics are pretty okay, and the gameplay is leveled out with moments of calm and situations of action. You fight a few types of enemies. The biggest ones being the Combine Overwatch units. The story plot is quite interesting as well. I've always had a deep interest in the way Valve has set up their stories.
So, what are the pros and cons? Well, while it is well made, it can be a bit glitchy with the Source Engine. The enemies are at times either boring to fight or are a bit one-sided. I wouldn't recommend for constant replay. Though, if you are patient with the game and don't burn yourself out on Half-Life 2, it can become like one of those books or movies you just keep coming back to read or watch over and over again. I know I've done that. So I recommend this to someone looking for an engaging story whilst also enjoying a bit of action on the side!

---Original Analysis of "Ezro"---
It was an innovative game, acclaimed by critics, and seen by many as the new model to follow for the genre shooter. Graphically, it was the best releases of the year, if not the best. For me, one of the best games ever created.
I do not come to talk about Half Life exactly, since everything is said. I come to talk about what happened next.
The Steam gaming platform was initially only an application from which you could download and play Half Life 2, called Tracker. At the time, Valve had not thought anything special for her, since it had been created with that sole purpose: to allow users to play Half Life 2. Nothing else.
Such was the success of this game that the company decided to continue its history through episodic releases. The first of June of 2006 was released Episode 1, and later, the 10 of October of 2007, Episode 2. Initially would be a trilogy of episodes that would give preamble to the next great game.
Time passed, and Episode 3 continued to be postponed and postponed, for reasons confused and still discussed.
Meanwhile, the Steam platform was gaining ground, thanks to which Valve agreed to host games of other companies in it. More games began to be published, more new users arrived; every year even more quickly. Valve continued to develop games for a while, to finish projects in which they were still working, but from Episode 3, nothing was said.
Steam was becoming more and more profitable for Valve. Thousands of developers were eager to sell their games on the platform, and with the rebates every winter and summer were more profitable than the launch of a game. This made Valve think that it was no longer necessary to make games. They preferred to continue adding cosmetic content to Team Fortress 2 and CS: GO, as it generated money more easily. As soon as they could, they took the simple route.
Not long ago, during the last 2 years, several Valve employees began to leave the company. Concept artists, voice actors, stage modelers ... and above all, writers. Writers who previously worked on scripts such as Portal 2, Left 4 Dead, Team Fortress 2 and, of course, Half Life 2. They left the company for an obvious reason: Valve no longer offered them any task they could apply their talents.
It seemed that Valve's plans were not to continue the sagas mentioned. Many fans speculated that perhaps the reason for this was that the dialogues and storyboards were already finished, and that only needed to be recorded in a video game. After 13 years without knowing our beloved series, there were still people who kept the hopes and looked forward to the return of Gordon Freeman.
Two days ago, on August 25, 2017, those hopes faded.
Half Life saga writer Marc Laidlaw, who had left the company 18 months earlier, revealed in his blog a letter containing what appeared to be a "fanfiction", camouflaged between modified and other names, but that was really everything the plot of what would be Episode 3 if it had ever come to be developed.
Marc was motivated to do this by realizing that after so much time of dedication and love for his work, Valve was no longer interested in the least to give a proper conclusion to the story and simply left the game to oblivion, while the fans continued to wait incessantly for the next track that would lead them to think that HL3 was close.
Sick of Valve's refusal and saddened by the fans, Marc gave us all the conclusion we both hoped for, in the form of text. What would have been a phenomenal game ended up becoming a blog entry of about 30 lines.
That's right, gentlemen. Gabe Newell preferred the easy money offered by both Steam and CS: GO instead of worrying about his biggest and most recognized series, letting her die as pathetically as possible. And as if that were not enough, he revealed not long ago that he is developing a card game, which will surely be an excuse to sell microtransactions.
You make me sick, Gaben. You make me sick, Valve. Great developers sold like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to the money, forgetting completely of what one day made them big. I hope it's worth it for you to have left an opportunity to go down in history as big as this, for a meager game of cards, hats and boxes with painted weapons. I will not remove this negative feedback until Valve replaces the fans in some way, for these 13 years of useless waiting that they made us go through.

What is Starward Rogue? Imagine if a neon-soaked SHMUP had a baby with a space-themed rogue-lite. There's a tl;dr "bottom line" section at the bottom.
.Game play.
You are a mech seeking to free your A.I. buddy from a dangerous, robot-infested dungeon. Or... something like that. You can use mouse and keyboard or gamepad. I prefer and used the latter, but movement is fluid and responsive either way.  You can shoot in eight directions (including diagonals) and your mech possesses a primary weapon, an energy weapon, and a missile--more on those later.
Every mech is unlocked from the very beginning, which is something that I really liked. Each has its own pro and con (i.e, this has more health, but a weaker arsenal or this has less health, but a bigger shield) and each plays substantially differently. My favourite thus far is the one with the flamethrower.
You get experience for killing enemies, which is a nice little RPG touch, and each level allows you to select a perk for your mech like more health or greater percentage of crits--adding greater diversity to each playthrough. Much in the manner of games like The Binding of Isaac, subsequent runs through the original dungeon opens up more floors and power ups.
After every run, successful or unsuccessful, you can view your stats regarding secret rooms found, accuracy, how many pieces of equipment you've unlocked, etc.
There are six levels of skill, from very easy to suicidal (not really, I just don't remember what the highest was) and they're all available right off the bat.
.Equipment.
There's a pretty wide variety of weapons, though I've found that the basic weapons tend to feel the same. It's the energy weapons and one-time use items that really vary up your combat and those can range from bullet-blocking shields to explosive traps.
Your weapons include your primary, which has infinite ammo, your special weapon, which uses energy that regenerates over time, and your missile launcher, which consumes missiles that can be found throughout your run. Interestingly enough, the missiles can also be used to block oncoming enemy fire, which is something to keep in mind when you find yourself in a particularly bullet-hellish situation.
.Enemies.
This gets a section of its own if only because the enemy bots found in Starward Rogue are unique and awesome looking. Some are fast and rush at you headlong, some
There are turrets that fire off bullets and can only be deactivated by clearing the room as well as mines and other floor traps that will damage you if you come into contact with them. There are also breakable objects which can be used as cover and sometimes conceal pickups. Some objects can only be broken by using missiles, adding an element of resource conservation.
And then there's the boss fights. These big, bad robots require you to memorize their attack patterns and they switch those up once they take enough of a beating. The enemy A.I. in general is pretty smart and even at normal difficulty I found that I had to be very careful of getting backed into corners or traps.
.Level design.
No two rooms look alike. Some rooms will be large and filled with traps and only a handful of enemies, while others will be a maze of corridors that become impossible to traverse thanks to enemy fire. The variety is substantial, but I'm sure if you played through several runs in one sitting, you'd start to see some repeats.
The level design also forces you to play accordingly or die horribly. In narrow, maze-like rooms, you'll be forced to slow down and try to remain behind cover. In larger, more spacious rooms, you'll be encouraged to dodge torrents of bullets by taking advantage of your full range of motion. In rooms with traps, you'll want to time your movements to avoid laser beams and take care where you step so as not to set off a chain reaction of explosions by stepping into a minefield.
.Graphics.
Lovely. The enemies hail down neon bullets that, and all the partical effects only add to the hectic sense that your life could end if you don't dodge well enough. That being said, the effects don't make it impossible to see your own shots or make it more difficult to find yourself on screen as I find happens in other titles. And, believe me: the screen *will* be flooded by bullets at many points in time during your run.
.Soundtrack.
One of my favourite things. It's chill and electronic--the perfect companion for the frantic game play.
.Bottom line.
If you're a fan of rogue-lites, pick this up. If you're a fan of shoot-em-ups, pick this up. There are difficulty settings for even the most casual of players, making Starward Rogue easy to pick up for gamers with varying levels of skill.

Far Cry Primal plays very much in the vein of Far Cry 3 and 4. The game feels familiar mechanically in that combat has the same weight and you can gather resources as in previous games, as well as tackle forts and bonfires (instead of radio towers). However, the prehistoric setting and the lack of vehicles and guns allows this entry to feel unique. Weapons must be crafted with resources found all throughout the map and there's a big focus on melee combat (though bows and throwable spears are present). Throwables are handled creatively as instead of grenades, you get jars full of bees, beserker poison and fire. There isn't much story present, though essentially you're fighting for the dominance of your tribe within your immediate inhabitable region. This isn't neccisarilly a bad thing, as the real appeal of the game is its gameplay, just as the other games are focused on.
While I do recommend the game, it does have a few issues. First, it's not immediately clear when you've finished it. I did all the "campaign" missions, only to be confused when there was no definitive end cinematic or even credits roll. While I did enjoy the hunting aspect of the game as well, I found that there were simply too many predators. I couldn't go anywhere without being constantly hounded by bears, wolves and sabertoothes all at once. The other Far Cry entries have you constantly bombarded by enemies as well (which I also find annoying) but you're at least left with the option of driving away. Here, you must confront pretty much all predators if they happen to catch sight of you. Last, for some people, they might have an issue with the basic layout of the map being incredibly similar to that of Far Cry 4. I can understand how some might find this "cheap", but the layout of the rivers and different terrain types (as well as variances of discoverable locations) make the map feel completely different. It also feels much different because you're walking or running everywhere as opposed to using vehicles.
If you've enjoyed previous entries of the series, you'll probably like this one too. It's unique, but still has enough staples of the series to feel familiar.

Exellent. With a capital E. The only flaws I can see are these: Story, which has been mentioned before on the forums, and arcen says they're aware of the lack in story and are working on that so it's not a concern. Items. There aren't that many things that switch things up a lot. Yes, there's the incredibilities, but i'm talking about something like mom's knife of brimstone from TBOI. Something less normal than, say typical glass cannon aka risky assassin. Finally, rear-burst turrets. They seem like a cool idea. Turrets that shoot bullets behind you which explode into more bullets sounds neat but they easily snipe with the extremely fast bullets that then explode, thus creating the bane of anyone who took risky assassin, which removes shields and reduces you to 1 health, thus causing anything that hits you instakill you. 1 health + nigh-unavoidible damage = ragequitting. I haven't mentioned any good things about this game yet, which is because everything else is exellent, however i'll go over the best things in this fantastic game here. Updates. Updates and bugfixes come faster than holidays, even more so if you don't count every obscure holiday you can think of(or look up on google). Enemy variety. The enemies aren't typical "flying thing that shoots bullets"esque tropes. Laser boomerangs? Check. Slow bullets that shoot fast but short range bullets behind them? Check. Bosses that use intricate bullet patterns to create a maze and then spawn minions that use slow-moving bullets to hinder your movement even more? Check. Difficulty.  The difficulty settings range from "Literally like 3 minutes of standing still for a boss to kill you" to "5 hits with bullet patterns that Touhou would be scared of". Anyhow, I give Starward Rogue 8.5/10 for an exellent roguelike.

Here's why I love this game: Jose 'Whiskey' Guzman.
Jose 'Whiskey' Guzman doesn't exist, but I will never forget him. My support trooper, he was the backbone of my X-Com team. He ran more missions than anyone else on the team and saved the lives of just about everyone at least once, popping smoke and deploying medkits. He was more than a medic- he had 54 confirmed kills and was a crack shot with a plasma rifle.
On his 28th mission the team hit heavy resistance securing a downed UFO. After tense fighting against  elite troops that left half the team wounded, a mech that we'd never seen appeared. This big ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ put two plasma rounds into our MEC trooper, critically wounding him. Whiskey sprinted to his side and stabilized him, saving his life. Afterward he tried to sprint to Carol 'Spider' Stevens, our wounded sniper, to pop a medkit on her. Passing a doorway the mech unexpectedly got an open shot on him, and put two rounds clean through his midsection. He died instantly.
I play on Ironman, which means no quickloading, and losing him hit me like I've rarely ever been hit by a game. I even thought about him the next day at work. In X-Com, every decision counts and death is permanent. Your squad members that survive and develop over many missions become something special, and when you lose one it can be absolutely devastating.
That sort of emotional investment is why I play games, and I can't recommend this one enough!

Half-Life 2 is a first-person shooter taking place after the events of Valve's Half-Life. In this game, you play as Gordon Freeman, an ever silent character who wields a crowbar and dons an HEV (Hazardous Environment) suit. I remember seeing this game years ago when I was young. Though, I mainly got it to run Gmod. However, I did play through it... a lot! And it was pretty fun. The mechanics are pretty okay, and the gameplay is leveled out with moments of calm and situations of action. You fight a few types of enemies. The biggest ones being the Combine Overwatch units. The story plot is quite interesting as well. I've always had a deep interest in the way Valve has set up their stories.
So, what are the pros and cons? Well, while it is well made, it can be a bit glitchy with the Source Engine. The enemies are at times either boring to fight or are a bit one-sided. I wouldn't recommend for constant replay. Though, if you are patient with the game and don't burn yourself out on Half-Life 2, it can become like one of those books or movies you just keep coming back to read or watch over and over again. I know I've done that. So I recommend this to someone looking for an engaging story whilst also enjoying a bit of action on the side!

Okay, now that I played for quite some time, I think I can update my review. I still recommend the game (at least the basic package once it goes on sale) but you should know a few things before you buy it:
1. PvP is not P2W. If someone tells you otherwise, they have no clue or have problems to understand what P2W really is. PvP is only affected by three things (in that exact order): Gear > Level > Skill. If you really want to deal the cards you should definitely plan on getting at least level 60. Higher is always better but you will grind hours for one percent of experience once you reach that level. Oh ... and you should get into a PvP guild or you will probably get your rear handed to you. PvP just happens in this game, especially on higher levels when people start to contest the lucractive grinding spots. These scuffles can quickly escalate to guild wars.
2. If you don't like PvP you can still consider looking into this. Questing and crafting will keep you busy until the end of time. You can choose to stay level 49 to be safe from any player aggression but I don't recommend that for your main character since you will miss out on a lot of content. Your crafting alts are on a different page. You get to level 56 rather quickly (58 is still possible with managable effort) which will enable you at least to reach all regions safely. If you do not contest the high end grind spots no one will bother with you anyway.
3. If you want to play this game seriously you should consider spending money on inventory slots, weight limit increases and a minimum of five pets. The pets alone will cost you about 60 bucks undiscounted so you have a rough estimate. You can theoretically snipe those off the marketplace but you will spend A LOT of time hoping for RNG to roll in your favor. The inventory and weight limit (the latter at least to some extend) can be bought with loyality which you get by logging in daily but it will take ages to accumulate.
4. This game feeds on your time. Whatever you want to do ingame will take time (there is not even a quicktravel system in place). The game can run as some sort of service in the background to allow your character to continue crafting his two thousand beers (takes about two hours, believe me when I say that's enough for one week) or keep fishing, walking around with a backpack to train your strength and many more things. In other games you need a bot which will get you banned while here all of that bot behaviour is integrated for everyone to use. The game seems to be designed to be never turned off.

I'm about 4 hours in and I'm enjoying Starward Rogue, it seems like a good mix of twin stick shooting and procedural dungeon crawling. I've been playing on normal difficulty and doing pretty well while still being challenged, as someone who doesn't usually play twin stick shooters that's a good balance for me. If you're more experienced in the genre you can ramp up the difficulty.
I would say that this game doesn't seem to have the breadth of features that other games in this genre have, for instance pickups seem to be mostly upgrades with little drawbacks, except for weapons which are more varied and have their ups and downs. In these kinds of games you usually get some risk/reward decisions with item pickups that you don't get much of here - you'll pretty much want to pick everything up. There are challenges on each level though, like don't use missiles to get a big boost next level sort of thing, which is a neat idea.
The character selection isn't huge, but varied enough to be interesting and they're all available from the start which is a big thumbs up from me. There aren't really any unlocks that I can see, which is great for someone with limited time.
Starward Rogue is a fun game that you can jump into and it wont suck thousands of hours of your life away, a run can be done start to finish in a couple of hours, more or less depending on skill. I recommend it.

Zen Bound 2 is a unique game in which you rotate wooden objects in order to wrap them with a limited length of rope. Wherever the rope touches an object, paint is applied to the surrounding area, and the goal is to cover the entire object with paint, while still having enough rope to reach the final tie-off point. Some levels introduce additional elements, like balls of paint that burst when touched with the rope to cover a larger area. You unlock additional objects as you complete levels, and while each set of objects starts easy, getting 100% completion on later ones can be a challenge. Zen Bound 2 is ultimately a puzzle game, in which you need to look for efficient ways to wrap the objects, although there are typically numerous possible solutions for scoring 100% on each level.
Visually, the game looks great, and despite being some years old at this point, the simple subject matter and attention to detail keeps things looking relatively realistic. The music is also well done and meditative, and overall the presentation is excellent.
The game's biggest flaw would have to be its controls. I've briefly tried mouse input, and it's awkward, to say the least. Zen Bound 2 was clearly designed with portable touchscreen devices in mind, and rotating blocks by clicking and dragging with a mouse tends to be unweildy. A laptop touchpad seems to be even worse, since the game only supports Macs for multi-touch input. There isn't an option to use a gamepad either. I found controls to be much better using the stylus on a Wacom graphics tablet for input, but that's not a peripheral most people are likely to own. And while you would think touchscreen input would be a natural choice, the game came out before touchscreen PCs became common, so touchscreen input on a PC simply doesn't work.
If you can get past the controls though, the game can provide a unique and challenging experience combined with meditative visuals and sound.

Latest Patch has changed the game significantly to appeal to more players. From the notes, there's no way I can't say ignore this game now and go back to cpma Q3.
After trying out the standalone again though, I'm glad that CA and Duel have 95% been untouched.
New heavy machinegun : Completely replaces the standard MG.
Auto hop : cg_autohop 0. You don't need this active, in fact it will mess up your stair timings and give you unwanted results. Also if you know how to strafe jump, this just slows you down.
Damage number display : Helps me out in knowing how much my rockets are doing, however it does allow you to track through walls better as long as the number is still up. Personally I would like to see this go.
New VO (Voice Over) : It was an unneeded change but after a while you can block it out.
Now for the worst of the worst...
Item timings : There's no need to count out your powerups anymore, you go near the PU spawn and it will tell you when it's up.
Last but not least, weapon loadout : No one, and I mean no one asked you to follow in activisions footsteps. I realize that you want to appeal to more gamers but quake was never meant to be easymode. To be waiting for an item spawn and only to have someone spawn right next to you and eat a rocket to the face or get railed isn't entirely what Q3/QL gameplay was supposed to be. You go build up your stack and then goto battle, you're not supposed to be babied. That's what CA is for, introducing this concept for FFA and TDM just means you're admitting defeat to CoD.

Devo ammettere che Telltale mi ha preso alla sprovvista in questo titolo. Dopo un playthrough a dir poco intenso, i miei pareri sono alquanto discordanti, quindi mi rimetterò all'eterno format pros & cons:
Da un lato abbiamo i Forrester, famiglia nobile del Nord celebre per coltivare "Ironwood", un legno dalle proprietà uniche. Da fan di lungo termine delle Cronache del Ghiaccio e del Fuoco, devo ammettere che la sceneggiatura di questa famiglia non ha, a mio parere, eguali nell'universo di G.R.R. Martin. Dalle sfaccettature dei personaggi alla storia della famiglia alla faida con i vicini Whitehill, tutto nelle prime puntate lascia presagire un avventura senza precedenti.
Dall'altro lato, purtropppo, abbiamo Game of Thrones.
Non fraintendetemi, il gioco è pensato per essere ambientato nella serie e raccontato attraverso la serie. Il cuore del problema sta nel fatto che, per dare evidenza a comparse di personaggi iconici (di cui non faccio spoiler) e al loro ruolo nella storia "principale", si toglie a quella dei Forrester, che di per se è un capolavoro. O meglio, avrebbe potuto esserlo.
Tutto ciò poi ha evidenti conseguenze sul sistema Telltale, in cui le scelte del giocatore scrivono la storia in tempo reale.
Capite benissimo che, se la storia dei Forrester è troppo legata a quella principale, il potere decisionale (e a volte le scelte effettive) del giocatore è limitato, poiché essa non può cambiare.
Più volte ho avuto la sensazione che una determinata scena potesse avere un solo esito, o che le mie alternative di dialogo fossere abbastanza indifferenti tra loro.
Detto ciò, vale la pena giocarlo? Io dico sì. Perchè, nonostante i suoi difetti, (probabilmente meno rilevanti per un neogiocatore Telltale o per chi non segue GoT) la saga dei Forrester amplia l'universo di Martin dandogli dettaglio, colore e personalità, rendendolo non solo un mondo di personaggi iconici, ma un mondo vivo, quasi realistico.
Se la serie manterrà lo stesso stile degli ultimi 2 episodi della saga ( a mio parere i più emozionanti, in cui GoT lascia pieno spazio alla storia dei Forrester) potrebbe essere un successo senza precedenti per Telltale

---Original Analysis of "Ezro"---
It was an innovative game, acclaimed by critics, and seen by many as the new model to follow for the genre shooter. Graphically, it was the best releases of the year, if not the best. For me, one of the best games ever created.
I do not come to talk about Half Life exactly, since everything is said. I come to talk about what happened next.
The Steam gaming platform was initially only an application from which you could download and play Half Life 2, called Tracker. At the time, Valve had not thought anything special for her, since it had been created with that sole purpose: to allow users to play Half Life 2. Nothing else.
Such was the success of this game that the company decided to continue its history through episodic releases. The first of June of 2006 was released Episode 1, and later, the 10 of October of 2007, Episode 2. Initially would be a trilogy of episodes that would give preamble to the next great game.
Time passed, and Episode 3 continued to be postponed and postponed, for reasons confused and still discussed.
Meanwhile, the Steam platform was gaining ground, thanks to which Valve agreed to host games of other companies in it. More games began to be published, more new users arrived; every year even more quickly. Valve continued to develop games for a while, to finish projects in which they were still working, but from Episode 3, nothing was said.
Steam was becoming more and more profitable for Valve. Thousands of developers were eager to sell their games on the platform, and with the rebates every winter and summer were more profitable than the launch of a game. This made Valve think that it was no longer necessary to make games. They preferred to continue adding cosmetic content to Team Fortress 2 and CS: GO, as it generated money more easily. As soon as they could, they took the simple route.
Not long ago, during the last 2 years, several Valve employees began to leave the company. Concept artists, voice actors, stage modelers ... and above all, writers. Writers who previously worked on scripts such as Portal 2, Left 4 Dead, Team Fortress 2 and, of course, Half Life 2. They left the company for an obvious reason: Valve no longer offered them any task they could apply their talents.
It seemed that Valve's plans were not to continue the sagas mentioned. Many fans speculated that perhaps the reason for this was that the dialogues and storyboards were already finished, and that only needed to be recorded in a video game. After 13 years without knowing our beloved series, there were still people who kept the hopes and looked forward to the return of Gordon Freeman.
Two days ago, on August 25, 2017, those hopes faded.
Half Life saga writer Marc Laidlaw, who had left the company 18 months earlier, revealed in his blog a letter containing what appeared to be a "fanfiction", camouflaged between modified and other names, but that was really everything the plot of what would be Episode 3 if it had ever come to be developed.
Marc was motivated to do this by realizing that after so much time of dedication and love for his work, Valve was no longer interested in the least to give a proper conclusion to the story and simply left the game to oblivion, while the fans continued to wait incessantly for the next track that would lead them to think that HL3 was close.
Sick of Valve's refusal and saddened by the fans, Marc gave us all the conclusion we both hoped for, in the form of text. What would have been a phenomenal game ended up becoming a blog entry of about 30 lines.
That's right, gentlemen. Gabe Newell preferred the easy money offered by both Steam and CS: GO instead of worrying about his biggest and most recognized series, letting her die as pathetically as possible. And as if that were not enough, he revealed not long ago that he is developing a card game, which will surely be an excuse to sell microtransactions.
You make me sick, Gaben. You make me sick, Valve. Great developers sold like ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to the money, forgetting completely of what one day made them big. I hope it's worth it for you to have left an opportunity to go down in history as big as this, for a meager game of cards, hats and boxes with painted weapons. I will not remove this negative feedback until Valve replaces the fans in some way, for these 13 years of useless waiting that they made us go through.

This is it. The final battle to finally crush the Federation. Everything was going according to plan, except for one, small hiccup. The Federation’s loyal messenger boy, who had managed to get all the way here. Now, he was the only thing standing in your path.
Federation Cruisers are typically not a problem, but this particular one, this little pain in the butt has managed to tear through at least seven sectors to get all the way here, and now it has repelled you twice. And it has fought with everything it had, and managed to counter every trick you could come up with. Their ship was on its last legs, but so was yours.
The battle was chaotic and fierce, and you lost several men. But so did they. In fact, your sensors picked up only a single life form remaining. Right at that moment of realization you’ve killed almost all the crew, you receive a hail from the ship. You answered hail and bring up the video screen. There was fire and smoke, but a visible silhouette of a Engi: The final living being on the ship. You smirked, expecting a surrender, but instead, got something very different.
The Engi held out it’s hand, and projected a hologram. A very simple hologram; one very easy to understand. It was a particular set of words that made your eyes widen with fear.
“YOU LOSE.”
Right than, the Federation Cruiser fired all its weapons, but so did you. As their ship broke apart on your monitor, your ship began shaking, and evacuation alarms began to sound. The Federation’s messenger boy, the eternal thorn in the Rebellion’s side, was dead.
But the Rebellion had lost.﻿

I'm not a SHMUP player. I'm not an 'action roguelike' player, either. To be honest? I bought this to support Arcen Games. I haven't always loved their games, but I love their brand of innovation, and I hate to see them in dire straits.
So I figured, "I bought the game--might as well give the game a try, right?" After a couple hours of play, it's pretty fun! Even if you suck at these things!
On 'Normal' difficulty, the pace of play is measured enough that navigating my way through "bullet heck" is as dependent on strategy as reflexes. And the variety of powerups is super cool! Every game is different after the first few upgrades. And there's such a variety that I haven't seen the same stuff twice. (To be fair, that's in two hours.)
Now, I've seen enough SHMUPs to know they can be very lush and beautiful productions. Arcen doesn't do "lush." But for those familiar with games like AI War and Last Federation, the graphics and controls are frankly better. Everything's clean and smooth, and it's enjoyable to discover the different variations on enemies. As with the loot, there's a whole, whole lot of enemy variety.
I can't say you're in for a fantastic journey through sound. The score and sound effects are pretty basic. You're probably going to want to play your own music in the background, but I do that with lots of games, so it's fine by me!
I'm playing with an X360 controller, which I imagine is how it's meant to be done.
In conclusion: I can recommend this as an amusement for casual players, especially if (like me) you're a fan of 'roguelike' genre conventions. It's not too punishing, even on the default difficulty level, and the design is clean and sharp. Why not give it a try?

Pretty good roguelike in the style of Binding of Isaac.  Doesn't have the item variety of BoI yet, but does anything?  This has a much more sci-fi feel, and incorporates a light touch of bullet-hell shooters (advancing to quite a lot of bullet hell by the end level) but also gives you multiple triggered weapon systems, many of which will destroy or affect enemy bullets.
There's a good variety of passive abilities, a lovely selection of actually differently behaving enemy types both large and small, and a pleasing variety of rooms.  The graphics and sound work just fine but the gameplay is probably the high point here.
There's a few annoying bits here and there, but as always Arcen is patching and updating on an amazingly frequent regular basis, so in the weeks and months since I write this review I'm sure many bugs will no longer exist, and new content will have been added.
If you like this style of game and you're looking for more, you should get it - it's good.

Hey everyone and this is my review about the game!
This is a Rogue-LITE bullet hell FAST PACED top view game.
You can have multiple File slots. (Up to 6)
There is a Toolbar at the bottom right with settings/Stats/Trophies and other things.
There are in-game Achievements.
You can change the in-game controls.
There are alot of Different Resolution sizes.
There is Screen/Sharpness Bar Slider.
There is a Volume/sound/voice/Combat bar slider.
You are able to play this game with a Xbox controller.
You are able to choose from 6 different MECHS. Sadly there are no "unlockable MECHS"
You are able to choose from 5 different difficulty settings. From Very easy to Very hard.
Each Mech has their own advantages and disadvantages, Power and weakness.
There is no Random button, so you have to choose a MECH.
I think the "Delete file" and "back to file select" are a bit too close to each other. There will be a warning notification however if you press the "delete" by accident.
There is a tutorial.
Text lines are voiced over.
Your hitbox is your head. Bullets won't damage and hurt you if it hits another part.
Music is weird and OKAY on the same time. (loops alot and if you get a bad soundtrack it could be even annoying too)
Music does need some variety.
There are passives buffs. (Example: You attack for 25% faster, Your damage is 25% lower).
If you press ESC,  you will see your equipped items. In the middle you will see a MAP.  However you can't see your active/consumables here.  So if you have forget about their stats. Well there is no way to look back, However you can see their effects.
You are able to see items on the Map and if you hover your mouse over the rooms. Then you are able to see which items. Only 1 icon will be shown on the map, so if there are more items in that current room then the only way to find out is by hovering the cursor over the rooms.
There are shops, You can trade Credits/Money for experience or items.
You have an experience bar and you are able to level up. If you kill enemies you will get experience.
You can choose 1 perk out of the 3 once you have gained a level.
There is a "Devil's room", You can trade your MAX health for items. So if an item is -5, You will permanently lose -5 HP for that current run.
There are "Health Shards", You have to see it like those collectable hearts from Legend of Zelda. Once you have enough Shards, you will gain 1+ Max HP.
I will explain about the ships a bit. I won't spoil too much. There are no unlockable or Secret Ships.
This is the Standard Overall ship. Nothing too Special about it. It's a good beginning MECH and it is easier to dodge bullets. You are able to see the MECH's Head, which is the only part that is able to hurt you. I personally don't like the secondary weapon.
This is one of those "High risk, high reward" Ships. He is very strong and kills enemies in no-time but his energy is on the low side and his range is very very limited. You have to be close in order to kill the enemies.
This is a ship that requires alot of patience but could be rewarding. Especially his secondary weapon. It places a landmine, which only could be good against big or fast enemies.
His missile makes him unique and a lifesaver too. It attract enemies bullets. So if you shoot the missile and bullets are already on your way. Well the Missile basically drag them away and makes you unharmed.
This ship pays off the longer your run goes. You need to gain more experience in order to level up compare to the other ones. But in return you will be able to find more cash and even KEYS! His secondary is a monster but not accurate, This is one of my favourite Mech's including Ship 5.
This is my other favourite Ship. He has weaker attack power but he has a companion that helps killing enemies. Secondary weapon is only powerful if you charge him up. Otherwise it won't offer much. Attack speed isn't high aswell and he is very vulnerable. A difficult ship but fun!
This could be a good second beginner's ship to see the enemy attack pattern. I find the idea from the unique power very well done but on the same time it slows down the game by alot. Enemies and bullets will stay still (even your own) if you are standing still aswell. So you could see them coming. Secondary weapon is powerful but the biggest downside that the ship has is surviving. Starts with only 3 HP and no shield makes him the most squishiest ship on the game.
There is no option to open the map only. You have to press ESC in order to open the map. It would be good if you only press 1 button and you will see only the (Zoomed) map.
Once you have cleared a room, You will hear a "notification" Sound.
Music Changes everytime if you enter a "Devil room". So if you want to hear a different music track, Go inside of the Devil room and go out again. Not happy with the soundtrack? then go back inside again.
Soundtracks keeps looping over on the current floor and there is no "Toggle to next song" button.
There are "Secret rooms", You are only able to destroy those walls with missiles.
I RECOMMEND TO GO THE OPTIONS/SETTINGS. Then go to GRAPHICS and slide the ZOOM BAR all the way to the left.
This will make the game a bit more easier and avoids annoying camera's. The game will be a bit more zoomed out and it will improve your gameplay.
I do see some Potential for Local Co-op. One with keyboard and the other one with Xbox controller.
The Run will be saved automatically, So if you decide to stop and play later again. You will load back on the current Floor and Run.
I wasn't aware of it but these are the same Developers from Valley of the wind. (i loved valley without wind 2).
Once you enter a new room and you do not move. You have the option to turn back or start the room. You can't attack if you are sitting there idle.
Sometimes the bullets could be difficult to see from the enemy. Because of bright background.
Enemy animations could be very basic/Predictable. Some doesn't have much Variety.
Sometimes you see "shiny glows" in a obstactle. If it is glowing Green/Blue, Then it will Contain a Health Shard. There is always at least 1 in a room and it is super easy to boost out your Health. I had once 3 of those Health shards in  a single room. You need 8 Health shards to get +1 Max HP. I think the chance to find those should be tuned down abit.
Challenge texts like "Open all containers on this floor before leaving to receive xx xxx xx ammount" overlaps the enemy Lifebar. Which will be difficult to see the enemy Life's bar.

I came here expecting to find loads of positive reviews and what i find is this.
Seems like playing the game of thrones(not the videogame, the fight for the iron throne is what i mean) is actually too hard on most people. What I dont get is how you would give it a bad review for that since quite frankly i think thats what it is supposed to be.
the art of the game is beautiful. Yes sure the graphics arent top notch, but what this game offers in terms of visuals just works perfectly for it. Characters look realistic, the way they act fits and they have so many little changes that can make up their expressions it adds up to a very realistic display of human interaction. Sometimes facial expressions can seem a bit odd or don't seem to fit 100% but it doesnt break immersion really. They did a great  job here in the end.
music fits well. not much i would remember as especially brilliant but it really works with the game. voice actors did great, really. and one song that is sung in the game really reminded me of what the national singing "the rains of castamere" made me feel like at the end of one of the seasons of the show. awesome.
now the gameplay is a lot harder to judge. people complain your choices dont matter in a game that is all but made up of decision making and i find myself disagreeing. I don't know even know one game that ever had me believe desicions made by the player had great influenze on the games outcome. this is not what this game is about. whoever read some of the books knows what playing the game of thrones comes down to in the very end. this game is in my opinion not about changing the game with your decisions. its about experiencing what its like to be forced to make the decisions. it makes you feel helpless, desperate even sad. it is rather realistic. as some mentioned here you mostly decide between bad and worse but it feels great when you understand you made a really hard decision knowing it would change almost nothing at all but knowing why you made the decision, what it meant to you and your character. the game sometimes even gives you immediate feedback on your decisions, which i admit can surely be seen as a bad point, but it also gave me a clear view of what im playing for. the illusion is, if you let yourself be drawn in, quite brilliant and entertains me to no end.
Another thing needs to be said about the QTS you find throughout the game along with the decison making. I have to say they felt a lot better playing with a gamepad so i encourage you to try that. all in all i do enjoy them. the way i see it you can really feel good completing a "stage" with perfect QTS, knowing you didnt mess up really feels great in the end. and more importantly they make up one of the solid pillars which hold the games foundation: Story, Immersion by choosing and interaction.
In the end i have to agree you might probably end up confused and not invested enough in the game if you do not know the books (or at least the show). One example is a reference to a past event you can choose to make during the game that is not explained by the game itself, more or lessing stripping you off one of 4 possible answers as you just dont have any clue what effect it might possibly have on the game.
TL;DR:
great visuals that work brilliantly with the game while not being up to todays standards in terms of graphic. (Review updated on August 14th 2016)
Now that I beat the 3 wardens and finally completed a full run, I think it's a good time to write a small review.
The game is a healthy mix of roguelite and bullethell. Think Binding of Isaac with mechs and lasers, where the huge selection of enemies all have very unique styles of attacks. But don't get scared by the Bullethell tag, it's not the "barf bullets all over your screen and call it a day" bullethell, it's more like "each pattern is a little puzzle you have to solve to dodge it" bullethell.
Controls are tight, which I think is pretty crucial for a game like this. I do recommend activating the option called "Use SHMUP-style controls" so you can stop your movements at a moment's notice. You'll be glad you did during most boss fights.
Difficulty-wise, the 5 levels of difficulty available before each run can give players of all skill levels a fun time.
-Very Easy: Enjoy the ride and learn at your own pace
-Easy: Quite forgiving
-Normal: Challenging
-Hard: Punishing
-Misery: Still in preparation, but a good description for it when it will be released should be "OH GOD, WHY?!"
For each run, you get to select a mech to use from a selection of 7 so far. You got the treasure hunter mech for extra cash and stuff, the flame tank to get a strong starting kit, the time manipulating mech that lets you stop the action to think/plan for a bit, the vanilla mech that's good at everything but doesn't have anything special per say, the magnetic mech that can break through any bullet pattern, the energy mech which can fire its secondary weapon for extended periods of time and finally, the humble mech that is all about shop discounts and money.
Weapons/items variety is pretty good from what I've seen. (Up to 260 so far if I look at the ingame menu) Which weapon would you pick? A super fast machinegun or a powerful flamethrower or a fancy phaser that can shoot through walls? Add to that a secondary energy weapon and a bunch of upgrades/modifiers and things can get crazy. Crazy fun that is. Consumable items were a bit underwhelming/overpriced, fortunately those were tweaked in an update and are now quite desirable/effective.
Graphic-wise, the game looks clean and colorful. You can spot enemy bullets without issue and it's easy on the eyes. What's not to love?
For the story, the tutorial does a good job of quickly explaining what's going on and what is expected of you. I thought the voice acting was pretty neat and the humor well dosed, but opinions on that may vary. It's short and pretty straightforward, but I personally like it that way.
The music isn't really my genre, but still found it well done and enjoyable. Doesn't detract from the experience and adds to it instead. There's a lack of variety in the number of music tracks available, but I remember reading the devs were planning on adding more later. So hopefully we'll get more tracks from their very talented music composer in the future.
Modding: The devs took extra care to make it easy for the community to make their own content for the game if they so desire. New enemies, new items, new mechs, new room layouts, new bosses, etc. I always appreciate it when devs put the effort to allow easy modding. I ended up making quite a few custom mechs of my own and it was indeed very easy.
Bugs and balance: Since this is an Arcen game, if something seems weird or just not fun, you can report it and the devs will listen. Plus, those guys are ridiculously fast at releasing updates. You reported getting stuck because of a glitch? Don't be surprised if you get an update a mere few hours later, fixing your issue the same day. How awesome is that?
Oh my, this review got a bit lengthy after all.
In conclusion, it's a very good Isaac-style roguelite with a very satisfying bullethell aspect that will keep you coming for one more run, over and over. Pure, concentrated fun filled game. Highly recommended.

Saints Row 4 is an odd game.
It feels like a cash-in on Saints Row 3 to me, and I haven't even played SR3 yet, so that says something.
But at the same time it's also something completely new, and definitely much more than a DLC could offer.
Bottom line, it's a good game TO AN EXTENT. You'll notice I have alot of hours. That is all from one single playthrough.
The core game is probably not much longer than 10 or 20 hours, but there is aLOT of side missions, collectibles, and customization. That being said, I cannot fathom playing another minute of it, especially not starting from the beginning.
The reason being, is that the game simply lacks challenge. This is not a challenging game, by any means. You are up to your ears in superpowers within the first maybe 3 or 4 hours of gameplay, you have guns out the♥♥♥♥♥ and you don't even need the bloody cars you've been collecting because you can just run faster and not have to bother going into your tab menu.
In all, this game has made me want, more than anything, to just play Saints Row 3 or 2. Because those games seem like they would have the same fun story line, with an actual challenge. Defeating enemies would feel much more gratifying if I felt like I was in mortal danger, instead of a super hero. And don't get me wrong, having super powers was REALLY fun, WHILE IT LASTED.
By the time you've collected as much stuff as you care to, and you've done all the side missions, and
, you will be BORED with having super powers AND defeating enemies, however tough, will feel meaningless and like a chore.
But still it's a good game for that time while it is fun.
TLDR:
It's good, but has very limited replayability.

I will admit, as a long time fan of the Far Cry franchise I let this one sit in my library for awhile out of fear that it would be too different from their last titles. I started playing the game two days ago. Do I regret getting this game? Lord no. Do I regret not playing it sooner? Uh, yeah.
Five minutes in, I already felt for the characters and the hardships they had to endure in this primitive landscape. Not only does Ubisoft immerse you in vivid storyline, but they also make sure that you don't get bored. This is achieved primarily by the use of making the landscape and the items in it crucial to building your village, upgrading your tools, and more or less progressing in the storyline, by giving each important character their own questline for you to follow, and having two tribes to thwart and four challenging beast hunts to complete.

The game is designed require communication and teamwork, which makes for escalating shouting matchesa and maybe the occasional gameplay. It's cleverly designed to force you to work together to win, unlike some games whose co-op modes seem a little shoehorned just for the sake of it.
If you have the necessary hardware (including friends) to host a couch gaming session, this game will not disappoint. The best thing about it is its accessbility. Casual gamers can easily relate to the cute visuals and simple, familiar Diner Dash-like game mechanics. Hardcore gamers and senior management on the other hand will appreciate the level of coordination and planning that is required in order to earn 3 stars in the co-op campaign levels.
That last comment is coming from someone who has spent around 200 hours playing Overwatch - a highly competitive game that has an optional co-op mode depending on whom you play with.
If you are keen on couch gaming on PC, this is an esssential.

Dustforce truly is a work of art. I don't mean that lightly. The way it's animated plus its music gives it that title in my book. I can find myself playing one level for an hour, maybe even hours at a time. The frustration of losing levels is filled with relaxation and calmness because of the ambient music. The way the levels are crafted is truly mindblowing. They had a system in which you had to perfect a level to earn a key, and you would use that key to earn more levels. In layman's terms, to earn more levels, you had to perfect current levels. They ditched that and added an XP system in which you gain more XP to earn a key the more levels you play and perfect. I'm very glad they added this system and was skeptical about buying it. But now that I did buy it, I do not regret it even for a second. One thing I really love about this game is how you don't have to unlock base levels. In a sense, this game is open world. That sense is that many levels are available to you, and you can choose whether you want to advance into more challenging levels, or stay where you're at. To get an S in completion, you have to sweep up EVERY leaf, and to get an S in Finesse, you have to maintain your combo throughout an entire level.
Another thing I absolutely enjoy about Dustforce is its expasive community. There are lots of Community Workshop maps for you to sharpen your skills on, and lots of people who can set a good example. I'm sure most of the people who get best times on all the levels have a Youtube channel, so you can probably catch them there. The community may or not be active, but it sure is good and friendly.
Overall, in terms of gameplay, music, artstyle, animation, and difficulty (it's not an easy game, but it's not that hard of a game either. It just depends on how much you want to play it), I rate this game:
10/10
BUY THIS GAME.

Tropico is a really interesting series.  In a time when the classic RTS is nearly dead on PC, the Tropico series really stands tall as a remaining vestiage from the old Westwood Studios days.  Now that's not to say that Tropico is a classic PC-styled RTS, because it isn't at all, but it does have that same sort of one-more-game feeling.
Tropico is interesting because you never directly control any of your citizens.  You really only can build things and watch and your people use them or not use them.  That may sound boring but it becomes addictive trying to balance the needs of your citizens, versus the missions that the game presents you with.  You may need to strengthen your economy but your citizens are not well educated enough to work in the factories... do you take the time to educate your citizens or do you invite foreign experts to help out or do you pass a law allowing uneducated to work in the factories even though it adds a large risk to their health and well-being?  These kinds of decisions are commonplace in Tropico.  At its very core I find that Tropico is slightly flawed in that each mission can be won by following a bit of a spreadsheet mentality and carefully crafting the perfect island... but finding that out is half the fun of the game.
Tropico uses an unusual asthetic, the island dictatorship, and combines it with an interesting tweek to traditional RTS roots and the result is pretty damn fun!  It's also a game with excellent humor and many tongue-in-cheek charactures of the cold war era.  I really recommend grabbing the full Tropico 4 game with DLC if you can find it for 30$ or less.  I got well over 60 hours playing through ONLY the campign of 4 and the expansion.  I only started playing custom games after about 60 hours of gametime, so it's well worth the value of your dollar spent.

Grim Dawn is a great ARPG that does a nice job of bringing together innovations from other games in one polished package.
Pros
+Deep skill system; lots of builds; lots of variations
+Beautiful graphics (the lighting during a lightning storm is especially noteworthy)
+Super atmospheric: music, art, design, everything
+Technical excellence: no bugs, no glitches, no lag
Cons
-Storyline is very much of its genre; I didn't ever feel compelled to move forward because of the story and wasn't ever surprised by the progression
-Loot is not particularly exciting; you'll spend lots of time examining every piece, but most is trash; the variety actually works against it I think -- you might look at hundreds of boots and end up keeping the same ones you've had for 10 levels; it's very common to find epic loot that isn't as good as lower tier stuff you found on minor enemies
-Voice acting is a mixed bag
If you enjoy Path of Exile, or any of the Diablo, Titan Quest, Myth, or Torchlight games, you'll probably like this one.  It's understandably dark in tone -- it has a Walking Dead/Warhammer 40K sort of vibe.  Whether you'll sink hundreds of hours into it like many others have is probably down to how much you like min-maxing and loot-grinding, but it's well worth a single play-through either way.

Short version of the review: If you like bullet-hell games that you can replay over and over with different characters and different abilities, with randomly generated floors and items, get this game.
Long version for those of you who want to know exactly what this game has to offer, and whether it excels in areas you want it to, here you go.
This game is, again, a bullet-hell game that places you in a robot that's going through several different floors on a huge station called the Megalith, which is surprisngly embedded in a sun. You get several different characters to use, all of which vary in stats (stats being your health, shields, damage, stuff like that), weapons, and some even have awesome side effects during the game. After you choose both the character and the difficulty, it drops you into a level. I'm pretty sure this game has the same floor level creation process as the Binding of Isaac. A large amount of pre-made rooms are set up, and then those rooms are randomly plotted around to create the floor that you traverse through. Anywho, the game has a lot of content right now. Lots of different varied enemies, lots of different room designs that make some rooms tricky to deal with, so on and so forth. The only thing this game lacks, in my opinion, is a lack of both MUSIC and ITEMS. The music, while awesome and catchy, does get old after a while. There are, like, 4-6 different loops (not including the boss music) that play during the different floors, and it gets kind of tiring after a while. I would really love to see more music added in the future. The next problem is the lack of items. Now, there is still quite an amount of items in the game. Different primary's, secondaries, attachments, useables, so on and so forth. Shops that offer you health/shield upgrades, and other things like that. But even with all that, there seems to be a lack of them. As I play the game more, I will change this if I notice a difference and there's actually, yknow, a LOT more then I've noticed. But until then, there ya go. It's a game that I would extremely recommend for it's price tag, and it's super fun.
