I'm personally not a huge fan of bullet hell type games, but I can't deny that Starward Rogue is well put together and enjoyable.
You pick a mech, choose your preferred difficulty, and head into a dungeon. Each mech has various pros and cons that set it apart from the others, and the difficulty choices encompass all types of players, whether you want a casual experience or a gruesome challenge.
Dungeons consists of various rooms. Most have enemies in them, which you have to kill before proceeding further, others have some kind of puzzles or obstacles such as lasers that go on and off in a pattern. You also pick up a variety of items and equipment for your mech to improve them for the duration of the run. At the end of the floor there's a boss, which you have to defeat in order to be able to descend to the next floor. Bosses all have unique attack behaviours and are generally very fun to fight. I'd say, this game is very similar to Binding of Isaac, except in a sci-fi setting.
Visuals are very pretty and shiny, despite being very simplistic. At first some stuff can be a tad confusing, like the glass floors overlooking space at first seemed like death drops/impassable places to me and it's not often easy to tell which of the obstacles are destructable and which aren't. Music is all right too. There are some nice upbeat tunes here and there, but I think the music in other Arcen games is way better.
It's a simple but fun gameplay. Don't expect deep tactics and strategy like in other Arcen games (such as Bionic Dues and The Last Federation), but if you just want to have some fast-paced fun and challenge your reflexes, then the game is well worth getting. It is a welcome change to see an indie dev that changes the formula in each of their games and does something new rather than churning out clones all the time.

Where to start ... simply I guess: this game is awesome.
This is by far the best example on how to remake a classic. The original game was a blast. The new version lives up to the name.
The one aspect I like the most is the immersion. As the base commander, station leader interact with you verbally each time you visit them and this really increases the feeling that you are the base commander. The whole strategic aspect available in the base is great. Mechanics are simple yet effective. You always have to decide on what to build/research/manufacture next, and there is never enough money. A good game is always found when you have to make tough decision. This is there the whole game.
Graphics are great, both in the strategic game and the tactical combat. The tactical game provides a good challenge and the AI does a fine job on keeping you on your toes, until your squad is experienced (mid-level) and carries the advanced equipment.  Enemy toughness does increase to keep the game challenging however, it would have been nice for the aliens to have some abilities, like their human counterpart.
This is a no brainer for anyone looking for a game with a mix of strategic elements with a heavy dose of turn-based tactical combat, all in a human vs alien invasion environment.

Zen Bound is a cute little game that focuses on wrapping objects with a rope, until you've covered as much topology as you can with it. The game looks beautiful and very serene, and has a pretty fitting soundtrack. At first impression, it all
together pretty well, considering how the puzzles are presented. You don't have a time limit, and the actual challenge of the game comes from very trial-and-error progression where you feel your way around the object and try to think best way to cover every nook and cranny. While this itself isn't problematic, I feel the game's overrall progression where you have to hit certain percentages of object coverage in order to unlock more objects feels very much against game's Zen theme and forces you to grind through the game - in order to unwrap more objects.
So basically, unless you really want to tie objects to perfection, this game probably won't impress you for a long. I feel like the game isn't made to be fun, and the puzzles are too abstract and physics-based in the same time to appeal for people looking for analytical challenge.

Welcome to my review of Starward Rogue, an unapolagetic bullethell roguelite fusion. As with any rogue, most of this is going to come down to gameplay, so let's just move on immediately!
Upon starting up a new save file for Starward Rogue, you will find yourself in a quick voiced tutorial that covers the basics and then sends you on your way. There are slow, default, and sprint movement speeds. Slow and normal speeds will be used to navigate mazes of bullets and traps carefully, while sprint is good for dodging quick enemies and bullets, as well as backtracking. You have your primary and secondary weaponfire, modules that can alter any number of things, and consumables that can also have a large variety of effects. The tutorial will also get you started on your way to recognizing enemy types and the way their bullet patterns work, as well as how a room might generate and how that will change the dynamics of combat based on their structure. There are traps and obstacles aplenty.
When looking at the stats screen pertaining to your save file, you can see that there is a total of: 124 enemies, 8 minibosses, 20 bosses, 13 condemned enemies, 223 items, and 11 incredibilities. Upon beating (as of the latest update) three 5-floor runs, you will unlock 7-floor runs. This is a downright impressive quantity for any game to feature, and yet the enemy types and bosses all seem balanced, weapons and items all seem to have their pros, cons, and uses, and you have 6 different options for what type of mech you wish to tackle it all with. The level of variety these possibilities produce, combined with the recognizable patterns and attack types of enemies, makes for a fun and challenging but fair experience. If that isn't the case for you, though, there are also 5 difficulty options to suit your needs! I should also mention that there are level-up perks, as well as health, currency, ammo, and exp drops. Even further, if you pick up a different weapon, consumable, or module it will swap their locations instead of overwrite the old with the new. Try something out for a few rooms and don't like it? You can just go back.
After 15 runs, I am at a measly 18% completion, and am still discovering interesting new room and floor layouts that catch me off guard. There are tiles you can't walk on, bombs you can't touch, barriers you can't pass, a variety of barriers that you or your enemies can still shoot past, timed and infinite lazers, turrets with various behaviors, etc. When you throw all of these into a room, of varying size and shape, in various formations, and then mix in a multitude of enemies with various attack patterns--some of which might make dodging impossible when combined, and stir it all up--you're in for a hectic, chaotic, fun-filled time! Thankfully, for scrubs like me, in a lot of situations simply taking cover between assaults is an option.
Even with death's strong attraction to me, I find myself compelled to deftly navigate the pretty, colorful volley of fireworks that are my enemy's bullets and laugh maniacally when they die with a satisfying explosion. Starward Rogue has a great concept and execution, and is just good old plain fun. With the right combination of hull, primary and secondary weapon, module, level-up perks, and upgrades I firmly believe that you will have an adrenaline-filled journey where you make a stupid mistake, die, curse the heavens, and then feel all the more eager to become similarly powerful and vanquish your enemies!
Here are the highlights: the main menu background art, beautiful. The interface, suitable and thematic, if a bit blue and large; good mix of retro and modern stylings. The textures and level design, fairly good, but not super amazing. I hate the green space background, but I once encountered a pink-yellow-orange background that was gorgeous and gave the game an amazing feel for that run. Super distinct, polished, and shiny would be a fault in this case, anyway, because the most important thing to see are the enemy attacks; displayed here in distinct, vivid colors and patterns. Finally, it is worth noting that the bosses have pretty detailed pixel art that I find lovely.
Great music, fits nicely, good when playing but can get old fast if you happen to alt tab for something. There are some nice subtle atmospheric sounds, and various other sounds that generally remind me of some of the better oldschool games around. It won't win any sound design of the year awards, but if you are a fan of rogues, sound is not the first thing on your mind.
Due to the quality gameplay, strong concept, good execution, massive variety, and an appealing mix of challenge and fairness, I recommend purchasing Starward Rogue at:

I can't really add much to the other reviews, except this observation. I have 57 friends who own this game. Yes, that's a lot, but one thing I notice is that the number of them that have played this game for more than an hour is only a very tiny proportion of that. The list of played time reads: 0.1, 0.1, 0.1, 0.2, 0.1, 0.1, then maybe a 5.8 scattered in there, then a whole bunch more 0.1's and 0.2's. To me, that isn't really acceptable. Not many other games that I own show that pattern.
As for what would explain it, I think the thing is, people play it a little bit, and realize how simple it is, and it doesn't seem to be getting more complex. The levels are repetitive, and sure there are a ton of them, and there is some variation in gameplay eventually with the balls of paint and so on, but it isn't varied *enough* to be engaging. A lot of people play the game for a few minutes and figure they've seen everything this game has to offer. I was one such person, years ago someone bought me this game as a gift, and I played a few minutes and that's it. Now later I'm returning to it just to make sure the gift was not in vain, that maybe there's more to this game than hundreds of repetitive levels that vary in only a tiny way from one another. But nope, I gave it another hour, and it's still repetitive.
I'm still positive about the game though, and believe it's worth trying just for its novelty value. This is still a positive review, just with a very large caveat that if you play it for a short while, and think you've seen everything this game has to offer, you are mostly right. Chances are if you buy this game you will play it for 0.1 or 0.2 hours only. But that can be okay, not every game needs to occupy you for 20+ hours -- and this game *can* do that, but only if you can stand repetition. I'd recommend this game just on the basis of its experimental nature though, it's worth playing a wide variety of games, especially offbeat ones like this. I see this game as an experiment, and a semi-successful but also semi-unsuccessful one. It probably *could* be made more varied and engaging, perhaps in a sequel, but it would take a lot more work to do so.

"I've heard it both ways."  is one of my favorite lines from my favorite show of all time, Psych.  As such, I shall give it to you BOTH ways.  A written review and, for those of you who prefer it, a link to my First Look video on Starward Rogue.
I'm not going to lie, I'm a really big Arcen Games fan.  I will say that I've thoroughly enjoyed every game of theirs that I have played, with the exception of one.  So, despite enjoying what Arcen does, I'm not a robot that likes everything.  :)
A little bit of info before the meat and potatoes of the review.   Tons of things about this game SCREAM Arcen and is a shoutout or pays homage to at least two of their other titles.  Many folks would say this is a cross between The Last Federation's sound, look, feel, lore, and Bionic Dues roguelike, walking mech thinggie.  :)  The main thing that sets it apart from both of those games is the combat.  So, where did the combat come from if it's inspired by turn based strategy games?
I was reading up on Starward Rogue while it was being developed and I learned that this game was actually the original concept for the battles in The Last Federation.  They opted to go away from the real time, bullet hell, twin stick shooter combat for turn-based combat.  Still, they really enjoyed what they had created and sat it aside for later use.  Thus, Starward Rogue was born.
I am not very amazingly good at bullet hell games.  I enjoy playing them and I have played several, but I usually do end up frustrated.  I love the range of difficulties in Starward Rogue.  Very Easy, Easy, Normal, Hard, & Misery.  It gives the hardcore bullet hell veterans plenty of challenge, while giving the average player a place to excel and enjoy, as well as newb scrubs like me a chance to shine (Or at least live longer than normal).
The gameplay mechanics are solid, the music (it's Arcen!) is great and very much reminds you of The Last Federation, and the controls work exactly as you would expect.  I love how your Mech gets updated visually as you get new equipment, change weapons, and add drones.  I will say many folks are turned off by Arcen's graphics, but I personally have never had any issue with them at all.  I am probably one of the few who actually like the graphics a lot.  :)
It has full controller support, which plays fantastically, and it also works well with a keyboard and mouse.  Additionally, it was designed with Modding in mind and has over the top mod support.  I think the Modding aspect is one of the things that will set Starward Rogue up for a fantastic future, beyond all the support, updates, and content I'm sure Arcen will bring, as they do with all their games.
If I had to say there was a con to this game it would be that the last boss owned the crap out of me!   Okay, that's not really a con, but still....thing destroyed my soul.  The only con I can think of is that there's no Steam Workshop for all the Modding posibilities....yet.  :)
So, if you're a fan of tons of projectiles flying at you, while you dodge and commit gigantically huge amounts of murder on sentient robots (or maybe hive mind controlled robots....or just robots), then go grab Starward Rogue and PLAY IT NOW!
Oh, also...I love that this has 1 negative review....how ludicrous!  Ahh well, some people!  #Arcen4President  Great job with another great game!  What?  I did warn you that I liked almost everything Arcen did!

I will admit, as a long time fan of the Far Cry franchise I let this one sit in my library for awhile out of fear that it would be too different from their last titles. I started playing the game two days ago. Do I regret getting this game? Lord no. Do I regret not playing it sooner? Uh, yeah.
Five minutes in, I already felt for the characters and the hardships they had to endure in this primitive landscape. Not only does Ubisoft immerse you in vivid storyline, but they also make sure that you don't get bored. This is achieved primarily by the use of making the landscape and the items in it crucial to building your village, upgrading your tools, and more or less progressing in the storyline, by giving each important character their own questline for you to follow, and having two tribes to thwart and four challenging beast hunts to complete.
The addition of trainable beasts only gave the game more depth, as well as provided an additional challenge. I began to feel as if it was my duty to collect each beast and find their unique skills and behaviors. I also enjoyed having to use the landscape fully in order to craft gear after each completed mission.
Over all, this game surely met and exceeded my expectations. Immersive storyline, new mechanics, lush graphics. I would highly recommend purchasing and trying it out if you too were hesitant to get it, or if you have never before played any of the Far Cry games.

Super Amazing Wagon Adventure is a side scrolling shooter. It's very clearly based on games from the 80s. You have to get your wagon from point A to point B... and shot things along the way. There are cool powerups, interesting little random events that may help or harm your run, traders to buy things from, and multiple forks in the road to keep the game fresh and replayable. There are also different unlockable wagons to use, each with their own advantages, disadvantages, and special quirks. There's not a whole lot more to say about the gameplay. It's mostly just automatically scrolling to the right as you move around the screen and shoot. It can be pretty easy or very hard depending on your choices and your luck. It's rather short, but highly replayable. I love the art style and the soundtrack is also pretty freakin' catchy. Plus the appropriate sound effects, of course. I really wish I could write a longer, more detailed review, but that's all there really is about it. It's fun, addictive, and only costs 3 bucks at full price. If you enjoy games you can complete in a sitting, this is great. And it keeps you coming back for more with the random events and different wagons. The only downside for this game is that... I wish there was more. More stuff in it. A longer trail. More events. Just... more everything. But I can't fault the game for any of that because what it DOES have is all great and makes for a wonderful experience that not many games aim to give you anymore. If you're thinking about it, just get it. You might not sink hundreds of hours into it, but the ones you DO put into it will all be worthwhile playtime, no filler.
Super Amazing Wagon Adventure gets an 8/10 for being a very fun little experience with lots of replayability and that throwback feeling.

I loved the first Alan Wake.
It was a very interesting take on the narrative and it's affect on the world around the player, and it saddened me to know that it's very hard that'll be a continuation for it, but when I heard of this game, I was a bit hopeful that it would at least let me play a bit more of what attracted me on the original game.
But that's not what happened.
This game, aside from a few elements, is not even that similar to what was the original Alan Wake, by being mostly an action game than a survival horror.
I tried, really hard to like this game but I just couldn't.
It has a cheap feeling to it, like it was very rushed to make a quick buck on the original, with only three maps that you have to re-visit three times, and in each visit there's very little change to them (mostly some of the NPCs interaction, enemies present and the missing pages being added), and they get even shorter when you get to the ending, unless you're searching for the missing pages (that aren't that many or hard to find), watch every Mr. Scratch video and radio interview (that are always in the same place).
It has only 5 important NPCs (Alan Wake, Mr. Scratch (just an Alan Wake model with different clothes and a dark aura) and three women you meet on each map that you must interect with to advance the game (seriously, if they were removed and replaced with writen notes left by some unseen NPC they would had the same impact in the game and plot).
Enemies are the usual Taken: small guys that run to you, big guys that are more resistant and causes more damage, huge guy with power tool that are even more resistant and causes even more damage. And there's the two new additions, guy that divide into two each time you shine your light into them and birds that fly into a random spot and fuse into a guy and turn back into birds to flee and return to attack, nothing very original or interesting.
They took the idea from the original Alan Wake, about writing changing the reality into a bit of a more literal form, where Alan would had written the pages and you need, in each stage, find a very specific page to indicate where and what you need to change to finish the stage, and the otter pages are more about lore of the place or stuff that's happening after the end of the first game (Barry started to manage the Old Gods Of Asgard, and the like), missing a lot of the original charm, where they give hints or mention about things thar are about to happen or that happened.
I didn't played the Arcade Mode, but I heard that it's a good play, but I didn't had the mood to play it after finishing the game.

Holy ♥♥♥♥, where do I start? This game was an amazingly awesome experience, and I regret that I let it rot for so long in my library. If you look casually at it, it is a gigantic mountain of colorful and perverted nonsense, weapons and explosions that make every Michael Bay movie look like new year in kindergarten, and eastereggs and jokes about pretty much every single game and movie that is kind of famous. Even though, I find that if you take the plot seriously, you have a great story with actual feelings, but not that they make you sad, oooooh no. They make you feel ♥♥♥♥ing great.
______________________________________________________________________
++Story:++
Congratulations! You just became the President of the USA! And your gang, the Saints, control everything in the white house along with you. But then, the Zin, an alien race, starts to invade earth. A brutal fight starts, and Zinyak, the evil overlord of the Zin, captures you and your team, and actually destroys earth entirely. You wake up in a simulation of a city called Steelport, and a journey begins that reminds extremely of the movie "Matrix". You goal is to save your crew, destabilize the simulation and kill Zinyak.
++Gameplay:++
The gameplay reminds very much of GTA. Open world, cars to steal, police, third person shooting battles and so on. But at some point in the story, you gain amazing superpowers. You run faster than any car can go, jump and climb buildings with amazing speed, you can upgrade your weapons so they do unbelieavable damage while having unlimited ammo, and you can even walk on water. So it is a funny version of GTA with actual build in cheats. That is great, because who play GTA without cheats anyways?
The city has 3 big parts to explore. Even though you can run super fast, you are faster by jet, and it takes at least 5 minutes to fly accross the whole map.
On the whole map, you have many different and fun minigames and sidequests to do. They give you money and EXP. With your EXP, you level up, which gives you the chance to upgrade everything with money. Get more ammo for your weapons, unlock weapons and cars, upgrade your stamina and health and such. At the end you have so much HP and ammo that you are nearly indestructible.
The missions always take place in the open world which prevents one way roads, and that feels fresh and good.
++Grafics:++
This game has amazingly well detailed grafics, even though its engine causes many models to glitch around, even though that looks funny as hell and is ok for a game like this. The light and reflection effects are well made, and the explosions breathtaking and fill you with adrenaline.
++Music:++
The music is great. I would have expected gangsta rappas everywhere, but this game has many many wubs of dubstep in it. I even think one mission had a theme made by Excision, and it sounded brutal and amazing. Also, you get a Dubstep cannon that kills with wubs. So what do you expect?
Along with wubs, you have rap, rock, oldies and classical music as well. I find it sad though that they did not have Metal. At least the Deathmetal Cannon (alternative form for the Dubstep Cannon) makes up for that.
++Features:++
Now, this is not really a feature, but this is what made me hate GTA V.
Now you all know how that psychopath, the black guy and the old thief guy (I honestly can not remember their names) are working together because they want money?
In Saints Row IV, you really have the feeling and the emotion that these people are doing this because they truely respect each other as actual friends. Lets just take the scene where the Boss (your char) sings with Pierce while they drive in a car to the next mission. ♥♥♥♥, they sing bad, even laugh while singing, but they have fun together, because they say that singing has always been their thing, and that shows me that these people have a relationship bigger than just working together to get some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ money. That give me as the player so much more enthusiasm to play this game, because the other characters welcome your character with open arms instead of being ready to backstab each other.
Honestly, I love how these characters are written.
_________________________________________________________________
In the end, Saints Row IV never takes anything serious, and when it does, it winks at you for you to know that everything happens in good fun.
Clearly recommended if you want something that is so dumb and random that it becomes beyond epic.
Oh, and buy it with the DLCs. They are in fact worth it.

In Far Cry Primal, you are tasked to single-handedly commit genocide on Neanderthals and an Aztec-inspired culture while demolishing local flora and fauna in "20,000 B.C. central Europe". Your paper-cutout pre-historic Rambo grinds through hundreds of repetitive missions and events systematically demarcated on a gigantic open-world map. Exploration consists of running towards the nearest colourful icon on the minimap.
You have at your disposal upgradable clubs, bows and beehives (instead of machetes, machine guns and grenades) with the goal of growing your own village and destroying everyone and everything else in the process. The combat is very well executed, sporting the most refined Far Cry system of base invasion, hunter-gathering and stealth-action to date. Investing in the obligatory skill-tree unlocks abilities that let you kill and craft faster as well as collect wild animals and ride some of them into battle brandishing a burning two-handed turtle-shell club.
Your bottomless bags of animal flesh and tree trunks, along with dozens of other consumables, allows you to upgrade your gear and build up your village which moves along the entertaining, well-produced story which is voiced in a made-up caveman language. This will breathe fresh air into the otherwise stale kill/collect/menu micromanagament loop and gives you a glimpse of how this undoubtedly talented studio might've produced a game less reliant on a management-mandated checklist of generic video game tropes.
Overall, it's a worthwhile experience if you go mostly for the story missions and soak in the unique atmosphere. The game options allow you to turn off all the intrisive UI elements and turn on permadeath, catering to those who want to eschew the standard Ubisoft-style player-handholding. The cartoonish levels of carnage and violence don't mesh well with the tone of the plot and character arcs, but if you are intrigued by the concept of a quasi-paleolithic era in video-game form, this is as good as it currently gets (on PC).

I am a huge fan of couch multiplayer, be it competitive or co-operative, and this game has been a thoroughly exciting co-op experience. The game is designed require communication and teamwork, which makes for escalating shouting matchesa and maybe the occasional gameplay. It's cleverly designed to force you to work together to win, unlike some games whose co-op modes seem a little shoehorned just for the sake of it.
If you have the necessary hardware (including friends) to host a couch gaming session, this game will not disappoint. The best thing about it is its accessbility. Casual gamers can easily relate to the cute visuals and simple, familiar Diner Dash-like game mechanics. Hardcore gamers and senior management on the other hand will appreciate the level of coordination and planning that is required in order to earn 3 stars in the co-op campaign levels.
That last comment is coming from someone who has spent around 200 hours playing Overwatch - a highly competitive game that has an optional co-op mode depending on whom you play with.
If you are keen on couch gaming on PC, this is an esssential.
10/10 if you are into casual couch gaming.

The whole strategic aspect available in the base is great. Mechanics are simple yet effective. You always have to decide on what to build/research/manufacture next, and there is never enough money. A good game is always found when you have to make tough decision. This is there the whole game.
Graphics are great, both in the strategic game and the tactical combat. The tactical game provides a good challenge and the AI does a fine job on keeping you on your toes, until your squad is experienced (mid-level) and carries the advanced equipment.  Enemy toughness does increase to keep the game challenging however, it would have been nice for the aliens to have some abilities, like their human counterpart.
This is a no brainer for anyone looking for a game with a mix of strategic elements with a heavy dose of turn-based tactical combat, all in a human vs alien invasion environment.

TL;DR
Starward Rogue is a crossover of SHMUP and Roguelite elements that blend seamlessly in this vibrant and explosive Sci-Fi twin stick shooter that gives you tons of variety to entertain you for days.
Pros
+ well balanced difficulties
+ unique enemies
+ tons of bosses
+ interesting level design
+ good soundtrack
Cons
- walls can be hard to see
- some traps are just plain annoying
- upgrades can be unclear
- lack of animations
Starward Rogue starts you off by immediately plopping you into a short tutorial which explains the mechanics through message prompts while a narrator named Rodney guides you with his goofy voice explaining the backstory. You are a disembodied head, and your sole use to is to control these mechanized warriors. You are replaceable, you are not someone special, you're just a cog in the machine that allows it's usage. The game reiterates this many times that it doesn't matter if you die because they can just replace you. You're a genetically modified space dragon that can regrow it's head upon death after a certain amount of time. You and many others in a similar situation to you are aboard the Megalith which is a giant ship in space that is lodged into a star, and your 'masters' have been paid handsomely to rescue Rodney from his metallic space cell. It is up to one of you to traverse the ship, combat it's many enemies, traps and hidden rooms in hopes of finding Rodney and maybe get yourself out of this hellhole. Is there any better motivation than that?
The tutorial is entertaining and short enough to keep you entertained while subtly showing you what to expect from a gameplay perspective. There are simple traps, revolving guns, and one special enemy which gives you a true glimpse of the future horrors to come. The game feels natural with a controller and the controls feels intuitive, very typical of twinstick shooters you control the direction of where you shoot with the right thumbstick and move with the left. You also have other weapons depending on the mech you choose, the standard mech has a gun that shoots infinite bullets, a rocket launcher and an energy weapon both with limited ammo. The energy weapon fully restocks after each new room you enter so it's a great wave clearer when you're overwhelmed by enemies. Once you finally clear the tutorial, you can pick a character to choose who you want to traverse the Megalith with.
There are 6 different mechs to choose from, all with their own strengths and weaknesses that will directly cater to almost any playstyle. There are also 5 difficulties to choose from, ranging from Very Easy to 'Misery' which hasn't been fully implemented yet but aspires to be Touhou levels of hard once it's finished. For my first run I decided to go with Normal which describes itself as meant for people who are experienced with SHMUPS or roguelikes. I'm fairly well acquainted with the genre with over 100 hours in Nuclear Throne, a game that is ruthless to it's players and refuses to hold your hand. The first thing I noticed was how well balanced the game felt on Normal, while it was a bit 'easy' for a roguelike veteran like myself it was nowhere near what I would consider a walk in the park for anyone except the most battlehardened SHMUPS players. I decided to give each difficulty a try to test them out, and each difficult felt very well balanced for the player it was intended to cater to. For reference, I died at the final boss on my first Normal run and completed both my runs on Very Easy and Easy. Hard felt a bit more natural, with enemies now having more attack patterns at their arsenal and you had lower health. At times I would die on the very first floor depending on which mech I chose.
One of the coolest mechs in the game is called Redshift, and his special is that he can control time. Time stops when he stops, and only starts to move forward when Redshift is either moving or shooting. This is such an interesting mechanic to fiddle with, as he only starts with 2hp and no shields but his special gives you much needed time to think about what move you're going to make next which is invaluable at higher difficulties.
Each run consists of 5 floors that you need to navigate and explore, each floor is filled with tons of rooms that are RNG based so no run will ever be identical. There are four types of rooms, enemies based, treasure based, shops, and bosses. Enemy based rooms are filled with robots who are hellbent on trying to kill you with shiny 80s inspired neon colour bullets. The doors behind you lock once you enter an enemy based floor meaning you're trapped until you clear the room of it's enemies. It almost feels like you're disco dancing while trying dodge all the colourful bullets being thrown at you along with the synth music thumping in the background.
One of the strongest elements of Starward Rogue are the enemies themselves and how they're designed for you to exploit their weaknesses and their attack pattern themselves. Some of the attacks enemies throw at you look impressive visually and pleasantly surprise you. Enemies would usually specialize in an ability like reflecting bullets off walls or slowly expanding bullets that would lay on the ground and cause contact damage if you didn't wait until it disappeared. Some enemies would have a shield that lasted indefinitely and their only weakness that you could exploit was shooting them from behind, at the same time there could be traps laying around the room that could take your bullets and reflect them in every direction. It was the variety of constantly finding interesting enemies and the element of being filled with traps like laser tripwires or spikes that enemies could hide behind would keep me on my toes at all times. But it was worth clearing all enemy based rooms because they would give you that sweet EXP to level up, and with each level up you were given a choice between 3 upgrades that would benefit you greatly. Level upgrades most commonly ranged between HP, damage or loot based, where I would always choose extra damage since the faster you killed an enemy the less dodging you would have to worry about.
When you weren't busy mowing down enemies, you would come across many rooms that were filled with treasure or power ups that would help you in your venture to the last floor. There were even secret rooms where you could sacrifice HP permanently for amazing upgrades such as infinite Energy but with a huge downside where it was only infinite until you received damage for the first time. There are countless weapons and items to be found, some of them adding onto your weapons or outright replacing them. If it's the latter, a box will pop up showing the specs of the weapon you own compared to the other weapon and a description of it's attack pattern.  One interesting moment I've come across is the time when I killed one of the merchants only to find out the stuff he was selling was replaced by super upgrades found nowhere else in the game, but the downside was that you could no longer buy items for the rest of that floor.
I reached the text limit right around here so I'll skip to my conclusion. I'm missing the last 3 paragraphs from my review.
Overall, Starward Rogue feels like a great entry to the Roguelite genre mixing it up with SHMUP and dungeon exploration elements makes it feel fresh and exciting. It isn't the prettiest game around but it is definitely one of the more fun roguelites. The gameplay is great and feels rewarding at higher difficulties for veterans of the genre but I could easily recommend it to anyone with it's well balanced difficulty settings and catchy music. I highly recommend this game to anyone who is a fan of twinstick shooters, or roguelites!

Tropico gives you so much freedom when it comes to creating your island. Not only is it a city builder (in a sense) it is a society sculptor. You can issue edicts or in more modern terms "executive orders" to put laws in place, as Tropicos Presidente that will change the way your islands inhabitants respect you.
The city building aspect is far from Sim City. It is a click and build, then 1 type of structure will be constructed everytime. The structures do not evolve like they do in Sim City. There are varieties of each structure (such as housing) but housing structures all come with different features and properties like less people per srtucture or people are happpier in that one house compred to another. Another very cool thing about Tropico's construction process is that you can place most buildings any where on the map; they don't all need to be connected to roads to operate. You also don't need power for your city to operate on a certain level of efficiency. If you want a more productive Tropico than you will need power, though.
The other big aspect of the game is the respect portion and groups of people who like you. The are about 10 groups who want your respect and they vary from nationalists,capitalists,environmentalist,militarists and even the USSR and many more. Don't forget your foreign relations. It's tough to please them all so you must find a balance.
In case you didn't find out already, this game is all about your import/exports. Generally it seems like you run a island full of slaves, but you can satify them all with high paying jobs and pull a nice profit, depending on what your island specializes in.

A twin stick shooter/bullet hell game where you take control of one of six mechs as you fight through 5 levels of a ship lodged inside a star to save something named Rodney from the ultimate boss Warden. Sounds pretty cool right? It is. This game is tons of fun, I've owned it for just a few days and already have more than 8 hours in it (might seem like a casual time for some, but for me that's quite a lot for a relatively short span of time). The controls are nice and fluid, the game boasts hundreds of items to pick up to augment your mech, and lots of weapons, attachments, bosses, minibosses, and enemies to make each play an indivual, enjoyable experience. With a catchy electronic soundtrack and nice graphics to top it off, the game really comes together.
Now that the good is out of the way, let me talk about just a few issues I have with the game.
I may just be bad, but from my experience there seems to be just a couple room types that are near impossible to come out unscathed. From clusters of enemies that mow you down to tight rooms where you get swarmed easily, some rooms just feel a tad unfair.
Another room type I for one have a big issue with is rooms where there's laser barriers everywhere that you have to sit and wait to turn off before weaving through to the next segment of the room, only to have to wait some more for the next barrier. It really breaks the flow of the game for me and since enemies are allowed to pass through these lasers without taking damage makes me really frustraded when I encounter such rooms. I feel like I take damage on those rooms because of the layout of the room itself, not because of some lack of skill on my part. I'll admit when I mess up, but in some cases I feel taking damage/dying outright is beyond my control sometimes.
Don't think I'm being critical because I don't enjoy the game, that's not the case. I really want this game to succeed because I'm having lots of fun with it and the company behind the game (Arcen Games) have had to lay employees off because this game hasn't brough as much money as they needed to sustain themselves. I feel with a few tweaks this game could be on par with some roguelikes I love like Isaac or NecroDancer, but as it stands it's showing a huge amount of potential but a few minor quirks get to me.
I would urge anyone who's interested in this game to pick it up. Support the developers, especially when Arcen Games is on the verge of collapse. $12 dollars isn't a huge amount to ask, even just getting 6 hours out of the game makes the expense worth it in my opinion.

TL;DR Recommended only for Game of Thrones and/or Telltale Games fans.
Main points:
1. It isn't a game as per all TtG titles, it is an interactive novel with some not so good QTEs.
2. Your choices are purely cosmetical, they don't matter. The game blatantly lies in your face, as per all other TtG titles. They give you an illusion and it works, especially in GoT world where choices of minor characters are of little to no influence in the grand scheme of things and against much better positioned players like Cersei, Tyrion, Ramsay or Margaery.
3. QTEs are somewhat annoying, there's too little time to react sometimes, unless you know beforehand - replaying the sequence when your char dies.
4. Writing is OKish if you are into GoT world, otherwise it's rather poor. Without GoT background it doesn't make much sense either.
5. Graphics and sounds fit the TtG style, no complaints here. Nothing spectacular either.
6. Controller recommended, for me it's unplayable with kb+m.
I like this product despite its flaws, but I am GoT and TtG fan and I accept the convention as it is. But if you are looking for a real game and want your choices to really matter, look elsewhere >> e.g. Bioware games.

Holy ♥♥♥♥, where do I start? This game was an amazingly awesome experience, and I regret that I let it rot for so long in my library. If you look casually at it, it is a gigantic mountain of colorful and perverted nonsense, weapons and explosions that make every Michael Bay movie look like new year in kindergarten, and eastereggs and jokes about pretty much every single game and movie that is kind of famous. Even though, I find that if you take the plot seriously, you have a great story with actual feelings, but not that they make you sad, oooooh no. They make you feel ♥♥♥♥ing great.
______________________________________________________________________
++Story:++
Congratulations! You just became the President of the USA! And your gang, the Saints, control everything in the white house along with you. But then, the Zin, an alien race, starts to invade earth. A brutal fight starts, and Zinyak, the evil overlord of the Zin, captures you and your team, and actually destroys earth entirely. You wake up in a simulation of a city called Steelport, and a journey begins that reminds extremely of the movie "Matrix". You goal is to save your crew, destabilize the simulation and kill Zinyak.
++Gameplay:++
The gameplay reminds very much of GTA. Open world, cars to steal, police, third person shooting battles and so on. But at some point in the story, you gain amazing superpowers. You run faster than any car can go, jump and climb buildings with amazing speed, you can upgrade your weapons so they do unbelieavable damage while having unlimited ammo, and you can even walk on water. So it is a funny version of GTA with actual build in cheats. That is great, because who play GTA without cheats anyways?
The city has 3 big parts to explore. Even though you can run super fast, you are faster by jet, and it takes at least 5 minutes to fly accross the whole map.
On the whole map, you have many different and fun minigames and sidequests to do. They give you money and EXP. With your EXP, you level up, which gives you the chance to upgrade everything with money. Get more ammo for your weapons, unlock weapons and cars, upgrade your stamina and health and such. At the end you have so much HP and ammo that you are nearly indestructible.
The missions always take place in the open world which prevents one way roads, and that feels fresh and good.
++Grafics:++
This game has amazingly well detailed grafics, even though its engine causes many models to glitch around, even though that looks funny as hell and is ok for a game like this. The light and reflection effects are well made, and the explosions breathtaking and fill you with adrenaline.
++Music:++
The music is great. I would have expected gangsta rappas everywhere, but this game has many many wubs of dubstep in it. I even think one mission had a theme made by Excision, and it sounded brutal and amazing. Also, you get a Dubstep cannon that kills with wubs. So what do you expect?
Along with wubs, you have rap, rock, oldies and classical music as well. I find it sad though that they did not have Metal. At least the Deathmetal Cannon (alternative form for the Dubstep Cannon) makes up for that.
++Features:++
Now, this is not really a feature, but this is what made me hate GTA V.
Now you all know how that psychopath, the black guy and the old thief guy (I honestly can not remember their names) are working together because they want money?
In Saints Row IV, you really have the feeling and the emotion that these people are doing this because they truely respect each other as actual friends. Lets just take the scene where the Boss (your char) sings with Pierce while they drive in a car to the next mission. ♥♥♥♥, they sing bad, even laugh while singing, but they have fun together, because they say that singing has always been their thing, and that shows me that these people have a relationship bigger than just working together to get some ♥♥♥♥♥♥ money. That give me as the player so much more enthusiasm to play this game, because the other characters welcome your character with open arms instead of being ready to backstab each other.
Honestly, I love how these characters are written.
_________________________________________________________________
In the end, Saints Row IV never takes anything serious, and when it does, it winks at you for you to know that everything happens in good fun.
Clearly recommended if you want something that is so dumb and random that it becomes beyond epic.
Oh, and buy it with the DLCs. They are in fact worth it.

Game of Thrones (GoT) is one of those games that you have to stick with a bit to really begin enjoying it. I found the opening chapter of GoT to be, well, dull. It was obviously setting up the context of the game. But, whereas in TellTale's other games (namely The Walking Dead and Wolf) the story was slowly built around the characters, it felt like in GoT the story took precedence. As such, I just didn't connect with Gared or the other characters introduced right at the end of the episode.
That said, once you get into espisode 2 - and especially by episode 3 - you become more invested in the story, and the pull that I loved in the other TellTale games becomes apparent, and I actually started caring about the decisions I made. And, boy, there are some tough choices to be made.
I know that, in GoT, there's no such thing as a fairytale ending, but I was not expecting the hardships in this game. To the point where I knew I was getting a bad outcome either way, so I would just turn off the game because I didn't want to have to choose between starving peasants or a pillaging army.
I think TellTale slip up a little in rushing to set up the events of GoT. An independent story in the world of Westeros would have worked well enough, I think. However, once you get past the slog of backstories and establishing story-arcs, the game picks up quick. I would call GoT my favourite in the series, even; had it not been for the opening episode.
But still, GoT is definitely worth your time and money.

Alan Wake returns, sort of. A short, 4-hour story accompanies a decent (but solo) arcade experience. But will players survive the re-used assets to complete the single-player campaign? That is the real question. Worth a purchase when discounted if you enjoyed the previous game, but there just isn’t a lot of content here.
Total size on my hard-drive: 2.4 GB
You can
.
+ Alan Wake is back. This takes place after the second “Special” episode of the first game.
+ Excellent (if occasionally low-res) graphics. Well-optimized.
+ New weapons. An assault rifle, sub-machine gun, auto-shotgun, crossbow – in keeping with American Nightmare’s focus as an arcade game, there are a number of new weapons that all handle and feel different. A big improvement over the first Alan Wake game, which only had a small number of weapons to choose from.
+ New enemies. Again, a by-product of the arcade focus, but the new enemies look nasty and fit right in with the world Alan Wake. Some don’t respond to light in the way you’d expect, so be careful.
+ Great sound design. Sometimes the tap-tap of footsteps is all you hear before you are attacked.
+ Short but great soundtrack from Petri Alanko once again. More great songs from Poets of the Fall as well.
+ The story is more of a pulp-style adventure, with garish over-acting from the villain and a Twilight Zone-style voice-over. A departure from the Stephen King-inspired first game, but it works well enough – especially in conjunction with the collectible manuscript pages, which supply a large amount of backstory.
+/- Collecting manuscript pages is required to unlock the more advanced weapons. Bad news for people who don’t want to be bothered with collectibles.
+/- Arcade mode is simple: fight hordes of “taken” and survive until the sun rises. The new guns and weapons, plus some well-designed arenas make this decent (if solitary) fun. Only five maps, and unlocking advanced weapons depends on how many manuscript pages you collected in the single-player story.
- The looping nature of the story results in reuse of the same three levels for the entire single-player campaign. Not only the levels, but Alan’s actions and most of the events are repeated as well. It’s a Groundhog Day / Source Code / Edge of Tomorrow style narrative gamble that might work on the first playthrough, but only hard-core fans will want to replay it.
- Though set after the events of the first game, not a proper sequel. More of a glimpse of what is happening with no time to go into detail.
I was (and am) happy to get more Alan Wake, but with a proper sequel being forever put off by Remedy, American Nightmare is a sad, short epilogue to what promised to be a unique suspense / horror franchise. Buy it (at a discount), enjoy it, and hope Alan Wake 2 will happen someday.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a a sequel to Alan Wake and as its predecessor it's a third person thriller. While the original game had a good presentation and tried to do something with an interesting premise, American Nightmare felt very cheap. First of, you have to play three maps three times in a row. Secondly, the story and its weak ending are forgettable although the villain wasn't too bad. Gameplay's core wasn't touched, but its parameters were slightely changed. Also, the flashlight is reloading its light much faster now. Together with new added weapons makes for a far easier gameplay. The good thing is that it seems to run much better without vsync than the first game for some reason.
+ new weapons
+ new enemies
+ runs well
+ potentially good villain in a bad story. that's why he can't really shine.
+ FOV slider
+ good looking environment
- repetitive gameplay since you are playing the same maps time after time
- bad story
- bad ending
- enemy type variety is too low
- much easier than before. also, too much ammo.
- very short. at least it was cheap
- bad voice acting in comparison to the original
Further information:
Increase the FOV in the settings. If you are playing with m/k, enable the direct aim in the settings.

Before i go into my review I would lke to say that i am still playing that game and haven't got a proper understanding of it YET this is just what i think at this point in time.
So i got bored one day and decided to give this game a shot. I gotta say the gameplay is really good infact it's the best gameplay in any mmo i've played to date. the controls are super responsive and it plays just as well as dmc did. you get the drill, you do combos on mobs in a fast pace style the more combos you do the more dmg output you give out. Their are LOTS of ways to mix combos together for each class which is great. changing class is like playing as another character, you'll always get something different. I have zero bad things to say in terms of the gameplay. If you like hack and slash games like god of war or dmc you'll enjoy this.
Now that i got that out the way let me talk about the crafting system. Listen, i haven't tried to craft much this game nor would i intend to. I think crafting and gathering is a chore and it trakes up too much of my time. It just isn't my thing but from what i've heard off of oher people the crafting in this is vast and very in depth. It's very hard for me to comment on the fun aspect in crafting seen as i hate it no matter what game it is. Those who craft on here however really like it so if it's your cup of tea you will most likely enjoy it too.
Now then let's cut to character creation! This is quite possibly the best character creation syetem i've seen in not just any mmo but any game in general. Theirs so many way to customise your character it's ridiculous. I was even able to make a character that looked like me irl almost perfectly. Even if you don't look normal it's still "possible" to create yourself on the game since it's possible to edit almost every part of the human body. Thats more than what i can for most games, this  I know for a fact will certianly not disappoint you.
Now lets talk about pve. This imo is where the game falls flat and loses most it's potential. It's sad too because the most important part of any game is haveing something to lean on, so in other words pve is your only option in terms of progression in the game. Alot of mmos now days play like work i mean literally work like a job or something.  every quest is always kills this collect that blah blah blah, it gets old fast and the mobs  all seem pretty much the same, unintersting mobs and easy AF to kill with so much as no effort put in. Don't get me wrong the, I love the exploration in the game and  immersive world that feels alive. But when i do go exploring it feels like zero prgression and i feel as though i have to do linear quests for progression which isn't a good feeling for me personally. Exploration isn't as rewaring like in a game like skyrim for example, it just feels like a waste of time. I can't comment on the endgame pve content since i haven't got that far yet but from what i've heard it's even more of a chore than doing quests. You basically kill the same mobs over and over to get better equiped but again i may be ignorant on this matter since i haven't got that far yet. I would like to know in the comments what endgame pve is like ;D. I may also update this review once i do indeed reach endgame and see it for myself.
As for pvp, i don't really care about it xD i'll probably toss an update if i ever try it out.
Overall, i really like the combat in the game and character creation. Pve can be fun but the fun aspect of pve only lasts so long for me.  Maybe if they change up the quests a little and add some actual challenge to the mix i'll certainly have a change of heart.
I still recomened it though seen as it's very cheap and looks and almost plays like an AAA title, also microtansactions in this game isn't the FULL goto. Instead it's just an option on the side..

What can I say about this game that hasn't been said before? Well over a decade old and Half-Life 2 still breathes with character and charm that hasnt aged a day. Once you can look past the dated models and textures in some areas, what you find is a bombastic sci-fi FPS puzzle solver. Memorable characters you will find yourself having strong positive or negative feelings for by the end. Stunning set-pieces and well constructed levels that will definitely test your platforming skills. An excellently paced and constructed story that will keep you trudging through to the very end. Well at least as far as Valve will let us trudge...
You'll shoot.
You'll run.
You'll beat things with a crowbar.
You'll even stack a box or two.
No library is complete without the Half-Life series and you won't regret adding it to yours. Especially if you can find a good deal on Half-Life 2 and its terrific follow-up episodes.

This is an action RPG from the makers of Titan Quest and there are enough similarities between the two games that this is basically Titan Quest 2 with a Dark Fantasy theme instead of Mythology.  I loved Titan Quest so this is not a bad thing.  If you liked the dual mastery system of Titan Quest then you would probably enjoy this game.  I really like the theory crafting you can do by experimenting with different character masteries, skills, devotions, items, etc.  There are so many ways to customize your character.  So many damage types....so many skills (and you can't get them all).  I don't like the theme as much as I did for Titan Quest though.  The story is "meh" for me.  I like the factions in the game and how you can kill certain monsters or complete quests to increase your standing with them.  And I like how there is a real incentive to do so since faction stores have nice loot if the faction likes you.  There is a ton of loot in this game.....maybe too much but there are filters you can set to hide loot below certain quality levels.
All that being said, somehow this game became my most played Steam game as of this writing. And thus far I haven't done anything past Veteran difficulty yet.  That is because I keep changing my mind on which character build I want to push to later difficulties first.  I wish I knew how much time I had alt-tabbed out of the game to look something up or look at builds.  I also think I would have enjoyed this game much more if I had played with friends like I did some back in the TQ days.
One thing to consider when playing this game is that this game is still actively patched/tweaked by the developers.  That is good but just keep in mind that your favorite character build could get nerfed.  Much like TQ though, just about any character can do well on Normal/Veteran and you may not notice weaknesses until the 2nd or 3rd difficulties.  Some builds are more dependent on loot/gear than others.
Note about expansions - I don't have the Crucible expansion which is basically just a gladiator type setting where you face wave after wave of enemies.  My understanding is that you can level quickly and get great loot quickly in the Crucible.  I do have the Ashes of Malmouth expansion that just came out in Oct 2017 and I consider it a must buy if you play the base game.  It basically adds another Act to the story, two new character classes, and many other things.
I have never enjoyed these games. Until now. This is a pretty fun game in the sense that you can be very serious with your civilization or you can just have fun, consequences be damned.

Welcome to the fourth installment of the popular 'Tropico' franchise. Highly acclaimed with a ton of rave reviews, but is this game as good as people say? Yes. Yes it is.
If you are new to the Tropico franchise like I was, then here is a very quick rundown of the game:
You are El Presidente, the leader of a small Carribean 'paradise' called Tropico. Your main aim is to transform Tropico, an underdeveloped and practically lifeless bunch of Islands, into a world superpower by any and all means necessary. You will  straight up notice some very funny parallels to the real world as Tropico is basically Cuba, and El Presidente is based off a number of socialist and communist figures such as Fidel Castro and Che Guevera.
Throughout the campaigns in the game you will have total control over Tropico which will see you lead your state onto the international platform for either good, or bad reasons. You will need to balance your popularity with your people by pleasing the various factions present within your society; something that is easier said than done. Similarly, you need to stay on the right side of the world superpowers as the game is based during the Cold War and your decisions will vary your popularity with the United States of America (US), or the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics (USSR). There are other world leaders but they don't threaten to invade you, well, as far as i'm aware anyway. Alongside all of this, you must work to transform Tropico by investing money into things like housing, welfare, food and resources, government, tourism, etc. Make sure you don't blow your budget too badly though because the world superpowers don't like broke countries. Also, prepare for major natural disasters that will kill your people, ruin your buildings and crops.
Some people may read this and say 'This is just a mix of the Sims/Cities mixed with Democracy or something like that'. In a way maybe it is, but here is why I think Tropico is way better. Political corruption is encouraged in the game.
Need to get more products out? Run a sweatshop. Rebels annoying you? Wire tap houses, impose martial law, conscript citizens into your army against their will. Getting too many immigrants and have shacks overunning your beautiful paradise? Force emigration. Faction leader or protesters becoming too popular? Have them eliminated or arrested for herecy. Minister of Foreign Affairs made a bad decision? Fire him and arrest him. . . See what I mean? How does this not sound fun?
If you like being the corrupt leader of Cuba and focusing more on being famous than the wellbeing of your citizens who you can force to never leave a state with poor housing, bad health conditions, slave labour, conscription, propeganda, rebels, frequent natural disasters, and 'accidents' or disappearences happening way too reguarly.. than this is the game for you.
Buy it. Play it. Live it.

In this game give you dark-background story as you are survivor similar to zombies apocalypse, but with demons, undeads, monsters etc. Plus the decision making is impact on me, somehow I made really bad hasty mistake and let some other survivor die without thinking ahead of consequences. A roguelite labyrinth lodged in the side of a star. Dodge gorgeous waves of bullets, claim weapons and upgrades, defeat The Warden, and rescue… Rodney?
That’s the description on Steam for the latest release from Arcen Games, ‘Starward Rouge’, and it’s quite on the money in my opinion. It’s a simple, easy to pick up top-down maze navigating shooter… think the maze portion of ‘Legend of Zelda’, except with a mech that shoots rockets.
Graphics wise, it’s decent, as is the sound work…. but of course the big factor is it fun, and the answer is of course yes. It’s a very easy game to learn, with a game pad, you can use the right stick to navigate, the left to fire your main weapon in numerous directions, the left trigger to spring, left bumper to pick up items, right trigger to fire rockets and right bumper for the energy weapons.
The mazes appear to randomize, so you don’t know exactly what you’re going to get, as you’ll see in my First Impressions game play video, I stumbled across boss battles rather frequently.
I do highly recommend this game for those looking for something fun, and something casual.

Overall this game is a good, solid ARPG.  There is good mechanics, such as the food concept that can be used to rapidly heal (which I think is better than the health globes of Diablo 3).  However, a few major issues make this not even close to my favorite ARPG.  Namely, the map design is way too labyrinthian.  The maps are pre-designed, but unfortunately I feel like randomly generated maps are done better than what these ones are.  Additionally, it all but begs you to back-track and replay areas, and it is just not that interesting or engaging to do so.  I did not, for instance, play through on higher difficulties because of this.
The other major issue I had with this game was the difficulty balance.  There would be times where I would easily breeze through enemies, but then hit this huge difficulty increase on a boss, wipe several times to it, until I widdled it down enough to kill it.  Or I would do full exploration of the map, and come up on enemies in the main path that are 3 - 5 levels above me.  This lead to some real frustrating moments.
Then finally, the ending is very disappointing.
All that being said, it gives a good chunk of fun, and if you can get past those issues, then you will enjoy this game.  I just feel like Torchlight, Path of Exile, or Diablo would be better choices then this game is.  I'm still giving it a recommendation though since I did play through it and had fun.

This is a great game. If you like skill based challenge with rogue-lite randomness and permadeath then this game is for you.
I find the challenge to be more skill based than knowledge based and for that it's a welcome change from BoI.  When I die in this game, it's because I screwed up. This is in stark constrast to BoI where I feel that half of my deaths are caused by wrong item choices based on incomplete knowledge of the possible item synergies because I haven't looked them up.
The choice of difficulty level is really satisfying. Normal is a fun challenge while hard is an impressive step up in difficulty without feeling like it is impossible one. It's definitely a bullet-hell game on the harder difficulties and trying to manage missing all of the bullet patterns while still hitting the bosses is a rewarding challenge.
EDIT:
My only complaints is that not all of the menu options in the game have intuitive controller mappings. For example, in the pause menu, it gives you a mouse like control to select options.  Lame.  But that doesn't take away from the fun you have while playing it.

When it comes to any Tell-tales game, you'll either love their games for the story or you feel like you aren't able to enjoy the story due to the game elements. In my case I just tried to like this game, since I am a big Game of Thrones (GoT) fan, but while playing it the videogame part ruined my enjoyment over and over again. Personally I would've rather watched this on Youtube or as a web series.
Now, you might be asking does this story include the main GoT characters. YES it does, you'll interact with Cersei Lannister and Tyrion Lannister a bunch and breathly meet a few other popular character from GoT.
Let's start with what things that stopped me from enjoying the game and you will be the judge of whether these things bother you or not. The biggest issue I had with this game, were the meaningless dialog choices, no matter what I said I would receive a generalised statement. Let me give you a minor-spoiler example:
Little things like these frustrate me a lot as it doesn't make any sense and tells me in the face that no matter what I'll do the story will go along the same. Now that isn't to say that you can make minor choices plus choosing between lives here and there. However, I felt like I hadn't any choice or my choices had hardly any impact throughout the game.

When it comes to action scenes, where you have to test your QTE skills. It doesn't sound too bad or off-putting, but try doing them with the horrible mouse acceleration, if you want to enjoy this game at least a bit, you'll need to play it with a controller. I also ran into the issue that I couldn't press a button in-time because of the performance issues the game has, even though the game isn't exactly a good looker.
Thus playing in the small levels, inbetween the cutscenes and dialogs,were you click here and there on items is surprisingly painful and annoying. Although you learn a bit more about the people or objects you click on, which does give you some immersion back.
In conclusion the game has a grim, but enjoyable story to tell, which you can only minor impact. If you can see past the issues I listed, are a GoT fan and have a controller you should be able to enjoy the game at least to a degree. I didn't outright hate it, but there is no way I am touching another Tell-tales game. I hope you make the right decision for yourself and thanks for reading.

"Luke, I am your father." But I am also in a videogame.
Yep, I'm reviewing a Star Wars game, whoop de-freaking-do.
Star Wars Battlefront 2, hmm. When I saw this at a half-price book store, and yes, this "half-price book store" had a videogame section, I thought this game was some sort of RTS strategy game. Boy, was I wrong. I actually bought this game at that "half-price book store" but it turned out that the disc didn't work so I returned it and later bought it on Steam.
Instead this game is an FPS. I never liked First Person Shooters, they left a bad taste in my mouth, but this one isn't that bad.
For starters, it has single player modes, and they're actually pretty good. FPS's usually rely on their multiplayer modes, focus less on single player, and/or give the player a very short single player campaign (except for Halo, which I have never played). In reality, this game actually took the cake with its single-player modes. The missions in the campaign are a bit demanding, but you eventually get used to them (after about five hours of RAAAGE). The turn-based/board-game/strategy single player conquest modes are actually pretty cool, but take forever to finish. I can't go one turn without running into some stupid  battle! Damn it, you stupid Separatists! Get your stupid ship away from me and my planets!
The AI is.....VERY topsy-turvy. In any of the single player modes you either have a very high or very low chance of winning due to your dumb-*** or smart-as-heck-*** computer teammates. In the campaign your teammates are VERY likely to get killed. Sometimes the computer is stupid, sometimes it's not. Sometimes you'll win very easily because the enemy is too stupid to know that it's losing.  I actually did an experiment, where during a battle in the conquest modes, I did absolutely nothing to prove that I had or hadn't had an influence on the battle, and I won. I believe I tested it again, and I lost. So I came to the conclusion that depending on the enemy's or my teammates AI would affect the battle, I had no influence at all. Well, I guess you have a little impact on the battle, but really you do not create a major influence. Unless you go crazy Rambo-style and happen to kill all the enemies without all your teammates getting killed, then it might turn the tables on the battle.
If you want to play this game's multiplayer modes, good luck. You won't find anyone playing this game anymore, this game is OLD. So if you DO actually find a server with actual people on it, go for it. Seriously though, nobody really plays this game anymore. Nonetheless, my opinion, even though true, shouldn't stop you from playing with complete strangers online in a game that's about ten years old in which just had a sequel/remake that is SO MUCH BETTER.
This game is good, but I didn't actually dive into how the gameplay is, sorry about that. I don't exactly have time to explain the gameplay, but I'll eventually update this review and give you the scoop.
So until then, have fun with Battlefront 4! (Which is NOT on Steam. Thanks a lot, Electronic Arts....)

Firstly; gotta love all these people giving HL2 negative reviews just because EPISODE 3 isn't being made. EPISODE 3. Nothing was ever said about Half-Life 3, just the 3rd Episode. A while ago, if I'm correct, Gabe said that they didn't want to do the episodic content for their games anymore. I may be wrong on that, but I'm almost certain that someone at Valve said something regarding episodic content for their games. Anyways, just because Episode 3 is dead doesn't mean the Half-Life franchise is dead. Half Life 3 may still happen; sure, since it'd be a new game, some plot holes would be left unanswered, but Marc Laidlaw answered most of those in his Episitle 3 post, so the slate is pretty much clean for a new Half-Life game in a new scenario.
ANYWAYS, it's time to get to my review.
Half-Life 2 follows Gordon Freeman, the titular hero from the first Half-Life, mysteriously appearing on a train to a city known only as "City 17". It's very quickly revealed that City 17 is a pretty dystopian society, with the Combine ruling over it, with Wallace Breen at the helm of the operation, located in the Citadel. It's up to Gordon Freeman to stop the Combine invasion, meeting a new friend or two along the way, as well as some old.
Overall, Half-Life 2 does a great job at delievering its story; it was one of the first games at the time to not have to take the player into a scripted cutscene event where they have no control over their player. In Half-Life 2, the player can move around and interact with most objects freely during story segments. It's a beautiful execution of a great story.
10/10
Half-Life 2 was the first game to use the Source engine, an amazing engine at the time. This engine simulated physics pretty damn accurately, and was astonishing for its time. This can be seen throughout the game, with physics puzzles and destructible objects and barriers. You can smash boxes open to reveal ammo boxes or healthkits hiding inside, or jump on them from one to the other to avoid toxic water. The firefighting is pretty good, too; no stupid health regen that modern games feature, but rather health stations and Combine charging stations used to refill the player's HEV suit at certain points in maps. Overall, this is some pretty impressive stuff for its time, if dated.
8/10
...Hot damn. For a game made in 2004, the graphics hold up extremely well. Half-Life 2 was very ahead of its time in this regard; if you played it now, it'd look pretty good compared to games that came out later than it. The Source engine also helped in this regard, allowing for some of the most human expressions seen in video games. You can very clearly see the emotion in each character as the story unfolds. With a few mods, the game can look even better and even more modern. Overall, this is a very strong part of Half-Life 2 for me.
10/10

There are morons I've seen call Half-Life 2 overrated.
Opinion is one thing, but there really isn't any unfounded nostalgia or hype surrounding this series. Half-Life 2 is a very intelligently and lovingly crafted experience. One with great thought put into its level design, and the general pacing and experience of the entire game. Yes it's a shooter, but it's not just going from fancy-looking shooting gallery to another different looking shooting gallery. It's a journey. You go from point A to point B and crazy things happens along the way. You get to drive two very different vehicles, go through a horrific town taken over by zombies, lead an army of alien bugs AND human beings, get to fight huge and very deadly alien machinery and more. All without cutscenes, with a silent protagonist and managing to make it all not awkward. Not to mention very likable and excellently voice-acted characters who leave an impression with just a few dozen voicelines. Overrated my♥♥♥♥♥ If you don't like it, just shut up and let people enjoy it.
Could do a negative review and give the finger to Gabe because it's likely the series will never be given closure... but this game is too good to click on that thumbs down button. If you've never played it fricking play it, it still holds up better than the vast majority of FPS today.
IMPORTANT: play the game through the mod ''Half-Life 2: Update''. You can find it on Steam. It's a graphical overhaul mod, but nothing drastic. It's a light touch to the graphics with improved lighting, effects and skyboxes, but nothing that clashes with the original (''lore-friendly''). Also fixes some bugs. Highly recommended.

This is an action RPG from the makers of Titan Quest and there are enough similarities between the two games that this is basically Titan Quest 2 with a Dark Fantasy theme instead of Mythology.  I loved Titan Quest so this is not a bad thing.  If you liked the dual mastery system of Titan Quest then you would probably enjoy this game.  I really like the theory crafting you can do by experimenting with different character masteries, skills, devotions, items, etc.  There are so many ways to customize your character.  So many damage types....so many skills (and you can't get them all).  I don't like the theme as much as I did for Titan Quest though.  The story is "meh" for me.  I like the factions in the game and how you can kill certain monsters or complete quests to increase your standing with them.  And I like how there is a real incentive to do so since faction stores have nice loot if the faction likes you.  There is a ton of loot in this game.....maybe too much but there are filters you can set to hide loot below certain quality levels.
All that being said, somehow this game became my most played Steam game as of this writing. And thus far I haven't done anything past Veteran difficulty yet.  That is because I keep changing my mind on which character build I want to push to later difficulties first.  I wish I knew how much time I had alt-tabbed out of the game to look something up or look at builds.  I also think I would have enjoyed this game much more if I had played with friends like I did some back in the TQ days.
One thing to consider when playing this game is that this game is still actively patched/tweaked by the developers.  That is good but just keep in mind that your favorite character build could get nerfed.  Much like TQ though, just about any character can do well on Normal/Veteran and you may not notice weaknesses until the 2nd or 3rd difficulties.  Some builds are more dependent on loot/gear than others.
Note about expansions - I don't have the Crucible expansion which is basically just a gladiator type setting where you face wave after wave of enemies.  My understanding is that you can level quickly and get great loot quickly in the Crucible.  I do have the Ashes of Malmouth expansion that just came out in Oct 2017 and I consider it a must buy if you play the base game.  It basically adds another Act to the story, two new character classes, and many other things.
