Overall this game is a good, solid ARPG.  There is good mechanics, such as the food concept that can be used to rapidly heal (which I think is better than the health globes of Diablo 3).  However, a few major issues make this not even close to my favorite ARPG.  Namely, the map design is way too labyrinthian.  The maps are pre-designed, but unfortunately I feel like randomly generated maps are done better than what these ones are.  Additionally, it all but begs you to back-track and replay areas, and it is just not that interesting or engaging to do so.  I did not, for instance, play through on higher difficulties because of this.
The other major issue I had with this game was the difficulty balance.  There would be times where I would easily breeze through enemies, but then hit this huge difficulty increase on a boss, wipe several times to it, until I widdled it down enough to kill it.  Or I would do full exploration of the map, and come up on enemies in the main path that are 3 - 5 levels above me.  This lead to some real frustrating moments.
Then finally, the ending is very disappointing.
All that being said, it gives a good chunk of fun, and if you can get past those issues, then you will enjoy this game.  I just feel like Torchlight, Path of Exile, or Diablo would be better choices then this game is.  I'm still giving it a recommendation though since I did play through it and had fun.

I consider myself a fairly casual/competitive gamer.  I do like the competitive side just to have fun and to have a little bit of a fresh and new experience with the games that I play.  I played Quake 3 a little bit and thought it was a great experience.  I discovered that there was a Quake Live, but I didn't play it for over a day.  Now that Quake Live has been brought to steam, I have had great amounts of fun than with any other game.  But, now that now there are these new mechanics that are added to the game, does that diminish the experience of this game?  From my point of view, I think no less of it.  With the additions and mechanics that have been introduced, it makes the game a little bit more balanced for people who just picked up the game, and nothing really has changed from my point of view.  From Total Biscuits point of view, that is understandable from a hardcore Quake fan.  But, there are servers with the classic mode that all the old players enjoy, so nothing is really at a loss.  However, it becomes an issue when the player has to pay for the lobby that they want.  It's extremely different as to which side you talk to.  If you are a newcomer to Quake, I would highly recommend that you give this game a try!  If your a hardcore Quake fan, I wouldn't say this is the end of Quake, and a few changes shouldn't cause the community to be up in arms about it.  Quake is still the fast paced genre that we all know and love, and the minor changes don't bother me.
Tl;dr: Quake is still a fun, fast paced game.  If you haven't tried it, I'm sure you will like it!

"Luke, I am your father." But I am also in a videogame.
Yep, I'm reviewing a Star Wars game, whoop de-freaking-do.
Star Wars Battlefront 2, hmm. When I saw this at a half-price book store, and yes, this "half-price book store" had a videogame section, I thought this game was some sort of RTS strategy game. Boy, was I wrong. I actually bought this game at that "half-price book store" but it turned out that the disc didn't work so I returned it and later bought it on Steam.
Instead this game is an FPS. I never liked First Person Shooters, they left a bad taste in my mouth, but this one isn't that bad.
For starters, it has single player modes, and they're actually pretty good. FPS's usually rely on their multiplayer modes, focus less on single player, and/or give the player a very short single player campaign (except for Halo, which I have never played). In reality, this game actually took the cake with its single-player modes. The missions in the campaign are a bit demanding, but you eventually get used to them (after about five hours of RAAAGE). The turn-based/board-game/strategy single player conquest modes are actually pretty cool, but take forever to finish. I can't go one turn without running into some stupid  battle! Damn it, you stupid Separatists! Get your stupid ship away from me and my planets!
The AI is.....VERY topsy-turvy. In any of the single player modes you either have a very high or very low chance of winning due to your dumb-*** or smart-as-heck-*** computer teammates. In the campaign your teammates are VERY likely to get killed. Sometimes the computer is stupid, sometimes it's not. Sometimes you'll win very easily because the enemy is too stupid to know that it's losing.  I actually did an experiment, where during a battle in the conquest modes, I did absolutely nothing to prove that I had or hadn't had an influence on the battle, and I won. I believe I tested it again, and I lost. So I came to the conclusion that depending on the enemy's or my teammates AI would affect the battle, I had no influence at all. Well, I guess you have a little impact on the battle, but really you do not create a major influence. Unless you go crazy Rambo-style and happen to kill all the enemies without all your teammates getting killed, then it might turn the tables on the battle.
If you want to play this game's multiplayer modes, good luck. You won't find anyone playing this game anymore, this game is OLD. So if you DO actually find a server with actual people on it, go for it. Seriously though, nobody really plays this game anymore. Nonetheless, my opinion, even though true, shouldn't stop you from playing with complete strangers online in a game that's about ten years old in which just had a sequel/remake that is SO MUCH BETTER.
This game is good, but I didn't actually dive into how the gameplay is, sorry about that. I don't exactly have time to explain the gameplay, but I'll eventually update this review and give you the scoop.
So until then, have fun with Battlefront 4! (Which is NOT on Steam. Thanks a lot, Electronic Arts....)

It is not without its issues though. For one the outlines of objects in the game have this oil painting like effect on them which is terrible. I'm not sure if this was some attempt to cover up errors in the models outlines or if it was some guy thinking "Yeah, soooo artistic" but either way it's very annoying. In most case you can ignore it, but when you have many thin objects together (I.E multiple swords on a sword rack) the whole image looks blury as it's the outline of individual objects that have this effect.
While I do love the story and the writing it can jump from character to character a little too often in some episodes. There's a few times where it cuts back to a character for all of two minutes before jumping to another and then another which can leave you with no time to settle in and makes it feel a bit rushed at times.
Some of the choices in this game are just down right unfair (In the best of ways) which leads to some pretty tense moments. I've played a lot of TTG. TWD Seasons 1 and 2, The Wolf Among Us, Batman, Tales from the borderlands etc.. but this is by far my favourite.

Don't get me wrong, this isn't a bad game. Just not good enough to recommend.
The gameplay is point and click puzzling solving which is actually pretty solid. The main problem is that the puzzles range in difficulty from easy to just plain crazily convuluted and overally complex. This makes the game feel tedious and frustrating. The challenge is all over the map and it breaks the game in my mind.
The game is relatively short, but I feel the price tag is justified for the amount of time you'll probably spend as you try to trudge through the puzzles. The game has a lot of gore, but they went a bit overboard with it, and it doesn't feel scary at all because of it. I do, however, feel that the art syle works for what they were trying to achieve and is one of the main highlights. The story is fragmented and poorly delivered, with no closure at the end.
It has no replayability. There is literally nothing different if you play the game a second time, unless you want to try and replay it for some achievements. Hardly seems worth it to randomly click the screen 5,000 times for a single lousy achievement. The "play the game for three hours" achievement seems bugged, so this screws those who likes to try and get a 100% rating in games.
Lastly, I had minor issues with the game in terms of funcationality. There's no options menu to fix the screen resolution, sound, etc. You're forced to play in full screen. This would be fine if my game didn't crash when I tried to alt tab out if it was necessary. This wasn't always the case, and luckily the game's auto saving is good, otherwise it would be a complete trainwreck.
Although an honest attempt was made and there are some good points, "tedious" is really the best way I can describe this as a whole.

It's a decent game.  I'm recommending it because this is the closest thing we're going to get to Alan Wake 2.  In reality we're not going to get Alan Wake 2 for a long time (if not ever) since Remedy is working on other projects.  The CEO of Remedy said this year that there is no second game in development.
American Nightmare is basically the beginning development material and prototypes that Alan Wake 2 was supposed to be.  But AW2 didn't happen and whatever material they had was packaged and rushed into this game.  I wouldn't even really call it a game.  It's extremely short (can finish it in like 3-4 hours) and it's more like an expansion.  You can tell how rushed this was due to the layout of the story itself (it's spoilers if I say, you'll have to see for yourself), the areas you're in, and the dialogue/story.
One thing that is annoying is that I wanted to replay the last chapter since I forgot to save a character and collect a collectable and some reason you start with only the sucky starting pistol and no other weapons and equipment.  Right off the bat you get the most powerful enemy thrown at you.  It doesn't help when you face two of these guys and lots more enemies moments later.
A good thing is that there is a lot of weapons to choose from and ammo and batteries is never short.  The problem is there is probably is only a few you're actually going to use due to their damage rates-like the revolver paired with the hunting rifle or carbine or AR.  Oh yeah they nerfed (made weaker) the flashbangs and flare gun.
Overall, I don't think this is even considered canon since there is so many unanswered questions from AW1 and the ending of this is left questionable along with the story itself.

Many games have the style of what Block N Load has, an FPS in a world you can build and destroy blocks... nearly all games that fit in this category fail miserably like Brick-Force.
Block N Load however doesn't, it stands tall on its own and has a lot to offer! Let's see what the game has!
Lots of heros, they are separated in 3 classes.
Brains who support the team and can do quite a bit of damage, while having limited movement and low health pools.
Brawns who are the bigger guys who can take hits, build spawns, radars and mines, and ontop can do a lot of damage to enemies and bases.
And Lastly are the skill pros who fit into small roles to help with the team, for an example Nigel the Sniper is a brillant partner to defend with, while Kira is a brillant option for attacking.
There's a lot of
between classes and all of them are unquie and memorable, plus if you don't like a certain hero, you can always try another! There are plenty of options to choose from!
Some of my personal favourites are...
Cogwheel the heavy hitting robot who can destory teams and bases with ease!
Sarge Stone who is a basic tough guy who can do a lot of damage and in a short time!
Nigel Longshot who is one of the most balanced Snipers ingaming and can set up lots of traps!
And Kreepy the Klown who scares his enemies into submission with his gloves and banana bombs!
Friendly
community, we are happy to help out new players who want to learn the game, by giving out advice and tips on how to do certain things, the only way you can anger/annoy us is by directly taunting people or making horrid balance suggestions, we welcome newcomers with open arms!
Easy to earn Ingame currency called Gold, you get some for your first win of the day, doing the tutorial, winning and daily events, you can easily earn 1000+ gold a day by doing your challenges and winning! You can then spend gold on heros and leveling up perks, which give you small bonuses and downsides to help give a more unique play style, for an example on Vander, you can get faster build speed, with higher build costs so you can become more offensive, and while attacking, you don't really need to worry about build costs.
Lots of blocks to build and destroy! Certain heros can carry certain blocks like Brain's Heal Stations and ammo, Brawn's radars and Spawn Points, and Skill's beartraps and fake blocks, all blocks are useful in their own way and none feel useless!
Lots of maps, plus you can make your own! Block N Load pretty much has unlimited maps since the community can create their own if the Dev's take a break from making their own!

I did not like playing this game.
The writing was poor, and poorly translated as well.
I know what the story is and where it ends, but how it got their is just, so, boring.
There are points in the game that you feel like, "Ohhh, boy, here we go! I wonder what this is all about!" But directly after these points you feel like, "Oh, we're.... we're not going to do anything with that? Oh, we, we just leave that there then. Um, alright then...."
There are many avenues that this game could have taken, but it seems to have chosen the most mundane one. I mean, it could have been better if it was arrived to in a better manner. I just didn't feel it. At no point in this game did I feel the slightest inclination of fear.
The voice over added nothing, very monotone, no real life. Also, I would figure an english speaker, which I only assume the voice over was, would be able to recognize the poor translation before recording the script. There are several blatant grammatical errors that are spoken, how did that get by?
1HEART game devs, you really should have presented this game to a native English speaker before release. It's distracting from the story to see these errors.
The art was enjoyable at most parts. Though the drawings of the girl and the villian seemed very silly, not scary at all, it just seemed poorly done.
These being said. some of the puzzles were actually really fun to work through! Really made you think.
But other challenges were impossible. A tool you find at the very end of the game is needed for a room in the middle? How is one supposed to know this? Theres nothing to lead one to think that this should be the case. The back and forth in this game gets a little out of hand.
TL:DR
Poor English writing, zero scare factor, decent puzzles. Pick up another point and click, like "I have no mouth and I must scream", or "Deponia". This one needed a few more weeks in game testing..... in the States or England, not Poland.

*UPDATED*
A pretty good revamp of a time-tested classic.
PROS:
+ Same frenetic Quake 3 Arena gameplay...with extras.
+ Choice of primary & secondary weapons allows you to start matches with your own play-style.
+ Spruced up graphics make Quake Live easy on the eyes.
+ Fully supported online community, like the original Q3A.
+ A one-time payment of $10. The monthly "Go Pro" subscription fee has been removed.
+ Modest hardware requirements for a "current gen" FPS.
CONS:
- Mac and Linux are not supported as of this review.
- Anything before Windows 7 (Vista, XP, 2000...) are not supported.
- Other FPSes of a Q3A ilk (OpenArena, Nexuiz Classic, Xonotic, Warsow) are available for FREE.
- Other FPSes of a Q3A ilk (OpenArena, Nexuiz Classic, Xonotic, Warsow) have lower hardware requirements.
- Other FPSes of a Q3A ilk (OpenArena, Nexuiz Classic, Xonotic, Warsow) run on Linux and Mac natively as well as Windows XP and later.
- Other FPSes of a Q3A ilk (OpenArena, Nexuiz Classic, Xonotic, Warsow) are DRM-FREE, and can be copied to your external hard-drive or burned to a disc for safe keeping.
- Quake III Gold can be had via
DRM-free, includes Team Arena, and runs on Mac and Linux via ioQuake3.
BOTTOM LINE:
Quake Live is pretty good at only $10 on Steam. However, Mac and Linux users will need to run Quake Live via Wine. Mac users in particular are often not savvy to programs like Wine. And Windows XP and Vista users are out in the cold.

It was hard for me to write this. You may go, aw, this guy has only barely 2-3 hours so I can't trust him. In most other games, you'd be right, but not this one. Quake is a multiplayer only as far as I can tell game with multiple gamemodes and multiple looks. All these are nice, except for a few issues. The first is the community: It is extremely hard to get better without being told "aim bettur". When I ask for some help, I want a real honest answer, not troll answers. I just get told to stop playing COD and HALO. That brings me to the learning curve. The Learning curve is EXTREMELEY Steep. Your gonna get rolfstomped on a couple occassions. Overcooked is a Shared/Split Screen Co-Op cooking game made by Ghost Town Games. Its gameplay focuses on the co-op element and I can say this game is definitely a 'hardcore' co-op. This game requires an intense coordination with your 'cookmates', quick reaction, time management, and a huge amount of focus.
Here's a bit of a lore to give you the idea of what's going on. Don't worry, these are all the intro of the game so they're not spoilers. Set in a "not so distant future", the world was coming to an end and a massive spaghetti meatballs monster is crushing the world. In order to survive, you need to cook onion and tomato salads to satisfy those delicious apocalyptic creatures. After you and your cookmates failed horribly, the Onion King sent you back to the past to train your cooking skills and save the world in the future.
You will now work in multiple different so-called kitchens in different environments, offering different challenges and foods to cook. Gameplay in general is 2-4 people playing as chefs, running around weirdly designed kitchens where they need to cook different types of foods to get enough money and achieve three stars. The kitchens are specially and well-designed by the devs to ensure you will coordinate with your friends. Some kitchen can be completely separated every several seconds, some kitchens only have one-person walkway, some kitchens have obstacles in them that will prevent you from moving around, some kitchens have mouses that will steal your food, etc.
In these specially designed kitchens, you need to cook different kind of foods like burgers and soups. The most common way to cook is: Take the ingredient - Boil/Fry the ingredients - Put it on a plate - Serve - Wash Dishes - Repeat. It may seems easy, but the kitchen and the overwhelming orders will create complete chaos (chaotic fun) if you don't coordinate well.
The main advantage of the gameplay is its 'reach'. Everyone can play this game as long as they are able to use a keyboard or a controller. To clarify my point, games like CSGO, Battlefield, Need For Speed, Dark Souls, and almost every game out there only attracts a very specific demography - male young adults. Co-Op Games like Overcooked, Gang Beasts, Monopoly, etc that successfuly created a friendly and fun co-op experience for all genders and ages are pretty uncommon to find these days. I saw several other reviews that gives this game a thumbs up because of 'My wife likes it' or 'My 7 years olds have a lot of fun with Overcooked' or ' My girlfriend loves this game' or other similar reasons. This is what makes this game so good - it has a co-op based gameplay that is fun for everyone and can be used to strengthen their players' bond with others. I personally also feel this benefit - I play this game with my sister who's not a gamer (she only plays PokemonGO and Reign) and she never plays any co-op or MP games with me before, yet we had a lot of fun playing Overcooked for hours.
But, I do have some things that I don't like from Overcooked. It's all of those splitting-kitchens, like the earthquake kitchen or the food truck kitchen. First of all, we thought it might be an interesting challenge to have the kitchen split every several seconds. But then, we realized there's really almost nothing to do when the kitchen separates. The intense yellings like 'I NEED MY TOMATOES NOW' or 'WHERE'S THE LETTUCE BURGERS OMFG IT'S ON FIRE' completely died out as soon as the kitchen splits. All we can do is chop stuff and wait until the kitchen's back. Or the worst part - wait until we can extinguish the other half part of the kitchen that's completely on fire. We both felt that it's a bit of a design 'flaw' - although it's not necessarily is - since it really 'killed' the co-op moments.
Overcooked is definitely one of the best split screen co-op games out there. You can enjoy it with your family, with your friends, with your soulmates or whoever. I highly recommend this game if you have some fun people to play with.
Thank you for reading!

If you are unfamiliar with Telltale Games, I'd like to start by advising that this is an interactive story where you make choices for the hero/heroine that you control and those changes will then tailor the story according to those choices, However, most of the time these choices will have a minor effect on the course of the tale and only a few choices will change things in major ways. This is fine because the focus in on telling a good story and Telltale tend to do this very well with excellent writing and a stable of very proficient actors. You WILL become emotionally invested in what is happening to your character and if this appeals to you then I would recommend any Telltale game to you.
For this specific game, a familiarity with the Game of Thrones TV series (at least up to Season 4) is strongly recommended if you wish to get the most out of the experience. If not, being familiar with the first three Song of Ice and Fire books that the TV series is based on would be fine. You can still enjoy the game if you are not familiar with the source material but you wouldn't get the best experience.
Now, a lot of reviewers have given this a thumbs down because the game and the story is too demoralizing. If you like your games/stories to be uplifting, where the heroes always win and the villains get their just desserts I would recommend that you stay away from this title - at least until future seasons are completed and the entire story arc is complete. This game is very much a product of the source material and you will find yourself struggling in a dark, depressing and unfair world where reality sucks. That is not to say that there won't be moments to cheer or glimmers of hope here and there but for the most part, the powerful will overcome the weak and you will be on the losing side.
Having said all this, we still have a compelling story with some great characters so if you really aren't afraid to immerse yourself in the world of Westeros for a few hours I would highly recommend giving this one a go.

An old school style point and click puzzle game focused on trying to instill a sense of dread, as a child lost in the dark.
At first, I felt drawn in by the voice acting and creepy cut-scene that draws you into this dark, twisted world, of two little girls alone in their house, and the haunted toys they take in with them. Whilst it's not exactly believable the parents would just HERP DERP leave their darling kiddies to go on a random holiday, the atmosphere of the game is well drawn for this point and click.
The scenes seem to be oil painted, using dark tones and chaotic strokes, and the music permeates the background as you go on this adventure, helping shape the mood of the game.
Now I really like the narrator's voice, though I find myself getting bored quite fast as it is slow paced. Not much really happens. You move from scene to scene, see some creepy looking objects, and the slowness of it, and lack of creeping fear in the background actually takes away the  sense of dread the game is clearly aiming to achieve. I don't feel that dread. I get more bored the further I make it through the scenes.
I also think the dialogue is a real letdown to what could otherwise be a good game. It's badly done. Like, really badly done. You can't help but notice how amazingly bad it is. I feel they didn't do much research on the English language at all.
The puzzles are quite good. Not so difficult but not so easy, either.
Nice, gothic style of graphics. Environments are moody and atmospheric.
Realistic controls
Creepy music
Good voice actor/narrator.
Story has potential.
Puzzles progress well.
Dialogue/writing feels off.  Incorrect or awkward use of words in sentences, and sometimes conjunctions/words are omitted, so it's not often grammatically correct.
Heartbeat sound isn't in synch with heart.
Doesn't seem to be a way to save your progress or know if you missed anything in a former scene.
TL;DR
A game that has a lot of potential, but sadly falls flat of what it can deliver. It's not very scary, and frankly, it's pretty boring. A shame, because the voice actor is good, and the drawings are nice. What especially dragged this game down was the bad use of  English language. For me, it ruined the game, but for others, maybe it's not so noticeable.

If you are thinking about buying the game then read this first before doing so. Here is my experience with the game so far.
At first, I really thought that this game would be great. However, as time went on, I soon realized that this game is a complete waste of time. Buckle up your seatbelts kids. It's adventure time.
TL;DR: This game sucks. Don't buy it.
Before I even started playing this game, I was really eager to get my hands on it because I would constantly see gameplay videos of BDO on YouTube. The graphics of the game really stood out to me, so I felt like I just had to get my hands and try it out for myself.
After I had gotten the game, I had a hard time getting use to it. The playstyle was different from what I was originally used to, and I struggled to find myself having fun with the game. Anyhow, it didn't take very long to get use to the new playstyle, and I soon found myself starting to enjoy the game overall.
The game itself has great aesthetics. Everywhere you go is visually appealing to the eye and it sort of adds to the realism of the game. The combat is different from other MMOs that I've played, but I think that it's great to have something different for a change. The idea of having a market place where items are already set at a certain price is cool because then players can't over charge you for more than what the item is worth. This may sound great and all, but here's what killed the game for me.
Yeah, BDO may be fun and all when you first start, but once you hit level 50 or so, it becomes difficult. You start to learn that it becomes a pain to level because the mobs that you are killing aren't giving you good exp anymore. In order to find places to level up faster, you need to find stronger mobs to kill. Great, sounds like a regular game to you right? That is until you realize that they literally gang up on you and destroy you like nothing. You then realize that you are undergeared and try to gear up for your grindfest. This is the point where you will find yourself feeling like you are not making anymore progress. The simplest way that I can make this is this:
In order to level up further into the game, you need to grind mobs. If you want to successfully grind the mobs, you need gears. To get gears good enough to grind mobs, you need money. And to get money, you need to do life skills. Yes. You will spend most of your time doing life skills.
At this point in the game, you aren't even playing the game anymore. I found myself constantly AFKing in the game in order to make money just to try and gear up. And even then I would spend 5 days just to make enough to buy 1 piece of armor. It's not worth it. The game just plays itself at that point and you will just find yourself stuck with nothing else to do. The only way to make the game less stressful is to spend some money in the game, but even then it only helps a bit. Not only that, but the game isn't pay to win. So if you're thinking about dropping money on the game in order to be "overpowered" then don't. Paying for cash shop items in this game is only for convience, so if you decide to drop money thinking that you'd be a top player then it'd be a waste.
This game had great potential, but unfortunately, it's just not fun at this point. Don't waste your time and money on this. Go find something else to play instead. You'll thank me later.

TLDR: Worth a try if you like ARPG's. Has some significant QOL improvement, but imo the masteries should be reworked a bit.
On some levels its Titan Quest 2.0.
On others its..not.
The setting is totally different and not for everyone, but the core of the game is more or less the same only much improved.
Examples:
+Auto-pickup items
+Better loot filter
+One-drop chests (chests that have 100% chance to drop epic item once in your game to prevent you not getting any good items for hours)
-Masteries
This is a tough one. The masteries in Titan Quest were very thematic for lack of a better word. Earth was based around fire damage. Storm was about frost and lightning. Warfare about melee combat. And so on.
In Grim Dawn however, masteries are much more mixed up. While I don't think this is a bad thing necessarily, I do feel that the masteries don't mix with eachother very well.
I keep going back to single-mastery characters because I don't feel like the classes complement eachother well. Sure you can stack modifiers by going arcanist-demolitionist for example, but I don't think the arcanist skills add anything aside from damage.
This is just my personal experience with the masteries and I can and probably am wrong, but I just wanted to put it in here.
+Art
I really like the art in this game. The coats, pistols and scrap-metal stuff really look awesome.
+Environment
For some reason I really like the environment in Grim Dawn. I think the map looks really nice.
All in all its worth a try if you like ARPG's. You will probably know if you like this game or not within 2 hours.

Fun.  Fierce.  Frustrating.  And like any other addict, you'll be coming back for more, even after getting schwacked by bad luck or poor design.
Luck is a big part of the game.  The exact same random event done 10 times can have 10 different consequences.  Maybe the guy you beamed down finds a lost person to join your crew.  Maybe he finds a weapon.  Maybe he gets eaten and dies.  Luck.  How much scrap, what events you find, and everything else will be random.  It's the nature of the beast.
But what isn't luck is making sure you don't overstretch your resources.  Can you give up 15 missiles in hopes of a better reward for helping someone?  If you're at 50 because you aren't using any, sure.  If you have 18 and have 2 missle guns...no.  Save for that cloaking device.  Don't bother with the clone-bay...or maybe you should.
Experiment.  You have to have a gameplan of how to run the ship, which you'll figure out after several awful runs.  There are many that work...but more that don't.  Find what works for you.  But keep your thumb on the spacebar and turn off numbered choice settings to save frustration.  You don't have to react fast, just pause the game and do what you need to.
This is easily one of the best games I've played in a while.  It doesn't rely on graphics to do it, just a little wit and plenty of gameplay choices.  Name your crew after characters from Star Trek, South Park, or whatever gives you a quick laugh.  As frustrating as it can be, remember that it's a game. You're not meant to win, you're meant to play.  Have fun.  That's pretty easy to do in this one.

I have only played for a short time thus far, but I am already in love with this criminally underrated and under promoted gem. The visuals are crisp and the juxtaposition of the dark (but detailed) backgrounds with the searing bursts of neon fire from enemies just works beautifully. Menus are slick and the developed provides a ton of flavor text, making it absurdly easy to navigate and use the options menu in particular. The in-game UI is unobtrusive and never gets in the way of the action, which becomes important as things turn chaotic. Controls are handled with aplomb and the player has just enough of a sense of weight to feel appropriate for mech fights. The devs even give the option for a weightless and snappy schmup style control feel. Combat itself is frenetic and possesses satisfying depth, rewarding the player with the ability to show off true skill in the midst of the madness. The general mix of exploration, upgrading, and combat are fleshed out and dialed in to provide what I consider to be near perfect pacing, and it is all backed up by the rare soundtrack that I actually turn UP.
If you like any element of this game, you will have an absolute blast with it. I bought it on sale for a couple dollars off, but I would not hesitate to pay the very reasonable $11.99. There is enough brilliant gameplay here to make it a legitimate no brainer.

Starward Rogue is a sci-fi roguelite with bullet hell influences. The game takes a lot of inspiration from Binding of Isaac. The basic structure is the same, although SR adds a lot of its own twists on top of it. It's also much more intense, often having a huge amount of bullets on screen at once.
There's a large variety of weapons. You can carry one of each type at once, and swap them with ones found in chests and stores. Energy weapons are interesting in that they have a limited amount of ammo, but automatically recharge whenever you change rooms. This is a clever way to encourage using the weapon regularly. There's also an experience system, along with selectable perks. All in all, the game has a good amount of depth, without feeling overwhelming.
You can pick from six different mechs at the beginning of a run. All of them have different starting loadouts and attributes. One of them starts out with an unique ability, which pauses the time whenever you stand still. This makes the game almost feel like a turn based game. It's pretty hard to use, but it's an interesting alternative way to play the game.
The camera can be zoomed out further than Steam's screenshots show. Doing this makes the game look a lot less claustrophobic. If you're using a 1080p monitor, the game shows a good amount of distance around you by default. For lower resolution displays, there's an option to zoom out the view. This is very handy, as being able to see the bullets from further away makes them easier to avoid.
The graphics are quite nice, featuring high resolution 2D graphics. The UI has a simple look to it, making it easy to read.
The soundtrack features a variety of upbeat electronic music. They're all good songs, and fit the game's atmosphere well.
Most of the game works well with a controller, but the menus were obviously made with a mouse in mind. Some of them require you to move a cursor around with the analog stick, which is a bit clunky.
There's more options than you usually see in 2D games. I especially enjoyed the option to switch to SHMUP style controls, which removes the friction from your movement. It makes the game feel a lot more responsive and familiar, for those who are used to playing bullet hell games.
I recommend Starward Rogue to anyone who enjoys roguelites or shoot em ups. It's a fun game, with few flaws. It's challenging, yet the difficulty rarely feels cheap. Arcen Games has a reputation for releasing interesting, yet flawed games. However, Starward Rogue is much more polished than their games usually are, so give it a shot.

Like most other space sim games, it takes a while for it to unravel itself and all its goodness. So don't trust any negative review with under 10 hours, and even that way, they haven't completed it, which I think is totally needed in this game to give it an honest rating.
This game is cruely overlooked but is well worth its time for any space sim fan.
Lots of things to do (main story, side quests, random missions, escort missions, trading, smuggling, bounty hunting, ...)
A main story giving a lot of different and surprising situations that keep the game fresh and enthralling.
A good twist compared to other games like this : you don't buy new ships, you evolve yours in a combinations of 3 different aspects, as you wish (and it changes the visual of course). You have to find artifacts for that, which pushes to exploration and add dynamics.
The graphics are really nice (even more considering it's from 2006), the different designs enjoyable.
The only flaws I'd see : some shortcuts missing, a bit more of a tutorial would be great, and more details about total energy balance too (sometimes getting the best weapons you can without thinking will just drag too much energy and empty your capacitors so fast that you won't be able to shoot often, so it's important).
In the end, nothing gamebreaking at all.
A really fun game not to miss for a lighter, but still demanding, experience in the genre.

This isn't normally the type of game I play, but I bought it anyway to support the devs. I'm actually having a lot more fun than I expected. I started out on normal but got killed multiple times in the first room floor. After I switched to Very Easy, it got a lot more fun. There are lots of different enemy types and each floor has multiple minibosses in addition to a main boss at the end. It's pretty chaotic, but there's also a lot of strategy. There's ammo management over three different weapons: a primary gun with unlimited ammo, an energy weapon that recharges every time you enter a new room, and a missile weapon that you have to find ammo for. Additionally you can collect credits which you can use to buy upgrades in shops and you also gain exp for killing enemies. After you gain enough exp, you gain a level and get to choose from one of three perks at random. There are also shops that let you buy powerful upgrades at the cost of some of your max health. These are pretty cool, and are an interesting risk vs reward system. You'll also find keycards throughout the levels which unlock secret chests and rooms, though there probably won't be enough for everything so you have to pick which you want more. For instance, you might have to choose between unlocking a loot chest or a shop which has defensive items. This isn't my favorite game of theirs, but it is a lot of fun for a couple hours at a time and I definitely see coming back to it again.

Overcooked is a Shared/Split Screen Co-Op cooking game made by Ghost Town Games. Its gameplay focuses on the co-op element and I can say this game is definitely a 'hardcore' co-op. This game requires an intense coordination with your 'cookmates', quick reaction, time management, and a huge amount of focus.
Here's a bit of a lore to give you the idea of what's going on. Don't worry, these are all the intro of the game so they're not spoilers. Set in a "not so distant future", the world was coming to an end and a massive spaghetti meatballs monster is crushing the world. In order to survive, you need to cook onion and tomato salads to satisfy those delicious apocalyptic creatures. After you and your cookmates failed horribly, the Onion King sent you back to the past to train your cooking skills and save the world in the future.
You will now work in multiple different so-called kitchens in different environments, offering different challenges and foods to cook. Gameplay in general is 2-4 people playing as chefs, running around weirdly designed kitchens where they need to cook different types of foods to get enough money and achieve three stars. The kitchens are specially and well-designed by the devs to ensure you will coordinate with your friends. Some kitchen can be completely separated every several seconds, some kitchens only have one-person walkway, some kitchens have obstacles in them that will prevent you from moving around, some kitchens have mouses that will steal your food, etc.
In these specially designed kitchens, you need to cook different kind of foods like burgers and soups. The most common way to cook is: Take the ingredient - Boil/Fry the ingredients - Put it on a plate - Serve - Wash Dishes - Repeat. It may seems easy, but the kitchen and the overwhelming orders will create complete chaos (chaotic fun) if you don't coordinate well.
The main advantage of the gameplay is its 'reach'. Everyone can play this game as long as they are able to use a keyboard or a controller. To clarify my point, games like CSGO, Battlefield, Need For Speed, Dark Souls, and almost every game out there only attracts a very specific demography - male young adults. Co-Op Games like Overcooked, Gang Beasts, Monopoly, etc that successfuly created a friendly and fun co-op experience for all genders and ages are pretty uncommon to find these days. I saw several other reviews that gives this game a thumbs up because of 'My wife likes it' or 'My 7 years olds have a lot of fun with Overcooked' or ' My girlfriend loves this game' or other similar reasons. This is what makes this game so good - it has a co-op based gameplay that is fun for everyone and can be used to strengthen their players' bond with others. I personally also feel this benefit - I play this game with my sister who's not a gamer (she only plays PokemonGO and Reign) and she never plays any co-op or MP games with me before, yet we had a lot of fun playing Overcooked for hours.
But, I do have some things that I don't like from Overcooked. It's all of those splitting-kitchens, like the earthquake kitchen or the food truck kitchen. First of all, we thought it might be an interesting challenge to have the kitchen split every several seconds. But then, we realized there's really almost nothing to do when the kitchen separates. The intense yellings like 'I NEED MY TOMATOES NOW' or 'WHERE'S THE LETTUCE BURGERS OMFG IT'S ON FIRE' completely died out as soon as the kitchen splits. All we can do is chop stuff and wait until the kitchen's back. Or the worst part - wait until we can extinguish the other half part of the kitchen that's completely on fire. We both felt that it's a bit of a design 'flaw' - although it's not necessarily is - since it really 'killed' the co-op moments.
Overcooked is definitely one of the best split screen co-op games out there. You can enjoy it with your family, with your friends, with your soulmates or whoever. I highly recommend this game if you have some fun people to play with.
Thank you for reading!

Two soldiers, one carrying the super-taser device and the other carrying a rocket launcher went around the outside. a hole would be blasted in the side of the ship, allowing for the quick subjugation of this fierce, elusive creature.
The soldiers took their positions.
The rocket was fired.

The beast turned around, angry and startled.
The device fired, sending a concentrated burst of electricity into the behemoth's body.
Stun failed.

With its simplistic design and elegant Asiatic music you would think this is a soothing game.  To me it is an intense mindbending challenge!  The object of the game is to get 100% coverage of a carved wooden shapes by wrapping it in as little of your length of rope as possible.  The rope is tied to one nail and you must tie it off (touch) to the finishing nail after getting at least the minimum amount of coverage.  The shapes and difficulty increase as you go.  It is really a wonder to me the amount of control you have moving the shape around as you work to wrap the rope around it.  It is extremely fluid.  If you are in the mood for something different, requiring mindfulness, and challenging then this is for you.

The game is good overall, becomes a bit grindy at times, but if you don't mind repetition, it's a pretty good sand box game (the story is just an excuse to get you going, but I have sadly seen much worse).
Personally I liked it especially because of the peculiar setting, which is recreated quite well I must say, not only graphically.
I purchased the game after all the patches had been released, including the survivor mode otherwise my comments would have probably been different.
The best part is having to make every bullet, or actually, every arrow count. I am not saying it because they are hard to come by.
In fact finding enough crafting materials, especially as you progress in the game, is quite easy, you just need to take the time to go around and gather them.
The challenging part is when you are busy fighting, especially if you are stuck inside a confined space like a cave, where you can't go looking for crafting materials if you run out, and you can only carry with you a limited amount of arrows, spears and so on (every weapon is throwable as well, in fact a thrown spear is probably the highest single target damage weapon in your arsenal).
The melee weapons can break at the worst time, and get consumed by the flame as they should if you put them on fire. It can become pretty intense when your weapon breaks in the middle of a fight and even if you have the resources to make a new one, you can't just put the game on pause (like drinking the potions in skyrim) and make a new one, it takes time, therefore you are forced to use another weapon if you have it, or to run away.
Because of the kind of weapons used, you also get to loot back the ammo from the enemy corpses or where you (or anyone else) missed (make sure you remember approximately the location of where you fired your shots and pick them up later, they are highlighted with the hunting vision).
In survivor mode is pretty tense to out at night, because the rate of predators roaming increases by a lot, and some of those can take you out in no time, especially cats that are fast and stealthy, and you won't see them coming unless you pay a lot of attention to the sound (mute the music and play with headphones is my advice) and the movement of the grass. Small tip: some beasts are not scared of fire...
The stealth part is okay, I must admit it's a bit too easy due to the lacking AI, but especially at the beginning, when you haven't unlocked most of the advanced weapons/skills, it can offer enough of a challenge in order to get the stealth XP bonus.
As mentioned before, I suggest you play it only in survivor mode, otherwise thanks to the owl bomb dropping ability, it becomes way too easy.
The melee combat is probably the weakest point. It works, they kept it very simple and could have used some more depth, but after all, despite being sure that it's not the real reason why they left it as it is (meaning they didn't want / didn't have the resources to make it better), it still makes sense for cavemen to swing without giving any further thoughts to things like parrying or dodging. It pretty much sums up to hitting first and hitting hard before the opponent can retaliate. Even better when you can avoid being spotted in the first place, although it's not always possible of course.
Most of the times you can use take downs/throw shards/spears/use the bow to kill from range with stealth, so the melee combat is not really a big issue (also keep in mind that not all take downs require stealth to perform, for example you can use "death from above" to jump on top of your enemy aware of your presence, it will still work if performed correctly and it's quite satisfying).
My only regret is that I couldn't play with permanent death enabled due to the insane amount of crashing I have been getting and that I still haven't managed to figure out why they happen. I am quite sure the ubisoft launcher is to blame and it's the main reason I have always stayed clear from any ubisoft game.
I got it this time because I fell in love with the setting and I found it on sale at 50%.
I still reccommend the game, but I prefer to mention the crashing, because it definitely took out a lot from my enjoyment of the game (especially since at least in survivor mode, the game saves by checkpoints, however if you crash in the middle of a mission, it will reset at the begginning of the first checkpoint)

This is my third and last Telltale game series.  The story and affect of your choices is the only saving grace to this type of game.
Story:
This game had huge promise, but it let me down bigly.  The first two episodes were very slow.  However, episode three and four grabbed my attention.  I was tired of licking boots and I was craving me some revenge.  There was no question in my mind that episode 5 and 6 would bring satisfaction.  However, I got no satisfaction at all.  I did not get to kill the big boss bad guy that crushed my family.  I did not sit on any thrones.  Most of the characters I played died horribly and there was no resolution to the question of whether the family should survive.
Choices:
Do your choices make a significant difference?  I haven't done extensive testing, but a quick internet search indicates that you are rail-roaded heavily.  I think the only choice of real significance is which male sibling survives to complete episode 5.
Gameplay:
Abismal, as with all Telltale games.  I felt rushed on 90% of the dialog with this game.  Eventually I realized I could pause long enough to think about the choices offered.  Lack of key mapping is a non-starter with me.  I'm not going to try and describe the action sequences, but lets just say they rely on you ability to push the indicated key quickly.

-Unlike other Telltale games, Telltale's GoT offering lacks true direction in terms of choice making. Braid is an incredibly hyped game, and one of the few that I think really deserves it. This game was revolutionary in its time.
Braid is a basic puzzle/platformer with an interesting philosophy: instead of punishing players for making mistakes, reward them for the lessons they learn. You get a variety of time-based powers, the most basic of which is to reverse time, allowing you to undo any bad move. But, this concept is explored very creatively. In one world, time is reversed by moving left and moves forward when you move right. In another, you can slow time down, but only for certain parts of the screen.
Some of the puzzles are very hard. I remember using a walkthrough for one or two of them.
Braid's story is an interesting metaphor that is delivered very well. It starts with a Mario-esque story, but the metaphor's depth is revealed by the end. The art and music are lovely.
Absolutely worth it for $10.

:: Summary
This was a very short playthrough (2hrs?). It does not substantially add to the Alan Wake story imo, but might be worth your time if you pick it up inexpensively. Note - this game features a "loop" mechanic, meaning you're gonna go through the main 3 sections a total of 3 times, with the subsquent runs being far shorter than the initial seequence.
-
I'd thought American Nightmare was a follow-up that would provide a solid wrap to the somewhat ambiguous ending in Alan Wake. Ultimately while the game does provide something like closure, American Nightmare feels quite divorced from the main Alan Wake title, to the point where this would have been an interesting indie project on its own. As is, it doesn't bring a lot of meat to the table, and feels pretty inessential - you don't have to play this to have appreciated Alan Wake on its own.
Comparisons below will be in contrast to the main Alan Wake title, since if you're playing this, you probably played the other one already.
:: Graphics
Textures are crisper in American Nightmare, colors a bit more vibrant (where they exist), and this game is prettier overall. Easy to run on an nVidia 1070.
:: Sound
Much like Alan Wake, American Nightmare's sound is unoffensive and has slight balance issues (softer gameplay, louder cutscenes). No special or noteworthy elements here, though I was starting to really dig one track in particular (tied to the "oil well" scene in the first act).
:: Gameplay
Shooting feels improved, flashlight recharge times are much faster than in Alan Wake (to the point where battery items are largely not needed), weapons options are increased with special options being found through weapon crates (unlocked after reaching certain collection goals). There are no multiple flashlight types in this game, and ammo types have become more universal (a Small Arms type, a Long Arms type, flares, and flashbangs). Special depots exist that can reload all your ammo in one button press instead of having to dive into a container of Revolver Ammo five or six times in a row.
The maps in American Nightmare are much more open and exploration-friendly than in Alan Wake. Each of the three major zones feels more like an open-world type game, particularly contrasted against Alan Wake's very dark and very linear forest corridors.
As a game, American Nightmare feels looser and plays faster than Alan Wake. This game also has an arcade mode, which makes sense given how differently the play feels. This title hangs a lot less on its story progression and has focused more on the execution of its action.
:: Story
...and that's where the cost is paid. Action was pretty great in American Nightmare but the story just sort of hangs on the skeleton, so to speak. While in Alan Wake the characters are very grounded in the events of the tale, the Alan you play in American Nightmare makes wry comments, talks to himself a bit with no one around, and occasionally drops lines "for the audience" (a la Uncharted, say).
Ultimately you realize you're caught in a looping series of events where you need to change things up just enough so that you can break the cycle. I thought it was kind of cute, as side-characters start recognizing what's going on and take pre-emptive steps to make your life simpler.
In the end the whole story only takes 2-3 hours total to wrap, and I found the whole work interesting enough for what it was, though I wouldn't advise spending serious money. If you can pick this up cheap or free, go for it, but this is a sub-$10 add on at best.

1Heart brings the heebie-jeebies in its fantastic art style and use of color and sound. From the moment the game loads the first odd cut scene, you know you are in for something weird, twisted, and probably not going to make alot of sense. That doesn't stop this title from packing everything you love about the genre into the game though. You have items that can be combined, puzzles, finding hidden objects, and feeling plenty lost 90% of the time. Veterans of the genre may enjoy the challenge that 1Heart offers, being a game that is very stingy with its hint system for better or worse. Those like me, who have some experience but only play on occasion may want to keep a handy guide on stand by as it is very easy to feel lost and confused as to what to do next. Despite this though, the puzzles are enjoyable, the game sticks to its theme unabashedly, and the voice acting guides the story, even if I found it slightly cheesy at times. In all 1Heart is a strange and twisted tale, it requires patience, luck, and most of all, lots of clicking. The game is well designed and looks fantastic. Just be aware of the nature of the beast. This isn't a game to hold your hand, simply put.

Weighed down by a narrative that lacks internal consistency, raises far more question than answers, and largely ignores plot threads brought up earlier, 1Heart struggles and fails to connect the dots in any way that would satisfy most players.
It does do a good job of establishing mood in some of its disjointed set pieces, and there are certainly times that hit exactly the right chord for horror, but it would be a stretch to say that any more than half of the puzzles in this game are actually fun to solve. Many times the game lacks internal consistency, letting you use a tool for one purpose in one region and then not in the same way in another, turning much of the game into a guess and check that I certainly didn't find enjoyable. The worst puzzles (without spoiling anything) count less on the player thinking their way through and instead rely on motor skills in ways that can only lead to annoyance for most, and perhaps bragging rights to few.
Unless you're desperate for a horror-themed adventure game, I'd say pass.

Trying to describe Black Desert Online is like trying to fight a Hydra. Every time a head gets cut off, more spawn in it's place. The best I can do is strike at the heart, and hope to convey the whole accurately.
===========
INTRODUCTION:
----------------
BDO is a new generation of MMORPG, there are obvious knock-off's from other games like TERA and Archeage, some new ideas that could be executed better, and a sprinkling of outdated/broken mechanics, but overall it's an improvement for the genre. While the Steam version of this game is primarily North American, progress updates come from the Korean version, which has the dedicated development team, KAKAO.
You'd better get used to hearing the name KAKAO, because it's often spoken with the same loathing as a hated politician. Whether it's because of the increasing trend of "Pay for Convenience", the disgusting optimisation resulting in minimal FPS in high pop zones or the disconnecting/always in maintenence servers that run little better than an EZ Bake oven, you'll have plenty of reason to join in using one of their many nicknames.
Sadly, the community isn't that much better, there's plenty of nice people to find, but you'll often come across people who are just there to wreck your day. Trying to use your double exp to grind? I'll kill you and take your grinding spot. Riding a horse between two major cities? I'll landmine the road for you. And frankly, listening to the public chat channels (between the guild recruitment/pearl trading spam) is like a milder version of 4Ch@n, complete with Trolls and Edgelords.
========
GAMEPLAY:
------------
The first thing you'll notice when you log into BDO is that they went in the opposite direction to simplifying the HUD, and decided to put EVERYTHING they could fit on the screen. This includes current transactions of the highly price-controlled player market, the war status of various Guilds you'll likely not care about for another couple months until you're looking to start Node Wars (GvG PvP), and many other varyingly unhelpful pop-ups.
Quests don't work the same as other MMOs, instead of rewarding overall level experience, you gain exp for "Contribution Points", which aside from having a dubious acronym, is vital for assembling an npc empire to produce various forms of passive income. I'm not going to describe how it all works here, you'll need a Cert III in Warehousing & Logisitics to understand it.
Thankfully, there's a plethora of incredibly bored people (like me right now...) who spend their time making guides and charts and tables, conduct business meetings and discuss guild politics, economics and ergonomics, so trying to find something to explain the constant confusion that comes from playing Black Desert Online, isn't very hard, just time-consuming like everything else in this game.
========
OBJECTIVE:
------------
If you're hoping for fun and excitement, it's a while off. The endgame primarily involves the typical forms of PvP and GvG, and anyone below Gearscore 400 (Attack Power + Defense Power = Gearscore, ignore Awakened Attack Power) is gunna have a bad time. The gear you'll need to reach 400 is both expensive and difficult to get off the (seriously in need of revision) player market and the only way you're going to afford that kind of scratch, is through lifeskilling.
Lifeskilling is for want of a better phrase, getting paid to afk while doing something. These things typically involve: Processing Wood/Ore, Auto Fishing, Crating, Horse Training, Cooking, Alchemy, and the Farming mechanics from Archeage. Like Archeage, all of these things revolve around using and regenerating energy, you chop trees for wood till you run out of energy, switch to an alt character, use their energy doing the same and when you run out of alts, regenerate your energy while you afk process the wood into refined forms for profit.
Black Desert Online has an in-depth mechanic where collecting knowledge adds to the maximum pool of energy. While this can be used to make huge gains, the average energy pool of a lvl 56 player, is usually around 120. (You start with 10) While it is entirely possible to flick through the encyclopedia of knowledge you've obtained while grinding/questing/lifeskilling, you'll find that many of the groups you've discovered are usually only missing one or two entries. This is where backtracking becomes painful, as you google every tiny detail you've missed, and where to find that stupid rock crab you failed to find the first time.
With some effort, a lvl 56 player can reach approx 200 max energy by the time they enter the Mediah region, but this requires a lot of googling names and locations, and a lot of harassing that ONE STUPID WATCHTOWER THAT WON'T PROC! Knowledge is controlled by RNG, you roll the dice to get the knowledge, and you roll again to see what grade of knowledge you get, with higher grades providing basic benefits that severely undercut the effort to get them. The primary benefit is that if you get 200 max energy on your main character, all of your alts will have it too (At the time of writing, I have 367 max energy).
=====
WHY?!:
-------
Black Desert Online is like a many-headed Hydra. While some heads are just plain greedy, hostile or sociopathic, there are others that are articulate, inventive and addictive. Having just finished collecting all the materials I needed for an Epheria Sail I started in July (the largest singleplayer boat in the game), I can say that while the days I spent collecting wood or refining steel ingots were tedious and bored the s**t out of me, I feel an unmistakable sense of achievement as it nears completion.
While I utterly hate the enhancing system of the game for taking all my money and breaking my gear all the time, having managed to crawl over the 400 GS mark makes a considerable difference to not only my PvE survivability, but also to my random experiences in PvP (which have a habit of finding me more often than I go looking).
In this game there's a tangible sense of progression. When you start out, you manage to scrape together a couple mil and use it to buy yourself a half-dead plough horse that struggles to race butterflies, but as you advance and you gain more and more disposable income, you start joining the other people sitting on the marketplace, waiting to snipe various items and gear. Eventually you make enough money and get lucky with a sale, and you manage to buy or breed yourself a new horse just like one of those you've seen flash by like a jet only a couple hundred times.
BDO is a new generation of MMORPG in the sense that instead of locking you into a linear lvling and gearing progression, it leaves you alone to figure out a lot of things for yourself. This is a double-edged sword as for clueless twits like me, it's difficult to get started and understanding the various elements of the game are daunting at the best of times, but this also gives you a feeling of freedom that few other MMORPGs of the age have struggled to create.
My 367 energy cap is all on me. There is nothing in BDO that tells me I need to do it, I do it because I want to. It's annoying and sometimes difficult (like when you have to talk to a broken-Amity NPC to get the knowledge pieces), but the feeling I get when I spend RL DAYS chopping wood with my obscene energy cap, is worth the time I spend hunting around filling in the gaps of my encyclopedia (you literally have one).
==========
THE VERDICT:
---------------
If you've read this far into my essay, you've probably already formed your own opinion of whether or not this is your sort of thing regardless of whether I reccommend it or not. If you want to spend hours grinding exp and doing heaps of google searches to increment numbers that give you a smug sense of satisfaction, then welcome to Black Desert Online.

Fun.  Fierce.  Frustrating.  And like any other addict, you'll be coming back for more, even after getting schwacked by bad luck or poor design.
Luck is a big part of the game.  The exact same random event done 10 times can have 10 different consequences.  Maybe the guy you beamed down finds a lost person to join your crew.  Maybe he finds a weapon.  Maybe he gets eaten and dies.  Luck.  How much scrap, what events you find, and everything else will be random.  It's the nature of the beast.
But what isn't luck is making sure you don't overstretch your resources.  Can you give up 15 missiles in hopes of a better reward for helping someone?  If you're at 50 because you aren't using any, sure.  If you have 18 and have 2 missle guns...no.  Save for that cloaking device.  Don't bother with the clone-bay...or maybe you should.
Experiment.  You have to have a gameplan of how to run the ship, which you'll figure out after several awful runs.  There are many that work...but more that don't.  Find what works for you.  But keep your thumb on the spacebar and turn off numbered choice settings to save frustration.  You don't have to react fast, just pause the game and do what you need to.
This is easily one of the best games I've played in a while.  It doesn't rely on graphics to do it, just a little wit and plenty of gameplay choices.  Name your crew after characters from Star Trek, South Park, or whatever gives you a quick laugh.  As frustrating as it can be, remember that it's a game. You're not meant to win, you're meant to play.  Have fun.  That's pretty easy to do in this one.

I'll recomend this game but only just barely.     It's a good Diablo clone but not a great one. Vendors almost always only ever have trash after you hit level 10, just like other diablo clones.
Skill choices/talent trees are ok, they have their own slight spin on them of course, Nothing hugely divergent, I did enjoy the side quest for a specfic skill set you get from unlocking shrines around the world.
There's multi-classing but I never used it myself, seemed pretty pointless for a game that rewards that you for specialzing your character by it's stats/equipment.  And the classes they do give you aren't terribly inspring, but that's probably my own personal taste, but at least they could have given them a better intro than a few pictures, and not picking one until you're already generated seemed an odd choice.

Music is good, some songs will stay with you, but they're all rather depressingly atmospheric.
All in all, I think the main flaw is thal this is a game that takes itself too seriously, it needed to have more fun and less grim darkness of the whatever it was trying to be all the time. If you love the RTS genre and you haven't played coh2... you're living a shell of a life. I've never played another RTS on the level of COH2. When the game first released in 2013, it was... okay. A promising start, but lacking in the polish and balance that it's predecessor had championed. But this game is a shining example of what can happen when a developer is truly committed to their work. Over the last few years, this has gone from a somewhat disappointing sequel, to a true masterpiece of a game. I'm still discovering new strategies and subtleties in my favorite maps after hundreds of hours of play.
And don't get put off by the DLC. You don't need it (although you might find yourself buying it just to support such a dedicated developer, as I have opted to do from time to time).
I could wax on about how many amazing maps there are, or how delightfully varied each faction is, but I'd still fail to capture just how much depth there is to this game and the franchise as a whole.
Simply put, if you haven't bought COH2, Steam is presenting you with an opportunity to correct a life failing. Click buy. You won't regret it.
(and no, I don't work for Relic. I just really love this game).

Theoretically, I should hate this game. The voice acting is terrible, I've fallen off of the map in one level, the economic element is tacked on, and the gameplay is repetitive. So why do I love this game?
With a little suspension of disbelief, it's really easy to become immersed in this. The universe is consistent, and makes sense on a grand scale. Even the terrible voice acting doesn't bring me out of it, because the lines were well written and the actors always nailed the timing, if not the emotion.
My favourite feature was the fact that I could drop all my cargo before a battle to improve how well I manoeuvre, then collect all my cargo at the end. Just once, I would have liked to face a powerful thief that would have picked up my cargo and gotten away successfully without destroying me to really hit home that possible tactic in this world, but it never happened. (I bet I probably could have done it to NPCs though.)
I also liked how well everything was tied together. Between the gameplay, movie sequences, and menu navigation, it was easy to see how big I was compared to my ship, how big the ship is compared to the satelite, and what radio communication looks like both inside and outside of gameplay. Most games never come close to achieving this level of cohesion and interconnectivity.
Overall, I liked it. As a game, it was okay at best, but as a new world to visit and experience, it is one of the best.

This game is great, and deserves your attention.
(the big one, TL;DR at the end of this section.)
This is a top-down, "twin-stick" style game.  Of course, being on PC you can play with mouse and keyboard OR a twin-stick controller like a 360 pad.  It's a rogue'lite'.. meaning, in this case, permadeath and procedurally generated floors.  Similar to games like Isaac, the rooms are hand-crafted but placed in randomized configurations, with randomized enemies, pickups, loot, etc.
You will be exploring labyrinths of rooms, finding powerups to make you stronger, gaining experience by killing enemies, fighting minibosses, and looking for secret rooms.  Each floor has a final boss that you typically must defeat before proceeding to the next floor.
I don't know how many room designs were made for this game, but it seems like a lot.  Some are small and square, some are very large, long, or wide.  Some have an optional obstacle course of sorts, with prizes for those skilled enough to attempt them.  The design of the room can really change how you'll fight the enemies within.  Some large enemy that was easy to fight in a big, wide-open room may be much harder if you find him in a room that is divided into narrower corridors, or full of environmental hazards.
You, and most of your enemies, fire bullets, beams, and other ranged attacks, and the game can be a little bullet-hellish, especially on some of the bosses that I've seen so far, who shoot in very bullet-hell-like patterns. This is what I like most about Starward Rogue.. most enemies fire different types of shots, in different configurations, meaning each one is a unique challenge, especially the bosses and larger enemies.  I've also come across a few very unique and well-designed bosses that break the mold a little bit, and add even more variety.  The enemy variety is top-notch.
The weapons, consumables, and upgrades that you can get are full of variety, as well.  Aside from the fact that there are several different mechs, with unique starting configurations, that you can play as; as you play, you'll come across chests, shops, boss drops, and other ways of obtaining new and interesting weapons.  Some are objectively better than others, while some are just a matter of preference, playstyle, or the 'right tool for the right job.'
Your main weapons consist of a main gun with infinite ammo, a subweapon that uses a universal ammo simply called "energy", and a missile launcher.  The subweapons tend to have the more unique effects (such as the Guardian Blaster, that fires a shotgun of bullets that can destroy enemy fire, as well as harm enemies), though there is plenty of variety to the main guns as well.  Missiles can be used offensively, but are often best saved for destroying obstacles that cannot otherwise be destroyed.
You can also carry one of many consumables, which each have their own effect that can be used once, and then the item is gone.  There is one slot for passive 'defensive' items.. and you can also find or purchase different robot buddies that will circle around you and do stuff.  On top of all of that, you can find all kinds of upgrade items, and collect as many of those as you like.
And that leads me to another strong plus for me. The game is not cryptic about what items do.  You can walk over something to see what it does before you pick it up, and the descriptions are usually pretty clear and straightforward.  It doesn't try to screw you over, force you to trial-and-error, or make you check a wiki to know what you're getting.
I almost forgot perks!  Basically, you gain experience, level up, and pick from one of 3 perks, similar to something like Nuclear Throne.  Simple, but another layer of complexity that may make you play your run differently, or give you more options when combating foes.
TL;DR: There are lots of weapons, enemies, items, room layouts, and just lots of variety in general.  Plays like a twin-stick shooter.  Procedurally generated floors comprised of hand-made rooms, similar to Isaac, with a bit of Geometry Wars and Nuclear Throne thrown in.
You can see them for yourself by watching the trailers, or looking at the screenshots.  There are some really cool-looking enemies, and each floor has it's own theme to the floors and walls.  The lasers and bullets are shiny and pretty.  You can see what you're doing, tell things apart, etc.  Overall, pretty good graphics, unless you just hate 2D games or something, for some reason.
Here's the thing about sound effects.. when they're good, you hardly notice them.  When they're bad, you notice.  I haven't really noticed anything bad, so they must be pretty good.  Nothing has really seemed out of place or ugly, to me.  There's a nice little sound effect to let you know when you've cleared a room.  The guns go tatatatatat and pew pew and fwooosh, and the explosions go boom..  What more do you want?
The music is okay, but it's not really my thing.  After a while, I turned it down a bit and found it more pleasant to have it faintly in the background  Other people will probably love the music, it's just not really what I like.
I have played using a 360 pad, and my mouse and keyboard.  Both work good.  I may slightly prefer mouse and keyboard, but the option of using a controller is nice if I want to sit back a bit and relax, or hook up to my TV and play from the bed or sofa.  Everything is rebindable, and the bindings make sense as-is.  I like that with my 360 controller, I can shoot at any angle with the right analog stick, or at 8 compass directions by holding the face buttons (individually, or two at a time for diagonals)
All aspects of the sound can be adjusted individually in the options menu.. and there are plenty of options for graphics and performance, too.  Fullscreen/window, resolution, refresh rate, scale.. even brightness, contrast, and sharpness! Nice!  And there are toggles to turn off shadows, reflections and such for people with slower computers.  Very good job on options.
I like this game, if you couldn't tell (duh).  It emulates the Isaac formula a bit, but definitely has its own thing going as well.  The game seems stable and I haven't noticed any bugs (except one time when the game seemed to hang on a black screen when I tried to start a run.  No biggie, at least it didn't ruin a run in progress.)  Nothing seems lazy or half♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and I'm struggling to think of any real 'cons' besides not personally caring much for the music, as mentioned.
Like most indie games, it's inexpensive and this is certainly well-worth the price.  And you really have to hand it to Arcen Games for always trying new things, and finding ways to bring twists to old ideas.  Even if their games aren't always the most popular, they have a few hits, and this is totally one of them.  So try Starward Rogue, and tell your friends about it if you like it.  At the time of writing, it's a hidden gem, but I hope to see more people discover it and play it.

A surpringly solid twin-stick shooter which takes inspiration from the best of the genre but doesn't just blindly follow in their footsteps.
Despite being pretty skeptical about Arcen pulling it off, I've conclued very fast that, fortunately, it is a pretty fun game! You can choose from 6 mechs who have different stats and some of which also start with some weapons or special skills that makes them unique. One of the mechs literally turns the game into SUPERHOT. For the uninitiated, SUPERHOT is a FPS where time flows only when you move so it basically turns from frantic battle for survival into a very chill experience.
Each mech has 4 slots, primary weapon with infinite ammo, secondary energy weapon with limited usage that refills upon entering a new room, limited ammo weapon like a rocket launcher that functions like bombs in Binding of Isaac for breaking stuff/killing enemies in emergency and lastly a consumable slot. Apart from that you can find drops that just upgrade or modify your mech without being restricted to slot.
The game starts you off at 5 floors in total, each floor is very Isaac-like with shops, miniboss rooms, secret rooms and floor boss. You also gain experience, upon leveling up you can choose a perk like becoming the Keymaster and getting 100 keys, seeing the non-special and later special rooms automatically on map or learning you gottagofast. Yes, game actually has sprint button for traversing long distances AND for use in boss fights. Some of them like the Hunter miniboss will actively chase you at higher-than-normal speed so you gotta put those mech legs to work.
The enemies use bullet hell patterns but on normal they are mostly avoidable even for someone like me who doesn't play typical bullet hell games like the Touhou series. That is, at least not until you increase the difficulty and/or get to the later floors. The difficulties alter enemy and boss patterns, among other things, which is really cool way to do difficulty tiers in general.
Overall, the game has pretty rad soundtrack even if it can get a bit repetitive during a longer session and solid gameplay with plenty to do on each floor and bosses that don't feel like copypasta of each other.
It's a good choice of a time-waster whether you've already played all the usual suspects or just getting into the genre. Highly recommended!
