Oh how I would love for Steam to have a Maybe option as well as Yes and No, because this game is a complete Maybe. I bought DarkStar One when it came out years ago. I was hoping it would be the next Freelancer, and it tried, but it didn't try hard enough.
DarkStar One has a lot of good points, but the biggest negative is the repetitiveness. Now if you've never played the game and have read some reviews here, you may think, "A lot of people talk about repetition, but just how bad could it be?" Bad. Really, really bad. It would be one thing if there were just a few mission TYPES that you had to do over and over, but you effectively do THE SAME MISSION over and over. I remember one in particular where you have to eavesdrop on a conversation (I think some crime lords are having a meeting or something). You always went to the EXACT same station type, parked in the EXACT same spot to do the eavesdropping, and then the people would have the EXACT same conversation, and at the EXACT same point in said conversation they would notice your presence. Then the EXACT same three ships would launch from the station and attack you. It got to the point where as soon as I was discovered I would fly over in front of the landing bay for the station and pick off the ships as they came out. It was an absolute slaughter. Good for me in terms of reward, but bad in terms of mind-numbing gameplay.
The mechanics of the game are fine, and it would be a lot of fun if there were more variation. If you ever played the first Assassin's Creed and got tired of the same thing over and over, this game is worse, and I would advise that you don't get it. If, on the other hand, you don't mind that sort of thing, then I say get this game. So yeah, it's a big Maybe.

What can I say. Thought this would be great since the first shots appeared, and lo and behold, it is. I give my game-assessment skills 10/10.
The real success of Overcooked is in building a game where the focus is not on individual mastery, but on social cooperation. That's of course the nature of co-op games in general to varying degrees, but in most co-op games you're probably going to do a whole lot better if a couple of players "get better" - they can kill more monsters or whatever, and carry the team to victory. And there's nothing wrong with that, lots of great games work like that. But it's lovely to play a game where the solution is almost never
, rather it's
.
Overcooked gives you tasks that always break down into very simple steps. Let's say you have to make a hamburger. The order queue will tell you it needs a meat pattie, lettuce and a bun (everything also needs to be on a plate). There are only two buttons: pick up/put down, and chop/wash. So a "burger" task is "made of" these smaller tasks:
-Pick up lettuce and put it on a chopping board.
-Chop lettuce.
-Pick up steak and put it on a chopping board.
-"Chop" (mince) steak.
-Put the steak on a frypan until it's cooked.
-Find a plate - if none are clean and available, pick up a dirty plate, wash it and put it down somewhere.
-Pick up a bun and put it on the plate.
-Pick up the lettuce and put it on the plate.
-Pick up the cooked meat and put it on the plate.
-Pick up the plate and take it to the conveyor belt.
These tasks can be done one by one all by one person making a whole burger, or as you will soon learn is important, parallelised so someone grabs fresh ingredients, someone does all the chopping, someone cooks (and doesn't burn things) etc. Organisation and communication are the words of the day.
Well, organisation and communication and
. Because while you will likely start out each level by deciding on roles and forming a sensible-sounding plan, whether that lasts is another matter entirely. Three burgers in, someone will realise they have nowhere to put the next one because nobody is washing plates. The cook is closest to the sink and rushes to get a plate washed, but in that time two frypans catch fire. The burger is tossed on the ground so someone can pick up a fire extinguisher, and subsequently falls onto the road and is lost forever because
the kitchen is actually a series of trucks driving down the highway. No burger, flaming ingredients, angry customers, no tip, a couch-ful of players falling around laughing, yelling at each other to GET THE BLOODY PLATES WASHED NEXT TIME, OH MY GOD!
Look, there are a couple of levels that are unfortunate difficulty spikes (my tip: sometimes a level will be easier if you play with one less player, due to some oddly scaling pass criteria), and the game technically can be played singleplayer but please don't do it. But that's really all I've got for criticisms. This is masterful co-op design; if you have a couple of friends and a night off it's worth every penny.

Braid is an incredibly hyped game, and one of the few that I think really deserves it. This game was revolutionary in its time.
Braid is a basic puzzle/platformer with an interesting philosophy: instead of punishing players for making mistakes, reward them for the lessons they learn. You get a variety of time-based powers, the most basic of which is to reverse time, allowing you to undo any bad move. But, this concept is explored very creatively. In one world, time is reversed by moving left and moves forward when you move right. In another, you can slow time down, but only for certain parts of the screen.
Some of the puzzles are very hard. I remember using a walkthrough for one or two of them.
Braid's story is an interesting metaphor that is delivered very well. It starts with a Mario-esque story, but the metaphor's depth is revealed by the end. The art and music are lovely.
Absolutely worth it for $10.

This is the first game I will not recommend.
This game has great graphics, sound design, and atmosphere. The story is intriguing and I was fairly satisfied with the ending (though it could have been better). I WANT to like this game, but I can't.
I love point and clicks, they have always been my favourite kind of game so I was rather excited to play this game. Boy, was I disapointed in its excecution.
The biggest issue is just that some of the puzzles are too convoluted or complicated in places, almost to the point of not making sense. Several puzzles I forced, but most I just had to look up a walkthrough. This usually isn't too big a deal for me, but it's highly agravated by some very minor things, for instance there is no indicator that you can pick up ANY of the objects you can pick up. This becomes a problem when those objects blend in with the environment or just look like nothing important. Another annoying thing is that items must be used in a very specific way: ex. you need frog's blood, you get an axe, you try to kill the frog using the axe, "what was I thinking?!", goes on merry way, later in the game gets butcher knife, that knife magically works on the frog! It's so bad, it's to the point where you will do something that seems logical and it fails, why? Because you need to do this task in a very specific way with a specific item. The other big thing hindering gameplay in the lack of hints. There are a total of 5 hints in the game, so far as I can tell, after that you get nothing. I had used all of the hints within the first 10 minutes of the game which was part of the reason I had to look up a walkthrough. The number of hints given just isn't enough considering the difficulty of the puzzles, if the hints would regenerate over time the game wouldn't be so frustrating.
Another critism I have is that you need to do actions multiple times in order to complete a task that could just be done all at once. It's a minor thing, but it's annoying to get 2 batteries (which look like one item in the inventory) and have to load them into the radio one at a time, just cut the crap, if you use an item to do something you should only have to use it once to get the job done.
Another small thing, is that there are a lot of grammatical errors in the descriptions (and I think at least one typo in a cutscene). This is such an easy thing to remedy while making a game; if you don't speak English and you make a game, just put out an advertisement saying you want someone to proofread your script, there are lots of people in the community, myself included, who would be willing to proofread your game FOR FREE. It's such a small thing but it does hurt the quality of your game.
All in all, these flaws amount to something that seriously hurts the game, like I said I want to like this game, and it was enjoyable and very atmospheric for the first 5-10 minutes, but by the end I was so frustrated it distracted me from any atmosphere there was. I repeat: I was actually creeped out at the beginning of the game and by the end I did not care, I just wanted to finish the game.
If really difficult puzzles are your thing you'll like it, if not it's not really worth your time.

Terrible narration, terrible translation (which the narrator ridiculously follows to a T, errors and all), and frustrating puzzles. I quit near the end during this maze puzzle, which requires you to navigate (with the mouse) long, thin twisting corridors without touching the sides. Ultimately, it just wasn't worth the frustration.

To begin with, I have never read any of the books nor watched the television show that inspired this game. I suspect that a fan of the television show would view this game quite a bit more favorably.
The biggest problem with the game is that none of your decisions really matter, even though the game constantly presents you with the illusion of choice. This becomes especially apparent in the final two chapters of the six chapter "series" as any hope of a satisfying conclusion to the story is stabbed, shot through with arrows, mutilated, and burned (not necessarily in that order).
This is also the least interactive Telltale game I've played. Your inventory is pointless, QTE events are simple and predictable (I never died during the course of the 10-hour playthrough), and the few opportunities to control the movements of your characters are perfunctory. You might as well just watch the television show.
All of that being said, there are some bright spots in the game. The character models are expressive and the art design is attractive. The voice acting is excellent. The game cuts rapidly between different characters in different locations ensuring that you never get too bored with any one scenario.
There are moments of genuine tension, too. A climactic showdown near the end of Episode 4 is a standout.
Ultimately, I would not recommend this game to anyone is isn't already totally sold on the Game of Thrones franchise.

Fun.  Fierce.  Frustrating.  And like any other addict, you'll be coming back for more, even after getting schwacked by bad luck or poor design.
Luck is a big part of the game.  The exact same random event done 10 times can have 10 different consequences.  Maybe the guy you beamed down finds a lost person to join your crew.  Maybe he finds a weapon.  Maybe he gets eaten and dies.  Luck.  How much scrap, what events you find, and everything else will be random.  It's the nature of the beast.
But what isn't luck is making sure you don't overstretch your resources.  Can you give up 15 missiles in hopes of a better reward for helping someone?  If you're at 50 because you aren't using any, sure.  If you have 18 and have 2 missle guns...no.  Save for that cloaking device.  Don't bother with the clone-bay...or maybe you should.
Experiment.  You have to have a gameplan of how to run the ship, which you'll figure out after several awful runs.  There are many that work...but more that don't.  Find what works for you.  But keep your thumb on the spacebar and turn off numbered choice settings to save frustration.  You don't have to react fast, just pause the game and do what you need to.
This is easily one of the best games I've played in a while.  It doesn't rely on graphics to do it, just a little wit and plenty of gameplay choices.  Name your crew after characters from Star Trek, South Park, or whatever gives you a quick laugh.  As frustrating as it can be, remember that it's a game. I've mentioned this before but I'm glad Arcen Games exists, even if I don't really enjoy most of their games. Every one of their titles tends to venture beyond the normal bounds of game design, mashing such disparate concepts as open worlds, puzzles, and zombies into a single title. Starward Rogue has earned the distinction of their most enjoyable game for me, perhaps because it doesn't go as far afield in design as the rest.
Starward Rogue places you in a head attached to a robot body stomping around the Megalith, a giant construct sticking out of a star. You get to pick one of seven wildly different bodies, from close-combat flame-spewers to a clever thing that freezes time when you're not moving. According to the tutorial you're here to rescue some AI dude, but that never really comes up during runs. Each of those runs is a top-down descent through five randomly-generated levels, featuring rooms of all shapes and sizes and enemy configurations and deadly traps. Armed with your gun, missiles, energy cannon, and whatever upgrades and single-use items you can find, you have to blast your way through tons of enemies, bosses, and minibosses to... win, I suppose. I've beaten it a few times and you just get a stat screen.
If this all sounds a lot like Binding of Isaac, that's because this is its manic sci-fi cousin. Your enemies are colorful drones and ships that will sling thousands of bullets at you in every arrangement imaginable. Much like the Touhou shmup games, bullets can curve, seek, chain, turn at right angles, form walls or fields or mazes, or perform even more dastardly maneuvers. That means you need to be prepared to do a lot of complex dodging and narrow escapes to survive a run. The health system is luckily quite generous, giving you a pool of health you can easily upgrade and also a shield or two (much harder to upgrade) that recharges for every room, essentially free hits. You also move quite fast and can freely sprint, which is a welcome addition and gives the game a much quicker pace than most.
Aside from the coins and keys you'll pick up, there are three classes of weapons, passive upgrades, and consumables to find. Weapons in particular tend to be few and far between but will completely change your style of play. Some guns fire through walls, some spread like flamethrowers, and some only work in melee range. Consumables can have similarly dramatic effects, like summoning temporary helpers and nuking everything in sight. You'll also level up and earn perks, but until level 10 or so those perks won't be very conspicuous, mostly being health or ammo upgrades. Oh, and there are permanent drone buddies you can find that provide some much-needed support, but can be easily confused with your foes.
And that brings me to my one real gripe with the game, the art style. Arcen tends to favor very bold, brash color schemes for their games, but too much variety in the palette can make important features hard to single out. Everything in Starward Rogue is brightly colored and detailed, but there's no real theme to the enemies, helpers, or even you. In huge battles everything can start to blend together, even moreso with thousands of glowing bullets flying around. The camera and the pace of your robot help keep it distinctive but I've started skipping the drone familiars because they almost always confuse me and get me killed.
The art style may be hit or miss, but the rest of the presentation is excellent. Arcen games often have somewhat shoddy menus and interfaces, but the ones here are clear and even a bit polished. All the information you need is readily available and easily navigable. There's also been an impressive amount of post-launch patches which have cleared out a lot of early bugs and jank, and rebalanced whole swathes of the game to provide a more even challenge. They even added in fast-travel around the level to make backtracking and exploring essentially painless.
What really keeps me coming back is just how plain ol' fun it is. The raw enjoyment of blasting hundreds of robots as you grow stronger and more unstoppable is in full force here. A pumping soundtrack helps keep you moving at breakneck speed as you look for the next boss to thrash. The difficulty is pretty even-handed as well, offering five different levels and ramping up steadily as you yourself grow stronger. With hundreds of enemies to encounter, tons of items to find, seven classes to master, and plenty of secrets to uncover, Starward Rogue is a worthy competitor in the arena of roguelike shooters.

I realize this isn't how reviews are normally done. I never claimed to be normal. I'm going to play through the game and post the various issues I've had here. Folks can decide if it's the kind of thing they'd expect in a game, or not.
Problem 0: [will never be resolved] flight physics. Sigh. Yet another "space" game that assumes space is a large bowl of clear mud, and that Newton was completely wrong. Freelancer got the right combination of proper space physics and simple controls. So far, I've not found another game whose developers actually understand anything about physics AND simplicity. Just for that, Darkstar One is going to have to be an awesome game to get a "recommended" from me.
Problem 1: [resolved, kind of]. Glad I got it for $2. Graphics are non-existent on my system. Cutscenes are the quality I'd expect, then I get an early 1980's mainframe VT100 "interface" during flight. Whether this is a bug, or by design, I don't know. And frankly, I don't care. If they sell a game with advertised gameplay graphics. that's what I expect.
RESOLUTION: reduce to lower screen resolution. Seems it can't handle the higher resolution, even if it claims it can.
Problem 2: [resolved] Tutorial says to select cargo container, but couldn't find it. Turns out text was a grey on darker grey background in an unexpected and unlabelled section of the target selection text list.  Grabbing and releasing container wasn't an issue, FINDING the damn thing was the issue. Future cargo containers should be easier to find. Things are always easier once you know how. Not very impressed with the organization of the target selection list.
Problem 3: [kludge found, not really resolved] crashes during combat. Often. Regularly. It's made the game almost unplayable at this point. Further analysis shows that it might be due to a combination dual-monitor setup and Darkstar not having a true "fullscreen" mode, but only a "borderless windowed" mode that they *call* "full screen". So the mouse goes off the edge of the screen when fighting, I click to fire, and it clicks on the desktop. Darkstar then crashes. Haven't found a way to force Darkstar to have true "full screen" mode where the mouse is restricted to the single screen. And yes, Darkstar crashes 90% of the time when I use Alt-Tab, and 100% of the time when I click on the desktop even when not in combat.
KLUDGE: use "WinKey"+P to cycle through display options. If your "main" monitor is (2), select "projector only". If your main monitor is (1), select "computer only". Then start the game. Pain in the a r s e, almost as bad as Steams Puritan-s h i t h e a d censoring system. Still looking for fix that tells Darkstar One to create a REAL "full screen", mouse-capturing option while leaving the other monitor alone.
Problem 4: [unresolved] Then there's what's almost become a trope in video games, the "let's screw the player over with a totally new interface that acts nothing like what they've been practicing with all this time, and make it a boss fight that you have to complete in order to continue the game". To be precise, the "flak" fight.  It's effectively a poorly done space-invaders mini-game, but written either by someone who really doesn't care about games, or someone who simply hates the people who buy their games. Either way, it has no place in Darkstar One. Just for that pile of steaming excrement, this game will never get anything other than "no recommended".  Opponents are pretty much invisible against the background until they get really close, the "radar" doesn't actually give accurate locations, nor does it give any idea of how far the opponents are. Unplayable, at least for me. I'm tired of wasting my time on this game.
Opinion: stay far, far away from this game, even if you get it for $2 it's not really worth it.

Darkstar One is like a mashup of sandbox space trading games and more quest / storyline driven games like "I-War 1" or "Freespace". It's a good job it does combine the two ideas together. Otherwise this game would not be quite so good.
The trading part of it is almost a complete rip of the original "X-Tension" - except MUCH lighter - you only have one ship to pilot (though that ship does evolve as the game progresses), there's hardly any weapons / equipment to spend your credits on, very few, and very repetitive, sandbox mode missions. In fact if this was the only aspect to the game, Darkstar One would be one of the most pathetic turkeys in history. Luckily this "X-Tension" part to the game plays only a support role to the main "quest" part of the game, enough to keep your ship equipped up to the challenge of the next sector's worth of quest missions. Which IS worth playing through. Again though, the spectre of "repetition" will haunt you throughout the entire game. Presentation wise the scenery is very nice for the time of it's release - but eye candy alone won't make a game a classic. This is not a classic. It's good, but not THAT good.
Your character Kayron Jarviss may as well be Guybrush Threepwood's wimpier brother. The taunts he uses against enemies are just laughable..... "I'm behind you (duckie)", "Oooh, nearly got you (schnookielumps)" etc..... seriously amusing!

Still, thanks to the continuous autosaves done at every available opportunity, you'll never find yourself loosing more than five minutes worth of effort!
It's 1000% worth the £1.19 that's it's currently on offer for the next few days, along two other titles! (After May 18th 2016 - you'll pay £6 for it by itself - not quite as good a deal)

This game was so awesome back in the day... and now it is again! It's incredible that a game this old (15 years! that's half my age!) has such a huge fan base now, all thanks to Steam. Servers are full and people are having loads of fun. To be honest, I didn't know QL even existed and I doubt that many people did. Who ever thought it would be a good idea to put this on Steam deserves a Nobel Prize.
QL stays very true to Q3A, in that the graphics are the same, the sounds are (mostly, except for the announcer) the same, and most importanly the speed, pace and feel of the game are the same. I just came back from my first two rounds of Free-for-All, and I'm pumped.
The one thing that immediately made me go "oh, ok... but wow!" was the fact that you get to pick your first two weapons now, instead of starting with the standard machine gun. They both come with a moderate amount of ammo, just to get you going again: it means you don't have to start hunting for a weapon before you set out to find your first victim. And that anyone who spawns near you is a real threat.
Another change is that all ammo packs now give you ammo for any weapon you are currently holding: if you're holding a Lightning Gun you get lightning ammo, if you're holding a Rocket Launcher you get rockets, etc. (although I'm not sure if this is also true for the BFG). It makes it easier to keep using you favourite weapons. Fortunately, the weapons are balanced enough (read: powered down) to make this fair. And if you still happen to run out of ammo, you can always use your trusty Gauntlet for a nice, humiliating melee kill.
There are other (but minor) gameplay changes as well, e.g.: you can see how much damage points you're dealing; powerups show their respawn time; there's a new green armour for 25 armour points.
One change I do not like but can accept is that there are no more "gibs" and gore (blood splatter) animations. It would have been nice to be able to turn these on, just to make it worth that extra rocket you fired at your opponent after he was already dead.
I was really cautious to install this "Free to Play" game, but thank god this one really is free to play in the normal sense of the word. You can, but absolutely genuinely positively do not have to pay any money what so ever. But you'll want to, just to support the developers and enable them to keep supporting this awesome retro-neo title.
Sadly, I have to end this review with a couple of notes to the developer:
1. A euro is not the same as a dollar
2. A dollar is not the same as a euro
3. ???
4. Profit!

is a 3D space craft action simulator. After learning information on a man responsible for your father's death, you inherit a ship called Darkstar One and set on a chase across the galaxy to uncover a plot against the Galactic Union.
: The game offers very intuitive controls that can easily be mastered by even the most novice to the genre, although difficulty might be light for a veteran. The galaxy is a large place with a huge amount of systems you gain access to as the story unfolds. Rather than changing ships, you upgrade the Darkstar One by uncovering mysterious alien artifacts hidden in asteroids or held by criminal gangs, allowing you to tailor your ship to your play style, be it hull strength & turrets, agility & firepower, or cargo & speed, but you still customize your weapons layout and special equipment to your needs.
: The story is the worst kind of unimaginative cliché that has its place in a kid's cartoon. The game is extremely repetitive, every system feels identical except for the color scheme, as you always jump in with a single trade station always located at the same distance from the jump gate, while enemy hideouts aren't even hidden by distance or debris fields and are often blatantly identified as "bandit hideout". But you're stuck tediously landing in each of them one by one, not by interest or desire to explore, but by necessity to find the very occasional side mission that unlocks some of the systems holding artifacts, as
aren't hidden at all and you'll know exactly where to find each of them. Graphics are awful by today's standard, textures are so low resolution that space backgrounds appear to be an overstretched 80x80 bitmap. The world itself is so bland you have no interest in doing trading or contracts as you quickly make more money then you can spend.

I'm really not sure what to say about this game. I got it as part of a bundle that had some other games I wanted in it. But it was an interesting experience playing it.
I have to say that it is a very unique form of puzzle game. You're given a 3D object in 3D space, and you attempt to tie it up with rope, and cover it in paint. A very simple game mechanic that can very quickly become complex. The levels themselves come in various complexities and styles.
Initially, I found managing the camera to be quite odd, but once I got the hang of it the game plays quite well.
The graphics in this game are not overy complex, but they do a fairly good job at detailing the materials of the the objects. The rope can get a bit glitchy at time, though.
This game has a calming "zen-like" soundtrack to go with your ropework. It fits very well.
I still don't think I fully understand the concept behind this game, but if you are into the whole "zen" and "calming" puzzle game experience, then this is definitely worth a buy.

One downside:
I'm not sure if it's by design but some maps was really difficult to do with 3 player co-op. I'm not sure if every level is fine tuned for any number of players (2,3,4). Some maps was "easy" to get 3 stars with 1-2 tries while the worst one so far required at least 10 attempts to even get 1 star. I think this is especially hard to balance when you have a level that is split in 2 and you have 3 players. Ideally you would want 1.5 person per side so you end up with work overload on one side where you have 1 person and waiting time on the side with 2 persons. This problem doesn't exist with 2 or 4 players as you always are evenly spread out.
We had a really good time and I can recommend this especially for co-op play!
That said, I would happily pay €10 for a multiplayer DLC. The number of times 4 player co-op will be possible is maybe 1-2 times per year for me, and that is if someone brings extra controllers. If my partner and I could just fire up a game with two friends joining in via the cyber webs we would not only have as fun as if they were at our place, but also we would actually play the game. The charm of this game is definately having 4 players working together and causing a mess. 2 player co-op will not be equally fun for us.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a story-driven Third-person shooter/adventure game. It employs an intersting narrative and intriguing, albeit minimalistic design.
THE GOOD
This game continues the story of the previous game, ALAN WAKE, which is rewarding as you are left with a bit of a cliffhanger from the last one (no spoilers here). The story here is intersting and keeps your attention. I love the Twilight Zone parallels here.
The combat is pretty solid and there are some exploratory elements here.
Combat arena challenge modes.
THE BAD
American Nightmare is, unfortunately, inferior to the original. It's shorter, plainer, and simply hollow when compared to the first game.
The gameplay is repetetive; this could be forgiven for the sake of telling a story, but the story here falls short of spectacular...it's interesting, but not thrilling as the last one was. And the primary element of Alan Wake is the story, and this one fell a bit flat.
Total Campaign runtime (for me) 3-4 hours.
CONCLUSION
This game is good for fans of the original, and I do recommend it as such. It's not going to be worth much to a casual player, however.
For those who do want to check out this game, $10 isn't really asking too much, but you're still better off grabbing it on sale.

Weapons are largely the same, with the addition of some alien tech and experimental weapons you get later in the game. Good times.
It's not a super-in-depth game, and if you just go from one mission to the next, you can solve the core game pretty quickly. But I like that because the developers didn't throw delaying stuff in simply to make it take longer to complete the main quest. And without cheats, it does take a little time to get good enough to solve all the missions at the Gold level.
So, I liked SR3 and that carried over to SR4 as well.

Honestly, I wanted to like this. The setup was there for a pretty intriguing game in the beginning. Two young sisters are left home alone by their parents and find a strange gift waiting at the front door. They take the gift inside to reveal two toys, which they then proceed to play with. They are suddenly attacked until one of the girls finds herself waking in a twisted world, forced to desperately search for her missing sister.
The atmosphere--particularly in the beginning--is very good. Strange, haunting landscapes. Great sound effects. Some pretty awesome artwork and interesting stylized cutscenes. But the glamor wears pretty thin, pretty fast.
The game is point-and-click, so it's to be expected that some of your goals may be obscure. You might have to do a bit of clicking and travelling around to get it. But there are also puzzles that really try your patience. Not so much challenging as simply time-consuming and frustrating (get ready to spend a hint--and you only get three--on navigating a complex maze with your mouse in total darkness and instant reset every time you touch the walls).
Nevermind the awful grammar (seriously, I understand that English is not the first language here, but if you're charging money, take the time to grammar-check. There are plenty of places online and offline that you can get your stuff checked for free). On that note, the narrative script is poorly written. Not just for the grammatical errors, but for its lack of consistency. One minute it's taking itself incredibly seriously, with a darkier-edgier tone. The next, it uses words that sound awkward and infantile in a tone that sounds like the narrator is intentionally hamming up his performance.
Of course, if a game is going to frustrate you with its mechanics, it should have a solid story to keep you engaged. This one falls woefully short. It meanders around with a barely coherent story and a rushed, tacked on preachy ending about the responsability of raising children or personal morality or ethics of something or other or whatever, Oh hey, look it's the end!

I got to the end asking myself : "what the hell went wrong ?!?!?!"
The demographic of my little GoT family was indeed not terrific. Must try again.

I enjoyed this game very much.  I tried 2 different classes but, I don't think I want to play MP or start another class.  Simply because for my tastes, there isn't enough depth in the build system and gear to make any memorable builds and that is what normally keeps me coming back again and again to games like this.
One of the biggest annoyances is the loot system which floods you with gear specific to classes you can't use and often gives you high-tier items that are significantly worse than the lower tier items.
I never really got any super rare items and nothing really build-expanding, however several times I got a really low-level weapon which came bound with a spell that I could add to my arsenal, and simply put, that one spell became so powerful (even though the element was not specific to my class!) that I ended up dragging the low-level item around with me to end-game because nothing comparable or better would ever seem to drop.  That's the kind of thing that makes you upset to be powerful.  It feels like the carrot of insanely awesome gear is always dangling in front of you but you never seem to get it.
All in all, I enjoyed the game very much and the scenery is breathtaking.  I did not enjoy having a billion crafting mats which never saw much meaningful use, and I don't like that the end part of the SP campaign requires a metric-ton of grinding if you want to complete it.  But as I've said in my above complaints the game doesn't really make me feel like playing more, the way a good AARPG loot gambling game should.
It is a thumbs-up, I just feel like the game is missing a lot of polish, as beautiful as it looks visually.  I mean polish in terms of the gameplay experience, the storytelling, the loot system, the spells, the combat, etc.
I give it a solid 7/10 game for a once-around play.

Darkstar One is basically a downgraded, linear version of the original Freelancer game. While, in it's own respect, it's a pretty decent game, don't expect any innovations. In Darkstar One, you play as a young, emerging escort pilot named Kayron, who's father has been recently deceased (probably been a few months to a year, doesn't say exactly). Eventually, Kayron learns the true nature of his father's demise and learns that a man named Jack Forrester was involved. Most of the game's story is gallavanting across the galaxy looking for this dude. In order to earn money to buy better stuff, you can perform contracts as a mercenary, become a bounty hunter and claim the rewards on pirates, become a pirate yourself and raid cargo ships for their goods, ship trade goods across sectors, or smuggle illegal contraband in a similar manner. Overall, it's an alright game. If you want a decent space sim style game to put some time into, pick this up on sale. If you're looking for a Star Citizen or X-series experience, look elsewhere.

I'm not usually the type who goes for pure puzzle games but this one looked interesting enough. And I have to say that this was one of the most relaxing gaming experiences I ever had. There's something meditative about wrapping all these wooden 3D models with rope to paint them. And while in theory the mechanic of painting these objects is fairly simple in execution it can lead to a few quite hard objects so it truly challenges your spatial visualization ability. Thankfully I have plenty of experience working with 3D modelling software so to me it's fairly straightforward how I have to use my mouse to rotate an object in the desired way, but I can imagine that for people who aren't used to this it can be quite challenging. It took me about 4 hours to play through the entire game and never did I feel bored with the experience. Yeah, there's no story to this it's simply gameplay that's presented with an excellent aesthetic - both visually and aurally - with high-resolution textures and very pleasing sound effects. 5 bucks for that, definitely worth it, though I probably need to mention that I bought it at a Humble Bundle for 20 cents, but still, it's worth the asking price if you buy it when it's not on sale somewhere.

This is a great game if you're like me - looking for a fairly simple sci-fi space sim.  It's very easy to jump right in as the tutorials do a good job of teaching the mechanics of the game.  It has a little bit of depth in terms of customizing your ship and whatnot but it is not overly complex.
This is not the game for people who are experienced players of the genre.  Anyone who has played many of this type of game will likely find this overly simplistic.  However, for the more casual player, it's a great deal of fun and is likely a good starting point for anyone wanting to get into the genre.  In terms of gameplay, it reminds me a bit of Freelancer (Digital Anvil/Microsoft - 2000).
The graphics and sound effects are quite good for 2006 (I don't know how the 2010 Xbox 360 version compares).  The flight mechanics, including fighting, exploration, docking, etc. are very smooth and easy to get used to.  I have read some reviews stating that it is repetitive and boring but again, that's probably from gamers who are looking for more complexity and depth that can be found in other games of the genre.
To sum up: DarkStar One is a great, entry-level space sim that is designed for simplicity and accessibility.  It is a lot of fun and very easy to pick up, even for someone unfamiliar with the genre.  It is not designed for seasoned veterans of the space sim genre and does not offer the depth of a game like Elite: Dangerous.  For anyone who wants a good stepping stone to get into the genre, this game is $10 well spent.

The bad part about it is that it makes mistakes that could've been (or even should have been) avoided. The main part: the intro. Yes, I get that it's going for a minimalistic approach. But a simple meter that displays which percentage you've 'covered' isn't too much to ask for, right? Or a visual feedback that you've completed the level.
Even more bothersome is that you have to actually exit the level to see which percentage you actually covered. Or whether you did reasonable, okay or great (not unimportant, as you need to know that for unlockable future things). There's no tutorial either. On one hand, it's not like this game is hard to wrap your head around, but nothing at all is just not enough.
And I'd love it if there were some options on the screen. It's like the only keyboard button to be used is 'escape' (which you'll need to press once you finished a level if you want to actually do anything but admire your wrapped present). I only accidentally stumbled upon the 'restart' option, and I think I'd rather have a rewind and forward button with it...though that may have been too hard to implement. Same for my wish to temporaly turn the object to glass and make anything but 20 cm of rope invisible...I'm sometimes just binding in the blind.
One thing that really shouldn't be that hard is an option to zoom in and out. For the same reasons already mentioned.
EDIT: just noticed that there's some sort of bug...there actually IS a percentage meter, as well as an indication of length. It's just not displayed on my monitor by default for some reason (I get it by alt-tabbing out of the game and then back in again...which for some reasons causes me not to be able to start a level :-\ ). Rather than deleting the above, I'll mention it. Perhaps my 1920x1080 resolution is to blame? :-\
Wow...seems like my last paragraph is quite a lot longer than my previous one. Don't let that fool you, though. I gave it a thumbs up for a reason: the game is certainly fun to play. And despite the mentioned quirks, you actually feel like you're in control of what you're doing. Which is something that isn't that common with 3D puzzlers...

Quake live is a relaunch of Quake 3, and that is not at all a horrible thing. In an era of braindead shooters, and boring movement through flat unistring levels, Quake scoffs your Modern military shooters and rocket jumps it’s way up a wall.
If “realism” is something you want in a game then Quake is not for you (why you want to portray “realism” in a game about killing people is another issue entirely). Quake is instead about creating interesting game dynamics. Physics and all sensibilities be damned, they’re secondary to good game play.
Quake has more than just a few things going for it. The movement is perhaps the most nuanced and complex in all of gaming, The weapons balanced and finetuned over a decade and a half of balancing, the level design is the best in any fps, and the community...well ok the community is mostly elitist jerks like any other internet game, but dammit they’re quake jerks, a special breed close to my heart, spouting out the truths of the PC faith (Always us optical mice, MX Cherry Reds forever, 120+ frames or I’m not even playing).
It’s free. Even if you have no interest in arena shooter I recommend you hop on in and get a quick history lesson with the granddaddy of FPS.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a nightmare indeed.  American citizenship not required.  Nor being Alan Wake.
Alan Wake was once a prolific writer now turned author of reality.  Trapped in a hostile realm he calls The Dark Place for almost two years.  Wake has escaped into the fictional town turned actual location of Night Springs, Arizona; the titular town of a low-budget psychological thriller TV series he once wrote for in his early days.  Having lost all contact with his former life; Wake has embarked on a quest to return to his world by using the powers that dwell in The Dark Place that respond to his creativity and rewrite reality.  American Nightmare centers on his hunt for his evil doppleganger, the elusive and powerful Mr.
.  Mr.
has taken Wake's identity in the real world, wreaking havoc with murders, maimings, and mind control, but is stuck keeping constant tabs on Wake to ensure he can't return.  Wake has brought with him a weapon; a manuscript that can change the world as he lives it, but the pages have been scattered and he'll have to track down Mr.
while collecting them to make use of their power.  Interesting as this all sounds, the story is short, uneventful, and save for Mr.
evil antics; lacks any level of emotional connection.
A third person shooter at its heart, American Nightmare pits Wake against a small variety of dark minions summoned by his quarry.  Most of his opponents make use of melee weapons, but a few break the mold by throwing bombs or bursting into a cloud of birds to reform behind Wake so they can make their attack.  The game arms players with a flashlight for burning away the dark shield that surrounds these Taken enemies, so that firearms (pistols, rifles, fully automatics, and shotguns) can be employed to finish them off.  Batteries drain when used, but the recharge is so fast that more often than not they will be fully charged by the time you finish shooting your target; completely negating any need for changing batteris in the majority of battles.  Flares can be used to buy Alan some space by warding back foes, and flashbangs strip away the darkness while knocking over or outright evaporating foes.  Flare guns are like mini rocket launchers, leaving a short-lived safety net in their wake.  Tapping the sprint key in the moment of a Taken's attack allows Alan to dodge out of the way.  His health is segemented, and while chunks recharge on their own; street lamps are used as temporary safe havens and healing stations.  Aside from the campaign, Amereican Nightmare also includes an arcade mode.  Wake is placed into an arena and must face waves of enemies with what tools he can find and last for ten minutes until the sun rises.  A slowly draining combo meter is built up for killing Taken to increase your score, but resets if Wake takes a hit.  Scattered throughout the campaign, players will find 53 pages of the manuscript.  These pages provide insight into the world and characters around, as well as events that will unfold, and changes that can be made to rewrite reality.  Also scattered throughout the campaign and arenas are weapon boxes that each have their own manuscript requirement before players can open them for use.  Radios provide further insight into the world outside Night Springs, and Mr.
sends sadistic messages to Wake through TV's that players can find.  On the whole, American Nightmare is far too easy.  The flashlight charges so fast, and the weapons are so powerful; that managing mobs is a breeze.  Especially with the use of flares and grenades.  The only true challenge is the Nightmare mode in the arena, but this difficulty feels a little forced.  Enemies have their health buffed by as much as 50%, and abandon attacking in increasing waves to simply spawn infinitely.  It feels cheap and unexciting.
Even here, Amereican Nightmare fails to impress.  Environments are bland and uniteresting.  Character model quality is low.  Outside of general combat, animations are very subpar.  Enemies mantle objects without touching them and very, very woodenly.  Wake reloads by moving his hand around his gun, but always pointing his flashlight at the center of the screen.  That's a broken wrist right there and not a loaded gun.  Wake himself is actually modeled after a real life actor, and the man plays both Alan Wake and Mr.
in the game's live action cutscenes.  Music is ambient beyond forgetability, save for a nice guitar riff at the motel and a few nice licensed tracks.  Character dialogue is mostly boring, but I did get a chuckle or two  Especially the stereotypical low-budget thriller narrator that describes Wake's journey.  Mr.
is a stand out character, but his writing isn't always the best and he has a lot of pauses that may be meant for drama but only come off as awkward.  Overall the game is rather shoddy in production, but at least its bug free.

At first, this game seems like a simple bullet-hell rogue-lite, but once you start getting into the game you realize it is so much more. I would, and have, recommended this game to a lot of my friends. This is the same price as a ticket, or two depending on where you live, to the movies. Of all the movies I've seen in the last two years, I wish I had found gems like this to replace them.
A lot of games like this focus on bullet patterns, leaving weapon tactics and level design as a secondary feature. Starward Rogue has excellent level design for their rooms. I'm still discovering new rooms, and finding that certain rooms work better with different tactics.
Mech design is also excellent. Some of the mechs play the same way, but there are a few that really shine in their gameplay design. I do feel that some of the mechs design make the game more difficult on top of making the player play differently.
There are some problems with the game. Achievements don't work, shops don't work sometimes, and the items aren't as random as you might think. This leads to some problems, but this doesn't detract from the gameplay. The shop and items are my biggest gripe, because I've often found myself finishing off a run with max money (I should be spending that money).
And plus, it's an Arcen game. In all the Arcen games I own, they have never failed to actively address bugs and issues in their games. For years.

I'm writing this after "only" one co-op session of 6 hours but I can already recommend the game. It's very beautiful and the gameplay is really fine tuned. Having a three star system for each level makes you wanna acieve three stars for all of them by trying to plan ahead only to end up screaming and laughing throughout the encounter.
One downside:
I'm not sure if it's by design but some maps was really difficult to do with 3 player co-op. I'm not sure if every level is fine tuned for any number of players (2,3,4). Some maps was "easy" to get 3 stars with 1-2 tries while the worst one so far required at least 10 attempts to even get 1 star. I think this is especially hard to balance when you have a level that is split in 2 and you have 3 players. Ideally you would want 1.5 person per side so you end up with work overload on one side where you have 1 person and waiting time on the side with 2 persons. This problem doesn't exist with 2 or 4 players as you always are evenly spread out.
We had a really good time and I can recommend this especially for co-op play!
That said, I would happily pay €10 for a multiplayer DLC. The number of times 4 player co-op will be possible is maybe 1-2 times per year for me, and that is if someone brings extra controllers. If my partner and I could just fire up a game with two friends joining in via the cyber webs we would not only have as fun as if they were at our place, but also we would actually play the game. The charm of this game is definately having 4 players working together and causing a mess. 2 player co-op will not be equally fun for us.

I would say it's only worth picking up if you are very patient, are interested in seeing more of the unique art style, and are willing to accept an abrupt and anticlimactic ending. Otherwise there are definitely  much more rewarding horror/atmospheric point and clicks out there.

Telltale Games’ Game of Thrones is, much like many of their other games, essentially a glorified Choose Your Own Adventure book. But, unlike some of their other games (The Walking Dead comes to mind), your choices feel like they mean very little in the grand scheme of things.
Compared to previous TTG games, the graphics in Game of Thrones seem to fall flat. While many of the scenes (particularly close up shots of characters in conversation) seem to do okay, for some reason there is a blur filter across most of the wide angle shots that just seems to chop up smaller items (like swords and torches). I believe the purpose was to make it appear hand-painted, but instead it messes up everything.
Speaking of hand-painted, however, there are some absolutely gorgeous backdrops that really do look like they were painted by hand. While few and far between, they were certainly a treat.
Also, in one of the very first scenes and the first plot-central death, there is a sword floating in mid air. Rather detrimental to the emotional atmosphere, really.
Quick-time events are the bane of my existence. I have always hated them. I like to lean back and relax when I am watching a cutscene (which make up about 90% of this game, to be fair) and having to jump up and press a button usually does not go well.
At least the combat felt engaging. Combat consists entirely of QTEs and pressing the correct button at the correct time. Yet, fighting off the Freys or chasing down the Whitehills felt so... real. It sucked me right in, to the point where I was wincing when I got hit, and I could feel my blade pierce an enemy’s chest. And it was FUN.
It is unfortunate, then, that it was all unnecessary. Since in the end, nothing really matters.
And now we get to the meat of this review. The Story.
I think most of my love for this game came merely from the fact that it took place in the Song of Ice and Fire settings, and how much I love the entire Game of Thrones story. So of course a game set in the same storyline would suck me right in.
And it did. And just like A Song of Ice and Fire, the storyline is bloody, depressing, and everyone you love dies. If you are expecting a story of grandiose heroism and victory, mayhap turn elsewhere. If you want to be stabbed in the heart multiple times and go to bed crying, then this is the game for you!
But don’t expect your choices to matter. Because, for the most part, the end is all the same.
Quick time events. Graphic glitches. And the fact that the choices I made were so insignificant that in the “Previously on” and “Next time on” (episodic game, y’know) the game would occasionally act like I had made a different choice entirely.
Despite all of it’s short comings, it was still a really fun game. But it does require some knowledge of the Game of Thrones universe. So keep that in mind.
I would say... don’t buy this game if you’re expecting something phenomenal. But if you want to get sucked in to a decent story and you can suspend your disbelief well, then it is definitely worth it.

Playing this as an older gamer, I was worried how I would do with a SHMUP roguelike. I'm a turn-based guy these days. You have to manage your ammunition as well as health, and you can't just mash fire buttons and get through. Some thought is required while dodging, you have to constantly plan your next target, attack angle, weapon choice and movement.
If you're worried that this is a reflex-based game, the more forgiving difficulties don't take away the fun, and it has a challenge for the brain as well as the spine. I didn't expect to really enjoy this, but I do; it's got that roguelike magic "let's see how far I can get *this* time" feeling.
Good job Arcen!

I enjoyed this game very much.  I tried 2 different classes but, I don't think I want to play MP or start another class.  Simply because for my tastes, there isn't enough depth in the build system and gear to make any memorable builds and that is what normally keeps me coming back again and again to games like this.
One of the biggest annoyances is the loot system which floods you with gear specific to classes you can't use and often gives you high-tier items that are significantly worse than the lower tier items.
I never really got any super rare items and nothing really build-expanding, however several times I got a really low-level weapon which came bound with a spell that I could add to my arsenal, and simply put, that one spell became so powerful (even though the element was not specific to my class!) that I ended up dragging the low-level item around with me to end-game because nothing comparable or better would ever seem to drop.  That's the kind of thing that makes you upset to be powerful.  It feels like the carrot of insanely awesome gear is always dangling in front of you but you never seem to get it.
All in all, I enjoyed the game very much and the scenery is breathtaking.  I did not enjoy having a billion crafting mats which never saw much meaningful use, and I don't like that the end part of the SP campaign requires a metric-ton of grinding if you want to complete it.  But as I've said in my above complaints the game doesn't really make me feel like playing more, the way a good AARPG loot gambling game should.
It is a thumbs-up, I just feel like the game is missing a lot of polish, as beautiful as it looks visually.  I mean polish in terms of the gameplay experience, the storytelling, the loot system, the spells, the combat, etc.
I give it a solid 7/10 game for a once-around play.

What is Xcom?
Imagine you're about to learn how to play chess (or a similarly cerebral board game). Only that in this "chess" game you get to keep your rooks and kings and queens as they survive each match, get to customize them and give them names and invent storylines and mythologies as they endure battle after battle, making you extremely protective of your chess pieces to the point of feeling physically ill when one of them dies at the hand of the enemy.
Oh, and your chess pieces now have big guns, rockets and grenades, and your opponent's chess pieces are not the same type as yours but aliens with superior weaponry, first-move advantage and, at times, blessed by the gods of the random number generator.
Add to all this a monopoly-ish side game in between each chess match were you have to balance your budget and improve your properties and equip your chess pieces with better and more powerful guns and explosives.
Did I mention that your opponent's chess pieces get stronger as time passes by? So you better hurry up!

Alright, since I played this sorry excuse for an XCOM game for 3 hours and can't get a refund any more, I guess all that's left to do is detail why I think it's a POS and why you shouldn't get it if like me, you've observered the hype around XCOM 2 but want to wait until it's properly patched and think about playing this in the meantime.
All that matters when approaching an enemy in this game is sight range. There can be concrete, a tree and whatever else between the enemy and you, his shot will just clip right through that stuff and still hit your characters. It of course works the other way around too but that doesn't change the fact that it's just dumb.
Because of this, there also really isn't much of a concept of tactical destruction of the environment any more. You simply can't choose to shoot a hole into a wall because you want to better ambush an enemy.
They even went so far as to justify this crappy mechanic by having animations where the characters will lean out of their cover time and time again, just so that they can get hit.
Contrary to any other strategy-based XCOM, Enemies don't always emerge from some aircraft or run around somewhere in the area already but will randomly fall from the sky. And I'm not exaggerating. That's what happens in some missions.
To top it all off, at least newbie snipers have to have enemies within their sight range to be able to fire on them. Which means that their radius of effectiveness is as big as that of someone with a shotgun.
I'd recommend Xenonauts over tihs instead. And if you've played that already... finish it on the highest difficulty. And if you - like me - have done even that... I don't know. Play anything else? Or maybe revisit the original X-COM games, via OpenXCom? I think I'll try that next.

Note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
Every so often, a game comes along that makes you go "why am I enjoying this so much?"
What makes me ask myself that question when it comes to this game is that 1) I do not enjoy punitive games with permadeath. 2) this is a punitive game with permadeath, yet 3) I enjoy this game! Yes, I utterly suck at it, I have yet to beat it once, and still...
Perhaps it is that this game does something that is woefully rare, it puts you as a captain of a single starship and lets you control the crew, the systems and so on, and it does this with graphics and mechanics that are simple, yet feels just right. Perhaps it is the brilliant soundtrack. Perhaps it is some weird mix of all this. Certainly, the premise is simple enough. You are being chased by rebels and need to get to your destination before they catch up with you, your journey takes you through a number of regions of space, where you encounter other ships and people that variously wants to trade with you, have you help them, or kill you. It's simple, fairly quick and very punishing...yet fun.
What saves the fun bit for me is the posibillity of scumsaving (backing up the save game file before it is erased upon your ship being blown up in the game, then restoring the file and trying again). Hey, I know many think that this is "playing wrong", but I both recommend it to those who find permadeath too punishing, and use it myself.
Pro:
*Places you in command of a starship.
*Simple yet fun mechanics.
*Graphics that seem "just right" for this game.
*Excellent soundtrack.
Con:
*No save / load option. This should at least be an option for those who want it.
*No "endless" mode where you can travel freely rather than being pursued.
Summary:

Zenbound 2 is a puzzle game which provides you with a rope and an object, and you are asked to wrap the rope around the object. Wherever the rope touches, a 'halo' of paint is applied, and the main goal is to cover as much of the object in paint as possible. Pins or nails are sometimes placed at strategic locations which can make the task easier or harder, based on your point of view.
Though at times, it can be frustrating to get the rope to stick or slide where and when you want it to, this is an engaging and brain-bending puzzle game. There are numerous solutions to each puzzle because of the nature of the paint mechanic, but as the difficulty increases, the objects get more complex, and the rope gets shorter, you have to carefully plan your paths to make sure that full contact is made at the right depth levels before you move to other areas.
100% completion is impossible, so if you strive for that satisfaction, don't search for it here. Casual puzzle gamers and people looking to burn 15-20 minutes at a time will love this.

I wish there was an option for 'Meh' for recommendations.
As far as Space Sim shooters go, this is definitely a good catch on the market. The learning curve is hardly a curve at all (if you are able to get on good terms with relativity of direction), and it will keep you going for a while.
However, at the time of writting this, 7 hours in, it's becoming more and more apparent just how repetitive this game becomes, and offers you no replay value. The missions are all pretty much the same ("Go there, kill things") and it turns into an incredible grind fest if you're a completionist like me. Eliminating all the gangs, liberating the systems, flying through asteroids for upgrades and a silly sidequest now and then that is even more repetitive if that's even possible.
The game would also like to suggest that there are multiple ways of making money and choosing different paths and sure, there are indeed multiple branches that you can gain reputation in, to become a Merchant or a Smuggler, a Mercenary or a Pirate, a Killer or a Bounty Hunter...
Well, except that Merchant and Smuggler are the same thing with a slight risk and much larger reward for Smuggler, Mercenary and Bounty Hunter are just you shooting the bad guys, Pirate is you shooting the good guys and stealing their stuff to sell for Mercenary or Smuggler, and Killer is the same thing except you shoot to kill. So really, not much of difference at all.
And even though there are indeed dozens and dozens of systems to explore, there really isn't a reason to. It's all the same anyway, slight differences here and there (image of a planet in the background, number of objects, possible sidemission/collectible (that you can see and check news stand about locations of beforehand)), but other than that, you're probably not going to visit a lot of systems for more than a few seconds while your jump drive recharges.
Anyway, to wrap it all up, I would only suggest this game if you want to play a space shooter. If you're looking for a trader game, I would suggest you look at other Kalypso titles, as the trading system isn't really all that great here. If you're looking for something you can pick up and play casually whenever you feel like blowing some space ships up, this is the game for you.

It's very hard for me not to recommend this considering how much time I've sunk into the web version of the game. Very few, if any shooters come (other than UT) close to the feel, pace, and delivery that Quake has. The skill needed to play the game has been visibly reduced, but this is still one of the shooters that will reward skill improvement greatly, and you will see yourself improve.
On the bad side, the iconic announcer has been replaced, which is a cardinal sin, and the free version somewhat lacks in the freedom to play with your friends or to play a very specific matchup.
Overall, the charm, the frantic pace, the skillshots, the rocket jumps and map travel are still there, and if you ever had a thing for Quake or UT type of arena FPSes, you'll find at least some of it here.
EDIT: After some time playing this game once again, and as well as looking what it turned into with all of the limitations if you're not paying for a subscription, I can no longer recommend this game in front of so many other shooters that do things so much better than Quake Live. I'm sorry guys, but you've finally managed to turn away your long time fan with this pay to pay ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
EDIT 2: The above change of mind was after the game was literally forcing the subscriptions down your throat. The newest pricing model has, unexpectedly, turned this game fun to play once again. There's a big issue with finding a server when you want to play, but this is the closest to the old QL that I used to love. Thanks for not ruining it!

Good graphics on this one. Never mind the naysayers. It's pretty standard fare for telltale games as far as telling you a predetermined story and letting you affect little details on the way. If you like Game of Thrones and Telltale you should like this. Just remember that playing as House Forrester is like playing as House Stark and currently Ned, Robb and Rickon are all dead. Figure Forrester will go through a similar attrition before things go their way and win probably won't happen in season one. You'll likely be disappointed regardless of your outcome and the game is overall a cruel experience, but depending on your choices there ARE countless little victories along the way. Nothing like kicking your attacker off the wall to warm your heart.
There's also this little gem of a feature in that at least once, a choice can end with everyone (good guys AND bad guys) being slaughtered and game over. Nice to have a death not caused by a missed button prompt for once.
All in all, one of the best Telltale experiences imo.

(Will write more when I have the time and patience to do so, I just wanted to add more to the positive review percentages since I find it to be a good game overall.)
The good:
Spectacular characters, great voice acting, nice soundtrack, and excellent writing. You will find yourself being sucked into this experience you'll never forget, and love the characters you spend the most time with, which happen to be the playable ones of course, plus their family.
The bad:
Low-poly textures on some models, some speech options are taken the wrong way by the character you're talking to or you end up saying something you didn't mean to, albeit rarely so, still an issue. Episode 6, the finale, ends up being a bit of a let-down, thankfully it gives hope for Season 2, however. Lacks replayability due to lack of branching stories since that would change the way the TV show goes on. You still have a good number of choices, though, and people who complain about this, well, I find them a bit too nitpicky. Fallout 4 has far less choices, still. I never played a Telltale game before so I wouldn't really know, but I'm viewing TTG's GoT as a game on its own and as one of two Game of Thrones games (this one being the better-known one), I just feel like we're already lucky to have this than nothing.
Anyway, I recommend getting this game if you love the show, I really do. You might feel a tad depressed throughout the game and that's what I was expecting anyway, after having just watched up to Season 5 (I watched S6 too but that was before then) at least one episode per day. I mean, seriously, it's GoT. Of course you'll have a lot of losses and few times winning. You're lucky to win anything at all in this universe. But yeah. If you're the weak of heart when it comes to characters that you care about dying and such, don't buy this game. If you want a heavy story-driven experience, this is perfect for you, well, that, and if you like Fantasy settings. And if you're like me and thought of getting this game despite the massive negative reviews on the page, as well as perhaps wanting it because you like or even love the show, you SHOULD get the game, preferably on a 50-75% sale since it'll probably lack replayability for you, too. I hope you enjoy the game if you do get it!

Do you like roguelites with a sense of progression?
Do you really like bullet hells?
I recommend giving this a shot.  Espcially if you've played Binding of Isaac(BoI) or Nuclear Throne(NT).
If there is one thing I have to give props for Arcen games beyond all else, it has to be consistently making games that feel unique, even in a genre (shump roguelite) that's been getting more and more attention as of late.
It focuses more on the bullet hell aspect, which is something that I didn't know that I wanted, but was sorely needed.  It does have the same design beats with keys and missiles that essentially act like bombs that can access secret rooms.  And it has NT's perk system when you level up.  Keep in mind though that for better or worse you can't break a run by getting essentially infinite items like in BoI.
The level design is fairly well done with the battles usually having some twist to them in terms of obstacles and layout.  The background graphics for the game can look a bit busy though, which means that you won't be able to instantly grasp what needs to be done in the room (like dodging spikes for instance).  However, you can easily see the bullets against the background, which has been a problem with some more colorful shmups.
The music is appropriately techno and fits with the mecha aesthetic.  Other than the menu (where you control the cursor with the control stick), the game works well on a controller, which is a plus.
There's also future support coming from the company itself.  And there's an active modding community that's been constantly adding more variety to the base game.  All Arcen has to do is to curate it before the created content gets patched in.
So it's not a clone.  Starward Rogue has its own take while still cherry picking the best of others in the genre.
A solid 8/10 that scratches an itch I've had for a while and a likely candidate for that part in my game library where I never uninstall.

A rouge-like bullet-hell that plays to the strengths of both.
This is not your father's rouge-like.
With older rouge-likes you have to sacrifice aesthetics for diversity, not so in star-ward rouge.
With older rouge-likes you have to explore a hundred rooms to find something interesting, not so in star-ward rouge.
With older rouge-likes you have to play dozens of hours to get your head around the basics, not so in star-ward rouge.
With older rouge-likes combat was boring, not so in star-ward rouge.
The core design of star-ward rouge, is that each room is an 'arena' and each level is required to have a set list of rooms. This means that while each level is different you are guaranteed to have an interested run every time. It also prevents you from being starved of interesting items/abilities because a shop keeper has spawned yet.
In short, if you like bullet-hells this game is for you. If you think games like crawl, but think they could use more accessibility this game is for you.

Note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
Every so often, a game comes along that makes you go "why am I enjoying this so much?"
What makes me ask myself that question when it comes to this game is that 1) I do not enjoy punitive games with permadeath. 2) this is a punitive game with permadeath, yet 3) I enjoy this game! Yes, I utterly suck at it, I have yet to beat it once, and still...
Perhaps it is that this game does something that is woefully rare, it puts you as a captain of a single starship and lets you control the crew, the systems and so on, and it does this with graphics and mechanics that are simple, yet feels just right. Perhaps it is the brilliant soundtrack. Perhaps it is some weird mix of all this. Certainly, the premise is simple enough. You are being chased by rebels and need to get to your destination before they catch up with you, your journey takes you through a number of regions of space, where you encounter other ships and people that variously wants to trade with you, have you help them, or kill you. It's simple, fairly quick and very punishing...yet fun.
What saves the fun bit for me is the posibillity of scumsaving (backing up the save game file before it is erased upon your ship being blown up in the game, then restoring the file and trying again). Hey, I know many think that this is "playing wrong", but I both recommend it to those who find permadeath too punishing, and use it myself.
Pro:
*Places you in command of a starship.
*Simple yet fun mechanics.
*Graphics that seem "just right" for this game.
*Excellent soundtrack.
Con:
*No save / load option. This should at least be an option for those who want it.
*No "endless" mode where you can travel freely rather than being pursued.
Summary:
FTL Advanced Edition is sadly marred by the lack of a save / load game system, and the absence of a mode where you can freely travel the galaxy without being pursued. Had this been added, this game would easly warrant an 8/10 rating for me, but so far, there is no sign of this being added. Despite this, FTL succeeds in being one of the best "starship captain simulation strategy games" ever. Granted, there aren't that much competition, but it is still a game well worth playing, especially if you can pick it up on a sale.  6/10 -Recommended.

Growing up, I had this cat.
She loved going outside, but was too wild to stay in the yard and out of traffic, so whenever she wanted to go out, we would hook her into a harness and let her roam the yard in that. My cat hated the harness, and as soon as it came out, she would turn into a puddle of fur, meat and disconnected bones that made threading her into the harness both an act of frustration and love.
Zen Bound 2 is a lot like that cat.
The object of the game is to wrap up an item with string, which places paint on the object. The objective is to completely cover each wooden effigy with paint. The main object in your arsenal is just to turn and rotate the item to slowly wrap it up, but the game includes nail bombs and paint bombs that also splash paint across the item. It's a simple enough premise in theory, and certainly something I had never come across before.
Perhaps it simply takes a certain type of person to appreciate this kind of game, but I found the puzzles in Zen Bound 2 frustrating me more than relaxing me, and the ambient sounds of rope pulling taut just made me go tense alongside it. I've seen other reviewers say it was soothing, though, so it all depends. The controls seemed tense and unforgiving to me, like I had little control over where the rope would fall, and what it stuck on or slid off of seems inconsistent.
You unlock new levels by covering a wide and delightful array of lovingly-rendered wooden figures, and each 'level' is represented by paper lanterns hanging from a tree. The aesthetic appeal of this game, with its clean and warm graphics, is undeniable, and even clever. I've only seen some of them so far, and look forward to unlocking the rest. The music is similarly Zen, very appropriate to the game.
I did encounter some freezing, stuttering, and long lag times, with items getting 'stuck' mid-turn and glitching out, along with the music and sound effects.
The fact that the game did not give me the experience I had expected doesn't mean I did not enjoy it, though, and find my own reasons to enjoy it. The game is challenging and maybe even punishing, as Perfection always is. There's more to this game than its claws.

Given wooden shapes (toys), some with nails, some with extra parts (read later), your goal is to wrap the toy in rope, from a given amount, As your rope touches the toy, the area of contact is painted, the aim being to "paint" the entire toy, or at least predetermined percentages.
The game features a few extra touches to help you on your way - such as nails to hook your rope onto, nail bombs which splat the nearby area of effect with paint when contacted, rope bombs which (attached to the rope) splatter the area with paint when in contact with the toy, and most importantly, the ability to wind back your rope to try again.
A truly brilliant game, and well worth the cost twice. A calming, almost minimalist gameplay style and visual makes it easier to contemplate what you need to do to get that obsessively desired 100%. The visuals are wonderful - shaded and detailed, while an out-of-focus background gives a feeling of containment within a world, it doesn't cramp your playing space. The audio features simple rope creaks and paint pops, all to an asian instrumental soundtrack.
The entire gam is tied together by trees - each puzzle being a hanging ornament on your tree, and your level rating being rated by your karma, giving the game a truly satisfying, yet calming whole.

Overcooked is an absolutely superb serving of local multiplayerage. It's fast, funny (and frequently furious): few games have ever make me laugh so much. It's super easy to pick up and play, and instantly rewarding.

Great soundtrack, too. Very highly recommended.

I salute the devs for keeping it local only - the online mode is likely to disappoint and put players off trying the real experience.
