I highly recommend this game, very fun. I have yet to have two matches which are the same, so the developers aren’t lying when they say that! Unlike so many other pvp games where the only difference between characters is the stats of the gun they’re using.
A unique experience, adding a bunch of insidious traps to your base before the match begins is very creative and enjoyable and also important to victory. This is a game where it is actually necessary to have at least one person camp, so if you like lying in wait, there’s something here for you because few people actually seem to want to do so in the game.
The characters have a great deal of variety, from ninjas who can teleport to yetis who call down avalanches to eye-talian construction workers with nailgun shotguns who build turrets you’ll not find a more diverse mix of special abilities and unique building components. There are also characters with a more traditional repertoire such as the Sarge, with his machine gun, rocket launcher and grenades or Cogwheel, a robot with high health and a minigun/cannon arm that builds mortar turrets that he activates with his special that then fire upon the beacon for great damage and lulz.

Speaking of lulz, though this game has cartoony graphics the humor is definitely more Adult Swim than Disney. Every character is a true stereotype but not in any sort of offensive way. The one-liners are quite enjoyable and reminiscent of impressions of various cultures around the world, often a strange mix of two. The Mexican ninja comes to mind. There are regularly three characters on rotation that you may use to get gold for unlocking a permanent character, and by leveling up these characters you get bonus gold in large quantities, encouraging trying all of them. You even get the bonus for the free rotation characters as you level them.
The maps are varied, featuring everything from symmetric opposing castles to green hilly areas that look similar to the backgrounds in the early levels of Super Mario World or Sonic the Hedgehog. If you don’t like a map, you can always remodel it with explosives to better suit your tastes.  You are able to dig into the various parts of the game world to construct tunnels and hidden alcoves where you may place healing/ammo stations or radars which reveal enemies and their defenses even through walls – very necessary to prevent the aforementioned tunnels from getting into your base and providing the enemy with cover and concealment to attack from. The maps range in size from just one base to destroy all the way up to three. There are even challenge maps which are single player and give a great currency reward simply for completion, with extra but smaller rewards for doing so in a shorter time.
There is no pay2win - all characters and abilities are able to be acquired without spending money though as tradition dictates, you may buy premium currency to unlock special skins as well as acquire characters faster, but you may NOT use this currency to buy perks. Perks must be acquired using the f2p currency you get from completing matches and challenges, and are more often side-grades rather than direct upgrades as they always remove one stat to buff another, though higher levels of the perk provide returns typically well worth the cost.
As a noob, I found myself able to have plenty of fun. It’s rare to run into a team so well organized that their experience allows them to completely trounce you without you even having a chance. This is in part due to the party system allowing only premades of three out of five in the casual mode, so both teams are bound to have at least one or two experienced players and a noob or two or three ;) . The game is very easy to get into, but the skill ceiling is very high. There are always better and more creative ways to do something, and any character may be used effectively for attack or defense, though some seem to favor one play style over another.
The colors are bright, the characters are colorful, and mass destruction abounds! Get this, and support a f2p game that is AAA quality and truly is not pay to win in any way.

Farcry primal is a prehistoric first person, hunter, gather, shooter developed by Ubisoft. Although taking place well before firearms, Farcry Primal still flows and plays like any modern Farcry game.
The core gameplay of farcry primal is pretty solid in its design. Primal plays like any resent farcry game, just with a change of timeline and weapons. The objectives are similar to other farcry games, including, hunting missions, taking outposts, clearing fog of war, and having psychedelic experiences.
Primal's story revolves around your characters culture. The Wenja need to reunite to survive, and fend off animals and neanderthals. The player quickly becomes a beast master, and is tasked with building up a village of Wenja, and taking over the land, clearing all threats.
Primal relies more on finding materials in order to craft weapons and upgrades, as well as upgrading your tribe members huts. These materials are located in certain areas of the map. (Such as south stone found to the south) these can be tedious to retrieve but can be rewarding. Players can unlock new tools and skills as they progress in the world.
Primal does a fair amount right:
The beast master missions are fantastic
Unique setting
Wide variety of animals to tame
Beautiful scenic environment
Satisfying to watch your beasts hunt
Watch your village grow
Primal does some things wrong:
Almost the same map from farcry 4
The combat isn't polished
Stealth isn't as big of an option
Some beast are useless
The game feels rushed
Overall primal is fairly solid title. At the cost of $49.99CND it is steep, however it is very much worth it if picked up on sale. Primal plays extremely well, and is quite good at pulling the players in. Pick it up and try it out.

I’ve followed this interesting developer for a few games now, most notably A Valley Without Wind and its sequel: two games that fused, oddly enough, turn-based strategy with Metroidvania-esque platform shooting. Arcen’s latest game Starward Rogue continues the dev’s tradition of fusing disparate genres together, in this case arcade shooters and roguelikes.
I say “disparate”; Starward Rogue isn’t the first game to combine roguelike elements with a shoot ’em up core, but it is the first I recall seeing designed around the principles of Japanese-style arcade shooters, particularly those of the “bullet hell” variety. That means intense, complex bullet patterns that you need to navigate through as well as enemies to defeat, and it makes for an exciting, very interesting take on a genre that all too often coasts along without any real innovation.
Starward Rogue casts you in the role of a severed head in a mech as you attempt to rescue someone called Rodney from the depths of a dungeon called the Megalith. I believe these two elements are a reference to one of Arcen’s other games, but it’s one I’m not familiar with at this time. Fortunately, no real knowledge of whatever the other game it’s referring to is required; it’s simply a bit of fanservice for those who have played the game’s spiritual predecessor. Rodney is an entertaining character in his own right, though my only direct contact with him so far has been in the tutorial sequence.
Starward Rogue‘s gameplay is balanced nicely between exploration and action. Each level of the Megalith is split into discrete rooms, each of which has to be cleared of enemies before you can move on to the next one. Unlike similar games such as The Binding of Isaac, though, Starward Rogue’s rooms are often more than a screen wide and tall, and there are a number of unique designs and layouts that you’ll encounter over the course of the game, which are then combined with various enemy and trap waves — the latter tending to be non-destroyable obstacles or gun turrets that will spew out hot fiery death as you try and take down the enemies, then deactivate when you’ve cleared the room.
Levelling up is a simple process: no stat allocation here, simply pick one of three randomly selected perks. These vary from increased damage to having a full map available from the start of the floor — and even being able to skip the rest of the floor you’re on. Alongside these passive bonuses you get from levelling, you can also equip and upgrade your infinite-ammo main gun, your recharging Energy-based weapon (which recharges when you enter a new room) and your limited-ammo Missile weapon. There are also various other passive upgrades you can collect, and one-shot consumable items that generally have some sort of “smart bomb” effect.
Much like the aforementioned The Binding of Isaac, Starward Rogue is a game intended to be replayed and rechallenged. There are a number of different mechs with which to play the game, and there’s a checklist of enemies and items you’ve found over the course of all your runs. There are also five difficulty levels to choose from, with Very Easy all but guaranteeing a full clear run unless you are the very worst kind of incompetent moron, and the highest difficulty claiming to offer difficulty on a par with the legendary Touhou series. And on top of that there are a bunch of achievements to earn, too, so it’s very much a game that will keep you busy for a long time if you get it — though it’s accessible enough to be able to pick up every so often for a quick blast even if you’ve left it alone for a while.
I completed a Very Easy run earlier — there’s no shame in starting either a roguelike or a shoot ’em up on the lowest difficulty, and this game is both! — and am already looking forward to giving it another shot soon. If you’re a fan of The Binding of Isaac and its ilk — “roguelites”, to use the popular term — then you could do far worse than give Starward Rogue a look.

I have at the time of writing this, nearly 30 hours of time in.  Most of this is me starting over again and again while I was recording my walkthrough videos.  With that in mind, I want to share my thoughts about this game with you.
First: Are you are a fast action, first person shooter, explode first ask questions later kind of person?
If you said yes and get bored reading a review half way through then this isn't the game for you.
This is a point and click adventure puzzle game.  There is no combat mechanic in it.  The game makes you think.  So if you enjoy puzzles and creative and/or critical thinking then this may be something you like.
Second: Are you used to games holding your hand?  Do you skip the dialog knowing the answer is in the journal or marked on the map for you?
If you said yes then this may not be the game for you either.
This game has a story and a plot.  This game has a clear direction your character is going in.  The difference is that it doesn't tell you what that is.  The character has no clue what is going on and so why should the game tell you?
Third: Are you a snob for perfect grammar and spelling?  Do you judge a game by its sound effects? music? graphics?
If you said yes then this may not be the game for you either.
This game was created by a polish company.  Words, Spelling, and Grammar don't always translate well the first time.  The development team is working on fixing that of course, but people like to take their shots when they can.  It's a translation issue not an intelligence issue.  Also the game isn't full of CGI or motion capture cut scenes.  They use very well done stills and limited animation paired with an excellent narrator and music to get the mood across.
There will always be someone who has something bad to say about a game.  Everyone is entitled to their opinions.  But look carefully at what they are saying before you judge the game by their words.  This game is thought out, well designed, and the challenges require observation, problem solving, and some skill.  Some of the puzzles are static puzzles, others are random,  but no puzzle is repeated in the game.
tl:dr ?
If this is where you skipped to don't buy the game.  It isn't a game for you.
If you are here for a summary? ok then.
Classic Point and Click Adventure Puzzle.  A throwback to the 90s
Good graphics and music set the mood and theme for the game.
Controls? they are exact, no room for error
Replay ability? low unless you are a completionist and want those achievements!

This is a pretty good title for the niche that it tries to represent, but I would not recommend this to a casual or regular gamer. In a nutshell, Starward Rogue is a twinstick shooter mixed with RPG and rogue-lite elements. You play as one of six mechas shooting enemies progressing from level to level and unlocking special weapons and skills.
The game is quite challenging and many casual players will be put off by the lack of other essentials:
-no catchy music
-graphics are sub par
-gameplay is limiting
There are however some good things about it, such as a variety in terms of gameplay when it comes to mechs. At least one of the mechs, gets a unique mechanic of stopping time and only advancing it when it moves around. Other than that though, I'd have to say "pass this unless you really lack a challenging twin stick shooter in your life and are okay with it being mediocre in other departments"
EDIT:
A lot of you inquired what I meant about "no catchy music".
If you play other Arcen titles you'll notice that sometimes despite really mediocre graphics, it's the sound effects and music that give their titles that extra atmosphere. A twin stick shooter title is also often dependent on some sort of a catchy and rhythmic melody that makes you want to come back to it over and over. This title however lacks that and it feels like a product that was pushed out of the door a bit too quick in that sense.
As for the gameplay being limiting: when I played this title it didn't draw me in even as a twin stick shooter. It felt impersonal. It didn't make me feel like I was the last survivor of a catastrophic disaster or had some strange reason to persevere and defeat the neverending overpowering enemies despite all odds. It just dropped me into the middle of a randomly generated level (thus the rogue part) and told me to go on my merry way using a somewhat generic control scheme, generic enemies and generic level layouts. Nothing really screamed "omg, I wanted to do this more". It was more of a "ok...well I died now should I really bother to do this again?"
All in all, it's an okay title and I definitely recommend supporting the indie game developers, but I feel like this title in particularly has been pushed out of the door a teeny bit too soon and most likely because the modern indie developers are under a lot of scrutiny when it comes to releasing games and competing with others.
So all in all, good title, but I wouldn't recommend it unless you want to donate money to an indie company because you support the industry.

Starward Rogue is fun, and worth your time and money.
It's a cross between Binding of Issac and Touhou, wherein you play as a mech shooting your way through five big levels of this starship, grabbing items and upgrades while you learn to better avoid the bullet hell patterns from the enemies. There's a solid range of difficulty levels, from easy to the forthcoming Misery mode, and I found Normal to be nicely balanced for me, and I'm merely decent at bullet hell games.
There are six mechs that change the gameplay in small (weapon changes) to huge ways - one mech will stop time unless you move or shoot, turning the game into this weird combination I'd call tactical, turn-based bullet-hell. I haven't seen anything like it, and I adore it - threading the needle to fight the bosses poses some tense questions - dodge or inflict more damage. But I digress: the standard mech is more than fun enough, presenting fast gameplay that caught me in the trap of "one more level!"
Your mech is armed with the standard bullet hell style infinite ammo shooter that you can aim with the mouse, a missile launcher, and an energy weapon that varies by mech - the basic mech has a bouncing ball of bullets, while the time-stop one has a machine gun burst.
There's a huge variety of weapons and items - I found myself a ghostly sword that would erase bullets directly in front of me at regular intervals, and I learned to love it - up until I got sloppy with a third floor boss and died. Whoops!
The levels are randomly generated pre-made rooms - some are mazes, some are open arenas, some have laser traps and other complications, and they're populated with a huge variety of enemies, each with their own bullet patterns.
Now - flaws. The music is good, but you'll hear the same tracks multiple times while playing.
... That's it. That's all I've got. The game seems balanced so far, I'm having a blast playing it, and the graphics are great. There's a nonobtrusive plot, the tutorial does its work, and I was able to easily put the game into windowed mode.
It's a top-down bullet hell shooter with roguelite elements with a lot of variety that presents some interesting twists on the genres - AND it's fun to play. Check it out!

Not having played any other game in the series, getting into Tropico 4 I was afraid of running face first into a learning curve wall, but was pleasantly surprised by the way the game was designed. It's intuitive and does a good job at explaining the core mechanics without holding your hand whilst talking down to you.
What I mean is that Tropico 4 is extremely accessible. You almost cannot lose unless you overreach something fierce. Even then, you can tell when things aren't working out, and you're more often than not given time to rectify the situation. The difficulty lies in the unique stipulations and events of each individual scenario, which actually switches the gameplay up to the point where you get to work with all your tools and not just do the same build over and over. I appreciate that, because it's a welcome change of pace from a lot of other strategy games where you just find "the best" way to play and then repeat until the end credits.
The ambience and tone of the game is spot on for what it goes for, keeping it light and humorous. It's chock-full of caricatured and satirized references to real life leaders and personalities, with plenty of jokes and easter eggs to keeps you entertained even when the gameplay starts getting repetetive and slow.
Graphically, it's ok without being especially impressive. Thankfully it's not going for impressive, though, but rather functionally, which it is. You can run it on most systems without any problems. Everything's clear and you won't have any problems getting into the mood of the game.
If you're an achievement hunter looking for another perfect clear, be aware that some of the "harder" achievements are rare because they're incredibly grind-heavy. I got stuck playing the same sandbox map over and over for more than 20 games after having cleared the campaigns, in order to get all character traits to level 5. Took hours and wasn't much fun after a while, although I hadn't maximized my char traits beforehand so some levels had been wasted.
When it comes to DLC, I would actually advice against getting "Modern Times", since the buildings you get completely break the game. You will get stuff that just replaces everything you can get in the base game, and all difficulty is thrown out the window. It could be fun for a couple of games or a long sandbox game, but it'll get tired and it'll get tired fast. Just isn't worth it in my opinion.
In conclusion, I warmly recommend it. Tropico 4 is a game that'll keep you busy for hours on end, and keep you entertained throughout. It's got character, atmosphere and tongue-in-cheek satire. It immerses you in the world of banana republics and continuously challenges you with new and innovative problems. Just don't bother with the "Modern Times" DLC, as it kind of breaks the flow of the game and makes it much too easy and simple. If it's on sale, get it! If it's not, but you like city builder strategy games, why not pick it up?

Note: Summary at the bottom of the review.
Every so often, a game comes along that makes you go "why am I enjoying this so much?"
What makes me ask myself that question when it comes to this game is that 1) I do not enjoy punitive games with permadeath. 2) this is a punitive game with permadeath, yet 3) I enjoy this game! Yes, I utterly suck at it, I have yet to beat it once, and still...
Perhaps it is that this game does something that is woefully rare, it puts you as a captain of a single starship and lets you control the crew, the systems and so on, and it does this with graphics and mechanics that are simple, yet feels just right. Perhaps it is the brilliant soundtrack. Perhaps it is some weird mix of all this. Certainly, the premise is simple enough. You are being chased by rebels and need to get to your destination before they catch up with you, your journey takes you through a number of regions of space, where you encounter other ships and people that variously wants to trade with you, have you help them, or kill you. It's simple, fairly quick and very punishing...yet fun.
What saves the fun bit for me is the posibillity of scumsaving (backing up the save game file before it is erased upon your ship being blown up in the game, then restoring the file and trying again). Hey, I know many think that this is "playing wrong", but I both recommend it to those who find permadeath too punishing, and use it myself.
Pro:
*Places you in command of a starship.
*Simple yet fun mechanics.
*Graphics that seem "just right" for this game.
*Excellent soundtrack.
Con:
*No save / load option. This should at least be an option for those who want it.
*No "endless" mode where you can travel freely rather than being pursued.
Summary:
FTL Advanced Edition is sadly marred by the lack of a save / load game system, and the absence of a mode where you can freely travel the galaxy without being pursued. Had this been added, this game would easly warrant an 8/10 rating for me, but so far, there is no sign of this being added. Despite this, FTL succeeds in being one of the best "starship captain simulation strategy games" ever. Granted, there aren't that much competition, but it is still a game well worth playing, especially if you can pick it up on a sale.  6/10 -Recommended.

I liked this game for the first 10 hours or so, which is ok, right?  It's not like this is a AAA release and it's going to be dirt cheap, right?
Well, for cheap you'll endure an super annoying and unasked for co-pilot, whom, much like her counterpart in X4: Rebirth, serves no real purpose and we're asked to believe that we would wouldn't just flush her out of the airlock at the earliest opportunity.
You've got one ship to fly that is upgradeable . . . but only if you can find the ancient artifacts it needs to grow.  Finding these artifacts becomes a central theme as you cannot upgrade to better weapons without first upgrading the Hull, Wings, and Engines.  You're even told at the very beginning that one should concentrate on the wings so that our intrepid pilot has more than one weapon firing forward.  IF one chooses to focus only on the wings, then when it comes to fire the weapons you drain your energy reserves so quickly that one will constantly be unable to fire your weapons at all.  You are, therefore, forced to upgrade each area with each level-up, which renders what should be a non-linear game into a hopelessly tedious affair with some really horrible writing.
If you must buy a space game, go with X3: Reunion or invest in Star Citizen.

This is a fairly divisive game. Of course, not everyone loved Alan Wake, but even its fans are split on American Nightmare. It's more Alan Wake, though I found the combat to feel a little better in this one than the original game, as the flashlight may have been a bit better in American Nightmare. The biggest point of contention for people playing this game is the timeloop. If you've seen Groundhog Day (or haven't), Bill Murray's character wakes up again and again, always on the same day with the same things happening, and he tries changing things each time.
The story and locations in American Nightmare go along those same lines. You will play through certain areas multiple times, and some folks get really♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off about that. Normally, I would be one of the first people to gripe about having to fight in the same areas, but the story angle of the loop really got me on board. Also, Alan and the ladies he meets in each area are remembering the loops, so he and they are actively changing things and doing things earlier than normal. For instance, you have to fix lights at one point in the game to drive away enemies, but after a loop, you don't have to fix the lights even though they got "un-fixed" thanks to the loop, because the lady remembered the time before, and she fixed the lights before you ever get there on the next go-around of the loop, so there's progress like that.
I thought it was pretty darn cool, and I was eager to see what would happen next. I can't recall, canonically, how this game's story meshes in with the original game, but I did like the story on its own merits, and would like to play it again sometime, after I play through the original Alan Wake and its DLCs again. Although I do recommend playing those first, if you're unable to get them due to Steam discontinuing their sale, I would certainly say playing American Nightmare if you get it on sale would be worth it, though you might want to briefly look up Alan Wake's story to understand it a bit better.
If playing a loop of 3 times through several repeat areas and some areas less than that, with characters starting to remember and react to things in prior loops that resulted in their deaths sounds like something you wouldn't enjoy, then you should probably steer clear, but if it sounds cool and you liked Alan Wake, you might enoy this game.

I both love and hate this game. The good is really good and the bad is really bad.
THE GOOD
- One of the best games when it comes to "making hard choices" because it is often life and death and almost never as black and white as good vs evil. Will you be loyal to your friend, or save your family?
- A chance to be immersed in the game of throne universe is also a very good point, and in this game it has been well done.
THE BAD
- Bad at making your choices matter. It often feels (and is a fact) that many "choices" result in the same outcomes. At first choices are fun because you think you are being clever or having a strategy and an outcome in mind. But as you start to realize how many of your choices don't matter at all, you lose interest and you just want to beat the game to be done with it.
- Episodic format is a nightmare. By the time a new episode is released you forget most of what you have done before. It really breaks immersion and kills any sens of continuity. And they made us wait for the last episode so long! I decided that I will never buy episodic games again until all episodes are out.
- The ending was very disapointing to me. None of the outcomes i was expecting happened, even the bad ones, because again a lot of the story is predetermined and you have little control. But worse than that, it didn't give any closure. Many story arcs stay open, and you realize they are milking them for future seasons which is very greedy and very disapointing.
CONCLUSION
I don't feel like I have accomplished anything. For this reason alone I was really tempted to vote it down. The game was fun as it was being played, but since it's a story game that promises that your choices matter, and none of what you seem to affect matters in the end it leaves a bad taste.
You know how bad it is? You make a choice, the character you interact with shows "he will remember this" a supposed indication that you did something that matters... then guess what, immediately that character DIES. And there is nothing you can do to save him. Why tell us he will remember if he is 100% dead? Just silly and discouraging.
Worse yet... the writers take the low road of just killing and killing characters for drama. I am fine with that, as long as it's a consequence or part of enhancing the story... but you never get a chance to save anyone. No matter what you do, eveything goes south and the writers seem to think that using this cookie cutter writing of just killing everyone is amazing writing. That's false. A good story is like a good paiting it needs contrast. It is also like music, it needs ups, downs, and silences. The music that is game of thrones just keeps on going down and down, never giving you a win that matters, not letting you save anyone, it's just downhill and just a monotone beep when you look at your experience.
For this reason it just leaves a bad taste.
(Comparison with tales from borderlands) I'd rather not have played it and discovered the telltales series with "tales of borderlands", which is definitely a great title and has less flaws than this one. For one being more based on humor than death and life situations makes it less prone on dispointing you when the story goes south, keeps going south, then takes a big final dive south. Game of thrones feels like a puzzle / strategy game in that you are making choices with a desired outcome in mind (for me i was trying to save the family at any price), and it dispoints when it just ignores you and does what it wanted to do anyway. Tales of borderlands is better because it truly feels like an adventure game where you experience the different situations, but you have no expectations and you are not wrestling difficulties to make something specific happen, so it it just works better, especially with the added humor.
In the end I recommend this game, but grab it on sale and dont' expect much from the ending. Just experience it for what it is, a chance to get immersed in the game of thrones universe and struggle with some difficult choices.

So I've decided to take the time to review this as space sims are a fave of mine - maybe they're yours too and you're on the fence about buying this or not.
I picked this up  for a fiver and can honestly say it was money well spent. There were a few teething issues (Which I'll discuss below) but overall, so far (about 5 hours in) its a solid, enjoyable space combat/trading/missions game that will not disappoint fans of Elite/Freelancer etc.
I had initially intended to run this on a Windows 8.1 laptop system, using my PS3 pad through the built in Xbox drivers - if you want to do this too, don't bother - it just simply doesn't work very well. I only got sporadic response from the pad before I gave in.
Secondly, the game will crash if you select certain resolutions - this can be fixed using a custom resolution (just Google Darkstar One custom resolution) but it was a bind having to mess about on both my laptop AND my desktop,
Since getting the game working, it's all been good. You start with a fairly basic ship and collect artifacts to upgrade it. You can pick up a variety of missions for cash, or just trade between systems if you like. Other reviewers have criticized the terrible voice acting and this is something I have to agree with - it is terrible for the most part, but the environmental speech from other pilots and space stations still adds to the atmosphere. I'm at the stage now where I've upgraded my ship three times and kitted it out with some reasonably decent gear. Blasting space pirates out of the sky is incredibly satisfying.
Pros at a glance:
Looks nice.
Lots to do.
Easy to pick up and easy to follow control system.
Interesting ship upgrading system and different upgrades.
A steal for the money being asked.
Cons at a glance:
Some technical niggles.
Voice acting is laughable.
No tracking of prices between space stations - back to pad and pen!
Some missions aren't clear enough about what you are expected to do - example: I picked up an escort mission and met my wingman outside the station - I hyperspaced to the target system and failed the mission because I hadn't got close enough to the wingman for him to jump first... a bit tiresome!
If you're still reading this, you're clearly in the right place - get it bought.

The goal of this game is to cook and serve a variety of meals quickly as a team of 1-4 players. This involves cleaning and grabbing a dish, picking up and preparing ingredients, not burning stuff (and if you do, putting out the fire), putting them together and then serving them.
The difficulty lies within how fast you prepare these dishes and how the level is set up. Sometimes you don't have everything on "your side" so you need to hand each other ingredients or done meals to get the job done.
Additionally, some levels come with environmental hazards which kill you and force you to wait a few seconds before respawning. Each level also has its own set of recipes which need to be cooked.
You can play together with up to two players per controller, each holding one side and having one stick to use each, meaning you only need two controllers minimum for four players.
The main story took about 10h to beat with three stars on every level (2 players). Alternatively, you can compete with each other in a face-off match and see who can cook more meals in the same time.

I was a backer for this game long before release. In addition to my 700+ Steam hours, I have probably at least that many outside of Steam in the standalone client. I can safely say that this is one of the very few Kickstarter/EA games I've invested in that turned out to be worth it.
In many ways, I view Grim Dawn as a spiritual successor to Titan Quest, Diablo 2, and even Dungeon Siege 2. Much of the gameplay and core mechanics have been carried over from Titan Quest, while much of the atmosphere and style of the gameworld feel reminiscent of Diablo 2 and Dungeon Siege 2 respectively. If you enjoyed any or all of those games, there is plenty to like here. It is not a perfect game and at times it's not an easy game, it has its ups as well as some downs, but it is definitely a good game. It's also pretty well-polished, and the tech is quite stable and doesn't require a beast of a PC to run well.
Crate Entertainment is a very small company, and you can tell that this is an RPG made by a group of people who love RPG's. Grim Dawn goes on sale on both Steam and Humble fairly often, and it's absolutely worth the price to show them some love. Do yourself a favor and check it out!
EDIT: I failed to note that there are some very excellent mods and utilities available for Grim Dawn. However, you'll have to seek them out on sites like Nexus as they are not available via Steam Workshop. The mod community for this game is quite small, but there are still some great mods available for both enhancing gameplay and QoL.

Here's a TL;DR: Great action RPG, good stories and lore, interesting classes. Poor performance, bugs (no, not the ones you squash in game), repetitive gameplay, lots of farming, good items for your build can be hard to get.
I love action RPGS. I really do. I could click things to death all day. This game scratched an itch I've felt since I stopped playing Path of Exile (not available in my region) and Torchlight 2. The game is a click and loot fest, which is great if you enjoy farming. Exploring areas, clearing out dungeons and caves and killing progressively tougher bosses is a lot of fun. You can also tweak and improve your build as you progress. A character that starts off with a sword and shield could be gunning down enemies with a rifle later on.
It's quite satisfying finding the next piece of armour that boosts your build, and there are tons online to follow if you ever get lost. The game also rewards players for exploration with hidden areas and experience rewards for reading about the world of Cairn. You will pick up diaries, notes and other scribblings of people as they try to cope in an incredibly hostile world that you, Player 1, plan to tame.
If this sounds exciting, by all means purchase and play the game. However, the game does have some shortcomings. Firstly, it can be a grindfest. Most new players will hit a "wall" on higher difficulties that will make them wonder why their unstoppable death machine is getting destroyed. The game requires players to research and seek answers online to improve their builds if they want to survive and thrive on Elite and Ultimate difficulties. When you complete normal, you unlock Elite and then Ultimate. If you don't have the time to figure out why weapon X doesn't work with armour Y, you're going to have a bunch of half baked, 40 something characters on your list. Those online builds are helpful but are also not a true reflection of the reality of the game: unless you cheat and use a mod to create items, be prepared to farm.
And boy will you farm. There is an arena mode in the game called The Crucible. It serves as a survival mode (sadly, no endless survival yet) but rewards players with great loot the more waves they face (up until 150). Crucible also has additional difficulties. But be prepared to spend a lot of time killing critters in the hope that an item you can use will drop. It will...eventually. Much of what you're going to find, however, will be for other characters. You could, in theory, build a character to farm items for any other builds you want to make. It is, however, frustating seeing another sorcerer or nightblade item drop when you really need a new weapon.
Very often you'll be hanging onto weapons and armour for 10 or more levels because you just cannot find something that will improve your build to the point that you can progress. When I started, I had to abandon my first character and try another one so I could farm items for the first. It's supposed to encourage players to make different characters and try different builds, but what if you don't want to start a new character? What if you're happy running around with two pistols and not a care in the world? Too bad, Crate will give you nothing but melee weapons and shields. Then when you need better shields, be prepared to see a million pistols and rifles drop.
Next, the gameplay. If you enjoy clicking things to death, it's great. But there is no real variety beyond "point cursor at enemy, hold down or press mouse buttons and watch until the red bar at the top disappears. Loot, rinse, repeat. There isn't a dodge or combo mechanic to change things up a bit. It's pretty straight forward in that regard but in 2017, players may want more from a game than just "heavy atmosphere point and click".
Then there's the bugs. Yes, there are bugs you can kill in game, but ever since the Ashes of Malmouth Expansion, the game is sometimes unplayable with all the crashes. I am at the point where I cannot progress with characters because of all the crashes. Hopefully Crate will fix this in an upcoming patch. Unfortunately, it means they might lose potential players until they fix these bugs. I imagine someone about to pick up a top level Legendary item only for the game to freeze before they can collect their loot. This destroys immersion and leaves players with the impression that the developers don't care.
If you just purchase the base game, you won't have all the nice shiny new stuff that comes with the expansion, but you won't have game crashing, rage inducing bugs. Until the crashes, the game was solid. I'd still recommend the game, but do wait until they fix the bugs.
Finally, the performance. I really wish this game was optimised better. It's annoying walking into a screen full of monsters and the fps drops on a pc that should be able to run it fine (I have a gtx 970 and a core i7). Be prepared to search online for fixes to the performance issues, again, something the devs should have worked on a bit more. Hopefully future patches will address some of these issues.
And don't listen to the fan boys. They will tell you the game is perfect, when it isn't. It's a 7/10, or a 7.5/10 without the bugs on a good day of farming.

FTL is one of my all-time favorite games, partially because every playthough is different. I'll start off by saying "Yes, this game can be incredibly difficult." Some playthroughs end after a few minutes, others in a few hours. Defeat can be extremely frustrating, especially when a random event kills off your pilot, or when you unknowingly arrive close to a star whose solar flares eventually burn your systems into oblivion. BUT it's the amazingly unique stories and chains of events that keep me coming back for more. For example, you may barely escape from the deadly combination of hostiles and a close star by venting the oxygen from the ship. The fire goes out without oxygen to burn, and you send two crewmen on a suicide mission to repair the broken oxygen systems before the rest of the crew sufficates. Your crippled ship escapes, manned by a skeleton crew. What comes next? Maybe a quick death. Or the discovery of a gattling laser for your arsenal. Prehaps your ship is boarded and your crew is killed. Or maybe a willing crewman from a small colony joins you. It was a dangerous journey, they knew that. But HornyFishMan, NuggleSnugg, and HurgaDerga had to do it. It was time they traveled to the West Coast in their trusty station wagon. Leading the group, HornyFishMan picks up his uzi. They hunt. Bandits attack. Some could even aim. They reach a river. They ford it. Boulders... so many boulders... and then the pirate ship attacked. Luckily, there was a rocket launcher in the river. A few quick shots, and it's down. Suck it, Blackbeard.
The group enters the Great Plains. Buffalo buffalo buffalo. The number of buffalo was absurd. HurgaDerga is impaled by a buffalo, and I swear he will be missed. NuggleSnugg and HornyFishMan go on. Horny is healed by health kits that was bought, along with a flame thrower, with the buffalo hide. Remember, the ones that killed HurgaDerga? Revenge is sweet. They see a woman in a red dress. HornyFishMan stops to see if she needs help. It wasn't a trap, and she needs no help. She thanks Horny and sends him away. A civil war battle is underway nearby. The group says hello. There were no survivors.
The group reaches another river. It was time the station wagon went underwater. Water buffalo water buffalo water buffalo. The group reaches an island. Horny notices supplies on the shore. He takes them. It was a trap! PELICANS! Luckily, he survives. They swim to shore.
They reach a mountain pass. Food supplies were running low, so they hunted. No bandits this time, but wolves. So many wolves. They find a trader. They use the wolves they murdered to buy a double-barreled uzi. There is a snow storm, yet the wolves continue to attack. ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s... They deal with the wolves, and see a strange figure in the distance... Horny investigates.
BIGFOOT! Horny runs at him, and having found another flamethrower in the snow, takes him down easily. It is now out of ammo, though, so he gets his double-barreled uzi back out. Infinite ammo rocks! He runs back to the wagon, and the snow storm was rough, so in their panic, they drive off a cliff.
Buffalo followed HornyFishMan and NuggleSnugg off the cliff. So many buffalo. They dodge all the buffalo, and manage to land safely in a river. Having lost their wheels, the station wagon became a raft. They navigated through boulders and fought off alligators. Then they reached a bandit ambush. The bandits attacked with shotguns on their rafts. Successfully defending themselves from the bandits, alligators, and boulders, the group could see the West coast. They almost made it! But then a bandit showed up. He had found some sort of steam boat. Lighting up the boat as much as possible, it wasn't enough. A bandit holding a shotgun on top of the steam boat fired, and Horny wasn't quick to the dodge. NuggleSnugg joined Hurga, after all this time. She came so far, and it didn't even matter. Horny, in all his rage, blew up the boat with his uzi, ending his bandit problem. Reaching shore, Horny shoots pelicans in celebration. He made it to the West coast, though he lost his best friends. He will never forget that fateful Super Amazing Wagon Adventure.

The story is ok, not great for a video game, but it would make a good book. There are new types of Taken that populate the world, and more weapons to take them down. But the game becomes repetitive as you work your way through three different maps three times as you try to complete the written story and escape.
I want to recommend this game if you loved Alan Wake, but don’t expect anything outstanding. If you are seeking an Alan Wake 2 you are more likely to be disappointed.

Having played Saints Row the Third when it was released, I was excited to hear about this expansion pack for the game. This expansion then became a full fledged $60.00 game. I refused to buy this, since the graphics upgrade was barely noticable, you were in the same location with the same buildings, and with a lot of re-used items from the previous game. So, once I got into PC gaming I saw this game on sale for $6.99 with every dlc with it. I gave it a chance, and I loved it. This game has jokes that fans of past games will love, and has some jokes that fall flat on their face. The story is very interesting, but lacks length. I would have prefered it if the story was twenty hours long. The side-quests are nice, and some prove useful; however, besides loyalty missions, there just is not much interesting stuff to do. The biggest problem wiht this game is also its best feature. The super powers. They are great fun and really enjoyable to use. It is a lot of fun to jump extremely high and run of the top of the tallest building and just glide. In reality, it would have been better that they had waited about three to four hours to give you these powers instead of right away. The "boss"/bad guy was really well done. There is one huge thing that happens in the game that makes me a little mad at, and I will not spoil it, but it happens after you get rescued. That is as much as I will say. All in all, this is a fun and interesting game to play. I give this game a score of 8/10, on sale. At thirty dollars for everything, I would give it a 6/10.

About 90% as good as "Freelancer," this game's flight and combat mechanics are easy to pick up and consistently rewarding. The just slightly campy (and lovably so) story is told well, too.
While some games in this genre focus on getting the next ship, "Darkstar One" is all about making one ship work for you. It's a slightly different take on the formula, and it's a good one. Also, the game is pretty forgiving, which is nice when similar titles can be "brickwall difficult" experiences.
I was actually quite surprised with how engaging "Darkstar One" turned out to be. Going in, I was prepared to be disappointed. Instead, I was enthralled.

I enjoyed this game. I was emotionally invested and thoroughly entertained. And yay for fanservice. If you love the show and/or Telltale, you'll have fun with it. However, I offer this recommendation with heavy criticism. This game failed to embody one of Game of Thrones' most important themes -- that of moral ambiguity. The "good guys" and "bad guys" were simply too clearly distinguished here, and the player is always on the "good" side. This is such a wasted opportunity for a game that holds player choice as its defining characteristic. I felt despair in my choices due to the bleakness of the situation but never felt torn apart by moral compromise. In any game, I always play "good." I played "good" here, and the outcome was hardly affected. For a story set in the Game of Thrones universe, this was not at all fitting. Also, Telltale, I know your selling point has always been story. But you fell flat with this story, which made the glaring lack of improvement in your visuals/gameplay all the more apparent.

Greetings El Presidente!  T4 brought back a lot of what people liked about T3 and polished a small amount of it.  I would have to agree with many people who said that the 4th installment didn't bring anything new or spectacular to it.  It did add some wonderful new innovations, but nothing that I'd call groundbreaking.
The Good:
+ An excellently performing graphic engine that's smooth and seamless for almost all views
+ A Caribbean soundtrack that makes you wish for a fruity drink
+ Strategic scenarios that largely feel well written
+ New traits for your Presidente
+ Great new buildings in the Modern Times expansion like the subway station can really help to fix problems on the island
The Bad:
- Some of the traits added would only be taken by those wanting a challenge or the stupid, some are just crippling
- Some of the later scenarios feel drawn out, like they are longer than they needed to be
- An anti-climactic ending for the single player campaign after what are quite a number of hours invested
Overall Impression:
If you like the Tropico series, installments 1 and 3, you will enjoy T4.  (The second game was similar, but thematically and execution-wise, was very different.)  But if you've played T3, don't pay full price for T4.  It's simply not different enough to merit paying full price.

Really good game in my opinion. I started playing this summer and i've quickly played 1000+ hours in just a few months. The game is really addicting with all its big and small features. Having houses, differents mounts and even boats make the game awesome and even more fun to play. Like every MMO there is a lot of text you have to read, which i have honestly just skipped most parts of. Even with little knowledge of the story there are still many other things that i look forward to do. As i write this review i have 1600 hours in the game and i have just entered Mediah, the fourth area in the game, which is actually really slow of me, but there are so much more than just questing to this game. Leveling life skills: Hunting, sailing, cooking is really fun as well. The ammount of detail that goes into life skills are amazing to me. Making a simple stew requires you to go down to the smallest detail, having you get raw materials, turn it into dough for example then continue from there. This process is really cool, but for a lot of things that i make it takes a lot of time, not just gathering all the rare materials for it but also the making.
But aside the good side of the game, there are of course a bad side as well. There are very few armor sets in the game that makes you look different in style. If you really want to look good in the game, you have to buy it, not just with in-game money but mostly with real money. This is also where the "p2w" aspect comes in. I would not say its a "p2w" kind of game but you can buy things like increased weight, inventory space and small gadgets that makes the game easier. You can also sell certain outfits on the market for in-game currency, but i wouldn't say it's a lot of money you can make from that. In the end, i would say this game would definitely be worth its low price. The low game price only compensates for the pearl shop where you buy things with real money. Not only  is the price now, but for an MMORPG there are no monthly cost, which is just aweomse. This game is a really good MMORPG and i would recommend it to anyone who likes RPG kind of games or similar.

Bitesize Review - Alan Wake's American Nightmare
The Good:
- Interesting locations
- Tighter controls than the original game
- Better optimization than the original game
- More gun options for the player to choose from
- Gathering Alan journal pages unlocks more guns for you to use
- Very interesting game, and way to do DLC
- Loved the music at the end of the DLC
The Bad:
- It reuses the same areas of the game over and over, does get a bit old by the end
- It's pretty short
The Verdict:
Overall if you were a fan of the original game but wanted more options in combat and tighter controls this DLC will correct most of those issues for you. The story of this DLC is interesting and it is told well, just like in the original game.
The way the story is told however does mean you visit the same locations over and over and over again which did get old by the time I finished the DLC. Much like with other similarly short games, I recommend buying this on sale. I did enjoy this though with it's gameplay improvements over the original game.

Zen Bound 2 is a calming puzzle solving game revolving (heh heh) around wrapping objects in varying shapes in rope to cover as much of the surface area as possible.
As a puzzler, the game isn't super. The game can't really be "worked out" in terms of puzzling your way through it, it's more of a "try it until you win" sort of game. It must be said though, that the relaxation part of it is quite good.
It's one of the only games I know of to market itself as calming, and to elicit such a response so well. The only other game I can think of really is Fez. The music is chill, light and ambient, and the sounds of the rope stretching and buckling, with paint pellets popping, is rather enjoyable.
Myself, I wasn't a huge fan of the game, and eventually just wanted to get through it. I completed all 10 trees within 3 hours, with 2-3 flowers on each level usually. The gimmick of the paint wrapping can get a bit tedious, but it's still a great game for what it is; a calming experience, and not so much a puzzle-solver.

If you get easily salty cos of bad game mechanics then you shouldn't play this game.
In general I'd suggest everyone to play this game with a walkthrough of it, so everytime when you get stuck you can check the walkthrough and progress further in the game. I play a lot of detective games and I got stuck a lot of times in this game, cos sometimes you literally have to find a bunch of hair somewhere which you can super easily overlook.
And if you reach the point in the game where you have to sneak past a guard and the guard dog: SAVE IMMEDIATELY! Because if you fail to sneak past them, the investigation is over and you have to re-load a save. Since this game does not have autosave, it has happened to me that I forgot to save for quite a while, got caught by the guards and lost progress of almost an hour.
And if you reach the point where you're in a forest which is kind of like a maze: SAVE IMMEDIATELY AGAIN! Because the same thing will happen again if you fail this mission.
Some of the puzzles did not make any sense to me, even with the help of the walkthrough. And the story can get super confusing at one point cos it's connected with so many side stories and I gotta admit that I lost track of what was happening halfway through the game. Still played it until the end cos I wanted to know who the murderer was.
All in all the game wasn't bad. Some mechanics were weird, some puzzles didn't make sense and the story is confusing but it still was an experience and fun to play through it. I'd say buy it when it's on sale so you won't regret spending the whole amount on it (let's be honest, the price is too high).

Important: It's local co-op (or single player) only, DON'T buy if you plan on playing multiplayer online. Also only one person can use keyboard at a time, so if you're playing with multiple people they WILL need controllers (you can also share a controller between two people).
Those warnings aside, I highly recommend checking this out for a local co-op game!
It's like Diner Dash mixed with a Mario Party game, it's so much fun. I've played it solo, as well as with one and two other people, and I definitely think the more the merrier. While it's doable single player (you get used to the controls fairly quickly swapping between the two characters), I think Overcooked thrives on the chaos that ensues from playing with others.
Normally we would play a map the first time completely winging it, which provided the most laughs and hecticness. Then if we didn't get all 3 stars, we'd go back and replay the level with somewhat of a plan on who is doing what.
The controls are generally responsive (note: we all played with Xbox controllers). I have had a bit of trouble with the darker maps not always being able to pick stuff up, but it might just be me being slightly off and not knowing due to the darkness. My friend had a little bit more trouble than me with the hitboxes seeming off (on the normal maps), having to try picking things up several times before it would work...but again I've not really had a problem.
I love that each kitchen adds something slightly new, whether it be a new recipe or various added challenges, so that each level is exciting and different. I also like that they don't include all of the previous challenges, so if you really don't like being on a boat for example you're not stuck being on it for the next several levels.
Definitely check this out, especially if you have friends to play with. I love couch co-op games and will be adding this to my list of favourites to play. :)

Short Answer - I'm pretty neutral on this one. There are lots of things the game did right, but there are a lot of things that put me off. So instead of straight out recommending it, I'd say wait for it to go on sale before getting it.
- Beautifully rendered open world, complete with day and night transitions and lots of other visuals.
- The world feels alive with lots of ambient sounds and lighting.
- Lots of diverse gear and customizations to choose from.
- I really like the devotion tree as an addition to the normal skill tree.
- Large sprawing open maps waiting to be explored.
- I have to say the musical score is pretty nice and works well with the world.
- Many impovments have been made over its predicessor, Titan Quest, including upgraded graphics and combat mechanics.
- Combat feels pretty stiff and clunky for an ARPG. Animations range from meh to eh. Many casting animations are clipped when using a weapon. Very distracting seeing your weapon blinking in and out everytime you attack. Once you see it, it cannot be unseen.
- Combat sound effects don't really feel punchy enough to convey a sense of power. Most seem pretty low key and bland, and don't really draw me into the experience of slaying hoards of monsters. For me this a very important aspect of the game.
- As far as active offensive skills go, there really arent that many to choose from when you get down to it - Most of the skill tree is composed of passive skills and modifiers. Many feel like they do the same thing - And many don't particulary feel interesting.
- Too many skills look very weak and uninspiring in the visual department. Combined with the sounds, I don't really get this sense that I'm kicking  ♥♥♥♥♥  and really taking it to the enemy. But don't take my word alone for it -- youtube demonstrations of the available skills for various classes and come to your own conclusion.
- Male / female characters pretty much look the same - Big and bulky. I'd even argue all classes look the same. Honestly I forgot what gender character I chose after I got all my gear slots filled.
To me in the end it seems like Titan Quest in a different time period with some improvments...and as a fan of norse mythology, while I do appreciate the improvments, I much prefer the setting of Titan Quest. Its not a bad game but for me the lack of hard hitting combat sounds, the shortage of active skills and the somewhat clunky combat system made for very repetitive and almost tiresome gameplay.

Positive part of my review.
Company of Heroes 2 is great.. with mods. The graphics are good, I mean, for a RTS. The resource management is pretty cool though, you'll need to funnel your small amounts of resources into whatever you need to counter your opponent. Unless you're playing with infinite resources, it's not all about clicks per second.
So far I have not delved too far into CoH2's campaign, but I look forward to it.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Negative part.
Want to let your computer go into standby mode? Too bad! The game will crash!.. or maybe Steam will crash. Or maybe your entire computer. There are drops in this game, but they are all practically useless and the good ones are scarce. I swear I have like 50 intel bulletins and next to no commanders or unit skins.
The FPS.. oh dear god the FPS.. 'nuff said.
As much as I hate to say it, this game is heavy on the DLC. You only get two factions to start out with, and even purchasing the DLC only gets you two more. Not to mention the campaign DLC.
Overall? I'd say it's worth it if you like solid resource management and don't mind buying a bit of DLC. CoH2 is also a bit overpriced if you ask me.
I'll leave you with these words. Relic, you did freaking awesome on Dawn of War I in my opinion, lots of races each with a different strategy, good unit variety, tanks are not too OP, (Bloodthirster is a bit much, but I don't really mind) fairly priced, (At least, right now it is) all the DLC is playable as STANDALONE GAMES. (Yes, yes, I know some of this game's DLC can be standalone aswell but at least DoW had some more content) But thats a review for another time.
Do I recommend Company of Heroes 2? Yes and no.

This game is basically if Michael Bay made a video game
First off, you get style points by killing people stylishly, need I say more? I will anyway
Pros:
-Can run on even the worst pc's, due to the not so next gen graphics, but they aren't horrible
-You can do awesome stunts, and get extra points doing it
-Third or First person (I like third person way more, with all the sliding it makes things easier to see)
-Easy controls, but different from most games
-Grenades, guns, punching, punching with guns
-Different classes have different perks and abilities (Not like tf2 classes where each class has a different character and gun)
-Very fun to play for short bursts, or maybe even long ones...
-Good and fun maps, not a whole lot, but you don't really need alot for this game
-You don't unlock anything, you start out with everything, and all the classes and guns are well balanced
Cons:
-Not alot of guns... only...... 7? Not counting the grenades
-Not alot of popularity, so usually there is only 2 or 3 servers with alot of people
-Some people use aimbot, every once in a while there will be one person in the server with a really high score and killing anyone who can see him, or he can see. Without missing. Ever (hence the "aim" in "aimbot")
Preference?
-No matchmaking, you choose the server, which is good for not getting in an empty server
-Graphics aren't super great, but its overall good, which means it runs great with great fps on almost any pc
-There is only 3 models you can use, which overall doesn't really matter to me, but maybe some people wouldn't like. but I doubt it

I won't compare Darkstar One directly to any of the Big Four.  In case you have no idea what I am talking about, then let me give you a hint:  The Big Four games in this genre start with the letters F, P and X.  (Two share the letter 'F' for their name.)  These games are held by many of space sim/combat games to be the pinnacle of the genre.
But I'm not going to invoke the Big Four in direct comparison to Darkstar One.  Comparing DSO to any of those has been done before in other reviews, and at times, I feel this comparison is unjustified, particularly when people say DSO isn't "as good" as the Big Four.
I suspect the developers of DSO have played the Big Four.  There's lots of elements from those games present in DSO -- And, in fact, I would argue that you couldn't MAKE a space sim/combat game without having those elements, either borrowed intentionally or re-created without realizing it.  It's like hold-left-dragging to select units in an RTS game.  That is an extremely common and intuitive manner to select lots of units.  It's become a common verb in RTS games, and in hind sight seems like a very obvious thing to implement and if you were to create an RTS today, you would implement mass-unit selection in that very manner.  To do otherwise would be unnatural and new players would complain.  Someone else found the most optimal verb for expressing an intent, and it's become a part of the building bible for the RTS genre.
Therefore, DSO uses a lot of the same verbs as the Big Four.  If you've played the Big Four, then practically nothing in DSO will seem out of place.  It's all there, it works like you expect it to, and that is what makes this game a lot of fun, even for someone such as myself.  I've played practically every major and note-worthy space sim/combat game out there, and that's not really much of a boast considering that I can only think of a dozen in my entire lifetime as a gamer.  This isn't a genre that gets a lot of attention.
DSO does it right and does it competently.
If you are a die-hard Big Four fan, you can't go wrong with DSO.  Just give it a chance.  The graphics are good, the voice-overs are decent, the plot and characters are okay, and the game mechanics are just fine.  There's all the elements you would expect from this genre:  Exploring, trading, bounty-hunting, alliance/allegiance shifting, pirates, Big Scary Aliens Doing Bad Stuff To Everyone, Mysteries to Uncover, etc.  The whole kit and kaboodle.
The only real issue with DSO is that it doesn't bring much new to the table aside from the single, upgradable ship instead of the more typical ladder-climbing of purchasing better ships.  I also like how they implemented the cargo carrying system, as it allows your super agile combat ship to suddenly take on the characteristics of a slow, vulnerable cargo vessel without forcing you to switch ships or land at a station first.  That was well thought out.
The game is well made and both looks pretty good and plays well enough for what it is.  And damn, you can't beat the price.  (Under $3 as of this review.  I would have gladly paid far more for this game, if I had known about it before hand.)
If you aren't a fan of the Big Four, and in fact if you are confused about what I am talking about:  Give DSO a try.  It's a good starting point for someone interested in this genre.  If you want more, then don't worry.  The Big Four are still around and you can pick them up at bargin prices.  (For the uninitiated, most of the Big Four are really old games.  Like, one of them is a DOS game!  See what I mean about this genre not getting much love and attention?)
DSO is worth it, no matter if you are a fanatic of the genre or not.  It's not going to blow you away, but it will provide many hours of solid, fun gaming and that's more than can be said for %90 of what is on Steam. :)
Kudos to the developer of DSO for making such an enjoyable game in this genre!

When I first played this game (about 3 years ago), I had a great feeling, as if I was a mastermind of a giant war operation. That was fun. Few years later, Enemy Within came out. I didn't see anything in it, so I passed. At first. Then I heard about a mod, called Long War, that made the game harder and... better. I thought I'd give it a try. I bought Enemy Within and Slingshot, downloaded the mod...
I've played Long War for about 8 months. Sure, there were long breaks from XCOM, sometimes months long. But I'm still going. The game is mostly same strategy, sure. But instead of feeling like a great asskicking mastermind I feel like... an insignificant distraction for alien forces. Every mission feels like a punch in the gut, and I'm lucky if every solder survived that mission. The funding from the Council is usually no enough, the soldiers are consantly panicking and sectoids are using same genetic thech we're using, so now they've got 5 points of health and a random ability.
XCOM 2 came out couple of days ago, right? I heard they made it harder then Enemy Unknown. Yeah, right. I'll still will try to beat EU with Long War mod. It will take time. Weeks, months, hell, maybe years. But it's too damn good to throw away like that.
So, in short, if you don't have the money to buy XCOM 2, like me, buy this one. Then install the Long War mod (after you finished the game, because it'll be impossible for new players), and pretend to use guerilla tactics. It's one of the best games out there, and you won't find such a rewarding expirience even in Dark Souls.

What's more to say, it's another great game from Telltale,
And i think this telltale game have the most difficult choices so far

Grim Dawn is an exceptionally mediocre game. It has lots of promise but like an early access title many parts are poorly executed and unintuitive. Don't mistake this for complexity though, while the game has that, this is unnecessary opacity.
You will find areas you cannot access but the game wont make that apparent and you may waste large amounts of time attempting to find off map areas that are quest locked.
You will scale your damage incorrectly because things like "Pierce" and "Bleed" are not "Physical" damage.
You will not know what consumable items have any value and the game will not explain their function in any clear manner.
You will open the devotion tab and not know anything, there is no way to clearly identify which constellation is associated with what damage type or compare different ones so you're either going to fumble through or google that it which certainly detracts from the experience.
I was hoping for an ARPG that would distract me from the glaring flaws that Path of Exile has but instead I found one that reminded me how good it is. Go play PoE instead. This game is... Meh.
Edit: A number of Grim Dawn fans have taken it upon themselves to insult my intelligence because I pointed out some glaring flaws the game has. Yeah, I'm sure after 2.5 times my current 18 hours I'd have stumbled past a few of these problems enough to know what to expect. I'm sure after... The 8000hours that "Powbam" has played I might have all the devotion options memorized and be able to easily remember which is comparably more efficient and powerful without referencing an external cheat sheet. I am maligning the lack of explanation for unintuitive mechanics and poor streamlining and these fans have become defensive. Ignore them.

Short Answer - I'm pretty neutral on this one. There are lots of things the game did right, but there are a lot of things that put me off. So instead of straight out recommending it, I'd say wait for it to go on sale before getting it.
- Beautifully rendered open world, complete with day and night transitions and lots of other visuals.
- The world feels alive with lots of ambient sounds and lighting.
- Lots of diverse gear and customizations to choose from.
- I really like the devotion tree as an addition to the normal skill tree.
- Large sprawing open maps waiting to be explored.
- I have to say the musical score is pretty nice and works well with the world.
- Many impovments have been made over its predicessor, Titan Quest, including upgraded graphics and combat mechanics.
- Combat feels pretty stiff and clunky for an ARPG. Animations range from meh to eh. Many casting animations are clipped when using a weapon. Very distracting seeing your weapon blinking in and out everytime you attack. Once you see it, it cannot be unseen.
- Combat sound effects don't really feel punchy enough to convey a sense of power. Most seem pretty low key and bland, and don't really draw me into the experience of slaying hoards of monsters. For me this a very important aspect of the game.
- As far as active offensive skills go, there really arent that many to choose from when you get down to it - Most of the skill tree is composed of passive skills and modifiers. Many feel like they do the same thing - And many don't particulary feel interesting.
- Too many skills look very weak and uninspiring in the visual department. Combined with the sounds, I don't really get this sense that I'm kicking  ♥♥♥♥♥  and really taking it to the enemy. But don't take my word alone for it -- youtube demonstrations of the available skills for various classes and come to your own conclusion.
- Male / female characters pretty much look the same - Big and bulky. I'd even argue all classes look the same. Honestly I forgot what gender character I chose after I got all my gear slots filled.
To me in the end it seems like Titan Quest in a different time period with some improvments...and as a fan of norse mythology, while I do appreciate the improvments, I much prefer the setting of Titan Quest. Its not a bad game but for me the lack of hard hitting combat sounds, the shortage of active skills and the somewhat clunky combat system made for very repetitive and almost tiresome gameplay.

Starward Rogue is rogue-lite, twinstick shooter set in a space style environement. It's a throwback to the old arcade/Atari days, rebuilt with modern graphics, and mechanics.
I won't go into a lot of detail here because I have created a YouTube video covering one of my runs, which shows all the elements of the game. But, I will provide the typical pros/cons.
+Rebindable Keys/Controller Buttons
+Good Soundtrack/Effects
+Large Variety of Items
+Large Variety of Enemies
+Decent Variety of Mechs (Player Vehicles)
+Creative Bosses/Mini-Bosses
+Athestically Pleasing
+Saves on Exit
+Unique Perks
-Spikes Can Be Hard To See
-Some Minor Bugs
-Aiming On Controller Feels Locked To Grid
-Tutorial Failed To Mention 1-2 Controls Vital To Gameplay (Or I Missed The Text Cue)
-No Long Term Progression/Unlocks - A Run Is Over When It's Over (Permadeath)
Think if Invaders + Defender + Binding of Isaac + Nuclear Throne had a love child, Starward Rogue would be the result. More in-depth review included in the YouTube video.

I am no Sherlock Holmes !
This is one of the earliest games in Sherlock Holmes series by Frogwares, and it shows its age.
Positive
+ It's a Sherlock Holmes game
Negative
- Story is overcomplicated, too many things, too many people, too many clues. And the game doesn't have a good system to track everything together.
- Gameplay elements are inconsistent. Sometimes actions require you to click on an object in the gameworld, sometimes you need to click the same object in inventory, or drag-and-drop two objects on top of each other, sometimes you need to use magnifying glass, sometimes you don't. It's a bit confusing.
- Crashes - There are few places that cause the game to crash consistently, loosing all your progress since the last save.
- Spot the dot - In some areas you literally need to find one small spec in one big room.
- Font in messages/books is unreadable !
Overall, there isn't really anything special about this, I would suggest trying newer games in the series, they are much more streamlined.

Customizing your ship with weapons and special abilities is the best part about this game. While space battles are well done, fun, and with good physics, it does get boring somewhat quickly. The main missions and side quests can be interesting as it progresses through the storyline, but it does not give you a feeling of great accomplishment as you go through them. The trading aspect of the game can and might as well be ignored completely. It provides you with minimal profits in comparison to the other means to acquire credits. Speaking of credits, I completed the game with 8.5 million credits in my possession. After a while, the amount of credits you accumulate will become obsolete, as you will have more than enough to get whatever you want. The game suffers from extreme repetitiveness, which also creates tedium and dullness when you do the same two or three activities over, and over, and over, and over. Simply put, the game is about 20 hours too long. The developers should have been more concise and implemented more diverse aspects in more ways than just this. The end game is surprisingly bland and unexciting. Also, throughout the game, you are given a false sense of freewill. Your progress is almost completely linear.

Secondly, a way too big part of my 4 hours of playtime was driving around in an airboat avoiding enemy fire and just trying to get away from those enemies as fast as possible while not getting much of a chance to explore your surroundings.
The parts where you fight zombies weren't good to me either since they seem to have the mental capacity of a three year old and most of them are cannonfodder rather than an actual enemy. The only thing they have going for them is that they have quite some HP and are seriously disgusting to look at.
I do think that the gravity gun is a really original weapon and that it was fun to use for a bit, but it did grow stale pretty quickly.
Lastly the game's story did seem interesting to me but I never got to finish it because the gameplay is much less interesting.

At first I thought 'Oh great another top-down shooter' and went into the game half hearted. Once the action started, I was immediately faced with fierce opposition & devastion. Overall, I find this game very fun to play. Things can get very frantic & unforgiving on harder difficulty settings which I think is great for diehard players. I fully recommend Starward Roque.

An addictive blend of a twin-stick shmup with procedural death labyrinth floors and per-run perks and item collection, this game is perhaps less "genre defying" than some of Arcen's releases, but it's certainly not cliché.
From the start, the game impresses with color. Like a variegated ballet, you weave through a diversity of bullet patterns and enemy types, clearing rooms and floors as you progress ever deeper into The Monolith. Each time you level up, you select a perk from a given set to customize your mech. Additionally, you find or acquire robot companions, attachments and other bonuses to further mutate the experience. This makes each run slightly different than the last, rewarding flexibility and adaptation.
There's so much content included with the base game, you'll be finding new items and enemies even after hours of playtime. A great strength of the game is how easily content can be added or modified. In fact, a portion of the included rooms, enemies and bosses were created by community members, vetted by Arcen and released with the game. Arcen has said they intend to release additional content for what is an already content rich game.
Easily worth the asking price and oozing with replayability. Each time I die, I say "
time, I'll try..." and the cycle starts anew.
Note: I was provided a Steam key for the game for participating in testing prior to release.
