Disclosure: I was provided a free copy and gave feedback on the game in the alpha/beta phases.
If you like Nuclear Throne and/or Binding of Isaac: Rebirth, this is an excellent game for you. If you don't, this is a great introduction to the rogue-lite genre.
Much like the aforementioned 2 games, this is a top-down rogue-lite with secrets and rooms of enemies. So what makes this one different?
- More interesting rooms. The rooms in Isaac and Throne are mostly afterthoughts -- simple arenas in which to fight enemies. Here, you generally get far more interesting patterns.
- More bullet hell. The other games take inspiration from the SHMUP genre, but they're too afraid to go all the way, preferring enemies that charge at you and simple bullets. Starward Rogue goes full SHMUP, with really cool bullet patterns that make dodging a real challenge. Think the Hush from Rebirth, but without the crazy HP.
- Cool sci-fi feel. This genre was really missing a true sci-fi setting, and this is it.
- Excellent *hi-res* art. Isn't it about time we got good art in rogue-lites? Why do they all want to use low-res art? The art here is beautiful and detailed. Each bullet glows with energy, and the explosions are satisfying.
- Explosions. Awesome explosions everywhere!
- Crazy good music. Seriously, just listen to the trailer.
- Easy to mod. Remember how Rebirth needed forever to give us modding tools? Well Starward Rogue has them out *now*. Make good enough rooms/enemies, and Arcen will even put them in the official game. How cool is that?
What I would like to see:
- A daily run. This has become standard among rogue-lites.
- Some co-op action, even if it's local only.
- Networking co-op would be even better.
All in all, I highly recommend this game.

I love me some detective adventure games where you got to gather clues and interrogate people. Games such as Discworld Noir and Under A Killing Moon do it really well and it's kinda sad that so few games in the genre exist. The Silver Earring is another of these games which does not rely upon "use item X with item Y" puzzles but rather on cross-examination, investigation and tying elements together.
It doesn't do it as well as the above-mentioned examples, however. In most areas the games is quite adequate but never more than that, and in some areas the game is rather poor. Here's a list of PRO's and CON's:
PRO
- The game keeps track of everything you collect & where you collected it in list-form. Same with dialogs and letters and other evidence. Very tidy and handy
- the Quiz between chapters is pretty well done and forces you to think for yourself
- the backdrops are pretty well designed
- the game has a nice attention to detail in true Sherlock Holmes fashion
- the murder mystery is actually quite engaging
CON
- the dialog is very hit & miss - some parts are simply poorly written while others are quite convincing. The voice actors are mostly average at best
- the characters you meet are not that interesting or simply break immersion by being unbelievable (the drunks outside for example)
- the interface is a bit of a chore to say the least.
- sometimes the game will let you "use" an object through dialog and sometimes you got to drag it onto a person - the game is very inconcistent like that. Since you pick up loads of items, this can be very tedious if you get stuck
- the game heavily relies on linearity - you need to find every single clue before it will continue which can be infuriating. A walkthrough is a must if you want to enjoy the game!
- the music is not very appropriate a lot of the time and harms the immersion.
- the Quiz requires every single answer to be correct and in two instances, I found that the question was confusing so I had to cheat.
- Holmes is even more of a jerk than the books make him out to be - he's plainly rude half the time.
Do I recommend this game? Just about but barely and only with a walkthrough. If you love murder mysteries, this is still a nice game if you can forgive its flaws ... .

The game is in many ways extremely flawed. The GUI is a complete pain, especially in portions where Sherlock needs to be moved around with precision, as he requires several second to just turn around, even when trying to avoid guards, and the game world is filled with invisible walls. The fixed third-person perspective also often turns the game into pixel hunt. Besides that, the game also pointlessly makes the player manually select dialogue options, even though all need to be cycled through, and all are recording in the journal, so there's no need to ever revisit them.
Meanwhile, the story does make for an entertaining enough whodunnit, which isn't dampened even by the dismal voice-acting. At the end of each chapter the game makes the player pick the right clues to yield the correct deduction, which is a neat feature, as it prompts the player to pay attention and use their noggin, instead of just clicking on everything and letting Sherlock do the reasoning. For most part, the deductions are sensible, too, though all the contrived puzzles people use to lock their saves and whathaveyou certainly push the limits of believability.

Before buying this game, be aware of these two things:
1. If you have an unusual monitor resolution, the game's hot spots may be improperly synced, making it impossible to interact with things. I was only able to fix this by switching to a different monitor. I've only heard of one other person having this problem, however.
2. There is a missable clue in the first chapter which breaks the game near the end. The game requires you to pick up all necessary clues before moving on except this glitched one. Consult a guide and save yourself the hours it'll take to start over.
All in all, Silver Earring has taken a huge step from Mystery of the Mummy. The story, gameplay, controls, and voice acting are all vastly improved. This game marks where the series really began to capture the traditional Sherlock Holmes vibe. Unlike many mystery games where the protagonist seems to be a complete idiot, Holmes is always a step ahead without leaving the player feeling completely lost. The end-of-chapter quizzes really help to keep you up with the story, so you don't find yourself simply clicking around with no idea what's going on.
Though the game is an overall improvement from it's predecessor, it does have its share of problems. The occasional typos and strange subtitles were more funny than annoying to me. The Action/Stealth sections can be a bit difficult as Holmes is not always easy to control, but with a few tries they can be mastered. For the most part, if you are forgiving of the game's age it will be easier to enjoy.

Having played through the previous Holmes games from Frogwares (I got the bundle), this represents a massive improvement compared to Mystery of the Mummy. The key crime occurs soon after you begin, and what follows is a (mostly) methodical investigation that mixes interrogation and evidence gathering/examining.
Having said that, the game is riddled with faults - a lot of the time you have to hunt for microscopic items to progress in the investigation, the placement of 'cursor spots' (for pathing and interactive points in the environment) is incredibly poor, the music is repetitive and dull, the translation for the English language version could have gone a lot better (and they could have used *any* font other than Comic Sans), the end of day quiz that summarises events doesn't tell you which answers are incorrect when you have to retry, inventory items have to combined in specific orders, and during the very lengthy conclusion, virtually *every* clue is explained, regardless of it's ultimate relevance.
Ultimately, unless you are a fan of the 'classic' Holmes, The Silver Earring will likely be a very dry, tedious experience, however, compared to the garbage that came before it, it can only be recommended on that merit.

This game feels abysmally one dimensional compared to earlier tell tale titles. If you're a massive fan of GoT you might genuinely enjoy this, however if you're a fan of games that adapt to your decisions, you needn't play this game. 90% or more of the choices you make are meaningless, nothing changes, sometimes not even the dialogue, the options are there purely to give you the illusion of choice. While definitely entertaining, and long enough to justify it on sale, I could not reccomend this at full price. This game is less your story, and more of a story that someone else wanted to tell.
For the bonus point, telltale has neglected to go back and check (for many dialogue options) that what you choose and what is actually said are consistent. In fact, there are many times where the voice actors dont even speak the entire line, if not for subtitles I would have missed this, I don't think it's ever been super important, but it's one of those small quality control things, I personally would expect from a game that has very little going for it.
Another thing, less to do with this game specifically, but TTG in general.  For a developer surviving off games with subpar  graphics, lack of actual gameplay, and being technically unimpressive, there are many super small details that they need to incorporate so that when their game finally crashes (and it will at least once) you don't need to sit through 15 minutes of dialogue you've already heard. E.g. There are no skip buttons for dialogue and no way to skip cutscenes, instead TT gives us two (2) pause buttons. This becomes rather frustrating, when you need to either restart the game due to crashing, or wish to change a decision. Without spoiling the game, suffice it to say I tried keeping a certain character alive but in fact all options lead to his death regaurdless, and the many hours I sunk into repeated dialogue, trying different combinations of choices, for nothing,  was very disappointing.

Coop seems to be an afterthought:
The teammate healthbar updates once every 2 seconds, there's no way to see which teammate is who on the map (Why is giving each player a different color so difficult?) so you can't really help eachother with aggro/CC when they're in trouble. There's no way to "view monsters" with some sort of overlay and with 4 people things get too chaotic to properly react to AoE. Host gets more experience due to a bug (He gets each "lore bonus" 4 times, for some reason), and you quickly get to be 2 levels above your party. There's no combat log. You have to guess what damage type monsters are doing. You have to guess how well your build is doing. This is even a bigger problem with coop. You can't tell if your build is good or your friends are just doing very good and making up for you.
Many things are not properly explained, the "codex" lacks tons of information. The wiki is barely kept up to date and also lacks a lot of information.
At the end of the day the only reason we're playing this is because we don't have anything else better to play together after almost tens of thousands of hours in every possible multiplayer games over a decade, from TF2 to Dota and borderlands. Don't look at it as Alan Wake 2. This is much more along the lines of expansion. It is much less horror-like than original game, instead going for atmosphere of solitude of three remote, almost desolate, locations located along the same road with a bit of mistery. It is also quite short and, fraknly, it needs to be because the entire game expolres one particular trope/gimmick, and while it does that very, very well, should it be longer, it would simply become tiresome. Disclaimer: Was part of the beta and received a free key, hours played are also going to be off as a result.
Review: As someone who is extremely unfamiliar with the genre of shmups and bullet hell, I found the game very easy to get in to and its controls very intuitive. The combat is fast-paced and diverse but also has a very tactical level to it as well; almost nothing shoots at random, so the game rewards being able to think as much as hair-trigger reflexes.
For the price, there's a lot of game to run at and good replayability, expanded even further by the difficulty levels. This is definitely not the sort of game where each boss you run into is just a slight reskin of the last. There's a huge amount of enemy and room variation. In all of my playtime, I've yet to feel like I've seen a room over and over. The game is also likely to see even further expansion in enemy types and rooms (amongst quite possibly a lot of other things) thanks to the level of modding that Arcen have enabled for the game and how supportive they are being about it as a developer.
Overall, I'd say it's definitely a very fun game, accessible to a wide range of skill levels and, had I not been in the beta, one that I'd be happily buying right now.

I've been a fan of Arcen Games for quite a long time now, and I own every game they've made.  They always create unique experiences that are hard - sometimes impossible - to find elsewhere.  Starward Rogue is no exception.  It's an action rogue-like with bullet hell influences.  You have 6 mechs to choose from, each with different stats.  During your game, you'll encounter tons of perks, equipment, and weapons to aid, or sometimes hinder, your quest.  There are bosses, enemies, and items to unlock on multiple playthroughs.  You'll fight through 5 pseudo randomly generated levels, each ending in a boss fight.  A single run should take around 30 minutes to an hour to complete, depending on your play-style and difficulty.  If you find it too easy or too hard, there are 5 difficulty levels to choose from.  Both keyboard/mouse and gamepad are equally playable.  All of the keys are rebindable, so it should be trivial to suit the controls to your taste.  Twin-stick shooter verterans will be perfectly at home.  All told, it's an awesome game that any fan of the genre should enjoy.

Disclaimer: Was part of the late private beta and received a free key for the game from the developer. My playtime exceeds the possible gameplay time since release on Steam cause of that.
Now onwards to the review.
Bullet extravaganza extraordinaire. Definitely shmup and roguelike gameplay. Everytime I play it it remembers me of the movie Tron. As always a magnificient soundtrack from Pablo Vega bringing back those pac-man era feelings.
In this game you play as one of 6 choosable mechs. Be it the Flame Tank (kinda beginners mech and my favorite), Red Shift aka time dilation mech (when you don't move or shoot time stands still), White Gloss (average mech with rail cannon), Indigo pole with its magnetic missile launcher that pulls any bullets towards it, Green Envy mech that is meant for players who like loot (higher chance to get credit/keycard) and Deep blue mech with weaker attack but with a droid companion from start.
Essentially each run is divided in to five to seven floors in which you fight through a procedually generated dungeon (from premade maps). You have rooms full of traps like laser beams blocking your way, fire canons shooting fireballs occasionally, moving walls trying to crush you depending on how you move. There are very thin bullets flying through air and blocking your way forcing you to slowly puzzle your way through them without getting killed. There are maze rooms with arrow mazes testing you if you can find the way to the middle where your award awaits (if it was worth the hussle who knows).
Each room you go through has its purpose. Some rooms are protecting bigger amount of health pack or health shards, (8 health shards increase your total healt) or a ton of credits. Some rooms are long hallways where treacherous nearly non beatable enemies await. Rooms with teleporter mazes (hm, which one is it going to get me to that blasted mini room? ).
There we have countless mini bosses that can make you pay for your mistake like Hunter who is trying to get you with his shield lines to make you go slower. Or Reaper who likes to lash you and kill you slowly. Then we have countless bosses that all have their personal bullet hells ready for you. There is Crystal Mother with its bullet and bullet lines and bullet walls. Wallmaster with its exchanging bullet walls. Labrinyth with its four henchmen and many many more. Every boss more or less has three stages with which he shows his anger at you after you injure him sufficiently.
With every floor that you reach and fight through the stakes grow and the game gets harder but not impossible.
This is one of those games where you think "Just one more run" aka "just one more turn" and the hours go past without you noticing that its already evening :) When you start the game you will ultimately die very fast but with each run the game will get easier when you begin to understand how to play and what the dangers are but remember nothing will save you from the bosses but your own skill :)
Highly recommended!
Will definitely rebuy it later for support.

The leap between Mystery of the Mummy and The Silver Earring is pretty astounding.  The Mystery of the Mummy was predominately a first-person (as in Myst/Riven) adventure with low resolution textures.  Two years later with The Silver Earring, the game becomes a point and click adventure with respectably nice graphics.
In this adventure, Holmes and Watson witness the murder of the host to a gun shot at a dinner party they were invited to but didn't see the shooter.  In fact no one saw the shooter, and it is up to Holmes and Watsons to gather testimonials, clues, and documents to solve the mystery.
Overall, it was a pleasant surprise.  The game looks largely pre-rendered, which meant the environment looks nice for such an old game, the trade-off being that people, who aren't pre-rendered, may be disproportionate in size to their surroundings.  For example, when Holmes stands next to a doorway, he might be much taller than it from one camera angle, but look perfectly fine in another.  My biggest gripe is that the controls can be clumsy when trying to control characters to move somewhere, being unresponsive at times unless the character is repositioned.
Despite the problem, it's still worth a playthrough.  Every now and then, Holmes and Watson summarize their findings and you're quizzed with Yes or No questions.  For each answer, you have to justify your choice by selecting the appropriate evidence/testimonial.  While the game provides color-coded indicators for choosing testimonial, evidince, or documents, it's pretty cool that it requires you to actually keep up with reading the findings in order to progress through the game.  The game provides a database to look back on previous conversations and findings so a pen and paper is not needed to keep records yourself.
This game is recommended on the note that the diminishing point is the clumsy controls.  On a last note, I played the game using DxWnd in order to put the game into windowed mode, which is not natively supported, otherwise the image will be stretched if you have a widescreen monitor.

Darkstar One is a space flight simulator in the trade/fight/explore genre that most people are familiar with from games like Elite and Freelancer. Darkstar One is not a game that deviates much from the tried and true, most of the features and design direction you find in Darkstar you will also find in the older successes of the genre.
You play the game as Kayron Jarvis, a young pilot who's father was recently killed through nefarious means and you set out to discover the truth. Of course you will quickly trip over a number of large conspiracies and eventually have to save the galaxy from an evil race of aliens. That is all standard.
To aid you in this quest you have the unique and powerful spaceship "Darkstar One" at your disposal. Unlike other games in the genre you will be stuck inside this one ship for the entirety of the game. That is not to say you will be stuck with the same capabilities for the entire game. As you progress through the game you will find artifacts for your Darkstar that will allow you to upgrade your ship with additional weapons and turrets.
Visually, Darkstar One looks pretty enough not to disappoint. The special effects are not overdone, and the visible part of the ship's cockpit feels gritty and natural. The design of the ships and other larger space vessels is striking at first, but it does become somewhat repetitive after a while.
The sound effects, while not top-notch were good enough to sort of blend into the gameplay seamlessly. The voice acting, on the other hand, is mysteriously void of the "acting" part. Blame it on the fact that the game was translated from German.
The biggest problem that Darkstar has by far is the fact that it simply feels like a pale copy of other, far more successful games in the genre. There is nothing in it to grab you while playing. The combat is overly simplistic after you master the controls and the story is about as engaging as the evening news. You almost get the feeling that Darkstar One was put together by people who either didn't know how to make an interesting game, or simply lacked the will to do it. Darkstar One is in need of fire and passion; it lacks the imagination and creativity needed to captivate the player. The gameplay feels flat and it becomes very tedious after a while. Even though the initial impressions may suggest differently, Darkstar One doesn't deliver the type of experience that space sim fans are looking for.
It's not a game I'd normally recommend to anyone but it just happens to be in a genre that is woefully short on quality these days so if you're fan of the genre you will probably end up playing this at some point regardless of it's faults.

First off, do I play this game: Sometimes.
Do I enjoy this game: About the first couple of missions.
Will I kill myself for giving this game a negative review: No, not really.
Xcom: Enemy Unkown and it's expansion are the continuations of a long-going series of tactics games where you kill alien invaders with your army of highly trained soldiers. Aesthetically everything's here, from the futuristic vehicles and guns, to the traditional-looking and ruthless aliens who see us as nothing more than cattle to be probed; quite frankly, this game's premise is rock-solid. However, the reason I cannot recommend this game to anyone is, because for $30, you're getting a good-looking mess of a tactics game that lacks any sense of fairness or satisfaction.
Now-now, I know what you're thinking: "SHUT UP YOU ♥♥♥♥♥♥, YOU'RE JUST BAD!" And I'd gladly take your word for it if it werent for the fact that, no, no I'm not, and in fact I'd even say that it's impossible to be good at this game. Anyone who's played a tactics game before knows how it works: You get a force of so-many people, moving them around a grid-like map, utilizing different terrains, angles, etc., and engaging the enemy's units before ending your turn. For the most-part, Xcom works in the same manner, as you take your soldiers and hop them from cover-to-cover, engaging aliens that pop up every now-and-again.
That's all well and good, until you get to realizing that you've missed a lot of high-percentage chances to hit your targets, or that your sniper just got critted while behind heavy cover, or that's the fifth time in a row that one of your soldiers has been hit by an enemy set up for overwatch. It's at this point that you start to wonder what exactly it is you're doing wrong, maybe you need to move here instead of there, maybe this loadout is better than that one? But eventually, like me, you come to the realization that Xcom is designed to be a game that you can't win through sheer will and problem-solving skills, but by luck.
In the grand scheme of the game's layout, there is really no way to win at Xcom other than to get lucky, which is a sad, but brutally true fact that nobody can deny. Almost no tactical decision you make will have any outcome on a battle because of the completely incompetent RNG system, which, for a tactics game, is a rather silly design choice. What's that? You moved your unit into the perfect spot to flank a suppressed enemy who you need to kill to save your medic's life? Sorry, the RNG isn't in your favor today, friend; rest in piece medic.
Keep in mind that I understand RNG is present in a lot of tactics games, and is supposed to represent many different factors of an engagement. But we're not talking about a guy with a sword swinging at a guy with a spear here, we're talking about a soldier behind a concrete wall being shot in the head with a pistol and instantly killed (am I supposed to believe that there's a percentage that the concrete wall didn't feel like doing it's job today?). But I could rant about this game's ridiculously idiotic and game-breaking RNG tables all day, and even then, it still wouldn't be enough to convince you this game is bad, especially if you're into rogue-likes.
So that's it then, Xcom is obviously not a game for regular tactics fans, seeing as there are no tactics involved, and the outcome of battles are based solely on what the computer feels like at that given moment. This game is obviously designed to be a rogue-like, which, it still fails as in every manner, and while I admit I don't like rogue-likes, I do know what makes them "good" and playable for other's.
The reason that Xcom fails as a roguelike is because it's progression is slow and at the mercy of a story, where-as most rogue-likes are about hitting that start button and seeing how far you can get before falling into an unavoidable pit. On top of that, one feature present in every rogue-like is some manner of progression through the form of unlocks, thus allowing you to start again with a special buff, making the game easier or at least giving you a more comfortable way to play. Xcom doesn't have that, if you lose the campaign, it's over, done, better luck next time amigo, combined with slow, unenthusiastic tactical combat sessions that amount to nothing more that "how much time can I waste on this screen before the game decides who wins?"
As a tactics game, this is completely unplayable, as a roguelike, maybe. In summary, this is a glorified, boring rogue-like being marketed as a "hard" tactics game for a price as unfair as it's RNG.

XCOM: Enemy Unkown + Enemy Within is not a story heavy game by any means.
The story is quite simple and generic: Aliens invade earth, you are the commander of an elite military group (XCOM) that has been tasked with stopping them at all costs and saving earth. That is the basic plot of the game.
There are a  few story twists (I won't spoil), none of them feel particulary surprising or unexpected and dont really develop the story much further. Even at the end of the game when
it feels underwhelming.
Also, while Enemy Within adds another faction, that is sympathetic to the aliens, into the mix, the plot and story is still the same. However, XCOM gives you the ability to name all of your soldiers, be it after friends, celebrities, famous figures, etc., which adds a very unique sense of depth and attachment.
For example - On one of my many playthroughs of the game I used my friends as my soldiers and this gave me an instant attachment to the characters. While playing on ironman, once I lost a soldier, that was it. Dead. No old save to save them. They were dead. And through this mode I honestly felt a sense of loss after one of my good friends, who had survived the majority of the game, died after being upgraded and ranked up through multiple mission successes. XCOM gives you the choice to MAKE your characters - something a lot of games don't.
Overall Story Score = 6/10 (Good)
XCOM is a turn-based strategy game, developed by Firaxis who have cemented themselves as masters of the genre.
The general gameplay of XCOM is split into two chunks.
Chunk one is the base building + management part of the game. This part of the game takes place at XCOM HQ and will have you, the commander, managing XCOM in every aspect - research, engineering, troop management, construction of new facilities for the HQ, UFO defence, management of the council, etc., this chunk of the game has a HUGE amount of depth, and while at first it can be a bit overwhelming, it's not too difficult to learn.
The second chunk of the game is the most exciting - fighting the aliens. This section of the game has you go out to abduction sites etc. and fight the alien attackers. The turn-based strategy element is excellently pulled off and works incredibly well and the general map design is amazing (although a few maps were not great).
Enemy Within also adds in some new elements which drastically change gameplay, including mech and bionic troops, more customisation, new enemies, a new enemy faction and MELD - a resource that is invaluable to you that in turn speeds up the game.
XCOM also has a multitude of game options such as damage roulette, randomised skills and the wonderful ironman mode. I would heavily advise playing on ironman mode - it makes XCOM the full package in my opinion. Ironman mode removes the ability to reload an earlier save, making the game much more intense as every move could be a wrong one, leading to the permanent death of one of your soldiers. It does add difficulty to the already difficult game - but trust me, its the best way to play.  Enemy Within also adds extra game modifiers to freshen the experience.
Upon starting the game for the first time, I remember feeling comfortable at first, thinking I was getting on fine with the game, doing well... Nope. XCOM has a habit of constantly reminding you that you are NOT the superior race, that the aliens are better than you and that they WILL hand your♥♥♥♥♥to you. multiple times. Please keep in mind I've only played through the game on normal difficulty. The harder ones will punish you for everything. However, I soon learned that the game was not unfairly difficult, it was simply the fault of me not paying attention to some parts of the game, such as, not researching the right things, etc. XCOM is a game that will make you suffer and say "try again you noob" until you learn how to utilise everything at your disposal to its fullest. This is what I personally love most about XCOM.
While the gameplay of XCOM in both the management and RTS sections is hugely fun, addictive and replayable, there is one problem I noticed while playing:
The 'chance to hit' system - I love this system, its perfect for XCOM - however - the problem is that sometimes it doesn't make sense at all. While most of the time the chance to hit is understandable and resonable, there have been a few occasions I have been point blank next to an enemy and had ridiculously low hit chance and my soldier has completely missed. most often this leads to their unfair demise.
Overall Gameplay Score = 9/10 (Masterful)
While XCOM is by no means a graphical master, it is also by no means a bad looking game.
The graphics options in XCOM are pretty good - AA, AO, texture settings, V-sync, etc. - Its all there (as you would expect from a good PC game). I run XCOM on a pretty good spec laptop (it can run Bioshock Infinite 60fps ultra (check my profile for full specs)) and I have no framerate dips what-so-ever - clean 60fps. XCOM is by no means a taxing game to run so older computers should be fine to run it. When it comes to texture quality and the general aesthetics of the game, I'm very, very happy. The textures look really nice even on medium to high settings and the lighting is pretty good as well. The general aethetic of the game is a dark, gritty, mysterious one, and the textures and lighting help emphisise this.
Overall Graphics Score = 7/10 (Great)

XCOM has some of the best sound design in any strategy game I've ever played. Only beaten by Civilization IV (also by Firaxis) due to that amazing menu music.
The general sounds of the game are amazing - the guns sound nice and the different sounds fit each weapon perfectly, the aliens sound terrifying sometimes and the little touches such as footsteps on different surfaces are really well done. Also every troop has multiple language options (more in Enemy Within) for all the different nationalities, however it misses out some that would be nice. When it comes to the music in the game - its perfect. Tracks add suspence when hunting the aliens and stress when fighting. Even the background track in the HQ, while repetative, never really gets old.
Overall Sound Score = 8/10 (Amazing)
The UI (user interface) for XCOM is incredibly user friendly and easy to use.
At the HQ the menus are split up nicely and the subsections well split up. In the battlefield the commands, map and info are a nice size and perfectly placed. Wether playing with just keyboard, keyboard and mouse or controller,  the game contols nicely. What's good: the setting is unique and cool, and it's what carries the game for a solid 12 hours or so. The graphics are beautiful, and there are new environments and creatures and enemies to discover around every corner. Like all the Far Cry games, it's got great atmosphere and the open world makes it incredibly immersive. Far Cry is my favorite video game series for this.
What's bad: Going back in time offers this great new setting, but since they went to a time BEFORE GUNS, the shooting obviously suffers. You get a melee club, bow and arrow, and spears, and that's pretty much it for weapons. It's just not quite as exciting without guns banging and cars exploding. The only improvement is they give you 2 types of melee attacks: heavy and light.
So to compensate you get magical powers. You command an owl to scout ahead and tag enemies. Then you command a lion to invade the camp and rip them apart. It's a cool idea that's fun the first few times, but it's ultimately shallow and overpowered. Taming is too simplistic: just throw meat to distract them, then walk up to them, press the tame button, and they're yours forever. If they ever take damage you can heal them, and if they ever die you can bring them back to life. So tame the biggest tiger you find, send him to crush the necks of all your enemies, and the game starts to get pretty easy for you while your tiger has all the fun. This is the first Far Cry where you're some kind of superhero wizard instead of just a regular guy fighting to survive. Can't say I like it.
Other than that it's mostly like Far Cry 3 and 4, with all the same highs and lows. Collect pelts and plants to upgrade your stuff, do missions, invade camps, grapple hook at the designated grapple hook spots. The map is revealed by walking through the world instead of by climbing towers. Fun to play with the minimap off and waypoints off for maximum immersion.
Primal is worth playing just for the awesome paleolithic atmosphere. I enjoyed most of my time hunting megafauna and bashing neanderthals, but I'm a little too burned out on the Far Cry formula to care to finish.  Far Cry 3 and 4 are better by virtue of having guns, so play those first if the setting doesn't especially tempt you. Or play 2 which is still the best.
P.S. This review is of normal mode, hard difficulty. Ubisoft later added a "survivor mode" which sounds like a better game: taming is harder, beasts can die, and you have stamina. Unfortunately I played it before they added that.
It's like The Sims with turn-based fighting. And aliens.

Diablo Who?
Ok, I'm being facetious when I said the above.  But that is basically how I feel when playing this game and all it's content.
The game itself is expansive, easily spanning (for me) about 45 hours on my first playthrough.  That only opens the game to real meat, which is the typical ARPG grind on higher difficulties.  You get through your first playthrough and you will be around level 60.  That then allows you to NG+ the game when you go onto the higher difficulties.  It's actually a pretty awesome system they have in place.  If you want to go back to your completed game, simply go back to the main menu, put the difficulty down to your original difficulty (normal/veteran), and this will allow you to play in that world.  If you wanted to take the time to increase your reputation with a certain faction or buy items that maybe you don't have access to yet on your higher level playthrough (such as a specific blue print for crafting).
Beyond that the game is a joy.  I did experience spike in difficulty when I played the Ashes of Malmouth expansion, but I got through.  My build was probably not that great, to be honest.  The map is expansive as well.  Just when I thought I was getting to an end of an area I would find a new way to go.  When I look at the world map I am still a bit blown away by it.  I actually have fond memories looking at it of things I did in each area, people I met, groups I am working towards getting a higher reputation with, things like that.
There are a bunch of classes to mix and match.  Expansive skill trees you can't use all of, lots of ways to build a character, a devotion system where you spend devotion points to passive and active skills you tie to your standard skill.
I have few complaints.  The maps are fun to explore, there are enemy heroes that come at a rate determined by your faction level with the "bad" factions, and a whole lot of loot to get.  One nice thing they do is they have a loot filter that essentially makes it so you only see loot at a certain level.  After about level 20, you don't care about yellow gear at all and the filter made it a joy to kill things again since my entire screen was not covered with yellow text.
I have only a few small complaints.  Enemies detect you through walls, and the fog of war clears through walls so you can see them over there.  They sometimes sit and attack the wall you are on the other side of, and my pets do the same.  It's only slightly annoying.  I have read on various forums that some arcane heroes (of the enemy factions) have some really annoying abilities like ones that cancel your toggled buff skills.  I can see that being really annoying.  While I love the map, some of the areas do feel kind of samey.  Part of me wants to see more varied environments.  There is one section, for example where it is snowy, but it's short lived.  I would like to see more areas like that.
This game is a must buy if you want to play and excellent ARPG.  I would expect no less considering the pedigree of the development talent.  It gives you that, "one more run" feel which more than once put me into the wee morning hours.  I thought I was done, but now I find myself sitting at work looking for fun builds that other people have done to start a new character on.  I look forward to their next expansion as well. Malmouth's content was pretty big in my opinion.  It increased the level cap, the devotion cap, added a huge new area to get to and explore, it was a steal at the price of it too.

"One day, the sun wil dim and spread..." -  wait, wrong game. That was the intro of Titan Quest, and it's Grim Dawn we're talking about! Honestly though, Grim Dawn feels an awful lot like TQ 2.0. Which is not very surprising, given the fact that Crate Entertainment, the studio that released Grim Dawn, was founded by the lead designer of Iron Lore, the studio that created Titan Quest.
As Titan Quest 2.0, Grim Dawn manages to deliver a well-designed and lore-rich world, hundreds of different items and - most importantly - well balanced classes. But let's get started with the world we get thrown in: We play as some guy or gal who was possessed by an Aetherial, pretty evil beings who want to take over the world. Due to the Aetherials, the future of mankind looks pretty, well, grim. But fear not, random dude will save the world! Admittedly, the story is pretty generic and nothing new, but it's the lore, the love for detail, that gives Grim Dawn its - excuse me please - grim setting. Little notes here and there show the desperate situation people are going through.
Like any other ARPG, Grim Dawn as well has hundreds of items to offer. Depending on the rarity of the item, its effects can range from the pretty standard "does x fire damage" to allowing you the use of unique and very powerful skills. Some of theses skills can either be activated or will activate on their own with a certain chance. It is true that these rare items may be the reason why your specific build works.
This brings me to the most impressive and , in my opinion, most enjoyable part of the game. Sure, you can choose from different classes and play accordingly - a tanky soldier, a ranged demolitionist, a spell-based arcanist... But maybe you want to create something seemingly insane? An arcanist with a mighty two-handed sword is as viable as a spell-slinging soldier - if you have spent your devotion points wisely. This interesting feature allows you to spend points on special skills and passives that can either complement your class and playstyle or allow for complete new tactics.
Despite all the great features, Grim Dawn has one fatal flaw: the ending is very disappointing, as is the final boss fight. Still, Grim Dawn is one of the best ARPGs, maybe even THE best right now and definitely worth its price. If you enjoyed Diabolo, Sacred or Titan Quest, you surely will enjoy Grim Dawn.

Grim Dawn is the Diablo 3 we never got.  Diablo 1 and 2 set a bar that Diablo 3 completely missed.
I love this game so much.  it's the only serious review I have made yet on Steam.
PROS:
- unique storytelling with a ton of interesting lore.
- refreshing character progression that lets you become a hybrid of two classes of your choice.
- Diablo-esque looting system, tons of weapons, armor and accessories that are randomly generated(if not part of a set) to keep you returning to the hunt for more.
- LAN and online play with subjectively no connection issues thus far.
- non-linear gameplay, never stale, in a beautifully crafted H.P. Lovecraft inspired world; it seems the developers pay a ton of attention to detail.
- Plenty of land and dungeons to explore with secrets and treasures to be found in nearly every crevice of the world.
- Easy learning curve; this game has a lot going on at first and can be a bit overwhelming but after only an hour of gameplay you'll understand the overall premise of progression in the game.
CONS:
- Inventory management can be a hassle if you mind taking trips back and forth to town to sell and manage your equipment and items to keep your character kicking butt and taking names.
So it's not even necessarily a CON.
So we'll just call it a "PROCON".
This game is great.
Do you like RPGs with a refreshing take on character progression in a huge world full of mystery and treasures?
If you answered yes then this is definitely the game to play.

This game is as addicting as it is hard. 9 times out of 10 I die on an adventure, but the idea of the possiblity of triggering a rare event is what makes you keep coming back to it. And it's not the kind of game that you have to warm up to either; I can just pick it up, play through an adventure, and leave if need be.
Personally, I like unlocking things. Even if I don't put it to frequent use, unlockables are very similar to accomplishments for me, so naturally I never get tired of SAWA. The numerous unlockables aren't just for keeping you engrossed in the game; they make you go for certain events that you may not have chosen otherwise (I'm talking about the rivers here). I personally don't like going into the desert with the snakes, scorpians, and vultures, but when I saw the locked Survival mode, I figured I'd go to try and unlock it. Because of this, I encountered new events that I never would've seen without the motivation to go back to that desert. Now I like alternating between different areas to see what kind of new or unlikely events I can trigger!
This isn't intended to be a hardcore game, but there are those kind of challenges for the people that always aim for the gold in video games. You know what kind of challenges I mean, and SAWA has them, namely the Random wagon, where you have to make it 50 days in Shuffle without dying. For those who haven't played Shuffle mode, it's a hard challenge. Take it from me.
SAWA is great for gamers of all types: casual, hardcore, completionists, you name it. I definitely recommend this game, even if it's for an hour.

I didn't have many expectations for this game. Lack of personal exposure to  games like this and Arcen's history of mostly making slower paced games made me wonder it it'll end up being any good. I'm glad to say I was wrong. Starward Rogue is a solid "roguelite" shooter with a varied selection of mechs to start with, plenty of powerful-feeling weapons, interesting enemy attack patterns (which there are a lot of) and nail-biting bossfights.
It's also hard. Sure, there's easy and very easy below normal difficulty but my pride won't allow me to use them. There's often very little room between all the bullets to navigate through and at least for me a good early run means I get overconfident and get smacked down hard before reaching the fifth level boss. Things are mostly manageable on normal but when kicking it up a notch to hard, the bullet hell part becomes quite obvious. To my  knowledge Misery difficulty bullet patterns didn't quite make it to 1.0 so it remains to be seen what kind of masochistic hell that ends up becoming.
Overall I was positively surprised how good it turned out to be and it'll probably become my go-to game when I don't have all evening to spend on gaming. I'll probably gift it to a friend too since the price is reasonable and I myself got it for free.

Although 'Alan Wake's American Nightmare' feels a bit dull and dragged out compared to the epic 'Alan Wake', there are a few reasons why I'd recommend this DLC. First of all, the gameplay is overall a lot better than in the main game. Alan runs faster, can sprint for longer time, he seems more prepared for battle and in general he is more effective in his combat. Second, the Birdman. This enemy is so impressive that it's a pity he wasn't included in the main game in the first place. Third, the premise of the story, which is very intriguing and twisted. Last but not least, the excellent atmosphere which drifts between dream and reality.
Unfortunately, the good gameplay is consumed in repeating the same routine over and over again, albeit with slight variations each time, to the point that it seems more like a tutorial of sorts and less like an actual game. I think the idea of reliving events to change reality is a fantastic one, but the way this is planned out in the DLC is somewhat uninspired. It's as if they had this great idea, but couldn't think of an equally good way to connect it to the game's plot. Somewhere midway, it starts feeling like a chore, and in the end, although there seems to be a resolution, you are still left with many questions unanswered. Moreover, the enemies are way too many for such a brief and repetitive game. I want to replay it so as to find the missing documents, but I am discouraged every time because I remember those persisting baddies that keep chasing me everywhere I go.
The DLC features also 'Fight Till Dawn', a pretty decent and fun game mode where you are challenged to survive for a set period of time in various areas of the story.

The progress the Franco-Ukrainian studio Frogwares has made between their first game, Sherlock Holmes: The Mystery of the Mummy from 2002 and The Silver Earring, released 2 years later, is astounding. While the first one was a flawed, mostly cheap looking and generic first person adventure game, more abusing than using the Sherlock Holmes theme and character (Wael Amr himself admitted something along those lines in one of the interviews if I remember correctly) - the studio seemed to learn quickly from their mistakes - and the far better budget the predecessor somehow assured is obvious.  This time it's catering as much as possible to the Holmesians and The Silver Earring, and a much more enjoyable, complex experience, if not without its flaws.
Gameplay is more or less typical point & click fare. Pixel hunting wasn't entirely eliminated, but is much, much more rare and less annoying than in the original. Inventory juggling is quite minimal and rare. Using items with people is rare and in perhaps all occasions but one, prompted by Sherlock, and using them together in the inventory itself. All the dialogues, clues, hints & papers are kept by the game and integrated in a sort of a "quiz" system, where you answer a series of questions using them as "proof" for the questions you're posed. While not perfectly executed, forced, and, perhaps, slightly clunky, it's an interesting system in any case. The game ensures you have everything you need I guess, by keeping you in one place / room / area until you find everything, which helps progress I guess. The puzzles are adequate, logical except for one with a safe (oh, you'll know which one it is) which requires a strange leap of logic. Though having a random character who just happens to dabble in inventions in the game is as cheesy a premise for introducing them as it gets. In general, it didn't thrill me, it didn't annoy me. OK enough.
Walking is an annoyance, however, moving is jittery in general, and clicking on a hotspot that's supposed to lead you to a place where the perspective changes doesn't guarantee that you'll get there, as Sherlock is prone to random bouts of turning in place indefinitely. Though you won't get stuck because of it. It just makes the one timed event and 2 that require timing more annoying than they should be for some.
The story & scenario are OK, and while it's not the best & original Sherlock scenario you'll ever see, it's fairly complex, with some good sides, and won't annoy the hell out of you like the first game. The voice acting is more convincing than last time (that's not saying much), though how and why couldn't they find a kid to play a kid, instead of an abysmal attempt by a grownup actor is beyond me - it depends on the character really.
Graphically it's a mixed bag, with character models ranging from pretty detailed (Holmes) to completely off (Watson... whose character isn't executed exactly flawlessly either). Some scenes are more or less nicely or adequately rendered, some feel rushed & unconvincing. Similar with cutscenes, generally unimpressive, but then you run into the "dominoes" one -> effective, very well directed & executed, showing there's quite some potential inside the team. And the outro was at the time, and maybe still is, one of the longest in a game ever (around 20 minutes... seemed shorter to me, but it might as well have been). While there are mild glitches here & there, miles ahead of its predecessor.
Music? Dvořák, Grieg, Schumann, Tchaikovsky. Need I say more? Well implemented too.
Overall, while, as a point & click adventure game, it will never be among your all time favorites, being a pretty much average adventure game as a whole, it has its good sides and there's no real reason for a p&c buff or a Sherlock fan not to seek it out (preferably in a bundle), so it gets a tentative recommendation... there are worse things to spend an afternoon on.

Sherlock Holmes: The Silver Earring was overall a very enjoyable puzzle adventure game. The game begins with the death of a wealthy businessman and leaves you to investigate the scene. The game will then take you to multiple connected locations as you attempts to piece together the murder and uncover the assassin and the motive for the murder. The game is set over 5 days of investigations and each day will have you visit a location and search it for clues and solve one or two puzzles with ranging difficulties (some puzzles were quite hard and confusing), at the end of each day you will summarise your findings in a quiz, which for me was probably the hardest part of the game. I found the story to be quite engaging and interesting overall with a good range of characters and locations and was well suited to a Sherlock story.
Overall 'Sherlock Holmes: The Silver Earring' was a good solid adventure game which presented a well written story and some good puzzles, taking around 9 - 10 hours to complete and with a very conclusive ending I would highly recommend it for adventure game enthusiasts.

This game is a tough one to rate. The artwork is standard telltale style which is good if you like it. Of course the meat of the game is in the story and I am left a little disappointed in the end.
***Spoiler Alert***
The whole story is built around House Forrester and how it's under threat so you spend the majority of the game strategising to save it. In the end my playthrough resulted in the house being lost and Asher being gravely wounded and running away. I didn't expect a fairy tale ending but I feel there I spent hours contributing to stories that never had their big pay off. I feel like there are too many loose ends.
The prime examples are Mira and Gared. You spent a lot of time playing these two characters, making important decisions but in the end it never leads anywhere. For Mira you spend all of your time in Kings Landing trying to help your family but in the end you had zero impact. I ended up marrying Morgryn but you don't see the continuation of that and how it helps your family.
You spend a lot of time with Gared in the night's watch and heading north of the wall to find the North Grove. I told the people there to march south to help Ironrath but that storyline ends with them marching off and this is what I mean by there is no huge pay off for some of the main characters.
As an individual game I would not recommend it because you will need to buy every upcoming season to finally see the end result of all of your hours of work. If you're okay with that then by all means buy it , otherwise i'd skip it. Other than that there are some performance issues. I had some problems getting it to launch and the game does not take tabbing out too well.

They try so hard to fit in Westeros that it end a bit fanservice, lots a moment are similars to the show and yet, you chose something and in the previously of next episode they say you chose differently.
I mean, we all knew where the Nothern way of dealing problem would lead to, but there seems to be no margin of choice.
However, this takes the point likessness of your actions to a new level. I was excited when I saw you were playing as characters of a lesser house. That would make sense. The game could show you some of the conflicts going on behind the scenes in the fight for the iron throne that don't make the cut for the TV show. (BTW the house your playing as is mentioned in the 5th book, A Dance with dragons.)
But TellTale didn't do that. They couldn't resist bringing in the cast from the Tv show which ultimately hurts the game. Because you already know the outcome of those character's life. It gives all the TV show characters "plot armor". Have the chance to kill one of them? Well, you know you can't. They aren't dead in the show, so you can't kill them here.
And it goes far beyond that. It's a running joke that your decisions don't matter in Telltale games. But they suceed when they create a convincing illusion of choice. But this game doesn't do that.
Let's say you get the mission to kill a guy. Everyone is telling you you're going to kill a guy. You arrive and start to beat him. You have a choice here. Be a sadist and really abuse him, or show restraint. Now if you have no plans for mercy, you might beat him and beat him until he's dead. But the game doesn't let you. Out of nowhere you have to let him live. And I'm not talking about some unexpected, his friends come to the rescue situation. I'm talking all of your allies are gung-ho, we're killing this guy, you start to torture him thinking, "why not? I'm going to kill him anyway." and then ouit of nowhere they go, "Actually, let's not kill him." and that's it. You get no choice in the matter. You end up with a godawful ending, even worser than Mass Effect 3 and thats saying ALOT.
Which brings us to the next issue, lack of continuity. As said before, regardless of your actions you're driving to a single resolution. But the game doesn't even acknowledge you actions on that road. You can permanantly main a character in one episode, and in the next episode he'll return right as rain.

Assassin’s Creed II, Batman: Arkham City, Borderlands 2. Never would I envision another game would barge in and join this prestigious list of games. Out of nowhere, comes XCOM: Enemy Unknown.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown is a turn based tactical warfare game where you command a squad of soldiers against aliens (classic). Expectations are set for you as commander to save human civilization and rid of the invading species. Right at the start, the game flung you into the mix of things with a steep learning curve. On the commanding side, you have to maintain panic levels that keep your ally countries to fund your XCOM project which is your main source of income. If you fail, they leave the XCOM project forever and you get zero funding from them onwards. The income is used to upgrade your base, weapons, and other perks. On the battlefield, keeping your squad members alive is crucial. The game runs on perma-death. If a squad member dies, he dies for good. After that, he can only be selected in the memorial and you can lookup on which mission he perished. Of course you can hire a new soldier but losing your best soldier on the field doesn’t feel good right. During combat, the way you inflict damage to your opponents is percentage based and relies heavily on positioning as well as flanking. Ever missed a 98%  point blank shot? Hell yeah. But when you hit that crucial 9% shot that saves your team from total annihilation. A sigh of relief. You will never have the calmness to expand your base as the game throws problems one after another at you. The brutal yet realistic nature of the game brings a satisfying gaming experience.
As mentioned, the game excels in turn based combat. It is realistic as it does not provide you an easy way out of sticky situations. An easy mission can be brutally difficult if patience is not taken into consideration. Charging into a swarm of enemies almost guarantees a death or two. What makes this game better is soldiers having distinct classes when ranking up. Each class will have their own skill tree. With each soldiers’ rank up, a skill can be selected between two choices to specialize the unit. You can choose having higher defense to soak up damage for your allies as a vanguard or increased critical chance while close up to the enemy to be that devastating spearhead your team desperately needs. Your team composition is solely up to you. Moreover, the underlying tension when in base or out in the field on uncertainties of what will happen next will keep you on your toes. I’ve spent hours in the game calculating my every movement, in which I thought I only spent minutes. This just signifies how immersive this game truly is. However, XCOM Enemy Unknown has its fair share of problems. The first noticeable flaw is graphical glitches. I saw my Japanese sniper nicknamed ‘Headshot’ charge up his plasma rifle to land a headshot while the plasma beam pierces through a friendly unit, a car, a wall AND then the alien’s head. In addition, switching elevation level in the game can be frustrating at times as layers of flooring are hard to navigate properly. The second issue is the random map generator. There is a limited pool of maps that is chosen for each mission and when you play a lot, you start to notice maps reoccurring, just from different angles where you start the mission from. The suburbs of USA look exactly the same as the that from India. Nevertheless, these imperfections don’t create much of an issue for an extremely flawless game, literally at 98%. With XCOM 2 just out, I might just be seduced into purchasing it seeing how good the prequel, XCOM: Enemy Unknown is.
Pros:
- In depth turn based tactical combat
- Realistic and unforgiving in nature
- Customizable and personalized team composition with plentiful options
- Tension loaded experience
Cons:
- Constant graphical glitches
- Repeating maps used for missions in different parts of the world
Rating: 9.8/10

This is a very casual and relaxing puzzle game that was originally released for touchscreen devices such as the iOS, Android and Maemo.
Objective of the game is simple. Tie ropes around 3D objects and try to cover as much of the object area while using as little rope as possible.
It gently introduces the player with simple objects at the beginning where you can afford to miss out a few inches of rope and gradually introducing more and more complex objects where every inch of rope must be carefully analyzed and conserved to prevent wastage.
Graphics are simple but look very nice and sharp. Music has a very alternative feel, and is soothing, relaxing and meditative.
Although the game's control scheme of using a mouse works well, there are times where it feels more suited for touchscreen devices which it was originally designed for.
Overall Rating: 8.0 / 10
Definitely worth to buy if you like very casual and relaxing puzzle games.

I am a casual gamer blazing through old PC classics that I always wanted to play but never had the PC to do so.
Half-Life 2 may be the most eye-opening game I've ever played in terms of what it has done to gaming since its release.
Almost anything worth remembering in an FPS game in the last 10+ years is in this game. I'm not going to pretend to know whether or not a lot of the mechanics in this game were revolutionary, but I have a good feeling that this game is the reason FPS games are where they are.
This game just feels original, it feels like it introduces a lot of what we've seen in FPS games even into the modern era. Somehow, it feels way ahead of its time even though it's not a terribly old game still. There are your regular FPS mechanics, driving mechanics, and even group-commanding mechanics all in this game. Even the gravity gun reminds of my recent trips through Portal, and how "specialty" weapons can really influence a game and its play.
All of these things may have existed in games, but this seems to have made them all so much better at the time of its release. You can really tell that this game influenced many of those that followed it. I'm not going to say anything else about the story or the game at this point you haven't heard elsewhere.
If you want to play Half-Life 2 & haven't ever, just play it NOW. I have no idea what all of the controvery stems from, but just based on this experience I'd have to say it's one of the best games to have ever been installed on my PC. I'm so glad I didn't let all of the negative reviews/comments about the developers keep me from this game.
I'm not from this day forward going to speak towards this game and how amazing it is. It's already well known and popular.
What I'm really glad to be able to say to others, is that I've experienced this game in full in my lifetime.

The Good: Solid visuals, great physics, unique design choice
The Bad: No extra modes, inconsistent difficulty, only good in short bursts
Who wound have thought winding rope on a wood figure would be fun? The guys at Secret Exit did and this is some simple fun here. While the graphics don't push anything the wooden figure models are nice and varied, but this is a more challenging puzzle game than you think. As you work your way up a tree you have three goals for each figure by covering 70%, 85%, and 99% of the allotted rope. When you wind the rope it will turn a painted color, but be careful because if you wind the rope tight that's lifted off the figure you can't get underneath. The physics are great with rope sliding off corners and falling into place like it should.
Some figures have nails that you can use to redirect the rope, but the art of this is how well you can wind the rope and cover the whole object. Some are easy and some are hard with lots of arms, legs, or pieces that can easily be covered up or roped off on accident. That's pretty much all there is to the game, but being such a unique puzzle game makes it great. There is nothing out there like this and you will have hours of fun here. Grim Dawn is a mixture of Titan Quest & Diablo 2.
It has the feel of Diablo 2 - hell on Cairn has been unleashed by people meddling with powerful entities who've been around since the creation of the world (Aetherials (pure magic) & Ch'thonics (Blood Magic) ). You are the survivor of an Aetherial possession attempt and are doing your best to help humanity survive. The core game provides you with chapters 1-4, the expansion provides chapters 5 & 6.
Game mechanics are akin to Titan Quest ( The developement team include some of the members of Iron Lore & Blizzard North). You pick one skill set at level 2, then pick a second at level 10. Base game has 6 sets, the expansion provides 2 more. You are able to build a fighter to best suit your playstyle, and can augment your skills through enchantments, magic items and shrines.
The game has 3 difficulty settings, with completion unlocking the next difficulty tier. Unlike D3, the game damage numbers are in the hundreds or low thousands, making them easier to grasp. My only niggle is the lack of voice overs for minor quest dialogues; all major characters have voices, but not all minor ones did in the vanilla game. Have yet to play expansion.

The game had great reviews and I wanted something to play other than Diablo 3, Path of Exile, Torchlight 2, and Titan Quest... but at the same time, I wanted to play all of those games wrapped up in one. Grim Dawn pretty much achieves that. And note: this review is more for the new player experienced with ARPGs; I am writing this as I level up my main... can't speak about replayability yet.
Why this game? Why not D3, POE, T2, TQ?
It's a new map, a different class system, a different specialization system, nice graphics... still a grindy ARPG, but aren't they all? Definitely lacking the "sparkles, sprinkles, shiny stars" and other polish from D3, but has more build complexity than D3. Doesn't have the cutesy graphics T2 has, but has a longer and deeper story mode. It has the raw, detailed graphics and themed storyline that TQ had, with a different, darker, grim story. Can be played offline, can be modded (but doesn't need to be!).
Pros?
It's an ARPG- plays well, balanced well, easy to pick up but complicated enough to keep you grinding for that next skill point. GD really shines with its in-game graphics; it's 3D modeling and texturing is phenomenal and its level design is very intricate, graphically. For an isometric ARPG, you can actually rotate the camera (!) and zoom in/out far and the graphics remain gorgeous. However, the 2D graphics (menus, windows) are lackluster- fully functional, well themed, but lacking fine polish. Also, development continues and, although continued features are bundled with expansions and priced DLC, the devs respond in forum, continue to advance the game, and it's fairly priced, not pay-to-win.
Cons?
Already mentioned the 2D graphics being lackluster. The server finder feels a decade old. Kind of grindy. Could use more polish. But if that's all the cons I can think of... then it's not half bad!
Summary?
Worth the $$. Put D3 away for a bit. It's like throwback TQ with a different story if you have many hours to kill.

The original X-COM: UFO Defense (more commonly known by its much more charismatic name UFO: Enemy Unknown by us Europeans) is a timeless masterpiece that I still go back to and replay every other year or so thanks to Xcomutil.  Filling its shoes is a near impossible task, and while XCOM admittedly (and somewhat expectedly) doesn't quite manage that (that honor goes to another game, Xenonauts) it succeeds in updating the core gameplay and ideas to a modern era of gaming.  The game is largely streamlined and in many ways oversimplified to better accommodate the modern (and in some ways the console) gamer; you have only one base, you have only one squad (albeit with rotating soldiers), you have a linear campaign, TUs  have been replaced by actions (of which every soldier can take two of each turn), Geoscape and council retention have turned into a weird satellite game and soldier stat progression has been replaced with classes and skill trees.  But underneath all these changes, it manages to retain the soul of what made X-COM a great game - the atmosphere, the tension and most importantly a wonderful tactical gameplay - the core premise is still all there.  In the end, it has become a very different, yet very similar, game that just keeps you coming back for more and more.   This core gameplay is significantly improved with the expansion Enemy Within, which also gets a strong recommendation for me, and the famous Long War mod makes the game a completely different, and uniquely frustrating, experience.  Buy it and play it.

Welcome back to Tropico my friends! Not much has changed since Tropico 3. There are new menus, new caricatures, new voice overs that lay on thick personality and accents. The graphics look the same and feel as if they're directly from Tropico 3. The are new disasters like tornadoes, tsunamis, droughts, and volcanoes. To compliment the disasters there are fire stations to put out the fires and a new weather station. To unlock edicts that help or opress your people, you'll not only need a ministry new to the series, but hire people to run each branch. You'll get to chose from viable candidates, or for a price you can import an expert. Buildings can now import resources. If you have a rum factory, but no sugar farms, you can simply import the sugar. There are also more foreign powers such as China, the UK and the Middle East. They won't donate money like the USA and USSR, but they'll give you goals to accomplish. There are new optional goals that you get by clicking the icons over buildings. New to the series is a quick build that will instantly construct a building for a price.
Tropico 4 is a surprisingly good city builder or rather a 3rd world simulator. It is very different than games like Sim City and Cities XL. Those two games are more macro city builders, where in two or three mouse clicks you can make city blocks where 1,000 people might live. With Tropico 4 and the Tropico series in general, you need to place each building, each road and your island along with the time it takes your construction company to build it. Your entire island might get to be 200 - 500 'Tropicans.'
Each Tropican has needs... Food, religion, job, healthcare, entertainment, safety and so on. The catch is every Tropican's needs have a certain weight to them based on what faction they believe in. Each faction has major and minor demands. The military will want more soldiers, so you need to build an army base. The religious faction will want a church or cathedral. The capitalist party will want privatization or upscale entertainment. The communist party will want you to enable the free public housing edict or have etiquette healthcare.
On top of that, you balance political relations with the USA and USSR. If they get too bad, one of the two will basically take over your country and it will be game over. It is interesting how many ways that you can get game over. The most common way to get a game over is to lose an election. You don't have to have elections even. You're in charge. If you don't want an election, the nationalist party will hate you and your loyalist party will love you. If you opt to have elections, it will be vise versca. People will call for early elections and when you have elections, you can see preliminary results and you can even sway (cheat) elections. Its all at the risk of a party's love.
It is pretty cool having to pick 3 things to make a speech about and then fulfill campaign promises, but its all pretty easy. Winning elections is pretty easy, especially compared to how difficult it was to win any elections in the original Tropico. It was so bad in that game, that it was almost impossible to win an election without stuffing the ballot box.
When citizens hate you, and there will be plenty that do, they will either peacefully protest or become rebels. Once you have enough rebels against you, they will attack your most remote buildings. Your army will then go fight them, but if the rebels outnumber your army, the rebel will win and the buildings will be destroyed. The rebels can attack your palace or flat out assassinate you for a game over.
Tropico has a single player campaign with 20 scenarios that each take an hour or two to complete. You don't just pick scenarios, you unlock them. Each scenario seems to have scenario specific events that only occur in the scenarios. Unlike Tropico 3, I don't get a sense in the scenarios of an ultimate goal I'm striving toward. I feel like I stumble into victory when its least expected. At the start of each scenario you can pick a player character from historical tropican dictators or make your own avatar. You can even make personality traits that will result in pros and cons. It can drastically change your play style if you are incorruptible and never have any crime or have a green thumb and have high farm yields at the cost of low factory production.
Your businesses, mines, farms, and everything requires citizens in them to function and make you money. Every citizen has different education levels that will impact who does what. So you need to build high schools and colleges. Once built, there are options to gear students to military or religion. You can also click vacant positions to hire foreign experts for a price. If you have more businesses than citizens, build an immigration office and let anyone into the country or change it to only let in skilled workers so you keep bums out of your country.
Nothing is done automatically. You place a building, then wait for your teamsters and construction crews to build it. The more crews and personnel you have working, the faster it'll get done. I'm happy with that. Its part of the realism. If there's a building you want developed faster, you can increase or decrease its priority. If its still taking too long, just have your avatar stand next to the building to get it done faster. The fire station works the same way.
The graphics are beautiful and you'll see every Tropican walking around, hopping in their car and driving to locations. The music is nice and very Tropican / Salsa music, but there's very little variety from Tropico 3. A few hours in I was bored with the music. The DJs feel gone for the most part. They're still in the game, but they do interviews with one liners here and there. The voice acting consists of great parodies of stereotypes. They really had fun embellishing on characters with tongue in cheek humor. The game knows you're all powerful and while being a dictator is usually seen as a horrifyingly negative thing, the humor twists it into a silly positive thing.
If you have Tropico 3, play Tropico 3. Tropico 4 is still a great game, but has a ton of DLC and feels like a cash grab with only minor upgrades. The menu feels more cumbersome and click heavy than Tropico 3. The disasters take way too long and it breaks the flow the game has. The quick build feature feels like a good addition that you don't have to use, but sometimes it takes forever for the construction crews to build, even with several construction offices at full capacity.

Following the likes of Wing Commander and the X-wing series, DarkStar One is certainly not an original concept, but it is still an incredible space opera--a well delivered story, great voice acting, an open galaxy, intuitive user interface, multiple side missions and other fun stuff will keep you entertained for many hours. Trade, smuggle goods, steal cargo, kill pirates, or just go postal and kill anyone you meet.
The limited side missions get repeatedly boring after a while, especially given the vast number of solar systems, but there are keyboard shortcuts for everything allowing you to skip most mundane tasks. The space combat is really enjoyable and gets progressively more difficult as the story progresses. Add ship upgrades and you ultimately become one bad hombre.
I got roughly 40 hours of enjoyment--your mileage may vary. This is not a space simulation--it is highly action based. Space shooter fans will not be disappointed.

Continuation of the bestselling production of Valve Software, which in 1998 set new standards in the genre of FPS shooting. The game takes place several years after the events shown in the original, and players reappear in the form of Gordon Freeman - a physicist from the Black Mesa laboratories, where as a result of the failed experiment alien life forms were brought to Earth. This time the plot is located in the fictitious city of City 17 and in its immediate vicinity. Our protagonist works for a secret government organization, and his task is to counter the aggressors of another dimension, which is supported by a representative of the earthly resistance - Alyx Vance. The second part of the game introduces a real revolution in technical issues, using the original Valve studio engine called Source. Its advantage is primarily excellent physics, allowing for to destroy virtually every element of the environment and use various objects as a shield or weapon.
