I LOVED this game, let me say that to start with. The powers are well balanced in that you can't really get away with not using one of them and there is motivation to upgrade them at that. The weapons are punchy and feel like you're doing damage except the submachine guns. I also love the freedom to customize, it's a bit over the top for some but it was a lot of fun and made it more imersive as you play as yourself, or a short, blue haired woman with tattoos and red eyes who can throw people with her mind.
However, while this is firmly on my list of favorite games for its self-awarness, characters, comedy, and fun, it is not without fault. Discounting how all the submachine guns fail to feel effective after 20 rounds to a zin's face my biggest issue was Johnny Gat, who does return from his disappearance early in the third game. They overhype Gat far too much for how little he does. I'm not saying he's not cool, but I am saying that he needs to do more for how awesome he is supposed to be. This may be a personal problem though; this was the first in the series I played, so Gat had to impress me in this game, which he fell shy of doing. I bought this game for ps3 originally only to buy this one again about a year later but Gat was sadly lacking something, and that was payoff. I played the third next, and he did leave an impression, albeit a weak one sadly, only to die shortly after that. Maybe in the second game he was a diety incarnate but i didnt play that, so it doesnt influence me.
The second major thing is the sidequesting. There are a lot of side activities in the simulation, which is good since most of them are fun, but the side missions are largely to do several activities and come back to the ship and get your reward. If you are like me this will actually shorten gameplay because you'll do them as you stumble across them, and since it still counts the mission can literally be launched and completed without ever entering the simulation knowing what to do.
If you've stuck with me this long then you must be wondering why I suggest you but it imidiately. In truth, this game does things so well that the issues pale in comparison. Maybe the bear was cut out and the side quests get redundant, so what? Its's fun while self aware and how every game series should end; madcap fun that pokes fun at all games and pop culture including itself with a genuinely hatable villain, likable characters which are more than stereotypes and actual humor. Is it perfect? No, but it is damn good.

If you are gifted the game and hit level 30, the person that gifted it to you gets some pretty sweet benefits, so right now heaps of people are looking to gift the game. visit the BDO subreddit and click one of the stickied threads, and you'll easily be able to obtain a free FULL copy of this game. I'ma use this review to address the cons that litter the reviews, give you an idea of what to expect
1. You need to leave your computer on 24/7.
You don't. You can if you want to, it's a nice option. But I don't. Not necessary.
3. Popping graphics.
Legitimately, this is something I don't notice. You might? But it's more than possible that you don't.
4. RNG.
Yes, the game becomes very RNG based. Is this is best method of advancing? Probably not. Just kidding, it really isn't. But. Everyone has the same luck as you do. You can't cheat luck. Everyone goes through the same system. No one is at a disadvantage, everyone gets lucky, every gets unlucky. However the RNG is not to a point where the lucky triumph over the hard working.
5. More RNG (Awakening the T8 courser)
Yo, literally like, 10 people have done this on this server. It's suppose to be damn ♥♥♥♥ing hard. It's suppose to be extremely rare. It's suppose to be something that if you see in a city, you stand in awe and admire that beautiful creature. It has such value to it, why would you want to make something like that easy to get?
6. Cash Shop Prices
This prices aren't the cheapest. Are they also necessary? Nope. Pay to convenience. Easy work around though. There's an amazing system in the game where a player can buy something from the cash shop with real money and sell it for in game money. This may sound pay to win, but it's actually amazing. This means that any cash shop item is accessible for a miniscule amount of in game money. You can buy a costume with 3 hours of grinding. This way, people that don't want to spend money on the game don't have to. People that want to save a miniscule amount of hours with buying from the cash shop and selling on the market (maximum 5 times a week) get to save those few hours. It's an easy win-win situation.
TLDR: Hit up the 7 day free trial. If you end up enjoying your time, which is more than likely, don't be afraid to give it a purchase. Massive updates so so often make for an ever improving experience. Plans for this game stray far into the future.
Small update: There were disconnect issues that pretty badly effected some peoples experiences within the game, mostly affecting only Americans, not others (like Australians) for some reason, even though we all play on the NA server. This has been addressed and fixed, and they recently give pretty sweet bonuses to all those who had bought the game early, including full copies of the game. So now all the servers are crowded again, unfortunately so the game won't be dying any time soon. And it's pretty awesome to see the towns and cities so lively, especially when so many people collaborate to kill the world bosses that spawn each day.

I bought this game on sale for about 8 bucks and ended up playing a bit oer 30 hours. For this price it was well an okay game ofr that time, however, I don't think it has anything too interesting going for itself (compared to other ARPGS of our time at least) and it's more tedious than fun in the later stages, so for anyone looking for a game/grinder they want to play long term, I would not recommend this.
The main two factors I think Grim Dawn messes up is that is has too much stuff and there's too little reward per time spent.
They have over 10 damage types alone and there's no smart drops or anything. Meaning, the amount of loot you find that's comepletely useless to you is huge. Still you gotta go over each piece, and check it's numerous stats, cause it "could" be an upgrade, effectively managing to make the suppsed rewarding part of the grind (i.e. getting the loot) into more of a tedious chore than anything. This is not only true for damage type but also just genreally what you can and can't wear. Usually when gear drops if it's an upgrade it's higher level than you can wear, so you gotta carry it around and then remember 2 hours later to equip it when you finally get those 2-4 level higher up where you can wear it.
The flipside is even worse when it comes to resistances. As is customary you will get resistance penalties in higher difficulties, but since you also have 10 different (yes, no kidding here) resistances you gotta keep in mind (plus armor ofc) it's a pain to try and juggle all of them. Again, keeping in mind that the gear is obviously random, so you can end up in a position of getting a nice upgrade, that you simply can't wear cause it messes up resistances. So you put it in the stash to all the other ones and hope at some point to take a few hours time to figure out IF there's a new combination of items you could wear that are an upgrade AND let you keep the resistances balanced.
If that sounds like fun to you, by all means, get the game, but for me (and I think in general) this is just really bad game design. It confuses having lots of stuff, with having meaningful interesting decisions to make. Overloading the player with options isn't what makes a game deep, it's having impactful decisions to make, which does and Grim Dawn fails at that imo.
Another thing would be the weird "difficulty" spike. I put it in quotes, cause I don't think getting one-shot has anything to do with difficulty, it's just bad game design in my opinion, as there's usually not a decision on the players part that has an impact on the outcome (as opposed to the player needing to make better or more complex decisions). So in GD you'll either find you kill mobs with one or two hits, or they seem to take almost forever to kill. On top of that, some boss/hero mobs just deal a ridiculous amount of damage in a very short time, meaning half the battle is running away to heal then coming back to get a few hits in, then repeating that over and over for 30-40 times until the boss is dead.
Part of that damage spike os no doubt the resistance problem I wrote about earlier, as there's usually a few resistances you won't have high enough and if you gt hit by that damage type you're just kinda screwed, but since there's 10 different resistances you also wouldn't want to just grind over and overfur jsut that one piece with this particular res on it either, since that's also kind of a waste of time, since it's not gonna do anything for most situations. (I mean ultimately you have to have all res, but while leveling trying to always res up seems just weird, since you also want to progress in the game and not stick to a few spots and grind over and over for one or two pieces until you can progress).
Another problem is disables, since there's no skills you have to make you immune or let you get out of immobilizes, freezes or stuns. So again it's either some gear with reduced stun/freeze/immobilize time, or (as I found out by chance at some point) using one time use potions that make you immune or severly reduce the time of those status effects. Problem being, they're also random drop or random recipe drop. Not only that, but since there's so many of those, you can't evn put it somewhere for convenient access, meaning in an actual fight, where all of a sudden you realize you need anti freeze pots, by the time you find it in the inventory you're most likely already dead. Again showing the same problem as earlier, which is "too much stuff".
Imo if you're looking for a ARPG, either go for Diablo 3 (if you're more casual) or Path of Exile (of you're looking for more depth and interesting build and gear choices). The main reason I played GD was cause I'm waiting for a new Path of Exile expansion at the moment, so once that's out I'll happily go back to that for another month or so of fun builds and engaging and rewarding gameplay

Pros:
+ A story worthy of being a part of the GoT mythos
+ Some truly heart-wrenching moments
+ Choices have weight and impact
+ Actors from the HBO series lend their voices
Cons:
- Artistic style leaves much to be desired
- Occastionally stiff animations
- Starts slow but picks up by Episode 3
Telltale has certainly made a name for itself over the last couple of years with its The Walking Dead series but beyond that most of their releases have been hit-or-miss. Not a lot of noise was made over Tales From the Borderlands, Back to the Future, or The Wolf Among Us but Game of Thrones was an entirely different animal whose success would've either kept the developer in a favorable light or upset fans of both the novel and television franchise.
Thankfully, Game of Thrones proves to be an entirely satisfying addition to this growing fictional universe.
Following a relatively unknown/unused Northern noble house from the mythos called Forrester, the player controls a number of characters associated with the family who find themselves on a slippery slope after the events of the Red Wedding. Much like the Starks, the tables turn on the Forresters quickly and utter annihilation seems inevitable. It's up to the player then to lead the surviving members of House Forrester as they try and navigate their way to survival through cunning and/or strength at their home in Ironrath, in the halls of the Red Keep in King's Landing, or at the Wall and beyond.
As is typical of a Telltale experience, the gameplay relies on player choices during conversations as well as quick-time events. Most of these selections will progress the game forward and have varying degrees of impact in the short and long term with only a very small few resulting in a "game over". Other than this, the player has very little control of what goes on. That being said, if these kinds of adventure titles aren't your thing you're not going to be satisfied.
However, those who can appreciate a good story will be more than pleased with the six episode experience. While it does get off to a rather slow start as you slog through seemingly mundane scenes in the first two episodes, by the third things really start to pick up, you start seeing some of the consequences your choices have brought, and in general the situation gets more and more grave for the Forresters - the stakes much, much higher. Once it gets going it's hard to walk away from and I'm glad I waited until all six episodes released to finally play it. There are some truly heart-wrenching moments here comparable to the despair of seeing Eddard Stark's execution, the shock and horror of the Red Wedding, and the satisfaction of Joffrey's slow and agonizing demise.
The story and characters are absolutely worthy of fitting into the existing literary and television universe and it does a brilliant job of blending the tale of the Forresters into the events between the Red Wedding and Tommen Baratheon's coronation (seasons 3 and 4 of the show) without distancing itself too far or getting too close to make the story seem impossible within the established mythos. Simply put, it's entirely plausible that this could've all gone on in the background of the novels and/or television show. Further supporting its credibility is the inclusion of a number of established characters voiced by their actual actors and actresses from the show. Seeing Jon Snow and Tyrion Lannister and hearing Kit Harrington and Peter Dinklage's voices does wonders for this game's believability and merit.
All-in-all perhaps the only gripe I can bring to the table is the artistic style and animation quality. Clearly, Telltale was going for something that evoked a living painting or pastel drawing but what we end up with is incredibly low resolution textures with noticeably jagged depth of field effects. I understand that the developer makes all their games with simplistic visual designs but I'm not entirely sure this was the way to go or at least at such a low level of quality. Making matters worse however is the shoddy animations. Certain scenes - like the fighting scenes - are done well enough but it's the more simplistic animations like characters walking, talking, etc that appear stiff and robotic. For me, there's nothing worse than that as it takes you right out of the moment when you see a character walk, come to a complete stop, turn 45 degrees, stop, and then start their walk animation again.
Simply put, Game of Thrones is a worthy addition to this ongoing literary and television franchise. It fits right in and does what the other two can not: lets the audience take a crack at surviving in this incredibly dark and brutal medieval fantasy world. If you enjoy this type of gameplay experience (or at least tolerate) this is a journey worth taking, and I for one am quite interested in seeing if Telltale will continue this series with a follow up.

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (/ˈɡɑːndi, ˈɡæn-/;[2] Hindustani: [ˈmoːɦənd̪aːs ˈkərəmtʃənd̪ ˈɡaːnd̪ʱi] ( listen); 2 October 1869 – 30 January 1948) was the preeminent leader of the Indian independence movement in British-ruled India. Employing nonviolent civil disobedience, Gandhi led India to independence and inspired movements for civil rights and freedom across the world. The honorific Mahatma (Sanskrit: "high-souled", "venerable")[3]—applied to him first in 1914 in South Africa,[4]—is now used worldwide. He is also called Bapu (Gujarati: endearment for "father",[5] "papa"[5][6]) in India. In common parlance in India he is often called Gandhiji. He is unofficially called the Father of the Nation.[7][8]
Born and raised in a Hindu merchant caste family in coastal Gujarat, western India, and trained in law at the Inner Temple, London, Gandhi first employed nonviolent civil disobedience as an expatriate lawyer in South Africa, in the resident Indian community's struggle for civil rights. After his return to India in 1915, he set about organising peasants, farmers, and urban labourers to protest against excessive land-tax and discrimination. Assuming leadership of the Indian National Congress in 1921, Gandhi led nationwide campaigns for easing poverty, expanding women's rights, building religious and ethnic amity, ending untouchability, but above all for achieving Swaraj or self-rule.
Gandhi famously led Indians in challenging the British-imposed salt tax with the 400 km (250 mi) Dandi Salt March in 1930, and later in calling for the British to Quit India in 1942. He was imprisoned for many years, upon many occasions, in both South Africa and India. Gandhi attempted to practise nonviolence and truth in all situations, and advocated that others do the same. He lived modestly in a self-sufficient residential community and wore the traditional Indian dhoti and shawl, woven with yarn hand-spun on a charkha. He ate simple vegetarian food, and also undertook long fasts as a means of both self-purification and social protest.
Gandhi's vision of an independent India based on religious pluralism, however, was challenged in the early 1940s by a new Muslim nationalism which was demanding a separate Muslim homeland carved out of India.[9] Eventually, in August 1947, Britain granted independence, but the British Indian Empire[9] was partitioned into two dominions, a Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan.[10] As many displaced Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs made their way to their new lands, religious violence broke out, especially in the Punjab and Bengal. Eschewing the official celebration of independence in Delhi, Gandhi visited the affected areas, attempting to provide solace. In the months following, he undertook several fasts unto death to promote religious harmony. The last of these, undertaken on 12 January 1948 when he was 78,[11] also had the indirect goal of pressuring India to pay out some cash assets owed to Pakistan.[11] Some Indians thought Gandhi was too accommodating.[11][12] Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist, assassinated Gandhi on 30 January 1948 by firing three bullets into his chest at point-blank range.[12]
His birthday, 2 October, is commemorated as Gandhi Jayanti, a national holiday, and world-wide as the International Day of Nonviolence.

I have a love/hate relationship with Telltale's games.
I love games that focus on telling a good story, without compromising gameplay. While Telltale's gameplay has been the same fare since their first Walking Dead (cutscenes with Quick TIme Events) - holding that against them at this point would seem silly.
As such, the gameplay is functional and what one would expect.
So let's rate it on it's main selling point; the storytelling.
In a well-told interactive story, you maintain the illusion of choice and player agency. We, as people, understand that TellTale can't *really* have hundreds of branching interactive paths for all those little 'such and so will remember this' messages they're so fond of throwing up in the upper left corner of your screen.
The trick then is to not show how empty your promises are *while* you're telling the story.
If the audience figures it out after the game, through a wiki or the forums or even a replay ... Hell, you've succeeded in making that first playthrough feel vibrant and alive.
And Game of Thrones, for all it's bluster and bravado falls absolutely flat.
The choices you're forced to make often make little sense, and when choosing diametrically opposed options, GoT isn't afraid to 'overrule' your first choice two spoken sentences later. It's the first thing you learn not to do to your players if you're GM'ing a pen and paper game, and a product that advertises itself as 'reacting to your choices' not even letting you get away with making the limited choices it *itself* presents you with ...
That's how you drop the curtain and strip players of the feeling of agency, and that's where my interest fades.
Then there's the story itself.
I'm a huge "A Song of Ice and Fire" fan, and I *like* Martin's 'gritty' fantasy setting.
I don't even mind the fact that the devs kill a lot of the characters they introduce you to. And I don't even mind they don't give you the chance to prevent it (though really - throw us a small victory here and there).
What I mind is that piling depressing event after depressing event is just poor storytelling.
I liked the first chapter. Dank. Depressing. Hopeless Odds.
Second chapter. Everything gets worse. Great!
Third chapter. Yeah, now we take your dignity too. Suck on it. I love it.
... but the golden rule of telling these stories is that after getting the player as down as you can get 'm ... you need to start offering 'm little bits of hope.
A goal. Things to strive towards. A way to, conceivably, come out on top.
The "Die Hard" idea. Poor Bruce Willis gets smacked around for over an hour, but he still gets to say 'ho ho ho' in the end.
The equivalent here is that you would choose the 'ho ho ho' option, but another NPC will tell you that's a poor idea and then your sister stabs you in the back for no conceivable reason instead, because that'd make the story more miserable.
So...
No.
It's a poor game for not maintaining the illusion of player agency.
It's a poor story for not offering a single glimmer of hope, not even to snatch it away and provide better storytelling through that avenue. Unless you're into that kind of thing. Then be my guest. Paint your windows black, and enjoy the ride.

Half-Life 2 is considered one of the best First Person Shooters to ever be created. But I cannot see why. I got this game as a birthday gift from the Orange Box because my friends told me that I would love it. But Half-Life 2 is a game that I cannot bring myself to finish because of how buggy, confusing, and difficult it is. Before you crusify me on the grounds for disliking a game because people enjoy it, let me explain:
First off: Half-Life 2 doesn't tell you ANYTHING. I counted multiple times where I ran around not knowing where to go, and there's no NPCs or guides to help you figure it out. I had to look up a guide during many points to figure out where to go. If I have to look up a guide to figure out where I need to go in the FIRST CHAPTER, there's something wrong with your game. Did you know you could get drinks from the soda machine to recover help? Did you know that the Health and Suit recharges RELOAD? No, because the game doesn't tell you that.
Secondly: Glitches. I counted 4 times where I ran into some glitch that either killed me for no reason, or made me reload an eariler save because of me or something else being stuck in a wall. I got flung into the air and fell to my death in Chapter 4 for no reason, and at the start of Chapter 11, I spawned inside a wall. I had to use NOCLIP to get myself out of a wall just because bad collision detection.
Finally: This game is REALLY hard. Even when playing on Easy, I found myself dying seemingly endless amounts of times from trying to escape from the Combine. The end of Water Hazard and Sand Traps were the most frustrating parts for me because of how often I died due to so many things attacking me. And combined with the fact that the game doesn't tell you that the soda machines give health and the chargers reload left me with low health alot of the time, further adding to my anger. I've never played a game before that made me both angry and bored.
I feel like Portal is a much better use of you $10 if you haven't played it before. I'm glad I didn't get hooked on the series, because if I did, I would be sad about Episode 3.

Black Desert Online is the MMO of the future
Black desert online has really suprised me with its aspects, but the thing the game truely pulls off best is it's PVP. From shortscale to large scale and even 1v1's held in a battle arena. Black desert has it all. The PVE has a grindy aspect to it, but they have added a feature that gives you a 200% XP boost for an hour every day. Which really motivates players to get out there and level up. The gear enchanting system is pure RNG, a lot of people have bad views on this but I personally love how it's RNG. Because all those times you fail makes up for the feeling you get when that Enchant says "Success". The pearl shop (Real Money For Stuff) has its pay to win aspects, but the pearl shop holds very usefull items e.g. Pets that pick up loot. Each pet is around 10 dollars and is worth every penny because it makes your life that much easier then having to break your finger by pressing r for hours on end. There is also a very good lifeskilling system, from venturing out into the deep sea and going fishing with your guild members, to cooking inside a house, Black desert truely has it all. Unlike other MMO's Black Desert holds no endgame, which some players find annoying and some players love. Personally I love how there isn't an endgame for BDO since it keeps you playing the game for longer. Most MMO's loose players after they reach endgame because they've done it all. But Black Desert has almost too many things you can invest time into.
I guarantee this game will draw you in, this game really has something for everyone to enjoy. Give this game a shot, this really is the MMO of the future

I bought this game on sale for about 8 bucks and ended up playing a bit oer 30 hours. For this price it was well an okay game ofr that time, however, I don't think it has anything too interesting going for itself (compared to other ARPGS of our time at least) and it's more tedious than fun in the later stages, so for anyone looking for a game/grinder they want to play long term, I would not recommend this.
The main two factors I think Grim Dawn messes up is that is has too much stuff and there's too little reward per time spent.
They have over 10 damage types alone and there's no smart drops or anything. Meaning, the amount of loot you find that's comepletely useless to you is huge. Still you gotta go over each piece, and check it's numerous stats, cause it "could" be an upgrade, effectively managing to make the suppsed rewarding part of the grind (i.e. getting the loot) into more of a tedious chore than anything. This is not only true for damage type but also just genreally what you can and can't wear. Usually when gear drops if it's an upgrade it's higher level than you can wear, so you gotta carry it around and then remember 2 hours later to equip it when you finally get those 2-4 level higher up where you can wear it.
The flipside is even worse when it comes to resistances. As is customary you will get resistance penalties in higher difficulties, but since you also have 10 different (yes, no kidding here) resistances you gotta keep in mind (plus armor ofc) it's a pain to try and juggle all of them. Again, keeping in mind that the gear is obviously random, so you can end up in a position of getting a nice upgrade, that you simply can't wear cause it messes up resistances. So you put it in the stash to all the other ones and hope at some point to take a few hours time to figure out IF there's a new combination of items you could wear that are an upgrade AND let you keep the resistances balanced.
If that sounds like fun to you, by all means, get the game, but for me (and I think in general) this is just really bad game design. It confuses having lots of stuff, with having meaningful interesting decisions to make. Overloading the player with options isn't what makes a game deep, it's having impactful decisions to make, which does and Grim Dawn fails at that imo.
Another thing would be the weird "difficulty" spike. I put it in quotes, cause I don't think getting one-shot has anything to do with difficulty, it's just bad game design in my opinion, as there's usually not a decision on the players part that has an impact on the outcome (as opposed to the player needing to make better or more complex decisions). So in GD you'll either find you kill mobs with one or two hits, or they seem to take almost forever to kill. On top of that, some boss/hero mobs just deal a ridiculous amount of damage in a very short time, meaning half the battle is running away to heal then coming back to get a few hits in, then repeating that over and over for 30-40 times until the boss is dead.
Part of that damage spike os no doubt the resistance problem I wrote about earlier, as there's usually a few resistances you won't have high enough and if you gt hit by that damage type you're just kinda screwed, but since there's 10 different resistances you also wouldn't want to just grind over and overfur jsut that one piece with this particular res on it either, since that's also kind of a waste of time, since it's not gonna do anything for most situations. (I mean ultimately you have to have all res, but while leveling trying to always res up seems just weird, since you also want to progress in the game and not stick to a few spots and grind over and over for one or two pieces until you can progress).
Another problem is disables, since there's no skills you have to make you immune or let you get out of immobilizes, freezes or stuns. So again it's either some gear with reduced stun/freeze/immobilize time, or (as I found out by chance at some point) using one time use potions that make you immune or severly reduce the time of those status effects. Problem being, they're also random drop or random recipe drop. Not only that, but since there's so many of those, you can't evn put it somewhere for convenient access, meaning in an actual fight, where all of a sudden you realize you need anti freeze pots, by the time you find it in the inventory you're most likely already dead. Again showing the same problem as earlier, which is "too much stuff".
Imo if you're looking for a ARPG, either go for Diablo 3 (if you're more casual) or Path of Exile (of you're looking for more depth and interesting build and gear choices). The main reason I played GD was cause I'm waiting for a new Path of Exile expansion at the moment, so once that's out I'll happily go back to that for another month or so of fun builds and engaging and rewarding gameplay
It'd surprise me if there's anyone out there that still hasn't played this. If you're that person, seriously... wtf?

If you'll like the game or not depends on if you like the setting, being cave-man style 10 000 BC. Using clubs, bows, spears, fire and tamed animals to fight enemies and get through the day.
It's a good game that is fun to play. Story is fairly simple and all dialogue is spoken in neanderthal so you'll spend a good bit of time reading subtitles.
The main story itself is pretty short but there are plenty of side-quests to do.
There is a lot more focus on crafting and collecting resources to build things such as weapons, ammo, upgrades for your gear and huts for your village.
Taming animals is very simple, but it's fun to send your saber-tooth tiger or giant cave bear into a camp and watching it wreak havoc.
Doing quests and killing things gives XP and eventually skill points that you use to make yourself more powerful.
The biggest issue with this game is the boss fights. there are roughly 4-5 bosses, all of whom break various rules the game has set and some feel really cheap and stupid. Some are just elites with a much larger health-bar, one has a constant poison around him, another is almost immune to damage besides getting icicles dropped on him and another has a bow that 1-shots you and can only be hurt by spears for some reason. You can't stealth kill them and if you're not properly prepared, you are ♥♥♥♥ed.
The apex edition and DLC is pretty meh. The mammoth missions are boring and you only get some animal reskins and early materials that aren't that special. Spec into gathering skills and collect things and you'll be fine.
I'm not sure if I can recommend it at full price since there's ultimately very little variety to the gameplay and it is essentially the shangri-la missions from fra-cry 4 turned into a full game. At a cheaper price, maybe 40-30$ and if the concept interests you. I had fun with it and can recommend this aswell as far-cry 3 and 4.

Unfortunatly, when there's a game like Black Desert that is filled with so much potential, the fact that it falls short just makes it hurts so much worse.
First: There both is and isn't a loot system
>The VAST majority of things that are dropped by monsters are non-items. They are items that serve literally no purpose other than to be traded in for gold. You can't do anything else with them.
>There are occassionally items that drop that are worth a bit more money, but even their use is a bit arguable.
>You will never pick up a weapon or piece of armor that is above the lowest tier.
Second: The upgrade system is probably one of the worst in modern gaming
>It's based on an concept of randomness that is designed to be time consuming.
>Part of me would like to break down why this system is so terrible, but honestly it would take way too much time. Just Google "Black Desert Upgrade Charts" and you'll get the general idea. There are probably twenty charts out there of people trying to figure out how to actually make this system work without it being a complete time-suck.
Third: The marketplace - The ingame, player to player selling system
>Because of the lack of a real loot system, and the highly daunting upgrade system, the marketplace is an absolute neccessity. You will literally spend hours and sometimes even days waiting for a certain peice of armor to appear in the marketplace, and then you have about twenty seconds to tag it to say that you want to buy it. But at the same time, god knows how many people are going to be doing the exact same thing, and the person that comes out with the peice of armor is the person out of that group who is randomly selected to win.
>Just as an example, yesterday I waited around for about five hours to bid on a few select items. Probably tagged about 20 items total because of how infrequently they were coming up. In those five hours with those twenty bids I did not win once. Welcome to the exciting world of Black Desert Online.

FTL is an amazing game that offers you that elusive chance to finally command your own spaceship like you've always dreamed. It's a great value for the money, especially with the advanced edition, with hundreds of potential hours in replay value as you unlock new ships to be played and experiment with new ways to play. The soundtrack itself is great and suits the game perfectly, conveying the mix of epic, nostalgia, and wonder. It's a real challenge that feels genuinely rewarding once you finally win. Kind of a mix between Firefly (you purchase various crew to perform different tasks on your small ship), Star Trek (you command a "Federation vessel" with a crew made of different races each with their own perks. Each crewman grows more effective at their task the more they do it), Star Wars (the basic save the galaxy idea), and Dark Souls in a way (Death comes often, but you learn from it each time) FTL is retro in appearance and difficulty, perhaps too difficult, even on easy, though I found myself enjoying each playthrough and coming back for more anyway. That's because each playthrough feels unique and the story you make up each time is new. While some of the same quests come up from time to time, and exploration feels rushed due to the enemy blocking your movement backward, FTL never feels stale or boring. Definitely rogue like with its randomness and newness, a bit like Oregon Trail even, with RTS combat and the classic strategic choosing of how and when to use your limited resources to ensure your best chance of survival, FTL is engaging but not tedious, easy to pick up but very in depth in customization and gameplay. Each game can last from fifteen minutes (if you find yourself dying early), to an hour and a half (if you reach the last level). You can close the game at any time and pick up where you left off, but there is no save function so the game keeps the tension and urgency. As you will have to make difficult choices and live with the decisions you've made, each game will frustrate you, but leave you fulfilled, which seems worth ten bucks for someone imaginative who's looking for a challenge and replay value, but doesn't have hours each day to invest. Definitely worth a look at the very least. Check out Angry Joe's review on Youtube to get a good idea. 9/10

Telltale's Game of Thrones delivers a rich story with many choices, many meaningless choices. Not only do your choices often feel hollow, with your character of the moment doing something that doesn't match up with the intent or your choice, but the choices presented epitomize the worst of CRPGs. They restrict you to obvious rails without giving you any ability to take a path you really want. These rails are most apparent in the form of plot holes: you are left to wonder how some events transpire the way they do when you objectively know they shouldn't have. This is poor writing.
Most choices adjust dialog or short term actions. Some few have more long term effects, but they are occluded enough that you won't feel that they have any impact for a long time to come. So you can rock the cart back and forth a bit, but it is still firmly on the rails with barely the veneer of agency. In this way the choices get in the way of the story rather than facilitate it, and you can often feel like it would have been better to just give you an animated movie.
This game is also marred by gameplay that consists of quicktime events and keyboard controls that are unchangeable from the outdated and pedestrian WASD configuration. This gameplay comes with little communication in how it works shy of using ESC to access menus to see the controls. The worst part isn't the controls themselves but that they are not integrated seemlessly into the experience. What controls you can use at any given time varies, which serves to take you out of the story rather than flowing with the story.
If this combination of features tickles your fancy, then it will be an awesome game. If not, then you will find the choices and gameplay to be barriers to enjoyment.

tl;dr if you liked Game of Thrones, and have watched up to season 5, and you like Telltale Games, then you will probably like this. Be prepared for all of your plans to come to ruin.
Warning:  Should watch the show first.  I think up until the end of season 4?
I watched all six seasons before playing this game and I'm glad I did.  I think the game occurs from the ends of season 3 to season 4 so watching to the end of season 4 should add the most depth to the came while preventing you from getting any spoilers for the show.
That said,  I enjoyed Game of Thrones, the show.  I wasn't terribly engaged, emotionally in it, but I enjoyed it.  Having said that, by the nature of the game, you will be more engaged because you control the characters.  You identify more with the characters and engage with them so you are more invested than you might be just watching a show.
And terrible, terrible things happen to those characters.  You will second guess every decision you make and regret a majority of them.  That makes the game somewhat uncomfortable to play and can be less rewarding when it feels like you will lose, no matter what option you choose.  Still, to me that engagement is a sign of how well it was done, and that makes it a good game, to me.
Also, I feel like the game was designed to have a second season, and that a lot of the rewards for your actions in the first season would probably play out in the second.
I went into the game with the same outlook as the show.  I decided to believe that all of my favorite characters would suffer a terrible fate and/or die, so I was always pleasantly surprised when they survived and/or things turned out well for them.
Notice:  I played this on Mac and I did have some technical glitches.  When I loaded the game, there was audio stuttering.  After playing the game for some time the audio stuttering went away or I no longed noticed it.  I restarted the game a few times and every time I had to set the resolution, which was annoying.  However, after passing the first save in the game, I believe that also saved my settings.  That's odd for a game not to save the settings until the game itself saves, but that seems to be how it works.
Also, on my controller, a rumblepad 2, my right trigger was actually right button or r1 instead of r2.
Sometimes, there were action sequences where I need to do an action quickly and it wasn't working.  In these situations I switched to mouse and keyboard to complete them.  I believe I had this issue in other telltale games as well.

Now that there is XCOM 2 on the horizon, I think it is a great time to talk about XCOM Enemy Unknown.
XCOM Enemy Unknown is a superb turn based strategy game, made by the combany that made the Civilization franchise. I would say that they are the grand masters of strategy, but some would argue back.
The gameplay is really nice. The mechanics compliment each other nicely, the enemy are not so samey and the meta game is really cool. There are the minor ''gripes'' though. The AI in the easier difficulties is poor at best, some say the game is repetitive, the upgrade system is boring/too linear etc. But those minor setbacks did not bother me. I dont care about the AI, I kind of liked that upgrade system and the battles were exhilarating. The risk of losing your Operatives created a bond between the player and it.
But I still hear people whine (The battles are 75% RnG, it is stupid, my Operative should have hit that with a 85% hit chance, now he is dead). Where I would say, but what about the decisions before that hit missed? Why did you need to put your mission on that one shot, if he missed you lose, if he had hit the enemy, they win. But why? there is not a single mission, where you have to take a risk like that. The only thing that can doom you in the mission, is your decisions. Sure the RnG is real in this game, but you do not have to pray to RnGeesus to help you on your mission, you do not.
XCOM Enemy Unknown is a good strategy game made by the people that know how to make a good strategy game. The game has a few issues, but every game can not be perfect. This is the part of the review, where i would put a score, but I will not, because scores are too arbitrary to make a difrence in the world. Just play the game for the most honest opinion.

On the harder difficulties quite a few creatures  can kill you in two hits. if only cause the game wont let them in one. Survival also is the best way to go in my opinion, just dont get too attached to anything around a sabertooth.

A classic of rope-wrap painting - a form of zen meditation where a paint-soaked rope is wound around a wooden sculpture to achieve interesting artistic patterns.
In Zen Bound 2, your objective is to wrap the rope around objects of increasing complexity to achieve a certain minimum of area being coated with the embedded beads of paint.
The first thing that can be noticed is the amazing music.  The soundtrack is relaxing and emotional, assisting players to maintain a steady, calm focus throughout their play.
Being a game that was originally designed for the iPad and ported to the PC, the developers managed to do an amazing job.  The interface is simple, and grants a medium of challenge in controlling the objects being painted.  Controls are fluid and manipulable, with few issues in translating finger swipes with mouse motions.
Graphics-wise, the objects seem hand-crafted and the paint works organically to provide an authentically painted look.  Shadows and artistic backgrounds flow and move to match lighting, enhancing the experience.
Physics can sometimes let the rope down by hurling it into a hyperdimensional realm where imploding is a normal factor of life.  It tends to resolve itself after a time, and still functions like rope even when it's observing space and time from a perspective beyond our comprehension.  Cthulhu f'tagn.
None to speak of.
Being able to share the finished products from within the game - say, creating a .gif of the object being rotated - would be amazing.
10/10 for a casual, and relaxing, meditation game where your challenge is in patience.  Secret Exit Ltd knew what they were aiming for, and hit it square on. Bravo.

If you enjoyed the original Alan Wake, you will probably find this satisfying to some degree.  The original game was very story-intensive whereas American Nightmare is very short on story and focuses almost exlusively on action/combat.  That isn't to say that this doesn't have a narrative, it is just minimal and not linear.  The combat elements seem to have been improved.  I did not enjoy this aspect of the original game, but for the most part it is executed well enough in this game.  There is a bigger variety of weapons, and although the combat mechanics are virtually identical, they seem to be refined to a degree, although perhaps this is a placebo effect.  Since this title relies primarily on combat, the designers have done a better job with ammo & supply placement.
As others have noted, you repeat the levels a few times and, although each time is a bit different, you're still ultimately going over travelled ground with basically identical objectives.  The game tries to offset this to some degree by incentivizing you to explore to collect items.  I did not care for this as wandering around exploring just resulted in getting attacked more thus wasting more ammo.
I'd be remiss if I didn't note that the character animations have improved over the first title.  There are only 4 characters really in this game.  Unlike the first Alan Wake, these don't look so atrocious (although they're not great either).
Although I do recommend this game, it isn't an extremely strong recommendation.  It's short, repetitive, the story is weak.  There is some charm to it, however, and if you liked the first game then consider this more like a DLC.  Only buy it if it's cheap and if  you liked the combat of the first game.

Half-Life 2 is considered one of the best First Person Shooters to ever be created. But I cannot see why. I got this game as a birthday gift from the Orange Box because my friends told me that I would love it. But Half-Life 2 is a game that I cannot bring myself to finish because of how buggy, confusing, and difficult it is. Before you crusify me on the grounds for disliking a game because people enjoy it, let me explain:
First off: Half-Life 2 doesn't tell you ANYTHING. I counted multiple times where I ran around not knowing where to go, and there's no NPCs or guides to help you figure it out. I had to look up a guide during many points to figure out where to go. If I have to look up a guide to figure out where I need to go in the FIRST CHAPTER, there's something wrong with your game. Did you know you could get drinks from the soda machine to recover help? Did you know that the Health and Suit recharges RELOAD? No, because the game doesn't tell you that.
Secondly: Glitches. I counted 4 times where I ran into some glitch that either killed me for no reason, or made me reload an eariler save because of me or something else being stuck in a wall. I got flung into the air and fell to my death in Chapter 4 for no reason, and at the start of Chapter 11, I spawned inside a wall. I had to use NOCLIP to get myself out of a wall just because bad collision detection.
Finally: This game is REALLY hard. Even when playing on Easy, I found myself dying seemingly endless amounts of times from trying to escape from the Combine. The end of Water Hazard and Sand Traps were the most frustrating parts for me because of how often I died due to so many things attacking me. And combined with the fact that the game doesn't tell you that the soda machines give health and the chargers reload left me with low health alot of the time, further adding to my anger. I've never played a game before that made me both angry and bored.
I feel like Portal is a much better use of you $10 if you haven't played it before. I'm glad I didn't get hooked on the series, because if I did, I would be sad about Episode 3.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is a stand-alone followup to the events of the DLC episodes of the original game. Too big for a DLC but not quite a sequel, its more of an expansion. Nightmare features what feels like quadruple the available weapons, faster flashlight energy regeneration, more responsive controls and more action-oriented encounters. There are some who decry Nightmare as of inferior quality to the base game, and while it does offer an explanation for why its the same three levels repeated three times with differences only in dialogue and enemy placement, that's still obvious repetition. Regardless of this, it really does play a lot better mechanically. It includes the obligatory wave survival mode for those inclined. It also offers an incentive for tracking down the manuscript pages beyond backstory, as they are required to access lockboxes new weapons- however, I found the most useful weapon to be the crossbow, accessible on the third level and found simply hanging on a tree, no manuscript pages necessary. A harder cap is placed on your flares and flashbangs, but ammunition is much more plentiful to account for the more frequent enemies encountered, as well as newer, tougher enemies.
We find a slightly older Alan, now in plaid work shirt and jeans instead of his stuffy tweed jacket, and much more experienced in facing the shadows that haunt him. Trapped in a Twilight Zone version of a Arizona highway-side town, Alan faces a cruel doppleganger called Mr. Scratch who claims to be everything he was too weak to be, but is really just a huge ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥, the manifestations of Alan's feelings of inadequacy as a writer and a husband. He has the opportunity to help a few people on the way.
American Nightmare is a good play, but it will make little sense to anyone who has not played the first game from a story standpoint. If you have the opportunity to play the first game I strongly recommend doing so before playing American Nightmare.

Now that there is XCOM 2 on the horizon, I think it is a great time to talk about XCOM Enemy Unknown.
XCOM Enemy Unknown is a superb turn based strategy game, made by the combany that made the Civilization franchise. I would say that they are the grand masters of strategy, but some would argue back.
The gameplay is really nice. The mechanics compliment each other nicely, the enemy are not so samey and the meta game is really cool. There are the minor ''gripes'' though. The AI in the easier difficulties is poor at best, some say the game is repetitive, the upgrade system is boring/too linear etc. But those minor setbacks did not bother me. I dont care about the AI, I kind of liked that upgrade system and the battles were exhilarating. The risk of losing your Operatives created a bond between the player and it.
But I still hear people whine (The battles are 75% RnG, it is stupid, my Operative should have hit that with a 85% hit chance, now he is dead). Where I would say, but what about the decisions before that hit missed? Why did you need to put your mission on that one shot, if he missed you lose, if he had hit the enemy, they win. But why? there is not a single mission, where you have to take a risk like that. The only thing that can doom you in the mission, is your decisions. Sure the RnG is real in this game, but you do not have to pray to RnGeesus to help you on your mission, you do not.
XCOM Enemy Unknown is a good strategy game made by the people that know how to make a good strategy game. The game has a few issues, but every game can not be perfect. This is the part of the review, where i would put a score, but I will not, because scores are too arbitrary to make a difrence in the world. Just play the game for the most honest opinion.

I'm somewhat mixed about the Game of Thrones game. I did like it overall so I'm going to click the thumbs up.
The first part of the game is quite memorable and full of interesting situations. You play a cast of characters focused on the struggles of a family that finds itself on the losing side. I liked this part more than the TV show it's derived from. The characters are relatable and full of personality, the dialogue is less solemn than the HBO show.
Many situations are heartbreaking: the game teaches you that every time you hold your head up proud, every time you try to retain a shred of dignity or honour, someone you care about will get hurt. It helps that you will really care about them; most of the time I was not ready to make that sacrifice. I often found myself in the mud; spat upon; drawing the contempt of my family and friends rather than putting them to pain. It relates to real life in this regard, at least from what I've seen of life.
The later chapters share some of the weaknesses of the source material. As the storylines stray away from the personal stories of family intricacies and politics, they start focusing on the exploits of the Targaryen broad in the warm countries and the stuff that happens North of the Wall, which are far less interesting or meaningful in my view. As the game plods to a somewhat uninspired climax, there's also more generic action of lower quality, becoming a bit harder to immerse into (in my playthrough I've seen characters shrugging arrows to the torso and stab wounds that undermined the previous feeling of realism)
The game's ending also suffers from shoddier craftsmanship; it lets you peer behind the veil to notice the illusion of choice and consequence.  As many reviewers pointed out, don't go expecting too much from the old catchphrase 'choices matter' as the experience is sometimes fairly clumsily railroaded; maybe somewhat more blatantly than other Telltale titles (or maybe you just notice it more if you've seen it before).
Still, the memorable moments hit hard and I enjoyed my time, so buy GoT on a sale if you want something with more heart and grit than your average videogame story. Don't expect perfection. It still holds more depth than 50% of TV shows stories, which is remarkable for a game with a strong sense of presence and a degree of agency.

WOW Where do I start!? This Game is outright amazing and it has taken me 500 hours of playtime to finally come up with a review, Im going to try to keep this short and not make it sound like a guide.
Black Desert Online (BDO) is an MMORPG if you dont know what this is think of games like Path of Exile or World of Warcraft. the game incoperates some amazing visuals with a very large scaled map, PvP and lots of Lifeskilling. However do keep in mind, I would only recommend this game to the person who has alot of free time on there hands (I do mean alot...) because after hitting level 56/57 Xp start to go up very very slowly and the game gets very challenging very quickly (Like 1-2% XP and hour of non stop grinding mobs / After level 59/60 it gets even worse) so if you dont have that free time you wont be doing an PvP any time soon, However this is an MMORPG AFTERALL! you can always lifeskill or AFK on some alt accounts to earn some cash fishing, or cooking etc. while u go to work or school. Overall for things to do in the game I give it a 10/10 and would say its an MMO for the Hardcore Player.
Compared to its competitors BDO Stacks up very well... Coming in at ($11 CAD) this game is a steal, looking at its main competitor WoW (World of Warcraft) which requires you to not only buy the game and its DLCs but also to a monthly fee! so for someone who doesnt have alot of free time paying memberships doesnt work well... another good side to BDO. Graphics wise to its competitors, I think its obvious... No matter what Price you get it for, on sale or not (Don't fall for those useless Bundles) BDO is a great game. It caters to the busy person who comutes to school or work who can sit AFK on an ALT making money, it caters to those who have free time who play for the PvP Aspect (which is amazing btw, totally level and gear mean everything and not much skill but the abilites and animations are amazing) or grinds for the Boss Gear, BDO is just an MMORPG meant for everyone. with no monthly fee you dont have to worry about playing as much to get your money's worth, and did I mention unlike WoW BDO has already had 3 Major Game updates / DLC given for free (Valenica Part I and II, and Kamasylvia Part I and Part II coming soon).
TL:DR - My Overall recomendation for BDO is a 10/10 a great looking game with lots to do at a great Price!

Quake Live was a free way to play, well, Quake. Specifically, an updated version of Quake 3, with some balance tweaks, the maps from Team Arena and the console ports built in, and some new ones as well. They did some "sanitizing", like removing blood and gore, but the fast and frantic action you wanted was still there, and in all the game types you could ask for.
The problem is, this wasn't making money. Offering fun and cool stuff for free, and then also offering the opportunity to spend some money to expand your gameplay experience should've been enough, but it wasn't. Why it wasn't is another conversation   entirely, though clearly someone up at Bethesda felt the solution lay somewhere within the product itself, not the delivery.
Now that Quake Live is finally available to a much, MUCH wider audience with the Steam launch, it's also come with major changes to the base gameplay that radically alter the fundamentals of how Quake Live plays. These changes are pretty terrible.
In all game types outside of Clan Arena and Duel, you will now choose two weapons to spawn with. Previously, you would pick up your weapons in the environment, like any other arena shooter. This piece alone removes all emphasis on item and map control, and entirely on "shoot dudes". While this may sound like a fine change to the uninitiated, part of what makes arena shooters stand out is the emphasis on outthinking your enemy and outplaying your enemy, rather than outshooting. If you were in control of the item spawns, you could turn things around that otherrwise would be dire. Without that mechanic, fights play out very similarily every time, and it gets old fast.
Premium members can host servers using the "classic" rules, but these servers are far and few between. The payment plans for Premium memberships have noticeably been changed with the release of this overhaul, and for the worse. Don't bend over and take it.
If I ever play another game with the Quake name and see loadouts and damage numbers flying out of guys when I shoot them, I'm ♥♥♥♥ing done.

It's a mother♥♥♥♥ing life simulator.
Every time you fall, you gain experience.
That's this game. I've recently beat Phase 1 of the boss, when 2 days ago, I could barely fly to sector 8 with the Kestrel.
And that's a life lesson.
The game simulates the randomness of life, and pushes you to be as living as you are in life.
And perhaps that's the missing link I only just recently noticed.
This game will frustrate, hence my vote being neutral. (I wish I could actually reflect this somehow)
But I can finally see what makes this game appeal to the masses.
The randomness isn't the problem. It's the game. And it's life. Because in life, you build experience. You build your tolerance to defeat. And you just keep going.
And well. Succeed at it. Thus is life. Thus is challenge. Thus is FTL
This is the final major edit.
Edit #1: Mostly the review stays the same (see below). The main difference I've noticed as per the second day of playing is just a slight improvement in knowledge after reading survival guides from online.
I don't know what to think of that. That shows a lack of accessibility to information in the game, but since the game sells on it... Eh.
Still personally think the difficulty is far too unforgiving, but maybe I just wasn't cut for perma-death roguelike.
Well if I eventually win, I guess its earned. If I ever reach sector 8 again. Having only reached it once in 13 hours, I'm slightly doubtful that will happen.
Main Review:
My friends are going to find this recommendation odd, and probably yell at me for it.
And I might change it myself, once I get past this frustration I am feeling.
I cannot in good conscience, recommend this to the standard gamer. This game isn't for the common taste, far from it. It's too difficult, too punishing without reward, and just too random to be worth any common gamer's (or even some hardcore gamer's) time. I play on easy, get to the boss, and die. Hell, let's strike out the "get to the boss" part.
You die. Alot. And you almost never are rewarded for it.  Oh hey, I unlocked a crappy Engi ship... Sigh.
Some people will have fun with this. The crowd that doesn't want to have his or her hand held while gaming will certainly love it. I still like it, mostly for the gameplay, combat, tactics. etc.
But having fun with it is far from the truth.
But this rating will change accordingly, as I'll probably eventually unlock some supership that actually gives me a reason to keep trying.
And for those FTL fans who are actually enjoying this, more power to you.
But I find it an experiment in torture.
TL; DR:
The game is a representation of the challenges of life. You win some, you loose alot. You build character and experience and eventually succeed.
But for those who are easily frustrated, or come to gaming as an escape from the realities of life.
This is not your game.
Neutral vote.

This one feels a bit like a prototype of what Alan Wake 2 could be. Consider it Alan Wake 1.5.
This one tweaks the combat gameplay a little bit because it focuses more on combat. Not that Alan Wake was an intense survival horror, but there certainly was more moments in that one where you felt like you had to watch your ammo than there is in this one. They've added more weapons this time around, which makes the combat have even more variety.
This originally was an Xbox Live Arcade game, so it's much more limited than a full game would be. But they do a good job with what they have. The story mode has essentially 3 levels that you replay 3 times each. Most other small games like this would do this in a way that makes you feel it's smaller scale, but the way they integrate it into the story and make it feel different each time was really nice.
I'm sure some people wouldn't like the way that this one feels more combat oriented than the original game, or perhaps the different tone or even the smaller amount of content, but I think it's a great little game. Certainly something that shows what Alan Wake 2 could be like.

This game made me extremely sad. We saw in it the plot for Alan Wake II, along with a collection of what would have been the new gameplay elements.
- New Enemies
- Alan Wake discovers rewriting reality
- The pseudo-horror theme was finally dropped in exchange for a more arcade shooter feel, which suited the story much better.
You can tell the sort of plot they would have gone with had this been a full Alan Wake II, as well.
The game would have placed us back in Alan Wake's Shoes some time after he'd learned to reshape reality. I assume the tutorial would have been the player helping Alan put the fictional Night Springs in the real Arizona. We'd meet Mr. Scratch after the fact, not before, although Alan could have had prior knowledge of him. We'd get more environments to explore than the gas station, the observatory, and the drive-in, rewriting reality to save the people who have been hurt by Mr. Scratch. And hopefully he'd meet a better end than a freaking Drive-in projector, one that he himself had played with hours before. Of course Barry, Rose, and that sheriff whose name escapes me would come back into play, if only because Mr. Scratch tried to manipulate them. In the end he'd get to see his wife again.
Honestly, I hope that if they ever make a real Alan Wake II, they do that and remove American Nightmare from the canon.  There was so much good material shown here that would have made for a great Alan Wake II. Too bad Remedy is too focused on all their other  IPs at the moment. Then again, if they chose to deal with the record company who screwed them over for Alan Wake 1, I wouldn't blame them for delaying the sequel a decade or two more.

This was a great, fun, engaging multiplayer game to play with friends in local co-op. The campaign was adequately challenging and varied. And the experience with others is great!
It should be restated though that as a single player game, it is tremendously lacking. It should not be considered viable to play it solo.
As a final thought: Recipies could be MUCH more complicated/difficult, and I do hope future content introduces new combinations of ingredients to bring challenge back into the kitchen for players who have already mastered all of the game's content.
Is it worth the full price? No, not for single player. Is it worth the full price, divided by how many players you expect to play with you? Yes, definitely. We were able to get roughly 6-7 hours out of it on the campaign alone. The versus modes improve on the replayability. However, you need 4 players to really enjoy it at that point.
Final Verdict: Great game, get it on sale unless you have 3 ready chefs standing by.

This game is a MUST play for anyone who loves Sci-Fi and tactical gameplay.

This is the first review I've felt motivated to write, perhaps because I've come out of this experience with a powerful feeling of disappointment, rather than a simple like/dislike.
I'm a huge fan of Game of Thrones and the Telltale games I've played so far (The Walking Dead and Wolf Among Us), but this played like a combination of the two made by someone with no idea of what makes either of those things great. All in all, the story is just an endless recycling of numerous plot beats from the TV show with nothing new to say about the setting, and a great number of places where the player's involvement is made to feel insignificant, if not outright irrelevant. Other than to shamelessly copy the entire Stark family plotline, I wonder why they even made this about a noble house and didn't just write a story about some peasants caught up in the conflict, considering the relentless beatdown you're given – presumably the danger of being original was just too great.
Coupled with some technical issues that first prevented me from playing the game at all and then forced me to replay entire scenes at least twice, I believe you can do far better in terms of Telltale offerings. I won't be on board for Season 2, and if I feel nostalgic for this one I'll just rewatch the first season of the TV show instead.
If you've bought it already, stick around for one of the worst attempts at a Northern/Received Pronunciation/South African accent you've ever heard in the form of Gwyn Whitehill, and also the ending presentation regarding your actions, which is actually a pretty interesting reflection on your playstyle. There was a lot of potential in forcing players to engage in the political doublespeak rat's nest of King's Landing, and on the occasions it does manifest it's a different experience from other interactions in Telltale, but it's not enough to carry the otherwise awful Hollywood writing on show here.

This isn't a game where you have the most massive armies, or you feel like the most badass commander. It's not quite the game that extreme micromanagers would enjoy. But more than any other game I have ever seen, including its predecessor and other RTS games of similar type, you get attached to units. You know everything about the units you have because you've had them for so long in the game, and then losing them makes you feel it both strategically and emotionally. You want to take revenge for that unit, you create another one of the same type but it just doesn't feel the same - everything feels like a troop that you sent out there and that you do not want to die.
Gamewise, this game has unbelievable gameplay options thanks to steam workshop and, with any luck, incoming mod support - not to mention the soon to be released expansion, Western Front Armies. This game, much like Dawn of War 1 to Dawn of War 2, does not quite feel like its predecessor - while they share a lot of similar aspects, many things feel different. Maps and armies are generally smaller, and the maps are also considerably more open with few, if any, obvious choke points. While some may complain this is a less fun gameplay mechanic, it's extremely realistic and can prove to be extremely fun and challenging, especially with the line of sight system that now rivals Men of War's same LoS system where objects, smoke, etc can block your units vision which opens up immense possibilites for stealth and flanking.
The only complaint I have is the snow mechanic - while it may look nice visually, they really didn't do as much with it as I wish they could have. Snow maps do not feel fun, but rather tedious, as you're forced to advance slowly due to cold weather. The maps also provide most sources of heat and such in strategic locations for you by default, meaning there's no real point to building fires other than rebuilding destroyed ones. Snow allows units to leave footprints and such, yes, but with maps that are generally smaller than the predecessor as mentioned, this really isn't necessary as the tracks simply wont continue far enough to be bothered with as units would likely be visible at the same time or very quickly after their tracks are noticed - not to mention tracks can only be left in deep snow, which is not abundant in the maps and areas where it is located can easily be avoided with no real tactical disadvantages.
This complaint aside though, this game is outstanding in the RTS department. It is not the same as other RTS games on the market, such as Men of War and such, and I wish people would stop comparing the two games. Looking at this game as it's own game, it is beyond fantastic and I could not have asked for a better sequel. (Aside from snow.)

Super Amazing Wagon Adventure is a randomly generated sidescrolling shooter that banks on a couple things: goofiness, nostalgia (slightly) and not caring too much about shooter games.
If I was to judge it purely based on its mechanics, it's not much more than mediocre. The weapon options are nothing too special, and the enemies mainly rely on strength of numbers to add challenge. The boss fights that I've experienced so far were OK but no big deal.
What really is entertaining is the silly nature of the entire endeavor. The game takes a lot of cues from Oregon Trail and basically makes fun of every option.
"There is a river. [Tom] has the brilliant idea to jump over it. Or, you could try fording it."
[Ford]
[Jump]
And then you can actually jump over the river if you want to.
Other times you might be attacked by modern cars or "inner demons", and the text that accompanies almost every event is weird and goofy. And it works almost every time, and because the game is so quick to play (the game I won probably took between 5-10 minutes) and there are a lot of options, it hasn't yet gotten old.
But it probably will eventually. And when I'm tired of seeing a million buffalo charge at me for the hundredth time, then I'll probably stop because all it has left are the mechanics, which, as stated, really aren't much special.
Still, it doesn't cost much, and it still plays much better than the far more tedious McPixel (I don't know why I feel the comparison is necessary - highly pixelated graphics and bite-size gameplay I guess, but nothing else much is in common so *shrug*) and I still foresee getting some quality time out of it, so I would recommend it!

A good roguelike is a game that features randomness, but also a tough-but-fair mentality.  They let you understand the randomness, prepare for it, and stack the deck and load the dice in your favor.  Good roguelikes are all about taking the time to get a good feel for the mechanics, and how best to manipulate a complex, nuanced world around you to the maximum effect, rather than just relying upon dumb luck.
This game isn't a good roguelike.
Prepare to experience the boredom of constantly restarting, hoping to get a good weapon which, if obtained, will ensure easy domination of the game, but instead losing most campaigns in the first or second sector because the RNG hates you.
Prepare for the "adventure" of trying to achieve long-term goals like unlocking other ships through events that are absolutely random, and require just plain craking the slot machine arm time after time after time until the RNG forgets to spite you.
I really like the fact you can design and build your own base.

When I first looked at this game, I was at first amazed that the new Tropico Game, be mindful I was always playing Tropico 3 for awhile.  Upon installing there were some new things that I liked, and some things I didn't like but in the overall It's a great game to try out.
Let's start off with the basics,
So like in Tropico 3 you own your island, want to provide the nourishment and economy of your island, that was easy at first, however what got me is the controls of the game, back in Tropico 3 the controls were alittle bit easier the ASWD keys also helped me around the island here, the ASWD don't really help, making you rely on the Arrow Keys.  Upon building my little paradise more to a standard economical side, I noticed that there were certain buildings that required ministers to unlock, which can be a downside if you are those SimCity 2013 fans that want to focus their needs but remember this isn't SimCity.  Upon having that, I got a cinematic and notification that a tornado has occurred.  Now this is where I get a bit upset at the disaster fix of Tropico 4 lacks in.  The Tornado rampaged itself through the heart of my little town, but none of the buildings the Tornado hit never really did collapse or fall apart, ONLY the house/building it was targeting.  It may lack in the disaster area there, but the rest of the disasters are pretty neat.
Upon finishing a few missions, the game sure has it's ups and downs but its disasters aren't really THAT helpful, sure I loved the missions and how some can upgrade your city to modern times, which really makes it great, however there are some moments where you want to revert back to those old buildings because they can save space sometimes.   In all, the Game is great and I recommend for those that liked/loved the Tropico or City Building series.
