Zombies, quite clearly, are monsters that get no shortage of love in the video game world. After all, take a brief glance through the Steam store, and you’ll find it only takes a matter of moments to find a title that pits you against the shambling undead in some way or another. This isn’t necessarily a bad thing when you consider the fact that there’s always some degree of satisfaction to be taken in turning a zombie’s brain into mush, but it does mean it’s hard to find something out there that keep things fresh and exciting. Enter Dying Light, and it’s rather novel solution to the problem; a healthy dose of… Parkour?
Yes, one of Dying Light’s main selling points comes in gracing you with the ability to jump and vault around its world like some sort of demented acrobat Dying Light’s main selling point is perhaps the ability to jump and vault around its map like a lunatic, using all the advantages that provides to swing the zombie apocalypse in your favour as you start to bash some skulls in. It’s a strange mix; the comparison that is always drawn is that’s it’s a hybrid of Dead Island’s violence and the free running from Mirror’s Edge, and in reality that’s pretty damn close to what you should expect.
It actually creates an interesting hybrid of gameplay styles, and in an odd way the gameplay shifts and mutates the more time you put into playing it. In the beginning, you’re a pathetic weakling - the game only just stops short of blatantly telling you to stay away from zombie encounters, and even taking one or two on at this point can lead to a quick and untimely death. Instead, your focus moves to scrambling from roof to roof in a desperate bid to stay away from confrontation, any daring attempts at attack generally taking the form of desperate hit and runs.
Yet as you progress and grow stronger, levelling up your character’s strength and agility whilst finding stronger weapons and supplies, you’ll find yourself hitting the streets and tackling things head on more and more. From the cowardly kitten, you become a slicing and dicing killing machine, and it’s really satisfying to do so. Yet you’re not done; the gameplay shifts again once gun-toting mercenaries come into play, becoming a war of attrition as you slowly creep through buildings taking pot-shots at your foes in what can best be described as a really odd version of Rainbow Six. It’s another piece that gets thrown into the survival stew, and you’d better get good at it fast lest you starve to death.
The clever thing with all this, however, comes in the way that the game can manipulate you into having to switch your approach at a moment’s notice. You might be majestically soaring between rooftops, only for an impromptu missed jump or loud noise to suddenly have the zombies bring the fight to you. On the opposite side of the spectrum, you might be happily slaughtering away, only for night to rapidly fall and make the really nasty stuff crawl out from the woodwork, causing a hasty retreat to the skies. It’s a really good way of keeping things fresh and not letting you remain complacent; you always need to be on your toes, lest you die. Not knowing what’s coming next is the main catalyst that will keep you playing; you don’t know what’s coming around the next corner, but you certainly want to find out.
Looking elsewhere, Dying Light’s story is a fairly cookie-cutter affair; you’re dropped in to recover a government file, but slowly and surely you find out the truth about what has occurred while battling fellow humans – the TRUE monsters, you see? It’s a story that comprises a sheer storm of clichés, and while the use of such clichés is executed reasonably well, this isn’t a narrative that’s going to stick in the memory for any extended period of time. It’s a healthily long campaign that’ll certainly keep you busy for many an hour, though. This is bolstered by many a side mission and challenge, and while many of them are a bit on the repetitive side (basically boiling down to glorified fetch quests), they all culminate into providing the game with a healthy lifespan.
Anything else? Well, the game looks pretty good graphically. I can’t say there’s much which astounded me visually, but it does manage to pull off some good looking vistas when it feels in the mood to do so. The default controls also felt a little cumbersome to me, but with the ability to remap things to your heart’s content (Or just grab a controller, which was my personal approach) it feels a bit unfair to moan about that. Finally, multiplayer is fun enough (if a little confusing at first), but I’d suggest turning the invasions off to begin with. Not doing so results in rival players having an irritating knack of appearing when you are in the middle of doing something important - cutting you off from your objective in the process.
Dying Light, therefore, is a commendable mash up of styles, which on paper perhaps looks like it shouldn’t work, but when put into practice provides a refreshing take on the zombie survival genre. The game’s ambition and scale manages to reach the lofty heights that you’ll often be climbing to, while its gameplay, just like the zombies, certainly has some bite to it.

Spoiler alert -- fake "achievements", you win them just by playing the game, which in many cases means simply leaving it switched on to run its course.
Not your standard RPG, but a narrative role that you need to watch constantly for dialogue choices and action prompts with limited time, just like in the real world.  Fiddly to play but as your finger-memory grows, settles down to "acceptable" -- it never becomes a joy to play, so it won't make it past the usual filters that determine which games make it big, and which flounder. Can't honestly say if this is better or worse than the OTHER Game of Thrones title, which was a disappointing generic clone based on a well-used game engine, its just different, sharing only the fact that the franchise deserves a better game than either offers....the only PLUS is that is saves the game automatically every couple of minutes so if you miss a screen prompt you don't need to wade back through the last half hour's narrative to replay it all, simply to spot the prompt you missed.  Graphics are reasonable, in an impressionistic sort of way, but you still get oddly angular wine bottles and other details where a little additional artistic application would have been a huge improvement.
You may not get a "feel" for this game until you reach chapter 3, where some very slightly interestinhg things begin to happen, so give it a bit of time before abandoning it out of sheer boredom (yes, it can be very dull in places).  Just watch those "achievemnents" mount up, you win them simply by playing the game, not doing anything special or difficult.

I am truly unable to understand why people rate so negatively this game at all. I found it perfect under many aspects.
Graphic
The graphic compartment of the game looks fabulous, the character customization is fine tuned and allows a precise creation of the kind of character you want, also, if you are lazy and want to make a character looking like some sort of celebrity you can because they have a huge library of fan-made characters that resembles anybody you want to look like. The game graphic itself is absolutely beautiful, and looks amazing, both the sunsets and the sea looks awesome, and the towns I seen so far are awesomely hand-crafted with a nice unique topology in a world full of details, useful details.
Combat
I found so far (I am level 30 dark knight) very easy, it's by no mean simple, I have dozens of skills and options I can choose from with nice combos and everything, my character seems umbelivably strong even with crappy equipment, I will have to tackle for harder challenges and see if anything can stop me at all, so far I've been doing areas for my level and pretty much wiped the floor with anything that moved. The combos are smooth, well rendered and beautiful looking, My knight dances while fights and has an awesome short range teleport move (that's the main reason for which I chose that class). it's simply relaxing fighting in that way.
Crafting
it's not complex like SWG but neither simplistic at all, I love the rough crafting that allows you to grind, heat, sift, chop, mix and do several kind of intuitive operations on raw materials to refine them or prepare them for crafting, the system is actually very smart alot of components are replaceable, so far I've just seen cooking but it does make the difference! it helped me to overcome a plethora of problems and helped me to do stuff that is actually useful! I can't wait to see what it has in store for the higher levels, or what I could create with alchemy or blacksmithing. Everything in this game seems to be made smartly. Everything counts, everything is useful, everything can be used and put to good use.
Auction house
it works!! at first I was befuddled by the plethora of... money the game threw at you, I thought the "millions" of silver was the actual gold of WoW for example, nope, the money has a huge range of uses and there's useful stuff you can buy off merchants for something like 10-15 silver each (and you soon have MILLIONS), the auction house prices are very affondable, I could even buy a 50 million item now if I wanted it, and I never seen super-rare things at billions at all. I am definitely not in the endgame but I can say there's no gold farmers here, everything seems awesomely balanced in it's complete lack of balance. Makes me think of the player driven economy of SWG! plus making money is easy and FUN! since there's hundreds of ways to make them!
Housing
incredible to say I had a house already the very second day of my playing, and I could buy furniture and arrange it as I wanted, I could even buy crafting stations and use them, and that is... awesome. The housing is fixed, you cannot place a house somewhere randomly, but you can choose between dozens of spots, in several cities and live in the very core of a town. so you can be next to your favourite spots and in familiar places, that creates a tremendous sense of belonging to a place.
Trade-management-life
I haven't explored trade but I did look at management, you can buy pretty much all the houses in a town, make dormitories for workers, make them storage, turn them into refineries, or shipyards, workshops to create tools, weapons, armors, safe asset banks to create money, make carpentry and furniture, and so on and then hire workers to do the job for you, they can even harvest nodes for you! I have several workers gathering for me copper and iron, I can even order them to produce me finished products giving them workshops to use and the materials to do, or just do that myself. it is a full game inside the game with several kind of different rules governed by stats that you can get with quests or simply by playing the way you like. One can also reach high levels by fishing or by crafting, not only by defeating monsters.
the workers can gain levels and get specialization getting better and better and has energy you can replenish with beer (that you create by cooking...) and they can be developed with skills and peculiarities as well.
Pets-mounts
you can have donkeys, to lug around trading items, you can have horses, you can have a wagon dragged by several horses, you can have a ship, you can pretty much travel the way you like, horses levels up, you can even tame your own, breed them, breed them with the skills you want, and become a better trainer of animals. they can get wounded they can die, and also you can combat while mounted. it is simply awesome how this is managed.
Ingame store
it's not pay to win, everything in the store is quite costly, the daily rewards for simply logging in are quite big, one can get rich quite fast by selling them and employ them in playing the game as they see fit. Several stuff in the ingame store looks cool and nice and is also useful, so it's a good thing to watch it closely, yet everything is optional, and archievable ingame playing.
social mingames and knowledge
several npcs have names and you can become their friends, speaking with them and doing mini-games to get them like you, by liking you they can drop you pieces of knowledge that goes to your whole family (the list of your characters), and also can get you unlock new quests, both unique and daily ones, and teach you things, recipes and everything else. Knowledge is power in this game and comes with a nice boon of xp and opportunities.
Everything counts
costumes counts, and gives bonuses, food counts, gear counts in ways I have to explore yet and looks super-customizable, just like everything else, the world feels alive, I see players running around, workers running around and gathering, I see wagons of players going around to trade, if you run alot you get better at running, if you eat alot hp goes up, if you carry huge weights on your back you get stronger and stronger and can carry more...
it is not a game for maxxers, it's not a game for people obsessed in doing everything because you cannot do everything, because nobody will be ever finished.
This is the game I dreamt for long long time. I guess I will end up with thousands of hours of playing time!

I'm a massive GoT fan and really enjoyed Telltale's TWD games, so I was really surprised that I disliked this game so much.  The cameos of characters from the show are fun at first, but feel forced and awkward.  It's like a weird sight-seeing tour where the game is trying to cram in as many familiar faces as it can, which detracted from the main plot a lot.  I thought the story was pretty good, but didn't have any particularly happy parts.  I know expecting that from Game of Thrones is stupid, but Telltale found a way to bring small moments of joy in the first TWD game that made you care about the characters.  All of the main characters go from one depressing scenario to the next.  There's no reward for surviving a crisis.  You're just pushed along to something else to make you miserable.  Even the books and the show have moments of characters finding solace in an unforgiving world, giving you the chance to enjoy following that character's journey.  I really wanted more from this game than I got.  I'd recommend playing TWD series instead.

So, this game is weird, and I don't know if I should recommend it yet or not... I've figured out some aspects of how it works and where it's going on, but I hope not all of them yet.
The statues you come across are save points, if you die, you respawn at them... There's a decay that spawns at where you start and works outward to slowly consume everything, if a save point is gobbled up, you won't spawn there anymore, so you constantly have to try and find a safe point further away from the decay.
You level by killing creatures and finding colored blocks and also finding statues... Everytime you level, you will be brough to the level room, where you can put the levels on a pedestal (I think), as you level, your shot becomes stronger, but the game also start to move faster, at some point it's recommended to turn the game speed to 'half' because it'll be going crazy fast otherwise.
When you reach certain points and defeat certain bosses, you will get an extra safe point that you can travel to, meaning, you have progress in the game even in death.
I havent gotten too far yet but this game is very pretty and a nice calming game, especially after something like TF2. :)  Pick it up!

If you came here from 15 Minutes of Game, you probably think this is some weird mindscrew puzzle game masquerading as a twin-stick shooter. It's not. It's just a twin-stick shooter, and TB, god bless him, has no patience. You're a dot, you shoot other dots, and they drop dots that you collect. When you level up, you get to pick an upgrade. That's the most complicated thing about it; if you move around and fire a little bit after placing a statue in each spot, you'll get an idea of what the upgrades do. There are save points every now and then, they're the satellite dish looking things.
It took me like... two minutes to work all that out. It is an incredibly simple game, and requires only the very smallest desire to experiment. If they made a tutorial for this game, people would likely joke about how unnecessary it is. You'd take one look at the thing telling you to shoot the thing so you can get the thing and say "oh yeah, haha, I've played this game like five hundred times."
Comparing it to other twin-sticks, it's fun, but not special. Pretty colors, simple gameplay. The one thing I'm disappointed about is the music. It's a huge letdown, especially considering "interactive music" was one of the features offered by the description. There aren't any good chiptunes here, it's just very weak bleepbloops all the way down. Bass Blocks was a terrible name for this game, because there isn't any.
I don't regret buying it at all, and if you like simple twin-sticks, you should probably get it, too. But I would've preferred paying $2.50. Wait for a sale event.

The scuptures range from easy to mind-boggling, and there are several game modes, such as the basic 'rope paints object' and 'only blobs attached to the rope paint the object' and 'only bombs attached to nails paint the object' which gives it some variety.

This isn't a game where you have the most massive armies, or you feel like the most badass commander. It's not quite the game that extreme micromanagers would enjoy. But more than any other game I have ever seen, including its predecessor and other RTS games of similar type, you get attached to units. You know everything about the units you have because you've had them for so long in the game, and then losing them makes you feel it both strategically and emotionally. You want to take revenge for that unit, you create another one of the same type but it just doesn't feel the same - everything feels like a troop that you sent out there and that you do not want to die.
Gamewise, this game has unbelievable gameplay options thanks to steam workshop and, with any luck, incoming mod support - not to mention the soon to be released expansion, Western Front Armies. This game, much like Dawn of War 1 to Dawn of War 2, does not quite feel like its predecessor - while they share a lot of similar aspects, many things feel different. Maps and armies are generally smaller, and the maps are also considerably more open with few, if any, obvious choke points. While some may complain this is a less fun gameplay mechanic, it's extremely realistic and can prove to be extremely fun and challenging, especially with the line of sight system that now rivals Men of War's same LoS system where objects, smoke, etc can block your units vision which opens up immense possibilites for stealth and flanking.
The only complaint I have is the snow mechanic - while it may look nice visually, they really didn't do as much with it as I wish they could have. Snow maps do not feel fun, but rather tedious, as you're forced to advance slowly due to cold weather. The maps also provide most sources of heat and such in strategic locations for you by default, meaning there's no real point to building fires other than rebuilding destroyed ones. Snow allows units to leave footprints and such, yes, but with maps that are generally smaller than the predecessor as mentioned, this really isn't necessary as the tracks simply wont continue far enough to be bothered with as units would likely be visible at the same time or very quickly after their tracks are noticed - not to mention tracks can only be left in deep snow, which is not abundant in the maps and areas where it is located can easily be avoided with no real tactical disadvantages.
This complaint aside though, this game is outstanding in the RTS department. It is not the same as other RTS games on the market, such as Men of War and such, and I wish people would stop comparing the two games. Looking at this game as it's own game, it is beyond fantastic and I could not have asked for a better sequel. (Aside from snow.)

Edit #2: 16 hours in, and 3rd day at it. I've started warming up to the game alot, and would probably have my recomendation at a neutral vote now. (but will reflect it as positive)
What you come to realize is that life is, well. Random. And this game is random. It's not a space simulator, it's more than that.
It's a mother♥♥♥♥ing life simulator.
Every time you fall, you gain experience.
That's this game. I've recently beat Phase 1 of the boss, when 2 days ago, I could barely fly to sector 8 with the Kestrel.
And that's a life lesson.
The game simulates the randomness of life, and pushes you to be as living as you are in life.
And perhaps that's the missing link I only just recently noticed.
This game will frustrate, hence my vote being neutral. (I wish I could actually reflect this somehow)
But I can finally see what makes this game appeal to the masses.
The randomness isn't the problem. It's the game. And it's life. Because in life, you build experience. You build your tolerance to defeat. And you just keep going.
And well. Succeed at it. Thus is life. Thus is challenge. Thus is FTL
This is the final major edit.
Edit #1: Mostly the review stays the same (see below). The main difference I've noticed as per the second day of playing is just a slight improvement in knowledge after reading survival guides from online.
I don't know what to think of that. That shows a lack of accessibility to information in the game, but since the game sells on it... Eh.

Main Review:
My friends are going to find this recommendation odd, and probably yell at me for it.
And I might change it myself, once I get past this frustration I am feeling.
I cannot in good conscience, recommend this to the standard gamer. This game isn't for the common taste, far from it. It's too difficult, too punishing without reward, and just too random to be worth any common gamer's (or even some hardcore gamer's) time. I play on easy, get to the boss, and die. Hell, let's strike out the "get to the boss" part.
You die. Alot. And you almost never are rewarded for it.  Oh hey, I unlocked a crappy Engi ship... Sigh.
Some people will have fun with this. The crowd that doesn't want to have his or her hand held while gaming will certainly love it. I still like it, mostly for the gameplay, combat, tactics. etc.
But having fun with it is far from the truth.
But this rating will change accordingly, as I'll probably eventually unlock some supership that actually gives me a reason to keep trying.
And for those FTL fans who are actually enjoying this, more power to you.
But I find it an experiment in torture.
TL; DR:
The game is a representation of the challenges of life. You win some, you loose alot. You build character and experience and eventually succeed.
But for those who are easily frustrated, or come to gaming as an escape from the realities of life.
This is not your game.

American Nightmare is something of an experiment with Remedy as they decided to create a side-story game that focused more so on its gameplay longevity than story. To put it more simply, if the Twin Peaks series could be comparable to the original Alan Wake, then American Nightmare is an episode of the Twilight Zone.
As you can tell by the five (more so six outside of Steam's playtime) hours I've played of American Nightmare, I do not find it as great as the original, which I have played for thirty hours. However, by no means do I think it's a bad game but something that was meant to demonstrate future plans for the series as well as refine the gameplay for the Xbox Live Summer Arcade rather than come up with an original story, and I'd hate to not review it as the original vanishes.
This game is an odd side-story as it takes place as a rerun episode of a story Alan Wake wrote that made him so popular in the spoofed Twilight Zone series, Night Springs. That sort of tone is kept throughout the entire experience as the impressive Rod Sterling impersonator keeps up the campy horror vibe throughout the entire experience.
The story is also a continuation, kind of, of the bonus episodes of the original Alan Wake with the alter-ego personality referred to as Mr. Scratch. There isn't much else to the story than the absurdity of the supernatural TV show plot and how it uses a game to restart a chain of events three times in order to tell the story, which means replaying the same three levels the same way three times in order to "beat" the game.
Now when I played this game I found the rewind feature an enjoyable but also disappointing aspect to the game. Initially, the rewinding of events is a compelling way to write a small side-story as you return with foreknowledge of what bad things will happen, and Alan will act on those changes in order to, hopefully, change the outcome. However, as for gameplay, this is where Remedy dropped the ball on this type of storytelling.
Instead of letting the player organically come up with the solution, which isn't far-fetched to suggest if there are only three levels total, then this experience might have worked better than how it's implemented. As of now, you have to fail two times in order to beat the game and there's no sense of reward from it. Even if it would break the "sequencing" of the game on repeated playthroughs, it could have added new challenges and other changes if you sequence-breaked the game to reveal more plot elements, combat options for difficulty as well as new weapons to use.
It's a shame that Remedy decided to play it safe, which is why I think this was meant as an enjoyable tech-demo for future games, as the gameplay refinements and additions would have benefited the gameplay from the original.
In addition to the story-mode of three levels, there is also the Resident Evil mercenaries-style mode where the player is given a score-time mode to rack up as many points to earn stars to progress. It is this mode that I think the core of American Nightmare is found.
Being able to more liberally play with the mechanics, especially in a campy horror game, is surprisingly an effective combination that works well to benefit what makes AN so good while offering so little. I don't personally enjoy leaderboards but challenge-room unlocks and skill-based challenges are incentives I do enjoy from these types of modes, and because the combat is so enjoyable it's worth the inclusion.
If anything is the sole reason for the gameplay being better, I think it has to be the significant amount of new weapons to utilize such as nailguns, magnums, sawed-off-shotguns and crossbows. Ammo management has been reduced to light-weaponry and heavy, but the small changes to the original weapons like damage output and gun-feel is what makes this change in combat versus fleeing highly satisfying.
This is probably what the developers had in mind when they first designed this game as a cheap thrill-ride to market on the Summer Arcade gaming craze on Xbox, and I can definitely appreciate the game in that regards even though I think they still missed quite an opportunity to incorporate more gameplay into their storytelling.
Now as far as I am aware this game was quite profitable for the type of market it appealed to and ever since then the development of Alan Wake 2 has been a pipe-dream many fans are still waiting for someday. I do not think this game is the reason is to blame.
Considering how long it took them to come up with and release the first game as well as the overall cult-following, this game may be the last game to hold that title of Alan Wake. If that is the case, then I can definitely say that nothing was lost in the creation of American Nightmare while also nothing notable was gained, so I hold no ill will toward it.
If it is the last title to bear that name, then I feel American Wasteland is a playable reminder of things that once was that could still be brought back someday, a lingering hope of meaning and of potential that will be taken away if it's also removed from the digital stores. In some ways, this game itself may embody the Wasteland T.S. Elliot wrote where all that was once grand and secure fell away into an emptiness that is harder to bear than simply being wrong.

The storyline is really good, the gameplay is awesome and i like the idea that there's more content to come. The only thing that i'd complain about is the lack of  server to play with different people, but this is not a problem since you can find those guys (and girls) in the discussion and maybe make new online friends, why not? So, right now i'm playing the new DLC, Ashes of Malmouth and i need to say this: this DLC (which is more like an expansion gives you two new classes, a new area and a lot of new features which you can read in the patch, i'm here to tell you why you should buy it) costs less than what Blizzard is charging for a DLC of an old/broken game (i'm sorry blizzard's fans, i played this game for a long time so i believe i can call it like that, if you don't agree, i respect, but this is my review) which comes with only one character.
My point: big companies used to create a lot of good games with great ideas, nowdays if you want the great ideas, give an indie company a chance. So, in conclusion, if you're a Diablo 2 fan which hasn't already found something to give you that joy you used to have when you played it, you should give Grim Dawn a chance, buy it on a sale (IMO even out of sale the price is still good), try from a friend's list, just give it a try.

Pretty great game. I came into this mostly blind, never playing previous XCOM titles, so I had no particular expectations going in and ended up feeling pretty satisfied with what was presented here. At its core, this is a turn-based tactical game that is fairly punishing if you make a miscalculated move. You play the role of commander of the XCOM project, an initiative tasked with thwarting an alien invasion. The meat of the game involves sending a squad of soldiers to various locals around the world to combat some pretty diverse alien invaders. Soldiers are divided into four classes: Assault, Heavy, Support, and Sniper, each with a unique set of abilities and primary weapons. Leveling up unlocks further abilities for each class, so it's important to keep seasoned soldiers alive. Which brings me to an important bit, if your soldiers die in a mission they are dead forever, so accurately assessing your situation in missions is critical. Debris and other structures provide cover, giving you some options when deciding to maneuver around the battlefield or bunker down and play defensively. These mechanics give you a lot to think about when planning your actions, resulting in pretty satisfying tactical gameplay.
Between missions you oversee the activities of your home base, which is kind of its own strategic mini-game. There's tons to do here, including researching upgrades, building new rooms/areas to expand the base's functions, recruiting new soldiers, and upgrading surveillance and interception tools to better combat the aliens. From here you also choose your missions and are able to observe in the state of the world regarding the invasion. Each major country has a panic meter, let it get too high and they pull their funding and benefits from the XCOM project. I actually quite enjoyed this aspect of the game, the extra strategic elements here make your choices feel like they have weight in the context of the scenario.
Overall the game is pretty solid. It's not without flaws, some recurring bugs and frustrating RNG (missing on a 99% chance to hit ) stand out as annoying, but doesn't sully the experience too badly. Personally I found the game to be an adequate challenge with normal settings, but there are higher difficulties and special modes (iron man mode for instance) that series veterans will likely appreciate. I'm more of an RTS guy in terms of strategy games, but I occasionally like to dabble in turn-based strategy games and I'm definitely glad I tried out this one. Highly recommended if you enjoy this kind of game.

I'm a tremendous fan of the Song of Ice and Fire series. Believe me, I wanted to like this game. I honestly wanted to. For a while, I actually did.
Then I completed it. That's when the rage set in.
My main problem with this game is how nothing you do really matters in the longrun. There is a policy I firmly believe in and constantly embrace: "The road ahead is filled with trials and tribulations, but no matter had dark the path may be, there should always be a light at the end of the tunnel."
You know what's at the end of this tunnel for this game? A VAST ♥♥♥♥ING ABYSS OF EMPTINESS.
Every episode involves the exact same formula: completely unlikeable, one-dimensional villains being absolutely horrible to the main characters and always getting the final laugh. The main characters struggle just to get by, but the entire literal world is against them. That would be fine, provided there was one ultimate outcome that involved some happiness for the characters. Or, at the very least, left the characters with some amount of hope that they would recover their losses.
Alas, it doesn't even offer THAT much.
I don't know what sociopaths devised this game, but even the most masochistic person I know would get no enjoyment whatsoever from enduring the hardships the Forresters have to endure. Making a "decision" in this game equates to little more than choosing how you'd like a group of thugs to beat you (without even the option to forgo a beating altogether).
I can stomach this sort of harsh reality when reading the books and watching the TV show, but I'd expect something different when playing a game. After a while, this routine of encountering worse and worse conditions becomes spiritually and emotionally draining.
Also, playing this game made me feel less sorry that Margaery is dead now.
All I can say is that if Telltale ever gets around to making Season 2 of this game, it had BETTER had a more pleasant conclusion than the abominable ending in THIS game.

Mohandas Karamchand Gandhi (/ˈɡɑːndi, ˈɡæn-/;[2] Hindustani: [ˈmoːɦənd̪aːs ˈkərəmtʃənd̪ ˈɡaːnd̪ʱi] ( listen); 2 October 1869 – 30 January 1948) was the preeminent leader of the Indian independence movement in British-ruled India. Employing nonviolent civil disobedience, Gandhi led India to independence and inspired movements for civil rights and freedom across the world. The honorific Mahatma (Sanskrit: "high-souled", "venerable")[3]—applied to him first in 1914 in South Africa,[4]—is now used worldwide. He is also called Bapu (Gujarati: endearment for "father",[5] "papa"[5][6]) in India. In common parlance in India he is often called Gandhiji. He is unofficially called the Father of the Nation.[7][8]
Born and raised in a Hindu merchant caste family in coastal Gujarat, western India, and trained in law at the Inner Temple, London, Gandhi first employed nonviolent civil disobedience as an expatriate lawyer in South Africa, in the resident Indian community's struggle for civil rights. After his return to India in 1915, he set about organising peasants, farmers, and urban labourers to protest against excessive land-tax and discrimination. Assuming leadership of the Indian National Congress in 1921, Gandhi led nationwide campaigns for easing poverty, expanding women's rights, building religious and ethnic amity, ending untouchability, but above all for achieving Swaraj or self-rule.
Gandhi famously led Indians in challenging the British-imposed salt tax with the 400 km (250 mi) Dandi Salt March in 1930, and later in calling for the British to Quit India in 1942. He was imprisoned for many years, upon many occasions, in both South Africa and India. Gandhi attempted to practise nonviolence and truth in all situations, and advocated that others do the same. He lived modestly in a self-sufficient residential community and wore the traditional Indian dhoti and shawl, woven with yarn hand-spun on a charkha. He ate simple vegetarian food, and also undertook long fasts as a means of both self-purification and social protest.
Gandhi's vision of an independent India based on religious pluralism, however, was challenged in the early 1940s by a new Muslim nationalism which was demanding a separate Muslim homeland carved out of India.[9] Eventually, in August 1947, Britain granted independence, but the British Indian Empire[9] was partitioned into two dominions, a Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan.[10] As many displaced Hindus, Muslims, and Sikhs made their way to their new lands, religious violence broke out, especially in the Punjab and Bengal. Eschewing the official celebration of independence in Delhi, Gandhi visited the affected areas, attempting to provide solace. In the months following, he undertook several fasts unto death to promote religious harmony. The last of these, undertaken on 12 January 1948 when he was 78,[11] also had the indirect goal of pressuring India to pay out some cash assets owed to Pakistan.[11] Some Indians thought Gandhi was too accommodating.[11][12] Nathuram Godse, a Hindu nationalist, assassinated Gandhi on 30 January 1948 by firing three bullets into his chest at point-blank range.[12]
His birthday, 2 October, is commemorated as Gandhi Jayanti, a national holiday, and world-wide as the International Day of Nonviolence.

Released in early 2017 (a strange time to release a game set at Christmas), The Thing with Mistletoes is a drama and romance otome novel, developed by Ran and published by Visual Wordplay. After Visual Wordplay’s Paranormal Teens, and Once Upon an All Hallow’s Eve, I wasn’t really sure if I wanted to give this one a shot, but it was rated very positively and I decided to give it a shot.
This is probably the only visual novel published by Visual Wordplay that I have actively enjoyed. You play as Lumina Duval, who has been left home alone with her 10 year old brother Vince for the week of Christmas. Lumi is excited for Christmas, it’s the best time of the year, and even the disappearances happening in her town can’t dampen her spirits. Of course, that is until Vince goes missing.
The first thing I noticed about this game was the artwork. It was very aesthetic and quite pleasant, but I couldn’t help but think the character design was rather… childish. It’s refreshing to see a new take on character designs in visual novels, done in a style that isn’t seen much in them, but it was rather humorous to see.
The second thing I noticed, was the cheerful Christmas music in the background, and honestly it was rather sickening. For a game released in February, that is being played all year round, I don’t think Christmas music itself, with songs such as Jingle Bells, was the best choice. It was rather annoying to be playing this in September and to hear all the constant Christmas music, to the point I had to just mute the game.
The story line is this is pretty well done – although I find it really unbelievable that their parents didn’t come home after Vince goes missing. It’s intriguing, and it has a hint of mystery, and doesn’t focus too much on the romantic side until later in the story, and that’s rather refreshing. It’s nice to see a story line that for once doesn’t seem washed out in a game like this, and it was a rather pleasant story line to read.
This isn’t the best visual novel I’ve read/played, but it’s for sure not the worst either. I’d definitely recommend giving this one a try.

One of the main appeal factors in gaming in the eyes of a fair few is the ability to vicariously experience happenings outside the players frame of reference and go through all the fun of taking a temporary holiday from your real life self, be it as a highly trained special forces badass to an alien monster with an innumerable amount of prehensile willies. However, for anyone wishing to realise their dreams of being a Carribbean dictator with solid gold statues and a numbered bank account in Switzerland has only the Tropico series to turn when it comes to realising their non-special forces or tentecular dreams.
Tropico 4 is the second most recent installment in this storied series of Bannana Republic simulators, tasking the player with adminstering a Carribbean island with the usual trappings of the sim genre, necessitating that you construct various buildings and grow your tropical "paradise" into a successful and thriving source on embezzlement mony for your ingame Swiss bank account. However, this is complicated by the fact that you also have to keep yourself in the good books of the islands resident factions, ranging from the intellectuals to the military, who will all hinder you in different ways if you fail to keep them satisfied. Compounding this is the balancing of international diplomacy among the various world powers, including the EU and China among the others outside of the USA and USSR, who can penalise you for scrwing them over in ways varying from the maritime invasion of the two superpowers to trade blockades for the minor powers, leaving the managing of your island nation as a delicate blencing act among a dozen different metaphorical plates with the eventual end goal of getting your financial incomings to the point of being able to swim in your earnings, Scrooge McDuck stylee.
As an installment in the series, the base game is just an iteration over the previous installment, meaning that owners of Tropico 3 might want to give this a pass. However, it is more sure-footed than the slighty chaotic mix of additions in Tropico 5, and the addition of the quite excellent Modern Times DLC adds a whole extra games worth of content and provides you with the tools and ability to bring your simulated Cuba-clone kicking and screaming into the 21st century, if you so desire.
So, in conclusion, Tropico 4 is an excellant example of the City Building genre that is only slighty made worse by its iterative status over the previous installment. Owners of Tropico 3 may want to pass over this one, but any newcomers can enjoy a sim with a wealth of content, a brilliant sense of humor, and a soundtrack that will worm its way into your head and leave with an unholy affection for Latin Jazz. Viva Numbered-bank-account-in-Switzerland!

For a story like Alice, it is very important to have crazy reality bending effects. There are many of those in this game like one-way doors, twisting rooms and power over time. Some stages were a lot better than other but even the worst parts were ok. This game may very well have the most awesome stage select area because of all the weird things that happen in it ( I wish entire game was like that ) For a movie based game I think they did a good job.
There is some platforming but it is very easy and linear. When your character comes to a cliff you have to press jump if you meant to go there. For the most part, you walking from point A to point B with decent puzzles and enemies in your way. 90% of the game is just collecting game currency which is hidden inside nearly every object in the game. You can spend your points on new skills if you find items that unlock them.

Each character starts with 1 button combat and usually a unique power like Slow, Shield Brake or invisibility. You can find 3 upgrades for each that add things like 3 hit combos, heavy attacks, and new special moves. Hitting enemy feels impactful but combat is mostly irrelevant since you respawn as soon as you die. The only way you really lose is if Alice gets dragged into a portal which comes with annoying cutscenes.

You can't access all the places until you get the specific character. Some good items are hidden in early areas so it gives you a reason to go back. The game is mostly linear but there are some secret and interactive places. You can probably explore it 100% in 12 hours. Navigation is slightly confusing but I like stage select area and web like level design.
You really have to utilize every single character except mouse who is your primary fighter. Sometimes a puzzle may require all of them. They were not very hard and I never got a stack ( i think its a good thing but I guess it depends on what you looking for ) I love how Hatter can use perspective power to create a path. It is kinda cool how there are some many things in the game which you can move or go through.
- overall mediocre but it has some good things going for it.The format of the game reminds me something you would play on PS1 and it feels nostalgic. Combat and platforming are not great but visual effects, secrets and intuitive puzzles make up for some of the problems.

I'm writing this from my partner's PC, because it's in the lounge room where the couch is, and that's where I'll be sleeping tonight.
She's been mad about Cook, Serve, Delicious for a while. She's got this habit of trying to max out every game she plays, and CSD scratches that itch nicely - it's a simple game that requires ridiculously quick thinking and forethought. I have neither of those things. So I bought her Overcooked today, because I thought it might help us to bond a little, the differences being the sweet little things that we find special in each other.
I realised my mistake when she slapped the controller out of my hand because I'd been impotently throwing lettuce at her for so long that she'd run out of space to stack burgers. If it weren't for my gentle Guiness-induced haze I'd have been a little worried about the long-term harm of this situation but, fuzzy and blind, we wandered on down the winding road to Singletown that Overcooked had paved for us. Soon I'd fallen off a truck while trying desperately to stop an onion rolling away from my precariously-perched pot. With a pot of delicious tomato soup in hand I'd been caught in a swarm of pedestrians and dragged kicking and screaming away from my street-side kitchen. At one point I'm fairly sure I saw a badger stealing my mushrooms.
So now I'm sitting on the couch, and she's unfriended me on Facebook. A++ would put relationship on the rocks again.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown + Enemy Within is a turn-based strategy game, where you also build a base as part of the secretly formed military organization called - XCOM. It's objective is to investigate and stop the alien invasion. There are two specific gameplay types in XCOM. Turn-based combat and base management, which involves resource allocation, decision making (everything has consequences) and a sort of artificial Risk/Reward system. Research and development of advanced weaponry, aviation and so on. There's not much to say about the actual gameplay, because it's turn based, but it provides a deep experience of learning different tactics, squad management and being able to outmaneuver the alien combatants.
- Replayability, due to the random nature of the game. (Second Wave options, Ironman)
- Vast ammounts of different weaponry, upgrades and modifications (Enemy Within)
- MEC's and Gene moding (Enemy Within)
- Alien autopsies and interrogations.
- Amazing soundtrack.
- Seeing a MEC perform a melee attack for the first time.
- More than one enemy faction, making the game even more intense (Enemy Within)
- Base building and an immersive resource management system.
- Tactical depth.
- Vast variety of different enemy types that all have different abilities and "danger" levels.
- Ironman mode, which makes every decision permanent and every mistake is punished.
- Highly destructive environment. Want to punch a hole with a rocket in a side of the building and shoot an alien in it's dome with your elite Sniper? Sure.
: Long War mod, which almost completely redesigns how the game plays. Though I would still recommend playing the "vanilla" game first. Makes the game more "friendly" for old school XCOM fans.
- Lack of a deeper soldier customization, even with all DLC's.
- Line of sight glitches, where sometimes you can't see the enemy, even if unobstructed.
- Slow pace of the game, due to the fact that on early on you can't scout effectively, without alerting the aliens.
- Mostly luck based gameplay.
- Steep learning curve, unforgiving beginning, which is arguably the hardest part of the game. (especially on Classic or Impossible).
- Psionic soldiers are available almost at the very end of the game, so you don't get to really enjoy them without grinding extra missions to level them up.
- First 1-2 in-game months are always a rush to build satelites, which can get repetative after a playthrough or two.
- Multiplayer is uninteresting. Would benefit from having an option to disable mind control troops in matchmaking.
- Virtually no engaging story, only a really basic narritive. No real incentive to give a hoot about the human race.
- Lacking variety in level design. Levels in China look the same as levels in UK.
- 1st time encountering Chryssalids without any advanced tech.
- Not much mission or objective variety (Enemy Within releaves this issue a bit).
- Soldier customization without "Enemy Within" and "Elite Soldier" Expansion/DLC.
- Interceptor and other aviation combat is underdeveloped and not interesting.
- Missing that 95%+ shot on Ironman.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within is a very solid effort at resurrecting the turn-based strategy legend of the 90's. It's fairly easy to pick up, but it will test your mettle in the long run. Features a lenghty campaign, albeit not having a very interesting story, it's still is more than worth it to play through it solely because of the satisfying combat, amazing soundtrack and the progressive expansion of XCOM, both in manpower and weaponry.
Would definitely recommend this game to anyone. Brilliant way to bring back a classic.

I would suggest anyone to pick this game up, unlike what many others say you don't need any of the items in the cash shop.  When the game is on sale for only 5.99 your not losing much on trying the game out.  The game may have been gifted to me to try out but I later upgraded my game version to the 30$ version.  Not because I needed any of the items it provided but because I wanted to show my support for the game and help the devs come out with more content.  There is enough content here for me to justify giving them a little more.
The only cons that I've come across is that this games fight with gold farmers ruined a few game mechanics for the rest of us such as a free market and being able to help your friends get geared up.  Because of this the game is considered to be a single player mmo by many players which aside from guild missions and pvp it really feels that way.  The other con being that they promote being AFK very heavily such as your workers don't do anything while your off.  Which honestly doesn't make any sense to me why do I have to be online for my workers to do♥♥♥♥♥♥  The other afk functions don't really bother me as much as this one.
If you put that aside though you will find that this game is pretty fun, theres many things to do outside of combat like fishing, cooking, crafting, node management, alchemy, horse taming/breeding and many other things.  This game is filled to the brim in content so if the combat gets stale take a brake from the combat and just go fishing or something to vary the gameplay a bit.
One thing I find brought up quite a bit is that people think the game is p2w....closest thing users that get to p2w is you can buy things in the pearl shop and sell them on the market.  Which the money that can be made this way can be also made through just playing the game and not many people do this anyway because the silver made from selling premium items on the market just isn't worth it for most players.   I actually wish that they sold for more so that people that didn't want to spend real money on the game would have more opportunities to get those premium pets or costumes because no one is selling them.  Also you can only sell 5 items a week through this.  So the "p2w" users can pay about $150 a week for what people that set their workers up effectively and go fish for a bit will make in about 3 hours....How is this pay to win again?
Anyway buy the game, play it for a bit see if you enjoy it.  If you want to support the devs get the adventurers or explorers pack.  For the 10-6 dollar price tag it's deffinetly something worth trying out, or you can also get the free trial on the official website, where you can lose nothing for giving the game a try.

Obviously a lot of people like the game, and it's pretty cheap, so if you're curious about it just get it in a sale and try it. However, I personally don't like it and for me it is a lot worse than other arpgs (TL2, VV, D3... haven't played PoE or VH).
The problem for me is that at least at the start of the game it's all just a left click snoozefest. It seems like this may get better later on, but the majority of the skills do not look interesting at all. I'm sure there's hidden gems there, but you have to really enjoy trying out different builds or reading about builds to get there.
Which brings us to the fact that you can respec your skills... but not all of them! I'd seen you could respec, so I just tried stuff, then it turns out you can't respec your mastery points which means my build is now ruined unless I get a char editor (which if you need that is a failing of the game). Why on earth they would do this is beyond me.
Gameplay seems very basic as well, hold down your left mouse button and occasionally walk back a bit if things start to get too close. Now I do read about people with elaborate builds with different skills, but again you really have to search to find this. I tried the demolitionist and nightblade and both made me feel like I was playing a left click simulator.
Lootwise, you get a LOT of items thrown at you. The problem for me is these have too many different stats and there's too much junk that's no good for your character. Perhaps this is cool if you like to theorycraft and calculate your damage, but for me it just made me give up on picking up those hundreds of items and poring over them to see if maybe one of them might be an improvement to my equipment.
All in all, this game seems too much like work to me, and not enough actual fun.
Not for the faint of heart.

I've never played any of the Far Cry games.  They looked good, but I never had the desire to get any of them until I saw this one.  Primal scratches the itch I sometimes have of an open world that does stealth well.  I can hide behind a tree or in some bushes and catch my enemy unaware and, if I can aim correctly, I can taken down 2 or 3 before they find where I am.  Primal scratches the itch I have for a game that allows a pet that doesn't box me in and I end up threatening to kill because it is getting on my nerves (looking at Fable 2 and 3).  Primal scratches the itch I sometimes get to do some ancient hunting.  I tried that in Skyrim, but 1 shotting a giant and 3 shotting a mammoth breaks it.
Pros:
- pretty good stealth system
- various pets
- interesting characters
+ The Ear-collecting woman scares me.  She clearly has PTSD.  Why is this a good thing?  The writing that went in for her.
Meh:
- Reminds me a lot of the Honest Hearts DLC for New Vegas.  I have called the main faction I have to fight against the 'White Legs' several times.  This is both good and bad as I really liked that DLC, but I find myself wanting to quit this game and go back to New Vegas to do that DLC.
Cons:
- I know there's a story there, but I have no desire to actually do it.
- I had more loyalty to the dude that saved me in the intro than I do the people living near my cave.
Primal is a fun game.  It's a good game for what it is: A relaxing experience with brief moments of panic as I run from bears/yaks/mammoths.  Is it worth full price?  I don't think so.

Captains log, stardate 20XX. I've just entered the purple teir 2 system after attacking my 3rd unarmed civilian vessel to salvage their scap. Tensions are high among the crew...sexual tension that is. That rock monster is such a tease, she knows she wants all this.
This is the life of captain in FTL. If you ever wanted to live out your fantasy of captain kurt, sexual fantasies and all (minus the sexual fantasies) then this game is for you. It plays more like a real time board game then a traditional video game, and I have to say I rather enjoy it.
The game is a Roguelike game with heavy RNG, but allows for different experiences in every playthrough. Many options abound to customize your ship, and you swap between an overworld map, and a battle screen for in system fights.
The strength of this game are also its greatest weakness. Yes RNG allows for different and unexpected play experiences, but it's also unexpected that I missed my 4th missile in a row, and that the next merchant does not sell fuel. Frustration goes hand in hand with exploration in this, yet if you can look past that the game has a lot to offer.

Double action boogaloo is fun. Thats all I can say. Well actually I can say more about this game, which in retrospect is more of a interactive action movie. Boogaloo revolves around 8 weapons and 3-4 characters, and each of them is running arund trying to murder eachother in the most stupid and action movie type way as possible. The game itself is a little confusing, and the controls are not exactly what one could call smooth, but it's still fun. each character is just a look for yourself, but you can choose perks and weapons to go along with your character. Weapons usually have a trait of either doing more damage/firerate/accuracy or something like that, with a sacrifice on "style points". These points when you gain 100 of them, give you a ability, such as being able to punch the everything out of someone, or have all guns be pinpoint accurate, or even give you an extra 4 seconds of SUPA SLOW MO. Did I mention the slowmotion? I don't think I did yet. Sometimes in the game, players will gain a certain amount of SlowMo. Slowmo can be used in Second increments, and does exactly what you think it does, it makes things go slow. This doesn't just effect you though, this affects EVERYONE ON THE MAP. Contrary to what you may think, it does not get annoying, it is awesome. The final thing that makes this game what it is is the right click. Right clicking will send you soaring towards your target, or if you hold Control, sliding. You can also use it to wall jump, climb up walls, and in general make things awesome. Go get this, the only thig you have to lose is time and hardrive space.

Quite a curious thing this Alice of a game, muchier than the Movie which lacked muchness as such.  Put on your best Futterwacken shoes for this Frabjous day as we celebrate one being better than the other, by one, its this one and not the other.  Zounding for one to be far yadder than the other, like being small or too tall.  We must hold up the movie to a mirror, going through the looking glass to arrive at this game, which was described in Alicespeak but now normalspeak.
This game from start to finish is a work of art in even the smallest of details.  Alice is not the playable character, players take on the roles of the characters of the movie, hot swapping back and forth.  These characters convey oddly more emotion than the movie with expressions, and camera shots one upping the great Tim Burton.  The character animations surpass the acting in the movie done with such detail in every expression that they convey.  There are TONS of extra recorded dialog and animations when just walking around, Alice may sit on a bench, point at things of interest.  This extra attention to detail is what shows this game stands out.  Many devs do the least to make a game, in this case they did more than they had to.  This is what being a game dev is about, not making the cheapest game on budget, but the best possible game within that budget.  These devs had impossible ideas, where they made the impossible, possible!
The musical score is incredible in the BIG budget way Disney can do but hasnt in nearly any of their games.  Incredible Voice Acting, most of the cast from the movie return to voice their characters in game.  The controls with controller are intuitive to the point of being a pick up and play game so everyone can enjoy it and share it locally via co-op with someone else.  Not a hard game, with puzzles that make sense, no need to google, just apply common sense.
The graphics are not great, their good, but they all work well making the world feel alive.  The Devs flex their skills to pay the bills with more breakable objects in this game than GTA V.  Killing enemies is fun, slashing grass is fun!  The sound effects make even slashing grass a fun thing to do and highly addictive though it serves no purpose really in the game.   Attacking the Queens Card Soldiers results in parts of their armor being knocked off, they can be one shot after upgrading skills, but knocking off their armor is very satisfying.
There are no steam achievements which is odd because the game does have achievements.  Completing achievements  which isnt hard, unlocks concept art.  This concept art with its detail is on the amazing level of Fallout.  If only we could get a physical artbook it looks so good and we only get a bit of it in game.  Sadly this studio is closed, because only the good die young.  Lets hope like a virus this French studio infects the rest of the gaming industry with their talent to make all our games more enjoyable for all of us.
Rating:  10/10  Value:  $14.99
Put on your Bee-ar goggles its time to go in depth on this ish.  Celebrate because in 2015, the 150th anniversary of Alice in Wonderland, this is the time to play an Alice game, this one, McGees or both?
Only 2 games ever made, came off better than their movie counterparts, this game and Wanted: Weapons of Fate.  Wanted fits right in with Alice, you may be asking yoruself how that is?  The studio who made Wanted is called Grin with pretty much the logo of the classic expression of our favorite Cheshire Cat.
You may be wondering why arent we playing Alice, why are we the side characters as if were just tagging along for the ride?  Alice in Wonderland was written in a Fantasy Genre created that merely followed the character as they wandered around, this type of storytelling was very popular in its day.  Another example is the author Charles Kingsleigh the father of Alice in the movie but not the book, who wrote Water Babies two years prior to Alice using the same storytelling style where we as readers go along for the ride on a fantastic journey.  The game trailer follows this storytelling style saying in BIG words "Follow Alice".
Tim Burton broke this golden rule, by making the movie through the eyes of Alice not about Alice.  A modern example of this storytelling style following the character around in a fantasy world is Mad Max.  Mad Max written by George Miller is not really about Max, its the audience following the character Max as things happen around the character just like Alice in Wonderland.  Meaning Max like Alice in wonderland is Max in Post-Apocalyptic Land. Hows that for dank?!?!
How is the game better than the movie?
The game takes HUGE liberties with the storytelling making it flow better than the movie.  Key moments in the story such as when Alice grows large meeting the Red Queen.  In the movie Alice sneaks into the garden with the Red Queen, she asks the rabbit for cake to be taller to save the Hatter.  She then scarfs it down for no reason in the movie, also no explanation as to why being taller would help save the Hatter.  In the game Alice is in the garden and needs to be bigger to get into a bigger door so she eats the cake from the rabbit but loving cake so much she eats too much becoming a giant.
In the movie Alice needs the Vorpal Sword guarded by the Bandersnatch who is missing an eye but the creature seems unhurt by this.  Alice then steals the eye from the mouse to get the sword not caring about the bandersnatch at all.  In the game its SHOWN that she sees the Bandersnatch in pain because its missing an eye.  Alice demands the eye to help the bandersnatch and get the vorpal sword, everyone wins, we can have both!
In the movie Alice is almost forced to fight the Jabberwocky.   In the game due to the battles the player goes through, Alice actually starts side commenting she feels more confident, then later invincible, growing beyond her control like a Marine in Full Metal Jacket.  By the end in the game when it is time to fight the Jabberwocky, the player is salty, Alice is ready to eat her own guts and ask for seconds.
In the end of the movie Alice wants to go home so is given a potion from the white queen.  Keep in mind Alice in the movie is a hero who just slayed a HUGE monster the Jabberwocky.  Now she wants to go back to a world where she is being forced to marry some guy and possibly be alone forever like her aunt???  This movie ending makes no sense.  This crappy cop-out like Dorothy in the Wizard Oz clicking her heels, because she wants to return to her inbred family on a dirt farm plagued by tornadoes is beyond belief.  In the game Alice is tricked into drinking the potion by the White Queen because she wasnt leaving which makes actual sense!  There is a great concept art that is unlocked showing all the characters waving, its real nice to see after that ending.
Does any of that crap that happens in the movie happen in the books?
Checked out the whole series and the answer is NO!
This game is better than the movie when held up to a mirror.  How far does this mirror analogy go of right and wrong, what sources do you have?
Long review short, this mirror mess may go all the way to the top of the US government.

I'm going to preface this review by stating that a majority of the reviews I've seen on here are biased as all hell, and that this long grind that people speak of is only needed if you want the creme de le creme. AKA Level 58 and above.
I'd also like to state that this is barely pay to win. Most people whine about how you can sell $30 items for thirty million silver, however, coming from a veteran, you can literally make around billions just by telling your workers to gather a specific thing and making your other workers make trade items out of it. Some may complain that pets and maids and all that are needed. Pets usually are used to pick stuff up for you, so if you don't want to spam R, there you go. The maids allow you to deposit and buy things on the go, so if you don't feel like travelling back to some random♥♥♥♥♥town to waste your exp boost, there you.
The main gripe people to seem to have is managing to buy weight and inventory space. Which is odd considering many MMO's have this pay for convience setup. Hell, even GW2, has some pay for convience.
Well, that's all I needed to say for the beginning, let's move to the pros and cons.
PROS:
Combat - The combat in this game is absolutely fantastic, it is the only thing that will make the grind bearable at times and will make you not want to kill yourself. Each of the animations feel great, the sounds and actions feel responsive. It's fantastic. Each of the classes, that aren't just the other gender of their counterpart, all feel pretty unique in their own way.
Graphics - I don't think I need to explain this, but it's pretty good. Just look at any basic screenshot and you'll see what I mean. The scenery varys drastically from some forest place, to some weird jungle and then a desert area. I mean, this might in theory be a con for you assuming you don't have a very high end system and then you'll have to run it at potato graphics.
Lore - There's this way of increasing your energy cap by gaining knowledge, which you get by completeing quests, killing things and letting your black spirit absorb their sould and talking to people or observing things. These are often surprisingly well written, providing some interesting background lore.
Guilds - I really enjoy the guild system that they've put forth. They're fantastic. Medium to extra large guilds can own territories called nodes. Nodes give you taxes and with those taxes you can pay out your various guild members. However, to own one of those nodes you must fight a node war with multiple allied guilds against other allied guilds. You need to communciate with your guild officers where to go and create multiple squadrons. Along with this, there are also territories that top tier guilds can own, which are basically just a collection of nodes and a city.
IN BETWEEN:
AFK - Most people argue that you need to remain heavily AFK during this, although after playing for a while, I'd argue against that. If you really just want a free ten million silver every day, then sure lifeskill away but besides that, it's not really AFK intensive. At the most you have autopathing if you don't want to really hold down W, although like most AFK activities it's not as efficent. Most of the lifeskills that require you to just press button even though it's incredibly boring in other games, are just AFK'd in BDO. Understandably, if you don't really like that idea of something being AFK in a game, however these are lifeskills. Not a really crucial part of the game per se but it can makes loads of money.
RNG - See, I'm sort of mixed on this. While the RNG is absolutely soul crushing and at times makes you want to kill yourself, it makes sense that it's there or everybody would have PEN, the highest enhancement one can get. It's easy to get to a mediocre level, TRI, but from that point onwards you'll probably wnat to kill yourself going TET and then PEN. The only real gripe I can find with this is with accesories breaking down when you fail. At the beginning of the game, it might not seem like a big deal since most only cost around four million, but boss accesories, which are very rare and can cost around twenty million to one hundred million, can also break when enhancing.
PVP - Personally, I love the gear based PVP because I have something to show for my grind and that each class has a very different playstyle if they're not the meta. However, I get if you don't really like that and you'd rather opt for something more casual and balanced. That's all I really have to say for it.
Community - If you're easily offended and don't like memes, you're probably going to think the community is incredibly toxic, it's hilarious as♥♥♥♥♥♥though so I don't care. Most of the higher levels tend to also be pretty hostile if you step into their grinding spot, because they'll just instantly deck you and tell you to go away. I couldn't really care for this because it's easy to fight back, but I know many people who were turned off from this game due to the community.
CONS:
Balance - Alright, stepping right into this, the classes are not balanced in the slightest. Now, most people will state that if you're good enough at a certain class you can faceroll anybody and while that might be true, the fact that it's easier for certain classes that faceroll is sort of a lead that the balance is very poor in this game. If you actually play the game, you'll know what I mean.
Explanation - To start off, the game explains almost nothing to you. A good portion of the beginning of the game will mostly involve you being shift-tabbed, googling how to do this or how to do this. The game is pretty complex with the only help it provides are some crafting notes where you can check what recipies you need.
Incredibly addictive, be careful of playing with friends, they can greatly hinder the experience if they themselves are inexperienced!
Wonderful game with a lot more depth than it appears to have on the surface. Roguelike in space which is both challenging and unique.

- By the time you start playing it and spends a few points in skills you almost immediately feel your character is what you expect him to be. Every skill point or devotion point makes a big difference on your character and you get a lot.
- Freeform character building: You have 6 (8) classes and they are very distinct from each other, and the game have you combine 2 of them, plus the devotion tree which requires careful planning ahead and helps you fine tune your character towards your playstyle. And don't worry, although at an ever incresing cost, you can respec skills and devotions (not class though) later.
- I only did one playthrough but it was 100% bug-free.
- Great graphics, good sountrack (very diablo-1-esque if you ask me), game runs perfect on my PC. I might be wrong but this game looks built with passion and attention to detail and feels good quality overall.
- Lots of lore and sidequests, secret places and places to explore.
- Played this with my xbox controller, it's no D3:UEE but it works great although I missed a way to quick-switch buttons (6 actions is probably not enough in a game with so many spells/skills).
- WoW-like faction system with faction vendors, makes the grind worth it.
- Awesome how game-changing your interactions with people around the world, considering this is an isometric ARPG.
- Garbage collector simulation. Afew hours in I just realized I had to ignore all magic+ drops to efficiently play the game and just loot from rare+ onwards. Way too much meaningless loot.
- Gear drops which completely ignore the way you are building your character. Considering the amount of freedom this game gives towards building your character, 9/10 gear drops are probably trash, you spend too much time delving through trash in your inventory.
- Too many damage types (fire ice lightning physical bleeding vitality chaos pet acid poison and I might be missing some), making it even harder to get the gear you need.
- No ladder play.
All and all, it's a pretty good game and a must-have for every ARPG fan. Expansion looks great, meaningful and great value also, these are the kinds of developers that put passion above greed and restore faith in the gaming industry.

TL;DR An absolutely superb ARPG, with a 'pick your own skill trees' approach which will keep you happily hacking away and looting for many hours
Set in a post-apocalyptic dark fantasy world Cairn, you set out to hack and slay your way through a variety of Undead, Beasts and Monstrosities in front of beautiful diverse landscapes. Two otherworldly factions, the C'thonians and Aetherials, have invaded this magic filled steampunk Era world, to fight out an ancient war between each other, leaving humans caught up in between and mostly ending up being used as fuel (for blood summons) or cannon fodder (as resurrected/mutated corpses). Instead of picking a character class from the start, you start out as a clean slate and get to pick any two of five (seven if you've got the expansion, which is well recommended) skill trees and combine them to create the ultimate hero aka monster killing machine of your dreams. Want to be a pet summoning gun slinger? Got it. A shield bearing tank who imbues their weapon with lightning? Go for it. On top of that there is a third 'skill tree' which is shared by all characters and looks like a sky with zodiac signs, each building on top and/or unlocking others and unlocking passive bonuses as well as new skills which can be tagged on top of skills from your other skill trees. The possibilities are endless.
Areas are large interconnected and create a beautiful and plausible landscape. Everything is hand crafted and not randomly generated, yet there is the odd cave entrance which may spawn randomly at different locations, creating a small bit of difference if you run through an area with your umpteenth character. It speaks to the design that, after 100 hours of gameplay, I am still delighted to find the odd hidden area in places I had previously thought to have fully explored.
Enemy design is great and even though is sometimes wished for a slight increase in variety (about 10%) things never get boring. Different damage categories also keep you on your toes, so your piercing resistant tank may still get a good wackin' if you walk into a new area where enemies favour something like vitality or aether damage.
On top of all of that you get a decent story (which in my opinion yet holds a lot potential to be expanded so much more), a fudge ton of loot, a crafting system including a variety of materials and runes, different factions who love/hate you and react by giving new quests/loot or sending more spawns against you and lastly the occasional small story decision which results in mostly minor changes to the world (but can also lead to some factions turning hostile).
For anyone having played Titan Quest and having enjoyed it or someonelooking for a solid break from Diablo, this one should be an instant no brain buy.
