I'll just put this out first: Alan Wake is overrated. Quite very overrated.
The first game had a cool concept and great original gameplay combat, where your weapon is not so much your gun but your flashlight. You have to shine at enemies shrouded in darkness to weaken them first before you can put in some bullet rounds.
Praise also goes out to the atmospheric setting, the narrative and theme of light vs darkness.
The game basically plays out like your typical ''run-here-run-there-do-specific-tasks'' game. Enemies are scripted to spawn at certain parts, kill them, run to area B, more enemies spawn later on, rinse and repeat.
American Nightmare is like a DLC to Alan Wake, but more like a separate game. Unlike Alan Wake part one, American Nightmare is based on a fictional story inside an already fictional story. A TV show in the game called ''Night Springs''.
The game features new weapons, including a very overpowered crossbow and just a few new different enemies.
Lastly, there's an Arcade mode for players to kill more and more darkness.
==============================================================
Now onto the problem with American Nightmare, it's truly...a nightmare. Just so boring and repetitive, it's a nightmare. It's such a very short game that is a shameful addon not worth the spend.
The game's campaign basically just consists of three, ONLY THREE desert maps. But since it's always nighttime 24/7, the desert feels more like an empty barren arena. I don't know why they put Alan Wake in a morning sunshine as the cover art when the entire game takes place at night. Even the first game had some daytime segments.
And you have to play these three maps all over again, not twice but THRICE. 'cos just when you reach the finale, the villian transports you back in time. Three times. Did I say three times? Yeah, three times.
And you have to perform the SAME objectives all over again. THREE. TIMES.
If you're thinking what I'm feeling, you know what I mean. This is the most shockingly cheap lazy as f**** way to extend a game's campaign. It would have been better if they at least had you start off somewhere new in the map or added new stuff, but no, you're literally playing the same three levels all over again, with only minor differences.
Altogether, playtime is 3 hours, and that's including me collecting all the manuscripts. Divide by three and you'll get how long the game would have been without the repetition. Only 1 hour of playtime.
===============================================================
And even if it's just 3x cheaper than the original game, I can't possibly find the enjoyment in this. Speaking of which, the game is just way too easy this time round. Due to the openness of maps, unlimited ammo stocks and faster flashlight recharge.  enemies are so, so much easier to spot and kill. Rarely did I ever have to resort to grenades, sticks or the flare gun to pull my way through.
On other hand, Arcade mode is the only thing making American Nightmare worthwhile, and puts you up to the challenge of surviving waves of enemies, testing your skill and might with the light vs dark combat. For once, things actually felt hard.
===========================================================
Overall, there's really not much to enjoy in Alan Wake AN, unless you're in it for the new arcade mode. You spend more time wasting time running across the night desert than doing much actual combat, by which, is also so repetitive, it makes me wanna cry.
A lazy game by all standards. It just stumps me how critics can give this the same score as Alan Wake 1 when it's basically just a dumbed down version of the original game.

I never played an Alan Wake game before, nor did I read any books (there are alan wake books right?), so I went into it completely unbiased, and ignorant. So for me at first it was about finding out what the heck I'm supposed to do.
Sure, "get the battery, get the cd, get the valve", but.. why! Good, there were some TVs that showed some lore and I found and listened to the manuscript pages I found, and I came to understand the underlying story.
A guy is, for whatever reason, in this weird place, which is not reality and not fiction, kinda both, and he needs to create the scene he was writing about himself, in order to change reality, and there is this evil twin controlling the enemies, which try to kill the character. Simple as that.
So I got the parts needed, did what had to be done. I did *not* know, that by taking the keys to the observatory, the game would literally stop, and put me to the observatory. I was teleported instantly, I did not have the chance to collect some manuscript pages I already knew the location of, and I was not able to go around everything to look for more.
Also I couldn't go back. That bugged me. Normally I would have loaded a previous save, go around everything - but there are no previous saves. You have one save. So I was stuck. I thought of 2 options, not playing the game anymore, or just going with it. In the end I just went with it. So I was in the second level, pretty much the same stuff like before. Get this, go there, fight enemies, go there, come here, here is what you needed, bye. Teleport to the third level.
Third level the same. Go there, do this, come here, blablabla. Then the final scene of the game, and boom.
You're back in the first level. What. So, the fourth level, being the first level, first thing you gotta do is go to the motel, like the first time you played the first level. This chick tells you, that she got every item you already had the first time you were there, except one thing. So yay, a little change, a little different this time. After that, everything the same, boom, motel, keys, observatory.
Again, this time the playthrough changed a bit, you already know that you need a specific thing, so you get it in advance, but, heck, of course you forgot *that thing* (I didn't, but the character did), so you had to go back and fix that, you go back, get what you want, teleport.
Last level, again, a bit different, again, last scene, boom, teleport to first level.
So the 7th level is the 4th level again, which already was the 1st level. This time the chick already got all the things and prepared them, so you go through that level even faster, in the observatory the chick also prepared some stuff and it is faster, and in the last level you simply start right at the point where you have to go first. Then you basically do the same thing like last time because nobody helped you this time, last scene and hey, finally it worked. The end.
And inbetween the enemie's strength and numbers rise, so does your firepower, I had to flee a lot, only to slowly advance back and kill those whatever they are. Taken.
So in conclusion, I knew what happened after basically the 9th level, when I started the second. I knew, that I would rewrite reality in a way that I win, and darkness fails. After the first time loop happened I knew, that I will have to do all the levels again, and looking into the missing manuscripts, I knew that I had to get 2 incomplete, and one complete part of manuscrupt in the observatory, so I knew I would have to play the 3 levels 3 times. It was very repetitive, very lame.
The game tried to compensate by advancing the character in his little quests so that I, the player, don't have to waste time on things I already did (twice), but it felt like the game / the developers knew, that this game is boring the way it is, that is not a good thing. When you already know, that your game is boring, and you try stuff to skip the boring parts, but it's the whole game, then you could have skipped the whole game.
Which is what I recommend to you.

XCOM: Enemy Unknown + Enemy Within is a turn-based strategy game, where you also build a base as part of the secretly formed military organization called - XCOM. It's objective is to investigate and stop the alien invasion. There are two specific gameplay types in XCOM. Turn-based combat and base management, which involves resource allocation, decision making (everything has consequences) and a sort of artificial Risk/Reward system. Research and development of advanced weaponry, aviation and so on. There's not much to say about the actual gameplay, because it's turn based, but it provides a deep experience of learning different tactics, squad management and being able to outmaneuver the alien combatants.
- Replayability, due to the random nature of the game. (Second Wave options, Ironman)
- Vast ammounts of different weaponry, upgrades and modifications (Enemy Within)
- MEC's and Gene moding (Enemy Within)
- Alien autopsies and interrogations.
- Amazing soundtrack.
- Seeing a MEC perform a melee attack for the first time.
- More than one enemy faction, making the game even more intense (Enemy Within)
- Base building and an immersive resource management system.
- Tactical depth.
- Vast variety of different enemy types that all have different abilities and "danger" levels.
- Ironman mode, which makes every decision permanent and every mistake is punished.
- Highly destructive environment. Want to punch a hole with a rocket in a side of the building and shoot an alien in it's dome with your elite Sniper? Sure.
: Long War mod, which almost completely redesigns how the game plays. Though I would still recommend playing the "vanilla" game first. Makes the game more "friendly" for old school XCOM fans.
- Lack of a deeper soldier customization, even with all DLC's.
- Line of sight glitches, where sometimes you can't see the enemy, even if unobstructed.
- Slow pace of the game, due to the fact that on early on you can't scout effectively, without alerting the aliens.
- Mostly luck based gameplay.
- Steep learning curve, unforgiving beginning, which is arguably the hardest part of the game. (especially on Classic or Impossible).
- Psionic soldiers are available almost at the very end of the game, so you don't get to really enjoy them without grinding extra missions to level them up.
- First 1-2 in-game months are always a rush to build satelites, which can get repetative after a playthrough or two.
- Multiplayer is uninteresting. Would benefit from having an option to disable mind control troops in matchmaking.
- Virtually no engaging story, only a really basic narritive. No real incentive to give a hoot about the human race.
- Lacking variety in level design. Levels in China look the same as levels in UK.
- 1st time encountering Chryssalids without any advanced tech.
- Not much mission or objective variety (Enemy Within releaves this issue a bit).
- Soldier customization without "Enemy Within" and "Elite Soldier" Expansion/DLC.
- Interceptor and other aviation combat is underdeveloped and not interesting.
- Missing that 95%+ shot on Ironman.
XCOM: Enemy Unknown/Within is a very solid effort at resurrecting the turn-based strategy legend of the 90's. It's fairly easy to pick up, but it will test your mettle in the long run. Features a lenghty campaign, albeit not having a very interesting story, it's still is more than worth it to play through it solely because of the satisfying combat, amazing soundtrack and the progressive expansion of XCOM, both in manpower and weaponry.
Would definitely recommend this game to anyone. Brilliant way to bring back a classic.
Can't wait for XCOM 2.

I'm going to preface this review by stating that a majority of the reviews I've seen on here are biased as all hell, and that this long grind that people speak of is only needed if you want the creme de le creme. AKA Level 58 and above.
I'd also like to state that this is barely pay to win. Most people whine about how you can sell $30 items for thirty million silver, however, coming from a veteran, you can literally make around billions just by telling your workers to gather a specific thing and making your other workers make trade items out of it. Some may complain that pets and maids and all that are needed. Pets usually are used to pick stuff up for you, so if you don't want to spam R, there you go. The maids allow you to deposit and buy things on the go, so if you don't feel like travelling back to some random♥♥♥♥♥town to waste your exp boost, there you.
The main gripe people to seem to have is managing to buy weight and inventory space. Which is odd considering many MMO's have this pay for convience setup. Hell, even GW2, has some pay for convience.
Well, that's all I needed to say for the beginning, let's move to the pros and cons.
PROS:
Combat - The combat in this game is absolutely fantastic, it is the only thing that will make the grind bearable at times and will make you not want to kill yourself. Each of the animations feel great, the sounds and actions feel responsive. It's fantastic. Each of the classes, that aren't just the other gender of their counterpart, all feel pretty unique in their own way.
Graphics - I don't think I need to explain this, but it's pretty good. Just look at any basic screenshot and you'll see what I mean. The scenery varys drastically from some forest place, to some weird jungle and then a desert area. I mean, this might in theory be a con for you assuming you don't have a very high end system and then you'll have to run it at potato graphics.
Lore - There's this way of increasing your energy cap by gaining knowledge, which you get by completeing quests, killing things and letting your black spirit absorb their sould and talking to people or observing things. These are often surprisingly well written, providing some interesting background lore.
Guilds - I really enjoy the guild system that they've put forth. They're fantastic. Medium to extra large guilds can own territories called nodes. Nodes give you taxes and with those taxes you can pay out your various guild members. However, to own one of those nodes you must fight a node war with multiple allied guilds against other allied guilds. You need to communciate with your guild officers where to go and create multiple squadrons. Along with this, there are also territories that top tier guilds can own, which are basically just a collection of nodes and a city.
IN BETWEEN:
AFK - Most people argue that you need to remain heavily AFK during this, although after playing for a while, I'd argue against that. If you really just want a free ten million silver every day, then sure lifeskill away but besides that, it's not really AFK intensive. At the most you have autopathing if you don't want to really hold down W, although like most AFK activities it's not as efficent. Most of the lifeskills that require you to just press button even though it's incredibly boring in other games, are just AFK'd in BDO. Understandably, if you don't really like that idea of something being AFK in a game, however these are lifeskills. Not a really crucial part of the game per se but it can makes loads of money.
RNG - See, I'm sort of mixed on this. While the RNG is absolutely soul crushing and at times makes you want to kill yourself, it makes sense that it's there or everybody would have PEN, the highest enhancement one can get. It's easy to get to a mediocre level, TRI, but from that point onwards you'll probably wnat to kill yourself going TET and then PEN. The only real gripe I can find with this is with accesories breaking down when you fail. At the beginning of the game, it might not seem like a big deal since most only cost around four million, but boss accesories, which are very rare and can cost around twenty million to one hundred million, can also break when enhancing.
PVP - Personally, I love the gear based PVP because I have something to show for my grind and that each class has a very different playstyle if they're not the meta. However, I get if you don't really like that and you'd rather opt for something more casual and balanced. That's all I really have to say for it.
Community - If you're easily offended and don't like memes, you're probably going to think the community is incredibly toxic, it's hilarious as♥♥♥♥♥♥though so I don't care. Most of the higher levels tend to also be pretty hostile if you step into their grinding spot, because they'll just instantly deck you and tell you to go away. I couldn't really care for this because it's easy to fight back, but I know many people who were turned off from this game due to the community.
CONS:
Balance - Alright, stepping right into this, the classes are not balanced in the slightest. Now, most people will state that if you're good enough at a certain class you can faceroll anybody and while that might be true, the fact that it's easier for certain classes that faceroll is sort of a lead that the balance is very poor in this game. If you actually play the game, you'll know what I mean.
Explanation - To start off, the game explains almost nothing to you. A good portion of the beginning of the game will mostly involve you being shift-tabbed, googling how to do this or how to do this. The game is pretty complex with the only help it provides are some crafting notes where you can check what recipies you need.

CONS:
-Story line is duller than a baseball bat...
No matter how strong my will was to actually wrap my head around this unique butterfly, I just couldn't get into it.
Well written plots have a way of grabbing your attention and pulling you into their world. Half the problem is that 99.99999999% of the story is conveyed through character dialogue (which I've played MANY games that pull this off extremely well), but it conveys it so poorly and with so little emotion that I quite honestly couldn't work up the brain power to give a damn.
Though I have to say that the most aggraviting part is that I mainly just found myself saying "WHO ARE YOU? WHY ARE YOU HERE? WHO AM I? WHY IS THIS HERE? WHAT AM I DOING!?!?!"
<INTRO>
"Hey there little black spirit who are you?"
"Idk."
"well who am I?"
"Can't tell you and you can't figure it out because you have amnesia."
"Oh, well what do I do now?"
"Kill stuff."
"and what happens then?"
"idk, you'll get more powerful and stuff so you can kill more stuff"
"oh...."
^ENTIRE PLOT IN A NUTSHELL^
- The learning curve on this game is steeper than trying climb a straight line up with virtigo.
The game acutally does quite well with teaching you the basics of fighting, using your inventory, and accepting quests. Beyond that you're completely on your own.
It took me 3 days to wrap my head around the bajillion freakin' buttons that slam into your face the second you hit the "ESC" button.
And remember how I said the plotline is dull? Well you REALLY want to avoid the sweet bliss of pounding that enter button during dialogue otherwise you'll miss out on some key play elements and quests. I made the the mistake of doing  just that and had to take in google's sweet loving embrace to actually figure out what buttons do what and how to actually play the 87% of the game that isn't just blazing through mobs.
- THE GRIND IS REAL
I don't just mean killing every single living thing you see. oh no no no. You'll get PLENTY of that just on the MAIN story line... I mean quite literaly almost EVERYTHING is grinding.
Want a horse? Grind that taming and breeding! You'll most definitely get some trash tiers thrown your way as a freeby, but you want a tier 8 or (god help you) a tier 9 without paying millions of your hard earned silver? Then ride that horse for hours until your tier 5 is level 30, let it make some sweet love, and pray to god you don't get dumped a tier 4 because the RNG god hates you.
Want a boat? If you want something that isn't complete trash it'll take you 14 days at the LEAST. Some people find this part fun, and I will admit that it can be immersive but altogether it just seems like more grinding to saner of the few.
Want some of those dank contribution (cough...storage...cough) points? Quests will be your only salvation. You may not care that little sally bumtickle lost 80 million of her cats all over the goddamn town, but she'll give you some of those points you so desperatley crave and need if you find them.
-Upgrading your equipment
MY. GOD. This by far has to be one of the most aggravating parts of the game.
In reality it really balances out. Your raw damage output is measured entirely by your sick gear...which isn't level capped...
So awesome right? Just upgrade your weapon til level +17 and you'll be OP and crush newbs right?
Correct! BUT SO WRONG.
after you upgrade your weapon to +7 it's all RNG from there. Your upgrade will normally fail the first time after +7  but by failing a weapon upgrade, your weapon's durability goes down by some god forsaken number (Which makes it inelligible to sell unless you have some of that Mem frag) and increases your chances of succeeding by +1. Makes sense right?
So the logical answer would be to buy a weapon already upgraded from the marketplace, except for the fact that no one is really filling that demand except 5 guys with neckbeards who praise the holy teachings of "FAILSTACK! THE GOD OF MERCY" and his lesser known and less endowed brother "RNG! THE GOD OF WHY DO YOU EVEN TRY"
armor goes up until +5 without consequences and jewelry uses another peice of the same jewelry to upgrade but it's stats don't double and if you fail you lose both.
- Notifications
Game: "HAHAHA LET ME TELL YOU EVERYTHING THATS HAPPENING EVERYWHERE WITH EVERY PLAYER!"
Player: "NOOOOOO. I JUST WANT TO READ THE CHAAAAAAT"
This one is short. The game by default will tell you absolutely everything that happening everywhere no matter how insignificant. You CAN turn this off, but in order to learn how to do so most players will go to chat...which is filled with literally EVERYTHING YOU DONT WANT TO KNOW ABOUT EVERYONE. Thus making it impossible to actually read the answer to your question.
-Customization
All your armor looks the same no matter what you have on. You CAN buy an outfit which will change all of that to an aesthetic of your choosing, but that costs real money dollars bruh.
The developers are quick to point out that you can buy outfits from the marketplace for silver... But supply most definitely does NOT meet demand. After all, people spend money on optimizing THEIR jiggle-physics, they could really care less about your silver, regardless of how much you spam "WTB TAMER OUTFIT PLZ" all across the whole frickin server.
-Pay to win?
No. nope nope nope. In general you will not really have a game winning advantage by paying real money dollars. You will however enjoy the game much much more, as since there are tons of pay-only buffs that will shave away that grind time quite a bit and make "RNG! THE GOD OF WHY DO YOU EVEN TRY" smile upon your newbness and grant you the power of kawaii in the way of pets, costumes, and actually getting a chance at undoing your screwups.
PROS:
-Character creator
This is by far one of the most advanced creators I've ever seen. You can literally change EVERY detail on your characters body so long as you don't try to give your girl characters a set of A's (The devs REALLY hate when you can't see all that work they poured into the jiggle physics) and you don't try to give your guy character a bigger bulge (what do you think this is? IMVU?)
-Content via Quests
I personally hate the quests... I really do... But there is never anything NOT to do in BDO. They put a huge amount of time into developing quests and the last person who tried to do a completionists run left their son their account info in their will after 84 YEARS of playing.
-Content via Life Skills
As I mentioned before, a good portion of this game IS NOT blazing through mobs. There is a ton to do, and to learn. In fact, you could play the entire game without ever even killing a single steel imp if you REALLY wanted to.
-Combat
My god. If Dark Souls nerfed their bosses and become an MMORPG, you essentially get the combat system in this game. It has by far one of the most fluid combat systems I have ever seen.
FINAL THOUGHTS:
Let me get serious and drop the memes real quick.
This is a GOOD GAME. It really is. It is just at this current time and point that it feels extremely unpolished and unfinished.
If the developers quadrupled the map size, raised the soft cap on levels to 100, and made the RNG more forgiving it would be 5000% more playable.
At this time and point the game is just way too small and unforgiving to be considered a good MMORPG.
By definition a game is something that someone plays for enjoyment, but the rewards don't justify the grind...
I WANT to understand this game, and I am VERY interested in whats going on... But at this point the plot is too far gone to fix. The amount of time poured into all of the dialogue is just too far developed to back track.
In total, if this game was still in beta I could justify someone putting their foot in the door and playing this game... I'll still play since I personally like it, but I can't recommend it.

TL;DR: It's a little short, but buy it if you have 1-3 friends who you like to play games with or hang out with occasionally, it will be one of the best times you've had with your friends. If you think you want to play it by yourself, skip it, it's impossible to play solo.
This is a great Co-Op game, really pulls you in and everyone has a blast playing it. It is a great party game to bust out whenever you have some bored friends over and looking to play a fun game for minutes to hours at a time. There are three small problems with it:
1. The campaign is pretty short, even for this type of game. Two friends and I beat the game in 3-4 hour sitting, with a fair amount of pauses for breaks. Then one friend and I went back and got all three stars in every level in another hour or so. Which brings me to my next point...
2. This is a game for a 2 or 4 person group. I had two friends with me, and it was near impossible to get three stars in a three player game, as the amount of points you need nearly doubles from two people to three. You can get to the boss with three people, but don't expect to 100% this with a three man party or BY YOURSELF.
3. THIS IS NOT A SINGLE PLAYER GAME. You may get about half way through, if you are really good, but you will not get enough stars to get anywhere close to the final stages. Period. The game trys to let you play two characters with one controller, but the amount of focus you have to put into what you are doing simply stops any single person in their tracks, and at some points in a stage you have to be looking at two completely different corners of your screen at the same time to be effectively managing your kitchen. It is simply nearly impossible to 3 star a level, let alone beat the game by yourself.

If you haven't played the series yet, and you have any interest in the city-building type of game, it's definitely worth a look.
Compared to a game like SimCity, Tropico is more mission-focused.  Islands have specific resources to exploit or ignore, and the infrastructure required for some industries means it's easier to focus entirely on one or two industries than it is to spread your resources around.  Tourism islands rely upon good press and expensive attractions bleeding visitor wallets dry, while farming or mining and industry can make for a relatively more stable economy (if one subject to the whims of international prices) but also require far more effort put into educating and housing the populace.
Also unlike SimCity, unhappiness is a much greater direct threat to your Presidential persona.  Especially early on, you'll be short on food, housing, healthcare, churches, and schools, and extremely short on resources to fulfil those needs.  In the interim, you've got a rebellion fomenting if you don't jury-rig a working city on the double.  Inversely, like with many of these types of games (like the older Pharaoh or Caeser games) once your miniature city starts working at all, you're in the clear, and there are rarely any real threats.  (Although now natural disasters can strike, as well as things like superpower conflicts, which make for late-game threats that Tropico 3 didn't have.)
You can play any level past completion of the objective, so you can just keep going until you have an island completely packed to the brim with bustling economic activity, and have money coming out the ears, if you so choose.
Tropico 3 is an important comparison to make because... there aren't really that many changes from Tropico 3.  Tropico 3 is cheaper, has the *EXACT SAME ENGINE, GRAPHICS, AND VOICES* and most of the mechanics are unchanged.  You might consider getting 3 first.  The differences are in disasters and mini-quests that pop up mid-mission, which DO keep the game feeling a little fresh, but if you're not certain on the series, but Tropico 3 on sale to test-drive the series.
Tropico 5 is out now, but unless you know you want it, it's probably worth waiting for all the changes that will likely be made to the base game to be made, and play 4 instead until 6 comes out, and 5 is finalized.

At first, I wanted to be a kind, benevolent dictator, in charge of my island which of course would be perfectly green, a land of equality, equal pay, a high living standard, jobs for every Tropican, a high level of schooling and a good member of the United Nations.
However, people kept complaining. At first, this was fine. Free Speech and all. But they were not working. Worse, they began to become rebels and attack the work of innocent, hard working Tropicans. "Right," I thought, "no more of that." I built guard posts around the nation to protect my other civilians and the economy which kept everyone fed and housed. After a while, the strikes became too much. "This right to protest is too inefficient", I thought, "and we just missed that freighter. We needed that boost to the economy." In a moment of Thatcher, I had the newly raised guards gun down some of the strikers. The rest returned to work. The right to protest had been removed, but people were happier as everyone got richer.
The environmentalists began to get angry. "It's too messy, too much industry, etc." I sighed. Look, did they like having money? Money to get houses? Electricity for movie theatres and hospitals? Wind Turbines simply don't do enough, we needed that gas Power Plant. We needed the jobs to keep the whole economy turning. I tried, I added gardens, I protected and grew new forests, but they continued to complain. So I stopped listening, and focused on the higher standard of living.
The U.S. came to me, demanding that I give them money, give this, give that, or "accidents can happen". But Agent Sasha instead never threatened me, referred to me as comrade and my islanders as Brothers. The Russians understood why I had to silence dissedence, and so we joined the Russians. At least they appreciated their people. The Americans... they didn't like this. But we stopped caring. We built assault rifles and using the funds from that, we built a nuclear weapon. Does it work? No idea, but it looks scary and shows the Americans that we MAY be able to blow something up. They stayed away and all was relatively well.
Now, schooling was fine, but a lot of Tropicans were starting to get funny ideas. They didn't understand that I was so strict because I was balancing the house of cards that was my economy. They had food, jobs, entertainment, a good house with fantastic conditions, they were safe from criminals and rebels and they could travel anywhere in the world (but mostly Russia, China and the MIddle East). If they had to not protest or speak against me, it was purely because I couldn't risk this going wrong. So I had to change a few things. I began to ask that schools make sure that children understood how fantastic our nation was, how corrupt the U.S. was, how our military kept us safe. A few people got a bit funny with that, but I needed to make sure this nation would continue after my death. I executed the rebels and burnt any book which said otherwise. People got iffy, but after a few years, they stopped caring. Good. Now we can continue in happiness.
Finally, my economy began to crumble. People refused to work the poorer jobs, they sat back on welfare and complained. They refused to pay the rent for better houses and built hovels on the side of roads. They committed crimes despite having social welfare. I couldn't make them work.
So, I built cheaper places for them to live, cheaper foods and easier work. But my towns were full, so I built them in another area. To support my now burdened economy, I had to import immigrants. Lots of them. A few people began to complain, but I shot them and they stopped. Now we have a high, middle, lower and underclass, which is executed often to save the economy.
However, Tropico is now making more money than ever, we're supporting every country that needs us, our people are famous for their money (when they can afford to travel), people order is perfect, there is no crime, you can go as far as you're willing to work, and you're safe.
You're welcome, my comrades.

Take the famous Oregon Trail, discard most of the historical facts and add a lot of random nonsense and you get Super Amazing Wagon Adventure!
Cruise through forests, fields, deserts and even underwater in your trusty wagon and try to stay alive!
And staying alive isn't so easy with almost everything out to get you! Bandits, wild animals, zombies and mother nature are trying to stop you from reaching your goal.
So what do you do? Offense is the best defense, right? So just shoot everything!
Your starting wagon gives you only a weak pistol, but you might find a lot of other weapons on your way, including shotguns, flamethrowers, bazookas and even an airstrike!

Company of Heroes 2 is a solid real-time strategy game. I can now say this game is better then CoH1.
I personaly enjoy this game it is:
Fun and challenging.
Good graphics, wonderful sound.
Stable! I don't remember it ever crashing on me.
The cold weather is interesting and well done.
I love the feel of the armies. Each fights diffrently.
Downside would be:
CoH2 is more expensive then CoH1. It has a lot of DLC content.
You have two starting armies: The Soviets and The Wehrmacht. The other armies: The US Forces, The German Oberkommando and The British Forces are "Sold Separately" and if you want to play them you will have to buy the armies.
There are side campaigns that are for sale. They're interesting, but not necessary. You would want a friend that also has them for the co-op missions because it's a pain fighting along side a computer, or (sometimes) worse a random person. Yes people can be much worse then a Hard computer...
Also Commanders are diffrent, and there are a lot more to choose from. Instead of only "Infantry, Airborne and Armor" Each commander has a spread of abilities, and there are commanders for sale. *Cough*$3.99*Cough*
The good news is you start with three useful commanders that pull their weight. And you can also earn commanders and intel (basicly small buffs) well playing for hundreds of hours.
Inspite of all of it... You can buy only the base game and still have fun. If you are a good leader you will be a force to be reckoned with, and you will crush the lesser commanders that bought all of the DLC thinking it would give them an edge only to find out they still suck, and it won't help them.

Having grown up playing online shooters such as Quake, you could understand how excited I was with the launch of Quake Live on Steam. I would consider myself a shooter fanatic, always playing the shooters that deserve my time, and skill. Quake, a simple, and fast paced shooter has become now a daily part of my life, only after a short relese of 2 days, and i'm sure i'll be back for more.
The game isn't all great, though. The classic Quake experience of knowing the map, times of weapon spwans, and even how much damage a gun will do to a un-armored and armored foe is totally swept away with many complexitys of Quake in Quake Live. A normal game allows loadouts, a putrid system for a game like Quake to have, while it also ruins the learning curve and challenge to many aspects of the game. For example, having not played Quake in years, I hopped in with the intent of rushing to the rocket launcher (a powerful weapon if controled accurately in the game) to only be surprised that in the menu, the option to start with ANY weapon in the games arsenal was available. Instantly my respect for players on higher end streaks was diminished, and the knowledge that any average joe could hop on and vaporize me with a railgun, was totally possible made the game suddenly alot less fun. I REALLY advice against this gameplay even if you are a begginer, Quake only makes itself into another generic FPS title that feels the need to compete, when it doesnt, it is better in almost all rights comnpared to other titles (ahem Call of Duty).
But my critism aside, gamemodes outside of the basic one are available, and the classic game modes and duels were ALL available here, to my relief. I find most of my time spent in Quake is the duel mode, 1v1 intense combat, knowing when weapons will spawn, and that my only hope of winning, is between me, and a super powerful laser gun. Not many games today do what Quake does, or offers such a simply unique, and simple experince that not only is fun to play, but is also very challenging. In fact, I beleive we may have a contender for the best FTP shooter this year, and certainly one of the best on steam currently. If you are a shooter fan of any kind, I highly recommend Quake Live.

Outside of the gameplay itself, this game is wonderfully written, has a very unique idea, and a hilarious story with lots of funny jabs at the nature of football.
Unfortunately, the gameplay itself just isn't up to scratch with the rest of the game. The mechanics themselves are fine, but just seem awkward. The tackling is inconsistent, the money per goal just seems random at times, the game lags immensely every kick off (at least for me) and in general the matches themselves are just monotonous.
This could be excused, as the jist of the gameplay is at least a very funny parody of football, with the offside and extra time mechanics being hilarious, but one things really ruined my opinion of this game. At the end of the story mode, the difficulty of the AI is just ridiculous - instead of being a genuine challenge, they can just kick the ball across the entirety of the pitch and score, while you can do literally nothing about it, and the final match really comes up to luck, and hoping that the AI don't just score out of nowhere like they can at any time.
Overall, this game is so close to being good for me, and I really do love the humour this game holds, but when a parody still fails to be fun, even in its own way, it's still not enjoyable as a video game, and means the game really has no replayability value. The only reason I played it as long as I did was to finish the storyline at least.

Far Cry Primal just feels like an old piece of chewing gum. Good quality chewing gum, but the taste has worn off a long time ago.
It has all the ingredients you would expect from a Far Cry episode. It looks amazing, you get to hunt, upgrade your weapons, unlock a bunch of nice stuff, free outposts, search for collectibles, kill lots of tribesman, gather plants. All very nice and all.......but....We know all that stuff...ther is no surprise anywhere. It took me about half an hour to "get" this game. Half an hour to understand what direction this game would be going.
At first i was excited to hunt for some prey. I wanted to feel like a stoneage hunter who stalks his prey and outsmart it using the right type of weapon and using the landscape in my advantage........Well....Far Cry gives you a big f#ck you in that regard. Instead of smart A.I. it just gives you numbers.......I mean life is literally everywhere. Walk for one minute and you'll encounter 20 goats, 15 deer, 10 wolves, 6 lions, 3 sabretooth tigers, a bunch of wooly mammoths and some people of friendly and enemy tribes. It does not feel like an actual jungle where the absence of obvious danger makes it all the more exiting. The thought there could be a dangerous animal around the corner is way more scary than being a 100% sure there is a dangerous animal.
The storyline is thin and characters are not to interesting. The NPC's give you tasks and you will do this tasks. That's about it. They've tried to make the NPC's weird or funny of tough, but you never get a "relationship" with them. Thet is no real character development and emotionally I would not give a single f#ck if the NPC would have died horrible deaths.
The language they speak sounds good and authentic, the voice acting however not always so spot on. For example "Urki the thinker" is a somewhat funny guy who does dumb things (won't spoil). But you can clearly hear an american redneck accent in his pronuciation. Maybe Far Cry's creators have done this on purpose to match his stupidity, but it just not works for me.
I have not finished the main story yet and I don't know if I will be finishing it. I kinda lost interest and at this point it's beginning to feel more and more like a chore than something I realy want to do.
My verdict: 6,5/10

Overcooked is a couch-coop cooking game that follow that age old recipe of 'collect the different engredients and put them together into the right dish'. It can be played only in couch coop, using keyboard and/or controller. The keyboard controls are fine, but I recommend using a controller.
I played through the campaing of the game in 2p coop in around 4 hours. The levels are split into five different themes, each with their own gimmick. The levels in each theme are varied and well designed. They are all designed in such a way as to try to mess up your ability to cook effectively, so finding the best way to divide the workload in each level is a large part of completing them.
Besides the campaign there is a competetive game mode which you unlock the levels for by playing through the campaign. The levels 9 available here brings the total number of level up to 35, which is fine if the competetive mode is something you and whoever you play with enjoy. If not, then the 26 levels of the campaign feels like a bit too few.
The lack of campaign levels is really my only problem with this game. The gameplay is great fun, and the more the merrier.
The music of the game reminds me of Back to the Future, Indiana Jones, and Generic-90'something-Family-Film. All in all it suits the game quite well.
The animations are pretty good as well, and the variety in design of the different available chefs (although mechanically identical) allows for many a laugh, and all fit the world perfectly.
All in all, as long as you can get together with 1-3 friends for some coudh-coop, I highly recommend this game. It can be played in single player, but I don't see why you would - The Game is designing for coop.

At first, I wanted to be a kind, benevolent dictator, in charge of my island which of course would be perfectly green, a land of equality, equal pay, a high living standard, jobs for every Tropican, a high level of schooling and a good member of the United Nations.
However, people kept complaining. At first, this was fine. Free Speech and all. But they were not working. Worse, they began to become rebels and attack the work of innocent, hard working Tropicans. "Right," I thought, "no more of that." I built guard posts around the nation to protect my other civilians and the economy which kept everyone fed and housed. After a while, the strikes became too much. "This right to protest is too inefficient", I thought, "and we just missed that freighter. We needed that boost to the economy." In a moment of Thatcher, I had the newly raised guards gun down some of the strikers. The rest returned to work. The right to protest had been removed, but people were happier as everyone got richer.
The environmentalists began to get angry. "It's too messy, too much industry, etc." I sighed. Look, did they like having money? Money to get houses? Electricity for movie theatres and hospitals? Wind Turbines simply don't do enough, we needed that gas Power Plant. We needed the jobs to keep the whole economy turning. I tried, I added gardens, I protected and grew new forests, but they continued to complain. So I stopped listening, and focused on the higher standard of living.
The U.S. came to me, demanding that I give them money, give this, give that, or "accidents can happen". But Agent Sasha instead never threatened me, referred to me as comrade and my islanders as Brothers. The Russians understood why I had to silence dissedence, and so we joined the Russians. At least they appreciated their people. The Americans... they didn't like this. But we stopped caring. We built assault rifles and using the funds from that, we built a nuclear weapon. Does it work? No idea, but it looks scary and shows the Americans that we MAY be able to blow something up. They stayed away and all was relatively well.
Now, schooling was fine, but a lot of Tropicans were starting to get funny ideas. They didn't understand that I was so strict because I was balancing the house of cards that was my economy. They had food, jobs, entertainment, a good house with fantastic conditions, they were safe from criminals and rebels and they could travel anywhere in the world (but mostly Russia, China and the MIddle East). If they had to not protest or speak against me, it was purely because I couldn't risk this going wrong. So I had to change a few things. I began to ask that schools make sure that children understood how fantastic our nation was, how corrupt the U.S. was, how our military kept us safe. A few people got a bit funny with that, but I needed to make sure this nation would continue after my death. I executed the rebels and burnt any book which said otherwise. People got iffy, but after a few years, they stopped caring. Good. Now we can continue in happiness.
Finally, my economy began to crumble. People refused to work the poorer jobs, they sat back on welfare and complained. They refused to pay the rent for better houses and built hovels on the side of roads. They committed crimes despite having social welfare. I couldn't make them work.
So, I built cheaper places for them to live, cheaper foods and easier work. But my towns were full, so I built them in another area. To support my now burdened economy, I had to import immigrants. Lots of them. A few people began to complain, but I shot them and they stopped. Now we have a high, middle, lower and underclass, which is executed often to save the economy.
However, Tropico is now making more money than ever, we're supporting every country that needs us, our people are famous for their money (when they can afford to travel), people order is perfect, there is no crime, you can go as far as you're willing to work, and you're safe.
You're welcome, my comrades.

One of my computer game memories is playing Diablo (the first). Diablo and the subsequent sequels have always been the shining examples of what the loot based hack and slash genre can be. The only game to come close is Torchlight. If you love skill trees then Path of Exile has crept up to be a standout as well.
Grim Dawn takes everything that is great about Diablo and spins it off into some very interesting routes. The base game does not have as great of loot cycle as Diablo but through content updates they have created a truely robust game. The only downside ot Grim Dawn is smaller playerbase.
The biggest upside to Grim Dawn is the skill tree depth while being much more navigable than Path of Exile. Trying out new class combos is enough to fuel multiple character runs through the game.
The visuals of the game are on par with the Genre but don't stand out. The spell effects are great but are resource hogs and could be better optimized.
The story is fine. Nothing amazing but I would say there is a story. Things happen for a reason.
If you like Diablo, PoE, or Torchlight give this a shot.

Although American Nightmare is a nice way to wrap up the ending of Alan Wake it falls very short in terms of storytelling and gameplay. There seems to be a competition between the voice acting and scripted dialogue, battling for the "Most Awful Delivery" award, but I'd say it was a tie.
It's a shame, I really enjoyed Alan Wake. I'm quite partial to small-town mysteries (Life is Strange, Twin Peaks, Deadly Premonition, Stranger Things) but American Nightmare took such a divergent path from its predecessor that it never really elicited a spark like the original did.
That doesn't make it a bad or unenjoyable experience... just an underwhelming one but it's still worth playing.

Alan Wake's American Nightmare is the sequel to Alan Wake and while it is not as good, it's still a great game. The game tells the story of how Alan returns to the real world. The story uses an interesting mechanic that is both good and bad. The player will play though the same levels a few times, with the same objectives but more enemies and more weapons to find. The causes the game to become repetitive and boring, since the player knows what the objectives are. This make sense from the story pespective, but doen't leave room for anything drastically new. There are a few twists and turns, but they are predictable or not very good. The gameplay is mostly the same, except for a few new weapons.  The game lasts for about 5 hours and are still very enjoyable, it's just not as good as the original.

Far Cry Primal just feels like an old piece of chewing gum. Good quality chewing gum, but the taste has worn off a long time ago.
It has all the ingredients you would expect from a Far Cry episode. It looks amazing, you get to hunt, upgrade your weapons, unlock a bunch of nice stuff, free outposts, search for collectibles, kill lots of tribesman, gather plants. All very nice and all.......but....We know all that stuff...ther is no surprise anywhere. It took me about half an hour to "get" this game. Half an hour to understand what direction this game would be going.
At first i was excited to hunt for some prey. I wanted to feel like a stoneage hunter who stalks his prey and outsmart it using the right type of weapon and using the landscape in my advantage........Well....Far Cry gives you a big f#ck you in that regard. Instead of smart A.I. it just gives you numbers.......I mean life is literally everywhere. Walk for one minute and you'll encounter 20 goats, 15 deer, 10 wolves, 6 lions, 3 sabretooth tigers, a bunch of wooly mammoths and some people of friendly and enemy tribes. It does not feel like an actual jungle where the absence of obvious danger makes it all the more exiting. The thought there could be a dangerous animal around the corner is way more scary than being a 100% sure there is a dangerous animal.
The storyline is thin and characters are not to interesting. The NPC's give you tasks and you will do this tasks. That's about it. They've tried to make the NPC's weird or funny of tough, but you never get a "relationship" with them. Thet is no real character development and emotionally I would not give a single f#ck if the NPC would have died horrible deaths.

Behold The Kickmen is an incredibly accurate representation of what soccer is, if it was described to you in a foreign language, from space. Now, I don’t claim to be a sports enthusiast. I used to play football and basketball when I was younger, but those days are long behind me. Occasionally I’ll dip my toes into an NBA 2K or an NHL 20XX, but I can’t say I’ve followed those sports in a long time. I suspect Dan Marshall, developer of Behold The Kickmen, is in a similar boat with soccer.
When I arrived at the main menu, I was presented with three choices. I could start a career, jump into a quick play game, or try the tutorial. I opted to go for quick play, so I could figure the mechanics out as I went. That’s when the personality of Behold The Kickmen really started to expose itself. I received an incredibly smarmy, yet accurate pop up notification saying that I should probably try the career mode first, as it slowly would teach me mechanics over time. I complied and attempted to start a career, and was greeted by another message with an even thicker coat of smarmy-ness drizzled all over it.
After my lovely experience with the tutorial, I was finally ready to jump into a career mode. I was given the opportunity to rename my team, and so Flankstank United was born. I was also given the chance to rename my star player, but I let him be.
So there I was, ready to play some soccer, except wait, Behold The Kickmen suddenly became a visual novel. Star player, Joey Flash, had some demons that his bitter rival Pedro kept taunting him about. Meanwhile, the coach of Flanksteak United seems to know less than I do about soccer, which to my knowledge is a requirement of being a coach. My goofy soccer game turned into a soap opera in an instant, and I couldn’t have been happier.
After the drama died down temporarily, I was able to play what seemed more and more like a mini-game in this entire package, soccer. Or some version of soccer I suppose. Remember when I said Behold The Kickmen was an accurate representation of soccer? I lied. Sure, there’s a ball and two goals, but I don’t think that actual soccer is played on a circular field. Nor do I think the “offside” rule just randomly occurs mid game punishing a played for being too far to the left. But hey, I’m not a soccer fan so I can’t say for sure.
For all the jokes and guffaws, Behold The Kickmen actually has some interesting mechanics. For instance, there’s a combo meter on screen at all times that accounts for passes, shots and tackles. You keep the chain going and eventually finish the combo off by scoring, or as the game calls it, having “Done a goal.” Finishing the combo grants you cash, and cash is key to growing your team.
In between matches and soap opera segments, you can take your hard earned cash and spend it on upgrades for various aspects of your team. Whether or not those upgrades actually affect gameplay is a question I have to ask, because I don’t entirely trust this game. But I hope at least one of the upgrades works, because when you start out, your players run painfully too slow and I would very much like that to change.
You can also unlock abilities like passing and sprinting (yes those are abilities) in career mode as well as things like advanced tackling techniques and being able to control the ball mid flight. You can also edit a 4-4-2. which I’m sure means something in real soccer, but once again, I don’t trust this game.
Behold the Kickmen may not be a hyper-realistic simulation of the world’s biggest sport, but rather a perfectly fine arcade style soccer game with a great sense of humor. It doesn’t have any multiplayer which is a little disappointing, but isn’t any worse of a game without it. The career and story mode seem to be the main draw thus far, and the writing is funny enough that I’m more than willing to stick it out till the end to see how it pans out.

Venture Forth is an homage to the cave-crawling RPG era of the early-to-mid 90s. It's got an extreme Zelda/Dark Cloud-like spelunking charm that will transport you to your formulative gaming years as a young child; that excitement you felt the first time you played as Link, broke a boulder and found a loot chest hidden behind it... such a satisfying experience.
Venture Forth is like that same experience, except it's been emboldened. There's a strange, satisfying lull to the depths of the lava cave: hidden nooks and crannies promise ph4t lewtz as a reward should you have the will to fully explore and search all the waters, cracks, and air vents the game lays sprawled out before you, and the upgrade mechanics and the way said mechanics tie into exploration in Venture Forth keeps you constantly wanting to move forward.
Every upgrade is extremely tangible and the build variety means that there's no real wrong/right/FotM spin-to-win way to win this game--if you want to be an Archer, you can. If you want to be a flame sword-wielding knight, you can. Claymore/Zweihander for cleaving foes in two more your fancy? Venture Forth can scratch that itch as well. And the best thing about the build variety?
. You won't be pigeonholed into a sword-and-board or op-as-balls-glass-cannon build in Venture Forth, and in this sandbox-esque class construction is where I draw and give much praise to the game's (re)playability.
Another mechanic I appreciated was the mapping system. VF uses a mapping system reminiscent of Metal Gear Solid or Rainbow Six. It's a globular, 3d representation of the space you're in and can effectively be brought forth like a hologram at any time. It's slightly confusing for the first 15-30 seconds but once you discern your character's orientation in relation to the rest of the map, you'll have no problem directing your path in no time.
My only complaint so far is with some hitboxes, especially during enemy skills that involve mobility (like their yellow dash attacks). On some smaller animals like Widowlings and Toothies, it can be incredibly hard to hit them with -anything-, especially if they start chain dashing. The best way to deal with these mobs (that I've found) is to just kite them until they reset, and then come back and rain a few Dragon Arrows on them from any one of your trusty bows.
Venture Forth gets a solid B from me. If it can iron out its hit animations/registry and improve some of the textures and models, I would think it near-flawless and probably toss it an A+. This is one of the better exploration-based ARPGs I've played in a while.

Short Review: Motivational training video for nihilists and self-pity enthusiasts.
Long Review: A "crush your hopes and dreams" simulator from Telltale Games, starring thinly veiled Stark expies, directed by Ramsay Bolton, produced by Ramsay Bolton, and written by Thomas Hobbes. Makes Upton Sinclair's "The Jungle" look like a Disneyland ride.
I know that A Song of Ice and Fire, like many semi-historical family sagas that deal with political intrigue, war and vice (e.g. The Accursed Kings, Money, The Godfather), is not exactly an optimistic work, and the TV show definitely plays up the eroticism and gore to unnecessary lengths (shock value sells), but Telltale's adaptation goes to whole new lengths of depressing pre-determined cynicism.
- Graphics: cel-shaded and actually pretty nice, stylistically; it gets awkward when a non-canon character shares screentime with a character from the TV show, however, because the TV-canon characters are voiced by the same performers and are modeled after them in stronger detail than the boring nonexistent characters. It's hard to take the game seriously if Margaery looks like a painting of the original actress while generic archvillain #2 looks like a potato with a wig.
- Story branching: Was it really necessary to base the game off the show instead of the original book series, and to introduce new, unique characters instead of familiar faces from the book? The result is basically the Stark saga, except even more disappointing and improbable.
The decisions matter diddly-squat in the long run. One would think that, perhaps, there would be different endings according to playstyle, at the very least three endings, one for players who chose integrity and virtue over cold-hearted shrewdness; a second for the opposite; and a third for the slow-pokes who missed the QTEs.
The replay value isn't high at all, because the story branches matter so little, that one is barely motivated to play a second time using alternate decisions. Not just the outcome of each episode and the entire season is basically the same no matter the choice, but the outcome of each scene boils down to the same thing. The branching is so trivial it's barely there.
For a game that boasts of tailoring gameplay to the player's decisions, it certainly lacks satisfactory branching and alternate endings. I can understand the difficulty of carrying over story branches in an episodic game, especially one that is based on an existing storyline, but as far as I can tell there were two solutions to surmount this problem:
1) don't brag about it being story-branching. Just leave it as a point-and-click and add a couple more scenes.
2) branch away from the existing storyline. /This did not have to follow the downfall of the Starks/. Fans of the show and book series would be interested in crafting their own "What if?" story, and new-comers to the franchise wouldn't be met with such a tidal wave of nihilism.
- Shock value: On the plus side, it isn't a smutty game (I don't think the world is ready for smutty celshaded Telltale adventures yet, or ever); on the down side, for what it lacks in smut it tries to make up for in gore and profanity. Gratuitous gore and profanity, but especially gore. A "blegh" simulator, basically.
- Mechanics: what mechanics? QTEs are not mechanics :<
- Genre: the game is like Britney Spears' stance on womanhood: too many QTEs to be a point and click, and not enough outcomes to be story-branching. Instead, it's a humiliating-cutscene-conga, made to cash in on a lucrative license.
- Alternate recommendations:
The Wolf Among Us and The Walking Dead (Season 1) remain the two best dramatic story-branching games from TellTale Games by far. Fans of the ASOIAF series should look into the /other/, earlier Game of Thrones game, an RPG that focuses on new but plausible characters and goes beyond the lore of the TV show.

While it is still in Early Access, and there are some quirks here and there, Venture Forth holds a lot of promise in regards to being a top-notch 3d adventure game! It gives as much as it takes, and believe me, while there will be some moments of frustration, there's also a lot to love about the game in general.
I really like the feeling of being in some underground lava caverns with who-knows-what. Small thoughts creep into your heart from time to time (Or at the top left) about locating the heart, finding the center, and every so often settling on despair. It's a nice, subtle poke in the side that urges you on.
Various areas are often hiding something, whether it's an item you need to continue forward or an over-powered weapon, the key to the game is to kill everything and explore everything, and to always check your inventory for special items that have dropped.  It feels like an adventure game that caters mostly to the inquisitive folk that want to explore every nook and cranny of an area. While I can't say I'm the same and I have gotten stuck on more than one occasion, I also wouldn't change the way a player progresses through the game. Some clues might be nice though!
The music is ambient, and I kind of wish there were a few more tracks, but I haven't reached the end of the game yet, so I don't know how long it takes to beat it.
The monsters are adorable, and I'd hug them to bits if they didn't hit me with arrows or bumrush me so much!
As mentioned before, there are some quirks here and there. I really had (and still do), have a bit of a time understanding the inventory system. It's fully customizable, but for new players who don't have many items in the first place, I haven't seen the need for so many slots and bars. Aaand maybe some more whispered clues when a player is stuck and doesn't know what to do or what to look for. I'm a sucky adventurer though, so that might just be me!
Overall, I really like this game and definitely recommend checking it out.

Far Cry Primal is enough of a departure from Far Cry 3 and 4 that it makes it a lot of fun. There are less weapons and the upgardes are relatively similar to the previous titles, but I didn't ever feel like this made the game worse in any way - you still have access to plenty of weapons (and let's be honest no one was constantly switching between weapons once you got the ones you liked maxed out anyway).
Aside from the fact that you're running through varied locations like lush forests and barren tundras, the lack of roads and cars makes the game feel more authentic in a way. You're constantly interacting with a wide range of wildlife with the new ability to tame some of them to serve as your companions - yes that means you get to tame a sabertooth tiger and ride it into battle to annihilate your enemies. I'll admit that having the beasts did make a large portion of the game fairly easy because you can just hang back and command them from afar to take out pretty much every enemy in a settlement you're trying to capture.
As with previous Far Cry's there are a ton of, admittedly repetitive and boring, tasks baked into the world. Doing them the first few times was fun, but once it became uninteresting I stopped doing them. The story missions are great and it's nice to have some side tasks to do as you're running from place to place, but there's only so many times I can go invade a cave and save my friends before I'm over it. This is a pretty standard Ubisoft thing so I would say it says more about the developers than it does about the game itself.
Overall my experience with the game was positive. The story is fun and decent, but nothing groundbreaking or overly compelling. The game looks great and runs well most of the time (1440p on High to Ultra settings with a 1070 netted me right around 60fps pretty consistently). I'd recommend it if you enjoyed the previous Far Cry games and are looking for something in the same vein, but different enough to feel like a new experience.

If you've read any of the reviews and the preamble on this page you'll have picked up on the conceit here, that it's a football game written by a non football fan who didn't do the research. And yet, you get the feeling that that may not be strictly true...
Certainly the general feel of the title is that of a less polished Sensible Soccer or Kick Off type title - both stalwarts of the arcade football genre. That the rules are quite blatantly wrong seems if anything to make things more accessible, the offside rule in particular.
My main gripe therefore is with the fact that this is only single player - the idea of having a knockabout with a more straightfaced FIFA or PES fan would make for a great experience, as the initial joke game feel gives way to something more arcadey. However, I can see how two player control in this setup would rapidly become unwieldy, as the ball moves very quickly, particularly in later matches.
I realise in this that I haven't covered the Story mode, which is the key to this game as currently set up. It's all a bit Speed Racer and manga in styling, with an overblown melodrama that suits this game to the ground. If football doesn't appeal, the secret future deathsport mode is worth a look, somehow combining the gameplay with a style more akin to early Bitmap Brothers titles (you know which one I mean).
One thing I would say though is do the tutorial mode first - for an arcade title, the controls can be a bit finicky compared to the one button and a stick approach of the aforementioned Kick Off type games. But yes, don't think of this as just a joke game, there is something of substance under the surface.

It's brutal, it's strange, it's got psychic slugs and stone golem Klingons. Use every ounce of cunning, guile, and luck to fight and sneak and salvage your ship through the dangerous, randomly generated systems between you and Federation command, all while merciless Rebels hunt you like a dog. Fire mighty weapons, equip strange technology, recruit weird aliens!
The music is notable in its ambient appeal and comfortable long-term listenability, the graphics, while not high tech, do a wonderful job of telling you precisely what you need to know about what's going on in your vessel. The gameplay is intuitive, and you can even use some interesting tricks like putting out fires by venting air into space. The game's challenges can be cruel, unfair, and hostile, but you're a spaceship captain! Deal with it!
Unlocking new equipment and vessels, discovering new tricks and devices, formulating new strategies, scrambling to fix it when things go wrong... It's everything a starship command sim should be. My only complaint is the rebel fleet's endless and insatiable pursuit... Many times I've had to abandon my explorations to escape them, leaving behind possibilities and treasures. But that is of course part of what gives the game urgency and pacing... So it's more a personal matter.

The first "rogue-like" game I've played, and it's damn brilliant and got me hooked to the genre. Basically, in a "rogue-like" you try to survive as long as possible - when you die, it's over. In this game, you control a lone space-ship navigating through different galaxies as you try not to die and ultimately take down the Federation ship that threatens the universe. The story is never really that important in "rogue-likes". What matters is the sense of tension and urgency as you navigate a harsh and cruel world in your the never-ending fight to survive. Each time you die, you learn, and try to get just a little bit further next time.
Because that's the core essence of a "rogue-like". Death. As hard as you will try to avoid it, you will die, and you will die a lot. The hope is that every time you do - you learn something from it. You learn what works, what doesn't. Is it better to upgrade your shields to block more attacks, or upgrade your engines to increase your evasion chance? Should you use lasers, ion cannons, missiles, or attack droids? You try one thing, then another, until you find a way that works for you. In a good rogue-like, (like this one, especially with the free Advanced Content patch), there are multiple ways that work, but there are still luck based events that can throw a wrench into your plans. So even if you get down a strategy that works, not every game will be the same.
So if all of that seems interesting to you, I'll get to the mechanics. You control a space-ship, with anywhere from 1-10(?) crew members. You can assign each member to boost one of the ships systems - be it the shields, weapons, engine, and of course you'll need a pilot. You travel throughout various galaxies, one space-jump at a time, where you'll encounter many events, good and bad, that will keep you on your toes and keep you constantly adjusting your tactics. Some events will reward you with new crew-members, weapons, or special items, Other events will force you to forfeit scrap, damage your ship, or even kill one of your crew-members. As you defeat enemy ships, or help out civilians, you get scrap, which is used to upgrade your ship and buy various weapons, crew members, as well as fuel, missiles, and droid parts. So you really have to balance what you use your precious scrap on.
In battle, you can control your weapons to shoot specific parts of the enemies ship - to disable the shields to inflict maximum damage, or disabling the engines to prevent them from getting away. You can pause whenever you want in battle giving you ample time to plan and execute your strategies. Obviously, the aim is to take down enemy ships while trying to minimize your own casualties. There are various ways to do this, whether it be disabling their weapons system via ion cannon, using missile launchers that bypass their shields, or activating droids that shoot down enemy projectiles, Again, you have to find out what works for you, but more importantly, you have to learn to work with what you got. Sometimes you have the choice of letting enemies surrender for a chance at getting more fuel or missiles, or blast them into space dust for more scraps.
Just as a word of warning, "rogue-likes" are usually pretty difficult, at least at first. It'll take you some time to get accustomed to the world, and probably even more time before you defeat the last boss. But that just makes victory so much sweeter. Each time you play, you get a little bit further, or at least learn something to get you a little further next time. If you like the idea of going through trial and error as you adapt to survive in a cruel, unforgiving world until you achieve victory, the final culmination of the sum of your experiences, then look no further, and pick up FTL today.

I genuinely love the writing and humor in this game. The character designs are delightful, and the satirical bent of the project is extremely charming.
But the game has serious technical problems. Tackling and passing are Russian Roulette in terms of whether they will actually do what the player wants; sometimes the tackling "possession" reticle appears, sometimes it doesn't, sometimes it appears and then disappears, sometimes it appears, changes color to the one that enables possession for the player, but the ball or the character just bounce off in another direction. For passing, sometimes it just flies across the field in the opposite direction. The A.I. is extremely buggy. Enemy teams have a tendency to run the ball into the corner where they get stuck until you try to tackle them, which serves only to dislodge them and run past you to score a goal. And things aren't better on the goalkeeping side. If anything, they're much worse. In terms of settings, attempts to turn down the grating music failed; turning the volume down did absolutely nothing. An opening prompt strongly recommends a controller, but the controller cannot select some menu items, requring a mouse and keyboard to navigate.
But the most egregious issue is not a glitch but a design choice: You can't change your character on defense. The game auto-selects the character that you're controlling and switches at random, presumably trying to select whoever is closest to the ball, but just as often selecting someone far behind the ball or in no position to reach the ball. If you try to tackle and it fails, you're stuck with that character until it auto-selects someone else, which might be fine except for the aforementioned hit detection issues and the fact that at least half the time the character the game switches you to is behind the opposing player with their stamina depleted because the A.I. was sprinting independently for some reason. The left trigger of the controller is totally open, too, which leaves room if the developer can figure out a way to patch in a way to cycle through nearby characters. A lot of the technical issues could be overcome if the player was able to quickly regain control by selecting another nearby character. It would probably help with some of the outrageous difficulty spikes, as well.
I didn't have a hard time winning, for the most part, but I had a hard time getting the game to respond accurately to my inputs.
I really hope the dev can figure out some of these issues, because as it stands it's a charming, funny, potentially addictive game marred by technical difficulties.

This game started out really fun. Then I made the mistake of winning a few matches; that's when I discovered that the game's difficult scales based on the assumption that you're able to bring in loads of money per goal, so that you can train your team to come at least vaguely close to keeping up with the AI. Alas, even after all the matches I've won and lost in the weeks since I bought this, I still score lots of 0/1 pound (note: not sure how to abbreviate pounds sterling appropriately, sry) goals, with the occasional 100-200 goals. I think I saw one for about 750 once....maybe. I may have imagined it. But since training is expensive, I quickly found myself in a spot where the AI was making laser-like passes and goals, stealing the ball from me at its whim, while I would apparently fail to even gather the ball after running right into it. While I'd love to take more of the blame for this, I fear that there may also be an issue of clunky controls that aren't nearly as responsive as this game needs them to be.
Despite having grown frustrated with the game early on, I was going to give it a positive recommendation....until I saw the patch notes for the 1.5 patch. The developer claimed that this patch addressed some of the negative feedback about this game, so I fired up the game again to see how different it felt. With my team in 17th place, the AI once again manhandled my team and I ended the match without bringing in a single penny. In 18th place, winning was too easy, but I didn't bring in nearly enough money for even a single upgrade to my team.  But goal scoring still feels just-managable enough that I don't feel like I can start doing whatever the game expects me to do to bring in more money when I finally score. In other words, same old poor scaling.
Even after the improvements, I still had a major problem: The automatic selection of which player you control. I can't count the number of times I've wanted to control a player who was actually near the ball (but couldn't, because the computer decides who you control), or the number of times when I've been charging in for a tackle, only to have the computer switch players so my slide tackle is done by someone neither near the ball nor even facing it. This, perhaps more than anything else, is what made the game frustrating for me. (A close second is when the computer starts intercepting every pass that comes near it, while my players do nothing of the sort. Or when the computer starts stealing the ball even time it wishes, while my attempts to steal are far less predictable.)
What mostly pushed me over the line toward a negative recommendation is the dev's statement of "it's supposed to be a difficult game." Upon reading this, I concluded the following: This isn't a difficult game, it's a poorly-designed game with awkward controls and a lack of attention to difficulty scaling. (Not to mention that the game does next-to-nothing to show the player how to succeed at the game's most important mechanic, that of maximizing money earned per goal.) Hearing the dev suggest otherwise sounds arrogant and out-of-touch to me.
Also, I've grown sick to death of the opening music, and button texts and match win/loss notes seem about as vacant as the typical meme...but they just keep showing up. In other words, I've quickly grown tired of this game's tedium and I don't want to fire up the game any more.
To be fair, the first couple hours with the game were quite fun, so if you think the price is low enough to see if you also enjoy it -- either at first, or possibly for much longer -- then, by all means, give it a go. The game certainly feels like it has loads of potential, when you first start playing.

With Battlefront coming out from EA in Open Beta, I reinstalled this because my potato computer couldn't hope to run the newest installment of this franchise. Luckily, I could run this on decently high graphics without my laptop exploding in front of me. So, let's get the review out of the way!
BF2 has a few different versions of single player (just like in BF), so let's start off with the campaign. It pits you as a clone trooper of the 501st, and gives a semi-detailed description of what those clones went through. While I'm not going to spoil too much for those who haven't played/seen a player do the campaign, it's sort of a tear jerker when you REALLY think about it.
For the second sort of SP, instant action, it doesn't come off as lacking. Each map you do has a  ton of variation, and even switching eras in the menu can somewhat alter how the game goes. Droids and Rebels have two of the most OP classes, but still easily countered so there's not really any bias because of the very limited numbers of them allowed at once. The most overpowered normal class is easily the Engineer, where you can end up killing half the enemy reinforcements with a single life if you're good enough. And prominent characters from each faction can be set to appear at different times/not at all once you kill or do enough, so that's a bit of a bonus.
The third type of SP is a glactic conquest thing that returns from the first game. Instead of just picking a planet to fight on, in here you have to manually send a fleet over to each enemy controlled planet and defeat all the forces on there. If you lose, you lose a fleet. If you win, you get the planet. That simple. With the addition of space battles, you can now have skirmishes in 'deep space' between planets, or battles for the planet in the space around it. Should you win those space battles, you then take the fight to the surface.
With Galactic Conquest, like the first game, you can chose a bonus when you fight. Unlike the first game, you have to buy them. And your troops. Until you do that, you're running around with a Pilot (for space battles) and a normal trooper. You could really win campaigns with just those two, but your enemy AI certainly won't stick to them. The consumables range from better blasters and armor, to being able to tote along a Hero/Villian for the duration of the battle. Certain ones won't work in space, so you can't play as General Grevious in a battle for the space above Naboo.
Now, on to the Multiplayer. For MP, it's basically just Instant Action. Except everyone only plays Hero Battles. So you can't really find any populated servers over, say 5 players, on any other map.
Overall, the game's a good game, but the AI could've REALLY used some more work. They do ridiculous things at the best of times, and it can be infuriating if you're playing a CTF game on Tatooine and a Jawa picks the flag up. When you don't have friendly fire enabled. I'd give it a 8/10, because it has a slight feeling of being a very late beta instead of a true game. That's just with instant action games, of course.
